cards.x: Foundation of business continuity planning.

puzzles.prompt: A $200,000 server has an exposure factor of 40%. What is the SLE in dollars?
puzzles.x: SLE = Asset Value × Exposure Factor = 200,000 × 0.4 = $80,000.

puzzles.prompt: With that $80,000 SLE and an ARO of 0.5 (once every two years), what is the ALE?
puzzles.x: ALE = SLE × ARO = 80,000 × 0.5 = $40,000 a year. Controls costing more than that per year are hard to justify.

decks.title: Application & AI Security
decks.summary: Secure coding, web attacks, and AI threats (new in SY0-801).

cards.q: What is SQL injection?
cards.a: Inserting SQL through input so the database runs it
cards.x: Fix with parameterised queries and least-privilege DB accounts.

cards.q: What is cross-site scripting (XSS)?
cards.a: Injecting script that runs in other users’ browsers
cards.x: Fix with output encoding and a Content Security Policy.

cards.q: What is CSRF?
cards.a: Tricking a logged-in user’s browser into sending an unwanted request
cards.x: Fix with anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies.

cards.q: What is a buffer overflow?
cards.a: Writing past a memory buffer’s bounds, possibly running code
cards.x: Mitigated by memory-safe languages, ASLR, and DEP.

cards.q: What is input validation?
cards.a: Checking input against expected type, length, and format
cards.x: Validate on the server; client-side checks are easily bypassed.

cards.q: What is code signing for?
cards.a: Proving software came from the publisher and wasn’t altered
cards.x: Protects the supply chain and users.

cards.q: What is SAST vs DAST?
cards.a: Static analysis of source vs dynamic testing of a running app
cards.x: Use both in CI/CD.

cards.q: What is prompt injection?
cards.a: Input that overrides an LLM’s instructions
cards.x: OWASP LLM01. Indirect injection hides instructions in documents or web pages.
wrong: SQL injection in an AI database

cards.q: What is data poisoning?
cards.a: Corrupting training data to manipulate a model
cards.x: Control training-data provenance and integrity.

cards.q: Why is excessive agency a risk in AI agents?
cards.a: An agent with broad tools can take harmful actions if manipulated
cards.x: Limit tools and permissions; require human approval for high-impact actions.

cards.q: What is an AI-enabled threat covered by newer Security+ objectives?
cards.a: Deepfakes and AI-generated phishing at scale
cards.x: Verify requests out of band; train staff on synthetic media.

cards.q: What is an SBOM?
cards.a: A software bill of materials: an inventory of components
cards.x: Lets you find affected systems fast when a library CVE drops.

tracks.title: Cybersecurity
tracks.tagline: Hands-on blue team and red team skills: SOC, web attacks, IR, and hunting.

decks.title: Linux & Command Line for Security
decks.summary: The shell skills every analyst and tester uses daily.

cards.q: Which command prints the current directory?
cards.a: pwd
cards.x: cd changes directory; ls lists it.

cards.q: Which command lists hidden files too?
cards.a: ls -la
cards.x: Hidden files start with a dot, like .bashrc.

cards.q: Which command searches text for a pattern?
cards.a: grep
cards.x: grep -i "failed" /var/log/auth.log finds failed logins.

cards.q: What does `chmod 600 key.pem` do?
cards.a: Owner read/write only; nobody else can access it
cards.x: r=4, w=2, x=1 for owner, group, others. SSH rejects world-readable private keys.

cards.q: Where are Linux password hashes stored?
cards.a: /etc/shadow
cards.x: /etc/passwd lists accounts but no longer holds hashes.

cards.q: Which log holds SSH/sudo authentication events on Debian/Ubuntu?
cards.a: /var/log/auth.log
cards.x: RHEL-family systems use /var/log/secure; journalctl on systemd.

cards.q: What does `sudo` do?
cards.a: Runs a command as another user, root by default
cards.x: Audit sudoers: overly broad sudo rules are a privilege escalation path.

cards.q: What does the pipe `|` do?
cards.a: Sends one command’s output into the next command’s input
cards.x: cat access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr counts repeat lines.

cards.q: What is a SUID binary?
cards.a: A program that runs with its owner’s privileges
cards.x: SUID-root binaries are a classic privilege escalation target (see GTFOBins).

cards.q: Which command shows running processes?
cards.a: ps aux (or top/htop)
cards.x: Look for odd parents, names, or high CPU.

cards.q: Which command lists listening sockets on modern Linux?
cards.a: ss -tulpn
cards.x: Shows TCP/UDP listeners with the owning process.

cards.q: What does `base64 -d` do?
cards.a: Decodes base64 text
cards.x: Base64 is encoding, not encryption; attackers use it to hide payloads.

puzzles.prompt: What octal mode gives the owner rw-, the group r--, and others ---?
puzzles.x: r=4, w=2, x=1. Owner 4+2=6, group 4, others 0, so 640.

puzzles.prompt: Permissions are bits too. Set the three low bits (r, w, x) of "others" to all on.
puzzles.x: 4 + 2 + 1 = 7, which is full rwx. That is the last digit of chmod 777, which is almost always a mistake.

decks.title: Frameworks: ATT&CK, Kill Chain, CSF
decks.summary: The shared maps defenders use to reason about attacks.

cards.q: What is MITRE ATT&CK?
cards.a: A knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques
cards.x: Tactics are the "why" (goal); techniques are the "how".

cards.q: Which ATT&CK tactic covers getting a first foothold?
cards.a: Initial Access
cards.x: e.g. phishing, exploiting public-facing apps, valid accounts.

cards.q: Which ATT&CK tactic covers staying on a system after reboot?
cards.a: Persistence
cards.x: e.g. scheduled tasks, run keys, new accounts.

cards.q: Which ATT&CK tactic covers moving to other hosts?
cards.a: Lateral Movement
cards.x: e.g. RDP, SMB/admin shares, pass-the-hash.

cards.q: First phase of the Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain?
cards.a: Reconnaissance
cards.x: Recon, Weaponization, Delivery, Exploitation, Installation, C2, Actions on Objectives.

cards.q: What are the NIST CSF 2.0 functions?
cards.a: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
cards.x: CSF 2.0 (2024) added Govern.
wrong: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover only

cards.q: What does the Diamond Model link together?
cards.a: Adversary, capability, infrastructure, victim
cards.x: Used in threat intelligence analysis.

cards.q: What is the Pyramid of Pain?
cards.a: IoC types ranked by how much blocking them hurts the attacker
cards.x: Hashes and IPs are trivial to change; TTPs are the hardest.

cards.q: What is STIX/TAXII?
cards.a: A format (STIX) and transport (TAXII) for sharing threat intel
cards.x: Lets tools exchange IoCs automatically.

cards.q: What is a purple team?
cards.a: Red and blue teams working together to improve detection
cards.x: Attack, observe detection, tune, repeat.

cards.q: What is OSINT?
cards.a: Intelligence from publicly available sources
cards.x: Search engines, social media, DNS, certificate transparency logs.

puzzles.prompt: Order the Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain.
puzzles.x: Break any link and the intrusion fails. The earlier you break it, the cheaper it is.

decks.title: Cryptography Deep Dive
decks.summary: Key exchange, certificates, PKI, and cipher types. (Domain 1.4)

cards.q: Two parties need a shared secret over a public channel. Which algorithm?
cards.a: Diffie-Hellman key exchange
cards.x: Each side combines its private value with the other’s public value to derive the same secret; eavesdroppers cannot.

cards.q: What is a digital envelope?
cards.a: A message encrypted with a fast symmetric key, which is itself encrypted asymmetrically
cards.x: Hybrid approach: symmetric speed plus asymmetric key distribution.

cards.q: DV vs OV vs EV certificates?
cards.a: Domain-validated (email check), Organization-validated (business identity), Extended-validation (rigorous vetting)
cards.x: Higher validation = more trust, but all three encrypt identically.

cards.q: When is a wildcard certificate the right choice?
cards.a: Many subdomains of one domain, e.g. *.example.com
cards.x: One compromised wildcard key affects every subdomain — scope the risk.

cards.q: When is a SAN certificate better than a wildcard?
cards.a: Multiple different domain names on one certificate
cards.x: SAN lists each name explicitly; wildcards cover only one domain’s subdomains.

cards.q: What is the risk of a self-signed certificate in production?
cards.a: No trusted third party vouches for it, so users get warnings and may accept fakes
cards.x: Fine for testing; production needs a trusted CA chain.

cards.q: What does key escrow mean?
cards.a: A trusted third party holds a copy of encryption keys for recovery
cards.x: Enables data recovery but creates a high-value target.

cards.q: HSM vs TPM in one line each?
cards.a: HSM: network-attached vault for keys and crypto ops; TPM: chip on the motherboard binding keys to one device
cards.x: HSMs serve many systems; TPMs anchor one machine’s boot and disk encryption.

cards.q: Block cipher vs stream cipher?
cards.a: Block ciphers encrypt fixed-size chunks; stream ciphers encrypt bit by bit
cards.x: AES is a block cipher; RC4 (deprecated) was a stream cipher.

cards.q: Why prefer AES-GCM over AES-CBC?
cards.a: GCM adds authenticated encryption: confidentiality plus integrity in one pass
cards.x: CBC alone needs a separate HMAC to detect tampering.

cards.q: Hashing vs encryption: what is the fundamental difference?
cards.a: Hashing is one-way and has no key; encryption is reversible with a key
cards.x: You cannot "decrypt" a hash — you can only recompute and compare.

cards.q: What are the steps of creating a digital signature?
cards.a: Hash the message, then encrypt the hash with the sender’s private key
cards.x: Verification reverses it: decrypt with the public key, re-hash, compare.

cards.q: A browser trusts a website’s certificate. What did it actually verify?
cards.a: The full chain: leaf signed by intermediate, intermediate by a trusted root
cards.x: Any break — expired, wrong name, untrusted root — triggers a warning.

cards.q: What happens if a root CA is compromised?
cards.a: Every certificate chaining to it becomes untrustworthy at once
cards.x: Root keys live offline in HSMs precisely because the blast radius is total.

cards.q: Why do CAs use intermediate certificates?
cards.a: To keep the root key offline: intermediates sign day-to-day certs
cards.x: A compromised intermediate can be revoked without replacing the root.

cards.q: What is certificate pinning?
cards.a: An app accepts only a specific certificate or key, ignoring the system trust store
cards.x: Defeats rogue-CA attacks but breaks when the pinned cert rotates.
wrong: Pinning a cert to a wall

cards.q: How often should encryption keys be rotated?
cards.a: On a defined schedule and immediately on suspected compromise or staff departure
cards.x: Rotation limits how much data one key protects.

cards.q: RSA-2048 vs ECC P-256: which is stronger per bit?
cards.a: ECC: a 256-bit curve rivals RSA-3072 with far less computation
cards.x: ECC suits mobile and constrained devices.

cards.q: What is steganography?
cards.a: Hiding data inside innocent-looking files, like text in an image
cards.x: Unlike encryption it hides the existence of the message, not just its content.

cards.q: Obfuscation vs encryption?
cards.a: Obfuscation only makes data hard to read; encryption makes it unreadable without the key
cards.x: Security by obscurity is not a control.

cards.q: What problem does a digital signature NOT solve?
cards.a: Confidentiality: a signed message is still readable by anyone
cards.x: Signatures prove origin and integrity, not secrecy — encrypt as well if needed.

cards.q: HMAC: what does it add over a plain hash?
cards.a: A secret key, so only key holders can create or verify the tag
cards.x: Proves both integrity and authenticity of a message.

cards.q: What is key derivation (e.g. HKDF)?
cards.a: Generating multiple working keys from one master secret
cards.x: TLS derives separate encryption and MAC keys per direction from the handshake secret.

cards.q: Why use ephemeral keys in a handshake?
cards.a: Each session gets fresh keys, so one compromise cannot decrypt other sessions
cards.x: This is the mechanism behind perfect forward secrecy.

cards.q: A developer hard-codes an AES key in the mobile app. What is wrong?
cards.a: Anyone who downloads the app can extract the key and decrypt everything
cards.x: Keys belong in a keystore, HSM, or derived per device — never in shipped code.

decks.title: Core Security Concepts
decks.summary: CIA, AAA, zero trust, physical security, and design principles. (Domain 1.1–1.3)

cards.q: Ransomware encrypts the file server. Which CIA goals are attacked?
cards.a: Availability first, then confidentiality if data is also stolen
cards.x: Double extortion adds a confidentiality breach to the availability loss.

cards.q: A database shows wrong account balances but no outage. Which goal failed?
cards.a: Integrity: the data is present and reachable but untrustworthy
cards.x: Backups restore availability; only verified clean copies restore integrity.

cards.q: A DDoS takes the web shop offline during a sale. Which goal?
cards.a: Availability
cards.x: Mitigate with CDN absorption, scrubbing, and rate limiting.

cards.q: An attacker sniffs unencrypted HTTP logins at a café. Which goal?
cards.a: Confidentiality
cards.x: HTTPS everywhere is the fix; HSTS enforces it.

cards.q: RAID, clustering, and generators protect which CIA goal?
cards.a: Availability
cards.x: Redundancy at every layer: power, network, systems, sites.

cards.q: Checksums and version control protect which goal?
cards.a: Integrity
cards.x: They detect unauthorised change, not eavesdropping.

cards.q: Authentication vs authorization vs accounting?
cards.a: Prove identity, grant permissions, log actions
cards.x: You authenticate to the VPN, are authorized to the finance share, and accounting records the access.

cards.q: What does the accounting part of AAA enable?
cards.a: Audit trails, billing, and forensic reconstruction
cards.x: Without accounting you cannot prove who did what.

cards.q: A badge opens the door but the log shows no entry. Which AAA failed?
cards.a: Accounting: authentication and authorization worked, the record did not
cards.x: Gaps in accounting blind incident response.

cards.q: Zero trust vs the old castle-and-moat model?
cards.a: No implicit trust by network location; verify every request continuously
cards.x: A compromised laptop inside the LAN gets no free pass.

cards.q: What is microsegmentation in zero trust?
cards.a: Dividing the network into tiny isolated zones with per-zone policy
cards.x: Limits lateral movement: breaching one segment does not open the rest.

cards.q: What does "continuous validation" mean in zero trust?
cards.a: Re-check identity, device health, and context throughout the session, not just at login
cards.x: A stolen session token alone should not grant lasting access.

cards.q: Policy engine vs policy administrator vs enforcement point?
cards.a: Engine decides, administrator configures, enforcement point applies the decision
cards.x: The NIST 800-207 logical components of a zero trust architecture.

cards.q: What does "assume breach" change in design?
cards.a: You build detection, segmentation, and least privilege as if attackers are already inside
cards.x: Backups, monitoring, and blast-radius limits become primary controls.

cards.q: Why does zero trust still need strong identity?
cards.a: Identity becomes the perimeter: every decision starts from "who and what"
cards.x: Weak identity collapses the whole model.

cards.q: A row of concrete posts blocks the lobby entrance. What are they?
cards.a: Bollards: anti-ram barriers against vehicle attacks
cards.x: Rated by crash standards; part of perimeter physical security.

cards.q: What is a mantrap (access control vestibule)?
cards.a: Two interlocked doors: the second opens only after the first closes and you authenticate
cards.x: Defeats tailgating and piggybacking.

cards.q: Why would a facility install a Faraday cage room?
cards.a: To block all radio signals: no Wi-Fi, cellular, or Bluetooth in or out
cards.x: Protects against wireless exfiltration and eavesdropping.

cards.q: What attack does a cable lock on a laptop prevent?
cards.a: Opportunistic theft of the device itself
cards.x: It does not stop a determined thief with cutters — layer it with encryption.

cards.q: Where should CCTV cameras go first?
cards.a: Entries, exits, server rooms, and other chokepoints
cards.x: Coverage of high-value areas beats blanket coverage of hallways.

cards.q: Visitor logs and escort policies enforce what?
cards.a: Accountability for non-employees inside secure areas
cards.x: Know who was where, when — and never leave visitors unescorted near sensitive zones.

cards.q: Fingerprint, iris, face, voice: what are these?
cards.a: Biometric authentication factors (something you are)
cards.x: They authenticate identity; they do not replace authorization.

cards.q: FAR vs FRR in biometrics?
cards.a: False Acceptance Rate (wrongly admitting) vs False Rejection Rate (wrongly denying)
cards.x: Lowering one raises the other; tune to the risk.

cards.q: What is CER (crossover error rate)?
cards.a: The point where FAR equals FRR: lower CER means a more accurate biometric
cards.x: Use it to compare biometric systems objectively.

cards.q: Why can’t you revoke a compromised fingerprint?
cards.a: Biometrics are permanent: you cannot issue a new fingerprint
cards.x: Use biometrics for convenience, pair with a revocable factor for high security.

cards.q: Smart card vs hardware token: what do they prove?
cards.a: Possession: something you have
cards.x: Combine with a PIN (knowledge) for true multi-factor.

cards.q: What is defense in depth?
cards.a: Layered controls so one failure does not mean breach
cards.x: If phishing beats training, MFA and EDR still stand in the way.

cards.q: What is separation of duties?
cards.a: Splitting critical tasks so no single person can complete fraud alone
cards.x: The person who approves payments cannot also issue them.

cards.q: What is implicit deny in access control?
cards.a: Default stance: deny everything not explicitly allowed
cards.x: The safe default behind allow-listing and firewall rules.

cards.q: Why enforce job rotation?
cards.a: It exposes fraud and removes single points of knowledge
cards.x: Someone covering a role may spot what the regular hid.

cards.q: Why require mandatory vacations?
cards.a: Fraud that needs constant cover unravels when the person is away
cards.x: A classic anti-fraud control in finance roles.

cards.q: What is dual control (two-person rule)?
cards.a: Two authorized people required to complete a sensitive action
cards.x: Used for key ceremonies, safe combinations, and large transfers.

cards.q: "Need to know" limits what?
cards.a: Access to information: only those who require it for their role
cards.x: Classification plus need-to-know equals least privilege for data.

cards.q: A policy says screens lock after 5 idle minutes. Which principle?
cards.a: Defense in depth applied to physical/logical access
cards.x: Layered with badges, clean desk, and encryption.

resources.title: ISC2 Certified in Cybersecurity (free course + exam)

decks.title: SOC Analyst Fundamentals
decks.summary: Triage, logs, alerts, and phishing analysis.

cards.q: What does SOC Tier 1 typically do?
cards.a: Alert triage: validate, enrich, escalate
cards.x: Tier 2 investigates deeper; Tier 3 hunts and handles major incidents.

cards.q: Windows Event ID 4625 means…
cards.a: A failed logon
cards.x: 4624 = successful logon; 4672 = special privileges assigned.

cards.q: Windows Event ID 4624 means…
cards.a: A successful logon
cards.x: Logon type 10 is RemoteInteractive (RDP).

cards.q: Windows Event ID 1102 means…
cards.a: The security audit log was cleared
cards.x: A strong indicator of anti-forensics.

cards.q: Windows Event ID 4720 means…
cards.a: A user account was created
cards.x: Unexpected accounts are a persistence indicator.

cards.q: Which email header field shows the path a message took?
cards.a: Received
cards.x: Read Received headers bottom to top.

cards.q: What do SPF, DKIM, and DMARC do?
cards.a: Authenticate email senders and set a policy for failures
cards.x: SPF = allowed servers; DKIM = signature; DMARC = alignment and policy.

cards.q: What is alert fatigue?
cards.a: Analysts overwhelmed by noisy alerts, missing real ones
cards.x: Tune detections, suppress known-good, automate enrichment.

cards.q: What is Sysmon?
cards.a: A free Microsoft tool that logs detailed process, network, and file events
cards.x: Event ID 1 = process creation with the full command line.

cards.q: What is a sandbox in malware analysis?
cards.a: An isolated environment to safely run suspicious files
cards.x: Observe behaviour: files dropped, registry keys, network calls.

cards.q: What does a file hash lookup (e.g. VirusTotal) tell you?
cards.a: Whether the exact file is known to be malicious
cards.x: A single changed byte changes the hash, so absence proves little.

cards.q: What does "true positive" mean for an alert?
cards.a: The alert fired and the activity really was malicious
cards.x: Track TP/FP rates to measure detection quality.
wrong: No alert fired for a real attack

cards.q: A server runs Telnet, FTP, and an old SMB version. What is the FIRST hardening step?
cards.a: Disable unneeded services and close unused ports
cards.x: Reduce the attack surface before patching: if nothing is listening, nothing can be exploited.

cards.q: What is OS hardening?
cards.a: Securing an OS by removing defaults, closing ports, and applying baselines
cards.x: Use CIS Benchmarks or STIGs as the starting template.

cards.q: BitLocker, FileVault, LUKS — what do they have in common?
cards.a: Full-disk encryption for Windows, macOS, and Linux
cards.x: Protects data at rest if the device is lost or stolen.

cards.q: EDR vs traditional antivirus: what is the key difference?
cards.a: EDR records behaviour and enables response; AV mostly matches signatures
cards.x: AV asks "is this known bad?"; EDR asks "what did this process just do?"

cards.q: Why does Security+ prefer application allow-listing over block-listing?
cards.a: Default-deny: only approved software runs, stopping unknown malware
cards.x: Block-listing chases an infinite list of badness.

cards.q: What is a host-based firewall’s job vs a network firewall’s?
cards.a: Controls traffic on that single machine, even off the corporate network
cards.x: Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security is the common example.

cards.q: A kiosk PC must boot the same clean image every restart. Which control?
cards.a: Reboot-to-restore or write-protected baseline image
cards.x: Prevents persistence of any change, malicious or accidental.

cards.q: Patch Tuesday is weekly, but a critical RCE drops on Thursday. What now?
cards.a: Out-of-band emergency patching per the patch management policy
cards.x: Criticality and active exploitation override the normal cadence.

cards.q: What does "secure baseline" mean in hardening?
cards.a: An approved, locked-down configuration every system is compared against
cards.x: Drift from baseline triggers remediation.

cards.q: Why disable Autorun/AutoPlay on Windows hosts?
cards.a: USB-borne malware would otherwise execute on insert
cards.x: A classic initial-access vector; disable via GPO.

cards.q: What is a CMDB used for in security operations?
cards.a: A single inventory of assets, owners, and configurations
cards.x: You cannot protect or patch what you do not know exists.

cards.q: Why tag assets (e.g. "crown-jewel", "pci-scope")?
cards.a: So controls, monitoring, and incident priority follow asset value
cards.x: Tagging drives data classification and handling rules.

cards.q: Data is labelled Public, Internal, Confidential. What is this?
cards.a: Data classification driving handling and protection requirements
cards.x: Classification decides encryption, sharing, and retention rules.

cards.q: A decommissioned drive held customer PII. How must it be disposed?
cards.a: Sanitised per NIST 800-88: clear, purge, or destroy to match sensitivity
cards.x: Purge or destroy for PII; a simple delete is not enough.

cards.q: What is the difference between wiping and degaussing?
cards.a: Wiping overwrites data; degaussing scrambles magnetic media with magnets
cards.x: Degaussing ruins HDDs and tapes but does nothing to SSDs or flash.

cards.q: Why does asset inventory matter for vulnerability management?
cards.a: Scans only find network-visible hosts; the CMDB reveals unmanaged shadow IT
cards.x: Unknown assets are unpatched assets.

cards.q: What does NAC check before letting a device on the network?
cards.a: Identity plus health: patched, AV current, compliant configuration
cards.x: Non-compliant devices are quarantined or remediated.

cards.q: 802.1X in one sentence?
cards.a: Port-based authentication: a device must authenticate before the switch port opens
cards.x: Uses EAP, commonly with RADIUS, on wired and WPA2/3-Enterprise wireless.

cards.q: Agent-based vs agentless NAC?
cards.a: An installed agent reports deep health; agentless probes with less detail
cards.x: Agentless suits BYOD and IoT that cannot run agents.

cards.q: Pre-admission vs post-admission NAC?
cards.a: Check before access vs continuously monitor after access is granted
cards.x: Post-admission catches a healthy device that later becomes compromised.

cards.q: Endpoint DLP vs network DLP: what is the difference?
cards.a: Endpoint DLP watches the device; network DLP inspects egress traffic
cards.x: Cloud DLP (CASB) covers SaaS. Layer them.

cards.q: An engineer emails 500 SSNs to a personal address. Which control should catch it?
cards.a: DLP with PII patterns on email egress
cards.x: Tune patterns so legitimate work is not blocked.

cards.q: What does DNS filtering block?
cards.a: Resolution of known-malicious domains: phishing, C2, malware delivery
cards.x: Stops the connection before it starts, for any protocol.

cards.q: Why filter DNS instead of only filtering web URLs?
cards.a: DNS covers every protocol and app, not just the browser
cards.x: Malware using its own resolver (DoH) is the bypass to watch for.

cards.q: A web filter blocks "gambling" and "adult" categories. What is it filtering by?
cards.a: URL/content category set by policy
cards.x: Also used for bandwidth and liability control.

cards.q: What does JML stand for in identity lifecycle?
cards.a: Joiner, Mover, Leaver: provision, adjust, deprovision access with role changes
cards.x: Automate it from the HR system to kill orphaned accounts.

cards.q: An employee is terminated Friday at 5pm. When should access be revoked?
cards.a: Immediately at termination, automated from HR
cards.x: Orphaned accounts are a top insider-threat vector.

cards.q: Rank by phishing resistance: SMS codes, authenticator app, hardware key
cards.a: Hardware key (FIDO2) > authenticator app (TOTP) > SMS
cards.x: SMS falls to SIM swapping; push alone suffers MFA fatigue.

cards.q: What does SSO give the security team besides convenience?
cards.a: One place to enforce MFA, login policy, and deprovisioning
cards.x: But it becomes a single point of failure — harden the IdP.

cards.q: SAML vs OIDC in one line each?
cards.a: SAML: XML-based SSO for enterprise apps; OIDC: modern JSON/REST SSO on OAuth2
cards.x: Both let one identity provider vouch for you to many apps.

cards.q: What is privileged access management (PAM)?
cards.a: Vaulting, rotating, and just-in-time issuing of admin credentials
cards.x: No standing domain-admin passwords; check out access per session.

cards.q: Why run periodic access reviews (recertification)?
cards.a: To remove accumulated, unneeded permissions — privilege creep
cards.x: Managers attest their team’s access is still required.

cards.q: A service account password has not changed in 4 years. What is the risk?
cards.a: Long-lived, rarely monitored credentials are ideal attacker persistence
cards.x: Rotate, vault, and scope service accounts to least privilege.

cards.q: What is just-in-time (JIT) admin access?
cards.a: Elevated rights granted for a limited window, then auto-revoked
cards.x: Removes standing privilege without slowing real work.

cards.q: An audit finds 40 enabled accounts for departed staff. What is the FIRST fix?
cards.a: Disable them now, then repair the HR-to-IT deprovisioning feed
cards.x: A process failure, not just a cleanup task.

decks.title: Threat Actors & Attack Vectors
decks.summary: Who attacks, why, and the social engineering they use.

cards.q: APT vs opportunistic attacker: what is the difference?
cards.a: APTs are resourced, patient, targeted; opportunistic actors spray broadly
cards.x: APTs dwell for months pursuing specific objectives; opportunistic actors blast ransomware and phishing widely.

cards.q: What motivates nation-state actors?
cards.a: Espionage, sabotage, and geopolitical advantage
cards.x: They have the deepest resources and the longest dwell times.

cards.q: What motivates hacktivists?
cards.a: Political or social causes — publicity over profit
cards.x: Defacements and DDoS are their typical loud tactics.

cards.q: Name the three insider threat types.
cards.a: Malicious, negligent, and compromised insiders
cards.x: Negligent insiders who click phishing cause as much damage as malicious ones.

cards.q: What motivates organized cybercrime?
cards.a: Direct financial gain: ransomware, fraud, theft
cards.x: They run ransomware-as-a-service like a business.

cards.q: What is the risk of shadow IT?
cards.a: Unsanctioned apps and systems outside security visibility
cards.x: A marketing SaaS holding customer data is a breach waiting to happen.

cards.q: What does TTP stand for?
cards.a: Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures — the attacker playbook
cards.x: ATT&CK catalogs TTPs so defenders detect patterns, not just indicators.

cards.q: Why profile which threat actors target you?
cards.a: It predicts their likely TTPs so defences match the real adversary
cards.x: A bank and a hospital face different actors.

cards.q: Hacktivist vs nation-state: how do their operations differ?
cards.a: Hacktivists want visibility; nation-states want stealthy persistence
cards.x: One defaces your homepage; the other lives in your network for a year.

cards.q: What is a "script kiddie"?
cards.a: An unskilled attacker using others’ ready-made tools
cards.x: Dangerous anyway: automated tools need no skill.

cards.q: What is corporate espionage in cyber terms?
cards.a: Stealing trade secrets for business advantage
cards.x: Insiders and APTs both do this work.

cards.q: Why do insiders bypass most perimeter defences?
cards.a: They already hold legitimate access and trust
cards.x: UEBA and least privilege are the countermeasures.

cards.q: What is an "evil maid" attack?
cards.a: Physical access to a device left unattended
cards.x: Full-disk encryption plus tamper-evident seals mitigate it.

cards.q: What is a supply chain attack?
cards.a: Compromising a vendor or update channel to reach its customers
cards.x: SolarWinds: one poisoned update, thousands of victims.

cards.q: Phishing vs spear phishing vs whaling?
cards.a: Bulk lures vs targeted individuals vs senior executives
cards.x: Whaling uses deeply researched pretexts against the C-suite.

cards.q: What is vishing?
cards.a: Voice phishing: fake calls impersonating trusted parties
cards.x: The classic is "IT support" asking for your MFA code.

cards.q: What is smishing?
cards.a: Phishing delivered via SMS or text messages
cards.x: Often fake delivery or bank alerts with malicious links.

cards.q: What is business email compromise (BEC)?
cards.a: Spoofed or hijacked executive email directing fraud like wire transfers
cards.x: BEC rarely carries malware — it abuses trust, so train finance staff specifically.

cards.q: What is pretexting?
cards.a: Inventing a scenario to extract information or access
cards.x: The "new IT contractor needs your password" call.

cards.q: What is baiting?
cards.a: Luring victims with something tempting: free USB, fake download
cards.x: The parking-lot USB drop is the classic.

cards.q: What is tailgating (piggybacking)?
cards.a: Following an authorized person through a secured door
cards.x: Mitigate with mantraps, turnstiles, and a challenge culture.

cards.q: What is a watering hole attack?
cards.a: Compromising websites your targets frequent
cards.x: Instead of attacking the target, poison their water supply.

cards.q: What is typosquatting?
cards.a: Registering lookalike domains such as micros0ft.com
cards.x: Used for phishing pages and credential harvesting.

cards.q: What is an influence campaign?
cards.a: Coordinated disinformation to shape opinion or behaviour
cards.x: Nation-states run them through fake personas and botnets.

cards.q: What is clone phishing?
cards.a: A legitimate email copied with malicious links swapped in
cards.x: Harder to spot because the original message was real.

cards.q: What is pharming?
cards.a: Redirecting users to fake sites via DNS poisoning
cards.x: Even a correctly typed URL lands on the attacker’s copy.

cards.q: What is scareware?
cards.a: Fake security warnings pushing bogus "fixes"
cards.x: Classic: "Your PC is infected! Call this number."

cards.q: Why does social engineering work?
cards.a: It exploits trust, urgency, and authority — not technology
cards.x: Defence is process and culture: verify out of band.

cards.q: What is dumpster diving (in security)?
cards.a: Recovering sensitive information from discarded trash
cards.x: Shredding policies exist because of this.

cards.q: What is shoulder surfing?
cards.a: Watching someone type credentials or PINs
cards.x: Privacy screens are the cheap fix.

cards.q: What is a quid pro quo attack?
cards.a: Offering a benefit in exchange for access or information
cards.x: "Free tech support" for your login credentials.

cards.q: Finance receives a vendor invoice with new bank details. What is the play?
cards.a: Verify the change via a known-good phone number, not email reply
cards.x: Vendor impersonation is a top BEC variant.

cards.q: What is a deepfake-enabled social engineering attack?
cards.a: AI-generated voice or video impersonating a trusted person
cards.x: Verify high-stakes requests through a second channel.

cards.q: What is elicitation?
cards.a: Drawing information out through casual conversation
cards.x: Skilled attackers never ask directly for secrets.

cards.q: What is war-driving?
cards.a: Driving around mapping Wi-Fi networks
cards.x: Finds rogue APs and weak encryption; defenders do it too.

cards.q: What is doxing?
cards.a: Publishing private information to shame or intimidate
cards.x: Protect executives’ personal data exposure.

decks.title: Malware Types
decks.summary: Ransomware to rootkits: what each does and how it spreads.

cards.q: What is ransomware?
cards.a: Malware that encrypts data and demands payment for the key
cards.x: Modern strains add double extortion: pay, or we leak it.

cards.q: What is double extortion ransomware?
cards.a: Encrypts data AND threatens to publish stolen data
cards.x: Backups alone do not defeat it — exfiltration already happened.

cards.q: What is a Trojan?
cards.a: Malware disguised as legitimate software
cards.x: Named for the Trojan horse: the user installs it willingly.

cards.q: What is a RAT?
cards.a: Remote Access Trojan: gives full remote control of the machine
cards.x: Hands the attacker a keyboard inside your network.

cards.q: Worm vs virus: what is the difference?
cards.a: Worms self-propagate; viruses need a host file and user action
cards.x: WannaCry wormed via EternalBlue; viruses attach to executables.

cards.q: What is fileless malware?
cards.a: Runs in memory via legitimate tools, with no disk binary
cards.x: PowerShell plus WMI plus registry: hard for AV, visible to EDR and Sysmon.

cards.q: What is a rootkit?
cards.a: Malware that hides by subverting the operating system itself
cards.x: Kernel-mode rootkits defeat most detection; rebuild from known-good media.

cards.q: What is a bootkit?
cards.a: A rootkit infecting the boot process, before the OS loads
cards.x: Survives OS reinstalls; Secure Boot mitigates it.

cards.q: What is a keylogger?
cards.a: Records keystrokes to steal credentials
cards.x: Hardware or software; phishing-resistant MFA blunts the payoff.

cards.q: What is spyware?
cards.a: Secretly monitors activity and exfiltrates data
cards.x: Often bundled with "free" software.

cards.q: What is a logic bomb?
cards.a: Malicious code that triggers on a condition or date
cards.x: The disgruntled admin’s revenge: fires when their account is deleted.

cards.q: What is a backdoor?
cards.a: A hidden access method bypassing normal authentication
cards.x: Planted by attackers — or left behind by vendors.

cards.q: What is a dropper?
cards.a: Malware whose only job is installing the real payload
cards.x: Small and evasive; the payload arrives later.

cards.q: Downloader vs dropper?
cards.a: A downloader fetches the payload remotely; a dropper carries it embedded
cards.x: Both are stage-one malware.

cards.q: What is a botnet?
cards.a: A network of compromised machines controlled as one
cards.x: Rented out for DDoS, spam, and crypto mining.

cards.q: What is cryptojacking?
cards.a: Stealing compute to mine cryptocurrency
cards.x: Look for unexplained CPU spikes, especially in browsers and cloud.

cards.q: What is a wiper?
cards.a: Destroys data with no recovery option — no ransom involved
cards.x: NotPetya posed as ransomware but was a wiper.

cards.q: Scareware vs ransomware?
cards.a: Scareware bluffs about infection; ransomware actually encrypts
cards.x: Both demand payment; only one has real leverage.

cards.q: What is ransomware-as-a-service?
cards.a: Criminals lease ransomware kits to affiliates for a cut
cards.x: It lowered the skill bar for ransomware attacks.

cards.q: What is process hollowing?
cards.a: Replacing a legitimate process’s memory with malicious code
cards.x: svchost.exe running ransomware: EDR catches the anomaly.

cards.q: What is DLL injection?
cards.a: Forcing a running process to load a malicious DLL
cards.x: Lets malware hide inside trusted processes.

cards.q: What is a packer (crypter)?
cards.a: Compresses or encrypts malware to evade signature detection
cards.x: High-entropy packed binaries are a static-analysis red flag.

cards.q: Polymorphic vs metamorphic malware?
cards.a: Polymorphic re-encrypts each copy; metamorphic rewrites its own code
cards.x: Both defeat hash-based detection.

cards.q: What is steganography in malware?
cards.a: Hiding payloads inside images or other innocent files
cards.x: A meme.png that drops a RAT.

cards.q: Why is macro malware still a top initial vector?
cards.a: Malicious Office macros arrive as trusted-looking attachments
cards.x: Disable macros by default; train users on the enable-content trap.

cards.q: What is malvertising?
cards.a: Malicious ads served through legitimate ad networks
cards.x: Even reputable sites can serve them — hence enterprise ad blockers.

cards.q: What is the top mobile malware vector?
cards.a: Trojanized apps and smishing links; sideloaded APKs on Android
cards.x: Stick to official stores and check app permissions.

cards.q: What is firmware/UEFI malware?
cards.a: Infects below the OS, surviving disk wipes
cards.x: Measured boot and firmware updates mitigate it.

cards.q: Adware: nuisance or threat?
cards.a: Both: aggressive ads, and often bundled spyware
cards.x: Treat unexpected adware as a compromise indicator.

decks.title: Web Application Attacks
decks.summary: OWASP Top 10 and PortSwigger-style labs.

cards.q: OWASP Top 10 (2021) #1 risk?
cards.a: Broken Access Control
cards.x: e.g. changing /account?id=123 to 124 (IDOR).

cards.q: What is IDOR?
cards.a: Accessing others’ objects by changing an identifier
cards.x: Insecure Direct Object Reference: enforce authorisation server-side on every request.

cards.q: What is SSRF?
cards.a: Making the server send requests to internal or unintended targets
cards.x: In cloud, SSRF can reach the metadata service (169.254.169.254). Use IMDSv2.

cards.q: What is path traversal?
cards.a: Using ../ sequences to read files outside the intended folder
cards.x: Canonicalise paths and use allow-lists.

cards.q: What is stored XSS?
cards.a: A malicious script saved on the server and served to every viewer
cards.x: Reflected XSS bounces off a single request; DOM XSS lives in client-side JS.
wrong: XSS that only affects the attacker

cards.q: Which cookie flag stops JavaScript from reading a cookie?
cards.a: HttpOnly
cards.x: Secure = HTTPS only; SameSite limits cross-site sending.

cards.q: What is a JWT weakness to test for?
cards.a: Accepting alg "none" or a weak/guessable signing key
cards.x: Always verify the signature with a fixed, expected algorithm.

cards.q: Which tool is the standard intercepting proxy for web testing?
cards.a: Burp Suite (Community edition is free)
cards.x: OWASP ZAP is a fully free alternative.

cards.q: What is command injection?
cards.a: Getting the server to run OS commands via input
cards.x: e.g. a ping form accepting "8.8.8.8; cat /etc/passwd".

cards.q: What is "Security Misconfiguration"?
cards.a: Insecure defaults, verbose errors, open storage, unneeded features
cards.x: Harden with baselines and automated config scanning.

cards.q: What is insecure deserialization?
cards.a: Turning untrusted serialized data into objects, enabling code execution
cards.x: Grouped under Software and Data Integrity Failures in 2021.

cards.q: What does a Content Security Policy do?
cards.a: Restricts which sources a page may load scripts and content from
cards.x: A strong defence-in-depth control against XSS.

decks.title: Penetration Testing Process
decks.summary: Scoping, recon, scanning, exploitation, and reporting.

cards.q: What must exist before any penetration test?
cards.a: Written authorisation and an agreed scope (rules of engagement)
cards.x: Without it, testing can be a crime.

cards.q: Black box vs white box testing?
cards.a: No prior knowledge vs full knowledge of the target
cards.x: Grey box is partial knowledge, e.g. a user account.

cards.q: What does `nmap -sS` do?
cards.a: A TCP SYN ("half-open") scan
cards.x: Sends SYN, reads SYN-ACK or RST, never completes the handshake.

cards.q: What does `nmap -sV` add?
cards.a: Service and version detection
cards.x: -O detects the OS; -A enables OS, version, scripts, and traceroute.

cards.q: Passive vs active reconnaissance?
cards.a: Gathering info without touching the target vs interacting directly
cards.x: WHOIS and OSINT are passive; port scanning is active.

cards.q: What is Metasploit?
cards.a: An exploitation framework with modules and payloads
cards.x: msfconsole; Meterpreter is its advanced payload.

cards.q: What is privilege escalation?
cards.a: Gaining higher permissions than initially obtained
cards.x: Vertical = user to admin; horizontal = one user to another.

cards.q: What is pass-the-hash?
cards.a: Authenticating with an NTLM hash instead of the password
cards.x: Mitigate with LAPS, Credential Guard, and tiered admin models.

cards.q: What is Kerberoasting?
cards.a: Requesting service tickets for SPN accounts and cracking them offline
cards.x: Use long random service account passwords or gMSAs.

cards.q: What tool cracks password hashes offline?
cards.a: Hashcat (or John the Ripper)
cards.x: GPU-accelerated; strong, slow hashes resist it.

cards.q: What goes first in a pentest report?
cards.a: An executive summary in business terms
cards.x: Then findings with severity, evidence, and remediation steps.

cards.q: What is pivoting?
cards.a: Using a compromised host to reach otherwise inaccessible networks
cards.x: e.g. SSH tunnels, SOCKS proxies, or chisel.

puzzles.prompt: Order the phases of a penetration test.
puzzles.x: Scoping with written authorisation comes first; the report is the actual deliverable.

decks.title: Detection Engineering
decks.summary: Writing and tuning detections: Sigma, YARA, and queries.

cards.q: What is Sigma?
cards.a: A generic, SIEM-agnostic format for log detection rules
cards.x: Convert one Sigma rule to Splunk, Elastic, Sentinel queries.

cards.q: What is YARA?
cards.a: Pattern-matching rules for identifying malware files
cards.x: Strings plus conditions, used by scanners and sandboxes.

cards.q: What is Snort/Suricata?
cards.a: Open-source network IDS/IPS engines
cards.x: Signature rules matched against network traffic.

cards.q: Signature vs anomaly detection?
cards.a: Matches known-bad patterns vs flags deviations from a baseline
cards.x: Signatures miss novel attacks; anomalies are noisier.

cards.q: Why map detections to ATT&CK techniques?
cards.a: To measure coverage and find gaps
cards.x: A heat map shows where you are blind.

cards.q: What is "detection as code"?
cards.a: Rules stored in git, tested, reviewed, and deployed via CI
cards.x: Brings software engineering discipline to SOC content.

cards.q: What is a common indicator of PowerShell abuse?
cards.a: Encoded commands (-enc) and download cradles
cards.x: Enable Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104).

cards.q: What is beaconing?
cards.a: Regular, periodic callbacks from malware to C2
cards.x: Detect by consistent intervals and sizes in network data.

cards.q: What is DNS tunnelling?
cards.a: Hiding data or C2 inside DNS queries and responses
cards.x: Look for long, high-entropy subdomains and high query volume.

cards.q: What is living off the land (LOLBins)?
cards.a: Abusing built-in OS tools like certutil or rundll32
cards.x: Hard to block; detect unusual parent/child processes and arguments.

cards.q: How do you validate that a detection works?
cards.a: Safely emulate the technique (e.g. Atomic Red Team) and confirm it fires
cards.x: Test in a lab or controlled environment first.

cards.q: Credentialed vs non-credentialed vulnerability scan?
cards.a: Credentialed logs in for deep findings; non-credentialed sees only network-exposed issues
cards.x: Credentialed finds missing patches and misconfigs but needs safe credentials and maintenance windows.

cards.q: CVSS 9.8 vs CVSS 4.2: what does the number tell you?
cards.a: Severity: 9.8 is Critical, 4.2 is Medium
cards.x: Ranges: None 0, Low 0.1–3.9, Medium 4.0–6.9, High 7.0–8.9, Critical 9.0–10.

cards.q: A CVSS vector reads AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U. What does it describe?
cards.a: Remotely exploitable, low complexity, no privileges or user interaction needed
cards.x: Worst-case exploitability — prioritise these first.

cards.q: Why is the CVSS base score alone not enough to prioritise?
cards.a: It ignores your environment: asset value, exposure, active exploitation
cards.x: Combine CVSS with EPSS, KEV, and asset criticality.

cards.q: A critical vuln has no patch yet. What is the compensating control play?
cards.a: Reduce exposure another way: isolate, block at firewall/WAF, disable the feature
cards.x: Document it as a risk acceptance or exception with an expiry date.

cards.q: What is a vulnerability exception — and its danger?
cards.a: Formal, time-boxed acceptance of risk; danger is exceptions that never expire
cards.x: Review exceptions on schedule or they become permanent holes.

cards.q: Agent-based vs network vulnerability scanning?
cards.a: Agents report continuously even off-network; network scans need the host reachable
cards.x: Agents suit laptops and cloud; network scans suit static infrastructure.

cards.q: Discovery scan vs vulnerability scan?
cards.a: Discovery finds live hosts and ports; vuln scan tests them for weaknesses
cards.x: Run discovery first so nothing hides from the vuln scan.

cards.q: How often should vulnerability scans run?
cards.a: Continuously or regularly — and after any significant change
cards.x: Plus an authenticated scan cadence for deep coverage.

cards.q: A scan flags 10,000 findings. What do you do FIRST?
cards.a: Prioritise by exploitability and asset criticality, not raw count
cards.x: KEV plus internet-facing plus crown jewels beats a giant spreadsheet.

cards.q: What is a false positive in vuln management, and why does it matter?
cards.a: A flagged issue that is not actually exploitable; it wastes remediation effort
cards.x: Validate before assigning work to engineers.

cards.q: Patch management: why have maintenance windows?
cards.a: To apply patches at agreed times that minimise business disruption
cards.x: Emergency patches can break the window for critical issues.

cards.q: In a SIEM pipeline, what does the collector/forwarder do?
cards.a: Gathers logs at the source and ships them to the SIEM
cards.x: Splunk Universal Forwarder, Winlogbeat, syslog-ng.

cards.q: What is log normalisation (parsing)?
cards.a: Converting varied log formats into one common schema
cards.x: Lets one query search firewall, Windows, and proxy logs together.

cards.q: Correlation rule vs simple alert: what is the difference?
cards.a: Correlation joins events: failed logins THEN a success from a new country
cards.x: Single-event alerts are noisier; correlation adds context.

cards.q: An analyst builds a dashboard of top blocked domains. What is a dashboard for?
cards.a: At-a-glance operational awareness, refreshed continuously
cards.x: Reports are point-in-time and distributable; dashboards are live.

cards.q: Hot vs warm vs cold log storage?
cards.a: Hot: fast, recent, searchable; warm: slower, months; cold: cheap compliance archive
cards.x: Match retention tiers to investigation vs legal needs.

cards.q: What is EPS and why does the SOC care?
cards.a: Events per second: the SIEM ingestion rate you are licensed for
cards.x: Exceeding EPS drops logs — tune noisy sources.

cards.q: A SIEM rule fires 5,000 times a day with 2 true positives. What is wrong?
cards.a: The rule lacks filtering — high noise, low fidelity
cards.x: Add allow-lists, thresholds, or correlation before disabling it.

cards.q: Why review logs even when no alert fired?
cards.a: Hunts and audits catch what detections missed
cards.x: Scheduled log review is a detective control.

cards.q: Playbook vs runbook?
cards.a: Playbook: automated SOAR workflow; runbook: human step-by-step procedure
cards.x: Automate the playbook once the runbook is proven in practice.

cards.q: A phishing email arrives. What is the ideal SOAR playbook?
cards.a: Extract URLs/attachments, detonate in sandbox, search mailboxes, quarantine, block IoCs
cards.x: Minutes instead of hours, executed consistently every time.

cards.q: What should you automate FIRST with SOAR?
cards.a: High-volume, low-judgment tasks: enrichment, ticketing, IoC blocking
cards.x: Keep humans on novel, ambiguous decisions.

cards.q: What is the risk of full auto-remediation with no human review?
cards.a: A false positive can cause an outage, e.g. isolating the CEO’s laptop
cards.x: Start human-in-the-loop, then graduate to automation.

cards.q: SOAR "orchestration" vs "automation"?
cards.a: Orchestration connects tools into one workflow; automation executes the steps
cards.x: Orchestration is the conductor, automation the musicians.

cards.q: Full packet capture vs NetFlow: when do you need each?
cards.a: PCAP for deep payload forensics; NetFlow for who-talked-to-whom at scale
cards.x: PCAP is heavy; NetFlow is metadata and cheap to keep long-term.

cards.q: What does NetFlow/IPFIX record?
cards.a: Flow metadata: source/dest IP and ports, protocol, bytes, timestamps
cards.x: No payload — but enough to spot beaconing and exfiltration.

cards.q: Syslog facility vs severity?
cards.a: Facility names the subsystem; severity rates urgency 0–7
cards.x: Facility examples: auth, kern, mail. Severity: 0 Emergency … 7 Debug. authpriv with failed logins is a hunting staple.

cards.q: CEF vs LEEF: what are they?
cards.a: Common structured log formats (ArcSight CEF, QRadar LEEF) that normalise parsing
cards.x: Structured logs beat regex on raw text.

cards.q: Network tap vs SPAN port for capture?
cards.a: Tap: passive copy, no loss; SPAN: switch mirror, may drop under load
cards.x: Taps for critical links and forensics.

cards.q: Why keep DHCP logs for incident response?
cards.a: They map IP-to-hostname/MAC at a point in time
cards.x: Without them, "which laptop was 10.4.2.88?" is unanswerable.

cards.q: What is metadata’s value when payloads are encrypted?
cards.a: TLS hides content but not endpoints, timing, sizes, and certificates
cards.x: JA3 fingerprints and flow sizes still betray C2.

cards.q: Vulnerability scan output as a SOC data source: what does it give?
cards.a: Known weaknesses per asset to contextualise incoming alerts
cards.x: An alert on a host with a matching critical CVE jumps the queue.

cards.q: An analyst needs the exact bytes of a suspicious download. Which source?
cards.a: Full packet capture, if retained for that window
cards.x: Otherwise proxy logs plus endpoint telemetry are the fallback.

cards.q: sFlow vs NetFlow?
cards.a: sFlow samples packets (1-in-N); NetFlow records every flow
cards.x: sFlow is lighter on high-speed links; NetFlow is more complete.

decks.title: Vulnerability Types & Mitigations
decks.summary: Zero-days to race conditions: the flaw classes Security+ tests.

cards.q: What is a zero-day vulnerability?
cards.a: A flaw exploited before the vendor knows about or patches it
cards.x: No patch exists yet — mitigate with isolation and monitoring.

cards.q: What is responsible disclosure?
cards.a: Reporting a flaw privately and giving the vendor time to fix
cards.x: Versus full disclosure: publishing immediately.

cards.q: What is a buffer overflow?
cards.a: Writing past a buffer’s bounds to corrupt memory or hijack execution
cards.x: Mitigated by safe languages, ASLR, DEP/NX, and stack canaries.

cards.q: What is ASLR?
cards.a: Randomizes memory layout so exploits cannot find their targets
cards.x: Address Space Layout Randomization; bypassed via info leaks.

cards.q: What is a race condition (TOCTOU)?
cards.a: Exploiting the gap between a security check and its use
cards.x: Time-of-check to time-of-use: the check passes, then the file is swapped.

cards.q: What is SQL injection?
cards.a: Inserting SQL into input to manipulate the database
cards.x: Fix it with parameterized queries — never concatenate SQL strings.

cards.q: What is blind SQL injection?
cards.a: SQLi where the attacker infers data from true/false responses
cards.x: Slower than classic SQLi but just as dangerous.

cards.q: What is cross-site scripting (XSS)?
cards.a: Injecting scripts that execute in victims’ browsers
cards.x: Steals sessions; fix with output encoding and Content Security Policy.

cards.q: Stored vs reflected vs DOM XSS?
cards.a: Stored: on server; reflected: one request; DOM: client-side JS
cards.x: Stored is the worst: every visitor gets hit.

cards.q: What is CSRF?
cards.a: Tricking a logged-in browser into performing unwanted actions
cards.x: Anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies mitigate it.

cards.q: What is XXE?
cards.a: XML parsers resolving external entities to read files or trigger SSRF
cards.x: Disable external entity resolution; prefer JSON.

cards.q: What is a replay attack?
cards.a: Capturing valid data — like an auth token — and re-sending it
cards.x: Mitigate with nonces and timestamps.

cards.q: What is session fixation?
cards.a: Forcing a victim to use an attacker-known session ID
cards.x: Regenerate session IDs at login.

cards.q: What is a downgrade attack?
cards.a: Forcing weaker crypto, e.g. stripping TLS down to HTTP
cards.x: HSTS and protocol version enforcement mitigate it.

cards.q: What is a side-channel attack?
cards.a: Extracting secrets from timing, power, or cache behaviour
cards.x: Spectre and Meltdown: constant-time code mitigates.

cards.q: What is an integer overflow?
cards.a: Arithmetic that wraps around, corrupting sizes and allocations
cards.x: A classic memory-corruption primitive.

cards.q: What is use-after-free?
cards.a: Using memory after it was freed, letting attackers control it
cards.x: A common browser-exploit primitive.

cards.q: What is LDAP injection?
cards.a: Manipulating directory queries through unsanitized input
cards.x: Same fix family as SQLi: parameterized and escaped queries.

cards.q: What is server-side template injection (SSTI)?
cards.a: Injecting template syntax that executes on the server
cards.x: It can escalate to remote code execution; sandbox templates.

cards.q: What is HTTP request smuggling?
cards.a: Desyncing front-end and back-end servers to poison requests
cards.x: CL.TE and TE.CL desyncs; fix with strict parsing.

cards.q: What is prototype pollution?
cards.a: JavaScript: polluting Object.prototype to alter application behaviour
cards.x: Freeze prototypes and validate merge keys.

cards.q: What is an open redirect?
cards.a: An app redirecting to an attacker URL via a parameter
cards.x: Phishing fuel: allow-list redirect targets.

cards.q: What is clickjacking?
cards.a: A transparent overlay tricking clicks onto hidden actions
cards.x: X-Frame-Options and frame-ancestors mitigate it.

cards.q: What is subdomain takeover?
cards.a: Claiming a dangling DNS record that points at a dead service
cards.x: Audit DNS records against actual resources.

cards.q: What is DNS cache poisoning?
cards.a: Corrupting resolver caches to redirect traffic
cards.x: DNSSEC and randomized source ports mitigate it.

cards.q: What is ARP spoofing?
cards.a: Poisoning ARP tables to intercept LAN traffic
cards.x: Dynamic ARP Inspection mitigates it.

cards.q: What is a man-in-the-middle attack?
cards.a: Secretly relaying or altering traffic between two parties
cards.x: Mutual authentication and certificate pinning mitigate it.

cards.q: Allow-list vs deny-list input validation?
cards.a: Allow known-good; deny known-bad — allow-listing wins
cards.x: Deny-lists always miss the next bypass.

cards.q: What is output encoding?
cards.a: Escaping data for its context so it cannot execute
cards.x: The XSS fix: encode for HTML, JS, or URL as appropriate.

cards.q: What is parameterized querying?
cards.a: Separating SQL code from data so input can never become code
cards.x: The definitive SQL injection fix.

cards.q: What is least privilege?
cards.a: Grant only the access needed — nothing more
cards.x: It limits the blast radius of any compromise.

cards.q: What is defence in depth?
cards.a: Layered controls so one failure is never fatal
cards.x: Firewall plus patching plus EDR plus backups — not one magic box.

cards.q: What is attack surface reduction?
cards.a: Removing unnecessary services, ports, and code
cards.x: You cannot exploit what is not there.

cards.q: Why is "security through obscurity" not enough?
cards.a: Hiding details fails once discovered — use it only as one layer
cards.x: Kerckhoffs’s principle: the system must be secure even when fully known.

cards.q: Patching cadence vs emergency patching?
cards.a: Routine schedule for normal fixes; out-of-band for critical active exploits
cards.x: Criticality and exploitation override the calendar.

cards.q: What is virtual patching?
cards.a: WAF/IPS rule shielding a flaw until patched
cards.x: Buys time for unpatchable legacy systems.

decks.title: Cloud Models & Virtualization Security
decks.summary: Shared responsibility, hypervisors, containers, and zero trust.

cards.q: IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS in one line each?
cards.a: IaaS: manage OS up; PaaS: code+data; SaaS: data+access
cards.x: The higher the stack, the less you control.

cards.q: Shared responsibility in IaaS: who secures what?
cards.a: Provider secures hardware and hypervisor; you secure OS, apps, and data
cards.x: Misconfiguring your half causes most cloud breaches.

cards.q: Shared responsibility in SaaS: what is still YOUR job?
cards.a: Users, access, data classification, and sharing settings
cards.x: The provider secures nearly everything else.

cards.q: Public vs private vs hybrid vs community cloud?
cards.a: Public: shared multi-tenant; private: dedicated; hybrid: both; community: shared by peers
cards.x: Hybrid is the common enterprise reality.

cards.q: What is "lift and shift" migration?
cards.a: Moving workloads to cloud unchanged
cards.x: Fast — but it carries on-prem weaknesses along.

cards.q: Cloud vs on-prem: the security trade-off?
cards.a: Cloud brings scale and managed controls, but shared fate and config risk
cards.x: You trade physical control for agility.

cards.q: What is the #1 cause of cloud breaches?
cards.a: Misconfiguration: public buckets, open security groups, exposed keys
cards.x: Automate guardrails so the safe path is the default.

cards.q: What is CSPM?
cards.a: Cloud Security Posture Management: continuous misconfiguration scanning
cards.x: It flags the public bucket before attackers find it.

cards.q: Type 1 vs Type 2 hypervisor?
cards.a: Type 1: bare metal; Type 2: on a host OS
cards.x: ESXi and Hyper-V vs VirtualBox and VMware Workstation.

cards.q: What is VM sprawl?
cards.a: Untracked VMs accumulating without owners or patches
cards.x: Unknown VMs are unpatched VMs.

cards.q: What is VM escape?
cards.a: Breaking from a guest out to the hypervisor or host
cards.x: Rare but catastrophic: one flaw compromises every tenant.

cards.q: Container vs VM: the security boundary difference?
cards.a: VMs isolate via hypervisor; containers share the host kernel
cards.x: A kernel bug escapes every container on the host.

cards.q: Why do bloated container images matter?
cards.a: They ship known CVEs in unused packages
cards.x: Use minimal or distroless images and scan in CI.

cards.q: Why run containers as non-root?
cards.a: A breakout as root owns the host; as nobody it stays contained
cards.x: Pair with read-only filesystems.

cards.q: What is Kubernetes RBAC for?
cards.a: Least-privilege access to cluster resources
cards.x: No cluster-admin for CI bots.

cards.q: What is a service mesh?
cards.a: mTLS and policy between microservices, e.g. Istio or Linkerd
cards.x: It encrypts east-west traffic by default.

cards.q: Serverless (FaaS): what is the security catch?
cards.a: Huge dependency attack surface; ephemeral does not mean invisible
cards.x: Scan functions like any code; scope IAM roles per function.

cards.q: Why is the cloud metadata service dangerous?
cards.a: SSRF to 169.254.169.254 can leak IAM credentials
cards.x: Enforce IMDSv2, which requires a token.

cards.q: Availability zone vs region?
cards.a: An AZ is an isolated datacenter; a region groups AZs
cards.x: Spread workloads across AZs for resilience.

cards.q: What is data residency?
cards.a: Legal requirement that data stay in certain geographies
cards.x: Pick regions to satisfy GDPR and contracts.

cards.q: What is a golden image?
cards.a: A hardened, pre-approved VM or container template
cards.x: Build once, scan it, deploy it everywhere.

cards.q: What is immutable infrastructure?
cards.a: Never patch running systems — replace them with new images
cards.x: It kills configuration drift and attacker persistence.

cards.q: IaC security: what do you scan for?
cards.a: Misconfigurations in Terraform or CloudFormation before deploy
cards.x: Checkov and tfsec run in CI.

cards.q: Secrets in images or repos: what is the rule?
cards.a: Never bake them in — inject at runtime from a vault
cards.x: Use a secrets manager, not environment files in git.

cards.q: What is a CASB?
cards.a: Cloud Access Security Broker: policy between users and cloud apps
cards.x: Discovers shadow IT and enforces DLP.

cards.q: What is SASE?
cards.a: Secure Access Service Edge: networking plus security as a cloud service
cards.x: ZTNA plus secure web gateway plus CASB, converged.

cards.q: What is zero trust architecture?
cards.a: Never trust, always verify: identity-aware, least-privilege access per request
cards.x: Assume breach; verify explicitly.

cards.q: Zero trust vs traditional VPN?
cards.a: VPN trusts the network; zero trust verifies every single request
cards.x: ZTNA replaces flat VPN access.

cards.q: What is microsegmentation in cloud?
cards.a: Per-workload network policies limiting lateral movement
cards.x: Compromised web tier cannot reach the database tier.

cards.q: Why scope IAM roles per function in serverless?
cards.a: A compromised function then holds minimal permissions
cards.x: Blast radius control for ephemeral code.

decks.title: Network Architecture & Segmentation
decks.summary: DMZs, VLANs, bastions, honeypots, and secure topologies.

cards.q: What is a DMZ?
cards.a: A buffer network between the untrusted internet and the internal LAN
cards.x: Firewalled on both sides.

cards.q: What belongs in a DMZ — and what never does?
cards.a: Web servers, mail relays, VPN concentrators in; databases never
cards.x: If the DMZ host falls, the database stays inside.

cards.q: VLAN vs subnet?
cards.a: VLAN: Layer 2 broadcast separation; subnet: Layer 3 addressing
cards.x: Often paired 1:1; double-tagging enables VLAN hopping.

cards.q: What is network segmentation for?
cards.a: Limiting lateral movement and blast radius
cards.x: A compromised HR laptop should never reach OT.

cards.q: What is microsegmentation?
cards.a: Per-workload policies, down to individual hosts
cards.x: Zero-trust networking: every flow needs an explicit rule.

cards.q: What is a jump server (bastion host)?
cards.a: A single hardened entry point into admin networks
cards.x: MFA it, log everything, allow-list sources.

cards.q: Why not RDP to servers directly from user VLANs?
cards.a: It exposes the management plane to every compromised laptop
cards.x: Route all admin access through the bastion.

cards.q: What is a honeypot?
cards.a: A decoy system that alerts the moment it is touched
cards.x: No legitimate user ever touches it — so alerts are high-fidelity.

cards.q: What is a honeynet?
cards.a: A network of honeypots simulating an enterprise
cards.x: Wastes attacker time and reveals their TTPs.

cards.q: What is a honeytoken?
cards.a: A fake credential or file that triggers an alert when used
cards.x: A bogus AWS key in code is an instant tripwire.

cards.q: What is an air gap?
cards.a: Physical isolation with no network path at all
cards.x: Strong — but USBs and insiders bridge gaps (Stuxnet).

cards.q: What is a data diode?
cards.a: Hardware allowing data flow in one direction only
cards.x: OT sends telemetry out; nothing comes back in.

cards.q: East-west vs north-south traffic?
cards.a: East-west: internal lateral; north-south: in and out of the network
cards.x: Firewalls watched north-south; zero trust watches both.

cards.q: What is a network choke point?
cards.a: A single controlled passage all traffic must cross
cards.x: Place inspection — IDS, proxy — there.

cards.q: What is switch port security?
cards.a: Limiting MAC addresses per port against rogue devices
cards.x: Sticky MACs plus violation shutdown.

cards.q: What is DHCP snooping?
cards.a: A switch feature trusting only legitimate DHCP servers
cards.x: It blocks rogue DHCP attacks.

cards.q: What is Dynamic ARP Inspection?
cards.a: Validates ARP against the DHCP snooping table
cards.x: It stops ARP spoofing and LAN man-in-the-middle.

cards.q: What is a private VLAN?
cards.a: Isolates hosts from each other within the same VLAN
cards.x: For DMZ hosts that should never talk to each other.

cards.q: What is an out-of-band management network?
cards.a: A separate network for admin interfaces like iDRAC and switch management
cards.x: It keeps management traffic off the production LAN.

cards.q: Stateful vs stateless firewall?
cards.a: Stateful tracks connections; stateless filters each packet alone
cards.x: Stateful is the modern default.

cards.q: What is a WAF?
cards.a: Web Application Firewall: filters HTTP attacks like SQLi and XSS
cards.x: Deploy in front of web apps and tune it so it does not break them.

cards.q: IDS vs IPS?
cards.a: IDS only alerts; IPS blocks inline
cards.x: IPS risks false-positive outages — tune in IDS mode first.

cards.q: What is a reverse proxy for security?
cards.a: Terminates client connections and hides origin servers
cards.x: WAF and TLS termination live here.

cards.q: What is a screened subnet?
cards.a: Another name for the DMZ architecture
cards.x: CompTIA loves this term.

cards.q: Why place public DNS or NTP in the DMZ?
cards.a: They must face the internet but a compromise must not reach inside
cards.x: Harden them; they are high-value targets.

decks.title: Secure Protocols, VPN & Wireless
decks.summary: TLS, IPSec, VPN designs, and locking down Wi-Fi.

cards.q: TLS 1.2 vs 1.3: why prefer 1.3?
cards.a: Faster handshakes, weak ciphers removed, more of the handshake encrypted
cards.x: Disable SSL and TLS 1.0/1.1 everywhere.

cards.q: What does TLS actually provide?
cards.a: Confidentiality, integrity, and server authentication
cards.x: Client certificates add mutual authentication.

cards.q: What is a certificate authority?
cards.a: A trusted third party that vouches for public keys
cards.x: Your browser ships a store of trusted CAs.

cards.q: Self-signed certificate: what is the risk?
cards.a: No third-party trust — users learn to click through warnings
cards.x: Fine for labs; never for production.

cards.q: What is certificate pinning?
cards.a: An app accepting only specific certificates, ignoring the CA store
cards.x: It defeats rogue-CA man-in-the-middle for that app.

cards.q: What is HSTS?
cards.a: A header forcing browsers to use HTTPS, blocking downgrades
cards.x: It mitigates SSL-stripping attacks.

cards.q: What is S/MIME?
cards.a: Email encryption and signing via certificates
cards.x: It protects message content end to end.

cards.q: What is STARTTLS?
cards.a: Upgrades a plaintext connection like SMTP to TLS
cards.x: Vulnerable to stripping if not enforced.

cards.q: SSH vs Telnet?
cards.a: SSH encrypts everything; Telnet is cleartext — never use Telnet
cards.x: SSH also tunnels traffic and transfers files via SCP/SFTP.

cards.q: SFTP vs FTPS?
cards.a: SFTP: over SSH:22; FTPS: FTP over TLS
cards.x: Prefer SFTP; both beat plaintext FTP.

cards.q: SNMPv3 vs v1/v2c?
cards.a: v3 adds authentication and encryption; v1/v2c use cleartext community strings
cards.x: "public" and "private" strings are not security.

cards.q: What is LDAPS?
cards.a: LDAP over TLS, typically on port 636
cards.x: It encrypts directory queries.

cards.q: What is DNSSEC?
cards.a: Cryptographic signatures validating DNS responses
cards.x: It stops cache poisoning — not eavesdropping (that is DoT/DoH).

cards.q: DoT vs DoH?
cards.a: DoT: port 853; DoH: port 443
cards.x: DoH blends with web traffic, complicating monitoring.

cards.q: IPSec transport vs tunnel mode?
cards.a: Transport encrypts the payload only; tunnel encrypts the whole packet
cards.x: Tunnel mode is for site-to-site VPNs.

cards.q: AH vs ESP in IPSec?
cards.a: AH authenticates; ESP encrypts and authenticates
cards.x: ESP is the modern choice.

cards.q: What is SRTP?
cards.a: Secure Real-time Transport Protocol: encrypted voice and video
cards.x: ZRTP adds key agreement for VoIP.

cards.q: Split tunnel vs full tunnel VPN?
cards.a: Split sends only corporate traffic via VPN; full sends everything
cards.x: Split is faster; full gives inspection and control.

cards.q: Site-to-site vs remote-access VPN?
cards.a: Site-to-site links networks; remote-access links individual users
cards.x: IPSec usually site-to-site; SSL VPN suits roaming users.

cards.q: What is always-on VPN?
cards.a: Connects automatically, even before user logon
cards.x: It ensures policy and patching apply off-network.

cards.q: WPA2 vs WPA3?
cards.a: WPA3 adds SAE against offline dictionary attacks plus stronger encryption
cards.x: WPA2-PSK falls to captured handshakes.

cards.q: WPA2-Enterprise vs Personal?
cards.a: Enterprise uses 802.1X per-user auth via RADIUS; Personal uses one shared PSK
cards.x: Shared PSKs cannot be revoked per user.

cards.q: What is SAE in WPA3?
cards.a: Simultaneous Authentication of Equals: password auth resisting offline cracking
cards.x: The Dragonfly handshake.

cards.q: What is a rogue access point?
cards.a: Unauthorized AP, or evil twin impersonating yours
cards.x: Wireless IPS and wired-side NAC detect them.

cards.q: What is an evil twin?
cards.a: A fake AP cloning a legitimate SSID to harvest credentials
cards.x: Verify certificates and distrust open "Free WiFi".

cards.q: What is wireless jamming?
cards.a: RF interference denying Wi-Fi availability
cards.x: A physical-layer denial of service; detect with spectrum analysis.

cards.q: What is a deauthentication attack?
cards.a: Spoofed deauth frames kicking clients off the AP
cards.x: It captures handshakes for cracking; 802.11w (PMF) mitigates.

cards.q: NFC security risks?
cards.a: Eavesdropping and relay attacks at close range
cards.x: Payment tokenization limits the damage.

cards.q: Bluetooth attack surface?
cards.a: Bluejacking, Bluesnarfing, and pairing interception
cards.x: Keep discoverable mode off and patch firmware.

cards.q: EAP-TLS vs PEAP?
cards.a: EAP-TLS uses certificates both ways; PEAP tunnels credentials inside TLS
cards.x: EAP-TLS is the gold standard for WPA3-Enterprise.

cards.q: Captive portal: what is the risk?
cards.a: Open network with a login page — traffic is visible before authentication
cards.x: Use a VPN on any captive portal.

cards.q: Why disable WPS?
cards.a: Its PIN is brute-forceable in hours
cards.x: It is a backdoor on most consumer routers.

cards.q: What is 802.11w (PMF)?
cards.a: Protected Management Frames: authenticates deauth and disassoc frames
cards.x: It blunts deauthentication attacks.

cards.q: Why prefer 5 GHz over 2.4 GHz for security-sensitive use?
cards.a: Less congestion and shorter range shrink the eavesdropping footprint
cards.x: Not encryption — just physics working for you.

decks.title: Risk Management & Business Continuity
decks.summary: Risk analysis, BIA, and keeping the business running. (Domain 5.1–5.2)

cards.q: Qualitative vs quantitative risk assessment?
cards.a: Qualitative uses ratings (high/medium/low); quantitative uses numbers (ALE in dollars)
cards.x: Qualitative is fast and cheap; quantitative needs data but justifies budgets.

cards.q: A risk matrix plots what against what?
cards.a: Likelihood against impact
cards.x: A "high likelihood × high impact" risk lands in the red corner demanding action.

cards.q: Inherent vs residual risk?
cards.a: Inherent: risk before controls; residual: risk left after controls
cards.x: You manage residual risk down to the appetite line — zero risk is not the goal.

cards.q: Risk appetite vs risk tolerance?
cards.a: Appetite: how much risk leadership will accept; tolerance: acceptable variation around it
cards.x: Appetite is strategic ("we accept moderate risk"); tolerance sets the guardrails.

cards.q: Who owns a risk?
cards.a: The business owner accountable if it materialises, not the security team
cards.x: Security advises and measures; the business decides and owns.

cards.q: Threat vs vulnerability vs risk in one line each?
cards.a: Threat: what could hurt you; vulnerability: the weakness; risk: likelihood × impact of the two meeting
cards.x: No vulnerability, no risk — even with active threats.

cards.q: When must a risk assessment be performed?
cards.a: Before new systems go live, after major changes, and on a recurring schedule
cards.x: Also after incidents and when the threat landscape shifts.

cards.q: SLE $50,000 with an ARO of 0.5. What is the ALE, and what does it justify?
cards.a: ALE $25,000: a control costing less than that per year is financially justified
cards.x: ALE turns security spending into a business decision.

cards.q: A $40k control reduces a $100k ALE to $30k. Is it worth it?
cards.a: Yes: $70k risk reduction beats $40k cost
cards.x: Compare annual control cost against annual risk reduction, not the sticker price.

cards.q: What does "risk acceptance" require?
cards.a: Formal sign-off by the risk owner with documentation
cards.x: Acceptance is a decision, not neglect — and it expires.

cards.q: Risk transfer: what are two common methods?
cards.a: Cyber insurance and outsourcing the risky function
cards.x: Transfer never removes all risk: you keep oversight and residual liability.

cards.q: When is risk avoidance the right call?
cards.a: When the activity’s risk outweighs its value and controls cannot fix it
cards.x: Example: decommissioning an unpatchable legacy system instead of protecting it.

cards.q: What is a key risk indicator (KRI)?
cards.a: A metric that warns risk is rising before loss occurs
cards.x: Example: unpatched criticals trending up predicts breach likelihood.

cards.q: How often should the risk register be reviewed?
cards.a: Continuously, with formal review at least quarterly or after major changes
cards.x: A stale register is decoration.

cards.q: A BIA is done. What are its three key outputs?
cards.a: Critical functions, RTO/RPO per function, and resource dependencies
cards.x: These outputs drive the entire continuity strategy and budget.

cards.q: What is Maximum Tolerable Downtime (MTD)?
cards.a: The longest an outage can last before the business faces existential harm
cards.x: RTO must fit inside MTD, or recovery is theatre.

cards.q: BCP vs DRP: who owns each?
cards.a: BCP: business leadership for whole-organisation continuity; DRP: IT for systems recovery
cards.x: DRP is a subset of BCP.

cards.q: What is succession planning in continuity?
cards.a: Named backups for every critical role, documented and trained
cards.x: Incidents do not wait for the one expert to return from holiday.

cards.q: Full vs incremental vs differential backup?
cards.a: Full: everything; incremental: changes since last backup of any kind; differential: changes since last full
cards.x: Incremental is fastest daily but slowest to restore; differential balances both.

cards.q: Tabletop vs functional vs full-interruption BC tests?
cards.a: Tabletop: talk through; functional: actually fail over systems; full interruption: run the business from the alternate site
cards.x: Escalate realism gradually; full interruption risks real disruption.

cards.q: How do you pick hot, warm, or cold alternate sites?
cards.a: Match site readiness and cost to each function’s RTO
cards.x: Seconds-to-minutes RTO buys hot; days of RTO tolerates cold.

cards.q: MTBF vs MTTR?
cards.a: Mean time between failures (reliability) vs mean time to repair (recoverability)
cards.x: Availability ≈ MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR).

cards.q: What is a single point of failure, and how do you find them?
cards.a: One component whose loss kills the service; find via architecture review and BIA dependencies
cards.x: Eliminate with redundancy or accept formally.

cards.q: Why geographically separate primary and recovery sites?
cards.a: One regional disaster must not take both
cards.x: Consider power grids, flood plains, and network paths — not just mileage.

cards.q: Backup generators: why test under load monthly?
cards.a: Untested generators fail when needed; wet-stacking and dead batteries hide until load
cards.x: A generator that has never carried the building is a hope, not a control.

cards.q: What belongs in a BC communications plan?
cards.a: Who contacts whom, via which out-of-band channels, with pre-drafted messages
cards.x: Include customers, staff families, regulators, and media — with alternates for each role.

cards.q: Why rehearse call trees instead of just publishing them?
cards.a: People change numbers and roles; a drill finds the dead branches
cards.x: An untested call tree fails at 2 a.m. exactly when needed.

cards.q: What is the "alternate processing" vs "alternate business" site distinction?
cards.a: Processing: IT systems failover; business: people have somewhere to work
cards.x: You need both or recovery stalls.

cards.q: A department’s RTO is 4 hours but its only backup is weekly tape. What is wrong?
