cards.a: RPO mismatch: a week of data loss exceeds what the business can tolerate
cards.x: Align backup frequency to RPO, recovery speed to RTO.

cards.q: Why involve HR in business continuity planning?
cards.a: Succession, emergency contacts, payroll continuity, and staff welfare during disruption
cards.x: People are the most critical continuity asset.

cards.q: What is a damage assessment team’s first job after a disaster?
cards.a: Determine what is hurt, what still works, and whether the site is safe to enter
cards.x: No recovery begins before safety is confirmed.

cards.q: How does cyber insurance fit into BC/DR?
cards.a: It transfers financial risk; it does not restore systems
cards.x: It funds recovery — it is not a recovery plan.

cards.q: What makes a risk assessment "continuous" rather than periodic?
cards.a: Feeding live telemetry — vuln scans, threat intel, control status — into risk ratings
cards.x: Annual spreadsheets miss risks that emerge in March.

cards.q: A vendor breach exposes your customer data. Whose incident is it?
cards.a: Yours: you own the risk to your customers regardless of who was breached
cards.x: Contracts should define notification duties and timelines in advance.

cards.q: What is risk aggregation?
cards.a: Small accepted risks combining into one unacceptable exposure
cards.x: Ten "low" risks on the same crown-jewel system equal one big problem.

cards.q: Why document risk acceptance with an expiry date?
cards.a: Accepted risks must be re-evaluated; the threat landscape moves on
cards.x: Permanent acceptances become invisible holes.

cards.q: What is the difference between a threat actor and a threat vector?
cards.a: Actor: who attacks; vector: how the attack arrives
cards.x: Phishing email (vector) sent by a criminal group (actor).

cards.q: A new regulation appears mid-year. What is the risk process?
cards.a: Assess applicability, gap-analyse current controls, plan remediation, update the register
cards.x: Compliance risk is still risk.

cards.q: What does "risk-based" vulnerability prioritisation mean?
cards.a: Patch by exploitability and asset value, not by CVSS alone
cards.x: A medium on a crown jewel beats a critical on a lab printer.

cards.q: Why track "time to remediate" for critical findings?
cards.a: It measures whether the vuln program actually reduces exposure
cards.x: A critical open for 200 days is an accepted risk wearing a disguise.

cards.q: What is a risk treatment plan?
cards.a: For each risk: the chosen response, actions, owners, deadlines, and residual rating
cards.x: The bridge between assessment and action.

cards.q: Who approves a risk treatment plan?
cards.a: Senior leadership or the board, since it commits budget and accepts residual risk
cards.x: Security proposes; the business disposes.

cards.q: What is "risk communication"?
cards.a: Reporting risks in business terms leadership can act on
cards.x: "$2M ALE with 30% likelihood" beats "CVE-2024-1234 is critical".

resources.title: ISC2 Certified in Cybersecurity (free course + exam)

decks.title: Compliance, Frameworks & Third-Party Risk
decks.summary: Laws, frameworks, audits, privacy, and vendor risk. (Domain 5.3–5.5)

cards.q: HIPAA: who must comply and what is protected?
cards.a: Covered entities and business associates; PHI — health data tied to identity
cards.x: The Security Rule mandates administrative, physical, and technical safeguards.

cards.q: HIPAA breach notification: what are the timelines?
cards.a: Notify affected individuals within 60 days; HHS promptly (media if 500+)
cards.x: Delays compound the violation.

cards.q: SOX: what does it demand of IT?
cards.a: Reliable financial reporting, which needs controlled IT systems (Section 404)
cards.x: Change management, access controls, and audit trails over financial systems.

cards.q: CCPA/CPRA: what rights do California consumers get?
cards.a: Know, delete, and opt out of sale/sharing of personal data
cards.x: Applies above revenue or data-volume thresholds; fines per violation.

cards.q: GLBA Safeguards Rule: who does it hit?
cards.a: Financial institutions: banks, lenders, even car dealerships offering financing
cards.x: Requires a written security program with risk assessment.

cards.q: FERPA protects what?
cards.a: Student education records: schools need consent to disclose them
cards.x: Parents (or adult students) can inspect and amend records.

cards.q: FISMA: what does it require of US federal systems?
cards.a: Categorise, select NIST 800-53 controls, assess, authorise, and continuously monitor
cards.x: The RMF operationalises FISMA compliance.

cards.q: PCI DSS: how many requirement families, and what is the headline?
cards.a: Twelve: build secure networks, protect cardholder data, manage vulns, control access, monitor, test, and maintain policy
cards.x: Applies to anyone storing, processing, or transmitting card data.

cards.q: PCI DSS merchant levels: what determines SAQ vs ROC?
cards.a: Transaction volume and breach history decide self-assessment vs on-site audit
cards.x: Level 1 merchants need a Report on Compliance by a QSA.

cards.q: GDPR data subject rights beyond breach notice?
cards.a: Access, rectification, erasure, portability, and objection to processing
cards.x: "Right to be forgotten" is the famous one — with legal exceptions.

cards.q: What is the ePrivacy Directive ("cookie law")?
cards.a: EU rules requiring consent before storing non-essential cookies or tracking
cards.x: Complements GDPR for electronic communications.

cards.q: The seven NIST RMF steps in order?
cards.a: Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor
cards.x: Authorisation is a risk decision by the authorizing official.

cards.a: 27001: certifiable requirements for an ISMS; 27002: the code of practice with control guidance
cards.x: Get certified against 27001 using 27002’s controls.

cards.q: ISO 27701 adds what to 27001?
cards.a: Privacy information management: PIMS controls for data controllers and processors
cards.x: Bridges ISO security management and GDPR-style privacy duties.

cards.q: CIS Controls v8: how are the 18 controls tiered?
cards.a: Implementation Groups IG1 (basic cyber hygiene), IG2 (more), IG3 (mature)
cards.x: Start at IG1: inventory, secure configs, patching, access control, backups.

cards.q: SOC 2: what are the five trust services criteria?
cards.a: Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, Privacy
cards.x: Security is mandatory; the others are added per engagement.

cards.q: What is the CSA Cloud Controls Matrix (CCM)?
cards.a: A cloud-specific control framework mapping to ISO, SOC 2, and others
cards.x: Use it to evaluate cloud provider security consistently.

cards.q: COBIT in one line?
cards.a: A governance framework linking enterprise goals to IT processes and controls
cards.x: ISACA’s answer to "is IT delivering business value securely?"

cards.q: What did NIST CSF 2.0’s new Govern function add?
cards.a: Organisational context, risk strategy, and supply-chain oversight as a top-level function
cards.x: Governance now sits above Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.

cards.q: FedRAMP: what is it for?
cards.a: Standardised security authorisation for US federal cloud services
cards.x: A FedRAMP authorisation spares each agency a separate review.

cards.q: What must an Acceptable Use Policy cover?
cards.a: Permitted and prohibited uses of systems, data handling, and consequences
cards.x: Everyone signs it; enforcement must be consistent to survive challenge.

cards.q: Password policy in the NIST 800-63B era?
cards.a: Long passphrases, no forced rotation without cause, check against breached lists
cards.x: Complexity theater is out; length and uniqueness are in.

cards.q: What does a data retention policy define?
cards.a: How long each data type is kept, then how it is destroyed
cards.x: Keep it for legal need, not forever: retention is also a breach multiplier.

cards.q: BYOD policy: what are the two technical pillars?
cards.a: MDM enrolment and containerisation separating work from personal data
cards.x: Plus remote wipe rights the user explicitly accepts.

cards.q: What does a remote work policy need beyond "use VPN"?
cards.a: Approved devices, encrypted storage, secure Wi-Fi expectations, and incident reporting
cards.x: Home networks are hostile territory.

cards.q: Why have a social media policy?
cards.a: To stop staff leaking sensitive info or damaging the brand online
cards.x: Cover personal vs official accounts and pre-publication review for sensitive roles.

cards.q: Data classification policy: what does it assign?
cards.a: Labels (Public/Internal/Confidential/Restricted) plus handling rules per label
cards.x: Classification without handling rules is decoration.

cards.q: Encryption policy: what must it specify?
cards.a: What data, which algorithms and key lengths, and who manages keys
cards.x: Mandate TLS 1.2+, AES-256, and HSM-backed CA keys where risk warrants.

cards.q: IR policy vs IR plan vs playbook?
cards.a: Policy: management intent; plan: organisation-wide approach; playbook: step-by-step for one scenario
cards.x: Policy authorises, plan organises, playbook executes.

cards.q: Change management policy: what does it require?
cards.a: Approval, impact analysis, testing, scheduled windows, and backout plans
cards.x: Emergency changes follow a fast-track path — still documented.

cards.q: Internal vs external audit: who do they serve?
cards.a: Internal serves management and the board; external serves regulators, customers, or the public
cards.x: Internal can be continuous; external is point-in-time and independent.

cards.q: What defines a good audit scope?
cards.a: Clear objectives, systems, time period, and criteria — agreed before fieldwork
cards.x: Scope creep wastes effort; scope gaps miss risk.

cards.q: SSAE 18: what is it?
cards.a: The auditing standard behind SOC 1, 2, and 3 reports
cards.x: An auditor opines on control design and operating effectiveness.

cards.q: What counts as audit evidence?
cards.a: Documents, logs, configurations, interviews, and direct observation
cards.x: Stronger evidence is independent and corroborated.

cards.q: Audit finding vs observation vs recommendation?
cards.a: Finding: control failed; observation: weakness noted; recommendation: how to fix
cards.x: Findings demand management response and dates.

cards.q: Compliance testing vs substantive testing in audits?
cards.a: Compliance: do controls operate as designed; substantive: are the numbers/data actually right
cards.x: Test the lock and also check the door stayed shut.

cards.q: What is continuous auditing?
cards.a: Automated, ongoing control testing instead of annual sampling
cards.x: Dashboards over spreadsheets.

cards.q: What is data minimization?
cards.a: Collect and keep only the personal data you actually need
cards.x: Less data means smaller breach blast radius and easier compliance.

cards.q: What is purpose limitation?
cards.a: Use personal data only for the purpose it was collected for
cards.x: Marketing reuse of support-ticket data violates it.

cards.q: PII vs PHI vs PCI data?
cards.a: PII: identifies a person; PHI: health data; PCI: cardholder data
cards.x: Different laws, different handling: know which regime each dataset triggers.

cards.q: What is data sovereignty?
cards.a: Data subject to the laws of the country where it resides
cards.x: Drives residency requirements and cloud region choices.

cards.q: Right to erasure: what is the hard part?
cards.a: Finding every copy: backups, logs, analytics, vendor systems
cards.x: Erasure must be verifiable across the data lifecycle.

cards.q: Opt-in vs opt-out consent?
cards.a: Opt-in: consent before collection; opt-out: collect until refused
cards.x: GDPR demands opt-in for most processing; opt-out is weaker.

cards.q: Privacy by design: what does it require?
cards.a: Bake privacy into systems from the start, not as a bolt-on
cards.x: The seven foundational principles from Ann Cavoukian.

cards.q: Data controller vs processor: who decides the "why"?
cards.a: Controller decides purposes and means; processor acts only on instructions
cards.x: Both have GDPR duties, but the controller carries primary accountability.

cards.q: Cross-border transfers under GDPR: what mechanisms?
cards.a: Adequacy decisions, Standard Contractual Clauses, or Binding Corporate Rules
cards.x: Schrems II killed Privacy Shield; SCCs need transfer assessments.

cards.q: De-identification vs anonymization?
cards.a: De-identification removes direct identifiers but re-ID may be possible; anonymization irreversibly prevents it
cards.x: Only true anonymization escapes GDPR scope.

cards.q: When is a DPIA required?
cards.a: Before high-risk processing: new tech, large-scale profiling, or sensitive data
cards.x: GDPR Article 35; consult the DPO and document mitigations.

cards.q: Vendor due diligence: what do you actually check?
cards.a: Security posture, financial health, compliance certs, and incident history
cards.x: Questionnaires plus evidence: SOC 2, pentest summaries, and references.

cards.q: What should a right-to-audit clause give you?
cards.a: The right to assess the vendor’s controls yourself or via a third party
cards.x: Without it you rely entirely on their marketing.

cards.q: SolarWinds taught what supply-chain lesson?
cards.a: Trusted vendor updates can carry malware to thousands at once
cards.x: Vet build pipelines, demand SBOMs, and segment vendor access.

cards.q: SLA: what three things must it define?
cards.a: Service levels, how they are measured, and remedies/credits for misses
cards.x: Without remedies it is a wish, not an agreement.

cards.q: SLA vs SLO vs SLI?
cards.a: SLA: contractual promise; SLO: internal target; SLI: the measured metric
cards.x: SLIs feed SLOs; SLO breaches trigger SLA consequences.

cards.q: What is fourth-party risk?
cards.a: Risk from your vendors’ vendors, whom you never vetted
cards.x: Map critical supply chains at least one layer deeper.

cards.q: Vendor offboarding: what must happen?
cards.a: Revoke access, retrieve data, confirm deletion, and close accounts
cards.x: Orphaned vendor VPN accounts are a classic breach path.

cards.q: Why include security requirements in procurement, not after signing?
cards.a: Leverage disappears after the contract is signed
cards.x: Bake in encryption, audit rights, breach notice, and data return up front.

decks.title: Incident Response & Forensics
decks.summary: Running an incident, preserving evidence, and recovery.

cards.q: Why take a memory image before shutting down?
cards.a: RAM holds processes, network connections, keys, and fileless malware
cards.x: Tools: WinPmem, LiME; analyse with Volatility.
wrong: It is required by the OS

cards.q: What is a forensic image vs a copy?
cards.a: A bit-for-bit copy including deleted and unallocated space
cards.x: Verify with a hash before and after.

cards.q: What does a write blocker do?
cards.a: Prevents any changes to evidence media during acquisition
cards.x: Preserves integrity and admissibility.

cards.q: What is a legal hold?
cards.a: An instruction to preserve relevant data from deletion
cards.x: Overrides normal retention schedules.

cards.q: What is timeline analysis?
cards.a: Ordering artefacts by time to reconstruct attacker actions
cards.x: Tools like Plaso build super-timelines.

cards.q: What is containment vs eradication?
cards.a: Stopping the spread vs removing the cause
cards.x: Then recover and monitor for re-infection.

cards.q: What is a lessons-learned review?
cards.a: A blameless post-incident review to improve controls
cards.x: Update playbooks and detections afterward.

cards.q: Why must communications during a major incident be out of band?
cards.a: The attacker may be watching normal email and chat
cards.x: Use a pre-arranged separate channel.

cards.q: What is an IR playbook?
cards.a: A predefined, step-by-step procedure for an incident type
cards.x: e.g. phishing, ransomware, compromised account.

cards.q: Who decides whether to notify regulators and customers?
cards.a: Leadership with legal counsel, per laws and contracts
cards.x: Deadlines vary: GDPR 72 hours; SEC material incidents within 4 business days.

cards.q: What is a key artefact for program execution on Windows?
cards.a: Prefetch files (and Amcache/ShimCache)
cards.x: Show what ran and when.

cards.q: The four NIST SP 800-61 incident response phases in order?
cards.a: Preparation; Detection & Analysis; Containment, Eradication & Recovery; Post-Incident Activity
cards.x: Preparation is where incidents are won or lost.

cards.q: What belongs in the Preparation phase?
cards.a: Playbooks, tooling, backups, contact lists, training, tabletop exercises
cards.x: You cannot invent process in the middle of an incident.

cards.q: Detection vs analysis: why are they one phase?
cards.a: An alert is not an incident until analysis confirms scope and impact
cards.x: Triage first: validate, then declare.

cards.q: Short-term vs long-term containment?
cards.a: Short-term: isolate now to stop the bleeding; long-term: hardened fixes while operating
cards.x: Pull the network cable first; rebuild cleanly after.

cards.q: Ransomware is spreading. Which containment strategy?
cards.a: Isolate affected hosts now — do NOT power off yet
cards.x: Powering off loses memory evidence and may trigger destructive payloads.

cards.q: When is wiping and rebuilding preferred over cleaning malware?
cards.a: When persistence is uncertain — rebuild from known-good media
cards.x: Cleaning cannot prove a rootkit is gone.

cards.q: What must happen BEFORE recovery (bringing systems back)?
cards.a: Eradication verified and a clean restore path confirmed
cards.x: Recovering into the same vulnerability just re-infects you.

cards.q: Post-incident activity: what are the two outputs?
cards.a: Lessons-learned review and concrete control improvements
cards.x: Feed findings back into detections and playbooks.

cards.q: What is a tabletop exercise?
cards.a: A discussion-based walkthrough of an incident scenario with stakeholders
cards.x: Tests the plan and the people without touching production.

cards.q: Who should be in the incident war room?
cards.a: IR lead, IT ops, comms/PR, legal, and business owners of affected systems
cards.x: Predefined roles beat an ad-hoc crowd.

cards.q: What is the order of volatility (RFC 3227)?
cards.a: RAM and running state first; disk and logs last
cards.x: Full order: registers/cache → RAM → network state → running processes → disk → logs → backups.

cards.q: What is chain of custody?
cards.a: Documented, unbroken record of who handled evidence, when, and why
cards.x: Gaps can make evidence inadmissible in court.

cards.q: Why hash evidence at acquisition?
cards.a: To prove later that the copy is identical to the original
cards.x: SHA-256 before and after; a mismatch means tainted evidence.

cards.q: An analyst finds a USB drive in the parking lot. What is forensically wrong with plugging it in?
cards.a: It alters metadata and risks malware; image with a write blocker first
cards.x: Curiosity is how incidents start.

cards.q: "Dead-box" vs "live" forensics?
cards.a: Dead-box: powered-off disk image; live: capture RAM from a running system
cards.x: Go live first for volatile data, then dead-box.

cards.q: RTO vs RPO?
cards.a: RTO: how fast to restore; RPO: how much data loss is tolerable
cards.x: RTO 4h / RPO 1h drives backup frequency and DR design.

cards.q: What is the 3-2-1 backup rule?
cards.a: 3 copies, 2 different media, 1 offsite or offline
cards.x: The offline/air-gapped copy defeats ransomware.

cards.q: Why must backups be tested, not just taken?
cards.a: Untested restores fail exactly when you need them most
cards.x: Ransomware groups target backups first.

cards.q: Business continuity vs disaster recovery?
cards.a: BC keeps the business running during disruption; DR restores IT systems after
cards.x: BC is the playbook, DR is the technical recovery.

cards.q: Hot site vs cold site?
cards.a: Hot: ready-to-run replica; cold: empty space to build out
cards.x: Warm is in between. Your RTO decides which you pay for.

cards.q: What is network segmentation’s role in containment?
cards.a: Pre-built segments let you quarantine a VLAN without killing the business
cards.x: Microsegmentation limits lateral movement by default.

cards.q: Why change all potentially exposed credentials during eradication?
cards.a: Attackers harvest credentials; any reused password re-opens the door
cards.x: Rotate service accounts and API keys too, not just user passwords.

cards.q: An exec wants to "just pay the ransom quietly." What is the IR-correct response?
cards.a: Escalate to leadership and legal; paying may not restore data
cards.x: Paying funds crime and may not restore data. The decision is business and legal — never the analyst’s alone.

cards.q: What goes in the first hour of a major incident?
cards.a: Declare, assemble the team, establish comms, begin scoping — not fixing
cards.x: Scope before action; premature fixes destroy evidence.

cards.q: Why keep a dedicated incident communications log?
cards.a: A timeline of who knew what when, for legal review
cards.x: Memory is unreliable under stress; regulators may ask too.

cards.q: What is root cause analysis in IR?
cards.a: Finding the underlying failure that allowed the incident, not just the malware
cards.x: Fix the cause (unpatched VPN), not only the symptom (ransomware).

cards.q: The same attack vector succeeds again three months later. What failed?
cards.a: Post-incident remediation was never implemented or verified
cards.x: Track action items to closure with owners and dates.

cards.q: What is the "preserve evidence vs resume business" tension?
cards.a: Forensics wants systems frozen; the business wants them back online
cards.x: Resolve it in the plan beforehand with leadership sign-off.

cards.q: Why involve legal early in a suspected breach?
cards.a: Privilege, notification duties, and evidence handling have legal consequences
cards.x: A misstep can create liability.

cards.q: What metric shows IR is improving over time?
cards.a: Mean time to detect/respond (MTTD/MTTR) trending down, repeat causes falling
cards.x: Measure, do not guess.

decks.title: Active Directory & Cloud Attacks
decks.summary: Enterprise identity attack paths and how to defend them.

cards.q: What is BloodHound used for?
cards.a: Mapping Active Directory attack paths to privileged accounts
cards.x: Defenders use it too, to remove risky paths.

cards.q: What is a Golden Ticket?
cards.a: A forged Kerberos TGT made with the KRBTGT account hash
cards.x: Grants domain-wide access. Remediate by resetting KRBTGT twice.

cards.q: What is DCSync?
cards.a: Impersonating a domain controller to pull password hashes
cards.x: Needs replication rights; monitor for Event ID 4662 with replication GUIDs.

cards.q: What does LAPS solve?
cards.a: Shared local admin passwords across machines
cards.x: Windows LAPS rotates a unique password per device.

cards.q: What is the tiered admin model?
cards.a: Separating admin accounts for DCs, servers, and workstations
cards.x: Stops credential theft on a laptop from exposing domain admins.

cards.q: What is MFA fatigue (push bombing)?
cards.a: Spamming push prompts until the user approves one
cards.x: Use number matching and phishing-resistant MFA.

cards.q: What is an adversary-in-the-middle phishing kit?
cards.a: A proxy that steals session cookies, bypassing standard MFA
cards.x: e.g. Evilginx. FIDO2/passkeys resist it.

cards.q: What is a common cloud initial access vector?
cards.a: Leaked access keys or misconfigured public storage
cards.x: Scan repos for secrets; block public buckets by default.

cards.q: What is an illicit OAuth consent grant?
cards.a: Tricking a user into granting a malicious app access to their data
cards.x: Restrict user consent and review app permissions.

cards.q: Why is the cloud control plane a critical attack surface?
cards.a: Whoever controls the IAM/API layer controls all resources
cards.x: Protect root/global admin with MFA, alerts, and break-glass procedures.

cards.q: What is token theft in cloud identity?
cards.a: Stealing session or refresh tokens to act as the user without the password
cards.x: Use token binding, short lifetimes, and conditional access.

decks.title: Threat Intelligence & Hunting
decks.summary: Turning intel into hunts and hunts into detections.

cards.q: Strategic vs tactical threat intelligence?
cards.a: Long-term trends for leaders vs TTPs/IoCs for defenders
cards.x: Operational intel covers specific campaigns.

cards.q: What is the intelligence lifecycle?
cards.a: Direction, collection, processing, analysis, dissemination, feedback
cards.x: Start from requirements, not feeds.

cards.q: What is a hunting hypothesis?
cards.a: A testable statement about attacker behaviour in your environment
cards.x: e.g. "Attackers use scheduled tasks for persistence on servers."

cards.q: What is the CISA KEV catalog for?
cards.a: Listing vulnerabilities known to be exploited in the wild
cards.x: Patch KEV items first. US federal agencies have deadlines.

cards.q: What does EPSS estimate?
cards.a: The probability a vulnerability will be exploited soon
cards.x: Combine it with CVSS and asset context to prioritise.

cards.q: What is attribution in threat intel?
cards.a: Identifying who is behind an attack
cards.x: Hard and often less useful than knowing TTPs.

cards.q: What is the TLP (Traffic Light Protocol)?
cards.a: Labels for how widely shared intel may be passed on
cards.x: TLP:RED (named recipients) to TLP:CLEAR (public).

cards.q: What is stack counting in hunting?
cards.a: Counting occurrences of a value to find rare outliers
cards.x: Rare autoruns or processes across a fleet stand out.

cards.q: What should a successful hunt produce?
cards.a: A new or improved automated detection
cards.x: Hunts that find nothing still document coverage.

cards.q: What is deception technology’s key advantage?
cards.a: Very high-fidelity alerts: legitimate users never touch decoys
cards.x: Honeytokens like fake credentials in memory catch lateral movement.

decks.title: Detection Lab Drills
decks.summary: Hunt the real traces from the CyberSecurity_Lab simulations (run them, then detect them).

cards.q: In the web-attack lab, what betrays credential stuffing (T1110)?
cards.a: A burst of 401s with many distinct usernames from one source hitting /login
cards.x: The lab’s auth_failure_threshold_exceeded event marks where the alert fires; chase any 401 burst that ends in a 200.

cards.q: What is the enumeration / dir-busting signature (T1595)?
cards.a: A 404 spike across many distinct paths from one source, with a few 200s revealing real content
cards.x: Hunt 404 rate and distinct-URL count per source; hits on /.git, /.env, /wp-admin are high signal.

cards.q: The SSRF drill aims a url= parameter at 169.254.169.254 — why is that the crown jewel?
cards.a: It is the cloud instance metadata endpoint; SSRF there can leak IAM credentials (T1552.005)
cards.x: A web tier should never fetch a user-supplied URL that resolves to link-local/loopback; enforce IMDSv2 and block link-local egress.
wrong: It is a DNS root server

cards.q: A file= parameter arrives as ..%2f..%2fetc/passwd. What is the detection lesson?
cards.a: Decode once before matching, and watch for double-encoding (%252e) that one decode leaves as %2e
cards.x: Path traversal (T1083) hides in encoded and mixed-slash forms; canonicalise, then confine to a base directory.
wrong: Trust the browser to normalise it

cards.q: In the DDoS lab, how do you tell a volumetric flood from slowloris?
cards.a: Volumetric = high requests/sec with connections reused; slowloris = concurrency climbs while requests never complete
cards.x: The lab exposes peak_rps vs peak_concurrent vs total_requests so each attack’s giveaway metric differs.

cards.q: The DDoS lab’s rapidreset vector models CVE-2023-44487. What is its signature?
cards.a: Streams/requests initiated far exceed completed ones; connections open then abort/RST immediately
cards.x: The lab’s aborted_connections metric climbs while total_requests stays low; over real HTTP/2 you see HEADERS then RST_STREAM.

cards.q: connflood vs volumetric — what distinguishes them at the victim?
cards.a: connflood opens a fresh socket per request (connections ≈ requests); volumetric reuses keep-alive (requests ≫ connections)
cards.x: Compare total_connections to total_requests; connection churn exhausts the accept queue and ephemeral ports.

cards.q: Why can the amplification lab measure a factor but never actually attack anyone?
cards.a: It does no source-IP spoofing, so the big responses return to the sender, not a forged victim
cards.x: Real reflection forges the victim’s IP as the query source; without spoofing you can study the factor safely.

cards.q: Which amplification profile has the highest factor, and on which UDP source port?
cards.a: NTP monlist (~556x) answering from UDP source port 123
cards.x: The lab’s ntp/ssdp/dns/memcached profiles each pair a query signature with a source port and realistic factor to hunt.

cards.q: In the gift-card lab, what on-disk trait flags the masquerading lure (T1036)?
cards.a: A double or mismatched extension — the name says .pdf/.txt but the real type is executable
cards.x: Correlate a downloaded file (MOTW / Zone.Identifier) with a later process-create where it executes.

cards.q: The lab’s persistence stage writes a Run key. Which telemetry catches it?
cards.a: Sysmon Event ID 12/13 (registry add/set) on ...\CurrentVersion\Run, or an Autoruns diff (T1547.001)
cards.x: Alert on new Run/RunOnce values that launch an interpreter or a file in a user-writable path.

cards.q: The persistence stage also simulates a scheduled task. What is the tell-tale log?
cards.a: Security Event ID 4698 (scheduled task created), or schtasks.exe in process telemetry (T1053.005)
cards.x: A new task with a logon/startup trigger running a script is classic persistence; baseline tasks and diff.

cards.q: How do you hunt the lab’s C2 beacon (T1071)?
cards.a: Look for periodicity, not volume: repeated check-ins to one destination at a near-constant interval
cards.x: Graph the evenly-spaced c2_beacon_sent timestamps; low bytes plus high regularity is the signal even with jitter.

cards.q: What is the point of each lab writing an events.jsonl file?
cards.a: It is the answer key: a ground-truth timeline to check what your tooling actually caught
cards.x: Run the drill, capture with Sysmon/EDR/Wireshark, then compare your detections against report and detect.

decks.title: Security Operations: SOC Scenarios
decks.summary: SIEM/SOAR triage, log analysis, and alert decisions as exam-style scenarios. (Domain 4.0)

cards.q: It’s 11:47 PM on a Friday. Your SIEM fires a critical alert: the account backup_svc just authenticated interactively to a domain controller from a workstation in the accounting VLAN, then ran whoami and net user. That account normally authenticates only from the backup server at 2 AM. You are the only analyst on shift. What is the most defensible first action?
cards.a: Disable the account and isolate the workstation from the network
cards.x: Anomalous authentication source plus reconnaissance commands is a lateral-movement pattern; containment comes before investigation because every minute of access is data loss.
wrong: Email the backup team to ask whether they are testing
Wait for a second alert to confirm the pattern
Restart the workstation to clear any malware

cards.q: Your SOC’s top alert fires 2,400 times a day: “possible lateral movement” on port 445 between endpoints and the print server. In six months it has produced one true positive. Analysts have started bulk-closing it without reading. What is the most defensible tuning change?
cards.a: Restrict the rule to non-server sources and require an admin logon, then measure for two weeks
cards.x: The fix for noisy alerts is precision, not silence: narrow the rule’s scope so it fires on genuinely suspicious conditions instead of disabling it or leaving analysts drowning.
wrong: Delete the rule entirely to stop the noise
Lower the severity to informational and keep bulk-closing
Route the alert to a mailbox nobody reads

cards.q: A finance clerk reports a suspicious email with an invoice attachment at 9:05 AM. By 9:20 AM, three more employees report the same email, and the mail gateway shows 60 copies delivered. The attachment hash is unknown. What should the SOAR playbook do first?
cards.a: Detonate the attachment in the sandbox while searching all mailboxes for the message and holding it for quarantine
cards.x: Triage scales by containing the blast radius first: find every copy, analyze the payload, then remove it — one analyst cannot race 60 inboxes by hand.
wrong: Delete the reported copy and tell the clerk to be careful
Block the sender’s domain and consider the incident handled
Forward the attachment to the whole security team for opinions

cards.q: Monday morning your SIEM shows EPS dropped 40% overnight for the firewall feed. No alerts fired about the feed itself. The SOC manager asks whether anything was missed. What is the most defensible first check?
cards.a: Verify the collector/forwarder on the firewall side and check for an ingestion gap in raw logs
cards.x: A silent drop in ingestion is a visibility failure, not quiet normality — the SIEM cannot alert on logs it never received.
wrong: Assume the weekend was simply quiet
Restart the SIEM and hope the feed recovers

cards.q: Two alerts fire for the same user within an hour: a failed VPN login from a new country, then a successful login from that country followed by a large SharePoint download. Individually each alert has a high false-positive rate. What is the most defensible action?
cards.a: Treat it as a probable compromised account: force re-authentication and revoke sessions before investigating
cards.x: Correlation is the whole point of SIEM: individually noisy signals compose into a strong indicator. Act on the pattern, not the single alert.
wrong: Close both alerts — the login succeeded, so it must be legitimate
Email the user asking if they are travelling
Disable the VPN for everyone until the user replies

cards.q: Legal asks for firewall logs from 14 months ago for a lawsuit. Your retention policy keeps hot logs 90 days, warm logs 12 months, and cold archives for 7 years. The SOC lead says the archive tapes are “somewhere”. What is the correct operational response?
cards.a: Restore the cold archive for that period, document the chain of custody, and hand legal the verified logs
cards.x: Retention tiers exist precisely for this: cold storage is the compliance archive. “Somewhere” means the retrieval process was never tested — fix that after this request.
wrong: Tell legal the logs are gone after 90 days
Pull the current warm logs and hope they cover it
Ask legal to narrow the request to the last 90 days

cards.q: NetFlow shows a workstation opening an HTTPS connection to the same external IP every 60 seconds, ±2 seconds, transferring about 4 KB each time, for six hours. The IP has no domain name and no threat-intel entry. The user insists they were “just browsing”. What is the most defensible conclusion?
cards.a: Treat it as likely C2 beaconing: isolate the host and capture memory before remediation
cards.x: Machine-regular intervals with tiny, consistent payloads are the beaconing signature; absence from intel feeds proves nothing about a fresh or private C2.
wrong: Accept the user’s explanation and close the ticket
Block the IP and take no further action
Wait for the endpoint agent to quarantine it automatically

cards.q: You are threat hunting in a 2,000-endpoint fleet. Your hypothesis: an attacker is using scheduled tasks for persistence. Which hunt is most likely to surface it?
cards.a: Stack-count scheduled task creation events (Event ID 4698) and investigate the rare outliers
cards.x: Hunting works by anomaly, not volume: legitimate scheduled tasks repeat thousands of times, so the rare outliers are where attackers hide.
wrong: Read every scheduled task on every endpoint manually
Count the total number of scheduled tasks in the fleet
Search for the word “malware” in task names

cards.q: Your IdP logs show a user received 47 MFA push prompts in 20 minutes at 3 AM, then approved one. Ten minutes later the account accessed the customer database it never normally touches. What is the most defensible first action?
cards.a: Disable the account, revoke its sessions, and require phishing-resistant MFA re-enrollment
cards.x: 47 prompts then an approval is push bombing, and the anomalous database access confirms session compromise. The session must die, and SMS/push alone must not be the re-entry path.
wrong: Ask the user whether they approved the prompt
Block the database from the user’s department
Change the user’s password but leave sessions active

cards.q: DLP flags an engineer uploading 12 GB of source code to a personal cloud drive over three nights. HR confirms the engineer resigned last week and their last day is Friday. No malware is involved. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Escalate immediately to management and legal as suspected insider data theft, preserving the DLP logs
cards.x: Departing employees exfiltrating data is the classic insider pattern; this is a personnel and legal matter first, a technical one second. Preserve evidence before confronting anyone.
wrong: Block the cloud drive and send the engineer a warning email
Assume it is a personal backup and close the alert

cards.q: A contractor’s account logs in from Chicago at 1:00 PM and from Singapore at 1:40 PM. The contractor’s manager says the contractor “travels a lot”. What is the most defensible action?
cards.a: Disable the account and revoke sessions pending verification — 40 minutes across 9,000 miles is not travel
cards.x: Impossible travel is physics, not policy: no manager’s assurance overrides an account in two places at once. Verify after containment, never before.
wrong: Accept the manager’s explanation and whitelist the contractor
Ask the contractor to confirm by email
Lower the alert threshold for contractors

cards.q: Your team of three analysts handles 400 phishing reports a month by hand. The CISO approved one SOAR automation project this quarter. What should it automate first?
cards.a: URL and attachment extraction, sandbox detonation, mailbox search, and IoC blocking for reported phish
cards.x: Automate the highest-volume, lowest-judgment workflow first: phishing triage is repetitive, time-sensitive, and proven. Incident command stays human.
wrong: Automated firing of employees who click links
A chatbot that tells users not to click

cards.q: During an incident review you discover the new cloud HR system sends no logs to the SIEM. It holds SSNs and banking details for 4,000 employees. What is the most defensible immediate action?
cards.a: Enable log forwarding from the HR system now and add a detection for anomalous bulk exports
cards.x: A system holding crown-jewel data with zero SIEM visibility is a blind spot, not a backlog item — coverage comes before perfect parsing.
wrong: Add it to next year’s SIEM onboarding plan
Assume the vendor’s own logging is sufficient
Block the HR system from the internet

cards.q: Forensic timeline analysis shows a workstation’s clock was 47 minutes behind the domain controller during the incident window. The SIEM correlated its events with firewall logs by timestamp. What is the impact on your investigation?
cards.a: Event ordering across sources is unreliable — re-correlate using relative offsets before drawing conclusions
cards.x: Correlation assumes synchronized clocks; a 47-minute skew can invert cause and effect. NTP is a security control, not just hygiene.
wrong: Timestamps are close enough; proceed as normal
Add 47 minutes to all firewall timestamps instead

cards.q: A Tier 1 analyst sees ransomware-like file extensions appearing on a file share, plus disabled shadow copies on two hosts. The runbook says “escalate suspected ransomware”. The analyst hesitates, not wanting to “cry wolf” on a Friday evening. What should the SOC’s culture and process dictate?
cards.a: Escalate immediately — suspected ransomware always meets the escalation bar, and no one is punished for a good-faith escalation
cards.x: Escalation criteria must be explicit and blameless: the cost of a delayed ransomware call dwarfs the cost of a false alarm. Hesitation is a process failure.
wrong: Wait until Monday so senior staff can look
Quietly restore the files from backup without telling anyone
Run a full antivirus scan first and escalate only if it finds something

cards.q: The CISO asks for “a report on phishing trends this quarter” and the SOC manager asks for “a dashboard of current phishing campaigns”. What is the correct distinction in what you deliver?
cards.a: The CISO gets a point-in-time report with trends and recommendations; the SOC gets a continuously refreshed dashboard for live operations
cards.x: Reports answer “what happened and what should we do”; dashboards answer “what is happening right now”. Mixing them up gives executives a blinking screen and analysts a stale PDF.
wrong: Send both of them the same dashboard link
Send both of them the same quarterly PDF
Dashboards are for executives; reports are for analysts

cards.q: An alert fires on a hash with no reputation hits. The analyst’s next step is enrichment before escalation. Which enrichment is most valuable?
cards.a: Detonate the file in a sandbox and pull parent process, command line, and network connections from EDR
cards.x: Unknown hashes are decided by behavior, not reputation: what the file did on the endpoint outweighs what no database knows about it.
wrong: Search the filename on Google and trust the first result
Email the file to the whole team for opinions
Check whether the file size looks suspicious

cards.q: Your DNS logs show one internal host generating 40,000 queries per hour to random-looking subdomains of a single domain, each 60+ characters of high-entropy text. Web proxy logs show nothing unusual. What is the most defensible conclusion and action?
cards.a: Likely DNS tunneling for data exfiltration or C2 — isolate the host and block the domain at the DNS layer
cards.x: High-volume, high-entropy DNS to one domain with no corresponding web traffic is the tunneling signature; DNS-layer blocking stops it for every protocol.
wrong: It is probably a misconfigured application; ignore it
Wait for the EDR to detect something

cards.q: Your SOC lead wants to prove the new EDR rules are working. She proposes tracking total alert volume. What metric should she track instead, and why?
cards.a: True-positive rate and mean time to detect/respond — volume can rise from noise while detection quality falls
cards.x: Alert volume measures noise, not security: a rule firing 10,000 times with 3 true positives is worse than one firing 10 times with 9. Measure outcomes.
wrong: Total alert volume is the right metric

cards.q: After a firewall firmware upgrade, the SIEM stops parsing its logs: events arrive but fields are empty, and the “top blocked ports” dashboard goes blank. No alerts fire. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Treat it as a detection outage: fix or update the parser immediately and backfill the raw logs so the gap is searchable
cards.x: Unparsed logs are invisible logs — dashboards and rules built on fields silently go blind. Raw retention is what makes the outage recoverable.
wrong: Wait for the vendor to fix it in the next release
Delete the old parser and start fresh
The firewall is still blocking, so nothing is lost

cards.q: Two tickets arrive: (1) a critical CVE on the public website’s WAF-protected login page, no exploit observed; (2) a medium-severity alert of data staging (large archives) on the finance file server by a service account. Which is the higher operational priority and why?
cards.a: The data-staging alert — observed adversary behavior on crown-jewel data outranks an unexploited CVE, even a critical one
cards.x: Severity classification must weigh observed malicious activity over theoretical severity: staging is a late-kill-chain step, while the CVE is a possibility behind a WAF.
wrong: The critical CVE — critical always outranks medium
Both are equal; work them in arrival order

cards.q: It’s 6 PM and you are handing a live triage to the night analyst: a suspicious PowerShell download cradle was blocked on a workstation, the user is the CFO’s executive assistant, and the EDR shows no further activity. What is the most defensible handoff?
cards.a: A written handoff with timeline, IoCs, what was blocked, what was NOT yet checked (persistence, lateral movement), and explicit next steps
cards.x: Shift handoffs are where investigations die: unstated assumptions become missed follow-ups. Document the open questions, not just the closed ones.
wrong: Tell them “the EDR handled it” and go home
Leave a sticky note saying “check the CFO’s assistant”
Email the CFO about the incident

cards.q: Your team subscribes to three commercial threat intel feeds. Analysts complain the feeds produce thousands of IoCs daily and nobody uses them. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Define detection requirements first, then auto-ingest only IoCs matching your environment into SIEM/SOAR with expiry dates
cards.x: Intel without requirements is noise: feeds must be filtered to what your stack can act on, and IoCs must expire or they become stale blocklists that break business.
wrong: Buy a fourth feed for better coverage
Block every IoC from all feeds immediately
Cancel the feeds and rely on web search alerts

cards.q: EDR flags a workstation: a signed binary sideloaded a malicious DLL, then opened an outbound connection. The user is in the middle of a client presentation on that machine. What is the most defensible action?
cards.a: Isolate the host from the network immediately — a confirmed compromise outranks the presentation
cards.x: DLL sideloading plus C2 is an active intrusion, not a suspicious alert; network isolation preserves the host for forensics while stopping the bleeding. The presentation can move.
wrong: Let the presentation finish, then investigate
Kill the malicious process but leave the network up
Ask the user to run antivirus when convenient

cards.q: A threat intel report says a ransomware affiliate is abusing WMI event subscriptions for persistence in manufacturing networks. You run a plant with 300 Windows hosts. What is the most defensible hunt?
cards.a: Query all hosts for WMI event consumers, filters, and bindings, and compare against a known-good baseline, investigating deviations
cards.x: Hunting starts from a hypothesis and a baseline: enumerate the mechanism everywhere, and the outliers — not the volume — reveal the attacker.
wrong: Disable WMI on all 300 hosts immediately
Search event logs for the word “ransomware”
Reimage all 300 hosts as a precaution

decks.title: Security Operations: Hardening & Vulnerability Scenarios
decks.summary: Patch prioritization, secure baselines, and asset decisions as exam-style scenarios. (Domain 4.0)

cards.q: It’s Tuesday. Your scanner flags: (1) a critical RCE on an internet-facing Exchange server with a public exploit, (2) a critical RCE on an internal HR server with no known exploit, (3) a high-severity flaw on 200 developer laptops. The change board meets Friday and hates emergency changes. What do you push for?
cards.a: Emergency out-of-band patching for the Exchange server today; the rest follow the normal Friday cycle
cards.x: Exposure plus active exploitability beats the calendar: an internet-facing, publicly exploited RCE cannot wait for the change board. Process serves risk, not the reverse.
wrong: Wait for Friday’s change board for all three
Patch the 200 laptops first since they are the most numerous
Patch the HR server first because HR data is sensitive

cards.q: A manufacturing line runs Windows XP controlling a $2M press. The vendor is defunct; no patch exists. The system must stay networked to the plant historian. What is the most defensible compensating control?
cards.a: Isolate it on a dedicated VLAN with strict firewall rules allowing only the historian, plus enhanced monitoring
cards.x: When patching is impossible, shrink exposure to the minimum viable: segmentation plus allow-listed traffic plus watching, documented as a risk exception with review.
wrong: Connect it to the internet so the vendor can remote in
Replace the press immediately regardless of cost
Do nothing — it has worked fine for years

cards.q: A quarterly audit finds 40 of 200 servers drifted from the CIS benchmark: mostly disabled audit logging and extra local admin accounts. The server team says the changes were “needed for troubleshooting”. What is the most defensible systemic fix?
cards.a: Re-apply the baseline via configuration management, require change tickets for deviations, and alert on drift
cards.x: Drift is the enemy of hardening: baselines enforced as code plus monitored exceptions turn “needed for troubleshooting” into a tracked, temporary, approved state.
wrong: Update the baseline to match whatever the servers currently look like
Manually fix the 40 servers once and move on
Disable auditing everywhere so the audit passes

cards.q: A pen test finds a forgotten Jenkins server, internet-facing, with default credentials — it was never in the CMDB. The CISO asks how this happens. What is the most defensible answer and fix?
cards.a: Unknown assets are unpatched assets: run continuous discovery scanning and reconcile it against the CMDB
cards.x: Vulnerability scans only see what they are pointed at; the CMDB is only as good as its inputs. Discovery must be continuous and reconciled, not assumed.
wrong: Fire whoever stood up the Jenkins server
Scan harder with the same scope
Assume this was a one-time mistake

cards.q: A vulnerability exception for an unpatched database was approved “temporarily” 18 months ago and renewed twice without review. The database holds customer PII and the compensating control (a WAF rule) was removed last year. What is the most defensible action?
cards.a: Escalate for immediate remediation or formal risk acceptance at the right authority level — the exception is void without its compensating control
cards.x: Exceptions are time-boxed risk acceptances, not permanent pardons: when the compensating control dies or reviews lapse, the exception dies with them.
wrong: Renew the exception for another year
Accept the risk verbally and move on
Delete the finding from the scanner

cards.q: A credentialed scan of the server fleet returns almost no findings, but an agentless network scan of the same fleet finds hundreds of missing patches. What is the most likely cause?
cards.a: The scan credentials are failing or lack privileges — validate the credential and its scope, then rescan
cards.x: A suspiciously clean credentialed scan usually means the scan never really authenticated; trust but verify the scan itself before celebrating.
wrong: The servers are fully patched; the network scan is wrong
The credentialed scan is always right

cards.q: Finance adopted a cloud expense app without IT review. It holds employee banking details and integrates with payroll via API. What is the most defensible immediate action?
cards.a: Bring it under governance: assess its security posture, enforce SSO/MFA and DLP, and put it in the asset inventory
cards.x: Shadow IT is a governance failure, not just a policy violation: the data already lives there, so the priority is securing it and preventing the next one, not punishment.
wrong: Block the app at the firewall immediately
Delete all the data in the app
Let finance keep using it unsupervised

cards.q: Facilities installed 60 smart thermostats on the corporate network, all with default admin passwords and no update mechanism. The vendor went bankrupt. What is the most defensible approach?
cards.a: Move them to an isolated IoT VLAN with no internet access, change what credentials can be changed, and monitor the segment
cards.x: Unpatchable IoT gets the same treatment as unpatchable legacy: segment, restrict, and watch. Default credentials on a flat network are an invitation.
wrong: Leave them — thermostats cannot be hacked
Put them on the guest Wi-Fi

cards.q: A critical zero-day patch is released for your VPN concentrators. The vendor warns the patch has known issues with a legacy client your sales team uses. Active exploitation is reported in the wild. What is the most defensible call?
cards.a: Patch immediately, accept the legacy-client breakage, and communicate the workaround — exploited zero-days outrank convenience
cards.x: Risk math: certain active exploitation of your remote-access edge beats a degraded experience for one legacy client. Test in parallel, don’t delay for it.
wrong: Wait for the next patch that fixes the legacy client
Patch half the concentrators and hope
Disable the VPN until a perfect patch exists

cards.q: A developer deploys cloud storage for a marketing site and leaves the bucket public, exposing 50,000 customer records. This is the third time this year. What is the most defensible systemic fix?
cards.a: Enforce organization-wide block-public-access defaults and add a CI check that fails builds creating public storage
cards.x: Repeat misconfigurations are a guardrail failure, not a training failure: make the insecure state impossible by default and catch it before deployment.
wrong: Send the developer to more training
Accept that buckets will sometimes be public

cards.q: An audit finds 30 decommissioned servers still powered on in a remote rack, unpatched for two years, still joined to the domain. What is the most defensible action?
cards.a: Isolate them immediately, verify no production dependencies, then decommission properly: wipe, remove from domain, update the CMDB
cards.x: Zombie servers are attacker infrastructure waiting to happen: powered-on, unpatched, and domain-joined is the worst combination. Verify dependencies before pulling the plug.
wrong: Just unplug them all right now
Leave them in case someone needs them

cards.q: Sales staff use personal phones for email under BYOD with no MDM. A phone with the CEO’s mailbox is stolen. What is the most defensible immediate action, and what should have existed?
cards.a: Revoke the device’s mail sessions and wipe corporate data via the mail platform’s remote wipe; MDM or app-level containerization should have existed
cards.x: Without MDM, your control plane is the identity layer: kill sessions and wipe the corporate container. BYOD without containerization is just hope.
wrong: Call the thief and ask for the phone back
Change the CEO’s password and do nothing else
Ban personal phones entirely starting tomorrow

cards.q: Your team deploys 50 new VMs a month from a golden image built in 2021. Scans show every new VM ships with the same 40 missing patches. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Rebuild the golden image monthly in a pipeline: patch, harden to baseline, scan, then promote
cards.x: Every manual build multiplies the same debt: an image pipeline makes secure the default instead of a monthly fire drill.

cards.q: A critical vulnerability is announced in the VPN client used by 800 remote workers. The vendor’s auto-update is broken and manual updates take 20 minutes each. What is the most defensible approach?
cards.a: Push the update via your endpoint management platform in waves, starting with the highest-risk users, and track compliance centrally
cards.x: Scale demands central push, not user goodwill: staged rollout with compliance tracking turns 800 manual updates into one controlled operation.
wrong: Email everyone asking them to update
Wait for the vendor to fix auto-update
Disable VPN access for anyone unpatched with no notice

cards.q: A CIS benchmark audit of workstations shows USB mass storage enabled everywhere, although policy requires it disabled. The helpdesk re-enabled it “for a VIP” months ago via GPO. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Restore the GPO to policy, scope a documented exception for the VIP with an expiry, and alert on future GPO changes to security settings
cards.x: One VIP exception silently became the fleet standard: exceptions must be scoped, expiring, and monitored — and security GPOs need change alerting.
wrong: Leave USB enabled; the VIP needs it
Disable USB in BIOS on every machine by hand

cards.q: A scan of your container registry finds critical CVEs in the base image used by 40 microservices. Rebuilding all 40 will take two sprints. What is the most defensible plan?
cards.a: Rebuild the base image now, prioritize rebuilding internet-facing services first, and put the rest on a tracked sprint plan with the risk formally accepted meanwhile
cards.x: Shared base images are single points of failure: fix the source, sequence by exposure, and make the residual risk explicit and owned — not silent.
wrong: Rebuild all 40 tonight regardless of testing
Delete the scan findings to keep velocity

cards.q: Your ERP runs on an OS going end-of-life in 60 days. The ERP vendor’s supported upgrade path costs $180k and six months. What is the most defensible plan?
cards.a: Buy extended support if available, isolate the ERP segment, harden monitoring, and fund the upgrade as a tracked project — not a surprise
cards.x: EOL without a plan is a choice to be breached: bridge with vendor support plus segmentation while the real migration gets a budget and a date.
wrong: Do nothing and hope attackers don’t notice
Disconnect the ERP from the network permanently

cards.q: Engineering ignores scanner findings because “everything is critical”. You propose SLAs. What is the most defensible SLA structure?
cards.a: Time-boxed by exploitability and exposure: internet-facing criticals in days, internal highs in weeks, with tracked exceptions — not one deadline for everything
cards.x: “Everything is critical” means nothing is: SLAs must encode risk so engineers feel the difference between an exposed RCE and a theoretical medium.
wrong: Only fix findings the auditors ask about

cards.q: A pen test report lists 15 findings. Management wants them all fixed by Friday. The top finding is “domain admin credentials in a helpdesk script”. What is the most defensible prioritization?
cards.a: Fix the credential exposure immediately as an emergency change; schedule the rest by risk with owners and dates
cards.x: Plaintext domain-admin credentials are a standing invitation, not a Friday task: separate the emergency from the plan, and assign every finding an owner.
wrong: Fix all 15 by Friday regardless of testing
Argue about the report’s accuracy first

cards.q: A misconfigured firewall push locks the SOC out of the management interface. The last config backup is six months old. What is the most defensible operational lesson and fix?
cards.a: Automate config backups on every change into version control, and test restores — configurations are assets too
cards.x: A six-month-old backup is barely a backup: config-as-code with tested restore turns a lockout into a ten-minute rollback.
wrong: Factory-reset the firewall and rebuild from memory
Blame the engineer who pushed the change

cards.q: A scan finds default credentials on 12 network printers, 3 UPS management cards, and the building’s badge system controller. What is the most defensible remediation order?
cards.a: Badge system controller first, then UPS cards, then printers — ordered by what an attacker gains
cards.x: Prioritize by blast radius: physical access control and power infrastructure outrank printers. Then eliminate the class of problem with a credential-change runbook for new devices.
wrong: Printers first — there are the most of them
All at once, no particular order

cards.q: You inherit a network with 200 unmanaged IoT devices (cameras, printers, sensors) on the flat corporate LAN. No inventory exists. What is the most defensible first step?
cards.a: Discover and inventory them, then move them to a segmented IoT VLAN with internet egress denied by default
cards.x: You cannot harden what you cannot see: inventory first, then segment. Flat networks turn every camera into a pivot point.
wrong: Change every default password today by hand

cards.q: The business wants to launch a customer portal in two weeks with two known high-severity findings unfixed. What is the most defensible path?
cards.a: Document formal risk acceptance signed at the right authority level, with compensating controls and a dated remediation plan — or delay launch
cards.x: “The business accepts the risk” is only real when it’s written, signed, time-boxed, and owned: verbal acceptance evaporates at the first incident.
wrong: Launch quietly and fix them later

cards.q: A security patch blue-screens 10% of workstations. The helpdesk is overwhelmed. What was missing, and what is the most defensible immediate action?
cards.a: A tested rollback plan and phased rollout were missing: halt the rollout, roll back affected hosts, and re-stage in smaller rings
cards.x: Patching without rings and rollback is gambling with the fleet: pilot, ring, monitor — and know how to reverse before you start.
wrong: Push the patch to the remaining 90% faster
Reimage all affected machines from scratch
Blame the vendor and stop patching

cards.q: The board asks “are we getting safer?” Your vuln program reports “10,000 findings closed this quarter”. What is the more defensible answer?
cards.a: Report mean time to remediate for KEV/exposed criticals, exception aging, and repeat findings — outcomes, not ticket counts
cards.x: Closed-ticket counts reward closing easy findings: the board needs to know how fast the dangerous ones die and whether the same ones keep coming back.
wrong: Show them the raw scanner dashboard

decks.title: Security Operations: Tooling & Identity Scenarios
decks.summary: EDR, NAC, DLP, IAM operations, and automation as exam-style scenarios. (Domain 4.0)

cards.q: EDR alerts: a process just disabled the endpoint agent’s service, then cleared the System event log. The host is a developer workstation with local admin rights. What is the most defensible first action?
cards.a: Isolate the host from the network immediately — tamper plus anti-forensics is an active intrusion until proven otherwise
cards.x: Attackers kill the agent before the real work: service tampering followed by log clearing is not a glitch, it is tradecraft. Isolate first.
wrong: Restart the EDR agent and see if it stays up
Ask the developer if they were testing something
Reinstall the agent and close the alert

cards.q: A new contractor laptop keeps getting quarantined by NAC for “missing patches”, but Windows Update shows it fully patched. The contractor is blocked from working. What is the most likely cause and fix?
cards.a: The NAC health check is reading a stale compliance cache or wrong update source — validate what the NAC agent actually checks and force a fresh assessment
cards.x: Quarantine loops are usually a telemetry mismatch, not a liar: verify the NAC’s definition of “patched” against the endpoint’s before bypassing the control.
wrong: Give the contractor a permanent NAC exception
Disable NAC for the whole contractor VLAN
Tell the contractor to reinstall Windows

cards.q: DLP blocks the legal team from emailing a redlined contract containing “SSN-like” numbers that are actually clause references. Legal is furious and demands DLP be turned off for them. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Tune the DLP pattern and add a scoped exception for legal’s document workflow with approval — not a blanket disable
cards.x: Blocking business is how DLP gets turned off permanently: tune the detector and exception the legitimate workflow narrowly, with sign-off, instead of surrendering the control.
wrong: Disable DLP for the entire legal department
Tell legal to stop using clause numbers
Turn off DLP globally until it is “fixed”

cards.q: The PAM vault is down for emergency maintenance and a production database is down. The on-call DBA asks for the break-glass domain admin password. What is the most defensible procedure?
cards.a: Release it per the break-glass procedure: dual control, time-boxed, fully logged, with mandatory rotation afterward
cards.x: Break-glass exists for exactly this — but it is a controlled exception: every use is witnessed, logged, and followed by rotation, or it becomes a backdoor.
wrong: Refuse — no vault, no access, let production stay down
Email the password to the DBA and the team
Give the DBA permanent domain admin to avoid this next time

cards.q: An audit finds a service account with domain admin rights, no owner, last password change six years ago, logging into 40 servers nightly for “backups” nobody can explain. What is the most defensible sequence?
cards.a: Scope what it actually touches, replace its function with a least-privilege managed account, then disable the old one — with a rollback window
cards.x: Ancient privileged service accounts are attacker persistence waiting to be discovered: understand the dependency before you cut it, or you break backups at 2 AM.
wrong: Disable it immediately with no investigation
Leave it alone — it might be important
Change its password and keep using it as-is

cards.q: Your SSO identity provider is down. Nobody can log into email, VPN, or the ticket system — including the SOC. What should have existed, and what is the most defensible immediate action?
cards.a: Break-glass local admin accounts and documented offline procedures should have existed; use them now and declare a major incident
cards.x: SSO is a single point of failure by design: the control for that is tested break-glass access plus runbooks that don’t live behind the SSO you just lost.
wrong: Wait for the IdP vendor to fix it
Disable MFA so people can log in directly

cards.q: Helpdesk receives a call: “Hi, this is the CFO, I’m locked out, please reset my MFA.” The caller ID shows the CFO’s number and the voice sounds right. The helpdesk tech is new. What is the most defensible procedure?
cards.a: Verify through an independent channel — call back on the known corporate number or require in-person/video verification — before any reset
cards.x: Caller ID is spoofable and voices are clonable: identity verification for privileged resets must use a channel the attacker doesn’t control.
wrong: Reset the MFA — the caller ID matches
Ask for the CFO’s password as verification
Refuse all MFA resets by policy

cards.q: The quarterly access review shows the marketing intern has write access to the production customer database, granted “temporarily” eight months ago. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Remove the access immediately and fix the review process so temporary grants actually expire
cards.x: Privilege creep is a process failure: temporary access without enforced expiry is permanent access. The review caught it — the process must now prevent it.
wrong: Leave it — the intern needs it for their project
Ask the intern to be careful

cards.q: EDR flags: rundll32.exe launching with a DLL from a user’s Downloads folder, then opening an outbound connection. The user says they were “installing a printer driver”. What is the most defensible action?
cards.a: Isolate the host and investigate — rundll32 sideloading a userland DLL with network egress is classic living-off-the-land tradecraft
cards.x: LOLBins abuse legitimate tools: the parent-child relationship plus the DLL’s location plus egress is the story, not the binary’s signature. Users’ explanations don’t override telemetry.
wrong: Allow it — rundll32 is a Windows component
Help the user finish the printer install
Whitelist rundll32 globally to reduce alerts

cards.q: Facilities wants 200 smart sensors on the corporate LAN. They can’t run agents and use shared default credentials. What is the most defensible NAC approach?
cards.a: Agentless NAC with device profiling: fingerprint, segment to an IoT VLAN, and restrict to required destinations only
cards.x: Devices that can’t run agents get profiled, not trusted: fingerprinting plus microsegmentation gives unmanageable devices a manageable network home.
wrong: Put them on the main LAN with the default credentials
Disable NAC for the sensor VLAN

cards.q: An employee uploads the customer list to a personal Google Drive from a managed laptop. Endpoint DLP is installed but didn’t fire. What is the most defensible investigation step?
cards.a: Check whether the DLP policy covers browser uploads to unsanctioned cloud apps and whether the agent was running — then close the gap
cards.x: A control that didn’t fire is a finding about the control: verify scope, agent health, and policy coverage before blaming the user.
wrong: Assume the DLP works and the upload was fine

cards.q: A new SOAR playbook auto-isolates any host with a “malware detected” alert. Overnight it isolated 30 hosts — including the payroll server — on a signature later confirmed a false positive. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Return the playbook to human-in-the-loop approval for high-impact actions, and require a staging period with alert-only mode for new automations
cards.x: Auto-remediation without a proving period turns a false positive into an outage: graduate automation from alert-only to approval to autonomous, by blast radius.
wrong: Let it keep running — payroll will recover
Make the playbook more aggressive to catch real malware

cards.q: HR onboarding is manual: IT creates accounts from emailed spreadsheets. Last month two new hires waited a week for access, and one ex-contractor kept VPN access for a month. What is the most defensible systemic fix?
cards.a: Drive provisioning and deprovisioning from the HR system of record with role-based templates and same-day revocation
cards.x: Manual JML is where orphaned accounts are born: the HR system knows who joined, moved, and left — make it the source of truth for identity.
wrong: Hire more IT staff to process spreadsheets faster
Give every new hire domain admin temporarily
Email spreadsheets are fine; the ex-contractor was a fluke

cards.q: A database admin needs emergency production access at 2 AM. PAM can grant it with full session recording. The DBA objects: “recording slows me down”. What is the most defensible stance?
cards.a: Grant it with recording enforced — privileged sessions are recorded, no exceptions, and performance concerns get engineered away
cards.x: Session recording is the accountability half of privileged access: JIT elevation without a record is just standing privilege with extra steps.
wrong: Skip recording this once for speed
Give the DBA the vault master password

cards.q: A red-team exercise shows the EDR missed a custom in-memory payload on servers, though it caught commodity malware on workstations. What is the most defensible conclusion?
cards.a: Tune and test EDR for server workloads specifically: memory scanning, script-block logging, and behavioral rules differ by platform
cards.x: EDR is not one control but a per-platform configuration: server workloads need their own policies, exclusions review, and adversary emulation — catching commodity malware is table stakes.
wrong: The EDR is useless; replace it

cards.q: An expired TLS certificate takes the customer portal offline for six hours. The cert was tracked in a spreadsheet nobody owned. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Automate certificate lifecycle management with ownership, expiry alerting, and auto-renewal where possible
cards.x: Certificates are identity infrastructure: spreadsheet-tracked expiry is an outage scheduled in advance. Automate issuance and renewal.

cards.q: Remote workers routinely disable the VPN “because it’s slow”, exposing their traffic on public Wi-Fi. What is the most defensible technical control?
cards.a: Enforce always-on VPN with kill-switch behavior via endpoint policy — the tunnel is not optional
cards.x: Security that depends on user diligence fails at scale: make the secure path the only path, then fix the performance complaint that drove the bypass.
wrong: Send a reminder email about VPN usage
Accept that remote work is insecure

cards.q: Engineers keep marking everything “Confidential”, so DLP blocks routine work and people start bypassing it. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Simplify to three usable labels with clear examples, train on real documents, and tune DLP to the labels that matter
cards.x: Classification that cries wolf trains people to ignore it: usable labels plus tuned enforcement beat a perfect taxonomy nobody follows.
wrong: Remove DLP so work isn’t blocked

cards.q: Developers share one “deploy” SSH key in a chat channel for production access. What is the most defensible replacement?
cards.a: Per-service identities in the PAM vault with short-lived credentials, checked out per deployment and fully audited
cards.x: Shared credentials destroy accountability and rotation: individual, vaulted, short-lived identities make “who did what” answerable.
wrong: Put the key in a shared password manager
It’s fine — the channel is private

cards.q: A file is both quarantined by EDR as malware and flagged by DLP as containing PII. The IR team and the privacy team both open tickets. What is the most defensible coordination?
cards.a: Run one coordinated response: contain the malware first, then assess the data exposure with privacy/legal — with a single incident commander
cards.x: One incident, one commander: malware containment and breach assessment are phases of the same response, not competing tickets.
wrong: Close the DLP ticket — malware matters more
Delete the file and close both tickets

cards.q: The guest Wi-Fi onboarding asks only for an email address, then grants full internet. A pen tester pivots from a guest device to the corporate LAN. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Isolate guest traffic completely (separate VLAN/firewall, client isolation, no corporate routes) and add captive-portal terms with rate limits
cards.x: Guest networks are untrusted by definition: the failure wasn’t the weak onboarding, it was the missing isolation between guest and corporate.
wrong: Require a password for guest Wi-Fi

cards.q: Managers rubber-stamp quarterly access reviews without reading them. What is the most defensible improvement?
cards.a: Show each manager what changed since last review and what the person actually used — review deltas and last-used data, not raw lists
cards.x: Rubber-stamping is a UX failure: reviewers approve what they can understand. Deltas plus usage data turn attestation into a real decision.

cards.q: An attacker with local admin stops the Windows Event Log service before running ransomware. The SIEM shows a gap. What control would have preserved the evidence?
cards.a: Forward logs in real time to the SIEM/collector — local logs are not the system of record
cards.x: An attacker with admin owns the local log store: real-time forwarding makes the SIEM the immutable copy, so local tampering leaves a visible gap instead of a clean slate.
wrong: Disable the Event Log service preemptively

cards.q: After acquiring a startup, their Google Workspace users need access to your Azure AD apps. IT proposes creating duplicate accounts for everyone. What is the most defensible approach?
cards.a: Federate the identity providers: trust their IdP via SAML/OIDC so one identity works everywhere with central policy
cards.x: Duplicate accounts double the attack surface and the deprovisioning burden: federation keeps one identity, one MFA policy, one kill switch.
wrong: Give everyone the startup’s admin passwords
Block the startup’s users until migration completes

cards.q: A pen test exfiltrates 2 GB via a USB drive from a workstation despite a “no USB” policy. The GPO was never actually linked. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Enforce USB mass-storage blocking via properly linked GPO/MDM, monitor for violations, and provide an approved encrypted-USB exception process
cards.x: Unenforced policy is theater: technical enforcement plus monitoring plus a legitimate exception path beats a rule nobody can follow.
wrong: Ban USB drives in the employee handbook

decks.title: Security Operations: Incident Response Scenarios
decks.summary: The full IR lifecycle — preparation to lessons learned — as exam-style scenarios. (Domain 4.0)

cards.q: At 8 AM the helpdesk reports “weird popups” on three machines in sales. By 9 AM it’s eleven machines across two departments. The IT manager wants to reimage all eleven immediately. What is the most defensible first move?
cards.a: Declare the incident, scope it (how many, how far, patient zero, vector) before reimaging anything
cards.x: Reimaging destroys evidence and doesn’t stop the vector: scope first — patient zero and the infection path — or you’ll reimage the same machines twice.
wrong: Wait and see if it spreads further
Email the whole company about the virus

cards.q: The CFO’s laptop is patient zero in a suspected breach. Forensics wants it untouched for imaging; the CFO has a board presentation in two hours. What is the most defensible resolution?
cards.a: Image the drive and memory now, then return a clean loaner for the presentation — evidence preserved, business continues
cards.x: “Forensics vs business” is a false choice when imaging takes an hour: capture first, then restore function. The plan for this should predate the incident.
wrong: Let the CFO keep using the laptop
Seize the laptop and cancel the presentation
Image it next week when convenient

cards.q: During an active breach investigation, IT’s normal retention job is about to purge 90-day-old proxy logs that may show initial access. Legal hasn’t been looped in yet. What is the most defensible action?
cards.a: Issue a litigation hold immediately: suspend the purge, preserve the logs, and loop in legal now
cards.x: Spoliation — destroying relevant evidence — can be worse than the breach: preservation duties trigger when litigation is reasonably anticipated, and the clock is already running.
wrong: Let the purge run — it’s automated
Copy the logs to a USB stick quietly

cards.q: An analyst images a suspect drive, stores the image on a shared folder “for the team”, and emails the hash to a colleague. Two weeks later legal asks for the chain of custody. What broke?
cards.a: Custody was never established: no documented handlers, no access control on the image, and the hash traveled separately from the evidence
cards.x: Chain of custody is a documented, unbroken record of who handled evidence and when: a shared folder and an emailed hash are gaps a defense attorney will drive through.
wrong: The analyst should have used a bigger drive

cards.q: You arrive at a running server suspected of hosting a rootkit. A junior analyst suggests pulling the power to “freeze everything”. What is the most defensible acquisition order?
cards.a: Capture volatile data first (memory, network connections, running processes), then disk — pulling power destroys the most valuable evidence
cards.x: Order of volatility: registers, cache, RAM, network state, then disk. A rootkit lives in memory; a powered-off box is a dead end.
wrong: Image the disk first, memory later
Reboot into safe mode and investigate

cards.q: Ransomware hit overnight. The attackers left a note with a chat link. The CEO wants to “just talk to them and see”. What is the most defensible position?
cards.a: No contact without leadership and legal directing it — and never pay without understanding decryption reliability and legal exposure
