cards.x: Negotiation is a business-legal decision with sanctions and reliability risks, not a curiosity errand: the CEO freelancing contact can create liability.
wrong: Let the CEO chat with them

cards.q: The CISO proposes a tabletop exercise simulating a ransomware attack on the ERP. Engineering groans: “we know the plan”. What is the most defensible argument for doing it?
cards.a: Tabletops test the people and the plan under pressure — most fail on communications and roles, not technical steps
cards.x: Nobody “knows the plan” until they’ve argued about it: tabletops surface the missing phone numbers, unclear authorities, and legal gaps before the real 2 AM call.
wrong: Skip it — the plan is documented
Do a real ransomware attack instead

cards.q: A breach exposed 50,000 customer records including SSNs. Engineering wants to “finish the investigation first” before telling anyone. What is the most defensible guidance?
cards.a: Start the notification clock with legal now — breach notification laws have hard deadlines that don’t wait for a complete investigation
cards.x: Investigation completeness and notification duty run in parallel: regulators measure from discovery, and “we were still investigating” is not a defense.
wrong: Finish the investigation first, then notify
Don’t notify — it hurts the stock price
Notify customers via social media immediately

cards.q: A major incident is underway and 40 people have joined the bridge, all talking. Nothing is getting decided. What is the most defensible structure?
cards.a: Establish incident command: one commander, defined roles (ops, comms, legal liaison, scribe), and move observers to a listen-only channel
cards.x: Incidents are managed, not meeting’d: command structure with a scribe turns chaos into decisions and a defensible timeline.
wrong: Wait for the chaos to settle naturally

cards.q: Post-incident review finds the breach came through an unpatched VPN — the same vector as an incident eight months ago. The previous review recommended patching it. What failed?
cards.a: Post-incident remediation tracking: recommendations without owners, dates, and verification are wishes, not fixes
cards.x: Lessons learned is a phase, not a meeting: every recommendation needs an owner, a deadline, and a verification check, or the same vector wins twice.
wrong: Eight months is too long to remember

cards.q: MTTR is dropping quarter over quarter, but analysts admit they close tickets at “containment” to look fast, while eradication drags on. What is the most defensible metric fix?
cards.a: Measure MTTD and MTTR to full eradication and verified recovery — and track repeat incidents separately
cards.x: Metrics drive behavior: defining “resolved” at containment optimizes for looking fast. Measure to true recovery, and watch for the same cause returning.

cards.q: Three systems are involved: a web server (patient zero, still running), an admin’s laptop (powered off by the user), and a file server (still serving production). In what order do you acquire evidence?
cards.a: Web server memory first (volatile, patient zero), then file server disk image (live acquisition), then the powered-off laptop last (its disk isn’t going anywhere)
cards.x: Volatility plus investigative value sets the order: live patient-zero memory first, then live systems, then dead boxes — which keep.
wrong: The laptop first since it’s off and easy
All at once with no priority

cards.q: A journalist tweets that your company was breached, with screenshots. The comms team wants to deny it until “we know everything”. What is the most defensible guidance?
cards.a: Acknowledge the investigation promptly with a holding statement; never deny what you haven’t verified — coordinate with legal
cards.x: Denying an unverified claim creates the second crisis when it proves true: a factual holding statement buys time without creating liability.

cards.q: Defense counsel challenges your forensic findings: “How do you know your imaging tool works correctly?” What is the most defensible answer?
cards.a: The tool is validated, the process is documented, hashes were verified at acquisition, and every step is in the chain of custody
cards.x: Admissibility rests on validated tools plus documented process: hash-verified images and an unbroken custody record answer the challenge before it’s asked.

cards.q: An attacker has compromised a cloud admin console session and is spinning up resources. The on-prem playbook says “isolate the host”. What is the most defensible cloud-native containment?
cards.a: Revoke the sessions and keys, attach a deny-all policy to the role, and snapshot affected resources for forensics — identity is the perimeter
cards.x: Cloud containment targets identity, not hosts: killing sessions and keys plus deny-all stops the bleeding; snapshots preserve evidence before termination.
wrong: Isolate an EC2 instance and call it done

cards.q: The post-incident review turns into finger-pointing at the junior admin who clicked the phish. Participation collapses. What is the most defensible facilitation?
cards.a: Refocus on systems: why did one click lead to domain compromise — missing MFA, flat network, no EDR — and make it blameless by rule
cards.x: Blameless reviews fix systems, blame fixes nothing: the question is never “who clicked” but “why did the architecture allow one click to matter”.
wrong: Fire the junior admin as an example
Cancel the review to avoid conflict

cards.q: A mid-size company has no IR team. The CFO asks whether the $50k/year IR retainer is worth it. What is the most defensible answer?
cards.a: Yes — a retainer buys guaranteed response SLAs, pre-staged tooling, and practiced contacts; building equivalent in-house costs far more
cards.x: Incident response is bought before you need it: without a retainer, you’re cold-calling firms during the worst week of the year at emergency rates.
wrong: No — the IT team can handle it
Buy cyber insurance instead of a retainer
Wait until the first breach, then decide

cards.q: Mid-incident, threat intel reports the ransomware group typically exfiltrates before encrypting, with a 72-hour dwell. You’re 24 hours in. What is the most defensible use of that intel?
cards.a: Hunt for exfiltration indicators now (large outbound transfers, staging) and prioritize containment of data paths alongside hosts
cards.x: Intel is only useful when it changes action: knowing the group’s playbook reorders your hunt toward exfiltration evidence while the window is still open.
wrong: File the intel report for later
Share the intel on social media

cards.q: Ransomware encrypted 200 servers. Clean backups exist. The business demands email first, but the IR team says identity infrastructure first. What is the most defensible restoration order?
cards.a: Identity and core infrastructure first (AD, DNS, backup systems), then business-critical apps in priority order — email after the foundation is clean
cards.x: Restore the trust fabric before the workload: bringing email up on a still-compromised identity system just re-infects it. Business priority applies within a safe sequence.
wrong: Email first — the business is always right
Pay the ransom instead of restoring

cards.q: After a painful investigation hampered by missing logs, the CISO asks what “forensic readiness” would have meant. What is the most defensible definition and first investment?
cards.a: The ability to investigate without scrambling: centralized logging with tested retention, defined evidence-handling procedures, and pre-staged tools — first investment is log coverage and retention
cards.x: Forensic readiness is preparation-phase work: you can’t buy visibility during an incident. Centralized, retained, tested logs are the foundation everything else stands on.
wrong: Buy the most expensive forensic suite
Hope the next incident is simpler

cards.q: Your EDR vendor pushes a bad update that bluescreens 5,000 endpoints — the vendor is the incident. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Activate the incident process with the vendor as a party: contain via safe-mode rollback procedures, communicate widely, and review supply-chain risk afterward
cards.x: When the tool is the threat, fall back to process: pre-planned rollback procedures and out-of-band comms matter more than the console you can’t reach.
wrong: Wait for the vendor to fix it silently

cards.q: Legal needs emails from a former employee’s SaaS mailbox for litigation. IT already deleted the account per the 30-day policy. What is the most defensible lesson?
cards.a: Litigation hold must suspend automated deletion: holds override retention policies, and SaaS offboarding must check for holds first
cards.x: Automated deletion is spoliation when a hold exists or is foreseeable: the offboarding workflow needs a legal-hold check before the delete button.
wrong: Ask the SaaS vendor to undelete quietly
Thirty days is thirty days — nothing to do

cards.q: A red-team exercise and a real intrusion overlap: the SOC can’t tell which alerts are the exercise. What failed, and what is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Exercise control failed: red-team activity must be tagged, time-boxed, and known to a trusted agent — with a kill phrase to distinguish real from exercise
cards.x: Uncontrolled exercises poison real detection: the trusted-agent model plus clear start/stop signals keeps the SOC’s real alerts trustworthy.
wrong: Let the SOC figure it out
Run exercises without telling anyone, always

cards.q: The board asks “could this happen again?” after a contained breach. What is the most defensible answer structure?
cards.a: What happened, root cause, what was fixed and verified, what residual risk remains, and what would detect it next time — honest, not reassuring
cards.x: “Never again” is a lie; the defensible answer shows the causal chain is broken, verified, and monitored — boards respect residual risk stated plainly.

cards.q: During a fast-moving incident, the scribe stops taking notes “to help with the actual work”. What is lost, and what is the most defensible correction?
cards.a: The defensible timeline is lost: who knew what when, what actions were taken and why — reassign a dedicated scribe immediately
cards.x: The timeline is built during the incident or never: it’s your legal record, your lessons-learned input, and your notification evidence. Scribing IS the actual work.
wrong: Notes slow things down — skip them
Reconstruct the timeline from memory later

decks.title: Threats & Attack Vectors: Scenarios
decks.summary: Attribution clues, initial-access choices, and vector response as exam-style scenarios. (Domain 2.0)

cards.q: Your manufacturing firm finds a breach: the attackers dwelled 11 months, stole CAD drawings slowly, left no ransom note, and used custom tooling. A ransomware crew hits your supplier the same week — loud, fast, double extortion. What is the most defensible attribution read?
cards.a: Two different actors: a patient espionage actor in your network and an opportunistic ransomware crew at your supplier
cards.x: Dwell time, tooling, and objectives separate APTs from ransomware crews: slow theft of IP with no note is espionage, loud fast extortion is e-crime. Never merge incidents by timing alone.
wrong: The ransomware crew is a false flag by the APT

cards.q: An engineer’s credentials are used at 3 AM from a foreign IP, but there is no malware, no phishing email, and the engineer swears they never travel. HR quietly notes the engineer was passed over for promotion last quarter. What is the most defensible hypothesis to test first?
cards.a: Insider misuse: someone with legitimate access acting on grievance — review access logs and data touched, not just malware
cards.x: Insider threats leave access logs instead of malware: authorized credentials, odd hours, data touched that matches no project. Test the human vector before chasing the technical one.
wrong: A brute-force attack from a botnet
The engineer is lying about phishing

cards.q: Three hospitals are hit the same day by identical ransomware. The only common factor: they all use the same MRI vendor, and the vendor pushed a “firmware update” yesterday. What is the most defensible first move?
cards.a: Isolate the vendor’s equipment and software from your network, verify the vendor’s compromise status out-of-band, and hunt for the update’s footprint
cards.x: A shared third party hitting multiple customers is a supply-chain compromise: the vendor’s signed update is the vector. Contain the vendor’s access first, then confirm with the vendor directly — not by email, which may be compromised too.
wrong: Reinstall the MRI machines from vendor media
Assume your staff clicked a phish

cards.q: A fintech’s admin panel is breached. Evidence: no phishing email found, but the internet-facing admin portal had RDP open with a weak password, and the first login came from a residential proxy. What is the most defensible conclusion about initial access?
cards.a: External exploitation of an exposed remote service — close RDP to the internet, enforce MFA, and audit what the session touched
cards.x: Attackers take the easiest path: exposed RDP with weak credentials needs no phishing. The fix is removing the exposure and MFA, not more email training.
wrong: A sophisticated phishing campaign you haven’t found yet
An insider who knew the password

cards.q: Twelve engineers at a game studio get malware the same week. Interviews find every infected machine visited the same indie game-dev forum in the last month. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Treat the forum as a watering hole: block it at the proxy, scan all visitors, and notify the forum operators — then hunt for what the malware did
cards.x: A shared benign site infecting one industry’s visitors is a watering hole. The site is the vector, so the response is blocking, sweeping everyone who visited, and notifying — the victims chose the site, the attackers chose the victims.
wrong: Reimage only the twelve machines and move on

cards.q: Finance gets an invoice from a long-time supplier, but the bank details changed. The email thread is genuine — the attacker hijacked the supplier’s mailbox mid-thread and slipped in new wiring instructions. What is the most defensible control that would have stopped this?
cards.a: Out-of-band verification of changed payment details by phone using a known number — never trust instructions inside the compromised channel
cards.x: Business email compromise defeats email verification because the channel itself is owned. Changed bank details always require a second, independent channel.

cards.q: A university’s website is defaced with political slogans the night before a controversial speaker’s talk. No data is stolen, no ransom demanded. What is the most defensible characterization and response?
cards.a: Hacktivist defacement: restore from known-good, review web app hardening, and treat it as a publicity attack rather than a data breach
cards.x: Hacktivists want an audience, not assets: defacement is loud by design. Restore, harden, and don’t over-rotate into a full data-breach response for a graffiti incident.

cards.q: Your SOC gets an alert at 2 AM. The “attacker” IP is your own red team’s documented range, but the engagement was supposed to end Friday — and it’s now Sunday. What is the most defensible action?
cards.a: Treat it as a real incident until the red-team lead confirms in person or by the agreed kill phrase — expired engagements don’t get the benefit of the doubt
cards.x: Red teams that overrun their window become indistinguishable from attackers. The trusted-agent model requires out-of-band confirmation; assuming “it’s just the red team” is how real breaches hide.
wrong: Ignore it — it’s the red team

cards.q: A logistics company’s drivers get SMS messages: “Your delivery route changed, tap to view” with a link. Several tap it on personal phones that also have the company MDM profile. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Treat it as smishing against the fleet: warn all drivers, check the MDM for sideloaded apps or profile changes, and block the domain
cards.x: Smishing targets the person, and personal-plus-work devices blur the blast radius. The response is fleet-wide warning plus MDM verification — the phones are company-managed endpoints.
wrong: Tell drivers to buy new phones
Ignore it — personal phones aren’t IT’s problem

cards.q: Attackers register yourbank-secure-login.com (you are “yourbank”) and harvest customer credentials for a week before anyone notices. What is the most defensible layered response?
cards.a: Takedown request to the registrar, force password resets for affected customers, publish a warning naming the exact domain, and monitor for variants
cards.x: Typosquatting is fought on four fronts at once: kill the domain, contain the credential theft, warn customers with specifics, and watch for lookalikes. Any one alone leaves the campaign alive.
wrong: Buy the domain from the attackers

cards.q: A hospital’s billing vendor is breached. The vendor had VPN access into the hospital network “for support”. Forensics finds the attackers pivoted from the vendor’s network into yours. What is the most defensible structural fix?
cards.a: Remove standing vendor VPN: replace with just-in-time, scoped, MFA’d access that expires, and segment vendor-reachable systems
cards.x: Trusted third-party access is a standing invitation: the fix is eliminating always-on vendor tunnels in favor of temporary, least-privilege access with MFA.
wrong: Give the vendor a stronger VPN password
Monitor the vendor’s network for them

cards.q: A retailer sees a burst of 40,000 login attempts in an hour: thousands of usernames, 2-3 passwords each, from residential IPs worldwide. What is the most defensible characterization and response?
cards.a: Credential stuffing with breached password lists: rate-limit, require MFA, and force resets on accounts that authenticated during the burst
cards.x: Low-and-slow across many usernames is stuffing, not brute force — lockouts won’t trigger, and the passwords are real ones from other breaches. MFA and anomaly-based throttling are the answers.
wrong: A DDoS attack — call the ISP

cards.q: A SaaS company’s customers report malware warnings from the company’s own download page. The page loads ads from a third-party network. What is the most defensible conclusion?
cards.a: Malvertising: the ad network is serving malicious creatives through your legitimate page — isolate the ad network, audit what ran, and notify customers
cards.x: Your page is the carrier, the ad network is the vector. Pull the ad network first, then determine exposure — customers trust your domain, which the attackers borrowed.

cards.q: An attacker drops infected USB drives labeled “Q3 Bonuses” in your parking lot. One is found plugged into a reception PC. What is the most defensible immediate response?
cards.a: Isolate the PC, scan and block the USB device IDs fleet-wide, and remind staff that found media goes to IT unplugged — then hunt for what ran
cards.x: Baiting works on curiosity: the response is containment of the plugged device, fleet-wide USB hygiene, and a culture where found drives are reported, not plugged in.
wrong: Ban USB drives and declare victory
Plug the other found drives in to “check” them

cards.q: A kiosk in your retail stores is found with a small hardware device between the keyboard and the PC. What is the most defensible conclusion and response?
cards.a: Physical keylogger (evil-maid style): treat all credentials typed on that kiosk as compromised, replace the hardware, and review camera footage and kiosk hardening
cards.x: Hardware between keyboard and PC is a keylogger until proven otherwise — every password typed there is burned. The fix is credential resets plus tamper-evident kiosk design.
wrong: It’s a USB hub — ignore it
Wipe the kiosk and move on

cards.q: A law firm’s partner gets a call: “IT support, we need your MFA code to fix the email outage.” There is no outage. What is the most defensible policy?
cards.a: MFA codes are never shared with anyone for any reason — the correct response is hang up and call the real helpdesk at the published number
cards.x: Vishing manufactures urgency to steal the one thing that defeats phishing. The rule must be absolute: codes are never spoken aloud, and “support” never calls asking for them.
wrong: Give the code if they sound professional
Disable MFA to avoid the hassle

cards.q: Your developers’ laptops beacon to a cloud storage domain every 90 seconds with tiny encrypted payloads. The domain is a legitimate file-sharing service. What is the most defensible conclusion?
cards.a: Likely C2 abusing a trusted cloud service: isolate a sample host, capture the traffic, and identify the process — legitimate services make excellent cover
cards.x: Attackers hide in trusted infrastructure: beaconing to a legitimate service is still beaconing. The service’s reputation doesn’t clear the behavior.
wrong: It’s the backup agent — ignore it

cards.q: After a breach, forensics finds the attackers used only built-in Windows tools — PowerShell, WMI, PsExec — and never dropped a malware binary. What does this tell you about detection strategy?
cards.a: Living-off-the-land techniques evade signature AV: you need behavioral detection, command-line logging, and allowlisting of admin tools
cards.x: No-binary attacks defeat file-based defenses entirely. If your detection starts at “malicious file”, LOLBins walk straight past it.

cards.q: A distributor notices its software update server pushing a signed update that nobody authored. The signing key was on that same server. What is the most defensible conclusion?
cards.a: The update infrastructure itself is compromised and the signing key is burned: revoke the key, rebuild the signing pipeline offline, and notify customers to distrust recent updates
cards.x: A signing key on the build server is a single point of failure: once the server falls, every “signed” artifact is suspect. The key must be revoked and the pipeline rebuilt from clean sources.
wrong: Push another update to fix it
The key is fine — it’s signed

cards.q: A company pays a ransomware demand, then gets hit by the same group six weeks later — this time wipers, no ransom note, no decryptor. What is the most defensible lesson?
cards.a: Paying marks you as willing to pay, and some payloads are destructive regardless: the strategy must be backups and containment, never ransom as a plan
cards.x: Ransom payment is not a transaction with a vendor — it funds the next attack and teaches the group you’ll pay. Wipers prove “decryption” was never guaranteed.
wrong: Pay double to get the decryptor

cards.q: An initial access broker’s listing appears on a forum: “Fortune 500 manufacturer, domain admin, $15k.” Three weeks later that manufacturer is hit with ransomware. What is the most defensible takeaway?
cards.a: Access and ransomware are often separate businesses: the broker sold the foothold, the affiliate deployed the payload — defend the initial-access phase, not just the ransomware
cards.x: The ransomware ecosystem is specialized: brokers sell access, affiliates encrypt. Killing the initial access (phishing, exposed services, valid accounts) starves the whole chain.
wrong: The broker is the ransomware author

cards.q: A government contractor’s cleared engineer is recruited on a professional network with a fake job offer, then asked to “review” documents that are actually exfiltration drops. What is the most defensible program response?
cards.a: Treat it as targeted elicitation: brief cleared staff on recruitment lures, report to counterintelligence contacts, and review what the engineer accessed
cards.x: Trusted-contact recruitment is a classic elicitation vector against cleared personnel. The response is awareness plus reporting — and quietly checking whether the hook already landed.
wrong: It’s just a job offer — ignore it

cards.q: Your threat intel feed says a ransomware affiliate is buying access to “any company running unpatched edge VPN.” Your edge VPN is two versions behind. What is the most defensible action today?
cards.a: Emergency-patch the VPN now and hunt for existing footholds — you are the exact profile being bought
cards.x: When intel names your exact configuration as the target, patching becomes emergency change, not next-quarter work. And patch the hole before assuming nobody walked through it.
wrong: Wait for the vendor’s next release

cards.q: A SaaS startup grants a third-party analytics app broad OAuth scopes “to try it out.” Months later the app vendor is breached and attacker sessions appear in customer tenants. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Revoke the app’s grants, scope all third-party OAuth to minimum necessary, require security review before any grant, and audit what the app touched
cards.x: OAuth grants are access: broad scopes given casually become the attacker’s keys. Treat third-party app grants like vendor access — least privilege, reviewed, revocable.

cards.q: During a merger, the acquired company’s network — with flat topology and no EDR — is connected to yours “temporarily.” Six weeks later, malware spreads from their segment to yours. What is the most defensible lesson?
cards.a: Never merge networks before security baselines: acquired networks stay isolated behind strict controls until they meet your standards
cards.x: M&A is a top attack vector because “temporary” connections become permanent with none of your controls. Integration order is: isolate, assess, remediate, then connect.
wrong: Disconnect everything and halt the merger

decks.title: Malware & Intrusion Scenarios
decks.summary: Identifying malware from behavior and choosing the response as exam-style scenarios. (Domain 2.0)

cards.q: A worm is spreading through your SMB shares: patient zero was one laptop, and now 40 machines are infected, each infecting others without any user action. What is the most defensible immediate response?
cards.a: Segment the network to stop lateral spread, then eradicate — worms propagate on their own, so containment is a network action, not a per-host one
cards.x: Worms self-propagate across the network: cleaning hosts one by one while the network stays flat just re-infects them. Stop the spread at the network layer first.

cards.q: An endpoint shows malicious behavior — outbound connections, injected threads — but every AV scan comes back clean and no malicious file exists on disk. What is the most defensible conclusion?
cards.a: Fileless malware running in memory: capture memory for forensics and use EDR behavioral blocking, because signature AV has nothing to find
cards.x: Fileless malware lives in RAM and legitimate processes: no file means no signature. Memory acquisition plus behavioral detection is the only path.
wrong: AV is broken — buy a new one

cards.q: A finance workstation beacons to an external IP every 120 seconds and someone is clearly typing-aware: windows open when the user is away, files accessed in odd order. What is the most defensible conclusion?
cards.a: Remote access trojan with a human operator: isolate the host, capture memory and network, and assume every credential typed there is compromised
cards.x: Interactive behavior — windows moving, files browsed — means a RAT with a live operator, not automated malware. Isolation plus memory forensics, and burn the credentials.

cards.q: An infected server keeps respawning malware after every cleanup: processes hide from Task Manager, AV is disabled on boot, and a “clean” scan finds nothing. What is the most defensible conclusion?
cards.a: Kernel-level rootkit: boot from known-good media or reimage from gold — you cannot trust any tool running on the compromised OS
cards.x: Rootkits subvert the OS itself: every tool you run on the infected system can lie to you. Trust must come from outside the compromised environment.

cards.q: A shared terminal in a warehouse shows a new process logging keystrokes. Fifty workers share that terminal, and it reaches the inventory system. What is the most defensible scope of response?
cards.a: Treat every credential typed on that terminal as compromised: force resets for all users of that terminal plus the inventory system accounts, then rebuild the terminal
cards.x: A keylogger on a shared terminal burns every credential typed there. The blast radius is every account, not just the machine.
wrong: Wipe the terminal and say nothing

cards.q: Ransomware hits, and the note says “we also have 2 TB of your data.” Clean offline backups exist. What is the most defensible response to the demand?
cards.a: Do not pay: restore from backups, engage legal and law enforcement, and prepare breach notification — the exfiltration already happened, payment buys nothing
cards.x: Double extortion defeats the “we have backups” defense: the data is already stolen. Paying doesn’t un-steal it; notification and legal process do the real work.
wrong: Pay quickly to stop the leak
Delete the backups to be safe

cards.q: A disgruntled admin is fired Friday. Monday, the payroll database is wiped. Logs show a scheduled task created three months ago by that admin’s account. What is the most defensible conclusion and fix?
cards.a: Logic bomb planted before termination: restore from clean backups and implement offboarding that revokes access and audits scheduled tasks immediately
cards.x: Logic bombs are time-delayed insider sabotage: the fix is both technical (restore, audit persistence mechanisms at offboarding) and procedural (same-day access revocation).

cards.q: An executive’s personal phone — used for work email — was infected by a sideloaded “productivity” app that reads messages and location. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Treat the device as compromised: revoke its mail and VPN access, force credential resets for accounts used on it, and enforce app-allowlisting via MDM
cards.x: BYOD means the personal device is a corporate attack surface. Sideloaded apps with broad permissions get everything; the response is revocation plus MDM enforcement.
wrong: Tell the executive to delete the app
Wipe the executive’s personal photos too

cards.q: Marketing PCs are slow and full of pop-ups, but no data has left the network. Forensics finds adware bundled with a “free” PDF tool — and the adware also logs browsing. What is the most defensible read?
cards.a: Adware with spyware behavior: remove it fleet-wide, find the bundling source, and treat the browsing data as exfiltrated
cards.x: “Just adware” still exfiltrates: bundling turns nuisance into data collection. The response matches the data risk, not the annoyance level.
wrong: Reimage one PC as an example

cards.q: A new malware strain changes its code with every infection. Signatures catch 10% of samples. What is the most defensible detection strategy?
cards.a: Behavioral and heuristic detection via EDR: judge what the code does, not what it looks like — polymorphic malware defeats static signatures by design
cards.x: Polymorphism exists to beat signatures: the defense moves to behavior — process trees, network patterns, and anomaly detection that don’t care about the bytes.

cards.q: An “invoice.docm” attachment, when opened, spawns PowerShell that downloads a payload. What is the most defensible enterprise fix?
cards.a: Block macros from the internet via Group Policy and detonate attachments in the sandbox — the macro is the execution vector
cards.x: Macro malware needs macros enabled: the enterprise fix is policy (block internet macros) plus detonation, not user training alone.
wrong: Tell users not to open invoices
Macros are safe if the sender is known

cards.q: Cleaned workstations keep getting reinfected within hours. The common factor: a shared USB drive used by the team, with a hidden autorun payload. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Disable autorun fleet-wide, scan and clean every shared drive, and re-clean the workstations after the vector is dead
cards.x: Reinfection means the vector is still alive: cleaning hosts while the USB still carries the payload is mopping with the tap running. Kill the vector, then clean.

cards.q: Ransomware hits, but the “offline” backups are encrypted too — the backup server was domain-joined and reachable. What is the most defensible lesson?
cards.a: Backups must be truly isolated: offline/air-gapped or immutable, on separate credentials — a reachable backup is just another target
cards.x: Ransomware hunts backups first. “Offline” that’s still network-reachable isn’t offline. Immutability and separate credentials are the actual controls.
wrong: Keep backups on the same network but hidden

cards.q: Cloud VMs show 100% CPU at 3 AM with no workload change, and the bill spikes. No data exfiltration is found. What is the most defensible conclusion?
cards.a: Cryptojacking: attackers are mining on your compute — find the initial access, kill the miners, and check for persistence and cost alerts
cards.x: Stolen compute is the quiet monetization: no data theft, just your bill. The response is eviction plus finding how they got in, and billing alerts as detection.

cards.q: A UEFI firmware scan flags an unknown module. The machine was “cleaned” twice by OS reinstall, but the persistence returns. What is the most defensible conclusion?
cards.a: Firmware-level persistence: reflash from vendor media or replace the hardware — OS reinstalls can’t reach below the OS
cards.x: Persistence below the OS survives every reinstall: the fix is firmware reflash from trusted media or hardware replacement, plus supply-chain review.
wrong: Throw the machine in the river

cards.q: A “free” system optimizer downloaded by an employee phones home with browser cookies and saved passwords. What is the most defensible classification and response?
cards.a: Trojan with credential-stealing behavior: remove it, force password resets for all accounts used on that machine, and review software policy
cards.x: Trojans arrive as wanted software and then betray the user: the response matches a credential compromise, not just an uninstall.

cards.q: Dozens of office IP cameras start scanning the internal network. They run ancient firmware the vendor no longer patches. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Isolate the cameras on a dedicated IoT VLAN with no internet or LAN access beyond the NVR, and plan replacement — they’re botnet recruits
cards.x: Unpatchable IoT becomes attacker infrastructure: since you can’t fix the firmware, you contain the devices. Segmentation is the compensating control.
wrong: Give the cameras internet access to “phone home”

cards.q: POS terminals at three stores start sending card data to an unknown server. The malware scrapes RAM, and disk scans find nothing. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Memory-scraping POS malware: isolate the terminals, engage the card brands and forensics (PCI scope), and rebuild from known-good images
cards.x: RAM scrapers live for the moment of the swipe: disk forensics finds little, so the response is isolation, brand notification, and rebuild — plus P2PE to shrink future scope.
wrong: Wipe one terminal as a test
Keep selling — the malware is small

cards.q: The ransom note demands payment but provides no way to identify your files, no chat, no proof of decryption — just a wallet address. What is the most defensible read?
cards.a: Likely a wiper, not ransomware: there is no recovery path, so don’t pay — focus entirely on containment and restoration
cards.x: Real ransomware operations run customer service; a wallet with no ID and no comms is destruction wearing a costume. Payment buys literally nothing.

cards.q: A decryptor for the exact ransomware strain is published by researchers (No More Ransom). What is the most defensible first step before restoring?
cards.a: Verify the decryptor matches your strain and test it on isolated copies — free, tested decryption beats both payment and full rebuilds
cards.x: Public decryptors exist for many strains: check before you pay or rebuild. Test on copies first, because the wrong decryptor can damage files.

cards.q: Images on an internal wiki contain hidden data exfiltrated via steganography. DLP sees only “image uploads.” What is the most defensible detection improvement?
cards.a: Inspect uploads by content and behavior, not just file type: flag anomalous upload volumes and destinations, and strip metadata on internal shares
cards.x: Steganography defeats type-based DLP: the defense is behavioral — who uploads how much to where — plus sanitizing files crossing trust boundaries.

cards.q: A browser extension installed by 200 employees silently exports session cookies to an external server. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Remove the extension fleet-wide via browser policy, revoke all active sessions, and allowlist extensions going forward
cards.x: Session cookies are authentication: their theft bypasses passwords and MFA. Kill the extension, kill the sessions, and take control of the extension catalog.
wrong: Uninstall it on your own machine

cards.q: The CFO wants to negotiate with the ransomware group directly “to save the consultant fees.” What is the most defensible guidance?
cards.a: Do not engage directly: route all contact through counsel and the IR firm — direct negotiation creates legal exposure and usually worsens terms
cards.x: Ransom negotiation is a legal and tactical minefield: sanctions risk, evidence handling, and professional negotiators exist for a reason. Amateurs pay more and risk more.

cards.q: Ransomware detonates Friday at 6 PM on a holiday weekend. The on-call analyst is alone and the IR retainer firm is slow to respond. What is the most defensible preparation lesson?
cards.a: Adversaries time attacks for skeleton crews: the IR plan must include holiday staffing, pre-authorized containment actions, and tested out-of-band comms
cards.x: Timing is a tactic: assume attacks land when you’re thinnest. Pre-authorization for containment and tested backup comms are what make the plan work at 6 PM Friday.

cards.q: A screensaver app on the CEO’s laptop records the screen every 30 seconds and uploads to a free hosting site. What is the most defensible classification?
cards.a: Spyware with visual exfiltration: remove it, assume all displayed data (including credentials and confidential docs) is compromised, and review exec device policy
cards.x: Screen capture bypasses every data control that watches files and keystrokes: what was visible is what was stolen. The response matches a full visual compromise.

decks.title: Social Engineering & Application Attack Scenarios
decks.summary: Phishing variants, credential attacks, and web exploitation as exam-style scenarios. (Domain 2.0)

cards.q: Your CFO receives an email that looks exactly like a board portal notification, with her name, the real meeting date, and a “view documents” link to a lookalike domain. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Treat it as spear phishing: do not click, verify the documents through the real portal or a phone call, and report it — personalization is the tell
cards.x: Spear phishing weaponizes real context: the more accurate the details, the more suspicious the link. Verification must use a channel the attacker doesn’t control.
wrong: Click — the details prove it’s real
Forward it to the whole board as a warning

cards.q: The CEO gets a call from “the bank’s fraud department” about “suspicious wires,” and is pressured to approve a “reversal” immediately. What is the most defensible policy?
cards.a: Hang up and call the bank back on the published number: no legitimate fraud department demands instant wire approvals by phone
cards.x: Whaling plus vishing manufactures authority and urgency. The defense is always the same: terminate the contact and re-establish it through a trusted channel.
wrong: Ask for their employee ID first
Call back the number they give you

cards.q: An attacker calls the helpdesk with an employee’s name, ID, and manager’s name — all from LinkedIn — and requests a password reset “because my phone died.” What is the most defensible procedure?
cards.a: Verify identity through a second factor the attacker can’t have (callback to the number on file, manager confirmation) — public details are not authentication
cards.x: Pretexting assembles public facts into a convincing story. Helpdesk verification must rely on secrets or out-of-band confirmation, never on facts anyone can Google.
wrong: Reset it — they knew the details
Ask for their mother’s maiden name (also public)
Reset it but tell the manager later

cards.q: A USB stick labeled “Salary Review 2026” is found in the lobby. An intern wants to plug it in to “see whose it is.” What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Do not plug it in: hand it to IT unplugged for safe inspection — curiosity is the attack
cards.x: Baiting converts curiosity into initial access. The rule is absolute: found media never touches a production machine; IT inspects it in isolation.
wrong: Plug it into a spare laptop
Open it on a Mac, those are safe

cards.q: Attendees at your industry conference find the event’s Wi-Fi login page replaced by a convincing fake harvesting credentials. What is the most defensible guidance for staff?
cards.a: Verify the network name with organizers, use VPN always, and treat any captive portal asking for corporate credentials as hostile until verified
cards.x: Evil-twin and portal phishing thrive at events: the fix is VPN-by-default plus a standing rule that corporate credentials never go into unverified portals.
wrong: Use cellular and skip the event Wi-Fi entirely — also fine but impractical as policy

cards.q: Employees receive texts about “missed package delivery” with a tracking link. The link leads to a credential-harvesting page mimicking the mail carrier. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Warn the company, block the domains, and remind staff that carriers never ask for credentials via text — report, don’t tap
cards.x: Smishing exploits routine life events. The organizational response is broadcast warning plus domain blocking; the individual rule is: delivery texts never need your password.

cards.q: Parking tickets appear on windshields with a QR code to “pay the fine.” The QR leads to a payment page that also installs a malicious profile. What is the most defensible guidance?
cards.a: Never scan unsolicited QR codes for payments: verify fines through the official city site or office, and treat QR codes as untrusted links
cards.x: Quishing hides the malicious URL behind pixels: you can’t hover a QR code. Unsolicited QR payment demands get verified through official channels, never scanned.
wrong: QR codes are safe by design
Pay cash to the person nearby

cards.q: A login page’s password manager refuses to autofill, the URL is yourb4nk.com, and the page asks for your full card number “for verification.” What is the most defensible conclusion?
cards.a: Credential-harvesting phishing page: close it, report it, and if anything was entered, reset credentials and watch for fraud
cards.x: Password managers are phishing detectors: refusal to autofill plus a lookalike domain plus over-collection of data is the full phishing signature.

cards.q: Your login form returns “user not found” vs “wrong password” differently, and attackers are enumerating valid accounts. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Return a generic “invalid credentials” for both cases and add rate limiting plus anomaly detection on the login endpoint
cards.x: Distinct error messages are an oracle for account enumeration. Generic errors plus throttling close the information leak without hurting real users.

cards.q: Attackers try thousands of username/password pairs from a breach dump against your VPN: 3 attempts per user, rotating IPs. Account lockouts never trigger. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: This is password spraying: enforce MFA, throttle by behavior not just count, and force resets on accounts that authenticated during the window
cards.x: Spraying stays under lockout thresholds by design: the defense is MFA plus behavioral rate-limiting, and treating any success during the window as compromise.
wrong: VPN logs are too noisy to matter

cards.q: A support ticket field reflects a customer’s input back to agents’ browsers unescaped, and an attacker’s ticket runs script in an admin’s session. What is the most defensible classification and fix?
cards.a: Stored XSS with session-hijack impact: output-encode all user content, set HttpOnly/SameSite on session cookies, and review stored data for payloads
cards.x: Stored XSS turns your app into the attacker’s delivery: every viewer is a victim. Encoding output plus hardened cookies contains it; then clean the stored payloads.
wrong: Tell agents not to open tickets

cards.q: Changing /invoice?id=1042 to id=1043 shows another customer’s invoice. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Enforce authorization server-side on every object access (IDOR fix): the session’s user must own the requested object — never trust the parameter
cards.x: IDOR is missing authorization, not missing authentication: the user is logged in, just looking at someone else’s data. Every object fetch must check ownership.

cards.q: An XML invoice upload triggers outbound connections to internal metadata endpoints. What is the most defensible conclusion and fix?
cards.a: XXE: the parser resolves external entities — disable external entity resolution and validate uploads; SSRF via XXE reaches cloud metadata
cards.x: XML parsers with external entities enabled become SSRF engines: in cloud, that path leads to instance credentials. Disable XXE and treat uploads as hostile.

cards.q: Your app serializes session state into a signed-but-not-encrypted cookie, and attackers are tampering with roles. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Stop trusting client-side state: keep authorization server-side and treat the cookie as an opaque token — signatures don’t stop replay or logic abuse
cards.x: Signed client state still lets attackers replay and probe: the fix is server-side sessions where the cookie is just a random identifier.

cards.q: A coupon code can be applied twice by double-clicking “redeem” fast, granting double credit. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Make redemption atomic server-side (single transaction, idempotency key): race conditions are fixed with atomicity, not with UI debouncing
cards.x: Race conditions exploit the gap between check and use: only server-side atomic operations close it. Client-side fixes are decorations.

cards.q: An API key for your payment processor is found in a public GitHub repo, committed 8 months ago. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Revoke and rotate the key immediately, audit all usage in that window for fraud, and add secrets scanning to CI — assume it was abused
cards.x: A public key is a compromised key: the window of exposure demands rotation plus a usage audit, and prevention means secrets never reach the repo via scanning.
wrong: The key is old, so it’s fine

cards.q: A password-reset link lets anyone set a session cookie value before logging in, keeping that session after login. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Regenerate the session ID at login (fixation fix): pre-login session identifiers must never survive authentication
cards.x: Session fixation plants the session before auth so the attacker already holds it: the fix is issuing a fresh session ID at the moment of login.

cards.q: An admin panel can be iframed by any site, and a crafted page tricks admins into clicking hidden “delete user” buttons. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Set X-Frame-Options/DENY or frame-ancestors and require anti-CSRF tokens on state-changing actions: clickjacking needs both framing and forgery defenses
cards.x: Clickjacking abuses the user’s authenticated browser: deny framing and require per-action tokens so forged requests fail even if framed.

cards.q: A file upload accepts “.jpg” but never checks content; attackers upload webshells renamed to .jpg. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Validate content server-side (magic bytes, re-encode images), store uploads outside the web root, and never execute the upload directory
cards.x: Extension checks are theater: the fix is content validation plus making the upload location non-executable and non-web-accessible.

cards.q: Attackers use your “forgot username” flow to harvest which email addresses have accounts, then target those users with phishing. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Make the flow ambiguous (“if an account exists, we’ve emailed it”) and throttle it: account enumeration feeds targeted phishing
cards.x: Helpful error messages are reconnaissance: the secure pattern confirms nothing while still serving legitimate users via email.

cards.q: A state-changing action (change email) happens via GET request with no token. A malicious link triggers it for logged-in users. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Require POST with anti-CSRF tokens on all state-changing actions: GET must never change state
cards.x: CSRF rides the victim’s authenticated browser: the fix is tokens on every mutation plus the HTTP-method discipline that makes GET safe.
wrong: GET is fine for small changes

cards.q: Your search box reflects the query into the page without encoding, and a crafted link pops an alert in victims’ browsers. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Output-encode the reflection (reflected XSS) and add Content-Security-Policy: encoding kills the payload, CSP contains what encoding misses
cards.x: Reflected XSS needs a victim to click, but clicks happen: encode output at the sink and layer CSP as defense in depth.

cards.q: A legacy app concatenates user input into SQL: admin’ OR ‘1’=’1’ -- logs in as admin. What is the most defensible permanent fix?
cards.a: Parameterized queries everywhere: separate code from data at the database driver — input sanitization alone is fragile
cards.x: Injection is a code/data boundary failure: parameters enforce the boundary structurally, while blacklists and escaping are bypassable.
wrong: It’s a legacy app — accept it

cards.q: Attackers order password resets for hundreds of users at once, flooding inboxes and the helpdesk — then call pretending to be IT “helping with the reset emails.” What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Throttle reset requests, warn users of the pattern, and train the helpdesk that a reset flood followed by “helpful” calls is a coordinated attack
cards.x: The flood is the setup: overwhelmed users plus a “helpful” caller equals credential handover. Throttling plus pattern-awareness breaks the play.

cards.q: A contractor’s laptop, used on your VPN, is found running a remote-access tool the contractor installed “for convenience.” What is the most defensible policy response?
cards.a: Prohibit unauthorized remote-access tools on any device touching the network, audit what it exposed, and enforce endpoint compliance before VPN access
cards.x: Shadow remote-access tools are unmanaged backdoors: the fix is policy plus technical enforcement — non-compliant endpoints don’t get VPN.

decks.title: Vulnerability Response & Mitigation Scenarios
decks.summary: Scan interpretation, zero-days, and compensating controls as exam-style scenarios. (Domain 2.0)

cards.q: An unauthenticated scan reports 4,000 “critical” findings, mostly version banners on a hardened Linux fleet that is fully patched. What is the most defensible interpretation?
cards.a: Likely false positives from banner-based detection: verify with credentialed scanning before treating any finding as real
cards.x: Unauthenticated scans guess from banners; credentialed scans verify from the package manager. Treating banner matches as findings burns the quarter on ghosts.

cards.q: A zero-day is announced for your exact firewall model, with active exploitation in the wild and no patch yet. What is the most defensible immediate posture?
cards.a: Apply compensating controls now: restrict management interfaces, deploy IPS signatures, increase monitoring — then patch the hour it drops
cards.x: Zero-days invert the order: when no patch exists, exposure reduction and detection become the patch. Waiting unprotected for the vendor is not a strategy.

cards.q: A CVSS 9.8 vulnerability sits on an isolated lab machine with no network route to production; a CVSS 7.5 sits on the internet-facing VPN. One emergency window exists. What is the most defensible choice?
cards.a: Patch the VPN: CVSS measures severity, risk measures your exposure — exploitability plus reachability outranks the number
cards.x: The number describes the flaw; your network describes the danger. An exposed 7.5 with a public exploit beats an unreachable 9.8 every time.

cards.q: The scan flags “missing critical patch” on servers your team patched last month. Spot checks show the patches are installed. What is the most defensible conclusion?
cards.a: False positive from stale scan data or version detection: re-scan with current plugins and credentialed access before reopening the work
cards.x: Scans lie in predictable ways: outdated plugins and banner checks flag patched systems. Verify the finding before re-doing the work.

cards.q: A network scan discovers 60 devices nobody recognizes: cameras, a 3D printer, and several “test” VMs. What is the most defensible conclusion?
cards.a: Shadow IT and unknown assets: quarantine them to a discovery VLAN, identify owners, and either onboard or remove — unscanned assets are unpatched assets
cards.x: You can’t protect what you don’t know: discovery must be continuous and reconciled. Unknown devices get contained first, identified second.
wrong: If nobody knows them, they’re harmless

cards.q: A pen test finds default credentials on 200 printers and cameras. What is the most defensible program-level fix?
cards.a: Change all defaults via centralized management, scan for remaining instances, and add default-credential checks to provisioning — one finding means a class of findings
cards.x: A single default-credential finding is never single: the fix is fleet-wide remediation plus a provisioning control so it can’t recur.

cards.q: A legacy payment terminal requires TLS 1.0, which PCI forbids. Replacing it takes nine months. What is the most defensible interim posture?
cards.a: Documented compensating control: isolate the terminal on its own segment, monitor all its traffic, restrict to the payment processor — with a dated replacement plan
cards.x: When the standard can’t be met yet, compensating controls plus a deadline are the defensible path. “We’ll fix it someday” is not a control.

cards.q: A researcher reports your password-reset tokens are predictable: requesting two resets reveals the pattern. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Use cryptographically random, single-use, expiring tokens generated server-side — predictable tokens are account-takeover tokens
cards.x: Token predictability is a design flaw, not a bug: randomness plus single-use plus expiry, generated where the attacker can’t observe the algorithm.
wrong: Make tokens longer but keep the pattern
Rate-limit resets and call it fixed

cards.q: Your login API responds 2ms faster for valid usernames than invalid ones, and attackers are timing it. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Constant-time comparison and uniform response handling: side channels leak through timing, so make valid and invalid paths indistinguishable
cards.x: Timing differences are information: the fix is making both code paths cost the same, plus the usual generic errors and throttling.

cards.q: A software composition scan finds a critical CVE in a logging library buried three dependencies deep in your flagship app. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Upgrade the dependency chain immediately and add SCA to CI so vulnerable libraries can’t merge — transitive dependencies are still your code
cards.x: Your app inherits its dependencies’ vulnerabilities: the fix is upgrade now plus automated composition scanning in the pipeline.
wrong: Wait for the next release cycle

cards.q: A container image scan reports 300 vulnerabilities in the base OS layer. What is the most defensible build fix?
cards.a: Switch to a minimal base image, rebuild regularly, and scan in CI — most of those vulns are packages your app never uses
cards.x: Fat base images import hundreds of irrelevant vulnerabilities: minimal bases plus automated rebuilds shrink the scan to what matters.
wrong: Containers are isolated, so it’s fine

cards.q: An MRI-adjacent workstation runs Windows 7, unpatchable, on the clinical network. What is the most defensible posture?
cards.a: Isolate it on a dedicated clinical segment with only required traffic allowed, monitor the segment, and document the exception with a review date
cards.x: Unpatchable medical systems get the standard treatment: micro-segmentation, allowlisted traffic, monitoring, and a dated risk exception — not hope.
wrong: Upgrade it anyway and break the MRI
Windows 7 is fine behind a firewall

cards.q: This month’s scan shows half the usual findings. Investigation finds the scan service account’s password expired mid-scan. What is the most defensible conclusion?
cards.a: The results are invalid: an unauthenticated partial scan — fix the credentials, re-run fully, and never report partial results as complete
cards.x: A scan that silently degrades to unauthenticated is worse than no scan: it reports confidence it doesn’t have. Credential health is part of scan integrity.

cards.q: A critical finding affects a system being decommissioned in 30 days; the fix costs $80k and a weekend outage. What is the most defensible decision?
cards.a: Formal risk acceptance with a 30-day expiry and compensating monitoring — not silent ignoring: the acceptance must be written, signed, and time-boxed
cards.x: Risk acceptance is a decision with paperwork and an expiry, not a shrug. Decommissioning on schedule is the remediation; the acceptance covers the gap.

cards.q: A researcher emails a detailed vulnerability report with a 90-day disclosure deadline. What is the most defensible process?
cards.a: Acknowledge promptly, validate, fix within the window, credit the researcher, and publish coordinated disclosure — the deadline is the deal
cards.x: Coordinated disclosure is a contract: good-faith researchers get validation, a fix timeline, and credit. Ghosting them converts allies into full-disclosure.
wrong: Fix it silently and deny everything

cards.q: Your bug bounty gets the same XSS report from five researchers in a week. What is the most defensible program response?
cards.a: Deduplicate to the first reporter, pay per policy, fix once, and add the pattern to your security testing — duplicates signal a systemic miss
cards.x: Duplicate reports mean the flaw class is widespread or your testing missed it: pay fairly, fix the instance, then hunt the pattern.

cards.q: A CSPM tool flags a storage bucket as public containing customer exports. Access logs show anonymous GETs for three weeks. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Make it private immediately, determine exactly what was accessed from the logs, and trigger the breach-notification process with legal — exposure plus access equals incident
cards.x: A public bucket is a finding; anonymous downloads make it a breach. Remediation is instant, but the logs decide whether notification duties trigger.
wrong: Make it private and say nothing

cards.q: A scan finds database credentials hardcoded in a mobile app shipped to 50,000 users. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Rotate the credentials immediately, scope the new ones to least privilege, audit usage, and move secrets to a vault with CI scanning to prevent recurrence
cards.x: Shipped secrets are public secrets: rotation is step one, but the window demands a usage audit, and prevention means secrets never compile into the app.
wrong: The app is already shipped — too late

cards.q: A server negotiates 3DES and TLS 1.0 with clients. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Disable weak protocols and ciphers, test client compatibility in stages, and monitor for breakage — negotiated weakness is attacker’s choice
cards.x: Protocol negotiation lets attackers pick the weakest option: the fix is removing the weak options server-side, with staged rollout to catch legacy clients.

cards.q: A DNS record points to a cloud storage bucket deleted last year. A researcher claims it and serves your branded phishing page. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Delete the dangling DNS record immediately and audit all DNS for dead cloud references — abandoned records are attacker real estate
cards.x: Subdomain takeover needs only a dangling record: the fix is DNS hygiene — remove dead references and continuously audit against live resources.

cards.q: An external researcher reports reading your internal wiki via a misconfigured reverse proxy. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Fix the proxy config, audit access logs for what was read, thank and credit the researcher — external reports are free pen tests
cards.x: Treat reporter findings like incident intel: remediate, scope via logs, and keep the relationship — hostile responses to helpers end the help.

cards.q: Your VPN concentrator has a KEV-listed vulnerability with active exploitation, and the patch needs a maintenance window. What is the most defensible call?
cards.a: Emergency change now: KEV plus active exploitation plus internet exposure is the textbook emergency — staged rollout, tested rollback, communicate
cards.x: KEV-listed and exploited in the wild collapses the change-management debate: this is what emergency windows exist for.

cards.q: A vulnerability is found in the backup software itself, with admin access to every backup job. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Patch the backup platform first, then verify backup integrity and test a restore — compromised backups undermine every recovery plan
cards.x: Backup infrastructure is the crown jewel: a flaw there threatens recovery itself. Patch it, then prove the backups are still trustworthy by restoring.
wrong: The backup vendor will handle it

cards.q: Vulnerability scans keep crashing the legacy order system during business hours. What is the most defensible scanning posture?
cards.a: Scan in maintenance windows with throttled intensity, plus agent-based scanning for fragile hosts — adapt the scan to the asset, don’t skip it
cards.x: Disruptive scanning gets skipped, and skipped assets stay vulnerable: the fix is gentler methods and better windows, not exemptions.

cards.q: Mean time to remediate criticals has climbed from 9 to 41 days over two quarters, while closed-ticket counts look great. What is the most defensible read?
cards.a: The program is optimizing easy wins: re-anchor on risk-based SLAs for exposed criticals and report aging — ticket counts reward the wrong behavior
cards.x: When MTTR climbs while closures look good, the team is closing easy findings. Leadership needs aging and exposure-weighted metrics, not counts.

decks.title: Security Architecture: Cloud & Virtualization Scenarios
decks.summary: Shared responsibility, IaC, containers, and cloud controls as exam-style scenarios. (Domain 3.0)

cards.q: A junior admin makes an S3 bucket public “temporarily” to share a build, and access logs show anonymous GETs for three days before anyone notices. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Restrict the bucket to private immediately, scope exactly what was accessed from the logs, and trigger the breach-notification process with legal if customer data was involved
cards.x: A public bucket is a finding; anonymous downloads make it a breach. Remediation is instant, but the logs decide whether notification duties trigger.
wrong: Make it private and say nothing — three days is nothing
Public buckets are a normal sharing pattern
Blame the junior admin and move on

cards.q: A developer runs company workloads in a personal AWS account “because procurement is slow”. The account has no CloudTrail and no SSO. What is the most defensible move?
cards.a: Migrate the workloads into the organization account with SSO and SCPs, then close or inventory the personal account
cards.x: Shadow cloud has no logging, no guardrails, no offboarding — work that lives outside the organization boundary is invisible to security.
wrong: Approve it as a pilot and leave it running
It is his account, so it is his problem
Block his credit card and hope for the best

cards.q: A CSPM scan flags 300 security groups open to 0.0.0.0/0 across 12 accounts. The app teams say “some of those are needed”. What is the most defensible approach?
cards.a: Triage before touching anything: required public services go behind the load balancer with narrowed rules, ephemeral leftovers get closed, everything under change control
cards.x: Blindly deleting 300 rules is an outage; ignoring them is exposure. The defensible path is classify, narrow, and control.
wrong: Delete all 300 rules at once and see what breaks
0.0.0.0/0 is fine if nothing bad happened yet
Open a ticket for each rule and wait

cards.q: Friday’s deploy went fine, but Monday’s Terraform plan shows 40 resources drifted from code after a weekend hotfix. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Reconcile the hotfix into code and re-apply so the state matches — unmanaged changes that stay become permanent infrastructure
cards.x: Drift is debt with a timer: the longer hotfixes live outside code, the more the next deploy surprises you. Codify it or lose the audit trail.
wrong: Delete the resources and redeploy from code
Disable Terraform so plans stop complaining

cards.q: A serverless function processes payments with an IAM role that has AdministratorAccess “because the docs example did”. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Scope the role to exactly the APIs the function calls, per function, with no wildcards
cards.x: Ephemeral code with standing admin privilege is the worst of both worlds: tiny blast radius only if the role is tiny. Scope it to the function’s actual calls.
wrong: Serverless is ephemeral, so admin is fine
Functions are too small to be attacked
Add more permissions to be safe

cards.q: The container registry allows pushing unsigned images, and production deploys whatever is tagged latest. What is the most defensible control?
cards.a: Require signed images and enforce an admission policy so only signed images run in production
cards.x: Unsigned images in prod mean anyone with push access owns the cluster. Signing plus admission control makes the registry a gate, not a shelf.
wrong: Latest tag is a deployment strategy
The registry is internal, so it is trusted

cards.q: A pen test shows the web app is vulnerable to SSRF, and the cloud metadata service still runs in IMDSv1 mode. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Enforce IMDSv2, which requires a token — a metadata request then needs the token, not just a URL fetch
cards.x: SSRF to 169.254.169.254 is the classic cloud credential theft: IMDSv2 breaks the one-request theft by requiring a PUT for the token first.
wrong: IMDSv1 is fine behind the firewall
Block 169.254.169.254 in the app code only

cards.q: The CI system deploys to Kubernetes with a cluster-admin service account. What is the most defensible change?
cards.a: Replace it with a namespace-scoped role granting only the verbs the pipeline needs
cards.x: Automation with cluster-admin is standing privilege that never sleeps: a compromised pipeline token becomes a cluster takeover. Scope the role to the job.
wrong: CI needs admin to work properly
Rotate the token monthly and keep admin

cards.q: The company runs AWS, Azure, and GCP, and nobody can list all production assets in one place. What is the most defensible first step?
cards.a: Aggregate into one inventory with consistent tagging via a CSPM or CMDB — you cannot protect what you cannot enumerate
cards.x: Multi-cloud without a single asset view is three blind spots. Tagging standards plus aggregation turn sprawl into an inventory.
wrong: Each cloud team manages its own list

cards.q: EU customers learn their data sits in a US region, and the contracts promise EU residency. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Migrate the data to an EU region and document the residency control — residency is a legal requirement, not a technical preference
cards.x: Data residency is decided by contracts and regulators, not latency. When the contract says EU, the region choice is compliance, not convenience.
wrong: The cloud is global, so residency is outdated
Ask the customers not to worry

cards.q: Development, staging, and production all live in one AWS account to “keep billing simple”. What is the most defensible change?
cards.a: Separate accounts under the organization with SCP guardrails — blast radius, logging, and billing separation all follow the account boundary
cards.x: One account means one failure domain: a dev mistake can delete prod, and you cannot tell whose spend is whose. Accounts are the cloud’s cheapest isolation.
wrong: One account is simpler and therefore safer

cards.q: CloudTrail is disabled in two regions “to save on storage costs”. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Re-enable it everywhere immediately — audit logging is not an optional line item
cards.x: The regions without trails are the regions attackers will find. Logging is the cheapest control in the building; cutting it is not savings.
wrong: Attackers only target the main region
Storage costs are a real security trade-off
Enable it only after an incident

cards.q: API keys are committed in the mobile app’s repo and also baked into the container image. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Rotate every exposed key now, move secrets to a vault injected at runtime, and add secret scanning to CI
cards.x: A committed secret is a public secret: rotation closes the window, but only vault-at-runtime plus scanning keeps it closed.
wrong: The repo is private, so the keys are safe
Rotate them at the next release

cards.q: The golden image pipeline broke two years ago, so every new VM starts from a 2023 base and gets patched at boot. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Rebuild the pipeline: minimal hardened base, monthly rebuilds, scan before deploy — patch-at-boot is drift with extra steps
cards.x: Images rot: every manual patch at boot is an untested, unaudited snowflake. Build once, scan it, deploy it everywhere.
wrong: Patch-at-boot is basically the same thing
2023 was a fine year for software

cards.q: A SaaS vendor you depend on announces a breach exposing customer data you store with them. What remains YOUR responsibility?
cards.a: Your users, access controls, data classification, sharing settings, and your own incident response — the provider secures the platform, not your configuration
cards.x: Shared responsibility does not end at the vendor’s breach notification: your half of the model is still yours. Review your side, rotate keys, audit sharing.
wrong: Immediately migrate to a new vendor

cards.q: The lift-and-shift migration kept the on-prem flat firewall rules “for compatibility”. What is the most defensible redesign?
cards.a: Rebuild with tiered security groups — web, app, data tiers with explicit flows — because flat rules in the cloud are still a flat network
cards.x: Lift-and-shift carries the old weaknesses along: compatibility with a bad design is not a reason to keep it. Segment in the cloud’s own primitives.

cards.q: A cryptominer is found on a production VM, and the bill spiked 40%. What is the most defensible first action?
cards.a: Isolate the instance, preserve it for forensics, rotate any credentials it could reach, then hunt for the entry point
cards.x: Mining is a symptom of compromise, not a billing problem: the instance is evidence, and the attacker’s keys are still valid until rotated.
wrong: Just terminate it and move on
Miners are a cost problem, not security
Pay the bill and increase the budget

cards.q: An internal API has no authentication “because it is only reachable internally”. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Add authentication and authorization anyway — internal reachability is not a control, especially after one phishing email
cards.x: The perimeter is porous: once an attacker is inside, unauthenticated “internal” APIs are free moves. Authenticate every API.
wrong: Internal APIs do not need auth
It is behind the firewall, so it is safe
Add auth only if it gets attacked

cards.q: A cross-account role trusts “*” as the principal for “flexibility”. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Scope the trust policy to the specific account and role, and require an external ID for third-party access
cards.x: A wildcard principal is an open door with a welcome mat: trust policies must name exactly who may assume the role, and external IDs stop confused-deputy attacks.
wrong: The * only applies to our accounts

cards.q: The entire platform runs in one region; the DR plan says “we will figure it out”. What is the most defensible architecture?
cards.a: At minimum multi-AZ for resilience, with a tested cross-region plan only if the RTO/RPO justify the cost — “figure it out” is not a plan
cards.x: Region choice is a business decision expressed in RTO/RPO: multi-AZ survives datacenter loss, cross-region survives regional loss, and both need testing.
wrong: One region is fine — clouds do not go down
Multi-region doubles the bill for nothing

cards.q: Compliance requires dedicated cryptographic hardware, but the team proposes KMS. What is the most defensible choice?
cards.a: If the requirement is single-tenant FIPS 140-2 Level 3, use CloudHSM; otherwise managed KMS is the defensible default
cards.x: Managed KMS is multi-tenant by design: when the auditor requires dedicated hardware boundaries, only a dedicated HSM satisfies it.

cards.q: Three-year-old IAM users with console access and no MFA belong to people who left. What is the most defensible program fix?
cards.a: Deprovision immediately and institute quarterly access reviews with automated deprovisioning on HR events
cards.x: Orphaned accounts are standing invitations: the fix is joiner-mover-leaver automation so access dies when employment does.
wrong: MFA is optional for old accounts

cards.q: Cloud backups live in the same account as production, and ransomware just encrypted both. What is the most defensible redesign?
cards.a: Separate backup account with Object Lock immutability — backups must survive the compromise of production
cards.x: A backup an attacker can delete is a copy, not a recovery plan. Immutability plus a separate account puts recovery outside the blast radius.

cards.q: The API gateway fronts 200 microservices with a single shared API key. What is the most defensible change?
cards.a: Per-client credentials with scopes and rotation, rate limiting per key — one shared key is one shared compromise
cards.x: A shared key means one leak revokes everyone or revokes nobody: per-client keys make compromise survivable.
wrong: Shared keys are easier to manage
Internal APIs do not need keys

cards.q: A production app authenticates to AWS with a static access key baked into the AMI, and the key is two years old. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Replace it with an IAM role attached to the instance — workload identity with automatic rotation — and revoke the static key
cards.x: Static keys are standing credentials that never expire on their own: roles for compute give the same access with no secret to steal, and rotation is automatic.
wrong: Baked-in keys are fine on private AMIs
Put the key in an env var instead

decks.title: Security Architecture: Network Design Scenarios
decks.summary: Segmentation, zero trust, VPN choices, and secure topologies as exam-style scenarios. (Domain 3.0)

cards.q: After a breach, the forensics team reports the attacker crossed from a phishing laptop to the domain controllers in 40 minutes on a flat /16. What is the most defensible architectural fix?
cards.a: Segment into tiered networks with firewall-enforced flows — user, server, and management tiers at minimum — so one compromised host is one failure, not the whole estate
cards.x: Lateral movement speed is a network-design metric: flat networks are a single failure domain. Segmentation turns a 40-minute domain takeover into a contained host.
wrong: Flat networks are faster to manage
Add more EDR and keep it flat

cards.q: A vendor needs access to one database for a week. The current answer is a full-tunnel VPN to the whole network. What is the most defensible alternative?
cards.a: Per-application access via ZTNA or a jump host with scoped credentials and session recording, time-boxed to the engagement
cards.x: A week of full-network VPN for one database is standing over-privilege: grant the application, not the network, and expire it automatically.
wrong: Full VPN is simpler for vendors
Open the firewall to their office IP

cards.q: Thirty branches run expensive MPLS; the proposal is SD-WAN with internet underlay. What is the most defensible evaluation?
cards.a: Compare encrypted overlay with centralized policy against the MPLS cost — SD-WAN wins on agility and price only if the overlay is encrypted and centrally controlled
cards.x: The transport decision is threat-model plus cost: unencrypted SD-WAN is just the internet, while MPLS bought you a private path you are giving up.
wrong: SD-WAN is always cheaper and safe

cards.q: Remote staff still use a legacy VPN concentrator, and helpdesk sees weekly credential-phishing reports. What is the most defensible direction?
cards.a: Migrate to ZTNA with device posture checks — per-app access that verifies identity and device on every request, not just at login
cards.x: VPN credentials are a single phishable secret guarding the whole network: ZTNA shrinks the blast radius to the one application.

cards.q: The OT network that runs the factory floor is routable from the corporate LAN “for convenience”. What is the most defensible architecture?
cards.a: Isolate OT behind a DMZ or data diode with only required flows, and monitor the boundary — convenience is how factories get ransomware
cards.x: IT/OT convergence without a boundary puts production lines one phishing email from the helpdesk: the diode or firewall makes the crossing deliberate.

cards.q: Guest Wi-Fi shares a VLAN with the point-of-sale terminals. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Separate SSID on its own VLAN with client isolation and a captive portal — guests must never share broadcast space with payment systems
cards.x: A guest device on the POS VLAN is a PCI failure and a pivot away from card data: segmentation is the control, not hoping guests behave.
wrong: VLANs are too complex for Wi-Fi

cards.q: Two hundred employees share one WPA2 pre-shared key, and the password is on a sticky note in the break room. What is the most defensible change?
cards.a: Move to enterprise 802.1X with per-user or per-device credentials — a shared PSK has no attribution and rotation means touching 200 devices
cards.x: Shared keys fail twice: you cannot tell who connected, and one departure forces a building-wide rotation. Per-user credentials fix both.

cards.q: An employee plugs in a personal travel router to “get better Wi-Fi”. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Remove it, scan for rogue devices with WIDS, and enforce port security plus 802.1X so unauthorized devices cannot join
