cards.x: Rogue APs bridge your secured network to an uncontrolled one: detection finds them, 802.1X and port security keep them off.

cards.q: The new IPS is inline and immediately starts blocking legitimate payroll traffic. What is the most defensible deployment?
cards.a: Run in detect-only mode first, tune out false positives, then enable blocking in stages
cards.x: Inline blocking with untuned signatures is a self-inflicted outage: the defensible rollout is IDS-mode tuning, then staged prevention.

cards.q: The DMZ web server has a direct rule to the internal database on 1433. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Remove it: the web tier talks to an app tier, and only the app tier reaches the database on required ports
cards.x: A compromised web server with a direct DB path is game over: tiering means each layer only reaches the next, never skips.

cards.q: The jump server — the only path into the server VLAN — has no MFA and keeps a shared admin password. What is the most defensible hardening?
cards.a: Enforce MFA, per-admin accounts, session recording, and source allow-listing — the bastion is the keys to the kingdom
cards.x: A bastion concentrates all admin access: without MFA and individual accountability, one phished password owns every server.

cards.q: IPv6 is enabled by default on all hosts but no firewall rules or monitoring cover it. What is the most defensible posture?
cards.a: Either manage it — firewall rules, RA guard, monitoring — or disable it where unused; an unmanaged protocol is an unmanaged attack surface
cards.x: Attackers love the protocol you forgot: IPv6 tunnels and rogue RAs bypass IPv4-only controls. Managed or off, never ignored.
wrong: IPv6 is the future, leave it

cards.q: The SOC sees DNS queries to random-looking domains every 30 seconds from a finance workstation. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Isolate the host, block outbound DNS except via the resolvers, and inspect — beaconing over DNS is a classic C2 channel
cards.x: DNS is the covert channel that firewalls wave through: periodic random domains are the tell. Force DNS through your resolvers and watch.
wrong: It is probably just Windows Update

cards.q: There is no packet capture or flow data at the internet edge — “the firewall logs are enough”. What is the most defensible addition?
cards.a: Full packet capture or at minimum NetFlow plus an NDR sensor at the edge — logs tell you what the firewall decided, not what happened
cards.x: Firewall logs are the bouncer’s diary: for forensics you need the actual traffic. Capture at the chokepoint before you need it.

cards.q: VoIP phones share the data VLAN with workstations. What is the most defensible change?
cards.a: Dedicated voice VLAN with 802.1X — segmentation by function, so a compromised laptop cannot reach the phone system
cards.x: Mixed voice and data means eavesdropping and toll fraud ride the same wire: a voice VLAN with authentication separates them.

cards.q: The entire datacenter hangs off one core switch with no redundancy. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Build a redundant core/distribution design — the core is a single point of failure for everything behind it
cards.x: Redundancy belongs where failure hurts most: one core switch means one failed power supply away from a total outage.
wrong: Buy a spare and keep it in the box

cards.q: All branch traffic backhauls through headquarters, and video calls crawl. What is the most defensible change?
cards.a: Local internet breakout with SASE policy enforcement — backhauling everything is latency, cost, and a single path
cards.x: Hairpinning SaaS traffic through HQ made sense in 2010: split-tunnel with cloud-delivered security keeps policy without the trombone.
wrong: The internet at branches is unsafe

cards.q: A MAC-flooding attack crashes the access switch’s CAM table, turning it into a hub. What is the most defensible mitigation?
cards.a: Port security with MAC limits, sticky learning, and violation shutdown — bound the table before it can be flooded
cards.x: CAM exhaustion is physics: limit addresses per port and shut violators down. The switch stops being a switch only if you let it.

cards.q: Cameras, badge readers, and HVAC controllers sit on the user LAN. What is the most defensible placement?
cards.a: Dedicated IoT VLAN with internet-only access and no path to the LAN — compromised cameras are botnet members waiting for orders
cards.x: IoT devices are unpatchable by design: the VLAN contains them, and no-LAN rules keep a Mirai moment from becoming your moment.
wrong: VLANs per device type is excessive

cards.q: Management interfaces (iDRAC, switch admin) are reachable from the user LAN. What is the most defensible change?
cards.a: Move them to an out-of-band management network, reachable only via the bastion — management planes are the highest-value targets
cards.x: An iDRAC on the user LAN is a backdoor with a web UI: one compromised laptop away from bare-metal control. Isolate the management plane.

cards.q: The firewall has 4,000 rules, and nobody knows what half of them do. What is the most defensible cleanup?
cards.a: Audit by hit counts, remove the unused, document the rest with owners and expiry — rule cruft hides real holes
cards.x: Firewall rules accrete like sediment: unused rules are unreviewed allow-lists. Measure, prune, and give every rule an owner and a reason.

cards.q: Server-to-server traffic inside the datacenter is completely uninspected. What is the most defensible addition?
cards.a: Microsegmentation or host-based firewalls on the servers — the perimeter-only model died when phishing did
cards.x: East-west is where ransomware lives: encrypt and policy the lateral paths, not just the front door.

cards.q: A second ISP is proposed “for redundancy” but both circuits enter through the same conduit. What is the most defensible design?
cards.a: Diverse physical paths and ideally diverse providers — shared conduit is a single backhoe away from dual failure
cards.x: Redundancy that shares a failure mode is theater: path diversity is the actual control.
wrong: One ISP with a good SLA

cards.q: The honeypot sits in the production VLAN and keeps alerting on the backup server’s scans. What is the most defensible placement?
cards.a: Isolated decoy segment with no production traffic — a honeypot among real systems produces noise and legal ambiguity
cards.x: Decoys only work when every touch is suspicious: production noise ruins the signal, and entrapping legitimate users creates liability.
wrong: Noise is fine, more alerts are better
The backup server is the attacker

cards.q: NAC is deployed in monitor mode and has been “almost ready” for two years. What is the most defensible push?
cards.a: Define the enforcement policy, pilot on one VLAN, then enforce in stages — monitor-mode forever is a dashboard, not a control
cards.x: NAC only works when it can say no: the blockers are always exceptions and politics, so pilot small and enforce deliberately.
wrong: NAC is too disruptive to enforce

decks.title: Security Architecture: Data Protection Scenarios
decks.summary: Classification, encryption, keys, and DLP as exam-style scenarios. (Domain 3.0)

cards.q: The company has no data classification — every file gets the same handling. What is the most defensible first step?
cards.a: Define classes (public, internal, confidential, restricted) with handling rules, then classify by business impact — controls follow classification
cards.x: Protection without classification is guesswork: you cannot encrypt “everything” sensibly. Classes tell each system what it is protecting and how hard.
wrong: Encrypt everything with the same key

cards.q: Application logs containing customer PII are shipped to a third-party analytics vendor. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Mask or tokenize PII in the pipeline before it leaves — logs inherit the sensitivity of the data they carry
cards.x: Logs are data too: once PII flows to a vendor, your breach surface includes their breach surface. Scrub at the boundary.
wrong: Ask users for consent in the logs

cards.q: The payment page still negotiates TLS 1.0 for “old clients”. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Disable TLS 1.0/1.1 and weak ciphers, in stages with compatibility monitoring — PCI forbids them and attackers negotiate down
cards.x: Protocol negotiation lets the attacker pick the weakest option: the server must remove the weak options, not hope clients choose well.
wrong: Old clients matter more than security

cards.q: The database uses transparent encryption, but the keys sit in a config file next to the database. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Move keys to a KMS or HSM with access controls and audit — encryption is only as strong as key protection
cards.x: A key beside the data is decoration: whoever reads the disk reads the key. Separate the key, control access to it, log every use.
wrong: Config files are protected by obscurity

cards.q: A laptop with the full HR database is stolen from a car, unencrypted, no MDM. What is the most defensible program fix?
cards.a: Full-disk encryption on all endpoints plus MDM with remote wipe — the device is already gone, so the control is the encryption
cards.x: Stolen hardware is a when, not an if: encryption makes the theft a hardware loss, not a breach. MDM adds the wipe for the window.

cards.q: DLP blocks the R&D team’s legitimate file shares daily, so they moved to personal drives. What is the most defensible tuning?
cards.a: Tune policies by data classification and user context with allowlisted workflows — blunt DLP gets bypassed, not obeyed
cards.x: A DLP that blocks real work teaches circumvention: precision policies plus approved paths keep both security and productivity.

cards.q: The new system must store card numbers for recurring billing. What is the most defensible design?
cards.a: Tokenize with the payment processor — store tokens, never the PAN — so card data never touches your systems
cards.x: The best way to protect card data is not to have it: tokenization removes PANs from your scope entirely. Encryption still leaves you holding the keys.
wrong: Encrypt the PANs in the database
Plaintext is fine behind the firewall

cards.q: Encryption keys have not been rotated in five years and the admin who created them left. What is the most defensible program fix?
cards.a: Scheduled rotation with versioned keys and automated re-encryption — old keys are standing risk
cards.x: Keys age like passwords: rotation limits the blast radius of a compromise nobody noticed. Automate it so it actually happens.

cards.q: Backup tapes go offsite unencrypted in a courier van. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Encrypt backups before they leave the building, with keys managed separately — a tape is just a hard drive in a van
cards.x: Offsite media is in the wild: unencrypted tapes make the courier a breach vector. Encrypt first, then transport.

cards.q: An employee emails a spreadsheet of SSNs to a personal address “to work from home”. What is the most defensible layered response?
cards.a: DLP and email encryption gateway to catch it, plus an approved remote-access path — the control gap is the missing legitimate way to work
cards.x: People exfiltrate through the easiest hole: block the bad path AND provide the good one, or the workaround just moves.

cards.q: Engineers sync laptops to a personal cloud drive with no policy. What is the most defensible control?
cards.a: Approved sync with DLP, device posture checks, and admin-controlled sharing — unmanaged sync is an exfiltration path wearing a productivity hat
cards.x: Shadow sync puts company data under personal accounts: bring it under policy with technical controls, not just a memo.
wrong: Cloud sync is the user’s business
Block all sync and watch productivity die

cards.q: Decommissioned drives are sold to a recycler without wiping “to save time”. What is the most defensible process?
cards.a: Sanitize per NIST 800-88 — clear, purge, or destroy based on media and classification — with certificates of destruction
cards.x: Resale without sanitization is a breach with extra steps: the buyer gets your data free. Sanitization level follows the data’s classification.

cards.q: The public website’s certificate expires at 3 AM on a holiday, and renewal is a manual ticket. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Automate issuance and renewal with ACME — certificates should never depend on a human remembering
cards.x: Manual certificate processes expire at the worst possible hour: automation plus expiry alerting makes renewal boring.

cards.q: An internal app uses a self-signed certificate, and users are trained to click through the warning. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Issue from an internal CA trusted by managed devices, or automate with ACME — self-signed trains users to ignore warnings
cards.x: Click-through training is anti-training: every bypassed warning teaches users that warnings do not matter. Proper certs restore the signal.

cards.q: The mobile app ships with a hardcoded database password used by 50,000 installs. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Rotate the credential immediately, scope the replacement to least privilege, audit usage, and move secrets to runtime injection with CI scanning
cards.x: Shipped secrets are public secrets: rotation closes the window, the audit tells you if it was used, and CI scanning keeps it from recurring.
wrong: The app is shipped — too late

cards.q: Analytics needs customer data, but privacy objects to sharing raw PII. What is the most defensible technique?
cards.a: Anonymize or aggregate so records cannot be linked to individuals — choose the technique by re-identification risk and regulation
cards.x: Masking keeps format but not privacy: true anonymization removes linkability. The technique follows the use case — analytics rarely needs real names.
wrong: Share raw data, analysts are trusted

cards.q: The company keeps every email and file for ten years “just in case”. What is the most defensible policy?
cards.a: A retention schedule with legal-hold process — keep what the law and business need, defensibly delete the rest
cards.x: Hoarding is liability: every retained byte is discoverable, breachable, and storable at cost. Retention is a schedule, not a sentiment.

cards.q: A third-party analytics SDK in the mobile app is caught sending contact lists to its servers. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Remove or replace the SDK, audit what it sent, disclose per policy — SDKs are third-party code running with your app’s permissions
cards.x: Your app’s permissions become the SDK’s permissions: vet SDKs like vendors, minimize their data, and monitor their traffic.

cards.q: USB drives are allowed on all workstations with no policy. What is the most defensible control?
cards.a: Block by default, allow only approved encrypted drives for defined roles — USB is both exfiltration and malware in a pocket
cards.x: Uncontrolled USB is a two-way hole: data walks out, malware walks in. Allowlist the need, encrypt the media, log the use.

cards.q: Sensitive documents are found on the shared printer daily. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Secure print with badge release — jobs print only when the owner is at the device
cards.x: Paper is data: the fix is making the printer hold the job until the human arrives, not hoping people hurry.
wrong: Printers are not a security issue

cards.q: A vendor screen-share session exposed the full customer database to their support tech. What is the most defensible control?
cards.a: Least-privilege views for support plus DLP on collaboration tools — the vendor sees only what the ticket needs
cards.x: Support access should be scoped to the problem: full-table views for a password reset is overexposure by design.
wrong: Vendors need full access to help

cards.q: The only copy of the master encryption key is with an admin who just resigned. What is the most defensible recovery design?
cards.a: M-of-N key recovery with split knowledge — no single person should be able to lose or walk away with the keys
cards.x: Single key holders are single points of failure and single points of coercion: split custody means the keys survive people.
wrong: Trust the admin to hand it over

cards.q: The messaging app offers “encrypted” chats, but the provider holds the keys. What is the most defensible read?
cards.a: That is transport-plus-storage encryption, not end-to-end: the provider can read everything — true E2EE keeps keys on the endpoints
cards.x: Who holds the keys decides who can read: provider-held keys mean provider access. E2EE is the only design where the provider cannot.

cards.q: A leaked board deck is traced by its unique watermark to one recipient. What made that possible?
cards.a: Forensic watermarking — per-recipient invisible marks that identify the source of a leak
cards.x: Watermarks do not prevent leaks; they attribute them. The deterrent is knowing the copy is traceable to you.

cards.q: Passwords are hashed with MD5 “because it is fast”. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Migrate to Argon2, bcrypt, or scrypt with unique salts — fast hashes are attacker-friendly hashes
cards.x: Password hashing must be slow by design: MD5 falls to GPUs in hours. Salts stop rainbow tables; work factors stop brute force.
wrong: MD5 is a hash, so it is fine

decks.title: Security Architecture: Resilience & Recovery Scenarios
decks.summary: Backups, DR, RTO/RPO, and HA as exam-style scenarios. (Domain 3.0)

cards.q: The only backup sits on the same SAN as production. What is the most defensible redesign?
cards.a: 3-2-1: three copies, two different media, one offsite — the backup must survive whatever kills production
cards.x: A backup sharing fate with production is a copy, not a recovery plan. The offsite copy is what survives fire, flood, and ransomware.

cards.q: The contract demands RPO of one hour, but backups run nightly. What is the most defensible change?
cards.a: Increase backup frequency to meet the RPO — architecture follows requirements, not the other way around
cards.x: RPO is the maximum data loss the business accepts: nightly backups guarantee up to 24 hours of loss. The schedule must satisfy the contract.

cards.q: Ransomware encrypted production and the online backups in the same night. What is the most defensible redesign?
cards.a: Immutable or offline copies — air-gapped, Object Lock, or tape — that no compromised credential can delete
cards.x: Online backups live in the blast radius: ransomware hunts them first. Immutability puts recovery outside the attacker’s reach.

cards.q: The DR plan was written three years ago and has never been tested. What is the most defensible program?
cards.a: Tabletop exercises, then simulations, then full failover tests on a cadence — an untested plan is a hope
cards.x: Plans rot: staff, systems, and vendors all changed. Testing graduates from discussion to simulation to real failover, on schedule.
wrong: DR is for natural disasters only

cards.q: A cold site is chosen to meet a two-hour RTO. What is the most defensible correction?
cards.a: Cold sites cannot meet a two-hour RTO — move to warm or hot, because recovery time follows site readiness
cards.x: Cold means empty building: procuring and restoring in two hours is fiction. The site type must match the RTO the business signed.
wrong: Cold sites are cheaper and fine

cards.q: The generator has never been load-tested; it “starts fine”. What is the most defensible program?
cards.a: Monthly load tests under real load — generators fail at 2 AM under load, not at noon idling
cards.x: Untested generators are the classic outage multiplier: the test must prove it carries the actual load, not just turns over.
wrong: Test it during the next outage

cards.q: The UPS holds ten minutes but the generator needs twenty to take load. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Size the UPS to bridge the gap with margin — the handoff must be continuous
cards.x: Power resilience is a chain: the UPS covers exactly the generator’s start time plus margin. A ten-minute bridge over a twenty-minute gap is an outage.
wrong: The generator will start faster in a real outage

cards.q: The company has one ISP and the SLA promises 99.99% uptime. What is the most defensible correction?
cards.a: Add a diverse second path — the SLA is a rebate promise, not uptime; single ISP is a single point of failure
cards.x: Carrier SLAs pay credits, not continuity: real availability comes from diverse paths, ideally diverse providers and entries.

cards.q: The load balancer is a single instance in front of everything. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: HA pair or anycast — the front door cannot be a single point of failure
cards.x: Every request crosses the load balancer: its failure is everyone’s failure. Redundant balancers with health checks fix it.

cards.q: The database runs on a single master with no replica. What is the most defensible change?
cards.a: Add replication or clustering matched to the RPO — a lone master makes every failure a data-loss window
cards.x: The replica is the RPO made real: without it, recovery means restoring from last night’s backup and losing the day.

cards.q: Backups complete nightly and report success, but nobody has ever restored one. What is the most defensible program?
cards.a: Scheduled restore tests — a backup without a tested restore is a prayer, not a plan
cards.x: Success reports measure the write, not the read: restores fail on corruption, missing keys, and wrong procedures. Test the read.

cards.q: The array runs RAID 5 across twelve 12TB drives. What is the most defensible concern?
cards.a: Rebuild time and URE risk: a second failure or unreadable sector during the multi-day rebuild kills the array
cards.x: RAID 5 rebuilds read every surviving disk: with huge drives the rebuild takes days, and one bad sector ends it. RAID 6/10 or erasure coding fits.

cards.q: Planned datacenter failover is set, but DNS TTLs are 24 hours. What is the most defensible preparation?
cards.a: Lower TTLs well before the cutover — long TTLs pin clients to the old site for a day
cards.x: DNS caching obeys the TTL you published yesterday: cutover speed is decided before the event, not during it.

cards.q: Nobody knows the graceful shutdown order, and the last outage corrupted the database. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: A documented, tested runbook with the order — databases before storage, apps before databases — because order matters
cards.x: Ungraceful shutdowns corrupt state: the runbook makes the order explicit and rehearsed, not improvised at 3 AM.

cards.q: The DR strategy is “we are in the cloud”. What is the most defensible correction?
cards.a: A region is not a DR plan: documented RTO/RPO, replicated data, tested failover runbooks — DR is a process, not a place
cards.x: Cloud regions fail too: without replication and tested procedures, “we are in the cloud” is a hope with a logo.

cards.q: Tape backups rotate to a storage room in the same building. What is the most defensible change?
cards.a: True offsite rotation — different facility, tested retrieval — because the building is the shared failure
cards.x: Fire, flood, and theft do not respect floors: offsite means a different risk zone, and retrieval must be proven, not assumed.

cards.q: A breach hits at midnight and nobody knows who notifies customers or regulators. What is the most defensible preparation?
cards.a: A crisis communication plan with named owners, templates, and legal review — silence is also a decision
cards.x: Notification duties have clocks: the plan names who decides, who writes, and who calls, before the midnight call happens.

cards.q: Only one engineer knows how to restore the backups, and she is on vacation. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Cross-training plus tested runbooks — the bus factor of one is an outage waiting for a holiday
cards.x: Recovery cannot depend on one person’s memory: document the procedure, train a second pair of hands, test together.

cards.q: Sales promises 99.9% uptime on a single-server deployment. What is the most defensible correction?
cards.a: 99.9% allows ~9 hours of downtime a year and still needs maintenance windows covered — single server cannot credibly promise it
cards.x: Availability math is unforgiving: promises must follow architecture. Redundancy, not optimism, delivers the nines.
wrong: Downtime does not count at night

cards.q: Snapshots are the only “backup” — same array, same site. What is the most defensible correction?
cards.a: Snapshots are not backups: they share the array’s fate — add true separate copies offsite
cards.x: A snapshot is a pointer, not a copy: array failure, ransomware, or site loss takes snapshots with it. Separate media, separate site.

cards.q: The DR plan was last updated before the cloud migration. What is the most defensible maintenance?
cards.a: Review the plan after every architecture change — a plan describing the old world fails in the new one
cards.x: DR plans rot with every migration: the review cadence must follow the change cadence, or the plan is fiction.
wrong: Update it after the next incident

cards.q: After ransomware, the CFO asks whether to just pay. What is the most defensible answer?
cards.a: Restore from clean, verified backups — payment funds crime, has no guarantee, and marks you as a payer
cards.x: Paying buys uncertainty: decryptors fail, data is already stolen, and payers get re-targeted. Tested backups are the answer.

cards.q: The alternate site’s configs are six months stale. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Continuous config replication or IaC-driven rebuilds — a stale site is a second outage wearing a DR costume
cards.x: Failover to stale configs fails differently but equally: the recovery site must track production, automatically.
wrong: DR sites do not need configs

cards.q: Every change window lacks a rollback plan “because rollbacks are admitting failure”. What is the most defensible standard?
cards.a: Every change ships with a tested backout plan — rollback is engineering discipline, not failure
cards.x: Changes fail: the question is whether failure is a 10-minute rollback or a 10-hour incident. Backout plans are mandatory.
wrong: Good changes do not need backout

cards.q: The same root cause has caused three outages this year, and each post-mortem recommended the same fix. What is the most defensible read?
cards.a: The lessons-learned process is broken: recommendations without owners and deadlines are suggestions, not fixes
cards.x: Repeat incidents are a management failure, not a technical one: track every action item to closure or the post-mortem was theater.

decks.title: Security Concepts: Scenarios
decks.summary: Zero trust, control types, AAA, and physical controls in real decisions.

cards.q: Your company still trusts anything inside the office network: no MFA on internal apps, flat VLANs, file shares open to everyone. The CEO asks where a zero-trust migration should start. What is the most defensible first move?
cards.a: Strong identity everywhere first — MFA on every account and app, before touching the network
cards.x: Identity is the new perimeter: without strong authentication, network segmentation just rearranges who the attacker impersonates. MFA kills the credential-reuse path that flat networks invite.
wrong: Rip out all VLANs and rebuild the network first
Buy a NAC appliance and call it zero trust
Put a bigger firewall at the internet edge

cards.q: The branch office runs a ten-year-old time-clock system that cannot do MFA and cannot be patched. Finance will not fund a replacement this year. What is the most defensible approach?
cards.a: Compensating controls: isolate it on its own segment, allow access only via jump host, and monitor it heavily
cards.x: When the ideal control is impossible, compensating controls reduce the risk to an acceptable level: isolation plus monitoring contains what patching and MFA would have prevented.
wrong: Leave it on the main network since it works
Disconnect it and make staff use paper timesheets
Open it to the internet so the vendor can maintain it

cards.q: The board wants 'defense in depth' but the budget covers one project. The CISO proposes adding a second firewall behind the first from the same vendor. What is the most defensible correction?
cards.a: Defense in depth means different layers, not duplicate boxes: WAF plus patching plus authentication plus monitoring
cards.x: Two identical firewalls fail identically to the same exploit. Real depth layers different control types — preventive, detective, corrective — across network, endpoint, identity, and data.
wrong: Two firewalls are exactly defense in depth
Spend it all on the most expensive firewall
One layer is fine if it is enterprise-grade

cards.q: An engineer proposes hiding the admin panel at a random URL instead of fixing its broken authentication. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Obscurity is not a control: fix the authentication; the hidden URL buys nothing against a scanner
cards.x: Security through obscurity fails the moment the secret leaks — and scanners find 'hidden' paths in minutes. It can supplement real controls but never replace them.
wrong: Hidden URLs are a valid primary control
Tell nobody the URL and it is fine

cards.q: The new SSO rollout covers authentication but nobody planned where the logs go. What is the most defensible gap to close?
cards.a: The accounting leg of AAA: SSO events must feed the SIEM with alerting, not just sit in the IdP console
cards.x: AAA is authentication, authorization, and accounting: without accounting, you cannot detect misuse of valid credentials — the exact scenario SSO centralizes.
wrong: SSO replaces the need for logging
Export logs once a quarter for the auditors
Logs are the IdP vendor's problem

cards.q: The firewall rulebase is ten years old, 3,000 rules, nobody knows what half of them do. What is the most defensible rebuild principle?
cards.a: Default deny with explicit, documented allows — and log the denies for tuning
cards.x: Implicit deny is the safe default: everything not explicitly permitted is blocked. A decade of accumulated allows is how attackers walk through 'enterprise' firewalls.
wrong: Migrate all 3,000 rules as-is to be safe
Default allow with blocks for known-bad IPs
Delete the firewall and use host firewalls

cards.q: A developer who writes code also deploys it straight to production. What is the most defensible separation?
cards.a: Split build and deploy: developers commit, a separate pipeline or role promotes to production
cards.x: Separation of duties means no single person can both create and release a change — it blocks both fraud and the 'oops, it worked on my laptop' outage.
wrong: Give the developer a second account for deploys
Require the developer to email before deploying

cards.q: The payroll administrator has processed every pay run alone for six years and resists vacations. What is the most defensible control?
cards.a: Mandatory vacation: someone else runs payroll for two consecutive weeks, which is how hidden fraud surfaces
cards.x: Mandatory vacations are a detective control — fraud that needs the perpetrator present to sustain itself breaks when they are gone.
wrong: Let her keep working; she is reliable
Move payroll to a new hire

cards.q: Wire transfers above $50,000 need two-person approval, but the CFO can override alone 'in emergencies'. What is the most defensible correction?
cards.a: No unilateral overrides: emergencies use a pre-defined second approver, because the override is the attack path
cards.x: Dual control fails the moment one person can bypass it — social engineers and fraudsters both aim straight at the exception process.
wrong: The CFO override is standard practice

cards.q: The 'assume breach' principle is adopted. A sales laptop is stolen from a hotel. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Treat it as compromised: rotate its credentials and keys, revoke sessions and certs — not just remote-wipe it
cards.x: Assume breach means acting as if the attacker already has access: a wipe command may never arrive, but rotated credentials are useless to a thief either way.
wrong: It had disk encryption, so nothing to do
Wait to see if anything happens

cards.q: A vendor RFP asks for the 'policy engine, policy administrator, and policy enforcement point' of your zero-trust design. What is the most defensible way to answer?
cards.a: Describe the three roles: engine decides, administrator configures, enforcement point applies the decision on the wire
cards.x: NIST SP 800-207 splits the job: the policy engine evaluates trust, the administrator pushes configuration, and enforcement points (agents, gateways) carry out allow/deny.
wrong: They are three brand names for a firewall
One appliance does all three, end of answer
Zero trust has no such components

cards.q: Users authenticate once in the morning and stay trusted all day, including on the finance system. What is the most defensible tightening?
cards.a: Step-up authentication and session re-validation on sensitive actions — trust must be continuous, not a morning event
cards.x: Continuous validation is a zero-trust pillar: a session hijacked at 10 AM inherits the morning's trust unless sensitive actions re-verify.
wrong: MFA once a year is enough

cards.q: Firewall change requests are approved by email from whoever is online. What is the most defensible approval control?
cards.a: Signed, ticketed approvals from a named approver — non-repudiation for every change
cards.x: Non-repudiation means the approver cannot later deny it: approvals need identity, timestamp, and a record — 'whoever was online' is none of those.

cards.q: The badge reader opens the door but the audit log shows no entry for a visitor who was inside. Which AAA element failed, and what is the fix?
cards.a: Accounting failed: the reader authenticated but did not log — fix the logging integration, because access without a record is invisible
cards.x: AAA breaks into three legs: the badge authenticated, the door authorized, but accounting (the record) failed. An access event nobody can reconstruct is a gap.
wrong: Nothing failed; the visitor was escorted

cards.q: A penetration test finds the guest Wi-Fi can reach the finance VLAN. What is the most defensible design principle violated?
cards.a: Segmentation with implicit deny between trust zones — guests should never route to internal VLANs
cards.x: Network segmentation enforces least privilege at the network layer: the guest zone's default route should be the internet, never internal segments.
wrong: The firewall is misconfigured, delete it

cards.q: The company wants to roll out biometrics for the data center. What is the most defensible enrollment caution?
cards.a: Biometrics cannot be revoked: pair them with a second factor and protect the templates like secrets
cards.x: You get ten fingers and two eyes for life — a compromised biometric is compromised forever. Treat templates as high-value data and never as a single factor.
wrong: Store templates in a shared folder for convenience
Fingerprints are unguessable, so one factor is fine

cards.q: Job rotation is proposed for the SOC but analysts fear losing expertise. What is the most defensible implementation?
cards.a: Rotate through roles with documented handovers — it spreads knowledge and surfaces hidden process gaps
cards.x: Rotation is both a security control and a resilience practice: it prevents single-person dependency and exposes processes that only work in one person's head.
wrong: Keep everyone fixed in their specialty
Rotate people out of the company

cards.q: A file share contains 'salary_2024_final_FINAL.xlsx' visible to the whole company. What is the most defensible classification fix?
cards.a: The data owner (HR leadership) classifies it, then access is restricted to need-to-know with the classification labeled
cards.x: Classification starts with the data owner — the business side that understands the data's value — and 'need to know' limits access to those with a legitimate purpose.
wrong: Everyone needs to see it for transparency
Rename the file to hide it

cards.q: The new office has a side door propped open for smokers, bypassing the badge reader. What is the most defensible physical fix?
cards.a: A mantrap or turnstile with enforced badging on every entry — every door is the perimeter
cards.x: Physical access control fails at the weakest door: tailgating defeats a $50,000 reader in seconds. Enforce badging at all entries, no exceptions.
wrong: Put up a sign asking people to close it
Remove the badge reader to save money
Smokers can use the front door only on weekends

cards.q: Honeytokens are proposed: fake credentials planted in the environment. What is the most defensible deployment?
cards.a: Place them where no legitimate user goes — any touch is a high-fidelity alert, and monitor them continuously
cards.x: Deception works when false positives are near zero: a honeytoken in a real workflow pages you about your own staff. Put it in attacker-only territory.
wrong: Plant them in the CEO's inbox
Tell all staff where they are

cards.q: The risk team asks whether a screen-lock policy is preventive or detective. What is the most defensible classification, and why does it matter?
cards.a: Preventive: it stops unauthorized use before it happens — classification matters because gap analysis must cover all control types
cards.x: Controls are classified by function (preventive/detective/corrective) and nature (technical/administrative/physical): a gap analysis that finds only detective controls has found a real gap.

cards.q: CCTV footage is reviewed only after incidents. What is the most defensible upgrade path?
cards.a: Monitored alarming on motion in restricted areas plus retained footage — detection in time to respond, not just to investigate
cards.x: Cameras nobody watches are forensic, not protective: pair recording with real-time alerting on the zones that matter.

cards.q: The change advisory board rubber-stamps firewall changes in bulk every Friday. What is the most defensible reform?
cards.a: Real review: risk assessment per change, testing evidence, and a backout plan — bulk approval is approval theater
cards.x: Change management is a preventive control: unreviewed changes are how outages and backdoors ship. Every change needs risk review and a rollback plan.
wrong: Approve faster to help the business

cards.q: An intern asks why the company bothers with 'least privilege' when everyone is trusted. What is the most defensible explanation?
cards.a: Trust is not the issue: least privilege limits blast radius, so one compromised account cannot reach everything
cards.x: Least privilege assumes credentials will be stolen: the damage is bounded by what the account could reach. 'Trusted' staff get phished too.
wrong: Least privilege slows work too much
Admins are exempt from least privilege

cards.q: The data center installed bollards, a mantrap, and badge readers — but the loading dock door is on a shared code. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Individual badges on every entry including the dock — shared codes cannot identify who entered
cards.x: Accountability requires attribution: a shared code authenticates 'someone with the code', which is no authentication at all for incident response.
wrong: Shared codes are fine for docks

decks.title: Cryptography & PKI: Scenarios
decks.summary: Algorithm choices, certificate lifecycles, and key management under pressure.

cards.q: Two services need to exchange large files securely over the internet. What is the most defensible design?
cards.a: TLS 1.2+ with strong ciphersuites — authenticated, standard, and maintained
cards.x: Use proven protocols: TLS gives confidentiality, integrity, and authentication in one maintained standard. Custom crypto is where breaches are born.
wrong: Base64-encode the files; it looks encrypted
Send them over plain FTP on a nonstandard port

cards.q: The app stores passwords with unsalted SHA-256 'because it is fast'. What is the most defensible correction?
cards.a: Switch to bcrypt, Argon2, or scrypt — slow, salted, memory-hard hashing designed for passwords
cards.x: Fast hashes are built for attackers: rainbow tables and GPUs chew through SHA-256. Password hashing must be deliberately slow and unique per password.
wrong: SHA-256 is a hash, so it is fine
Store them in a separate database table

cards.q: Two companies with no prior relationship must agree on a shared secret over a public channel. What is the most defensible mechanism?
cards.a: Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE) with authentication — forward-secret key agreement
cards.x: DH lets two parties derive a shared secret over a public channel; ephemeral keys plus authentication add forward secrecy and MITM resistance.
wrong: Use the same password on both sides

cards.q: Log files must prove they were not tampered with in transit to the SIEM. What is the most defensible mechanism?
cards.a: HMAC with a shared key — integrity plus authenticity of the sender
cards.x: A plain hash proves nothing about who sent it; HMAC binds the integrity check to a secret only the sender holds.
wrong: Zip the logs with a password

cards.q: The public website's certificate expires on launch day and nobody noticed. What is the most defensible program?
cards.a: Automated issuance and renewal (ACME) with expiry alerting — certificates must never depend on memory
cards.x: Certificate expiry is a solved operational problem: automation renews, monitoring alerts. A launch-day outage from an expired cert is a process failure.
wrong: One person owns all renewals manually

cards.q: The company needs certificates for forty subdomains of one domain. What is the most defensible choice?
cards.a: A wildcard certificate, understanding that one compromised key affects all forty subdomains
cards.x: Wildcards trade operational simplicity for blast radius: scope the risk deliberately, protect the private key accordingly, and prefer SAN certs for distinct names.
wrong: Forty individual certificates managed by hand
One certificate shared across unrelated domains

cards.q: The internal HR portal uses a self-signed certificate and staff click through warnings daily. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Deploy an internal CA, distribute its root to managed devices, and issue proper certificates
cards.x: Warning fatigue is the real vulnerability: staff trained to click through cert warnings will click through a real MITM too. Internal PKI removes the warnings legitimately.
wrong: Tell staff the warnings are normal
Move HR to the public internet with a public cert

cards.q: Encrypted backups need key recovery if the admin leaves, but no single person should hold the keys. What is the most defensible design?
cards.a: M-of-N key recovery: key split so any M of N custodians can reconstruct it
cards.x: Escrow must survive both departure and compromise: M-of-N means no single custodian can abuse the keys, and the organization cannot be locked out by one absence.
wrong: Email the keys to the team

cards.q: TLS 1.0 is still enabled 'for legacy clients'. What is the most defensible action?
cards.a: Disable it: segment the legacy clients and give them a migration path — obsolete protocols are an attacker's on-ramp
cards.x: TLS 1.0 has known weaknesses (BEAST and more). Keeping it for a handful of clients exposes everyone negotiating down to it.
wrong: Enable SSL 3.0 too for older clients
Legacy clients can use HTTP instead

cards.q: Database backups of 4 TB must be encrypted. What is the most defensible approach?
cards.a: AES-256 for the data, with the data key wrapped asymmetrically — hybrid encryption
cards.x: Symmetric ciphers handle bulk data; asymmetric handles key distribution. RSA-encrypting 4 TB directly is absurd; hybrid is the standard pattern.

cards.q: Release builds must prove they came from the build pipeline. What is the most defensible mechanism?
cards.a: Sign artifacts with a pipeline-held key and verify the signature before deploy
cards.x: Code signing gives authenticity and integrity: the deploy trusts the signature, not the network path the artifact traveled.
wrong: Trust artifacts from the build server implicitly

cards.q: How should the company detect certificates fraudulently issued for its domains?
cards.a: Monitor Certificate Transparency logs for your domains and alert on unexpected issuance
cards.x: CT logs make all public issuance visible: monitoring them catches misissued or attacker-obtained certificates for your names.
wrong: Check the website manually each morning
CT logs are the CA's problem
Buy more certificates to crowd out fakes

cards.q: Payment-card keys need the strongest protection for PCI. What is the most defensible storage?
cards.a: A hardware security module (HSM) — tamper-resistant, FIPS-validated key operations
cards.x: HSMs perform crypto inside hardened hardware that resists extraction; software keystores cannot make the same assurance to an auditor.
wrong: A config file with tight permissions
The HSM is overkill; use the app server
Split keys across two config files

cards.q: The board asks about quantum computers breaking encryption. What is the most defensible strategy?
cards.a: Crypto agility: inventory where each algorithm is used, prefer hybrid post-quantum options where available, plan migration
cards.x: Panic-migrating is as bad as ignoring it: agility — the ability to swap algorithms — plus an inventory is the defensible posture while standards settle.
wrong: Ignore it; quantum is decades away
Migrate everything to untested algorithms now
Double all key lengths and declare victory

cards.q: File deduplication uses SHA-256 hashes to skip identical uploads. What is the most defensible security caveat?
cards.a: Hashes confirm integrity, but dedup leaks whether a file already exists — separate the integrity check from the storage decision
cards.x: Content-defined storage has a side channel: an attacker can probe for the existence of files. Integrity hashing is fine; the dedup oracle needs handling.
wrong: SHA-256 is broken, stop using it

cards.q: Executives want 'encrypted email' for board materials. What is the most defensible deployment?
cards.a: S/MIME or PGP with managed keys and a clear key-recovery story — not just a 'confidential' banner
cards.x: Real email encryption needs key management: issuance, revocation, recovery, and training. A banner changes nothing about who can read the message.

cards.q: Encryption keys are rotated 'when someone remembers'. What is the most defensible rotation program?
cards.a: Scheduled rotation plus event-driven rotation (departures, suspected compromise) — automated where possible
cards.x: Rotation limits the value of a stolen key: schedule it like patching, trigger it like incident response, and automate both.

cards.q: The app encrypts session tokens with AES-CBC and no MAC. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Switch to an authenticated mode (AES-GCM) or add HMAC — unauthenticated encryption invites padding-oracle attacks
cards.x: CBC without integrity lets attackers tamper with ciphertext and learn plaintext through error oracles. Authenticated encryption is the standard.

cards.q: A partner proposes 'Diffie-Hellman' for a new integration with no mention of authentication. What is the most defensible objection?
cards.a: Unauthenticated DH is MITM-trivial: require authenticated ECDHE (signed or pre-shared authenticated)
cards.x: DH without authentication lets an attacker sit in the middle of both handshakes. The fix is authenticating the exchange, not abandoning DH.
wrong: Use a longer DH group and skip auth

cards.q: API keys are committed to the repo 'temporarily' and end up in container images. What is the most defensible practice?
cards.a: A secrets manager or vault with runtime injection — secrets never live in code, images, or chat
cards.x: Committed secrets are compromised secrets: repos are copied, images are shared, and 'temporary' lasts years. Inject at runtime from a vault.
wrong: Private repo, so it is fine

cards.q: The security team wants revocation checking that does not phone home for every user. What is the most defensible mechanism?
cards.a: OCSP stapling: the server presents a fresh revocation proof with the handshake
cards.x: Stapling gives clients revocation status without per-user OCSP queries — no privacy leak, no extra round trip, no soft-fail downgrade pressure.
wrong: CRLs downloaded hourly by every client

cards.q: The password-reset flow generates tokens with MD5 of the timestamp. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Replace with a CSPRNG-generated token of sufficient length — unpredictability, not hashing, is the requirement
cards.x: Reset tokens must be unguessable: MD5-of-timestamp is predictable to anyone who knows roughly when it was issued. Use the OS random source.
wrong: MD5 is a hash, so tokens are safe
Add a secret salt to the MD5

cards.q: Laptops have OS passwords but no disk encryption. What is the most defensible upgrade?
cards.a: Full-disk encryption with TPM plus PIN — the password alone does nothing against a removed drive
cards.x: An OS password is a software gate on a running system; pull the drive and it is gone. FDE with hardware-bound keys protects the data at rest.

cards.q: A vendor pitches 'blockchain-based audit logs' for a single-company system. What is the most defensible evaluation?
cards.a: Reject the blockchain: a hash-chained, signed log gives the same tamper-evidence without the complexity
cards.x: Blockchains solve multi-party trust without a central authority — a single company's log needs integrity, which signatures and hash chains provide.

cards.q: The new CA's root keys are generated on an admin's laptop 'to save time'. What is the most defensible process?
cards.a: A witnessed key ceremony: offline HSM, split knowledge, documented procedure — the root's birth is its most vulnerable moment
cards.x: A compromised root key compromises everything it ever signs. Ceremonies with witnesses, offline hardware, and split custody make the generation trustworthy.
wrong: Generate it in the cloud for convenience

decks.title: Risk Management: Scenarios
decks.summary: ALE math, risk treatments, and ownership in business decisions.

cards.q: A flood scenario has an SLE of $200,000 and an ARO of 0.3. A $40,000 control would cut the ALE to $10,000. What is the most defensible decision?
cards.a: Buy it: the ALE is $60,000 and the control saves $50,000 a year for $40,000
cards.x: ALE = SLE × ARO = $60,000. A control is justified when its cost is below the ALE reduction ($50,000) — the math decides, not the sticker price.
wrong: Skip the math; buy every control

cards.q: The board wants risk 'in dollars' but the team only has a red-yellow-green matrix. What is the most defensible approach?
cards.a: Quantitative analysis for the board decision (ALE, cost-benefit) while keeping qualitative triage for speed
cards.x: Quantitative speaks the board's language — dollars and probabilities; qualitative is faster for prioritization. Use each where it fits.
wrong: The matrix is enough for the board
Quantitative is too hard; skip it

cards.q: MFA is deployed on the VPN. The CISO asks whether phishing risk is now gone. What is the most defensible answer?
cards.a: No: the remaining risk is residual risk — reduced but present, and it must be formally accepted
cards.x: Controls reduce inherent risk to residual risk; residual risk never hits zero and needs explicit acceptance by the risk owner.

cards.q: The company buys cyber insurance and outsources the SOC. Has the risk been eliminated?
cards.a: No: that is risk transfer and sharing — the breach is still your breach, and the risk remains on your register
cards.x: Transfer moves the financial impact, not the risk itself: customers and regulators still hold you accountable.
wrong: Delete it from the risk register

cards.q: A legacy app cannot be secured and holds no critical data. What is the most defensible risk strategy?
cards.a: Risk avoidance: decommission it — eliminating the asset eliminates the risk
cards.x: Avoidance is legitimate when the asset's value does not justify its risk cost: retire what you cannot defend.

cards.q: The business accepts the risk of running an unpatched server for six months pending an upgrade. What is the most defensible documentation?
cards.a: A signed risk acceptance with the owner, the compensating controls, and an expiry date
cards.x: Acceptance is a formal decision: named owner, what mitigates it meanwhile, and when it expires — verbal acceptance is no acceptance.
wrong: A verbal OK from the manager
Email the team that it is fine

cards.q: Failed logins on the VPN spike 400% in a week. What is the most defensible use of this metric?
cards.a: Treat it as a key risk indicator for credential attacks and trigger the playbook threshold
cards.x: KRIs are early-warning metrics tied to specific risks: define the threshold in advance so the spike drives action, not just a graph.
wrong: Wait for a breach to act

cards.q: The risk register lists 'ransomware' but no owner. Who should own it, and why does it matter?
cards.a: The business unit head whose operations stop — ownership drives funding and decisions
cards.x: Risk owners are business owners: they have the authority to fund mitigation or formally accept. Unowned risks are unmanaged risks.
wrong: The security team owns all risks
The CEO owns every risk personally

cards.q: Incident records show 3 ransomware scares in 2 years across the industry peer group. What ARO should the analysis use, and why?
cards.a: ARO 1.5 — three events over two years — because ARO is the expected annual frequency
cards.x: ARO comes from history: count events over time. Peer data fills gaps when your own history is thin.

cards.q: A $80,000 control addresses a $50,000 ALE. What is the most defensible conclusion?
cards.a: Not cost-effective as-is: find a cheaper control or accept the risk — never spend more than the risk
cards.x: Security economics: control cost must stay under the ALE reduction. An $80k control on a $50k risk destroys value.
wrong: Buy it and the $40k one too

cards.q: Three 'low' risks all affect the same customer database. What is the most defensible read?
cards.a: Aggregate them: correlated lows on one asset can equal a medium or high — assess together
cards.x: Risk aggregation: risks are not independent when they share an asset. The register must show the combined exposure.

cards.q: The scanner lists 5,000 findings; the team can fix 50 this quarter. What is the most defensible prioritization?
cards.a: Risk-based: internet-facing, exploitable, on critical assets first — severity times exposure times value
cards.x: Risk-based vulnerability management weighs exploitability and asset value, not raw counts or CVSS alone.

cards.q: Critical findings have sat open 200 days with no SLA. What is the most defensible program change?
cards.a: Time-to-remediate SLAs by severity with escalation — what gets measured gets fixed
cards.x: Remediation SLAs turn findings into commitments: criticals in days, highs in weeks, with escalation when they slip.

cards.q: A new privacy regulation takes effect mid-year. What is the most defensible risk process?
cards.a: Treat it as a compliance risk: gap analysis, assign an owner, track remediation in the register
cards.x: Regulatory change is a risk event: assess the gap between current state and the new requirement, then manage it like any risk.

cards.q: The risk register is reviewed annually. What is the most defensible cadence?
cards.a: Quarterly plus after major changes — risks move faster than annual reviews
cards.x: Annual reviews describe last year's risk: tie reviews to the change cadence and threat landscape.

cards.q: Threat intel reports a new ransomware strain targeting your sector. What is the most defensible use?
cards.a: Feed it into continuous risk assessment: update likelihoods, check controls, brief owners
cards.x: Continuous assessment keeps the register alive: intel updates likelihood, control tests update effectiveness.
wrong: File it for the annual review

cards.q: The CFO proposes self-insuring instead of buying cyber insurance. What is the most defensible analysis?
cards.a: Compare the expected loss (ALE) against premium plus retained risk — self-insurance is formal risk retention with reserves, not ignoring the risk
cards.x: Retention is a valid treatment when the organization can absorb the loss: fund the reserve, define the triggers, and revisit annually. Skipping insurance without reserves is just hope.
wrong: Self-insurance means no incident plan needed
Buy insurance and keep no reserves

cards.q: The board sets 'zero breaches' as the risk appetite. What is the most defensible correction?
cards.a: Appetite must be realistic: define the amount of risk the business will take to operate, with tolerance bands
cards.x: Risk appetite is the level of risk the organization accepts in pursuit of objectives; 'zero' is a fantasy that drives risk underground.

cards.q: Risk acceptance is documented 'until further notice'. What is the most defensible correction?
cards.a: Add an expiry date and a re-assessment trigger — acceptances must be time-bound
cards.x: Risk changes: an open-ended acceptance becomes permanent by neglect. Expiry forces the decision to be revisited.

cards.q: The assessment finds the only DNS admin credentials are held by one contractor. What is the most defensible treatment?
cards.a: Mitigate the single point of failure: cross-train, split duties, document — then reassess the residual risk
cards.x: Key-person risk is operational risk: redundancy and documentation reduce it; the register then reflects the lower residual.

cards.q: A $2M revenue system has no backup and the business 'accepts' the risk verbally. What is the most defensible escalation?
cards.a: Put the acceptance in writing with the true ALE exposed — verbal acceptance of existential risk is negligence
cards.x: Acceptance requires understanding: quantify the loss, name the owner, sign it. Unsigned acceptance of a $2M exposure is not a decision.

cards.q: Two departments dispute who owns the risk of a shared SaaS platform. What is the most defensible resolution?
cards.a: Assign one risk owner — the party with the most at stake and the budget to act — and record it
cards.x: Shared ownership is no ownership: one named owner with authority, others as stakeholders.

decks.title: Governance, Audit & Compliance: Scenarios
decks.summary: Policies, audits, regulations, and privacy in real situations.

cards.q: The CISO must document the encryption requirement, the approved algorithms, and the key-generation steps. What is the most defensible document split?
cards.a: Policy states the requirement, the standard names AES-256, the procedure gives the key-generation steps
cards.x: Policy (what and why, executive-approved), standard (the specific rule), procedure (the how-to steps) — each has a different author and audience.

cards.q: Enterprise customers demand independent assurance before signing. What is the most defensible audit to commission?
cards.a: An external audit (e.g., SOC 2 Type II) — independent attestation for relying parties
cards.x: External audits serve outsiders: independence is the point. Internal audit serves management readiness.

cards.q: The audit scope says 'review security' with no systems, period, or criteria named. What is the most defensible correction?
cards.a: Define scope precisely: systems in scope, the period, and the criteria — vague scope produces vague assurance
cards.x: A good audit scope names what, when, and against what standard. 'Review security' lets the auditor — or the auditee — dodge the hard parts.

cards.q: The auditor's finding says access reviews are undocumented. The team disagrees. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: A remediation plan with an owner and a date — argue the facts once, then fix the gap
cards.x: Audit findings get management responses: accept and remediate with a timeline, or rebut with evidence. Endless argument is the worst option.

cards.q: The auditor asks for evidence that patches were applied. What is the most defensible evidence?
cards.a: System-generated reports with integrity (immutable logs, signed reports) — not screenshots alone
cards.x: Good evidence is sufficient, reliable, and tamper-evident: tool output beats screenshots, which anyone can fabricate.
wrong: A screenshot of the update screen

cards.q: The SaaS company signs its first EU customers. What is the most defensible compliance move?
cards.a: Treat GDPR as applicable: data processing agreements, data-subject rights workflows, 72-hour breach notification
cards.x: GDPR follows the data subject: serving EU residents triggers it regardless of where the company sits.
wrong: GDPR is only for EU companies
Block EU signups instead of complying

cards.q: A US clinic wants the platform to store patient records. What is the most defensible requirement?
cards.a: HIPAA compliance with a signed BAA covering every vendor touching PHI
cards.x: PHI in scope means HIPAA: administrative, technical, and physical safeguards, plus business associate agreements down the chain.
wrong: Encrypt it and HIPAA is satisfied

cards.q: The startup starts taking credit cards directly. What is the most defensible scoping decision?
cards.a: Reduce PCI DSS scope first: tokenization or P2PE so card data never touches your systems
cards.x: Scope reduction is the highest-ROI PCI move: if cardholder data never enters your environment, most requirements fall away.
wrong: PCI applies only to big companies
Scope is whatever the auditor says

cards.q: California users sign up in volume. What is the most defensible privacy posture?
cards.a: CCPA/CPRA compliance: opt-out of sale/sharing, deletion and access request workflows
cards.x: California grants consumers rights over their data: honor opt-outs and deletion requests with real processes, not a buried email address.
wrong: California law does not apply online
Add a cookie banner and stop

cards.q: A Fortune 500 prospect requires 'SOC 2' before procurement. What is the most defensible path?
cards.a: SOC 2 Type II over 6-12 months against the relevant trust criteria — Type I alone rarely satisfies procurement
cards.x: Type II tests operating effectiveness over time; Type I is a point-in-time design review. Enterprise procurement wants the former.
wrong: Type I is faster and equivalent
SOC 2 is only for cloud companies

cards.q: Control evidence is gathered in a two-week scramble before each audit. What is the most defensible program?
cards.a: Continuous auditing: automate evidence collection so controls are provable any day
cards.x: Audit readiness is a daily state, not a seasonal panic: automated evidence makes assurance continuous and cheaper.

cards.q: The app collects SSNs 'in case we need them later'. What is the most defensible data decision?
cards.a: Stop collecting them: data minimization — hold only what the purpose requires
cards.x: Every data element held is breach liability: minimization deletes the 'just in case' fields that become the headline.

cards.q: Marketing wants to reuse support-chat transcripts for ad targeting. What is the most defensible answer?
cards.a: No without fresh consent: purpose limitation — data collected for support cannot be repurposed silently
cards.x: Purpose limitation binds data to the purpose it was collected for. New purpose needs a new legal basis.

cards.q: The contract must define who is controller and who is processor. What is the most defensible assignment?
cards.a: The customer (who decides purposes) is controller; you (who processes on their behalf) are processor — written in the DPA
cards.x: Controller decides the 'why', processor handles the 'how': the DPA must reflect reality, because obligations follow the role.
wrong: Roles do not matter in contracts

cards.q: A breach is confirmed at 2 AM. When does the 72-hour GDPR notification clock start?
cards.a: At awareness: when the organization has a reasonable degree of certainty — which is why the runbook pre-assigns the decision
cards.x: The clock starts when you know, not when you finish investigating: pre-named owners and templates make 72 hours achievable.

cards.q: An emergency firewall change is needed during an active attack. What is the most defensible change process?
cards.a: Make the change, document it fully, and hold the post-implementation review — emergencies compress process, not eliminate it
cards.x: Change management bends in emergencies but does not break: the review happens after, with the same rigor.

cards.q: Staff use personal cloud drives for work files and IT finds out during an incident. What is the most defensible policy fix?
cards.a: An acceptable-use policy defining approved storage, plus technical enforcement — policy before the next incident, not after
cards.x: AUP sets the rules of the road: what is allowed, what is monitored, and the consequences. Enforcement makes it real.
wrong: Cloud drives are convenient; allow them

cards.q: Who should approve the information security policy?
cards.a: Executive leadership approves; the CISO drafts — authority must sit above the function it governs
cards.x: Policy needs teeth: approval at the top gives it organizational weight that a security-team memo lacks.
wrong: The CISO approves their own policy

cards.q: The company passes every audit but gets breached through an unpatched test server. What is the most defensible lesson?
cards.a: Compliance is a floor, not a ceiling: keep hardening beyond the checklist — audits sample, attackers do not
cards.x: Audits verify a sample against a standard at a point in time. Security is continuous; the checklist is the minimum.
wrong: The auditor missed it; blame them

cards.q: The board has never rehearsed a breach. What is the most defensible exercise?
cards.a: A tabletop with executives: walk the ransomware scenario, assign decisions, find the gaps before they are real
cards.x: Boards make breach decisions (pay? disclose? shut down?): rehearsing them in a tabletop is cheaper than improvising at midnight.
wrong: Send them the IR plan to read

cards.q: A new hire asks for the difference between a guideline and a standard. What is the most defensible answer?
cards.a: Standards are mandatory rules; guidelines are recommended best practices — one is enforced, the other advised
cards.x: The hierarchy matters for enforcement: violate a standard and face consequences; deviate from a guideline with justification.

cards.q: Regulators ask for proof of 'continuous compliance'. What is the most defensible evidence?
cards.a: Automated control monitoring with dashboards and trend data — proof the controls operate, not just exist
cards.x: Continuous compliance is demonstrated by continuous evidence: monitoring that shows controls working every day.

decks.title: Third-Party & Continuity Governance: Scenarios
decks.summary: Vendor assessment, contracts, and exit strategies that work.

cards.q: A new vendor will process customer data. What is the most defensible onboarding gate?
cards.a: A completed security assessment — SOC 2 Type II or equivalent evidence — before signing
cards.x: Trust but verify before the contract: assess the vendor's security posture while you still have leverage, not after the data flows.

cards.q: The vendor proudly shows a clean SOC 2 opinion letter. What is the most defensible review?
cards.a: Read the full report: the period covered, the exceptions, and whether your services are in scope
cards.x: The opinion letter is the headline; the exceptions and scope are the story. A clean opinion on someone else's systems helps you not at all.

cards.q: The contract needs terms, the project needs a work description, and uptime needs teeth. What is the most defensible document split?
cards.a: MSA for master terms, SOW for the specific work, SLA for performance metrics and remedies
cards.x: MSA governs the relationship, the SOW describes each engagement, and the SLA makes performance measurable and enforceable.

cards.q: The SaaS contract is silent on who owns the data. What is the most defensible clause to demand?
cards.a: You own your data: the vendor must return it on request and destroy it on exit, certified
cards.x: Data ownership in writing prevents the hostage scenario: without it, your data is leverage at renewal time.
wrong: The vendor owns what you upload

cards.q: A critical vendor refuses any audit rights. What is the most defensible position?
cards.a: Reserve the right to audit in the contract — walk away from critical vendors who refuse
cards.x: Right-to-audit is your verification lever: a critical vendor with no audit rights is a black box holding your risk.
wrong: Audit rights are never used anyway

cards.q: The vendor notifies you of a breach affecting your data — three weeks after they knew. What is the most defensible contractual fix?
cards.a: A defined breach-notification window (e.g., 72 hours) plus your right to invoke your own IR
cards.x: Notification timing is negotiated before the incident: the contract should set the clock and preserve your response rights.

cards.q: Your vendor uses subcontractors you have never heard of. What is the most defensible requirement?
cards.a: Disclosure and approval rights over fourth parties — your risk extends down the chain
cards.x: Fourth-party risk is your risk: the contract should name subprocessors and require notice before changes.

cards.q: The BIA is complete. How should it drive vendor management?
cards.a: Tier vendors by the RTO/RPO impact of their failure — critical vendors get deeper assessment
cards.x: The BIA tells you what the business cannot lose: vendor criticality follows business impact, not spend.
wrong: All vendors get the same review
BIA is for internal systems only

cards.q: The company depends on one SaaS for billing with no exit plan. What is the most defensible preparation?
cards.a: A tested exit strategy: proven data export, documented migration path, contractual cooperation
cards.x: Exit is a capability, not a hope: prove you can leave before you must, while the relationship is good.

cards.q: One engineer at the vendor knows your entire integration. What is the most defensible mitigation?
cards.a: Key-person provisions or dual-sourcing: no critical function should depend on one human
cards.x: Succession risk applies to vendors too: contractual continuity commitments or a second source for critical functions.

cards.q: The vendor wants your architecture diagrams before the security review. What is the most defensible sequence?
cards.a: Mutual NDA first, then the tailored security review — protect your information while assessing theirs
cards.x: Due diligence is bidirectional: NDA before disclosure, and the review scaled to the data they will touch.
wrong: Skip the NDA to move fast

cards.q: Two business-critical functions now depend on a single vendor. What is the most defensible read?
cards.a: Concentration risk: diversify or negotiate stronger protections — one failure becomes two outages
cards.x: Vendor consolidation creates correlated failure: assess what one vendor's outage, breach, or price hike costs you twice.
wrong: One throat to choke is a strategy

cards.q: The SLA promises 99.9% uptime with service credits. What is the most defensible understanding?
cards.a: Credits compensate; they do not restore — negotiate termination rights for chronic misses, not just credits
cards.x: SLA credits are rebates, not recovery: real protection is the right to exit when performance chronically fails.

cards.q: A critical library in your product has no SBOM entry and an unknown maintainer. What is the most defensible action?
cards.a: Generate the SBOM, assess the component's risk, and monitor it for vulnerabilities like any vendor
cards.x: Open source is third-party code: inventory it, track its vulns, and have a replacement plan.

cards.q: The cloud provider says 'security is our job'. What is the most defensible understanding?
cards.a: Shared responsibility: the provider secures the cloud, you secure what you put in it — data, access, config
cards.x: The shared responsibility model draws the line: misconfigured storage and weak IAM are always your breach, never the provider's.

cards.q: Your vendor is acquired by a competitor's parent company. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Re-assess: new ownership can change security posture, roadmaps, and conflicts of interest
cards.x: Acquisitions reset assumptions: reassess the vendor as if new, because in important ways it is.

cards.q: Support staff offshore will access customer data. What is the most defensible control?
cards.a: Data residency and access clauses: defined regions, least privilege, logged access
cards.x: Cross-border support is a data-transfer decision: contract the where, the who, and the logging before granting access.

cards.q: The three-year vendor contract is up for renewal. What is the most defensible use of the moment?
cards.a: Raise the bar: MFA, logging, breach-notification terms — renewal is your leverage point
cards.x: Renewal is when you have power: bake in the security terms you wish you had, priced into the deal.

cards.q: Every vendor gets the same 200-question security questionnaire. What is the most defensible tailoring?
cards.a: Scale the review to data access and criticality — deep dives for critical vendors, light touch for low-risk
cards.x: Risk-based due diligence: a catering vendor and a payroll processor do not merit the same interrogation.

cards.q: The BIA names the order-entry system as tier 1 with a 4-hour RTO, but its vendor contract has no recovery commitment. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Align the contract to the BIA: negotiated recovery commitments matching the tier — the BIA is toothless without them
cards.x: Business impact analysis must flow into vendor obligations: tier-1 systems need contractual recovery to match.

cards.q: The vendor's incident response plan has never been tested with your team. What is the most defensible preparation?
cards.a: A joint tabletop: walk a vendor-breach scenario together before it is real
cards.x: Shared incidents need shared rehearsal: the tabletop reveals who calls whom, who decides, and where the contract helps or hinders.

cards.q: A startup vendor offers 70% off for a three-year prepay. What is the most defensible evaluation?
cards.a: Weigh the discount against lock-in, viability, and exit cost — cheap today can be expensive at renewal
cards.x: Prepay trades cash for commitment: assess the vendor's viability and your exit options before the discount seduces you.

tracks.title: Cloud Computing
tracks.tagline: Service models to Well-Architected design to cloud-native security.

decks.title: Cloud Concepts
decks.summary: NIST definition, service and deployment models, shared responsibility.

cards.q: How many essential characteristics does NIST SP 800-145 define?
cards.x: On-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, measured service.

cards.q: In IaaS, who manages the operating system?
cards.a: The customer
cards.x: The provider manages hardware, virtualisation, and facilities.

cards.q: In SaaS, what does the customer still manage?
cards.a: Their data, users, and access configuration
cards.x: Identity and data are always the customer’s responsibility.

cards.q: Which service model is AWS Lambda / Azure Functions?
cards.a: Serverless / FaaS (a form of PaaS)
cards.x: You deploy functions; the provider runs and scales servers.

cards.q: What is a hybrid cloud?
cards.a: A mix of on-premises/private and public cloud working together
cards.x: Community cloud is shared by organisations with common needs.

cards.q: What is the shared responsibility model?
cards.a: The provider secures "of" the cloud; the customer secures "in" the cloud
cards.x: The split shifts depending on IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS.

cards.q: CapEx vs OpEx: cloud shifts spending to…
cards.a: OpEx (pay as you go)
cards.x: No up-front hardware purchase.

cards.q: What is elasticity?
cards.a: Automatically scaling resources up and down with demand
cards.x: Scalability is the ability to grow; elasticity is doing it automatically, both ways.

cards.q: What is a region vs an availability zone?
cards.a: Geographic area vs isolated data centre(s) within it
cards.x: Spread workloads across AZs for high availability.
wrong: A region is one data centre

cards.q: What is an edge location?
cards.a: A site that caches content close to users (CDN)
cards.x: e.g. CloudFront, Azure Front Door, Cloud CDN.

cards.q: What is vendor lock-in?
cards.a: Dependence on one provider’s proprietary services
cards.x: Mitigate with open standards, containers, and portable IaC.

puzzles.prompt: Order these models from MOST to LEAST customer responsibility.
puzzles.x: Each step up hands more of the stack to the provider. Data and identity always stay yours.

decks.title: Core Services Across AWS, Azure & GCP
decks.summary: Compute, storage, database, and networking equivalents.

cards.q: AWS virtual machines are called…
cards.a: EC2
cards.x: Azure: Virtual Machines; GCP: Compute Engine.

cards.q: AWS object storage is…
cards.a: S3
cards.x: Azure: Blob Storage; GCP: Cloud Storage.

cards.q: AWS block storage attached to EC2 is…
cards.a: EBS
cards.x: Like a virtual disk. EFS is shared file storage.

cards.q: AWS managed relational database service is…
cards.a: RDS (and Aurora)
cards.x: Azure SQL Database; GCP Cloud SQL.

cards.q: AWS managed NoSQL key-value database is…
cards.a: DynamoDB
cards.x: Azure Cosmos DB; GCP Firestore/Bigtable.

cards.q: What is the AWS isolated virtual network called?
cards.a: VPC
cards.x: Azure: VNet; GCP: VPC (global).

cards.q: AWS identity service is…
cards.a: IAM (plus IAM Identity Center for SSO)
cards.x: Azure: Entra ID; GCP: Cloud IAM.

cards.q: AWS service that records API calls for auditing?
cards.a: CloudTrail
cards.x: Azure: Activity Log; GCP: Cloud Audit Logs.

cards.q: AWS metrics and logs monitoring service?
cards.a: CloudWatch
cards.x: Azure Monitor; GCP Cloud Monitoring/Logging.

cards.q: AWS managed Kubernetes is…
cards.a: EKS
cards.x: Azure AKS; GCP GKE.

cards.q: Which S3 storage class suits rarely accessed archives?
cards.a: Glacier (Deep Archive for the cheapest)
cards.x: Retrieval takes minutes to hours.

cards.q: What does AWS Organizations provide?
cards.a: Central management of multiple accounts with policies (SCPs)
cards.x: Multi-account is the recommended isolation boundary.

cards.q: Azure’s virtual machine service is called…
cards.a: Azure Virtual Machines
cards.x: The direct equivalent of EC2.

cards.q: GCP’s virtual machine service is called…
cards.a: Compute Engine
cards.x: The direct equivalent of EC2.

cards.q: Azure’s object storage service is…
cards.a: Blob Storage
cards.x: The direct equivalent of S3.

cards.q: GCP’s object storage service is…
cards.a: Cloud Storage
cards.x: The direct equivalent of S3.

cards.q: Azure’s managed relational database is…
cards.a: Azure SQL Database
cards.x: The direct equivalent of RDS; Azure also offers managed PostgreSQL/MySQL.

cards.q: GCP’s managed relational database is…
cards.a: Cloud SQL
cards.x: The direct equivalent of RDS for MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server.

cards.q: Azure’s isolated virtual network is called…
cards.a: Virtual Network (VNet)
cards.x: The direct equivalent of an AWS VPC; subnets and peering work similarly.

cards.q: GCP’s virtual network is…
