cards.a: VPC, and it is global rather than regional
cards.x: One GCP VPC spans all regions, unlike AWS and Azure regional networks.

cards.q: Azure’s identity service is…
cards.a: Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD)
cards.x: The direct equivalent of AWS IAM for users and SSO.

cards.q: GCP’s identity service is…
cards.a: Cloud IAM
cards.x: The direct equivalent of AWS IAM for users, groups, and roles.

cards.q: Azure’s monitoring service is…
cards.a: Azure Monitor (metrics, logs, alerts)
cards.x: The direct equivalent of CloudWatch.

cards.q: GCP’s monitoring service is…
cards.a: Cloud Monitoring (formerly Stackdriver)
cards.x: The direct equivalent of CloudWatch.

cards.q: Azure’s serverless function service is…
cards.a: Azure Functions
cards.x: The direct equivalent of AWS Lambda.

cards.q: GCP’s serverless compute options are…
cards.a: Cloud Functions and Cloud Run
cards.x: Cloud Run runs any container serverlessly; both match Lambda use cases.

cards.q: Azure’s managed Kubernetes is…
cards.a: AKS (Azure Kubernetes Service)
cards.x: The direct equivalent of EKS; GCP’s is GKE.

resources.title: AWS Skill Builder: Cloud Practitioner Essentials

decks.title: Pricing, Support & Governance Basics
decks.summary: Pricing models, cost tools, and tagging.

cards.q: Which EC2 pricing model is cheapest for interruptible jobs?
cards.a: Spot instances
cards.x: Up to ~90% off, but AWS can reclaim them with 2 minutes’ notice.

cards.q: Which pricing model suits steady 1-3 year workloads?
cards.a: Reserved Instances or Savings Plans
cards.x: Commit in exchange for large discounts.

cards.q: Why tag cloud resources?
cards.a: Cost allocation, ownership, automation, and policy
cards.x: e.g. owner, environment, cost-center tags.

cards.q: What does a budget alert do?
cards.a: Notifies you when spend crosses a threshold
cards.x: Set one on day one of any cloud account.

cards.q: What is egress cost?
cards.a: Charges for data leaving the cloud
cards.x: Ingress is usually free; cross-region and internet egress cost money.

cards.q: What is rightsizing?
cards.a: Matching instance size to actual usage
cards.x: Often the quickest cost win.

cards.q: What is FinOps?
cards.a: Collaborative cloud financial management across engineering and finance
cards.x: Inform, optimise, operate.

cards.q: What is TCO?
cards.a: Total cost of ownership including hidden operational costs
cards.x: Compare on-prem power, staff, and hardware refresh against cloud.

cards.q: Why should the root account not be used day to day?
cards.a: It has unrestricted power and cannot be limited by IAM policies
cards.x: Enable MFA, lock away credentials, use role-based admin accounts.

cards.q: What is a landing zone?
cards.a: A pre-configured, secure multi-account baseline
cards.x: AWS Control Tower, Azure Landing Zones.

resources.title: AWS Skill Builder: Cloud Practitioner Essentials

decks.title: Cloud Networking
decks.summary: VPC design, subnets, gateways, and connectivity.

cards.q: What makes a subnet "public" in AWS?
cards.a: Its route table has a route to an Internet Gateway
cards.x: Private subnets route outbound via a NAT gateway.

cards.q: What does a NAT gateway allow?
cards.a: Outbound internet from private subnets, no inbound initiation
cards.x: Used for patches and API calls from private instances.

cards.q: Security group vs network ACL?
cards.a: Stateful, instance-level vs stateless, subnet-level
cards.x: SGs allow only; NACLs allow and deny, evaluated by rule number.

cards.q: What is VPC peering?
cards.a: A private connection between two VPCs
cards.x: Not transitive. Transit Gateway scales hub-and-spoke.

cards.q: Private dedicated link from on-prem to AWS?
cards.a: Direct Connect
cards.x: Azure ExpressRoute; GCP Cloud Interconnect.

cards.q: What does a VPC endpoint (PrivateLink) do?
cards.a: Reaches cloud services privately without the public internet
cards.x: Gateway endpoints for S3/DynamoDB; interface endpoints for others.
wrong: Opens the VPC to the internet

cards.q: Which load balancer works at Layer 7 with path routing?
cards.a: Application Load Balancer
cards.x: NLB is Layer 4, extreme performance, static IPs.

cards.q: What does Route 53 provide?
cards.a: DNS with health checks and routing policies
cards.x: Latency-based, weighted, failover, and geolocation routing.

cards.q: Why avoid overlapping CIDR blocks across VPCs?
cards.a: Overlapping ranges cannot be peered or routed cleanly
cards.x: Plan IP space centrally before you build.

cards.q: What is a bastion host, and the modern alternative?
cards.a: A hardened jump box; now often replaced by SSM Session Manager
cards.x: Session Manager needs no open inbound ports and logs sessions.

cards.q: What are VPC Flow Logs?
cards.a: Records of IP traffic metadata in and out of network interfaces
cards.x: Essential for investigations; do not contain payloads.

resources.title: AWS Skill Builder: Cloud Practitioner Essentials

puzzles.prompt: Your VPC is 10.0.0.0/16. Slide to the prefix that gives each subnet 4,096 addresses.
puzzles.x: /20 leaves 12 host bits: 2^12 = 4,096 addresses, so the /16 splits into 16 subnets. AWS reserves 5 IPs in each subnet.

decks.title: Well-Architected Design
decks.summary: The six pillars, HA/DR patterns, and scaling.

cards.q: How many pillars does the AWS Well-Architected Framework have?
cards.x: Operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimisation, sustainability.

cards.q: Which pillar was added most recently (2021)?
cards.a: Sustainability
cards.x: Minimise the environmental impact of workloads.

cards.q: What is horizontal scaling?
cards.a: Adding more instances
cards.x: Vertical scaling is making one instance bigger.

cards.q: Why design stateless application tiers?
cards.a: Any instance can serve any request, so scaling and failover are easy
cards.x: Store sessions in a shared cache or database.

cards.q: DR strategy with the lowest cost and slowest recovery?
cards.a: Backup and restore
cards.x: Then pilot light, warm standby, and multi-site active/active.

cards.q: What is pilot light DR?
cards.a: Core data replicated and minimal services running, scaled up on failover
cards.x: Faster than backup/restore, cheaper than warm standby.

cards.q: What is loose coupling?
cards.a: Components interact through queues or APIs so failures don’t cascade
cards.x: SQS, SNS, and EventBridge decouple services.

cards.q: What does an Auto Scaling group do?
cards.a: Maintains and adjusts instance count based on health and demand
cards.x: Replaces failed instances automatically.

cards.q: What is a multi-AZ database deployment?
cards.a: A synchronous standby in another AZ with automatic failover
cards.x: Read replicas are for scaling reads, often asynchronous.
wrong: A read replica in another region

cards.q: What is immutable infrastructure?
cards.a: Replacing servers with new images rather than patching in place
cards.x: Reduces configuration drift.
wrong: Servers that never change or update

cards.q: What is blue/green deployment?
cards.a: Running two environments and switching traffic to the new one
cards.x: Canary shifts a small share of traffic first.

resources.title: AWS Skill Builder: Cloud Practitioner Essentials

puzzles.prompt: Order the DR strategies from cheapest (slowest) to most expensive (fastest).
puzzles.x: Pick the cheapest one that still meets the business RTO and RPO.

decks.title: Containers, Kubernetes & IaC
decks.summary: Docker, Kubernetes objects, Terraform, and CI/CD.

cards.q: Container vs virtual machine?
cards.a: Containers share the host kernel; VMs each run a full OS
cards.x: Containers are lighter; VMs give stronger isolation.

cards.q: What is a Dockerfile?
cards.a: A recipe of instructions to build a container image
cards.x: Each instruction creates a cached layer.

cards.q: What is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes?
cards.a: Pod
cards.x: One or more containers sharing network and storage.

cards.q: What does a Kubernetes Deployment manage?
cards.a: A desired number of pod replicas and rolling updates
cards.x: Uses ReplicaSets under the hood.

cards.q: What does a Kubernetes Service provide?
cards.a: A stable IP/DNS name load-balancing to a set of pods
cards.x: Types: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer.

cards.q: Are Kubernetes Secrets encrypted by default?
cards.a: No, only base64-encoded unless encryption at rest is configured
cards.x: Enable etcd encryption or use an external secrets manager.

cards.q: What does a NetworkPolicy do?
cards.a: Restricts which pods can talk to which
cards.x: Pods can talk to each other freely until policies apply.

cards.q: What does `terraform plan` do?
cards.a: Shows the changes Terraform would make, without making them
cards.x: Review the plan in pull requests before apply.

cards.q: Why store Terraform state remotely with locking?
cards.a: Prevents concurrent corruption and shares state safely
cards.x: State can contain secrets: encrypt it and restrict access.

cards.q: What is GitOps?
cards.a: Git as the source of truth; an agent reconciles the cluster to it
cards.x: Argo CD and Flux are common tools.

cards.q: Why run containers as non-root?
cards.a: Limits damage if the container is compromised
cards.x: Also drop capabilities and use read-only file systems.

decks.title: Cloud Security Engineering
decks.summary: IAM policy, encryption, detection, and posture management.

cards.q: In AWS IAM policy evaluation, what always wins?
cards.a: An explicit Deny
cards.x: Default is implicit deny; an explicit allow is needed; explicit deny overrides all.

cards.q: What is an SCP?
cards.a: A Service Control Policy setting maximum permissions for accounts in an Org
cards.x: SCPs do not grant permissions; they set guardrails.

cards.q: Why prefer IAM roles over long-lived access keys?
cards.a: Roles provide short-lived, automatically rotated credentials
cards.x: Use roles for EC2, Lambda, and CI (OIDC federation).
wrong: Keys cannot be used in code

cards.q: What is envelope encryption?
cards.a: Data encrypted with a data key, which is itself encrypted by a master key
cards.x: KMS holds the master key; data keys are used locally.

cards.q: What is CSPM?
cards.a: Cloud Security Posture Management: continuous misconfiguration detection
cards.x: Checks against benchmarks such as CIS.

cards.q: What is CNAPP?
cards.a: A unified platform combining CSPM, CWPP, CIEM, and more
cards.x: Cloud-Native Application Protection Platform.

cards.q: What does AWS GuardDuty do?
cards.a: Threat detection from CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs
cards.x: Azure: Defender for Cloud; GCP: Security Command Center.

cards.q: Why enforce IMDSv2 on EC2?
cards.a: It requires a session token, blocking most SSRF credential theft
cards.x: The Capital One breach (2019) involved SSRF to instance metadata.

cards.q: What is S3 Block Public Access?
cards.a: Account/bucket settings that override any public ACL or policy
cards.x: Enable it at the account level by default.

cards.q: What is CIEM?
cards.a: Managing cloud entitlements to find excessive permissions
cards.x: Most cloud identities use a tiny share of what they are granted.

cards.q: What is a break-glass account?
cards.a: A tightly controlled emergency admin account
cards.x: Monitored, MFA protected, used only when normal access fails.

decks.title: Cloud Security Governance (CCSP concepts)
decks.summary: Data lifecycle, legal, and assurance in the cloud.

cards.q: What are the stages of the CSA cloud data lifecycle?
cards.a: Create, store, use, share, archive, destroy
cards.x: Apply controls at each stage.

cards.q: What is crypto-shredding?
cards.a: Destroying the encryption keys so encrypted data is unrecoverable
cards.x: The practical way to sanitise data in the cloud.

cards.q: What is data sovereignty?
cards.a: Data is subject to the laws of the country where it is stored
cards.x: Drives region selection and residency controls.

cards.q: What is the CSA Cloud Controls Matrix?
cards.a: A cloud-specific security control framework
cards.x: The CSA STAR registry publishes provider assessments.

cards.q: What does BYOK / HYOK mean?
cards.a: Bring your own key / hold your own key for provider encryption
cards.x: More control over keys, more operational responsibility.

cards.q: Why is e-discovery harder in the cloud?
cards.a: Data is distributed, multi-tenant, and controlled by the provider
cards.x: Contracts must define legal hold and access support.

cards.q: What is multi-tenancy risk?
cards.a: Isolation failures could expose data between customers
cards.x: Providers mitigate with hypervisor and logical isolation.

cards.q: What should a cloud SLA define?
cards.a: Availability targets, support response, and remedies
cards.x: Service credits rarely cover real business losses.

cards.q: What is the "right to audit" issue in cloud?
cards.a: Providers rarely allow customer audits; you rely on third-party reports
cards.x: Use SOC 2, ISO 27001, and FedRAMP attestations.

cards.q: What is FedRAMP?
cards.a: The US government authorisation programme for cloud services
cards.x: Low, Moderate, and High baselines based on NIST SP 800-53.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-145: Definition of Cloud Computing

decks.title: Reliability & Observability
decks.summary: SLOs, error budgets, the three pillars, and chaos engineering.

cards.q: SLI vs SLO vs SLA?
cards.a: Measured indicator vs internal target vs contractual promise
cards.x: e.g. SLI latency; SLO 99.9% under 300 ms; SLA with penalties.

cards.q: What is an error budget?
cards.a: The allowed unreliability implied by the SLO
cards.x: 99.9% monthly allows about 43 minutes of downtime.

cards.q: What are the three pillars of observability?
cards.a: Metrics, logs, traces
cards.x: OpenTelemetry is the open standard for collecting all three.

cards.q: What are the four golden signals?
cards.a: Latency, traffic, errors, saturation
cards.x: From the Google SRE book.

cards.q: What is distributed tracing for?
cards.a: Following one request across many services
cards.x: Finds the slow or failing hop.

cards.q: What is chaos engineering?
cards.a: Deliberately injecting failures to test resilience
cards.x: Start small in staging, with a defined blast radius.

cards.q: What makes an alert actionable?
cards.a: It signals user impact and has a clear response
cards.x: Alert on symptoms (SLO burn), not every cause.

cards.q: What is a blameless postmortem?
cards.a: An incident review focused on systems, not individuals
cards.x: Encourages honest reporting.

cards.q: What is toil in SRE?
cards.a: Manual, repetitive, automatable operational work
cards.x: Google SRE aims to keep it under 50% of time.

cards.q: What does a readiness probe do in Kubernetes?
cards.a: Keeps traffic away from a pod until it can serve
cards.x: Liveness probes restart stuck containers.

puzzles.prompt: A 30-day month with a 99.9% availability SLO allows how many minutes of downtime?
puzzles.x: 30 × 24 × 60 = 43,200 minutes, and 0.1% of that is 43.2 minutes. That is your error budget.

tracks.title: AWS Solutions Architect
tracks.tagline: Design secure, resilient, high-performing, cost-optimized architectures on AWS.

decks.title: IAM: Identity & Access
decks.summary: Users, roles, policies, MFA, and least-privilege design. (Domain 1)

cards.q: A company wants developers to access AWS but never with long-lived credentials. What should they use?
cards.a: IAM roles with short-lived temporary credentials
cards.x: Roles issue temporary credentials via STS; never embed access keys in code or on EC2.
wrong: IAM users with access keys rotated yearly

cards.q: What is the difference between an IAM identity policy and a resource policy?
cards.a: Identity policies attach to users/groups/roles; resource policies attach to resources like S3 buckets
cards.x: S3 bucket policies and KMS key policies are resource policies; most other services use identity policies.
wrong: Identity policies are for S3 only

cards.q: An explicit Deny in any applicable IAM policy results in…
cards.a: Access denied, regardless of any Allow
cards.x: Explicit deny always wins in policy evaluation logic.
wrong: Access allowed if another policy allows it

cards.q: How should an application running on EC2 access an S3 bucket?
cards.a: An IAM role attached via an instance profile
cards.x: The instance gets temporary credentials automatically; no keys stored on disk.
wrong: Embed an access key in the application config
Open the bucket to public read

cards.q: What does MFA Delete protect in S3?
cards.a: Accidental or malicious permanent deletion of object versions
cards.x: Requires MFA to delete versions or change versioning state; must be enabled by the root account.

cards.q: A developer needs S3 read access for 2 hours to debug production. Best practice?
cards.a: Assume a role with scoped-down permissions using STS
cards.x: Temporary, least-privilege, and auditable; avoids standing permissions.
wrong: Create an IAM user with S3FullAccess
Make the bucket public for 2 hours

cards.q: What is an IAM permission boundary?
cards.a: A maximum-permissions guardrail for an IAM entity
cards.x: Effective permissions are the intersection of the boundary and identity policies.

cards.q: How can you find unused IAM permissions to tighten toward least privilege?
cards.a: IAM Access Analyzer with unused-access findings
cards.x: It analyses CloudTrail to suggest policy refinements.

cards.q: Cross-account access: Account A’s Lambda must read Account B’s S3 bucket. What is required?
cards.a: A role in Account B that Account A can assume, plus a bucket policy allowing it
cards.x: Trust policy on the role plus resource policy on the bucket; both sides must permit.
wrong: An IAM user in Account A with S3FullAccess
Copy the bucket to Account A

cards.q: Why must the AWS root user have MFA enabled and its keys locked away?
cards.a: Root cannot be restricted by IAM policies and has full power
cards.x: Enable MFA, never use root day-to-day, use break-glass admin roles.
wrong: Root cannot use the console otherwise

cards.q: What is IAM Identity Center used for?
cards.a: Central workforce access to multiple AWS accounts and applications
cards.x: One identity, permission sets per account; replaces per-account IAM users.

cards.q: An S3 bucket policy denies all principals except a specific VPC endpoint. Which condition makes this work?
cards.a: aws:SourceVpce (or aws:SourceVpc)
cards.x: Keeps S3 traffic off the public internet while restricting which networks reach the bucket.

cards.q: What do service control policies (SCPs) do?
cards.a: Set maximum permissions across accounts in an Organization
cards.x: SCPs never grant permissions; they filter what identity policies can allow.

cards.q: A CI/CD pipeline in GitHub Actions must deploy to AWS. Most secure approach?
cards.a: OIDC federation with an IAM role (no stored secrets)
cards.x: Short-lived tokens via the OIDC provider; nothing to rotate or leak.
wrong: A long-lived access key in repo secrets

cards.q: What is the purpose of IAM policy conditions?
cards.a: Restrict when, where, and how a permission applies (IP, MFA, time, tags)
cards.x: e.g. aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent or aws:SourceIp conditions.

cards.q: Two engineers need identical permissions that change often. How to manage this?
cards.a: An IAM group (or role) with managed policies attached once
cards.x: Change the policy in one place; users inherit it.
wrong: Copy inline policies to each user

cards.q: What does the iam:PassRole permission control?
cards.a: Who may pass a role to an AWS service (e.g. EC2, Lambda)
cards.x: Without it, a user could escalate by attaching a privileged role to a resource they control.

cards.q: How often should IAM access keys be rotated, per best practice?
cards.a: Regularly (e.g. every 90 days) — and prefer roles to eliminate keys
cards.x: Delete unused keys; rotate active keys on a schedule.

decks.title: VPC & Network Security
decks.summary: Security groups vs NACLs, WAF, Shield, PrivateLink, and private connectivity. (Domain 1)

cards.q: A web server in a public subnet must accept HTTPS only from the internet. How?
cards.a: Security group allowing 443 inbound from 0.0.0.0/0
cards.x: Security groups are stateful and instance-level; use them as the primary filter.

cards.q: What is the key difference between security groups and NACLs?
cards.a: SGs are stateful and attach to instances/ENIs; NACLs are stateless and attach to subnets
cards.x: SGs evaluate allow rules only; NACLs evaluate numbered allow and deny rules.

cards.q: A database in a private subnet must be reachable only from app servers. Best design?
cards.a: DB security group allowing inbound only from the app servers’ security group
cards.x: Referencing security group IDs is more robust than IP ranges.
wrong: Put the database in a public subnet
Use a NACL to allow all traffic

cards.q: How can EC2 instances in private subnets reach S3 without traversing the internet?
cards.a: A VPC gateway endpoint for S3
cards.x: Gateway endpoints are free and keep traffic on the AWS network.

cards.q: What does AWS WAF protect against?
cards.a: Layer-7 attacks like SQL injection and XSS
cards.x: Attach to ALB, CloudFront, or API Gateway; use AWS managed rules.

cards.q: What is the difference between AWS Shield Standard and Advanced?
cards.a: Standard is free automatic DDoS protection; Advanced adds 24/7 DRT support and cost protection
cards.x: Advanced also brings custom mitigations for larger, sophisticated attacks.

cards.q: An application needs DDoS protection plus a web application firewall. Which combination?
cards.a: Shield Advanced for L3/L4 DDoS plus WAF for L7 rules
cards.x: They complement each other at different layers.

cards.q: A company wants to inspect all outbound VPC traffic centrally. Which architecture?
cards.a: Egress VPC with firewall appliances behind a Gateway Load Balancer
cards.x: Route spoke VPC traffic through the inspection VPC via Transit Gateway.
wrong: Open all outbound in each VPC

cards.q: What is AWS PrivateLink (interface VPC endpoints) used for?
cards.a: Private connectivity to AWS services or SaaS without internet exposure
cards.x: Traffic stays on the AWS network via endpoint network interfaces.

cards.q: In what order are NACL rules evaluated?
cards.a: Lowest rule number first; first match wins
cards.x: Use small increments (100, 110) so rules can be inserted later.

cards.q: You need stateful-allow plus explicit-deny filtering at the subnet boundary. Which control?
cards.a: Network ACL
cards.x: NACLs are the subnet-level stateless filter; security groups cannot deny.

cards.q: How do on-premises users get private access to an internal ALB?
cards.a: AWS Client VPN or Site-to-Site VPN into the VPC
cards.x: Client VPN provides mutual-TLS authenticated access to VPC resources.

cards.q: What does enabling S3 Block Public Access at the account level do?
cards.a: Overrides any bucket policy or ACL that would make buckets public
cards.x: A preventive guardrail; enable by default in every account.

cards.q: An EC2 instance was compromised. What is the fastest network-level containment?
cards.a: Change its security group to isolate it (remove inbound/outbound)
cards.x: Faster and reversible versus terminating; preserve the instance for forensics.

cards.q: Which service flags exposed access keys and unintended cross-account access?
cards.a: IAM Access Analyzer
cards.x: Also validates policies against best practices.

cards.q: For defense in depth, where should packet filtering happen?
cards.a: At multiple layers: security groups, NACLs, WAF, and host firewalls
cards.x: No single control should be the only barrier.

cards.q: A Lambda in a VPC must call a third-party HTTPS API. What is required?
cards.a: A NAT gateway (or VPC endpoint) for outbound internet from private subnets
cards.x: Lambda in a VPC loses default internet access; provide a route out.
wrong: An internet gateway on the Lambda
A public IP on the Lambda

cards.q: How do you restrict S3 access so it only works from your VPC?
cards.a: Bucket policy condition on aws:SourceVpc or aws:SourceVpce
cards.x: Combined with a VPC endpoint, S3 never traverses the public internet.
wrong: A security group on the bucket

decks.title: Encryption & Data Protection
decks.summary: KMS, SSE options, Secrets Manager, ACM, and S3 protection. (Domain 1)

cards.q: What is the difference between SSE-S3 and SSE-KMS?
cards.a: SSE-S3 uses S3-managed keys; SSE-KMS uses KMS keys you control with audit trails
cards.x: SSE-KMS adds CloudTrail logging of key usage and granular key policies.

cards.q: When should you use SSE-C instead of SSE-S3?
cards.a: When you must supply and manage your own encryption keys per request
cards.x: You provide the key with each request; S3 never stores it.

cards.q: What is envelope encryption?
cards.a: Data encrypted with a data key that is itself encrypted by a KMS master key
cards.x: Data keys do bulk encryption locally; KMS protects the keys.

cards.q: A company needs automatic yearly rotation of encryption keys. Which KMS feature?
cards.a: Automatic rotation for customer-managed symmetric keys
cards.x: Enable it on the CMK; rotation is transparent to applications.

cards.q: Where should database credentials for an application be stored?
cards.a: AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation
cards.x: Parameter Store SecureString is cheaper for non-rotating config; Secrets Manager rotates.

cards.q: Secrets Manager vs Systems Manager Parameter Store?
cards.a: Secrets Manager adds automatic rotation and cross-account sharing; Parameter Store is cheaper for plain config
cards.x: Use Parameter Store for non-secret config, Secrets Manager for credentials.

cards.q: How do you prove who accessed a KMS key and when?
cards.a: CloudTrail logs every KMS API call (with SSE-KMS, not SSE-S3)
cards.x: Key-usage auditing is a major reason to choose SSE-KMS over SSE-S3.

cards.q: What does ACM (Certificate Manager) provide?
cards.a: Free public TLS certificates with automatic renewal for AWS services
cards.x: Use with ALB, CloudFront, and API Gateway; private CA available for internal certs.

cards.q: EBS volumes must be encrypted to meet compliance. How?
cards.a: Enable EBS encryption by default in the region (or per volume with a KMS key)
cards.x: Snapshots of encrypted volumes are encrypted too.

cards.q: What is S3 Object Lock used for?
cards.a: WORM compliance: prevent object deletion or modification for a retention period
cards.x: Governance mode allows privileged deletes; Compliance mode blocks even root.

cards.q: How does S3 versioning help with ransomware protection?
cards.a: Deleted or overwritten objects remain recoverable as prior versions
cards.x: Combine with MFA Delete and Object Lock for strong protection.

cards.q: A KMS key policy is a…
cards.a: Resource policy controlling who can use and administer the key
cards.x: Key administrators vs key users; cross-account use requires key-policy permission.

cards.q: What does AWS Macie do?
cards.a: Discovers and classifies sensitive data (PII, credentials) in S3
cards.x: Uses machine learning; alerts on exposed sensitive data.

cards.q: Where should TLS be terminated for an internet-facing app?
cards.a: At the ALB or CloudFront, with HTTPS to backends as needed
cards.x: Offloads crypto from instances; ACM provides free certificates.

cards.q: How do you encrypt an existing unencrypted RDS database?
cards.a: Take a snapshot, copy it with encryption enabled, restore to a new instance
cards.x: You cannot encrypt an existing instance in place.
wrong: Enable a checkbox on the live DB

cards.q: A company must keep encryption keys in single-tenant hardware. Which option?
cards.a: CloudHSM (dedicated HSM) or KMS with external key store
cards.x: CloudHSM gives exclusive hardware control; KMS custom key stores can use CloudHSM backing.

cards.q: What does enabling default S3 bucket encryption do?
cards.a: Automatically encrypts all new objects with SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS
cards.x: No application changes needed; applies to uploads without encryption headers.

cards.q: An application needs FIPS 140-2 validated cryptography. Which KMS consideration?
cards.a: Use KMS with FIPS endpoints in a compliant region
cards.x: KMS offers FIPS 140-2 validated endpoints; check the region’s compliance scope.

decks.title: Highly Available Compute
decks.summary: Multi-AZ, ALB/NLB, Auto Scaling, and Route 53 routing. (Domain 2)

cards.q: An application must survive an AZ failure with no manual intervention. Which design?
cards.a: Multi-AZ deployment: ALB across AZs with an Auto Scaling group spanning subnets
cards.x: ALB routes around failed AZs; ASG replaces instances automatically.

cards.q: ALB vs NLB: when should you choose NLB?
cards.a: Extreme performance, static IPs, or non-HTTP TCP/UDP traffic
cards.x: NLB handles millions of requests/sec at Layer 4 with ultra-low latency.

cards.q: What is the difference between target-group health checks and Route 53 health checks?
cards.a: Target groups check instance health for the load balancer; Route 53 checks endpoints for DNS failover
cards.x: Both remove unhealthy targets from rotation at their own layer.

cards.q: An Auto Scaling group should scale on request count per target. Which policy?
cards.a: Target tracking scaling on ALBRequestCountPerTarget
cards.x: Maintains steady load per instance by adding or removing capacity.

cards.q: How does an ASG replace an unhealthy instance?
cards.a: Terminates it and launches a replacement from the launch template
cards.x: Health checks combine EC2 status with optional ELB health checks.
wrong: It notifies but takes no action

cards.q: Route 53 failover routing is used for…
cards.a: Active-passive DNS failover to a standby endpoint
cards.x: Health checks determine when to flip to the secondary.

cards.q: Weighted routing in Route 53 is useful for…
cards.a: Blue/green deployments and canary releases via DNS
cards.x: Shift 10% of traffic to the new version, then increase.

cards.q: Geolocation vs geoproximity routing?
cards.a: Geolocation routes by user location; geoproximity routes by distance with bias control
cards.x: Geoproximity can shift traffic gradually between regions.

cards.q: A stateful web app stores sessions on local disk. What breaks when scaling?
cards.a: Sessions are lost when requests hit different instances or replacements
cards.x: Fix: store sessions in ElastiCache/DynamoDB, or enable ALB stickiness.

cards.q: What is the purpose of ASG lifecycle hooks?
cards.a: Pause instance launch/termination to run custom actions (warm-up, log drain)
cards.x: e.g. finish in-flight requests before termination.

cards.q: Multi-AZ RDS vs read replica: which provides automatic failover?
cards.a: Multi-AZ standby (synchronous) fails over automatically; read replicas do not
cards.x: Read replicas scale reads and can be promoted manually.

cards.q: How many AZs should a production VPC span at minimum?
cards.a: At least two; three preferred
cards.x: Two AZs survive one AZ failure; three tolerates more and balances ASG better.

cards.q: What is a Gateway Load Balancer used for?
cards.a: Deploying third-party virtual appliances (firewalls, IDS) transparently
cards.x: GENEVE encapsulation; scales appliances with demand.

cards.q: An application needs session affinity. Where is it configured?
cards.a: ALB target group stickiness (duration-based cookies)
cards.x: Prefer stateless design; use stickiness only when required.

cards.q: What happens to in-flight requests during an ASG scale-in?
cards.a: Connection draining (deregistration delay) lets them complete
cards.x: Default 300s on ALB target groups; tune to application needs.

cards.q: A single-instance legacy app cannot scale but must auto-recover from AZ failure. How?
cards.a: Place it behind an ALB in an ASG with min=1/max=1
cards.x: The ASG replaces the instance automatically if the AZ or instance fails.

cards.q: What is Route 53 Application Recovery Controller used for?
cards.a: Readiness checks and routing controls for multi-region failover
cards.x: Zonal shift moves traffic away from an impaired AZ quickly.

cards.q: Why spread ASG instances across AZs even for a dev workload?
cards.a: Automatic recovery if an AZ has issues, at no extra cost
cards.x: Balanced AZs are the default best practice.

decks.title: Decoupling with Queues & Events
decks.summary: SQS, SNS, EventBridge, and Step Functions for resilient flows. (Domain 2)

cards.q: A web tier gets traffic spikes that overwhelm the backend. Which pattern absorbs bursts?
cards.a: SQS queue between web tier and workers (buffering)
cards.x: The queue decouples producers from consumers; workers scale independently.

cards.q: SQS standard vs FIFO queues?
cards.a: Standard: best-effort ordering, at-least-once; FIFO: strict ordering and deduplication
cards.x: FIFO has lower throughput (300 TPS default, higher in batch mode).

cards.q: What is an SQS dead-letter queue for?
cards.a: Isolating messages that fail processing after max receives
cards.x: Alerts you to poison messages without blocking the queue.

cards.q: When should you use SNS instead of SQS?
cards.a: Fan-out: one message to many subscribers (push model)
cards.x: SNS topics push to SQS queues, Lambda, email, SMS, and HTTP endpoints.

cards.q: How do SQS visibility timeouts prevent duplicate processing?
cards.a: A received message hides for the timeout; if not deleted, it reappears
cards.x: Set the timeout longer than processing time; use heartbeats for long jobs.

cards.q: An order workflow has sequential steps with retries and human approval. Which service?
cards.a: Step Functions (state-machine orchestration)
cards.x: Visual workflows with built-in error handling, retries, and wait states.

cards.q: EventBridge vs SNS: when to choose EventBridge?
cards.a: Event-driven routing with rules, filtering, and SaaS event sources
cards.x: Event buses route events to targets based on patterns; great for choreography.

cards.q: What makes consumers idempotent, and why does SQS require it?
cards.a: Handling duplicate deliveries safely; standard queues deliver at-least-once
cards.x: Design workers so reprocessing the same message is harmless.

cards.q: A Lambda processes S3 uploads but throttling causes data loss. What fixes it?
cards.a: S3 event → SQS queue → Lambda (buffered, with DLQ and retries)
cards.x: Direct S3→Lambda has limited retries; a queue absorbs spikes.

cards.q: Short vs long polling in SQS?
cards.a: Long polling waits up to 20s for messages, cutting cost and latency
cards.x: Long polling is almost always the right choice.

cards.q: How do you fan out one order event to inventory, billing, and shipping workers?
cards.a: SNS topic with three SQS queue subscriptions
cards.x: Each team consumes independently; add or remove subscribers freely.

cards.q: A saga across microservices needs compensation on failure. Which AWS service?
cards.a: Step Functions with catch/retry and compensating states
cards.x: Orchestrates distributed transactions with rollback logic.

cards.q: What is EventBridge Scheduler used for?
cards.a: Cron-like scheduled invocations of 200+ AWS targets
cards.x: Replaces scheduled CloudWatch Events rules with more flexibility.

cards.q: Messages must be processed in exact order per customer. Which design?
cards.a: SQS FIFO with MessageGroupId per customer
cards.x: Ordering is guaranteed within a group; groups process in parallel.

cards.q: How do you handle a downstream API that rate-limits your workers?
cards.a: SQS with throttled consumer concurrency plus exponential backoff
cards.x: The queue smooths bursts; backoff respects the API’s limits.

cards.q: What is the maximum SQS message retention period?
cards.a: 14 days
cards.x: Default is 4 days; DLQs preserve failed messages for analysis.

cards.q: When would you choose Kinesis Data Streams over SQS?
cards.a: Ordered, replayable, high-throughput streaming with multiple consumers
cards.x: Kinesis retains records 24h–365d and supports real-time analytics.

cards.q: A decoupled architecture’s main resilience benefit?
cards.a: One component’s failure or slowness does not cascade to others
cards.x: Queues and async patterns isolate faults and enable independent scaling.

decks.title: Backup & Disaster Recovery
decks.summary: RTO/RPO, DR strategies, Aurora Global, and backup automation. (Domain 2)

cards.q: RTO vs RPO?
cards.a: RTO: how fast to recover; RPO: how much data loss is acceptable
cards.x: RTO 4h / RPO 1h means back online in 4 hours losing at most 1 hour of data.

cards.q: Cheapest DR strategy — and the slowest to recover?
cards.a: Backup and restore
cards.x: Then pilot light, warm standby, and multi-site active/active in rising cost and speed.

cards.q: What is pilot light DR?
cards.a: Minimal core (e.g. replicated DB) always running; scale out on failover
cards.x: Faster than backup/restore, cheaper than warm standby.

cards.q: Warm standby vs multi-site active/active?
cards.a: Warm standby runs scaled-down; active/active runs full capacity in both
cards.x: Active/active has near-zero RTO but roughly double the cost.

cards.q: How does S3 Cross-Region Replication help DR?
cards.a: Async object copy to another region for regional failover
cards.x: Requires versioning; can replicate to multiple destinations.

cards.q: RDS automated backups vs manual snapshots?
cards.a: Automated: 1–35 day retention with point-in-time recovery; manual snapshots persist until deleted
cards.x: Copy snapshots cross-region for DR.

cards.q: What is AWS Backup used for?
cards.a: Central policy-based backup across EC2, RDS, EFS, DynamoDB, and S3
cards.x: One schedule, retention, and compliance reporting for many services.

cards.q: How do you test a DR plan without impacting production?
cards.a: Failover drills in an isolated environment
cards.x: Test restores regularly; untested backups are not backups.

cards.q: Aurora Global Database provides…
cards.a: Cross-region read replicas with sub-second lag and fast failover
cards.x: RPO around 1 second, RTO around 1 minute for regional recovery.

cards.q: What is the 3-2-1 backup rule in AWS terms?
cards.a: 3 copies, 2 media/types, 1 offsite (e.g. cross-region)
cards.x: S3 versioning + cross-region replication + Backup Vault Lock.

cards.q: How does AWS Backup Vault Lock help against ransomware?
cards.a: WORM: prevents backup deletion before retention expires
cards.x: Even compromised admin credentials cannot delete locked recovery points.

cards.q: An application needs seconds-level RPO across regions for its database. Which option?
cards.a: Aurora Global Database or DynamoDB global tables
cards.x: Both offer multi-region replication with fast failover.

cards.q: What should a failover runbook contain?
cards.a: Exact steps, verification checks, rollback plan, and contact list
cards.x: Automate with Systems Manager or Step Functions where possible.

cards.q: How do you keep AMIs current for fast instance recovery?
cards.a: Automated AMI pipeline (e.g. EC2 Image Builder) on a schedule
cards.x: Stale AMIs mean long patching during recovery.

cards.q: Route 53 health checks for DR failover should monitor…
cards.a: The actual application endpoint, not just the server
cards.x: Fail over only when the app is truly unhealthy; use thresholds to avoid flapping.

cards.q: What is the difference between a snapshot and an AMI?
cards.a: Snapshot: point-in-time disk copy; AMI: snapshot plus launch metadata
cards.x: AMIs launch instances; snapshots restore volumes.

cards.q: For a multi-region active/passive web app, how is traffic failed over?
cards.a: Route 53 failover routing with health checks
cards.x: DNS TTL controls how fast clients switch; keep TTLs low.

cards.q: Why must KMS-encrypted data replicated cross-region be planned carefully?
cards.a: The destination region needs access to a valid KMS key
cards.x: Use multi-Region keys or re-encrypt with destination-region keys.

decks.title: Storage Selection
decks.summary: S3 vs EBS vs EFS vs instance store — picking the right store. (Domain 3)

cards.q: A workload needs shared file storage for 100 EC2 instances across AZs. Which service?
cards.a: Amazon EFS
cards.x: NFS shared filesystem, scales automatically, multi-AZ.

cards.q: EBS vs instance store: the key durability difference?
cards.a: EBS persists independently of the instance; instance store is ephemeral
cards.x: Never put irreplaceable data on instance store.

cards.q: Which EBS volume for a latency-sensitive database needing 64,000 IOPS?
cards.a: io2 Block Express
cards.x: Sub-millisecond latency and high durability; gp3 is the general-purpose default.

cards.q: When is EFS Infrequent Access the right choice?
cards.a: Files accessed rarely but needing millisecond retrieval
cards.x: Lifecycle policies move cold files automatically; cheaper than Standard.

cards.q: A Windows workload needs SMB shared storage on AWS. Which service?
cards.a: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
cards.x: Native SMB with AD integration; FSx for Lustre suits HPC.

cards.q: S3 vs EFS vs EBS: which for a data lake queried by Athena?
cards.a: S3
cards.x: Object storage with unlimited scale; Athena queries S3 directly.

cards.q: What is S3 Transfer Acceleration used for?
cards.a: Faster uploads over long distances via CloudFront edge locations
cards.x: Helps distributed uploaders; combine with multipart upload.

cards.q: How do you speed up large S3 uploads from one host?
cards.a: Multipart upload (parallel parts)
cards.x: Improves throughput and retry granularity for large objects.

cards.q: EBS gp3 vs gp2: what changed?
cards.a: gp3 decouples IOPS/throughput from size and costs less
cards.x: Baseline 3,000 IOPS included; provision extra independently.

cards.q: A CMS needs shared POSIX storage across AZs with file locking. Which?
cards.a: EFS
cards.x: NFSv4 with strong consistency; mounts on many instances at once.

cards.q: What is S3 Object Lambda for?
cards.a: Transform S3 objects on retrieval (redact PII, resize images)
cards.x: No data duplication; Lambda modifies the GET response.

cards.q: When should you use AWS Storage Gateway?
cards.a: Hybrid: on-prem apps need cloud-backed file, volume, or tape storage
cards.x: File Gateway presents S3 as NFS/SMB.

cards.q: EBS snapshots are…
cards.a: Incremental block-level backups stored in S3
cards.x: First snapshot is full; later ones store only changed blocks.

cards.q: How can two instances share one EBS volume for a clustered filesystem?
cards.a: EBS Multi-Attach (io1/io2, Nitro instances, same AZ)
cards.x: The cluster software must handle concurrent writes.

cards.q: S3 Select vs Athena: when is S3 Select better?
cards.a: Retrieving a subset of rows/columns from a single object
cards.x: Server-side filtering reduces transfer; Athena queries many objects with SQL.

cards.q: What does S3 strong read-after-write consistency enable?
cards.a: Safe read-immediately-after-write patterns without workarounds
cards.x: Applies to all S3 operations.

cards.q: A video render farm needs high-throughput shared scratch space. Which FSx?
cards.a: FSx for Lustre
cards.x: HPC-optimized, integrates with S3 as the durable store.

cards.q: How do you move 50 TB from on-prem to S3 with limited bandwidth?
cards.a: AWS DataSync (online) or Snowball (offline shipment)
cards.x: DataSync automates and validates; Snowball ships petabytes physically.

decks.title: Database Selection
decks.summary: RDS vs Aurora vs DynamoDB vs Redshift — the right engine. (Domain 3)

cards.q: A workload needs single-digit-millisecond reads at massive scale with flexible schema. Which database?
cards.a: DynamoDB
cards.x: Managed NoSQL key-value/document store.

cards.q: RDS vs Aurora: when is Aurora worth the premium?
cards.a: Need higher throughput, sub-30s failover, or Global Database
cards.x: Aurora replicates 6 ways across 3 AZs with continuous backup to S3.

cards.q: A reporting workload runs complex joins over petabytes. Which service?
cards.a: Redshift (data warehouse)
cards.x: Columnar storage and MPP for analytics; not for OLTP.

cards.q: How do RDS read replicas differ from a Multi-AZ standby?
cards.a: Replicas scale reads (async, promotable); standby is for HA failover (sync)
cards.x: Different purposes: performance vs availability.

cards.q: DynamoDB partition key design: what causes hot partitions?
cards.a: Uneven access concentrated on a few key values
cards.x: Use high-cardinality keys; add write sharding for hot keys.

cards.q: What is DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)?
cards.a: In-memory cache for DynamoDB (microsecond reads)
cards.x: Write-through; no application changes beyond the endpoint.

cards.q: When should you choose RDS over DynamoDB?
cards.a: Complex joins, multi-table transactions, or an existing SQL app
cards.x: The relational model fits structured, relational data.

cards.q: What is Aurora Serverless v2 for?
cards.a: Auto-scaling relational capacity for variable workloads
cards.x: Scales in fine increments; pay per ACU-second.

cards.q: Migrate Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL with minimal downtime. Which service?
cards.a: AWS DMS with ongoing replication
cards.x: DMS migrates and replicates changes until cutover; SCT converts schema.

cards.q: ElastiCache Redis vs Memcached: when Redis?
cards.a: Need persistence, pub/sub, sorted sets, or replication
cards.x: Memcached is simpler for pure caching; Redis is richer.

cards.q: How do you reduce DynamoDB costs for spiky read traffic?
cards.a: DAX caching plus on-demand or auto-scaling capacity
cards.x: Cache absorbs peaks; avoid over-provisioned RCUs.

cards.q: What is an Aurora reader endpoint used for?
cards.a: Load-balancing reads across replicas
cards.x: Writer endpoint goes to the primary; reader spreads SELECTs.

cards.q: A fraud-detection workload needs millisecond graph traversals. Which database?
cards.a: Neptune
cards.x: Purpose-built graph DB; relational engines cannot traverse efficiently.

cards.q: DocumentDB is best for…
cards.a: MongoDB-compatible document workloads
cards.x: JSON documents with flexible schema on managed infrastructure.

cards.q: How does RDS Proxy help Lambda-heavy workloads?
cards.a: Connection pooling: reuses DB connections across invocations
cards.x: Prevents connection exhaustion from thousands of concurrent functions.

cards.q: What is the purpose of DynamoDB Global Tables?
cards.a: Multi-region active-active replication with sub-second latency
cards.x: For globally distributed apps needing local reads and writes.

cards.q: Timestream is designed for…
cards.a: Time-series data (IoT, metrics) with automatic tiering
cards.x: Purpose-built; cheaper than relational for timestamped data.

cards.q: Choosing between provisioned and on-demand DynamoDB?
cards.a: On-demand for unpredictable/spiky; provisioned (+auto-scaling) for steady predictable
cards.x: On-demand costs more per request but needs zero capacity planning.

decks.title: Caching & Content Delivery
decks.summary: CloudFront, Global Accelerator, ElastiCache, and edge patterns. (Domain 3)

cards.q: A global audience needs low-latency static content. Which service?
cards.a: CloudFront CDN
cards.x: Caches at edge locations; integrates with S3, ALB, and WAF.

cards.q: CloudFront vs Global Accelerator: when Global Accelerator?
cards.a: Non-HTTP protocols, static IPs, or fastest path for dynamic content
cards.x: Anycast IPs route to the optimal edge; CloudFront is HTTP(S) caching.

cards.q: How do CloudFront signed URLs/cookies restrict content?
cards.a: Time-limited, optionally IP-bound URLs for private content
cards.x: Your app generates them; CloudFront validates the signature.

cards.q: CloudFront Functions vs Lambda@Edge?
cards.a: CloudFront Functions: lightweight edge logic; Lambda@Edge: full compute at edge
cards.x: Functions for header rewrites; Lambda@Edge for auth and heavier transforms.

cards.q: ElastiCache for a leaderboard with sorted scores: Redis or Memcached?
cards.a: Redis (sorted sets)
cards.x: Native data structures beat application-level sorting.

cards.q: How do you cache database queries without code changes?
cards.a: ElastiCache with lazy loading (cache-aside)
cards.x: Check cache, fall back to DB, populate cache on miss.

cards.q: What is API Gateway caching for?
cards.a: Reducing backend load by caching responses at the edge
cards.x: TTL per method; cache key on parameters.

cards.q: A CloudFront distribution must serve private S3 content. How?
cards.a: Origin Access Control (OAC) with a bucket policy allowing CloudFront
cards.x: OAC replaces legacy OAI; the bucket stays private.

cards.q: How do you invalidate CloudFront cache after a deployment?
cards.a: Create an invalidation for changed paths (or version filenames)
cards.x: Invalidations cost beyond the free tier; versioned filenames avoid them.

cards.q: What problem do Global Accelerator’s static anycast IPs solve?
cards.a: Clients whitelist fixed IPs while traffic routes optimally
cards.x: Two static IPs with health-checked endpoint failover.

cards.q: Cache-aside vs write-through: which for a read-heavy catalog?
cards.a: Cache-aside (lazy loading)
cards.x: Populate on miss; simple and resilient to cache failure.

cards.q: How do you reduce cross-AZ data-transfer costs for chatty services?
cards.a: Keep traffic in-AZ where possible; use zonal endpoints
cards.x: Cross-AZ traffic is billed; design locality-aware routing.

cards.q: What is the benefit of CloudFront origin failover?
cards.a: Automatic failover to a backup origin on errors
cards.x: Origin groups: primary S3, secondary backup.

cards.q: DAX vs ElastiCache: when DAX?
cards.a: Caching specifically for DynamoDB with zero application changes
cards.x: DAX speaks the DynamoDB API; ElastiCache is general-purpose.

cards.q: How does Route 53 latency-based routing improve performance?
cards.a: Directs users to the lowest-latency region
cards.x: Combine with health checks for resilient multi-region routing.

cards.q: A gaming leaderboard needs sub-millisecond reads globally. Which design?
cards.a: DynamoDB Global Tables with DAX
cards.x: Local reads/writes everywhere plus microsecond caching.

cards.q: What is the CloudFront price-class option for?
cards.a: Limiting edge locations to reduce cost
cards.x: Price Class 100: US/EU only; 200 adds Asia; All is global.

cards.q: How do you handle thundering herd on cache expiry?
cards.a: Staggered TTLs, request coalescing, or probabilistic early refresh
cards.x: Prevents all clients hitting the database simultaneously.

decks.title: Compute Cost Optimization
decks.summary: EC2 pricing models, Savings Plans, rightsizing, and Graviton. (Domain 4)

cards.q: A steady web tier runs 24/7 for 2 years. Cheapest EC2 option?
cards.a: Compute Savings Plan or Reserved Instances (1–3yr commit)
cards.x: Up to ~72% off On-Demand; Savings Plans flex across instance types.

cards.q: Batch jobs that tolerate interruption and run nightly. Cheapest?
cards.a: Spot Instances
cards.x: Up to 90% off; design for the 2-minute interruption notice.

cards.q: EC2 Instance Savings Plan vs Compute Savings Plan?
cards.a: Compute: flexible across family, region, even Fargate/Lambda; EC2: deeper discount, locked to family/region
cards.x: Choose flexibility vs maximum discount.

cards.q: What does Compute Optimizer recommend?
cards.a: Rightsizing: optimal instance types from utilization history
cards.x: Also covers EBS, Lambda, and ECS; integrates with Cost Explorer.

cards.q: How do Graviton instances reduce cost?
cards.a: Better price-performance (up to 40%) for compatible workloads
cards.x: ARM-based; test compatibility before migrating.

cards.q: When is Lambda cheaper than EC2 for an API?
cards.a: Spiky or infrequent traffic; pay per invocation vs idle servers
cards.x: Sustained high traffic often favors EC2 or ECS.

cards.q: What is the risk of over-provisioned ASG minimums?
cards.a: Paying for idle capacity 24/7
cards.x: Set min to the true baseline; use scheduled or target-tracking for peaks.

cards.q: How do Spot Fleets improve on single Spot requests?
cards.a: Diversify across instance types and AZs with capacity-optimized allocation
cards.x: Reduces interruption rate; combine with an On-Demand base.

cards.q: A dev environment runs 8h/day on weekdays. How to avoid paying 24/7?
cards.a: Scheduled start/stop (Instance Scheduler)
cards.x: Nights and weekends off cuts roughly 70% of cost.

cards.q: What is the key advantage of Savings Plans over Reserved Instances?
cards.a: Flexibility: apply across families, sizes, regions, and compute services
cards.x: Slightly lower maximum discount than standard RIs in exchange.

cards.q: How do you find idle EC2 instances wasting money?
cards.a: Cost Explorer + Compute Optimizer; look for under 5% CPU over weeks
cards.x: Also check unattached EBS volumes and old snapshots.

cards.q: Fargate vs EC2 for containers: the cost consideration?
cards.a: Fargate: no idle host cost, pay per task; EC2: cheaper at high steady utilization
cards.x: Break-even depends on utilization; Fargate wins for variable loads.

cards.q: What is the AWS Free Tier’s main cost trap?
cards.a: Exceeding limits or forgetting resources after 12 months
cards.x: Set billing alerts and budgets from day one.

cards.q: How do Dedicated Hosts differ in cost from Dedicated Instances?
cards.a: Hosts: per-socket licensing control, highest cost; Instances: single-tenant hardware
cards.x: Hosts suit BYOL compliance; instances suit isolation needs.

cards.q: Why use multiple AWS accounts for cost management?
cards.a: Separate bills, blast radius, and SCP guardrails per team and environment
cards.x: Organizations with consolidated billing keeps volume discounts.

cards.q: What does the Cost and Usage Report (CUR) provide?
cards.a: Granular hourly billing data for analysis in Athena or QuickSight
cards.x: The most detailed cost source; feeds FinOps dashboards.

cards.q: How do you commit to compute for the best discount with flexibility?
cards.a: Compute Savings Plans (1 or 3 year)
cards.x: Applies to EC2, Fargate, and Lambda across regions.

cards.q: Startup traffic is unpredictable. Which pricing avoids commitment risk?
cards.a: On-Demand with Auto Scaling, then Savings Plans once baselines emerge
cards.x: Commit only to the steady-state baseline you can measure.

decks.title: Storage & Data Cost Optimization
decks.summary: S3 tiers, lifecycle policies, transfer costs, and Athena. (Domain 4)

cards.q: Logs are rarely accessed after 30 days but kept 7 years. Cheapest S3 strategy?
cards.a: Lifecycle: Standard → Infrequent Access → Glacier Deep Archive
cards.x: Deep Archive is about $1/TB/month; retrieval takes 12–48h.

cards.q: S3 Intelligent-Tiering is best when…
cards.a: Access patterns are unknown or unpredictable
cards.x: Auto-moves between frequent, infrequent, and archive tiers; small monitoring fee.

cards.q: S3 Standard-IA vs One Zone-IA?
cards.a: One Zone-IA is cheaper but stores in a single AZ (less resilient)
cards.x: Use One Zone-IA only for easily reproducible data.

cards.q: What is the minimum-billable-size concern with Glacier?
cards.a: Small objects incur per-object metadata overhead
cards.x: Aggregate tiny files before archiving.

cards.q: How do you avoid S3 request costs dominating a high-request workload?
cards.a: Reduce request counts: bigger objects, caching, fewer LIST operations
cards.x: Requests are billed per thousand; LISTs add up fast.

cards.q: How do EBS snapshot costs accrue?
cards.a: Per GB-month of changed blocks stored in S3
cards.x: Delete stale snapshots; use DLM lifecycle policies.

cards.q: What is S3 Storage Lens for?
cards.a: Visibility into storage usage and cost anomalies across accounts
cards.x: Finds incomplete multipart uploads and cold buckets.

cards.q: Data transfer OUT to the internet vs between AZs?
cards.a: Internet egress ~$0.09/GB; cross-AZ ~$0.01/GB
cards.x: Keep traffic in-AZ or in-region where possible.

cards.q: How do you cut CloudFront costs for a high-traffic site?
cards.a: Price class limits, longer caching TTLs, Origin Shield, compression
cards.x: Most savings come from higher cache-hit ratios.

cards.q: What are incomplete multipart uploads costing you?
cards.a: Abandoned parts billed as Standard storage until aborted
cards.x: Add a lifecycle rule to abort incomplete uploads after N days.

cards.q: S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode affects cost how?
cards.a: Objects cannot be deleted early; you pay the full retention
cards.x: Plan retention carefully; there is no early-delete workaround.

cards.q: When does S3 Replication increase cost?
cards.a: Cross-region replication doubles storage plus transfer fees
cards.x: Replicate selectively with filters, not whole buckets.

cards.q: How do you rightsize EBS volumes?
cards.a: Monitor with CloudWatch; downsize gp3 and strip unused provisioned IOPS
cards.x: gp3 lets you tune IOPS and throughput independently of size.

cards.q: Cheapest way to retain 7 years of compliance logs?
cards.a: S3 Glacier Deep Archive with Object Lock
cards.x: About $1/TB/month; Vault Lock for compliance mode.

cards.q: Why tag S3 buckets with cost-center tags?
cards.a: Cost Explorer breaks spend down by tag for chargeback
cards.x: Activate cost-allocation tags in the Billing console.

cards.q: A data lake’s Athena queries are expensive. How do you cut cost?
cards.a: Partition, compress (Parquet), and limit scanned data
cards.x: Athena bills per TB scanned; format matters enormously.

cards.q: What is the AWS Pricing Calculator used for?
cards.a: Estimating architecture cost before building
cards.x: Model alternatives; export estimates for approval.

cards.q: A startup stores 100 TB of backups accessed once a year for audits. Cheapest tier?
cards.a: S3 Glacier Deep Archive
cards.x: Lowest storage cost; 12–48h retrieval is fine for annual audits.

tracks.title: CySA+
tracks.tagline: SOC analyst skills: detection, vulnerability management, and incident response, aligned to CS0-003.

decks.title: SOC Foundations
decks.summary: SOC tiers, alert triage, SIEM basics, and core analyst metrics. (Domain 1.0)

cards.q: What is the primary role of a Tier 1 SOC analyst?
cards.a: Triage incoming alerts and escalate confirmed incidents
cards.x: Tier 1 filters noise and does initial investigation; Tier 2 performs deep analysis and Tier 3 does threat hunting.

cards.q: What distinguishes a true positive from a false positive?
cards.a: A true positive is an alert for a real malicious event; a false positive flags benign activity
cards.x: A false negative — a missed attack — is the most dangerous outcome.
wrong: A true positive is always critical severity
A false positive means the SIEM is broken

cards.q: What is alert fatigue?
cards.a: Analysts become desensitized by excessive false positives and risk missing real threats
cards.x: Solved through tuning, correlation, and SOAR automation.

cards.q: What does a SIEM do?
cards.a: Collects, normalizes, and correlates logs to detect security events
cards.x: It provides central visibility; it does not block traffic inline.

cards.q: Which data sources typically feed a SIEM?
cards.a: Firewalls, IDS/IPS, EDR, servers, identity systems, and cloud audit logs
cards.x: Breadth of telemetry determines detection quality.

cards.q: What is log normalization?
cards.a: Converting logs from different formats into a common schema
cards.x: Normalization enables correlation across vendors and products.

cards.q: What is the difference between an event and an incident?
cards.a: An event is any observable occurrence; an incident is an event confirmed as a policy or security violation
cards.x: Only incidents trigger the formal incident response process.
wrong: An incident is always less severe

cards.q: What is the alert queue in SOC workflow?
cards.a: The prioritized list of alerts analysts work through
cards.x: Prioritized by severity, asset criticality, and threat intel context.

cards.q: What is mean time to detect (MTTD)?
cards.a: The average time from compromise to detection
cards.x: Lower MTTD limits attacker dwell time.

cards.q: What is mean time to respond (MTTR)?
cards.a: The average time from detection to containment or remediation
cards.x: A key SOC efficiency metric tracked over time.

cards.q: What is dwell time?
cards.a: How long an attacker remains undetected in the environment
cards.x: Industry averages are measured in days to weeks; hunting reduces it.
wrong: The time a user stays logged in
The length of a SOC shift

cards.q: What is a runbook?
cards.a: A documented step-by-step procedure for handling a specific alert type
cards.x: Runbooks ensure consistent Tier 1 response.

cards.q: What is a playbook?
cards.a: A broader conditional response plan linking multiple runbooks, tools, and decisions
cards.x: SOAR platforms automate playbooks.

cards.q: What is ticket enrichment?
cards.a: Automatically adding context such as asset owner, threat intel, and related alerts to a ticket
cards.x: Enrichment speeds up triage decisions.

cards.q: How do severity and priority differ in triage?
cards.a: Severity is the technical impact of the event; priority is the response order based on severity plus business context
cards.x: A compromised domain controller outranks a compromised print server.
wrong: Priority is always higher than severity

cards.q: What is the typical SOC escalation path?
cards.a: Tier 1 triage → Tier 2 investigation → Tier 3 hunting and IR → management
cards.x: The path is defined in the incident response plan.

cards.q: What is a baseline in security monitoring?
cards.a: A profile of normal behavior used to spot anomalies
cards.x: Deviations from baseline trigger investigation.

cards.q: Why does asset criticality matter in alert triage?
cards.a: More important systems raise an alert’s response priority
cards.x: A domain controller alert outranks a print server alert.
wrong: It determines the SIEM license cost

cards.q: How do IDS and IPS differ in SOC workflow?
cards.a: An IDS alerts for analyst review; an IPS blocks inline and its blocks become events to verify
cards.x: Poorly tuned IPS rules can disrupt legitimate business traffic.
wrong: An IDS blocks; an IPS only alerts

cards.q: What is continuous monitoring?
cards.a: The ongoing collection and analysis of security telemetry
cards.x: Required by frameworks such as NIST CSF; not a once-a-year audit.

decks.title: Vulnerability Scanning Basics
decks.summary: Scan types, CVSS fundamentals, and remediation concepts. (Domain 2.0)

cards.q: What is vulnerability scanning?
cards.a: Automated discovery of known weaknesses in systems
cards.x: It finds flaws; penetration testing exploits them to prove impact.

cards.q: How do credentialed and non-credentialed scans differ?
cards.a: Credentialed scans authenticate and see configuration detail; non-credentialed scans show the attacker’s external view
cards.x: Credentialed scans find missing patches; non-credentialed scans find exposed services.

cards.q: What is an agent-based vulnerability scan?
cards.a: A lightweight agent on the host reports vulnerabilities continuously
cards.x: Works well for remote, roaming, or intermittently offline assets.
wrong: A scan run by a human agent
A scan of physical security guards
A scan that requires no software

cards.q: What is CVSS?
cards.a: An open standard for scoring vulnerability severity from 0.0 to 10.0
cards.x: It has base, temporal, and environmental metric groups.

cards.q: What does a CVSS score of 9.8 indicate?
cards.a: Critical severity
cards.x: Scores of 9.0–10.0 are critical, but score alone does not equal organizational risk.

cards.q: What is a CVE?
cards.a: A unique public identifier for a known vulnerability, formatted CVE-YYYY-NNNNN
cards.x: CVEs enable common referencing across tools and teams.

cards.q: What is the NVD?
cards.a: NIST’s database of CVEs with CVSS scores and references
cards.x: The primary US source analysts consult for vulnerability details.

cards.q: What is a false positive in vulnerability scanning?
cards.a: A reported vulnerability that does not actually exist
cards.x: Validate findings before committing to patching sprints.

cards.q: What is a false negative in vulnerability scanning?
cards.a: A real vulnerability the scan failed to detect
cards.x: False negatives are more dangerous than false positives.

cards.q: What is vulnerability remediation?
cards.a: Fully fixing the root cause, usually by patching or reconfiguring
cards.x: Remediation is preferred over temporary workarounds.

cards.q: What is vulnerability mitigation?
cards.a: Reducing exposure without fully fixing the flaw, for example with compensating controls
cards.x: Used when patching is not immediately possible.
wrong: Pretending the flaw does not exist

cards.q: What is a vulnerability exception (risk acceptance)?
cards.a: Formal documented acceptance of a vulnerability’s risk by an owner
cards.x: Exceptions require sign-off and an expiry date.

cards.q: What is patch management?
cards.a: The process of testing and deploying updates on a schedule
cards.x: Includes rollback planning for failed patches.

cards.q: What is a maintenance window?
cards.a: A scheduled period for disruptive changes such as patching
cards.x: Minimizes business impact of reboots and outages.

cards.q: How does a vulnerability assessment differ from a penetration test?
cards.a: An assessment finds and reports weaknesses; a pentest exploits them to prove impact
cards.x: CySA+ focuses primarily on the assessment and analysis side.

cards.q: What is configuration compliance scanning?
cards.a: Checking systems against secure baselines such as CIS Benchmarks
cards.x: Finds drift from approved configurations.

cards.q: What is a CIS Benchmark?
cards.a: Consensus-based secure configuration guidance for platforms and applications
cards.x: Used as audit baselines for hardening.

cards.q: What does scan scope mean?
cards.a: The defined set of assets included in a vulnerability scan
cards.x: Scanning outside scope can be disruptive or unauthorized.

cards.q: Why are scans often scheduled during off-hours?
cards.a: Scanning can degrade performance or crash fragile systems
cards.x: Legacy and OT systems are especially sensitive to scan traffic.

cards.q: What is vulnerability chaining?
cards.a: Combining multiple lower-severity flaws into a serious exploit path
cards.x: Prioritize findings with attack-path context, not just single scores.

decks.title: SIEM Correlation & SOAR
decks.summary: Correlation rules, tuning, automation playbooks, and threat intel integration. (Domain 1.0)

cards.q: What is event correlation in a SIEM?
cards.a: Linking related events across sources into a single incident view
cards.x: Example: failed logins followed by a successful login and data exfiltration.

cards.q: What is a correlation rule?
cards.a: Logic that fires an alert when a defined pattern of events occurs
cards.x: Example: five failed logins in two minutes from one source.

cards.q: What is aggregation in SIEM processing?
cards.a: Combining similar events into one to reduce alert volume
cards.x: Prevents alert storms from repeated identical events.

cards.q: What is a SIEM use case?
cards.a: A defined detection scenario mapped to a specific threat
cards.x: Example: impossible-travel detection for compromised accounts.

cards.q: How do you tune a noisy detection rule?
cards.a: Adjust thresholds, add allowlists, and require additional corroborating events
cards.x: Measure the false positive rate before and after tuning.

cards.q: What is SOAR?
cards.a: Security orchestration, automation, and response: automated playbooks that act on alerts
cards.x: It enriches, contains, and tickets without manual clicks.

cards.q: What can SOAR automate during triage?
cards.a: Enrichment, ticket creation, IP blocking, account disablement, and evidence collection
cards.x: Humans should still approve high-impact destructive actions.

cards.q: What is a SOAR playbook trigger?
cards.a: The alert condition that starts a sequence of automated actions
cards.x: Example: a phishing alert triggers URL detonation and mailbox search.

cards.q: What is the main risk of fully automated SOAR response?
cards.a: Automated containment can disrupt legitimate business activity
cards.x: Use human-in-the-loop approval for destructive actions like network isolation.

cards.q: What does threat intelligence feed integration add to a SIEM?
cards.a: Automatic matching of observed indicators against known-bad IOCs
cards.x: Known threats get triaged faster with less analyst effort.

cards.q: What is the difference between an IOC and an IOA?
cards.a: An IOC is an artifact of compromise such as a hash or IP; an IOA is a behavior pattern such as living-off-the-land techniques
cards.x: IOAs survive attacker infrastructure changes better than IOCs.
wrong: IOCs are behaviors; IOAs are hashes

cards.q: What are STIX and TAXII?
cards.a: Standards for sharing threat intelligence: STIX is the format, TAXII the transport
cards.x: They enable machine-readable intel sharing between organizations.

cards.q: What is log retention and why does it matter to analysts?
cards.a: How long logs are kept; it determines the forensic lookback window
cards.x: Compliance often mandates a year or more of retention.

cards.q: What is EPS in SIEM sizing?
cards.a: Events per second: the ingest rate the SIEM must handle
cards.x: Under-licensing EPS causes dropped events and blind spots.

cards.q: What is a parser in SIEM architecture?
cards.a: Code that extracts fields from raw logs into the SIEM’s schema
cards.x: A parser is needed for each log source type.

cards.q: How do agent and agentless log collection differ?
cards.a: An agent is software on the host forwarding logs; agentless collection has the SIEM pull via syslog or WMI
cards.x: Agents provide richer endpoint telemetry.

cards.q: What is UEBA?
cards.a: User and entity behavior analytics: baselining normal behavior to flag anomalies
cards.x: Effective against insider threats and compromised accounts.

cards.q: What is a watchlist in a SIEM?
cards.a: A custom list of entities such as IPs, users, or domains to alert on
cards.x: Useful for VIP accounts and known-bad infrastructure.

cards.q: Scenario: the SIEM fires “multiple failed VPN logins followed by a success from a new country.” What is the likely assessment?
cards.a: Likely account takeover via brute force; force a password reset and review session activity
cards.x: Corroborate with impossible-travel logic and MFA logs.

cards.q: Scenario: an alert fires for a known-malicious IP communicating with a workstation. What is the efficient SOAR-driven response?
cards.a: Auto-isolate the host, block the IP at the perimeter, enrich the ticket, and assign to Tier 2
cards.x: Automation handles containment while the analyst investigates scope.
wrong: Ignore it as a false positive

decks.title: Threat Hunting & Telemetry Analysis
decks.summary: Hunting hypotheses, network, endpoint, and email analysis techniques. (Domain 1.0)

cards.q: What is threat hunting?
cards.a: Proactive, hypothesis-driven searching for threats that evaded automated detection
cards.x: It assumes breach and hunts beyond existing alerts.

cards.q: What is a hunting hypothesis?
cards.a: An educated guess about attacker behavior to test against telemetry
cards.x: Example: “attackers use WMI for lateral movement in this environment.”
wrong: A random guess with no basis

cards.q: What are the steps of the threat hunting loop?
cards.a: Hypothesize, investigate, uncover, and inform or improve
cards.x: Findings feed back into new detections and hypotheses.

cards.q: What is intel-driven threat hunting?
cards.a: Starting from threat reports and known actor TTPs
cards.x: Map the hunt to MITRE ATT&CK techniques.

cards.q: What is data-driven threat hunting?
cards.a: Exploring telemetry for anomalies without a specific intelligence lead
cards.x: Uses clustering and outlier analysis on large datasets.

cards.q: What network evidence indicates C2 beaconing?
cards.a: Regular, low-volume callbacks at fixed intervals, often with slight jitter
cards.x: Look for periodicity in NetFlow and DNS logs.

cards.q: What does DNS tunneling look like in logs?
cards.a: Long encoded subdomains with high query volume to rarely seen domains
cards.x: Data is exfiltrated inside DNS queries.

cards.q: What is NetFlow analysis used for?
cards.a: Determining who talked to whom, when, and how much — without payload content
cards.x: Reveals lateral movement and exfiltration patterns.

cards.q: What endpoint artifacts suggest process injection?
cards.a: Unexpected parent-child process relationships, such as Word spawning PowerShell
cards.x: EDR telemetry is the primary source for this analysis.

cards.q: What is living-off-the-land (LotL)?
cards.a: Attackers using legitimate system tools like PowerShell, WMI, and PsExec to evade detection
cards.x: Requires behavior-based detection rather than signature matching.

cards.q: Which email headers help investigate phishing?
cards.a: Return-Path, the Received chain, and SPF, DKIM, and DMARC results
cards.x: They reveal spoofing and the true sending infrastructure.

cards.q: What is URL detonation?
cards.a: Safely opening a suspicious link in a sandbox to observe its behavior
cards.x: A standard step in phishing email triage.

cards.q: What indicates a successful phishing compromise?
cards.a: Credential entry on a lookalike domain, followed by impossible travel or new mailbox rules
cards.x: Check for auto-forwarding rules created by the attacker.

cards.q: How do attackers abuse mailbox rules for persistence?
cards.a: Creating auto-forwarding rules or rules that delete security alerts
cards.x: Hunt for recently created or modified inbox rules after phishing.

cards.q: What is memory forensics used for?
cards.a: Finding fileless malware, injected code, and encryption keys in RAM
cards.x: Memory is volatile: capture it before rebooting.

cards.q: What is the order of volatility?
cards.a: Collect the most volatile evidence first: CPU cache and RAM before disk, then logs and archives
cards.x: Rebooting destroys the most valuable forensic evidence.

cards.q: What is timeline analysis in forensics?
cards.a: Ordering artifacts by timestamp to reconstruct the attack sequence
cards.x: Super-timelines combine disk, log, and registry timestamps.

cards.q: What is file carving?
cards.a: Recovering deleted files from unallocated disk space
cards.x: Useful when attackers delete logs or tools.

cards.q: Scenario: EDR shows rundll32.exe with no command line making external connections. What is the assessment?
cards.a: Highly suspicious; rundll32 is a common living-off-the-land loader — isolate the host and capture memory
cards.x: Legitimate rundll32 use almost always has a visible command line.

cards.q: Scenario: DNS logs show 10,000 queries to random-looking subdomains of a single domain in one hour. What is the assessment?
cards.a: Likely DNS tunneling or exfiltration — block the domain and inspect the source host
cards.x: The entropy and volume pattern is the key indicator.

decks.title: Vulnerability Prioritization & Response
decks.summary: EPSS, KEV, risk-based prioritization, and remediation workflows. (Domain 2.0)

cards.q: What is EPSS?
cards.a: The Exploit Prediction Scoring System: the estimated probability a vulnerability will be exploited in the next 30 days
cards.x: Prioritize high-EPSS flaws over high-CVSS flaws with no exploit activity.

cards.q: Why is CVSS alone insufficient for prioritization?
cards.a: It measures severity, not likelihood of exploitation or asset context
cards.x: Combine CVSS with EPSS, KEV status, and asset criticality.

cards.q: What is the CISA KEV catalog?
cards.a: The list of vulnerabilities known to be actively exploited in the wild
cards.x: US federal agencies must remediate KEV entries by binding deadlines.

cards.q: How do you prioritize a CVSS 9.8 with no known exploit versus a CVSS 7.5 listed in KEV?
cards.a: Remediate the KEV-listed flaw first: known exploitation beats theoretical severity
cards.x: Risk equals likelihood times impact, not score alone.

cards.q: How do remediation, mitigation, and acceptance differ?
cards.a: Remediation fixes the root cause; mitigation reduces exposure; acceptance formally documents the risk
cards.x: The choice depends on feasibility, cost, and risk appetite.

cards.q: When is mitigation preferred over remediation?
cards.a: When no patch exists, the system is legacy, or a change freeze is in effect
cards.x: Deploy compensating controls until remediation is possible.

cards.q: What is a compensating control for an unpatchable server?
cards.a: Network segmentation, IPS signatures, or restricted access around the vulnerable system
cards.x: Document it in the risk exception with an expiry date.

cards.q: What is vulnerability validation?
cards.a: Confirming a scanner finding is real and exploitable before acting on it
cards.x: Validation eliminates false positives before remediation work begins.

cards.q: What role does penetration testing play in vulnerability management?
cards.a: It validates exploitability and finds scanner blind spots
cards.x: Pentesting complements scanning; it does not replace it.

cards.q: What is continuous vulnerability management?
cards.a: Ongoing cycles of discovery, prioritization, and remediation
cards.x: Modern programs scan continuously, not annually.

cards.q: What is threat-informed prioritization?
cards.a: Weighting vulnerabilities by active threat intelligence relevant to your sector
cards.x: Example: prioritizing CVEs that ransomware groups are currently exploiting.

cards.q: What is a remediation SLA?
cards.a: A deadline for fixing vulnerabilities based on severity, such as criticals within 15 days
cards.x: SLA compliance is tracked as a core security metric.

cards.q: What is a vulnerability exception workflow?
cards.a: Request, risk assessment, owner approval, expiry date, and periodic review
cards.x: Exceptions must expire; otherwise accepted risk accumulates silently.

cards.q: What is the risk of indefinite vulnerability exceptions?
cards.a: Accepted risk accumulates until it becomes breach material
cards.x: Review exceptions at least quarterly.

cards.q: What is configuration drift?
cards.a: Systems gradually diverging from their secure baselines over time
cards.x: Compliance scanning detects drift between audits.

cards.q: Why run both authenticated and unauthenticated scans?
cards.a: Authenticated scans find missing patches and misconfigurations; unauthenticated scans find exposed services
cards.x: Each shows a different view of the attack surface.

cards.q: Scenario: a scanner flags Log4Shell on 200 hosts, threat intel shows active exploitation, and 10 hosts are internet-facing. What is the priority order?
cards.a: Patch internet-facing hosts first, then internal hosts ordered by EPSS, KEV status, and asset criticality
cards.x: Exposure plus exploitability drives the order, not alphabetical lists.

cards.q: What is a vulnerability disclosure program?
cards.a: An official channel for researchers to report flaws to the vendor
cards.x: It is distinct from a bug bounty, which pays for reports.

cards.q: What is coordinated vulnerability disclosure?
cards.a: The vendor remediates before the flaw is publicly released
cards.x: It protects users during the window between discovery and patching.

cards.q: Which metrics show vulnerability program health?
cards.a: Mean time to remediate by severity, percentage of criticals past SLA, and scan coverage
cards.x: Report trends over time, not just raw counts.

decks.title: Incident Response & Forensics
decks.summary: IR phases, containment and recovery, digital forensics, and legal considerations. (Domain 3.0)

cards.q: What are the NIST SP 800-61 incident response phases?
cards.a: Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication, and Recovery; Post-Incident Activity
