cards.x: The foundational lifecycle every IR plan follows.

cards.q: What happens during the preparation phase?
cards.a: Building the IR team, tooling, playbooks, and communication plans
cards.x: Tabletop exercises validate readiness before a real incident.

cards.q: What is the first priority when ransomware is confirmed on a host?
cards.a: Contain it: isolate the host from the network immediately
cards.x: Stop lateral spread before beginning detailed analysis.

cards.q: What is the difference between short-term and long-term containment?
cards.a: Short-term containment isolates the threat now; long-term containment provides temporary clean systems to restore service
cards.x: It balances stopping spread against business disruption.

cards.q: What is eradication in incident response?
cards.a: Removing all attacker presence: malware, backdoors, and persistence mechanisms
cards.x: Verify eradication with clean scans before recovery.

cards.q: What is recovery in incident response?
cards.a: Restoring systems to normal operation from known-good backups or images
cards.x: Monitor closely for reinfection after recovery.

cards.q: What is the purpose of the post-incident lessons-learned review?
cards.a: Blameless analysis of what happened and how to improve people, process, and technology
cards.x: Findings feed playbook and control updates.

cards.q: What is digital forensics?
cards.a: The scientific collection and analysis of digital evidence
cards.x: Methodology preserves the evidence’s admissibility.

cards.q: What is chain of custody?
cards.a: The documented record of who handled evidence, when, and how
cards.x: An unbroken chain is required for evidence to be admissible.

cards.q: What is a forensic image?
cards.a: A bit-for-bit copy of storage media used for analysis
cards.x: The original media stays pristine and hashed.

cards.q: What does write-blocking do in forensics?
cards.a: Hardware or software that prevents any writes to evidence media
cards.x: It preserves hash integrity of the original evidence.

cards.q: What is legal counsel’s role in incident response?
cards.a: Protecting privilege, managing breach notification obligations, and liaising with law enforcement
cards.x: Engage legal early in significant incidents.

cards.q: What is the tension between evidence preservation and business continuity?
cards.a: Forensics wants systems frozen; the business wants them restored quickly
cards.x: Predefined criteria in the IR plan resolve the conflict.

cards.q: How do you contain a compromised cloud account?
cards.a: Revoke sessions and access keys, block API access, and snapshot resources for forensics
cards.x: Cloud containment is typically faster than on-premises.

cards.q: What is the difference between an incident and a breach?
cards.a: A breach is confirmed unauthorized acquisition of data; an incident is any broader security event
cards.x: Breach determination triggers notification laws.

cards.q: Should analysts perform attack attribution?
cards.a: Generally avoid definitive attribution; focus on TTPs and remediation
cards.x: Attribution is difficult and rarely changes the response.

cards.q: What is a war room in incident response?
cards.a: A centralized coordination space or channel with defined roles during major incidents
cards.x: Keeps communications structured under pressure.

cards.q: What is an IR retainer?
cards.a: A pre-contracted external incident response firm for surge support
cards.x: It is far faster than procuring help mid-crisis.

cards.q: Scenario: EDR quarantines malware on a finance workstation, and the user reports odd wire transfer instructions. What are the next steps?
cards.a: Treat as potential BEC plus compromise: isolate the host, check mailbox rules, and verify transactions out-of-band
cards.x: Correlate endpoint and email telemetry before deciding scope.

cards.q: Scenario: logs show data staged in a zip on a server with a large outbound transfer at 2 AM. What is the phase and action?
cards.a: Likely exfiltration in progress: contain the host and preserve the archive as evidence, then scope before eradication
cards.x: Do not delete the staged data; it is evidence.

decks.title: Attack Frameworks & Threat-Informed Defense
decks.summary: MITRE ATT&CK, the cyber kill chain, and the diamond model. (Domain 3.0)

cards.q: What is MITRE ATT&CK?
cards.a: A knowledge base of adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures
cards.x: Analysts map detections and incidents to its technique IDs.

cards.q: What is the difference between a tactic, technique, and procedure in ATT&CK?
cards.a: A tactic is the adversary’s goal, a technique is how they achieve it, and a procedure is the specific implementation
cards.x: Example: Persistence (tactic) via Registry Run Keys (technique).

cards.q: What are the phases of the cyber kill chain?
cards.a: Reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, and actions on objectives
cards.x: Breaking any link stops the attack.

cards.q: How does ATT&CK improve on the kill chain for analysts?
cards.a: It is non-linear and far more granular, reflecting how real attacks loop and skip phases
cards.x: The kill chain is a useful model but too rigid alone.

cards.q: What is the diamond model of intrusion analysis?
cards.a: A framework linking adversary, capability, infrastructure, and victim with analytic pivoting
cards.x: Pivoting across vertices enriches investigations.

cards.q: Which ATT&CK tactic covers credential dumping such as LSASS access?
cards.a: Credential Access
cards.x: Technique T1003 covers OS credential dumping.

cards.q: Which ATT&CK tactic covers scheduled tasks used for persistence?
cards.a: Persistence
cards.x: Technique T1053 covers scheduled task and job abuse.

cards.q: What is lateral movement in ATT&CK?
cards.a: Techniques adversaries use to move through the environment, such as PsExec, RDP, and WMI
cards.x: Detect it via anomalous use of admin protocols.

cards.q: What is defense evasion in ATT&CK?
cards.a: Techniques adversaries use to avoid detection, such as obfuscation and disabling security tools
cards.x: Fileless attacks live primarily in this tactic.

cards.q: What is exfiltration in ATT&CK?
cards.a: Techniques for stealing data, such as automated transfer, exfiltration over C2, or via cloud storage
cards.x: DLP and egress monitoring counter it.

cards.q: What is initial access in ATT&CK?
cards.a: The techniques used to gain the first foothold, such as phishing, exploits, or valid accounts
cards.x: Hardening email and patching internet-facing systems cut it off.

cards.q: What is privilege escalation in ATT&CK?
cards.a: Techniques for gaining higher-level permissions, such as exploitation or token manipulation
cards.x: Least privilege limits the blast radius.

cards.q: How do you map a SIEM use case to ATT&CK?
cards.a: Tie each detection to specific tactic and technique IDs
cards.x: Mapping reveals coverage gaps in the detection program.

cards.q: What is ATT&CK Navigator used for?
cards.a: Visualizing technique coverage across defenses as heatmaps
cards.x: It shows detection maturity per technique.

cards.q: What is threat-informed defense?
cards.a: Prioritizing controls against the TTPs most relevant to your sector and threat landscape
cards.x: It combines threat intel with ATT&CK mapping.

cards.q: Why are TTP-based detections more durable than IOC-based ones?
cards.a: TTPs describe attacker behavior, which changes slowly; IOCs are artifacts that attackers rotate quickly
cards.x: Behavioral detections age far better than hash or IP blocklists.

cards.q: Scenario: an attacker used valid VPN credentials, moved via WMI, then staged data for theft. Which kill chain phases apply?
cards.a: Delivery and exploitation via valid accounts, installation and C2, then actions on objectives — with phases collapsed through legitimate access
cards.x: Valid credentials let attackers skip early kill chain phases.

cards.q: What is MITRE D3FEND in relation to ATT&CK?
cards.a: A knowledge base of defensive techniques mapped against offensive TTPs
cards.x: It guides countermeasure selection for observed techniques.

cards.q: What is an adversary emulation exercise?
cards.a: Simulating a specific threat actor’s TTPs to test defensive controls
cards.x: A purple-team activity bridging red and blue teams.

cards.q: Why map incidents to ATT&CK after response?
cards.a: It standardizes reporting and reveals systemic detection gaps
cards.x: The mapping feeds detection engineering improvements.

decks.title: Reporting & Stakeholder Communication
decks.summary: Security metrics, executive communication, and compliance reporting. (Domain 4.0)

cards.q: What belongs in an executive incident summary?
cards.a: Business impact, scope, actions taken, and next steps — without technical jargon
cards.x: Executives need decisions, not packet captures.

cards.q: How are MTTD and MTTR used in reporting?
cards.a: As trend metrics showing detection and response efficiency over time
cards.x: Improving trends demonstrate program value to leadership.

cards.q: What is a vulnerability aging metric?
cards.a: How long vulnerabilities remain open past their remediation SLA
cards.x: It shows remediation discipline, not just scan counts.

cards.q: What is scan coverage as a metric?
cards.a: The percentage of assets scanned during the period
cards.x: Unscanned assets are blind spots in the program.

cards.q: How do metrics differ from KPIs?
cards.a: Metrics measure activity; KPIs tie measurements to business objectives
cards.x: “Critical vulnerabilities remediated within SLA” is a KPI.

cards.q: Who are the stakeholders in incident response?
cards.a: Executives, legal, public relations, IT, HR, customers, and regulators
cards.x: A predefined communications plan covers each audience.

cards.q: What is a stakeholder communication matrix?
cards.a: A plan defining who gets told what, when, and by whom during an incident
cards.x: It prevents leaks, rumors, and confused messaging.

cards.q: What must a breach notification include?
cards.a: What happened, the types of data affected, steps taken, and contact information
cards.x: Timelines and content requirements vary by regulation.

cards.q: What is the GDPR 72-hour rule?
cards.a: Supervisory authorities must be notified within 72 hours of becoming aware of a breach
cards.x: Affected individuals are notified when there is high risk to them.

cards.q: What is attorney-client privilege in incident response?
cards.a: Legal counsel directing the investigation so findings are protected
cards.x: Engage counsel early in significant incidents.

cards.q: What is a lessons-learned report?
cards.a: A blameless post-incident analysis with assigned action items
cards.x: Each improvement gets an owner and a deadline.

cards.q: How should technical findings be presented to non-technical audiences?
cards.a: Lead with risk and business impact, using analogies and visuals
cards.x: Avoid acronym soup; translate technical detail into decisions.

cards.q: What does a risk register entry for a vulnerability contain?
cards.a: Description, severity, owner, remediation plan, and deadline
cards.x: It creates accountability for each accepted or open risk.

cards.q: Which compliance frameworks require vulnerability management reporting?
cards.a: PCI DSS, HIPAA, SOC 2, and ISO 27001
cards.x: They require evidence of a continuous, documented process.

cards.q: How do an incident report and a forensic report differ?
cards.a: An incident report covers timeline and business impact; a forensic report details technical evidence
cards.x: They serve different audiences and purposes.
wrong: Forensic reports go to the press

cards.q: Why document “what went well” in post-incident reviews?
cards.a: It reinforces effective controls and recognizes good team actions
cards.x: Balanced reviews build a stronger security culture.

cards.q: What is trend reporting in SOC metrics?
cards.a: Showing alert volume, true positive rate, and MTTR over time
cards.x: Trends justify staffing, tooling, and budget decisions.

cards.q: Scenario: the board asks “are we secure?” How should the analyst answer?
cards.a: With risk framing: top risks, mitigation status, and trends — never absolute claims
cards.x: “Secure” is not a state; risk management is the honest answer.

cards.q: What is responsible disclosure communication?
cards.a: Coordinated, factual public statements made after remediation, prepared with PR and legal
cards.x: It controls the narrative instead of letting rumors spread.

cards.q: What should a SOC shift handoff note include?
cards.a: Open investigations, pending actions, and items to watch
cards.x: Good handoffs prevent dropped incidents between shifts.

tracks.title: AWS Security Specialty
tracks.tagline: Detect, protect, and govern AWS workloads at the specialty level.

decks.title: Threat Detection Services
decks.summary: GuardDuty, Security Hub, and Macie fundamentals. (Domain 1.0)

cards.q: What log sources does GuardDuty analyse without any agent installed?
cards.a: CloudTrail management events, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS query logs (plus S3, EBS, RDS, Lambda, and EKS findings where enabled)
cards.x: GuardDuty is agentless; it consumes logs AWS already collects.
wrong: EC2 system logs, application logs, and CloudWatch metrics
Inspector scan results and Config snapshots

cards.q: A GuardDuty finding reports an EC2 instance communicating with a known malicious domain. What is the recommended first containment step?
cards.a: Isolate the instance by replacing its security group with one that denies all traffic, then snapshot for forensics
cards.x: Containment before eradication preserves evidence and stops lateral movement.
wrong: Reboot the instance and rotate all IAM keys
Disable GuardDuty to stop alert noise

cards.q: What is the primary purpose of AWS Security Hub?
cards.a: Aggregate security findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, and partners into the ASFF standard format with CIS benchmark checks
cards.x: One console for posture; it does not itself detect threats.

cards.q: Which service uses machine learning to discover PII and PHI in S3 buckets?
cards.a: Amazon Macie
cards.x: Macie scans S3 objects and classifies sensitive data types.

cards.q: GuardDuty is enabled in one region. Does it protect resources in other regions?
cards.a: No, GuardDuty is regional and must be enabled per region (use Organizations delegated admin to enable centrally)
cards.x: Most security services are regional; enable them everywhere you operate.
wrong: Yes, it is global like IAM
No, GuardDuty cannot be multi-region at all

cards.q: What does a GuardDuty "high" severity finding for IAM (e.g. anomalous API calls) typically indicate?
cards.a: Potentially compromised credentials being used from an unusual location or in an unusual pattern
cards.x: Treat IAM findings as credential compromise until proven otherwise.

cards.q: How does Amazon Detective help during incident response?
cards.a: It builds visual entity graphs linking GuardDuty findings to users, roles, and IP addresses over time
cards.x: Detective answers "what else did this actor touch" without manual log correlation.

cards.q: What is the difference between a GuardDuty finding and a Security Hub insight?
cards.a: A finding is a single detection event; an insight is a grouped collection of related findings matching a pattern
cards.x: Insights help prioritise, e.g. all findings tied to one instance.
wrong: Findings are manual, insights are automatic
Insights are raw logs, findings are summaries

cards.q: Which GuardDuty protection plan covers S3 data events (object-level API calls)?
cards.a: The S3 protection plan, which must be enabled separately from the foundational threat detection
cards.x: S3 data events cost extra because of their volume; enable selectively.
wrong: It is included by default in every account

cards.q: A company needs centralised threat detection across 50 AWS accounts. What is the best approach?
cards.a: Enable GuardDuty in every region via Organizations with a delegated administrator account
cards.x: Delegated admin gives one pane of glass without cross-account role juggling.
wrong: Enable GuardDuty in the management account only
Create one IAM role per account and check manually

cards.q: What does it mean that Security Hub findings use the ASFF format?
cards.a: AWS Security Finding Format normalises severity, resources, and remediation across all integrated products
cards.x: Standard fields let automation and SIEMs parse any finding uniformly.
wrong: Findings are encrypted with ASFF keys

cards.q: Macie reports a bucket containing unencrypted national ID numbers. What two actions should follow?
cards.a: Enable default encryption on the bucket and restrict access with bucket policies plus Block Public Access
cards.x: Remediate the exposure, then protect the data class going forward.

decks.title: Security Logging Foundations
decks.summary: CloudTrail, CloudWatch Logs, metrics, and alarms. (Domain 2.0)

cards.q: What is the difference between CloudTrail management events and data events?
cards.a: Management events log control-plane API calls (free, on by default); data events log data-plane calls like S3 object access and Lambda invocations (extra cost)
cards.x: Enable data events selectively on sensitive buckets.
wrong: Data events are free, management events cost extra
Management events only exist in GovCloud

cards.q: Where should CloudTrail logs be stored to prevent tampering by a compromised admin?
cards.a: A dedicated, locked-down log-archive account with MFA Delete and restricted write access
cards.x: Separation of duties: attackers who own a workload account cannot erase their trail.
wrong: In the same account as the workloads

cards.q: What does CloudTrail Insights detect?
cards.a: Unusual API activity such as spikes in call volume or anomalous patterns that may indicate misuse
cards.x: Insights surfaces statistical anomalies, not signature matches.

cards.q: How do you query CloudTrail logs across months of history with SQL?
cards.a: Enable CloudTrail Lake (or Athena on the S3 log bucket) and run SQL against the event data store
cards.x: Lake gives up to 7 years retention with SQL; Athena queries raw S3 files.

cards.q: What is the purpose of a CloudWatch Logs metric filter?
cards.a: Extract numeric metrics from log patterns (e.g. count of "AccessDenied") to trigger alarms
cards.x: Turns log text into actionable signals.

cards.q: An alarm must fire when there are more than 5 failed console logins in 10 minutes. Which components do you need?
cards.a: A metric filter on the CloudTrail log group plus a CloudWatch alarm on the resulting metric
cards.x: Filter creates the metric; the alarm evaluates it.
wrong: A GuardDuty finding and an SNS topic
A Config rule and a Lambda function
An IAM policy and CloudTrail Insights

cards.q: What is the retention risk of CloudWatch Logs with the default setting?
cards.a: Log groups retain logs indefinitely (Never Expire) unless you set a retention period
cards.x: Set retention deliberately; indefinite storage wastes money and complicates scoping.

cards.q: How can CloudTrail be configured so that no region is left unmonitored?
cards.a: Create an organization trail that logs all regions and delivers to one central bucket
cards.x: An org trail in the management account covers every member account and region.
wrong: CloudTrail is global by default with no setup

cards.q: What does enabling CloudTrail log file validation provide?
cards.a: Digest files with hashes that prove log files were not modified or deleted after delivery
cards.x: Validation detects tampering; it does not prevent deletion of the bucket itself.

cards.q: Which CloudWatch feature can automatically remediate, e.g. reboot an impaired EC2 instance?
cards.a: CloudWatch alarms with EC2 actions (stop, terminate, reboot, recover)
cards.x: Alarms can invoke EC2 actions, Auto Scaling policies, or SNS notifications.

cards.q: What is the difference between CloudWatch Events and EventBridge?
cards.a: EventBridge is the evolved service: same event bus concept plus SaaS integrations, schema registry, and archives
cards.x: Use EventBridge for new event-driven automation.

cards.q: A security team needs near-real-time alerts on root account usage. What is the minimal setup?
cards.a: CloudTrail org trail plus a metric filter for root API calls and a CloudWatch alarm to SNS
cards.x: Root usage should be rare; any occurrence deserves an immediate page.

cards.q: Why send VPC Flow Logs to S3 instead of CloudWatch Logs for long-term analysis?
cards.a: S3 is far cheaper for high-volume, long-retention storage and works directly with Athena
cards.x: CloudWatch Logs suits real-time alerting; S3 suits cheap archival analytics.
wrong: S3 encrypts automatically, CloudWatch does not

cards.q: What information do VPC Flow Logs NOT contain?
cards.a: Packet payloads; they record metadata only (IPs, ports, protocol, bytes, action)
cards.x: Flow logs show who talked to whom, not what was said.

decks.title: IAM Foundations
decks.summary: Users, roles, policies, and MFA for least privilege. (Domain 4.0)

cards.q: In IAM policy evaluation, which statement always wins?
cards.a: An explicit Deny
cards.x: Evaluation order: default implicit deny, then explicit allow, then explicit deny overrides everything.
wrong: The identity-based policy over the resource policy

cards.q: Why should applications on EC2 use IAM roles instead of access keys?
cards.a: Roles provide temporary credentials that rotate automatically via the instance metadata service
cards.x: Long-lived keys get leaked; roles eliminate the secret to steal.
wrong: Access keys do not work on EC2

cards.q: What is the difference between an identity-based policy and a resource-based policy?
cards.a: Identity policies attach to users/groups/roles; resource policies attach to resources like S3 buckets and KMS keys
cards.x: Cross-account access typically needs both sides to allow.
wrong: Resource policies only exist for EC2
Identity policies cannot grant S3 access

cards.q: A developer needs S3 read access for 2 hours to debug an issue. What is the most secure approach?
cards.a: Assume a role with the needed permissions; credentials expire automatically
cards.x: Temporary elevation beats permanent permission grants.
wrong: Create an IAM user with permanent keys

cards.q: What does enforcing MFA for IAM users protect against?
cards.a: Credential theft: a stolen password alone is no longer enough to authenticate
cards.x: Require MFA especially for console access and privileged roles.
wrong: Phishing of the MFA device itself

cards.q: What is an IAM instance profile?
cards.a: A container that passes an IAM role to an EC2 instance
cards.x: The instance assumes the role and gets temporary credentials.

cards.q: Which IAM policy element specifies the API actions allowed?
cards.a: Action
cards.x: Resource scopes where, Condition constrains when, Effect allows or denies.

cards.q: What is the purpose of the IAM Policy Simulator?
cards.a: Test whether a policy grants or denies specific actions before deploying it
cards.x: Validate least-privilege changes without breaking production.

cards.q: Why is the root user dangerous even with a strong password?
cards.a: It has unrestricted permissions that no IAM policy or SCP can limit
cards.x: Lock it with MFA, never use it daily, monitor it with alarms.
wrong: It is billed at a higher rate

cards.q: What does the IAM credential report show?
cards.a: Password/key age, MFA status, and last-used timestamps for all IAM users
cards.x: Use it to find stale keys and users without MFA.

cards.q: A policy allows s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::data/*. What happens for arn:aws:s3:::data (the bucket itself)?
cards.a: Denied (implicitly): the resource ARN covers objects, not the bucket; ListBucket needs the bucket ARN
cards.x: S3 ARNs distinguish bucket-level from object-level permissions.

cards.q: What is the AWS managed policy "ReadOnlyAccess" appropriate for?
cards.a: Auditors and read-only tooling that need visibility across services without modification rights
cards.x: It is broad; scope it down for production workloads.

cards.q: How does IAM Access Analyzer help with least privilege?
cards.a: It identifies unused permissions and generates policies based on actual CloudTrail activity
cards.x: Rightsize policies from observed behaviour, not guesses.
wrong: It blocks all unused permissions automatically

cards.q: What is the difference between AWS managed and customer managed IAM policies?
cards.a: AWS managed policies are maintained by AWS and update automatically; customer managed policies are versioned and controlled by you
cards.x: Prefer customer managed for anything you must audit or freeze.
wrong: Customer managed policies cannot be attached to roles
AWS managed policies are always more secure

decks.title: Incident Response Playbooks
decks.summary: Detective, containment, eradication, and recovery in AWS. (Domain 1.0)

cards.q: During IR, how does Amazon Detective shorten investigation time?
cards.a: It pre-correlates GuardDuty findings into timelines of IP, user, and role activity across accounts
cards.x: Analysts pivot from one finding to the full blast radius in clicks.

cards.q: What is the correct order of operations for a compromised EC2 instance?
cards.a: Detect and scope, contain (isolate networking), collect forensic snapshots, eradicate, recover, lessons learned
cards.x: Never skip containment; wiping first destroys evidence.

cards.q: How should forensic disk images be preserved for a compromised EBS volume?
cards.a: Create EBS snapshots, share/copy them to a dedicated forensic account, and restrict access
cards.x: Snapshots are point-in-time and immutable; isolation keeps the chain of custody.
wrong: Copy files to an S3 public bucket

cards.q: What is the fastest way to revoke a compromised IAM user session immediately?
cards.a: Attach an inline policy with an explicit deny keyed on aws:TokenIssueTime, or delete/deactivate the user and their keys
cards.x: Killing keys alone does not invalidate already-issued temporary session tokens.
wrong: Wait for the session to expire

cards.q: Which service can automatically remediate a GuardDuty finding, e.g. isolate an instance?
cards.a: EventBridge rules matching GuardDuty findings can trigger Lambda or SSM Automation runbooks
cards.x: Detection to response in seconds without human clicks.

cards.q: What should an incident response runbook for ransomware on EBS include?
cards.a: Isolate instances, snapshot volumes before any change, check for encrypted volumes and unfamiliar snapshots shared from other accounts
cards.x: Attackers share malicious AMIs/snapshots; verify provenance.
wrong: Delete all snapshots to save cost

cards.q: How does Security Hub help prioritise during a multi-account incident?
cards.a: Insights group related findings (e.g. all findings on one instance) and CIS controls show blast radius
cards.x: One prioritised queue instead of dozens of account consoles.

cards.q: What is a "game day" in the context of AWS incident response?
cards.a: A simulated incident exercise that tests detection, runbooks, and team coordination before a real event
cards.x: Practice the playbook; the exam expects preparation over improvisation.

cards.q: After containing a compromised Lambda function, what must be rotated?
cards.a: Any credentials, keys, or tokens the function could access, plus the function code and layers if tampered
cards.x: Assume the execution role and environment variables were exposed.

cards.q: Which AWS service provides a managed digital forensics workflow for EC2?
cards.a: There is none fully managed; the pattern is EBS snapshots plus Inspector/Detective analysis in an isolated forensic account
cards.x: Know the building blocks rather than expecting one button.

cards.q: What is the role of AWS Artifact during incident response?
cards.a: It provides on-demand access to AWS compliance reports (SOC 2, ISO) that may be needed for breach notification evidence
cards.x: Regulators and customers will ask for them; have them ready.

cards.q: Why should IR runbooks be tested with least-privilege automation roles?
cards.a: Over-permissive response automation can itself become an attack path or cause outages
cards.x: Scope Lambda/SSM remediation roles to exactly the actions the playbook needs.
wrong: Automation is never allowed in IR

decks.title: Monitoring and Log Analysis
decks.summary: Config, Flow Logs, Athena, and centralised analysis. (Domain 2.0)

cards.q: What does AWS Config record that CloudTrail does not?
cards.a: Configuration history and compliance state of resources over time (what it looks like now vs before)
cards.x: CloudTrail logs who did what; Config tracks what the resource became.

cards.q: How do AWS Config rules differ from Security Hub standards?
cards.a: Config rules evaluate resource compliance continuously; Security Hub aggregates findings including Config evaluations
cards.x: Config is the sensor; Security Hub is one dashboard that consumes it.
wrong: Config rules only work in one region

cards.q: What is a Config conformance pack?
cards.a: A bundled set of Config rules and remediation actions deployed as one package (e.g. CIS benchmark)
cards.x: Deploy baseline compliance across accounts quickly.

cards.q: How do you analyse VPC Flow Logs at scale for a compromised IP across 30 days?
cards.a: Store flow logs in S3 and query with Athena using SQL on time-bounded partitions
cards.x: Partition by date; full scans of unpartitioned data are slow and costly.

cards.q: What is the cheapest way to retain 7 years of CloudTrail for audit?
cards.a: An organization trail to S3 with lifecycle policies transitioning to Glacier/Deep Archive
cards.x: Compliance retention does not need hot queryable storage.

cards.q: When would you choose CloudTrail Lake over Athena for log analysis?
cards.a: When you need immutable, queryable event storage with SQL and up to 7-year retention managed by AWS
cards.x: Lake is purpose-built; Athena is flexible but you manage the S3 lifecycle.

cards.q: What does enabling "all regions" on a trail protect against?
cards.a: An attacker operating in a region where logging was never enabled
cards.x: Future regions are included automatically.
wrong: Nothing, regions are logged by default
It doubles the cost with no benefit

cards.q: How can KMS-encrypted CloudWatch Logs be shared with a central security account?
cards.a: Resource-based log destination policies plus KMS key policies granting the central account decrypt rights
cards.x: Both the log destination and the key must authorise the consumer.

cards.q: What is CloudWatch Logs Insights used for during IR?
cards.a: Ad-hoc queries over log groups to find indicators (e.g. all 403s from one IP in the last hour)
cards.x: Faster than exporting when logs are already centralised.

cards.q: Which S3 feature proves log files have not been altered, complementing CloudTrail digest validation?
cards.a: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode on the log bucket
cards.x: WORM storage: not even the root user can delete until retention expires.

cards.q: What is the security value of AWS Config timeline view?
cards.a: It shows exactly when a resource drifted from compliant to non-compliant and which API call caused it
cards.x: Attribution plus state history in one view.

cards.q: How do you detect S3 bucket policy changes in near real time?
cards.a: Config rule detecting non-compliant bucket policies plus EventBridge on Config compliance-change events to SNS/Lambda
cards.x: Detect the drift, then notify or auto-remediate.

cards.q: What is an AWS Config aggregator used for?
cards.a: Collect Config data from multiple accounts and regions into one view for central compliance
cards.x: Essential for multi-account governance.

cards.q: Why should CloudTrail data events be enabled selectively rather than everywhere?
cards.a: Data events (S3 object, Lambda) are high-volume and billed per event; enable them on sensitive resources only
cards.x: Management events already cover control-plane activity for free.

cards.q: What does "management events" read vs write separation allow in CloudTrail?
cards.a: Log read-only API calls separately from mutating calls to cut volume while keeping change history
cards.x: Many orgs log writes always and reads only for sensitive services.

decks.title: Network Security Controls
decks.summary: VPC design, NACLs vs security groups, WAF, and Shield. (Domain 3.0)

cards.q: A security group and a NACL both filter traffic. What is the key behavioural difference?
cards.a: Security groups are stateful (return traffic auto-allowed) and allow-only; NACLs are stateless (each direction evaluated) and support deny rules
cards.x: Ephemeral ports matter for NACLs; security groups handle them automatically.
wrong: NACLs are stateful, security groups are not

cards.q: NACL rules are evaluated in which order?
cards.a: Ascending rule number; the first match wins, so put specific denies on low numbers
cards.x: Rule 100 beats rule 200 regardless of allow or deny.

cards.q: An application needs HTTPS from the internet but SSH only from a bastion subnet. How many security groups and what rules?
cards.a: Two: a web SG allowing 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 and an app SG allowing 22 only from the web SG (referenced by SG ID, not IP)
cards.x: Referencing SG IDs keeps rules correct when instances scale.
wrong: One SG with all ports open
One SG allowing 22 and 443 from anywhere

cards.q: What is the primary use case for AWS WAF?
cards.a: Filtering Layer 7 web traffic (SQLi, XSS, bot control) in front of ALB, CloudFront, or API Gateway
cards.x: WAF is not a network firewall; pair it with security groups and NACLs.

cards.q: What is the difference between a WAF rate-based rule and AWS Shield Advanced?
cards.a: Rate-based rules block request floods at Layer 7 per IP; Shield Advanced protects Layers 3/4/7 against DDoS with DRT support
cards.x: Use both: WAF for application abuse, Shield for volumetric attacks.
wrong: Rate-based rules only work on EC2

cards.q: When should you use WAF managed rule groups versus custom rules?
cards.a: Managed groups for common threats (OWASP Top 10, known bad inputs); custom rules for business logic like blocking specific paths or headers
cards.x: Start managed, add custom for your app specifics.

cards.q: What does AWS Shield Standard provide at no extra cost?
cards.a: Automatic DDoS protection for CloudFront, Route 53, ALB, and Elastic IPs
cards.x: Always on; Advanced adds cost, DRT, and cost protection.

cards.q: A multi-tier VPC needs web, app, and data subnets. What is the most secure layout?
cards.a: Public subnets for load balancers only; app and data in private subnets across at least two AZs with NAT for outbound
cards.x: No instance that users reach directly should hold data.
wrong: Data tier in public subnets with strong SGs

cards.q: Why are VPC endpoints (PrivateLink) a security improvement over internet gateways for AWS service access?
cards.a: Traffic to S3, DynamoDB, and other services stays on the AWS private network and can be restricted by endpoint policies
cards.x: No public IPs, no internet exposure, policy control per endpoint.
wrong: They are faster than Direct Connect

cards.q: What is the difference between a gateway endpoint and an interface endpoint?
cards.a: Gateway endpoints (S3, DynamoDB) are free route-table targets; interface endpoints (most other services) are ENIs with hourly plus data charges
cards.x: Design for cost: gateways where available.

cards.q: How do you prevent an EC2 instance from reaching the internet while still allowing SSM?
cards.a: Private subnet with no NAT/IGW route plus VPC interface endpoints for SSM, EC2 Messages, and SSM Messages
cards.x: Session Manager works without any internet path.

cards.q: What is AWS Network Firewall used for that security groups cannot do?
cards.a: Stateful, centrally-managed Layer 3-7 inspection with Suricata rules across VPCs
cards.x: Use it as a transit inspection point; SGs remain per-instance.

cards.q: In a hub-and-spoke Transit Gateway design, where should inspection appliances sit?
cards.a: In a dedicated security VPC attached to the transit gateway, so all spoke traffic routes through inspection
cards.x: Centralised control without per-VPC appliances.

cards.q: What does enabling "Block Public Access" at the account level guarantee for S3?
cards.a: No bucket in the account can become public via ACLs or policies, regardless of individual bucket settings
cards.x: It is the single most effective S3 guardrail.

cards.q: A WAF is blocking legitimate traffic after a managed rule update. What is the safest immediate response?
cards.a: Switch the rule to Count mode to log matches without blocking, then tune exclusions
cards.x: Count mode gives visibility without outage.

cards.q: What is the security benefit of separate AWS accounts per environment over one account with IAM separation?
cards.a: Blast-radius isolation: SCPs, separate CloudTrail, and no accidental cross-environment privilege paths
cards.x: Multi-account is the AWS-recommended security boundary.
wrong: It removes the need for VPCs

decks.title: Advanced IAM and Federation
decks.summary: SCPs, permission boundaries, cross-account roles, Cognito, and SSO. (Domain 4.0)

cards.q: What is the critical limitation of Service Control Policies (SCPs)?
cards.a: They never grant permissions; they only set the maximum allowed, and they do not apply to the management account
cards.x: An SCP allow without an identity policy allow still denies.
wrong: They apply to the management account

cards.q: When would you use an IAM permission boundary instead of an SCP?
cards.a: To delegate limited admin to developers: they can create roles but never exceed the boundary, within a single account
cards.x: Boundaries enable safe delegation; SCPs govern whole accounts.

cards.q: A partner needs read access to one S3 bucket in your account. What is the most secure pattern?
cards.a: A cross-account IAM role with an external ID and a trust policy limited to the partner account, scoped to that bucket
cards.x: External ID prevents confused-deputy attacks.
wrong: Create an IAM user for the partner with permanent keys

cards.q: What is the confused deputy problem in cross-account roles?
cards.a: A malicious party tricks your role into acting on their behalf by omitting the external ID check
cards.x: Always require a unique external ID for third-party trust policies.

cards.q: Cognito User Pools vs Identity Pools: which does what?
cards.a: User Pools authenticate users (sign-up/sign-in, MFA); Identity Pools federate identities to get temporary AWS credentials
cards.x: User Pools are the directory; Identity Pools are the AWS access broker.
wrong: User Pools grant S3 access directly

cards.q: What is IAM Identity Center (successor to AWS SSO) used for?
cards.a: Centralised workforce SSO across AWS accounts and business apps with permission sets
cards.x: One identity, many accounts, no long-lived keys.

cards.q: How should CI/CD pipelines authenticate to AWS without long-lived keys?
cards.a: OIDC federation from the identity provider (e.g. GitHub Actions) to assume a short-lived role
cards.x: No static secrets to rotate or leak.
wrong: Embed access keys in the repo
Share one IAM user across pipelines

cards.q: What does the IAM condition key aws:PrincipalOrgID enforce?
cards.a: That the call comes from an account inside your Organization, blocking exfiltration to external accounts
cards.x: Use it in S3 bucket and KMS key policies for data-perimeter guardrails.
wrong: The principal is the root user

cards.q: A key policy and an IAM policy both matter for KMS. Why?
cards.a: KMS evaluates both: the key policy is the primary gate and cross-account access requires the key policy to allow it
cards.x: Unlike S3, KMS defaults to key-policy-only control.
wrong: IAM policies are ignored for KMS

cards.q: What is the purpose of IAM Access Analyzer unused-access findings?
cards.a: Flag permissions granted but never used so policies can be tightened toward least privilege
cards.x: Feed findings into a regular access-review cycle.

cards.q: How do you enforce MFA for all privileged role assumptions?
cards.a: Add an MFA condition (aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent) to the role trust policy
cards.x: The trust policy is the gate; conditions there apply before any session starts.
wrong: Enable MFA on the EC2 instance

cards.q: What is the difference between a service-linked role and a service role?
cards.a: Service-linked roles are predefined by AWS services and cannot have their permissions edited; service roles are customer-created
cards.x: Prefer service-linked where available for least privilege by default.
wrong: Service-linked roles need manual key rotation

decks.title: Data Protection and Encryption
decks.summary: KMS, S3 encryption, CloudHSM, ACM, and Macie. (Domain 5.0)

cards.q: What are the three KMS key types and when is each appropriate?
cards.a: AWS managed (default, AWS controls rotation), customer managed (you control policy and rotation), AWS owned (service-internal)
cards.x: Use customer managed keys for sensitive data needing audit control.

cards.q: A KMS key policy allows the key for one account, but an IAM policy in another account also allows it. Does cross-account decryption work?
cards.a: Only if the key policy explicitly allows the external account; IAM allow alone is insufficient for KMS
cards.x: KMS defaults to key-policy authority unlike most services.

cards.q: What is envelope encryption and why does KMS use it?
cards.a: Data is encrypted with a data key; the data key is encrypted by the KMS key, so plaintext keys never leave your code boundary longer than needed
cards.x: GenerateDataKey returns both plaintext (use then discard) and encrypted (store) versions.

cards.q: When should you use a KMS grant instead of editing the key policy?
cards.a: For temporary, programmatic delegation (e.g. an AWS service needs limited key use) without changing the durable policy
cards.x: Grants are scoped, expirable delegations.

cards.q: What does automatic key rotation do for customer managed KMS keys?
cards.a: Generates new backing key material yearly while retaining old material so existing ciphertext still decrypts
cards.x: Rotation without re-encryption: AWS keeps prior key versions.

cards.q: SSE-S3 vs SSE-KMS vs SSE-C: which gives you audit trail of every decryption?
cards.a: SSE-KMS, because each use is logged to CloudTrail with the requesting identity
cards.x: SSE-S3 is free and simple; SSE-C means you manage keys entirely.

cards.q: What are S3 Bucket Keys and why do they matter for cost?
cards.a: A bucket-level KMS data key reused for objects, cutting KMS API calls (and cost) by up to 99% for high-volume buckets
cards.x: Enable bucket keys whenever using SSE-KMS at scale.

cards.q: A compliance rule requires that AWS personnel cannot access encryption keys. Which option satisfies it?
cards.a: CloudHSM (dedicated, single-tenant HSM) or KMS with external key store (XKS)
cards.x: Standard KMS is multi-tenant AWS-managed; CloudHSM gives exclusive control.

cards.q: What is the practical difference between CloudHSM and KMS?
cards.a: CloudHSM is dedicated single-tenant hardware you manage (FIPS 140-2 Level 3); KMS is multi-tenant AWS-managed with simpler APIs
cards.x: Choose CloudHSM for regulatory mandates; KMS for everything else.

cards.q: How do you ensure TLS certificates for an ALB are always valid without manual renewal?
cards.a: Use ACM public certificates with DNS validation; ACM renews automatically when the validation record persists
cards.x: Email-validated certs cannot auto-renew reliably.
wrong: ACM certificates cannot be used on ALBs

cards.q: Can an ACM public certificate private key be exported?
cards.a: No; ACM-managed keys never leave the service (use ACM Private CA or CloudHSM for exportable keys)
cards.x: This is a security feature, not a limitation, for most use cases.

cards.q: What is the most secure way to store database credentials for an application on EC2?
cards.a: Secrets Manager with automatic rotation and retrieval via the SDK at runtime
cards.x: Never in environment variables, code, or Parameter Store plaintext.
wrong: In Systems Manager Parameter Store as String

cards.q: Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store SecureString: when does Secrets Manager win?
cards.a: When you need automatic rotation, cross-account sharing, or RDS-integrated rotation
cards.x: Parameter Store is cheaper for static config; Secrets Manager for true secrets.

cards.q: How does Macie help meet data protection obligations beyond initial discovery?
cards.a: Continuous monitoring of S3 for new sensitive data plus automated findings to Security Hub for response
cards.x: Discovery is day one; Macie watches for drift.

cards.q: What S3 feature lets you require encryption on every object upload?
cards.a: Default bucket encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS) plus a bucket policy denying PutObject without the encryption header
cards.x: Belt and suspenders: default plus explicit deny.

cards.q: A company must prove that deleted data is unrecoverable in the cloud. What is the accepted method?
cards.a: Crypto-shredding: destroy the KMS key material so ciphertext can never be decrypted
cards.x: Deleting S3 objects alone leaves replicated copies; killing keys is definitive.

cards.q: What does EBS default encryption at the account level protect against?
cards.a: Snapshot sharing mistakes and stolen volumes: every new EBS volume and snapshot is encrypted automatically
cards.x: Enable it in every region; it does not encrypt pre-existing volumes.

cards.q: How do you share an encrypted RDS snapshot with another account?
cards.a: Share the snapshot and grant the target account use of the KMS key via the key policy
cards.x: Both the snapshot share and key permission are required.
wrong: Only the management account can share

cards.q: What is the risk of using AWS managed KMS keys for highly sensitive data?
cards.a: You cannot view or edit the key policy, set rotation, or get the same audit granularity as customer managed keys
cards.x: The exam expects customer managed keys for regulated data.

cards.q: How should TLS be enforced for data in transit to an S3 bucket?
cards.a: Bucket policy denying requests where aws:SecureTransport is false
cards.x: The canonical condition key for TLS enforcement.

cards.q: What is Certificate Transparency monitoring in ACM useful for?
cards.a: Detecting misissued or unauthorized certificates for your domains via public CT logs
cards.x: Catches rogue issuance early.

cards.q: A Lambda function needs to decrypt with KMS. What is the least-privilege setup?
cards.a: Execution role with kms:Decrypt scoped to the specific key ARN plus the key policy allowing the role
cards.x: Scope both the IAM policy and consider key policy constraints.
wrong: Store the key in an env var

cards.q: What does S3 Object Lock in compliance mode guarantee?
cards.a: WORM immutability: objects cannot be deleted or overwritten until retention expires, not even by root
cards.x: Required for SEC 17a-4 style retention.

cards.q: How do VPC endpoint policies improve data protection for S3 access?
cards.a: They restrict which buckets and actions are reachable through the endpoint, containing exfiltration paths
cards.x: Even with broad IAM, the endpoint policy can deny sensitive buckets.

cards.q: What is the purpose of KMS multi-Region keys?
cards.a: Encrypt once and decrypt in other regions without re-encryption, for DR and global apps
cards.x: Key material replicates; each region still logs independently.

cards.q: Why is client-side encryption still relevant when SSE-KMS exists?
cards.a: Data is encrypted before it reaches AWS, so AWS never sees plaintext (needed for strict zero-trust requirements)
cards.x: Trade-off: you own key management and lose some service features.

cards.q: What must be true for CloudTrail log file encryption with KMS (SSE-KMS)?
cards.a: The KMS key policy must allow CloudTrail to encrypt (kms:GenerateDataKey) and be in the same region as the trail
cards.x: A misconfigured key policy silently breaks log delivery.
wrong: Any key in any region works
The key must be AWS managed

cards.q: How does AWS Backup help the data protection story?
cards.a: Centralised, policy-driven backups with vault lock (WORM) across services and accounts
cards.x: Vault Lock gives ransomware-resistant recovery points.

decks.title: Secure Compute and Workload Hardening
decks.summary: Inspector, Systems Manager, and EC2/EKS hardening. (Domain 3.0)

cards.q: What does Amazon Inspector assess that GuardDuty does not?
cards.a: Software vulnerabilities and network reachability in EC2, ECR images, and Lambda code
cards.x: Inspector finds patchable CVEs; GuardDuty finds active malicious behaviour.

cards.q: How should Inspector findings be operationalised at scale?
cards.a: Aggregate to Security Hub, prioritise by exploitability, and auto-remediate patching via Systems Manager Patch Manager
cards.x: Findings without a remediation pipeline are just noise.

cards.q: Why is SSM Session Manager more secure than SSH with key pairs?
cards.a: No inbound ports, no long-lived keys, IAM-authenticated sessions with full CloudTrail/CloudWatch logging
cards.x: Removes the entire SSH key management problem.

cards.q: What does Systems Manager Patch Manager provide for compliance?
cards.a: Scheduled, automated patching with baselines and compliance reporting across fleets
cards.x: Prove patch state to auditors centrally.

cards.q: How do you prevent EC2 instances from being launched without IMDSv2?
cards.a: An SCP or IAM policy denying RunInstances unless MetadataHttpTokens is required, plus Config rule monitoring
cards.x: Guardrail plus detective control.

cards.q: What was the security lesson of the 2019 Capital One breach for AWS architects?
cards.a: SSRF against IMDSv1 let an attacker steal role credentials; enforce IMDSv2 and least-privilege roles
cards.x: The exam loves this case: metadata service plus overbroad role.

cards.q: How should EKS cluster endpoint access be secured?
cards.a: Private endpoint with authorized networks or bastion/VPN access; never a public endpoint open to 0.0.0.0/0
cards.x: Public EKS endpoints are a top misconfiguration.

cards.q: What does EKS Pod Identity (or IRSA) solve?
cards.a: Fine-grained IAM permissions per pod without sharing node role credentials
cards.x: Each service account gets exactly the AWS access it needs.

cards.q: Why run Inspector on ECR images in the CI/CD pipeline?
cards.a: Catch OS and language-package CVEs before deployment, blocking vulnerable images from reaching production
cards.x: Shift-left: fail the build, not the audit.

cards.q: What is the secure way to give a third-party scanner access to your VPC?
cards.a: A cross-account role with external ID scoped to read-only, time-boxed, and monitored via CloudTrail
cards.x: No shared credentials, full audit trail, easy revocation.
wrong: Open the security groups to their IP

cards.q: How does AWS Firewall Manager help multi-account infrastructure security?
cards.a: Centrally deploy WAF rules, Shield Advanced, and security groups/NACL policies across Organizations
cards.x: One policy, every account compliant.

cards.q: What is the purpose of EC2 Image Builder in a secure pipeline?
cards.a: Produce hardened, tested, versioned AMIs automatically so every instance launches compliant
cards.x: Golden images eliminate snowflake servers.

cards.q: A Lambda function processes PII. What are the top three hardening steps?
cards.a: Least-privilege execution role, VPC deployment with no internet unless needed, and environment variables encrypted with KMS
cards.x: Scope identity, network, and secrets together.
wrong: Put it in a public subnet
Store secrets in plain env vars

cards.q: How do you detect a crypto-miner on EC2 quickly?
cards.a: GuardDuty CryptoCurrency finding plus CloudWatch CPU anomaly alarms and Inspector for the initial-access CVE
cards.x: Detection layers: behaviour, metrics, vulnerabilities.

cards.q: What does enabling Nitro Enclaves provide for EC2 workloads?
cards.a: Isolated, attested compute environments for processing highly sensitive data like crypto keys
cards.x: No persistent storage, no admin access, cryptographic attestation.

cards.q: Why should Auto Scaling launch templates enforce IMDSv2 and encrypted EBS?
cards.a: Every instance launched by the fleet inherits the secure baseline automatically
cards.x: Secure defaults at the template level beat per-instance fixes.

decks.title: Security Governance at Scale
decks.summary: Organizations, Control Tower, Config rules, and auditability. (Domain 6.0)

cards.q: What is the recommended AWS account structure for security?
cards.a: A management account plus separate accounts per workload/environment, governed by SCPs and centralised logging
cards.x: Account boundaries are the strongest isolation AWS offers.

cards.q: What is the difference between preventive and detective guardrails in Control Tower?
cards.a: Preventive (SCPs) block non-compliant actions; detective (Config rules) flag them after the fact
cards.x: Prevent what you can; detect the rest.

cards.q: How does a delegated administrator account improve security operations?
cards.a: Security tooling (GuardDuty, Security Hub, Macie) is managed centrally without using the management account daily
cards.x: The management account stays locked down; security admins work in the delegated account.

cards.q: What is the purpose of the log archive account in a landing zone?
cards.a: Immutable, centralised storage for CloudTrail and Config logs from all accounts
cards.x: Tamper-evident audit trail separated from workload accounts.

cards.q: How do SCPs and permission boundaries work together?
cards.a: SCPs cap what an entire account can do; permission boundaries cap what delegated admins can grant within an account
cards.x: Two layers: account ceiling, then delegation ceiling.

cards.q: What is AWS Control Tower Account Factory?
cards.a: Standardised, pre-approved account provisioning with baselines applied automatically
cards.x: Every new account is born compliant.

cards.q: How can Config conformance packs prove CIS benchmark compliance to auditors?
cards.a: Deploy the CIS pack across the organization; non-compliant resources and history export as evidence
cards.x: Continuous evidence beats point-in-time screenshots.

cards.q: What is the security value of tagging strategy enforced by policy?
cards.a: Tags drive automation: SCPs, Config rules, and cost allocation all key off consistent tags
cards.x: Untagged resources escape governance.

cards.q: How should cross-account CloudTrail be queried during an incident?
cards.a: From the log archive account using Athena or CloudTrail Lake over the centralised S3 bucket
cards.x: One query surface for every account.

cards.q: What does AWS Audit Manager provide?
cards.a: Continuous evidence collection mapped to frameworks (CIS, PCI, HIPAA) for audit readiness
cards.x: Turns Config and CloudTrail data into auditor-friendly reports.

cards.q: Why require MFA Delete on the log archive S3 bucket?
cards.a: Even a compromised admin cannot permanently delete versioned log objects without the MFA device
cards.x: Protects the audit trail from insider or attacker deletion.

cards.q: What is the principle behind "deny by default" SCPs for new accounts?
cards.a: New accounts start with minimal allowed services; teams request expansion through change control
cards.x: Least privilege applied at the organization level.

cards.q: How does IAM Access Analyzer help govern at organization scale?
cards.a: Centrally surface unused permissions, public resource exposure, and cross-account access across accounts
cards.x: One dashboard for entitlement risk.
wrong: It only works in one account

cards.q: What is a detective control for ensuring encryption standards across 100 accounts?
cards.a: A Config aggregator rule checking default encryption plus Security Hub CIS controls reporting centrally
cards.x: Detect drift everywhere from one place.

cards.q: When an employee leaves, what is the correct AWS offboarding sequence?
cards.a: Disable SSO/IAM access first, revoke sessions and rotate shared secrets, then remove from groups after handover
cards.x: Access removal before account deletion preserves audit continuity.

cards.q: What should a cloud security baseline document define?
cards.a: Required guardrails: SCPs, Config rules, logging destinations, encryption defaults, and network patterns
cards.x: Codify the non-negotiables; automate their enforcement.

cards.q: How do you prove to regulators that no production data left the region?
cards.a: VPC endpoint policies plus SCPs denying cross-region actions, evidenced by Config history and CloudTrail
cards.x: Prevent, then prove with logs.

cards.q: What is the role of AWS Artifact in governance?
cards.a: On-demand third-party audit reports (SOC 2, ISO 27001, PCI) for customer and regulator assurance
cards.x: Due diligence without auditing AWS yourself.

cards.q: Why separate the management account from all workloads?
cards.a: A compromised workload can never reach billing, Organizations, or SCP controls; the management account has minimal attack surface
cards.x: The most privileged account does the least.

cards.q: What is drift detection in CloudFormation and why does it matter for governance?
cards.a: It identifies resources changed outside IaC so compliance state matches the approved template
cards.x: ClickOps undermines every guardrail; detect it.

cards.q: How should security findings be routed to the right team automatically?
cards.a: Security Hub custom insights plus EventBridge rules routing by account, severity, and resource tags to team channels
cards.x: Findings die in inboxes; route them to owners.

cards.q: What is the minimum audit trail an SCS-C02 architect should design for?
cards.a: Org-wide CloudTrail with validation to a locked log archive, Config recording everywhere, and 1+ year retention
cards.x: You cannot investigate what you did not record.

tracks.title: AI Engineering
tracks.tagline: ML fundamentals to production LLM apps, agents, and AI security.

decks.title: Machine Learning Basics
decks.summary: Supervised vs unsupervised, training, and overfitting.

cards.q: Supervised learning uses…
cards.a: Labelled examples (inputs with known answers)
cards.x: Classification and regression are supervised.

cards.q: Clustering customers without labels is…
cards.a: Unsupervised learning
cards.x: k-means is a classic clustering algorithm.

cards.q: Learning by trial and reward is…
cards.a: Reinforcement learning
cards.x: RLHF uses it to align language models with human preferences.

cards.q: Predicting a house price is which task?
cards.a: Regression
cards.x: Predicting a category (spam/not spam) is classification.

cards.q: What is overfitting?
cards.a: A model memorises training data and fails on new data
cards.x: Symptom: high training accuracy, low validation accuracy.
wrong: A model too simple to learn

cards.q: What is underfitting?
cards.a: A model too simple to capture the pattern
cards.x: Poor accuracy on both training and validation data.

cards.q: Why split data into train, validation, and test sets?
cards.a: To tune on one set and measure true generalisation on unseen data
cards.x: Never tune on the test set, or its score is no longer honest.

cards.q: What is a feature?
cards.a: An input variable the model uses
cards.x: The label is the output you want to predict.

cards.q: What does a loss function measure?
cards.a: How wrong the model’s predictions are
cards.x: Training minimises the loss.

cards.q: What is gradient descent?
cards.a: Adjusting parameters step by step in the direction that reduces loss
cards.x: The learning rate sets the step size.

cards.q: Why is precision vs recall important for a malware detector?
cards.a: Precision = few false alarms; recall = few missed threats
cards.x: There is usually a trade-off; F1 balances the two.

cards.q: Why can accuracy mislead on imbalanced data?
cards.a: Predicting the majority class scores high while missing the rare class
cards.x: If 1% is fraud, "never fraud" is 99% accurate.

puzzles.prompt: A malware model flags 50 files: 40 are truly malicious, 10 are clean. What is its precision (%)?
puzzles.x: Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 40 / 50 = 80%. It says nothing about the malware it missed; that is recall.

puzzles.prompt: Order a basic ML workflow.
puzzles.x: Touch the test set only once, at the end, or its score stops being honest.

decks.title: Neural Networks & Deep Learning
decks.summary: Neurons, backprop, and architectures.

cards.q: What does an activation function add?
cards.a: Non-linearity, so networks can learn complex patterns
cards.x: ReLU is the common default: max(0, x).

cards.q: What is backpropagation?
cards.a: Computing each weight’s gradient of the loss via the chain rule
cards.x: Karpathy’s micrograd builds it from scratch.

cards.q: What is an epoch?
cards.a: One full pass over the training data
cards.x: A batch is a subset processed in one step.

cards.q: Which architecture was classic for images?
cards.a: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs)
cards.x: Vision transformers now compete strongly.

cards.q: Which architecture underlies modern LLMs?
cards.a: The Transformer
cards.x: Introduced in "Attention Is All You Need" (2017).

cards.q: What does self-attention let a model do?
cards.a: Weigh how relevant every token is to every other token
cards.x: Captures long-range context in parallel.

cards.q: What is transfer learning?
cards.a: Starting from a pretrained model and adapting it to a new task
cards.x: Much less data and compute than training from scratch.

cards.q: What is dropout?
cards.a: Randomly disabling neurons during training to reduce overfitting
cards.x: Disabled at inference time.

cards.q: Why are GPUs used for deep learning?
cards.a: They run massive numbers of matrix operations in parallel
cards.x: TPUs and other accelerators do the same.

cards.q: What is a parameter in a neural network?
cards.a: A learned weight or bias
cards.x: Model size is often quoted in parameters, e.g. 70B.

cards.q: What is a hyperparameter?
cards.a: A setting chosen before training, like learning rate or batch size
cards.x: Tune them on the validation set.

resources.title: Andrej Karpathy: Neural Networks Zero to Hero

decks.title: LLM Fundamentals
decks.summary: Tokens, context windows, sampling, and prompting.

cards.q: What is a token?
cards.a: A chunk of text (often part of a word) the model processes
cards.x: Pricing and limits are counted in tokens.

cards.q: What is the context window?
cards.a: The maximum tokens the model can consider at once
cards.x: Includes system prompt, conversation, documents, and output.

cards.q: What does temperature control?
cards.a: Randomness of sampling
cards.x: Low = focused and repeatable; high = more varied.

cards.q: What is a hallucination?
cards.a: Confident but false or fabricated output
cards.x: Reduce with grounding (RAG), citations, and verification.

cards.q: What is a system prompt?
cards.a: Instructions that set the model’s role and rules for a conversation
cards.x: Put persistent guidance and constraints here.

cards.q: What is few-shot prompting?
cards.a: Including examples of the desired input and output in the prompt
cards.x: Zero-shot gives no examples.

cards.q: What does pretraining do?
cards.a: Learns general language by predicting the next token on huge text corpora
cards.x: Fine-tuning and RLHF then shape behaviour.
wrong: Aligns the model to human values

cards.q: What is an embedding?
cards.a: A vector representing meaning, so similar text lands close together
cards.x: Used for semantic search and RAG.

cards.q: Why ask a model to answer in structured JSON?
cards.a: So code can reliably parse and validate the output
cards.x: Many APIs offer structured outputs or tool schemas to enforce it.

cards.q: What is a knowledge cutoff?
cards.a: The date after which the model has no training data
cards.x: Use search or retrieval for newer facts.

cards.q: Open-weight vs closed model?
cards.a: Weights downloadable and self-hostable vs accessed only via an API
cards.x: Trade-off: control and privacy vs capability and managed operations.

decks.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
decks.summary: Chunking, vector search, and grounding answers.

cards.q: What is RAG?
cards.a: Retrieving relevant documents and adding them to the prompt
cards.x: Grounds answers in your data without retraining.

cards.q: Why chunk documents for RAG?
cards.a: To retrieve focused passages that fit the context window
cards.x: Chunk size and overlap strongly affect quality.

cards.q: What does a vector database store?
cards.a: Embeddings, indexed for fast similarity search
cards.x: e.g. pgvector, Pinecone, Weaviate, FAISS.

cards.q: Which similarity metric is common for embeddings?
cards.a: Cosine similarity
cards.x: Measures the angle between vectors.

cards.q: What is hybrid search?
cards.a: Combining keyword (BM25) and vector search
cards.x: Keywords catch exact terms like error codes; vectors catch meaning.

cards.q: What does a reranker do?
cards.a: Re-scores retrieved chunks for relevance before prompting
cards.x: Improves precision of the final context.

cards.q: Key security control for enterprise RAG?
cards.a: Enforce the user’s document permissions at retrieval time
cards.x: Otherwise the bot leaks data users are not allowed to see.

cards.q: Why ask a RAG system to cite sources?
cards.a: Users can verify claims and spot hallucinations
cards.x: Pair with "say you don’t know if the context lacks the answer".

cards.q: RAG vs fine-tuning for fresh company facts?
cards.a: RAG: update the documents, no retraining
cards.x: Fine-tuning is better for style, format, or narrow skills.

cards.q: What is indirect prompt injection in RAG?
cards.a: Malicious instructions hidden inside retrieved documents
cards.x: Treat retrieved content as data, never as instructions.
wrong: A user typing a bad prompt

cards.q: What does RAG evaluation measure?
cards.a: Retrieval relevance plus answer faithfulness to the context
cards.x: Build a labelled question set and measure both.

puzzles.prompt: Order a RAG pipeline, from indexing to answering.
items: Generate an answer with the chunks in context
puzzles.x: The first three steps run ahead of time (indexing); the last three run on every question.

decks.title: LLM APIs, Tools & Structured Output
decks.summary: Calling models from code, tool use, streaming, and cost.

cards.q: What is tool use (function calling)?
cards.a: The model requests a function call with arguments; your code runs it and returns results
cards.x: The model never runs code itself; your app executes and validates.
wrong: The model runs code on your server

cards.q: Why define tools with a JSON Schema?
cards.a: So the model produces valid, typed arguments
cards.x: Always validate arguments server-side anyway.

cards.q: What does streaming a response provide?
cards.a: Tokens arrive as they are generated, improving perceived latency
cards.x: Typically delivered over Server-Sent Events.

cards.q: What is prompt caching?
cards.a: Reusing a processed prompt prefix across calls to cut cost and latency
cards.x: Put stable content (system prompt, docs) first so it can be cached.

cards.q: How should you handle HTTP 429 from an LLM API?
cards.a: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter
cards.x: 429 means rate limited. Respect retry-after headers.

cards.q: Where must API keys for an LLM live in a web app?
cards.a: On the server, never in browser code
cards.x: Anything shipped to the browser is public.

cards.q: How are LLM API costs usually charged?
cards.a: Per input and output token
cards.x: Output tokens are typically priced higher than input.

cards.q: What is model routing?
cards.a: Sending easy tasks to small models and hard ones to large models
cards.x: Balances cost, latency, and quality.

cards.q: Why set max output tokens?
cards.a: Caps cost and latency and prevents runaway responses
cards.x: Too low truncates answers, so check the stop reason.

cards.q: What is an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server?
cards.a: A standard way to expose tools and data to AI applications
cards.x: An open protocol; treat third-party servers as untrusted code.

cards.q: What does "grounding" a model output mean?
cards.a: Tying answers to supplied sources or tool results
cards.x: Reduces hallucination and enables citations.

decks.title: Fine-tuning & Evaluation
decks.summary: When to fine-tune, LoRA, and building evals.

cards.q: When is fine-tuning the right tool?
cards.a: Consistent style, format, or a narrow task that prompting can’t achieve
cards.x: Try prompting and RAG first; they are cheaper to iterate on.

cards.q: What is LoRA?
cards.a: Training small low-rank adapter matrices instead of all weights
cards.x: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning; QLoRA adds 4-bit quantisation.

cards.q: What is quantisation?
cards.a: Storing weights in lower precision (e.g. 8-bit, 4-bit) to save memory
cards.x: Some quality loss, big savings on hardware.

cards.q: What is an "eval" in AI engineering?
cards.a: A repeatable test set measuring model or app quality
cards.x: Run evals on every prompt or model change, like unit tests.

cards.q: What is LLM-as-a-judge?
cards.a: Using a model to grade outputs against a rubric
cards.x: Calibrate it against human grades; watch for bias.

cards.q: Why is benchmark contamination a problem?
cards.a: Test data leaked into training inflates scores
cards.x: Build private evals from your own use cases.

cards.q: What is catastrophic forgetting?
cards.a: Fine-tuning erodes previously learned general abilities
cards.x: Mitigate with adapters, mixed data, and low learning rates.

cards.q: What is a golden dataset?
cards.a: Curated inputs with expected outputs used for regression testing
cards.x: Grow it from real failures in production.

cards.q: What is distillation?
cards.a: Training a small model to imitate a larger one
cards.x: Cheaper inference at some quality cost.

cards.q: Why log prompts and outputs in production?
cards.a: For debugging, evals, abuse detection, and audits
cards.x: Redact PII and control access to logs.

decks.title: Agents & Orchestration
decks.summary: Agent loops, planning, memory, and safe autonomy.

cards.q: What is an AI agent?
cards.a: An LLM in a loop that chooses tools and actions toward a goal
cards.x: Observe, think, act, repeat until done.

cards.q: Workflow vs agent?
cards.a: Predefined code paths vs the model deciding its own steps
cards.x: Prefer the simplest workflow that works; add autonomy only when needed.

cards.q: What is the orchestrator-worker pattern?
cards.a: A lead model splits a task and delegates subtasks to worker agents
cards.x: Good for broad research; costs more tokens.

cards.q: What is human-in-the-loop?
cards.a: Requiring human approval for high-impact actions
cards.x: e.g. sending money, deleting data, emailing customers.

cards.q: Why give agents least-privilege credentials?
cards.a: A manipulated agent can only do limited damage
cards.x: Scope tokens per tool; sandbox code execution.

cards.q: What is agent memory?
cards.a: Persisting useful information across steps or sessions
cards.x: Short-term = context; long-term = external store or files.

cards.q: What is context engineering?
cards.a: Curating exactly what goes into the context window at each step
cards.x: Too much noise degrades reasoning; summarise and prune.

cards.q: Why sandbox agent code execution?
cards.a: Generated code may be buggy or malicious
cards.x: Isolated containers, no secrets, network egress controls.

cards.q: What is the "lethal trifecta" for agent data exfiltration?
cards.a: Private data access + untrusted content + a way to send data out
cards.x: Remove at least one leg to break the attack.

cards.q: How do you evaluate an agent?
cards.a: Task success rate on realistic scenarios, plus cost, steps, and safety
cards.x: Inspect transcripts, not just final answers.

cards.q: What is a guardrail in an AI system?
cards.a: A check that blocks or corrects unsafe inputs, outputs, or actions
cards.x: Input filters, output validators, tool allow-lists, rate limits.

decks.title: AI Security (OWASP LLM Top 10)
decks.summary: Attacks on LLM apps and how to defend them.

cards.q: OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025) #1?
cards.a: Prompt Injection
cards.x: Direct (user) and indirect (content) injection.

cards.q: What is sensitive information disclosure in LLM apps?
cards.a: The model reveals PII, secrets, or confidential data
cards.x: Minimise data in context; filter outputs; control access.

cards.q: What is improper output handling?
cards.a: Passing model output unchecked into browsers, shells, or SQL
cards.x: Treat LLM output as untrusted user input: encode and validate.

cards.q: What is system prompt leakage?
cards.a: Attackers extracting hidden instructions or secrets from the system prompt
cards.x: Never put credentials or security logic in prompts.

cards.q: What is unbounded consumption?
cards.a: Abuse that drives up cost or exhausts resources
cards.x: Rate limits, quotas, max tokens, and budget alerts.

cards.q: What is model or data supply-chain risk?
cards.a: Tampered models, datasets, or plugins from third parties
cards.x: Verify sources, pin versions, scan model files (e.g. prefer safetensors over pickle).

cards.q: What is a jailbreak?
cards.a: Prompts crafted to bypass a model’s safety behaviour
cards.x: A form of prompt injection aimed at policies.

cards.q: What is vector and embedding weakness (LLM08)?
cards.a: Attacks via poisoned or leaked embeddings in RAG stores
cards.x: Apply access control and integrity checks to vector stores.

cards.q: What is MITRE ATLAS?
cards.a: An ATT&CK-style knowledge base of attacks on AI systems
cards.x: Use it for AI threat modelling.

cards.q: Best mitigation mindset for prompt injection?
cards.a: Assume it will succeed; limit what a compromised model can do
cards.x: Least privilege, human approval, output validation, isolation.

cards.q: What is model inversion / extraction?
cards.a: Recovering training data or cloning a model via repeated queries
cards.x: Rate-limit, monitor query patterns, and avoid training on secrets.

decks.title: AI Governance & Risk
decks.summary: NIST AI RMF, EU AI Act, and responsible AI in practice.

cards.q: What are the NIST AI RMF core functions?
cards.a: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage
cards.x: Govern is cross-cutting; the Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) extends it.

cards.q: What approach does the EU AI Act take?
cards.a: Risk-based tiers: unacceptable, high, limited, minimal risk
cards.x: Unacceptable-risk practices are banned; high-risk systems carry strict obligations.

cards.q: Which ISO standard defines an AI management system?
cards.a: ISO/IEC 42001
cards.x: The AI counterpart to ISO 27001 for security management.

cards.q: What is algorithmic bias?
cards.a: Systematically unfair outcomes for certain groups
cards.x: Often inherited from skewed training data.

cards.q: What is explainability?
cards.a: Being able to show why a model produced an output
cards.x: SHAP and LIME explain feature contributions for classic ML.

cards.q: What is a model card?
cards.a: Documentation of a model’s intended use, data, limits, and evaluations
cards.x: Datasheets do the same for datasets.

cards.q: Why maintain an AI inventory?
cards.a: You cannot govern or secure AI systems you don’t know about
cards.x: Includes shadow AI: staff pasting data into public tools.

cards.q: What is a key data-protection risk of public AI tools?
cards.a: Staff pasting confidential data that may be retained or used for training
cards.x: Use approved enterprise tools with clear data policies.

cards.q: Who should own AI risk in an organisation?
cards.a: Business leadership with a cross-functional governance group
cards.x: Security, legal, privacy, data science, and business owners together.

cards.q: What is red teaming an AI system?
cards.a: Adversarially probing it for harmful, unsafe, or insecure behaviour
cards.x: Do it before launch and after major changes.

tracks.title: CISSP Capstone
tracks.tagline: All 8 domains, managerial mindset first. The destination of the roadmap.

decks.title: Think Like a Manager
decks.summary: How CISSP questions want you to reason.

cards.q: What is always the first priority in a CISSP answer?
cards.a: Human safety
cards.x: Life safety beats data, systems, and money every time.

cards.q: Who is ultimately accountable for security in an organisation?
cards.a: Senior management
cards.x: Responsibility can be delegated; accountability cannot.

cards.q: CISSP answers favour which role’s viewpoint?
cards.a: A risk advisor to the business, not a technician
cards.x: Pick answers that align security with business goals.

cards.q: What should come before choosing any control?
cards.a: Understanding the risk and business requirements
cards.x: Assess, then treat. Technology is rarely the first answer.

cards.q: What are the four canons of the ISC2 Code of Ethics, in order?
cards.a: Protect society; act honourably; serve principals competently; advance the profession
cards.x: When canons conflict, apply them in that order.
wrong: Serve employer; protect data; obey law; teach
Act legally; be fast; be cheap; be secure
Protect data; protect systems; protect users; protect self

cards.q: What is due care vs due diligence?
cards.a: Due care = doing the right thing; due diligence = verifying it is done
cards.x: Negligence is failing at due care.

cards.q: What is the best "first step" in most CISSP scenarios?
cards.a: Gather facts or consult policy and stakeholders before acting
cards.x: Avoid drastic unilateral actions.

cards.q: How much should a control cost at most?
cards.a: No more than the value of the asset it protects
cards.x: Cost-benefit: annual control cost < reduction in ALE.

cards.q: What is defence in depth?
cards.a: Multiple layered controls so one failure isn’t fatal
cards.x: Administrative, technical, and physical layers.

cards.q: What exam format does CISSP English use (2026)?
cards.a: CAT: 100-150 items in 3 hours, pass at 700/1000
cards.x: CAT = computerised adaptive testing.

cards.q: Experience required for full CISSP certification?
cards.a: 5 years paid work in 2+ of the 8 domains
cards.x: A degree or approved cert can waive 1 year. Otherwise pass as an Associate of ISC2.

resources.title: Destination Certification CISSP MindMaps (free videos + PDF)

puzzles.prompt: Order the ISC2 Code of Ethics canons by priority.
items: Protect society, the common good, and the infrastructure
Act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly, and legally
Provide diligent and competent service to principals
puzzles.x: When canons conflict, the higher one wins. Society comes before your employer.

decks.title: Domain 1: Security & Risk Management (16%)
decks.summary: Governance, risk, legal, BCP, and personnel security.

cards.q: Quantitative vs qualitative risk analysis?
cards.a: Monetary values (ALE) vs ratings like high/medium/low
cards.x: Most organisations blend both.

cards.q: What are the NIST RMF (SP 800-37) steps?
cards.a: Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor
cards.x: Authorisation is the management decision to accept residual risk.

cards.q: What is residual risk?
cards.a: Risk remaining after controls are applied
cards.x: Total risk − controls = residual; management must accept it.

cards.q: What is the goal of a Business Continuity Plan?
cards.a: Keep critical business functions running during a disruption
