cards.x: DRP is the IT-focused subset that restores systems.

cards.q: What is MTD (maximum tolerable downtime)?
cards.a: The longest a function can be down before unacceptable damage
cards.x: RTO must be less than or equal to MTD.

cards.q: Which legal concept protects a trade secret?
cards.a: Keeping it secret with reasonable protections (NDAs, access control)
cards.x: No registration; protection lasts while it stays secret.

cards.q: How long does a US utility patent generally last?
cards.a: 20 years from filing
cards.x: Copyright lasts life of author + 70 years; trademarks can renew indefinitely.

cards.q: What is separation of duties?
cards.a: Splitting critical tasks so no one person can commit fraud alone
cards.x: Collusion is then required. Job rotation and mandatory vacations help detect fraud.

cards.q: What is a supply chain risk management (SCRM) control?
cards.a: Assessing and monitoring vendors, including their suppliers
cards.x: Includes SBOMs, contract requirements, and right-to-audit clauses.

cards.q: What does ISO/IEC 27001 specify?
cards.a: Requirements for an information security management system (ISMS)
cards.x: ISO 27002 provides the control guidance.

cards.q: What is threat modelling with STRIDE?
cards.a: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Info disclosure, DoS, Elevation of privilege
cards.x: A Microsoft method for design-time threat analysis.

cards.q: Who must be involved when terminating an employee’s access?
cards.a: HR and IT together, revoking access at or before notification
cards.x: Collect assets and disable accounts promptly.

resources.title: Inside Cloud and Security: CISSP Exam Cram (free videos)

puzzles.prompt: Order the NIST Risk Management Framework steps.
puzzles.x: "People Can See I Am Always Monitoring." Authorize is the executive decision to accept residual risk.

puzzles.prompt: A risk has an ALE of $50,000. A control cuts it to $10,000 and costs $15,000 a year. What is the control’s annual value?
puzzles.x: (ALE before − ALE after) − annual control cost = (50,000 − 10,000) − 15,000 = $25,000. It is positive, so the control is worth it.

decks.title: Domain 1: GRC Deep Dive (16%)
decks.summary: BCP/DRP, control types, policy hierarchy, and personnel security.

cards.q: BCP vs DRP?
cards.a: BCP keeps critical business functions running; DRP restores IT systems
cards.x: The DRP is the IT-focused subset of the wider business continuity effort.
wrong: BCP restores servers; DRP runs the business

cards.q: What does a BCP contain?
cards.a: BIA, recovery strategies, plan invocation, roles, communications, and maintenance
cards.x: It is owned by the business, not just IT.

cards.q: What does a DRP contain?
cards.a: System recovery procedures, RTO/RPO targets, backup and restore steps, alternate site details
cards.x: One DRP per critical system or site is common.

cards.q: What does a Business Impact Analysis (BIA) identify?
cards.a: Critical functions, dependencies, MTD, RTO/RPO, and financial and operational impacts
cards.x: The BIA drives both BCP and DRP priorities.

cards.q: RTO vs RPO?
cards.a: RTO is how fast to restore service; RPO is how much data loss is tolerable
cards.x: RTO must be within MTD; RPO sets the backup frequency.

cards.q: What is a structured walkthrough (tabletop) DR test?
cards.a: The team discusses the recovery plan step by step without touching systems
cards.x: Cheap, discussion-based, and good for finding plan gaps.

cards.q: What is a simulation DR test?
cards.a: The team practices recovery in a simulated scenario without failing over production
cards.x: More realistic than a walkthrough, still non-disruptive.

cards.q: What is a parallel DR test?
cards.a: Recovery systems run alongside production to validate the plan without cutover
cards.x: Close to real, but needs duplicate capacity.

cards.q: Preventive vs detective vs corrective controls?
cards.a: Prevent incidents; detect them in progress; restore afterwards
cards.x: Firewall rules prevent; IDS detects; backups correct.

cards.q: Deterrent vs preventive control?
cards.a: A deterrent discourages attack (signs, policies); a preventive blocks it (locks, firewalls)
cards.x: Deterrents rely on the attacker choosing not to act.

cards.q: What are recovery and compensating controls?
cards.a: Recovery restores operations (backups, failover); compensating substitutes when the primary control is not feasible
cards.x: A compensating control must provide equivalent protection.

cards.q: Administrative vs technical vs physical controls?
cards.a: Policies and training; enforced by systems (firewalls, encryption); guards, locks, cameras
cards.x: CISSP calls these control categories; types are preventive/detective/corrective.

cards.q: Policy vs standard vs procedure vs guideline?
cards.a: Policy states mandatory intent; standard gives mandatory specifics; procedure is step-by-step; guideline is recommended
cards.x: Policy needs senior management sign-off.

cards.q: Why require mandatory vacations?
cards.a: So someone else performs the duties and may spot fraud or irregularities
cards.x: A classic detective control against employee fraud.

cards.q: What is the security benefit of job rotation?
cards.a: It reduces fraud opportunity and eliminates single points of knowledge
cards.x: Pairs with separation of duties and mandatory vacations.

resources.title: Destination Certification CISSP MindMaps (free videos + PDF)

decks.title: Domain 2: Asset Security (10%)
decks.summary: Classification, ownership, retention, and sanitisation.

cards.q: What is the first step in asset security?
cards.a: Identify and inventory assets
cards.x: You cannot protect what you don’t know you have.

cards.q: Who classifies data?
cards.a: The data owner
cards.x: Custodians implement the protection the owner specifies.

cards.q: US government classification levels, highest first?
cards.a: Top Secret, Secret, Confidential (plus Unclassified)
cards.x: Commercial equivalents: confidential/proprietary, private, sensitive, public.

cards.q: What is data remanence?
cards.a: Residual data left on media after deletion
cards.x: Why sanitisation matters.

cards.q: Clearing vs purging vs destruction?
cards.a: Overwrite for reuse inside; stronger methods for reuse outside; physically destroy
cards.x: NIST SP 800-88 defines Clear, Purge, Destroy.

cards.q: Does degaussing work on SSDs?
cards.a: No, SSDs are not magnetic
cards.x: Use cryptographic erase, vendor secure erase, or physical destruction.

cards.q: What is a data retention policy for?
cards.a: Keeping data only as long as legally and operationally needed
cards.x: Over-retention increases breach impact and e-discovery costs.

cards.q: Data controller vs data processor (GDPR)?
cards.a: Controller decides purpose and means; processor acts on its behalf
cards.x: A cloud provider is typically a processor.

cards.q: What is scoping and tailoring a baseline?
cards.a: Selecting relevant controls, then adjusting them to the environment
cards.x: Start from a standard baseline like NIST SP 800-53.

cards.q: What is pseudonymisation?
cards.a: Replacing identifiers so data can’t be linked to a person without extra info
cards.x: Still personal data under GDPR; anonymised data is not.

cards.q: What does DRM protect?
cards.a: Use of digital content after distribution
cards.x: Controls copying, printing, and forwarding.

resources.title: Destination Certification CISSP MindMaps (free videos + PDF)

decks.title: Domain 2: Asset Security Deep Dive (10%)
decks.summary: Data lifecycle, legal holds, DLP, and cloud data controls.

cards.q: What are the phases of the data lifecycle?
cards.a: Create, store, use, share, archive, destroy
cards.x: Protection must follow the data through every phase, not just storage.

cards.q: Data owner vs steward vs custodian?
cards.a: Owner is accountable and classifies; steward manages quality and handling; custodian maintains the systems
cards.x: The owner decides, the steward oversees daily handling, the custodian operates.

cards.q: How do handling requirements differ by classification?
cards.a: Higher classifications need marking, encryption, and strict access control; public data needs integrity only
cards.x: Handling rules must be written, trained, and enforced.
wrong: All data is handled the same

cards.q: What typically sets a data retention period?
cards.a: Legal and regulatory requirements plus business need, whichever is longer
cards.x: Document the justification for each retention period.

cards.q: What is a legal hold (litigation hold)?
cards.a: Suspending normal destruction so relevant data is preserved for litigation
cards.x: Destroying data under a hold can be ruled spoliation of evidence.

cards.q: Do backups fall under retention and legal holds?
cards.a: Yes: backups and archives must follow retention schedules, and holds extend to them
cards.x: A hold that misses backups is a failed hold.

cards.q: What does network DLP inspect?
cards.a: Data in motion at egress points: email, web uploads, and file transfers
cards.x: It can block, quarantine, or encrypt on policy violation.

cards.q: What does endpoint DLP control?
cards.a: USB drives, printing, clipboard, and local storage on devices
cards.x: Stops the "sneakernet" exfiltration path.

cards.q: How is DLP applied to cloud and SaaS?
cards.a: Cloud-native DLP or a CASB scanning uploads, sharing links, and collaboration apps
cards.x: Shadow IT discovery is a common CASB win.

cards.q: What actions can DLP take on a violation?
cards.a: Block, quarantine, encrypt, or alert, according to policy
cards.x: Start in monitor/alert mode before enforcing blocks.

cards.q: Who owns data stored in a SaaS application?
cards.a: The customer (the data owner), not the provider
cards.x: Contracts should state this explicitly, with return and deletion terms.

cards.q: What is data sovereignty?
cards.a: Data is subject to the laws of the country where it is stored or processed
cards.x: It drives cloud region selection for regulated data.

cards.q: Data residency vs data sovereignty?
cards.a: Residency is where data is stored; sovereignty is whose laws apply
cards.x: You can meet residency and still fail sovereignty.

cards.q: Which controls protect data in IaaS?
cards.a: Customer-managed keys (BYOK), storage encryption, and private endpoints
cards.x: In IaaS you own the data and OS layers; the provider owns the hypervisor down.

cards.q: What do data discovery and classification tools do?
cards.a: Automatically scan stores to find and label sensitive data like PII or card numbers
cards.x: You cannot apply handling rules to data you have not found.

resources.title: Destination Certification CISSP MindMaps (free videos + PDF)

decks.title: Domain 3: Security Architecture & Engineering (13%)
decks.summary: Security models, secure design, crypto, and physical security.

cards.q: Bell-LaPadula enforces which goal?
cards.a: Confidentiality: no read up, no write down
cards.x: Military classification model.

cards.q: Biba enforces which goal?
cards.a: Integrity: no read down, no write up
cards.x: The inverse of Bell-LaPadula.

cards.q: Which model prevents conflicts of interest?
cards.a: Brewer-Nash (Chinese Wall)
cards.x: Access changes dynamically based on prior access.

cards.q: Clark-Wilson enforces integrity using…
cards.a: Well-formed transactions and separation of duties
cards.x: Users access data only through programs (the access triple).

cards.q: What is a trusted computing base (TCB)?
cards.a: All hardware, firmware, and software enforcing the security policy
cards.x: The reference monitor mediates all access and must be tamper-proof.

cards.q: What does a TPM provide?
cards.a: A hardware root of trust for keys, measured boot, and attestation
cards.x: Used by BitLocker to seal disk keys.

cards.q: What is Common Criteria?
cards.a: An international framework for evaluating security products (EAL1-7)
cards.x: Protection profiles define requirements.

cards.q: Which fire suppression is best for data centres?
cards.a: Clean agents (e.g. FM-200) or pre-action sprinklers
cards.x: Pre-action fills pipes only after detection, reducing accidental water damage.

cards.q: What is a side-channel attack?
cards.a: Extracting secrets from timing, power, or emissions
cards.x: Spectre and Meltdown exploited CPU speculative execution.

cards.q: Secure design principle: "fail securely" means…
cards.a: On failure, the system defaults to a secure state
cards.x: Also: secure defaults, least privilege, zero trust, privacy by design.

cards.q: What is the key length/strength trade-off of ECC vs RSA?
cards.a: ECC gives equal strength with much shorter keys
cards.x: 256-bit ECC ≈ 3072-bit RSA.

cards.q: What does a CPTED approach use?
cards.a: Environmental design (lighting, sightlines, landscaping) to deter crime
cards.x: Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design.

resources.title: Destination Certification CISSP MindMaps (free videos + PDF)

decks.title: Domain 4: Communication & Network Security (13%)
decks.summary: Secure network architecture, protocols, and channels.

cards.q: At which OSI layer does IPsec operate?
cards.a: Layer 3 (Network)
cards.x: TLS is usually placed at Layer 4-6 depending on the model used.

cards.q: IPsec AH vs ESP?
cards.a: AH = integrity and authentication only; ESP adds confidentiality
cards.x: ESP is what most VPNs use.

cards.q: IPsec transport vs tunnel mode?
cards.a: Transport protects payload; tunnel encapsulates the whole packet
cards.x: Site-to-site VPNs use tunnel mode.

cards.q: What is micro-segmentation?
cards.a: Fine-grained policies isolating individual workloads
cards.x: A zero trust building block, limits lateral movement.

cards.q: What does EAP-TLS require?
cards.a: Certificates on both the client and the server
cards.x: Strongest common 802.1X method. PEAP needs only a server cert.

cards.q: What is converged networking (e.g. FCoE, iSCSI, VoIP)?
cards.a: Carrying storage, voice, or other traffic over standard IP/Ethernet
cards.x: Convenient, but widens the attack surface of those services.

cards.q: What is a CDN’s security benefit?
cards.a: Absorbs DDoS and shields origin servers
cards.x: Often combined with a WAF at the edge.

cards.q: Which protocol secures DNS responses with signatures?
cards.a: DNSSEC
cards.x: Provides integrity and authenticity, not confidentiality. DoH/DoT add encryption.

cards.q: What is a bastion/jump host’s role?
cards.a: A single hardened, monitored entry point to a secure zone
cards.x: Increasingly replaced by ZTNA brokers.

cards.q: What does network segmentation mainly limit?
cards.a: Blast radius and lateral movement
cards.x: A PCI DSS scope-reduction technique too.

cards.q: What does ZTNA replace?
cards.a: Broad VPN access with per-application, identity-aware access
cards.x: Zero Trust Network Access; users never land "on the network".

cards.q: What is a key risk of IoT devices on corporate networks?
cards.a: Weak, rarely patched devices becoming pivot points
cards.x: Put them on isolated segments with strict egress.

decks.title: Domain 5: Identity & Access Management (13%)
decks.summary: Identification, authentication, authorisation, and lifecycle.

cards.q: What is the order of access control steps?
cards.a: Identification, authentication, authorisation, accountability
cards.x: Claim identity, prove it, get permissions, get logged.

cards.q: Biometric Type I error is…
cards.a: False rejection (a valid user denied)
cards.x: Type II is false acceptance, the more serious security failure.

cards.q: What is the Crossover Error Rate (CER)?
cards.a: Where false rejection and false acceptance rates are equal
cards.x: Lower CER = more accurate biometric system.

cards.q: What is Kerberos’ trusted third party?
cards.a: The KDC (Key Distribution Center)
cards.x: Includes the Authentication Service and Ticket-Granting Service.

cards.q: Kerberos’ main weakness?
cards.a: The KDC is a single point of failure and requires time sync
cards.x: Clock skew beyond 5 minutes (default) breaks authentication.

cards.q: What is federated identity?
cards.a: Trusting identities issued by another organisation’s IdP
cards.x: SAML, OIDC, and WS-Federation implement it.

cards.q: What is JIT (just-in-time) access?
cards.a: Granting elevated rights only when needed, for a limited time
cards.x: Eliminates standing privilege.

cards.q: Why perform periodic access reviews?
cards.a: To remove privilege creep and orphaned accounts
cards.x: Managers recertify their team’s access.

cards.q: What does NIST SP 800-63B advise on passwords?
cards.a: Favour length, screen against breached lists, no forced periodic rotation
cards.x: Change passwords only on evidence of compromise.

cards.q: What is session management’s key control?
cards.a: Timeouts, secure tokens, and re-authentication for sensitive actions
cards.x: Invalidate sessions on logout and password change.

cards.q: What is a risk-based / conditional access policy?
cards.a: Adjusting requirements based on context like device, location, and risk score
cards.x: e.g. require MFA from unknown devices, block impossible travel.

decks.title: Domain 6: Security Assessment & Testing (12%)
decks.summary: Audits, vulnerability assessment, pentesting, and metrics.

cards.q: Vulnerability assessment vs penetration test?
cards.a: Finding and ranking weaknesses vs actively exploiting them
cards.x: Pentests prove impact; both need authorisation.

cards.q: First-party vs second-party vs third-party audit?
cards.a: Internal audit by own staff vs audit by a customer or partner vs audit by an independent firm
cards.x: First-party audits are internal; second-party audits are external but by an interested party; third-party audits are independent and carry the most weight.

cards.q: SOC 1 vs SOC 2 vs SOC 3?
cards.a: Financial controls vs security/trust controls (detailed) vs public summary
cards.x: SOC 2 covers the Trust Services Criteria.

cards.q: What is synthetic transaction monitoring?
cards.a: Scripted simulated user activity to test availability and performance
cards.x: Real user monitoring (RUM) observes actual users.

cards.q: What is fuzz testing?
cards.a: Feeding malformed or random input to find crashes and bugs
cards.x: Mutation fuzzing alters valid input; generation fuzzing builds from a spec.

cards.q: What is misuse case testing?
cards.a: Testing how an attacker might abuse the system’s functionality
cards.x: The adversarial counterpart of use cases.

cards.q: What are KPIs vs KRIs?
cards.a: Performance indicators (past results) vs risk indicators (early warnings)
cards.x: Report both to leadership in business terms.

cards.q: What is code coverage vs interface testing?
cards.a: How much code tests exercised vs testing interactions between components
cards.x: Interface testing covers APIs, UIs, and physical interfaces.

cards.q: What is a breach and attack simulation (BAS)?
cards.a: Automated, continuous safe emulation of attacks to validate controls
cards.x: Complements periodic pentests.

cards.q: Why must audit logs be protected?
cards.a: Attackers alter or delete them to hide activity
cards.x: Centralise, restrict access, and use write-once or integrity checks.

cards.q: What does a regression test confirm?
cards.a: A change did not break existing functionality
cards.x: Run the regression suite automatically on every change, so a fix in one place cannot silently break something that used to work.

decks.title: Domain 7: Security Operations (13%)
decks.summary: Investigations, logging, IR, recovery, and physical safety.

cards.q: What does the (ISC)² incident management process begin with?
cards.a: Detection, then response (containment)
cards.x: Detection, response, mitigation, reporting, recovery, remediation, lessons learned.

cards.q: What is the best evidence rule?
cards.a: Courts prefer original evidence over copies
cards.x: Forensic images with verified hashes are accepted as duplicates.

cards.q: Which evidence type is hearsay?
cards.a: Second-hand information not from direct knowledge
cards.x: Business records made in the normal course can be an exception.

cards.q: What are the types of investigation?
cards.a: Administrative, criminal, civil, regulatory
cards.x: Criminal requires "beyond reasonable doubt"; civil "preponderance of evidence".

cards.q: Full vs incremental vs differential backup restore?
cards.a: Full + last differential, or full + every incremental since
cards.x: Incremental: fast backup, slow restore. Differential: the reverse.

cards.q: Which DR test is least disruptive?
cards.a: Read-through / checklist review
cards.x: Then walk-through (tabletop), simulation, parallel, and full interruption.

cards.q: Which DR test is most disruptive (and risky)?
cards.a: Full interruption test
cards.x: Production actually fails over; do it rarely and carefully.

cards.q: What is entrapment vs enticement?
cards.a: Inducing a crime (illegal) vs luring someone already intent (legal)
cards.x: Honeypots are enticement if used properly.

cards.q: What is patch management’s correct sequence?
cards.a: Evaluate, test, approve, deploy, verify
cards.x: Emergency patches still follow an expedited change process.

cards.q: What does a SIEM correlation rule do?
cards.a: Links related events across sources into one meaningful alert
cards.x: e.g. failed logons followed by success from a new country.

cards.q: What is a key principle of personnel safety during an emergency?
cards.a: Evacuate people first; systems and data are secondary
cards.x: Doors fail safe (unlocked) for life safety.

cards.q: What is the role of egress monitoring?
cards.a: Detecting data leaving the organisation, e.g. exfiltration
cards.x: DLP, proxy logs, and NetFlow support it.

puzzles.prompt: Order the DR test types from least to most disruptive.
puzzles.x: Only run a full interruption test when you are confident, and with management approval.

decks.title: Domain 8: Software Development Security (10%)
decks.summary: SDLC, DevSecOps, secure coding, and software acquisition.

cards.q: When should security be integrated into the SDLC?
cards.a: From the very start: requirements and design
cards.x: Fixing flaws later costs far more. "Shift left".
wrong: At the end of the project

cards.q: What does the SAMM or BSIMM model measure?
cards.a: Software security programme maturity
cards.x: OWASP SAMM is open; BSIMM is descriptive, based on real firms.

cards.q: What is the CMMI maturity level for "optimising"?
cards.a: Level 5
cards.x: 1 Initial, 2 Managed, 3 Defined, 4 Quantitatively Managed, 5 Optimising.

cards.q: What is DevSecOps?
cards.a: Building automated security into DevOps pipelines
cards.x: SAST, SCA, DAST, IaC scanning, and secrets scanning in CI/CD.

cards.q: What is software composition analysis (SCA)?
cards.a: Identifying third-party components and their known vulnerabilities
cards.x: Produces or consumes SBOMs.

cards.q: What is a polymorphic object vs polyinstantiation?
cards.a: Same interface, different behaviour vs multiple versions of data per clearance
cards.x: Polyinstantiation prevents inference in MAC databases.

cards.q: What is an API security top risk?
cards.a: Broken object-level authorisation (BOLA)
cards.x: OWASP API Top 10 #1: check the caller owns each object.

cards.q: What is code escrow?
cards.a: A third party holds source code in case the vendor fails
cards.x: Protects buyers of critical commercial software.

cards.q: What does an ACID database transaction guarantee?
cards.a: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
cards.x: Ensures integrity of transactions.

cards.q: What is the risk of AI coding assistants in the SDLC?
cards.a: Insecure or licence-problematic code accepted without review
cards.x: Keep human review, SAST, and SCA on generated code.

cards.q: What is a sandbox in software security?
cards.a: A restricted environment that limits what code can do
cards.x: Browsers sandbox tabs; mobile apps are sandboxed.

cards.q: What should acquired (third-party) software be assessed for?
cards.a: Security requirements, vendor practices, and contractual obligations
cards.x: Includes SaaS: review SOC 2 reports and data handling terms.

cards.q: What is the waterfall model?
cards.a: Sequential phases where each completes before the next begins
cards.x: Requirements, design, implementation, verification, maintenance; revisiting earlier phases is costly.

cards.q: What is agile development?
cards.a: Iterative, incremental delivery with close customer collaboration
cards.x: Working software in short cycles; requirements evolve with feedback.

cards.q: What are the Scrum roles?
cards.a: Product owner, Scrum master, and the development team
cards.x: The product owner prioritises the backlog; the Scrum master removes impediments.

cards.q: What are the Scrum ceremonies?
cards.a: Sprint planning, daily standup, sprint review, and retrospective
cards.x: Time-boxed events that keep each sprint inspectable and adaptable.

cards.q: What is the spiral model?
cards.a: Iterative development with explicit risk analysis in every cycle
cards.x: Each loop: plan, assess risk, engineer, evaluate. Good for large, risky projects.

cards.q: What is RAD (rapid application development)?
cards.a: Prototype-driven development with fast iterations and heavy user involvement
cards.x: Speed comes with a risk of weak security controls if they are not designed in.

cards.q: SAST vs DAST?
cards.a: SAST analyses source code (white box); DAST tests the running application (black box)
cards.x: SAST finds flaws early; DAST finds runtime issues SAST cannot see. Use both.

cards.q: Waterfall vs agile: where does security fit?
cards.a: Waterfall bakes security gates into each phase; agile needs security in every sprint’s definition of done
cards.x: Either way, security is continuous, not a final phase.

cards.q: What is the "definition of done" from a security view?
cards.a: Acceptance criteria that include security checks: no high-severity findings, secrets scanned, dependencies reviewed
cards.x: It makes security a release gate in agile teams.

cards.q: What is a security champion?
cards.a: A developer trained to promote secure practices within their team
cards.x: Scales AppSec by embedding security knowledge in every squad.

puzzles.prompt: Order the CMMI maturity levels from 1 to 5.
puzzles.x: Maturity grows from ad hoc work to measured, continuously improving processes.

decks.title: D1 Capstone: Scenario Judgment
decks.summary: Risk-first decisions: compensating controls, BIA gaps, and policy exceptions.

cards.q: Scenario: A risk assessment finds a critical vulnerability in the order database, but no patch exists and the business cannot take it offline. What is the BEST immediate action?
cards.a: Apply a compensating control (e.g. WAF rule, network segmentation) and document the residual risk
cards.x: When you cannot remediate, you compensate: reduce likelihood or impact another way, record it, and get formal risk acceptance. Doing nothing is not an option.
wrong: Disconnect the database immediately regardless of business impact
Accept the risk silently and do nothing
Wait for the vendor patch with no interim measures

cards.q: Scenario: The BIA sets a 4-hour RTO for order processing, but the DR plan restores it in 12 hours. What should you do FIRST?
cards.a: Report the gap to management and initiate a strategy review
cards.x: The BIA defines the requirement; the plan must meet it. The gap is a risk decision for management, not something to quietly accept or unilaterally rebuild.
wrong: Rewrite the entire DR plan yourself over the weekend

cards.q: Scenario: A new privacy regulation takes effect in six months and affects your EU customer data. As security manager, what do you do FIRST?
cards.a: Perform a gap analysis of current controls against the regulation
cards.x: You cannot plan remediation until you know what is missing. Assess first, then roadmap, then implement.
wrong: Hire a data protection officer immediately
Wait for the legal team to tell you exactly what to do

cards.q: Scenario: A senior executive requests an exception to the MFA policy for convenience. What is the BEST response?
cards.a: Require formal documented risk acceptance by the system owner, with compensating controls
cards.x: Policy exceptions are legitimate only through the exception process: documented, time-bound, risk-accepted. "Because I am senior" is not a control.
wrong: Grant it — executives are low-risk targets
Grant it quietly to avoid conflict
Remove MFA for everyone so the policy is "fair"

resources.title: Destination Certification CISSP MindMaps (free videos + PDF)

decks.title: D2 Capstone: Scenario Judgment
decks.summary: Data handling under pressure: departing staff, test data, and legal holds.

cards.q: Scenario: An employee with access to customer PII resigns today. From a data-security view, what matters FIRST?
cards.a: Revoke their access immediately, then sanitise or reassign their devices per the media-handling policy
cards.x: Containment before cleanup: cut off access so nothing more can leave, then handle data remanence on the hardware.
wrong: Quick-format their laptop for the next hire
Let them keep the laptop until their last day
Only delete their user account next week

cards.q: Scenario: Marketing asks to copy production customer data into the test environment to "speed up QA". What is the BEST answer?
cards.a: Refuse — use masked, anonymised, or synthetic data instead
cards.x: Test environments rarely carry production-grade controls. Real PII in test is a breach waiting for an auditor (or an attacker) to find.
wrong: Allow it — faster testing helps the business
Allow a partial copy to limit exposure
Allow it if they promise to delete it afterwards

cards.q: Scenario: Legal issues a litigation hold covering six months of email. What must happen FIRST?
cards.a: Suspend normal retention and destruction for the affected data
cards.x: A legal hold overrides the retention schedule. Destroying held data is spoliation, with serious legal consequences.
wrong: Delete old mailboxes to free up space
Email all staff the details of the lawsuit

resources.title: Destination Certification CISSP MindMaps (free videos + PDF)

decks.title: D3 Capstone: Scenario Judgment
decks.summary: Architecture trade-offs: fail-secure design, layered controls, and key management.

cards.q: Scenario: You are reviewing the design of a new payment application. If a component fails unexpectedly, what is the MOST important design property?
cards.a: Fail-secure (fail closed): failures deny access rather than grant it
cards.x: A failure that opens access turns every bug into a vulnerability. Deny by default, even — especially — when things break.
wrong: Log verbose errors to the end user

cards.q: Scenario: The team debates firewall versus IPS for the data-centre edge. What is the BEST recommendation?
cards.a: Deploy both: firewall for access control, IPS for threat prevention — defence in depth
cards.x: They are different control functions, not substitutes. Layering means one control's miss is another's catch.
wrong: An IPS fully replaces the firewall

cards.q: Scenario: A cloud design stores encryption keys alongside the encrypted data in the same account with the same admins. What is wrong?
cards.a: It violates key-management separation: keys need their own security domain (KMS/HSM, split duties)
cards.x: Whoever compromises the account gets both lock and key. Keys and data must have different access paths.
wrong: Nothing — it is convenient and cheap
Keys belong in application source code instead
Encryption adds no value in the cloud

resources.title: Destination Certification CISSP MindMaps (free videos + PDF)

decks.title: D4 Capstone: Scenario Judgment
decks.summary: Network defence scenarios: VPNs, evasion, and segmentation.

cards.q: Scenario: Branch-office traffic to headquarters must cross the public internet. What is the MOST appropriate protection?
cards.a: A site-to-site IPsec VPN
cards.x: VPNs provide confidentiality and integrity over untrusted networks — the standard answer for site interconnect.
wrong: Port forwarding on the branch router

cards.q: Scenario: Your IDS is missing attacks that use crafted fragmented packets to evade signatures. What is the BEST defence?
cards.a: Normalise and reassemble fragments at the IPS before inspection
cards.x: Evasion by fragmentation works only if inspection sees fragments. Reassemble first, then match signatures.
wrong: Turn off the IDS to stop the noise

cards.q: Scenario: Guest Wi-Fi and the corporate LAN will share the same switches and firewall. What is the FIRST design step?
cards.a: Segment them into separate VLANs and firewall zones
cards.x: Guests are untrusted by definition. Segmentation contains lateral movement before anything else is tuned.
wrong: Just give guests a strong Wi-Fi password
Put guests on the same VLAN for simplicity

resources.title: Destination Certification CISSP MindMaps (free videos + PDF)

decks.title: D5 Capstone: Scenario Judgment
decks.summary: Identity decisions: federation, session theft, and exposed secrets.

cards.q: Scenario: A new SaaS HR tool must let staff sign in with corporate credentials, but passwords must never be shared with the vendor. What is the BEST standard to use?
cards.a: SAML (or OIDC) federation against the corporate identity provider
cards.x: Federation delegates authentication to the IdP; the application never sees a password. SAML for enterprise SSO, OIDC for modern web apps.
wrong: Store corporate passwords in the SaaS app
Issue one shared service account to all staff
Email temporary passwords to new users

cards.q: Scenario: An administrator's session was hijacked even though MFA was enforced at login. Which control would BEST have limited the damage?
cards.a: Short session timeouts with step-up re-authentication for privileged actions
cards.x: MFA proves identity at login; session controls bound the blast radius after a theft. The more powerful the session, the shorter its leash.
wrong: MFA prompts on every single click

cards.q: Scenario: A developer committed a production API key to a public repository an hour ago. What do you do FIRST?
cards.a: Revoke and rotate the key immediately, then investigate the exposure
cards.x: A published secret is a compromised secret. Containment (rotation) cannot wait for the investigation to finish.
wrong: Delete the repository and hope nobody saw it
Monitor the key for misuse before acting

resources.title: Destination Certification CISSP MindMaps (free videos + PDF)

decks.title: D6 Capstone: Scenario Judgment
decks.summary: Testing triage: pentests, finding prioritisation, and vendor claims.

cards.q: Scenario: Before a major release you want the BEST assurance against vulnerabilities in the running application. Which test do you choose?
cards.a: Penetration testing
cards.x: Pentests simulate real attackers against the running system. SAST examines source; DAST automates black-box checks; neither replaces adversarial testing.

cards.q: Scenario: A vulnerability scan returns 500 findings across the estate. How do you prioritise FIRST?
cards.a: By risk: exploitability combined with business impact (internet-facing critical systems first)
cards.x: Scanners report technical severity, not your risk. A critical on an isolated lab box matters less than a high on the payment server.
wrong: Ignore anything first found over 90 days ago

cards.q: Scenario: A vendor claims SOC 2 compliance during procurement. Before signing, what should you do?
cards.a: Read the actual SOC 2 report — scope, period, and any qualifications
cards.x: Third-party risk management runs on evidence, not claims. Check what was audited, when, and what the auditor qualified.
wrong: Take the claim at face value
Ask for a bigger discount instead
Demand ISO 27001 sight unseen as well

resources.title: Destination Certification CISSP MindMaps (free videos + PDF)

decks.title: D7 Capstone: Scenario Judgment
decks.summary: Operations under fire: containment, alert triage, and learning.

cards.q: Scenario: The SOC watches ransomware actively encrypting file shares RIGHT NOW. What is the FIRST action?
cards.a: Isolate the affected systems from the network
cards.x: Incident response runs contain → eradicate → recover. Stopping the spread comes before forensics, backups, or blame.
wrong: Delete the encrypted files to stop it

cards.q: Scenario: A 3am alert reports a single failed login for one user. How should the SOC treat it?
cards.a: Low priority: baseline noise unless corroborated by other indicators
cards.x: Triage is about fidelity. One failed login is expected background noise; five hundred from one IP is an incident.

cards.q: Scenario: An incident is resolved and systems are restored. What is the MOST important step before closing it?
cards.a: Hold a lessons-learned review and update playbooks and controls
cards.x: Without the post-incident review the same incident will recur. Improvement — not closure speed — is the goal.
wrong: Delete the tickets to keep metrics clean
Discipline the user who clicked the link
Close it fast to protect the MTTR metric

resources.title: Destination Certification CISSP MindMaps (free videos + PDF)

decks.title: D8 Capstone: Scenario Judgment
decks.summary: Secure development calls: supply chain, secrets, and shift-left.

cards.q: Scenario: Developers want to adopt a popular open-source library. What should happen FIRST?
cards.a: Assess its licence, maintenance health, and known vulnerabilities (SCA)
cards.x: Supply-chain due diligence: licence compatibility, commit activity, and CVE history before a line of it ships.
wrong: Use it — popular open source is inherently safe
Check only the GitHub star count

cards.q: Scenario: A code review finds hardcoded AWS keys in the repository. What is the BEST immediate fix?
cards.a: Revoke and rotate the keys, move secrets to a vault, add pre-commit secret scanning
cards.x: The committed secret is compromised the moment it is pushed. Revoke first, then fix the process so it cannot recur.
wrong: Restrict repo access and keep using the keys
Email the team asking them not to use the keys

cards.q: Scenario: Leadership asks where in the SDLC a security bug is cheapest to fix. What is the correct answer?
cards.a: As early as possible — requirements and design (shift-left)
cards.x: Remediation cost grows exponentially through the lifecycle. Threat modelling in design is orders of magnitude cheaper than an emergency patch in production.
wrong: In production — real-world feedback is fastest
The cost is the same at every phase

resources.title: Destination Certification CISSP MindMaps (free videos + PDF)

tracks.title: Linux Administration
tracks.tagline: Own the command line: the OS that runs the cloud, the SOC, and every server.

decks.title: Command Line & Filesystem
decks.summary: Navigating, creating, moving, and finding files from the shell.

cards.q: What does `pwd` print?
cards.a: The current working directory as an absolute path
cards.x: pwd = "print working directory". It answers "where am I?", e.g. /home/ana.

cards.q: Which command lists files with details, including hidden ones?
cards.a: `ls -la`
cards.x: -l is the long format, -a shows dotfiles (names starting with .).

cards.q: What is the difference between an absolute and a relative path?
cards.a: Absolute starts at / (root); relative starts from the current directory
cards.x: /etc/ssh works from anywhere; ../logs only works from the right place.
wrong: There is no difference on Linux

cards.q: What does `cd ~` do?
cards.a: Goes to your home directory
cards.x: ~ expands to $HOME. `cd` alone does the same thing.

cards.q: Which command creates nested directories in one step?
cards.a: `mkdir -p projects/2026/q1`
cards.x: -p creates missing parents and does not error if the directory already exists.

cards.q: What does `rm -rf dir/` do, and why is it dangerous?
cards.a: Recursively force-deletes dir/ with no prompt and no undo
cards.x: -r walks into subdirectories, -f skips confirmation. There is no trash can.

cards.q: How do you find a file named "app.log" anywhere under /var?
cards.a: `find /var -name "app.log"`
cards.x: find walks the tree; -name matches the basename. Quote the pattern so the shell does not glob it.

cards.q: What does `man ls` show you?
cards.a: The manual page documenting ls
cards.x: man pages are the built-in docs: q quits, / searches inside.
wrong: The last 10 lines of ls output

cards.q: What does pressing Tab do in a shell?
cards.a: Autocompletes the current word
cards.x: Press twice to list candidates. It works for commands, paths, and (often) options.
wrong: Sends SIGINT to the foreground job

cards.q: How do you re-run the previous command with sudo?
cards.a: `sudo !!`
cards.x: !! expands to the last command, so this is the classic "permission denied, try again" fix.

decks.title: Permissions & Ownership
decks.summary: rwx, chmod, chown, umask, and the special bits.

cards.q: In `-rwxr-xr--`, what do the three rwx groups mean?
cards.a: Owner, group, others
cards.x: Positions 2-4 are the owner, 5-7 the group, 8-10 everyone else.

cards.q: What numeric mode is `rwxr-xr-x`?
What numeric mode is `rw-r--r--`?
cards.x: rw- = 6, r-- = 4, r-- = 4. The classic default for data files.

cards.q: Which command gives the owner full access, the group read-only, and others nothing on file.sh?
cards.a: `chmod 740 file.sh`
cards.x: 7 = rwx for owner, 4 = r-- for group, 0 = --- for others.

cards.q: What does `chmod u+x script.sh` do?
cards.a: Adds execute permission for the owner only
cards.x: u = user/owner, g = group, o = others, a = all. Use - to remove: `chmod go-w file`.

cards.q: Which command makes ana the owner and devs the group of file?
cards.a: `chown ana:devs file`
cards.x: Only root (or sudo) can give away ownership. chgrp changes just the group.

cards.q: With umask 022, what permissions does a new file get?
cards.x: Files start at 666 minus the umask (666 - 022 = 644); directories start at 777, giving 755.

cards.q: What does the SUID bit on an executable do?
cards.a: It runs with the file owner's privileges
cards.x: Classic example: /usr/bin/passwd runs as root so normal users can change their own password. Shown as an s: -rwsr-xr-x.
wrong: It runs the file at boot
It hides the file from ls

cards.q: What does the sticky bit on /tmp do?
cards.a: Only a file's owner (or root) can delete or rename it
cards.x: Everyone can write to /tmp, but the sticky bit (t in drwxrwxrwt) stops users deleting each other's files.

cards.q: What does SGID on a directory do?
cards.a: New files in it inherit the directory's group
cards.x: Useful for shared project folders: `chmod g+s shared/`. Shown as s in the group execute slot.
wrong: New files inherit the directory's owner

decks.title: Users, Groups & sudo
decks.summary: Accounts, /etc/passwd, groups, and safe privilege escalation.

cards.q: Which file holds one line of account info per user?
cards.a: /etc/passwd
cards.x: Username, UID, GID, home directory, shell. Passwords have not lived here for decades.

cards.q: Where are password hashes actually stored?
cards.a: /etc/shadow, readable only by root
cards.x: Shadow also holds ageing policy: expiry, warning days, inactivity lockout.

cards.q: What does UID 0 signify?
cards.a: The superuser (root)
cards.x: Any account with UID 0 has full root privileges, whatever its name.

cards.q: Which command creates user ana with a home directory?
cards.a: `useradd -m ana`
cards.x: -m creates /home/ana. Then set a password with `passwd ana`.

cards.q: What does the `id` command show?
cards.a: Your UID, GID, and group memberships
cards.x: `id ana` shows another user's. Handy when debugging "permission denied".

cards.q: Which command adds ana to the docker group?
cards.a: `usermod -aG docker ana`
cards.x: -a appends; without it, -G replaces every supplementary group — a classic footgun.

cards.q: What does `sudo` do?
cards.a: Runs a command with elevated privileges per the sudoers policy
cards.x: It asks for YOUR password (not root's) and logs the command.

cards.q: Why must you edit sudoers with `visudo`?
cards.a: It validates the syntax before saving
cards.x: One typo in sudoers can lock every admin out of root access.
wrong: It is faster than other editors

cards.q: What is the practical difference between `su -` and `sudo -i`?
cards.a: `su -` needs the root password; `sudo -i` uses your password and is logged
cards.x: sudo also allows fine-grained rules (e.g. "may restart nginx only") instead of all-or-nothing root.

cards.q: Which command locks ana's account without deleting it?
cards.a: `usermod -L ana` (or `passwd -l ana`)
cards.x: Locking disables password login; -U unlocks. The files and home directory stay put.

decks.title: Text Processing Pipelines
decks.summary: grep, pipes, redirection, cut, sort, sed, and awk.

cards.q: What does the pipe `|` do?
cards.a: Feeds one command's stdout into the next command's stdin
cards.x: `dmesg | grep -i usb` searches kernel messages for "usb".
wrong: Chains commands to run on failure

cards.q: What is the difference between `>` and `>>`?
cards.a: `>` overwrites the file; `>>` appends to it
cards.x: Both create the file if missing. `>` on the wrong file is how data loss happens.

cards.q: Which command prints lines containing "Failed" in auth.log?
cards.a: `grep "Failed" /var/log/auth.log`
cards.x: grep searches text with patterns; add -i to ignore case, -r to recurse directories.

cards.q: What does `grep -ci "error" app.log` print?
cards.a: The count of lines mentioning "error", case-insensitively
cards.x: -c counts matching lines (not occurrences), -i ignores case.
wrong: The number of times the word appears

cards.q: What does `2>` redirect?
cards.a: Standard error
cards.x: Every process has stdin (0), stdout (1), stderr (2). Plain `>` is shorthand for `1>`.

cards.q: How do you discard both stdout and stderr of a noisy command?
cards.a: `command > /dev/null 2>&1`
cards.x: /dev/null is the bit bucket; 2>&1 merges stderr into wherever stdout goes.

cards.q: What does `cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd` print?
cards.a: The usernames (first colon-separated field of each line)
cards.x: -d sets the delimiter, -f picks fields; -f1,3 picks fields 1 and 3.
wrong: The last field of each line

cards.q: What does `sort access.log | uniq -c | sort -rn | head` do?
cards.a: Shows the most frequent lines first, with counts
cards.x: uniq only collapses adjacent duplicates, so sort first; -c counts, -rn sorts numerically in reverse.
wrong: Sorts and deletes the original file

cards.q: What does `awk -F: '{print $1}' /etc/passwd` do?
cards.a: Prints the first colon-separated field of each line
cards.x: -F sets the field separator; $1, $2 are fields, $0 is the whole line.

cards.q: How do you replace "foo" with "bar" everywhere in file.txt, in place?
cards.a: `sed -i 's/foo/bar/g' file.txt`
cards.x: s/// is substitute, g means global (all occurrences per line), -i edits the file in place.

decks.title: Package Management
decks.summary: apt/dnf, repositories, and keeping systems updated.

cards.q: Which package tools belong to which distro family?
cards.a: apt/dpkg on Debian/Ubuntu; dnf/rpm on RHEL/Fedora
cards.x: dpkg/rpm are the low-level tools; apt/dnf resolve dependencies from repositories.
wrong: yum on Ubuntu, apt on Fedora

cards.q: What is the difference between `apt update` and `apt upgrade`?
cards.a: `update` refreshes the package index; `upgrade` installs newer versions
cards.x: Always update first, or upgrade works from a stale list.

cards.q: Which command installs nginx on Ubuntu?
cards.a: `sudo apt install nginx`
cards.x: On Fedora/RHEL it is `sudo dnf install nginx`.

cards.q: How do you list installed packages matching "ssh" on Debian?
cards.a: `dpkg -l | grep ssh`
cards.x: On RHEL/Fedora: `rpm -qa | grep ssh`.

cards.q: How do you find which package owns /usr/bin/curl?
cards.a: `dpkg -S /usr/bin/curl` on Debian; `rpm -qf` on RHEL
cards.x: Useful when a binary misbehaves and you want its package version and config files.

cards.q: What do `apt remove` / `dnf remove` leave behind?
cards.a: Configuration files
cards.x: Use `apt purge` (or remove then clean /etc) for full removal; configs in /home are never touched.

cards.q: Where do apt repository definitions live?
cards.a: /etc/apt/sources.list and /etc/apt/sources.list.d/
cards.x: dnf/yum repos live in /etc/yum.repos.d/.

cards.q: Why prefer the distro repository over a random .deb/.rpm download?
cards.a: Signed, verified, dependency-resolved, and updated automatically
cards.x: A stray .deb gets no security updates — how breaches start.

cards.q: What does `apt autoremove` do?
cards.a: Removes packages that were auto-installed as dependencies and are no longer needed
cards.x: Safe cleanup after uninstalling software.

cards.q: What should you do before a major upgrade on a production server?
cards.a: Back up (or snapshot), read the release notes, and test in staging first
cards.x: Never upgrade production on a Friday afternoon without a rollback plan.
wrong: Run it Friday at 5pm and hope

decks.title: systemd & Services
decks.summary: systemctl, journalctl, units, and timers.

cards.q: Which command shows whether nginx is running and enabled?
cards.a: `systemctl status nginx`
cards.x: Shows active state, enabled state, recent log lines, and the main PID.

cards.q: What is the difference between `systemctl start` and `systemctl enable`?
cards.a: `start` runs it now; `enable` makes it start at boot
cards.x: You usually want both: `systemctl enable --now nginx`.

cards.q: Which command tails a service's logs live?
cards.a: `journalctl -u nginx -f`
cards.x: -u filters by unit, -f follows. Add --since "10 min ago" to bound it.

cards.q: What replaced SysV runlevels in systemd?
cards.a: Targets, e.g. multi-user.target and graphical.target
cards.x: `systemctl get-default` shows the boot target; `isolate` switches to one.

cards.q: Where do your custom unit files go?
cards.a: /etc/systemd/system/
cards.x: Distro units live in /lib/systemd/system — override them with drop-ins, never edit in place.

cards.q: What does `systemctl daemon-reload` do?
cards.a: Reloads unit file definitions after you edit them
cards.x: Run it after adding or changing any .service file, before start/enable.

cards.q: What is a systemd timer?
cards.a: A cron-like scheduler: a .timer unit that triggers a .service unit
cards.x: Timers give you journald logging and dependency handling that cron lacks.
wrong: A timeout that kills hung services

cards.q: How do you list services that failed?
cards.a: `systemctl --failed`
cards.x: Then `journalctl -u <name>` for the actual error.

cards.q: What does `journalctl --since "1 hour ago" -p err` show?
cards.a: Error-priority messages from the last hour
cards.x: -p filters by priority: emerg, alert, crit, err, warning, notice, info, debug.

cards.q: For a config change, why prefer `reload` over `restart`?
cards.a: `reload` rereads config without dropping connections; `restart` stops the process first
cards.x: Not every service implements reload — check `systemctl reload-or-restart`.

decks.title: Networking Tools
decks.summary: ip, ss, curl, ssh, and the files behind name resolution.

cards.q: What is the modern replacement for `ifconfig`?
cards.a: `ip addr` (from iproute2)
cards.x: ifconfig is deprecated on Linux. `ip -brief addr` gives a compact view.

cards.q: What is the modern replacement for `netstat -tulpn`?
cards.a: `ss -tulpn`
cards.x: ss is faster (reads kernel directly). Flags: TCP/UDP, listening, processes, numeric.

cards.q: Which command shows the routing table?
cards.a: `ip route`
cards.x: `ip route get 8.8.8.8` even tells you which interface and source IP would be used.

cards.q: What does `curl -I https://example.com` do?
cards.a: Sends a HEAD request and prints only the response headers
cards.x: Quick way to check status codes, redirects, and server banners without downloading the body.

cards.q: How do you copy file.txt to /tmp/ on a remote server over SSH?
cards.a: `scp file.txt user@host:/tmp/`
cards.x: Add -r for directories. rsync is better for repeated syncs.

cards.q: Where does Linux check hostnames before asking DNS?
cards.a: /etc/hosts
cards.x: The lookup order is controlled by /etc/nsswitch.conf.

cards.q: What does /etc/resolv.conf configure?
cards.a: Which DNS servers (nameservers) to query
cards.x: On systemd systems it is often a stub pointing at systemd-resolved.

cards.q: What does `ping -c 4 host` do?
cards.a: Sends 4 ICMP echo requests, then stops
cards.x: Plain `ping` on Linux runs forever; -c counts. -i sets the interval.

cards.q: How do you test whether port 443 is open on a host?
cards.a: `nc -vz host 443` (or `curl -vk https://host:443`)
cards.x: ping cannot test ports — ICMP has no port concept.

cards.q: What does `ssh -i ~/.ssh/deploy.pem user@host` do?
cards.a: Connects using that specific private key file
cards.x: Useful for automation and jump hosts with per-environment keys.
wrong: Copies the key to the host

decks.title: Bash Scripting
decks.summary: Variables, conditionals, loops, functions, and safe scripting.

cards.q: What should the first line of a bash script be?
cards.a: `#!/usr/bin/env bash`
cards.x: The shebang tells the kernel which interpreter to run. env finds bash via PATH, so it is portable.

cards.q: How do you make script.sh executable and run it?
cards.a: `chmod +x script.sh`, then `./script.sh`
cards.x: The ./ matters: the current directory is not in PATH by default (a security feature).

cards.q: What does `$?` hold?
cards.a: The exit code of the last command (0 means success)
cards.x: Check it right after the command — any command, even echo, overwrites it.
wrong: The process ID of the script

cards.q: What is the difference between `$@`, `$*`, and `$#`?
cards.a: `$@`/`$*` are the arguments; `$#` is how many there are
cards.x: Always use `"$@"` (quoted): it keeps each argument intact even with spaces.

cards.q: How do you test whether a file exists?
cards.a: `if [ -f "$file" ]; then ... fi`
cards.x: -f regular file, -d directory, -z empty string, -n non-empty. Quote the variable.

cards.q: What does `set -euo pipefail` at the top of a script do?
cards.a: Exits on any error, treats unset variables as errors, and catches pipeline failures
cards.x: The single best line for scripts that must not silently keep going after a failure.

cards.q: Why quote variables as `"$name"`?
cards.a: Prevents word splitting and glob expansion on values with spaces
cards.x: Unquoted `$file` with "my report.txt" becomes two arguments.
wrong: Quoting is required by shell syntax

cards.q: What does `for f in *.log; do gzip "$f"; done` do?
cards.a: Compresses every .log file in the current directory
cards.x: The glob expands before the loop runs; quote "$f" for names with spaces.

cards.q: What is the safe way to read a file line by line?
cards.a: `while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file`
cards.x: -r keeps backslashes literal; IFS= preserves leading/trailing whitespace. Never `for line in $(cat file)`.

cards.q: How does a bash function return data to its caller?
cards.a: Exit status via `return N` (0-255); real data goes on stdout
cards.x: `result=$(myfunc)` captures stdout. `return "text"` does not work.

decks.title: Logs & Troubleshooting
decks.summary: Finding evidence: journald, /var/log, and resource tools.

cards.q: Where do most traditional service logs live?
cards.a: /var/log/ (syslog, auth.log, nginx/, ...)
cards.x: Structured apps may log to journald instead — check both when hunting.

cards.q: Which command follows a log file live?
cards.a: `tail -f /var/log/syslog`
cards.x: -f follows new lines as written. `tail -F` also survives log rotation.

cards.q: What does `dmesg | tail` show?
cards.a: Recent kernel ring-buffer messages: boot, hardware, drivers
cards.x: USB disconnects, OOM kills, and disk errors all appear here first.

cards.q: How do you check filesystem free space vs directory sizes?
cards.a: `df -h` for filesystems; `du -sh *` for directories
cards.x: "No space left" with free inodes? Check `df -i` — millions of tiny files exhaust inodes first.

cards.q: Which command shows processes sorted by CPU usage?
cards.a: `top` (then P) or the friendlier `htop`
cards.x: In top: M sorts by memory, k kills a PID, q quits.

cards.q: What does `ps aux | grep nginx` tell you?
cards.a: The nginx processes: user, PID, CPU%, memory, command
cards.x: Look for unexpected processes here during incident triage.

cards.q: How do you find which process listens on port 8080?
cards.a: `ss -tulpn | grep 8080` (or `lsof -i :8080`)
cards.x: The -p flag reveals the PID and process name — gold during triage.

cards.q: What does `uptime` report?
cards.a: Current time, how long the system has run, logged-in users, load averages
cards.x: Three load numbers = 1, 5, 15 minute averages of runnable processes.

cards.q: How do you read the three load-average numbers?
cards.a: Average runnable processes over 1, 5, and 15 minutes
cards.x: Sustained load above your CPU core count means queuing — investigate with top.

cards.q: What is `strace` for?
cards.a: Tracing a process's system calls
cards.x: `strace -p <pid>` or `strace -e openat cmd` reveals exactly which files a failing program touches.

decks.title: Linux Security Basics
decks.summary: SSH hardening, firewalls, patching, and least privilege.

cards.q: What is the single biggest SSH hardening step?
cards.a: Key-based auth only: disable passwords and root login
cards.x: In /etc/sshd_config: PasswordAuthentication no, PermitRootLogin no. Then `systemctl reload sshd`.
wrong: Expose port 22 to the whole internet

cards.q: What does `ufw allow 22/tcp` do?
cards.a: Opens SSH through the Uncomplicated Firewall
cards.x: Default-deny first: `ufw default deny incoming`, then allow only what you need.

cards.q: firewalld vs ufw — which is which?
cards.a: firewalld is RHEL's zone-based firewall (firewall-cmd); ufw is Ubuntu's simpler iptables/nftables frontend
cards.x: Both are frontends; the packet filter underneath is nftables on modern systems.

cards.q: What does fail2ban do?
cards.a: Bans IPs after repeated failed logins, by watching the logs
cards.x: Classic brute-force mitigation for SSH. It inserts temporary firewall rules.

cards.q: Why enable automatic security updates (unattended-upgrades / dnf-automatic)?
cards.a: Patches land promptly without relying on a human remembering
cards.x: Scope it to security updates on servers; full upgrades still deserve a maintenance window.

cards.q: What does least privilege mean in practice?
cards.a: Every account and service gets only the permissions its job needs
cards.x: No shared root passwords, no blanket sudo ALL, no world-writable config.

cards.q: Why shouldn't services run as root?
cards.a: A compromised service then owns the entire box
cards.x: Create a dedicated low-privilege service account per daemon (nginx, postgres, ...).
wrong: Services cannot run as root at all

cards.q: What do AIDE and Tripwire do?
cards.a: File integrity monitoring: alert when system binaries or configs change unexpectedly
cards.x: Establish the baseline right after a clean install, then monitor the drift.

cards.q: Why must `~/.ssh/id_rsa` be mode 600?
cards.a: SSH refuses private keys readable by anyone else
cards.x: The client errors out with "UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE" rather than risk leaking it.
wrong: It shares the key with your group
It encrypts the key on disk

cards.q: What is the checklist before exposing a Linux server to the internet?
cards.a: Patched, SSH keys-only with no root login, firewall default-deny with only needed ports, brute-force protection, tested backups
cards.x: Do this in order, verify each step, and re-check after every major change.

tracks.title: Terraform
tracks.tagline: Infrastructure as Code: define, plan and provision cloud infra safely.

decks.title: IaC & Terraform Basics
decks.summary: What Infrastructure as Code is, and where Terraform fits.

cards.q: What is Infrastructure as Code (IaC)?
cards.a: Managing infrastructure through machine-readable config files instead of manual clicks
cards.x: The config is versioned, reviewed and reproducible like application code.

cards.q: Is Terraform declarative or imperative?
cards.a: Declarative — you describe the desired end state
cards.x: You say *what* you want; Terraform figures out the steps to get there.

cards.q: What language does Terraform configuration use?
cards.a: HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language)
cards.x: HCL is human-readable; Terraform can also read JSON (.tf.json).

cards.q: What file extension do Terraform config files use?
cards.a: .tf
cards.x: Terraform loads every .tf file in the working directory and merges them.

cards.q: What is a Terraform provider?
cards.a: A plugin that lets Terraform manage a specific platform (AWS, Azure, Kubernetes…)
cards.x: Providers expose resources and data sources for their API.

cards.q: What does a provider do with your credentials?
cards.a: Authenticates to the target API to create and read resources
cards.x: Credentials come from env vars, shared files or the provider block — never hard-code them.

cards.q: Which is NOT a benefit of IaC?
cards.a: It removes the need to understand the cloud platform
cards.x: IaC gives versioning, repeatability and review — but you still need to know the platform.

cards.q: What is "idempotence" in Terraform?
cards.a: Applying the same config repeatedly converges to the same state with no extra changes
cards.x: A second apply with no config change is a no-op.

cards.q: Where does Terraform record what it has created?
cards.a: In a state file (terraform.tfstate)
cards.x: State maps your config to real-world resource ids.

cards.q: Terraform vs Ansible, in one line?
cards.a: Terraform provisions infrastructure (declarative state); Ansible configures it (procedural)
cards.x: They are complementary: Terraform builds the server, Ansible installs software on it.

cards.q: What is a Terraform "resource"?
cards.a: A block describing one infrastructure object Terraform manages
cards.x: e.g. an aws_instance, a dns record, a storage bucket.

decks.title: The Core Workflow
decks.summary: init → plan → apply, plus fmt, validate and destroy.

cards.q: What does `terraform init` do?
cards.a: Initialises the working directory: downloads providers and sets up the backend
cards.x: Run it first, and again whenever providers, modules or the backend change.

cards.q: What does `terraform plan` do?
cards.a: Shows the changes Terraform *would* make, without making them
cards.x: A dry run: it compares desired config to current state.

cards.q: What does `terraform apply` do?
cards.a: Executes the plan to create, update or delete real resources
cards.x: It shows the plan and asks for confirmation unless -auto-approve is set.

cards.q: What does `terraform destroy` do?
cards.a: Deletes all resources tracked in the state
cards.x: It is `apply` toward an empty desired state; it also shows a plan first.

cards.q: What does `terraform fmt` do?
cards.a: Rewrites config files to the canonical style and indentation
cards.x: Keeps diffs clean; run it (or -check) in CI.

cards.q: What does `terraform validate` do?
cards.a: Checks the config is syntactically valid and internally consistent
cards.x: It does not talk to any provider or check real infrastructure.

cards.q: In `plan` output, what does a `+` mean?
cards.a: A resource will be created
cards.x: `~` means update in place, `-` destroy, `-/+` replace.

cards.q: In `plan` output, what does `-/+` mean?
cards.a: The resource will be destroyed and recreated (replaced)
cards.x: A changed immutable argument forces replacement.

cards.q: How do you preview a destroy without doing it?
cards.a: terraform plan -destroy
cards.x: It shows exactly what would be removed.

cards.q: What does `-auto-approve` do on apply?
cards.a: Skips the interactive "yes" confirmation
cards.x: Useful in CI; dangerous interactively — it applies immediately.

cards.q: Why save a plan file (`terraform plan -out`)?
cards.a: So `apply` runs exactly that reviewed plan, with no drift between preview and apply
cards.x: Guarantees what you reviewed is what gets applied.

puzzles.prompt: Put the core Terraform workflow in order for a first run.
puzzles.x: init downloads providers and sets up the backend, validate checks the config, plan previews the change, apply makes it real.

puzzles.prompt: How many resources does a plan showing "2 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy" apply in total (add + change + destroy)?
puzzles.x: A plan summarises the actions: 2 creates + 1 update + 0 deletes = 3 resource actions.

decks.title: Resources & Data Sources
decks.summary: Resource blocks, references, dependencies and reading existing infra.

cards.q: What are the two labels in `resource "aws_instance" "web" {}`?
cards.a: The resource type (aws_instance) and a local name (web)
cards.x: Together they form the address aws_instance.web.

cards.q: How do you reference another resource's attribute?
cards.a: <type>.<name>.<attribute>, e.g. aws_vpc.main.id
cards.x: Referencing an attribute also creates an implicit dependency.

cards.q: What is an implicit dependency?
cards.a: A dependency Terraform infers because one resource references another
cards.x: Terraform builds a graph and orders creation automatically.
wrong: A dependency you must always declare

cards.q: When do you need `depends_on`?
cards.a: When a dependency exists but is not expressed through a reference
cards.x: It forces ordering Terraform cannot infer.

cards.q: What is a data source?
cards.a: A read-only lookup of information defined outside this config
cards.x: e.g. data "aws_ami" "latest" finds an existing image id.

cards.q: How do you reference a data source?
cards.a: data.<type>.<name>.<attribute>
cards.x: e.g. data.aws_ami.latest.id.

cards.q: Difference between an argument and an attribute?
cards.a: Arguments are inputs you set; attributes are values exported after creation
cards.x: e.g. you set `ami`; you read the exported `id`.

cards.q: What is the `terraform` block for?
cards.a: Settings for Terraform itself: required_version, required_providers and the backend
cards.x: It configures the tool, not infrastructure.

cards.q: Why pin `required_providers` versions?
cards.a: So a new provider release cannot silently change behaviour or break your config
cards.x: Pin with version constraints like "~> 5.0".
wrong: It is required for every resource

cards.q: What does the constraint `~> 5.1` allow?
cards.a: >= 5.1.0 and < 5.2.0 (patch updates only)
cards.x: The pessimistic operator locks the left-most unpinned segment.

decks.title: Variables, Outputs & Locals
decks.summary: Parameterise configs with inputs, locals and outputs.

cards.q: How do you declare an input variable?
cards.a: A `variable "name" {}` block, optionally with type, default and description
cards.x: Reference it as var.name.

cards.q: How do you reference an input variable?
cards.a: var.<name>
cards.x: e.g. var.region.

cards.q: What happens if a variable has no default and no value is supplied?
cards.a: Terraform prompts for it (or errors in non-interactive runs)
cards.x: Provide values via -var, a .tfvars file or env vars.

cards.q: Which file is auto-loaded for variable values?
cards.a: terraform.tfvars (and *.auto.tfvars)
cards.x: Other .tfvars files need -var-file.

cards.q: How do you set a variable from an environment variable?
cards.a: Prefix it with TF_VAR_, e.g. TF_VAR_region=us-east-1
cards.x: Handy for secrets and CI.

cards.q: What is a `local` value?
cards.a: A named expression computed once and reused, referenced as local.<name>
cards.x: Locals reduce repetition; they are not inputs.

cards.q: What is an `output`?
cards.a: A value a config exposes after apply (and to parent modules)
cards.x: Shown by `terraform output`; used to wire modules together.

cards.q: How do you hide a sensitive value from CLI output?
cards.a: Mark the variable or output `sensitive = true`
cards.x: It is redacted in plan/apply output (but still stored in state).

cards.q: Does `sensitive = true` encrypt the value in state?
cards.a: No — state still stores it in plaintext; protect the state itself
cards.x: Use an encrypted remote backend and tight access controls.

cards.q: What variable types can you declare?
cards.a: string, number, bool, list, set, map, object and tuple
cards.x: Type constraints catch mistakes early.

cards.q: What does `nullable = false` on a variable do?
cards.a: Forbids the value null, so a default is always used instead
cards.x: Prevents null from propagating into resources.

decks.title: Expressions & Functions
decks.summary: Conditionals, for-expressions, and built-in functions.

cards.q: What is Terraform's ternary conditional syntax?
cards.a: condition ? true_value : false_value
cards.x: e.g. var.prod ? "m5.large" : "t3.micro".

cards.q: What does a `for` expression do?
cards.a: Transforms one collection into another, e.g. [for s in var.list : upper(s)]
cards.x: Use { } to build a map instead of a list.

cards.q: What does the splat expression `aws_instance.web[*].id` give you?
cards.a: A list of the id attribute from every instance in that resource
cards.x: Shorthand for [for i in aws_instance.web : i.id].

cards.q: What does `length()` return for a list?
cards.a: The number of elements
cards.x: Also works on maps and strings.

cards.q: What does `lookup(map, key, default)` do?
cards.a: Returns the map value for key, or the default if the key is absent
cards.x: Prefer map[key] with a known key; lookup adds a fallback.

cards.q: What does `coalesce(a, b, c)` return?
cards.a: The first non-null, non-empty argument
cards.x: Great for "use this, else fall back to that".

cards.q: How do you read a value from a JSON string?
cards.a: jsondecode(str) — turns JSON text into a Terraform value
cards.x: jsonencode() goes the other way.

cards.q: What does `templatefile(path, vars)` do?
cards.a: Renders a template file with the given variables into a string
cards.x: Used for user-data, config files, policy documents.

cards.q: What does the `try()` function do?
cards.a: Returns the first argument that evaluates without error
cards.x: Useful for optional/maybe-missing attributes.

cards.q: What is string interpolation in HCL?
cards.a: Embedding an expression in a string with ${ ... }
cards.x: e.g. "web-${var.env}". Avoid it where a bare reference works.

decks.title: State & Backends
decks.summary: Remote state, locking, and why state matters.

cards.q: Why should teams use remote state instead of a local file?
cards.a: So everyone shares one source of truth and runs do not clobber each other
cards.x: Local state on laptops diverges and leaks secrets.

cards.q: What is a Terraform backend?
cards.a: Where state is stored and how operations run (local, s3, remote, etc.)
cards.x: e.g. the s3 backend stores state in a bucket.

cards.q: Why is state locking important?
cards.a: It stops two applies from modifying the same state at once and corrupting it
cards.x: e.g. S3 backend uses DynamoDB (or S3 native) for the lock.

cards.q: What does `terraform_remote_state` let you do?
cards.a: Read the outputs of another configuration's state
cards.x: A read-only way to share values between stacks.

cards.q: Why NEVER edit terraform.tfstate by hand?
cards.a: You can corrupt the mapping; use state commands instead
cards.x: Use terraform state mv/rm/import and plan to reconcile.

cards.q: What does `terraform state list` show?
cards.a: Every resource address Terraform is tracking in state
cards.x: A quick inventory of managed resources.

cards.q: What does `terraform state rm <addr>` do?
cards.a: Removes a resource from state WITHOUT destroying the real resource
cards.x: Terraform then stops managing it.

cards.q: What does `terraform state mv` do?
cards.a: Renames/moves a resource's address in state (e.g. after refactoring)
cards.x: Avoids a needless destroy/recreate when you rename.

cards.q: What is "drift"?
cards.a: When real infrastructure changes outside Terraform, diverging from state
cards.x: A plan (or refresh) detects it; apply reconciles it.

cards.q: Should the state file be committed to git?
cards.a: No — it holds secrets and shifting ids; use a secured remote backend
cards.x: Add terraform.tfstate* to .gitignore.

decks.title: Modules
decks.summary: Reusable, composable infrastructure building blocks.

cards.q: What is a Terraform module?
cards.a: A reusable container of .tf files called with inputs and returning outputs
cards.x: Every config is itself the "root module".

cards.q: How do you call a module?
cards.a: A `module "name" { source = "..." }` block with input arguments
cards.x: Reference its outputs as module.name.<output>.

cards.q: What does the `source` argument accept?
cards.a: A local path, a registry address, a git URL, etc.
cards.x: e.g. "./modules/vpc" or "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws".

cards.q: Why pin a module `version`?
cards.a: So a new module release cannot change your infra unexpectedly
cards.x: Version constraints work like provider ones.

cards.q: How do you expose a value from a module to its caller?
cards.a: Declare an `output` in the module
cards.x: The parent reads module.<name>.<output>.

cards.q: How do you pass data INTO a module?
cards.a: Set its declared input variables as arguments in the module block
cards.x: The module reads them as var.<name>.

cards.q: What makes a good module boundary?
cards.a: A cohesive, reusable unit with a clear input/output contract
cards.x: e.g. a "vpc" module, not "all of prod".

cards.q: Can a module call other modules?
cards.a: Yes — modules compose, forming a tree from the root module
cards.x: Keep nesting shallow for readability.

cards.q: What is the Terraform Registry?
cards.a: A public catalog of reusable providers and modules
cards.x: registry.terraform.io; verified modules are marked.

cards.q: Where should provider configuration live?
cards.a: In the root module; pass providers to child modules explicitly if needed
cards.x: Child modules should not define their own provider blocks for normal use.

decks.title: Meta-Arguments & Lifecycle
decks.summary: count, for_each, lifecycle, dynamic blocks and provisioners.

cards.q: What does the `count` meta-argument do?
cards.a: Creates N copies of a resource, indexed count.index
cards.x: Address them as <res>[0], <res>[1]…

cards.q: What does `for_each` do, and why prefer it over count?
cards.a: Creates one instance per key in a map/set; stable keys survive list edits
cards.x: With count, removing a middle item re-indexes and churns resources.

cards.q: Inside a for_each resource, what are each.key and each.value?
cards.a: The current key and value from the map/set being iterated
cards.x: Use them to configure each instance.

cards.q: What does `lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }` do?
cards.a: Creates the replacement before destroying the old resource
cards.x: Avoids downtime when a change forces replacement.

cards.q: What does `prevent_destroy = true` do?
cards.a: Makes Terraform error rather than destroy that resource
cards.x: A guardrail for critical resources like a database.

cards.q: What does `ignore_changes` do?
cards.a: Tells Terraform to ignore drift on specific attributes after creation
cards.x: e.g. ignore tags mutated by another system.

cards.q: What is a `dynamic` block for?
cards.a: Generating repeatable nested blocks (e.g. many ingress rules) from a collection
cards.x: It loops nested blocks the way for_each loops resources.

cards.q: Why are provisioners a "last resort"?
cards.a: They are imperative, run only on create/destroy, and are not tracked in state
cards.x: Prefer provider resources, cloud-init or config tools instead.

cards.q: What does a `null_resource` (or terraform_data) commonly do?
cards.a: Runs provisioners or triggers tied to arbitrary values, with nothing to create
cards.x: A workaround when no real resource fits.

cards.q: What does the `terraform_data` resource replace?
cards.a: The older null_resource pattern, without needing the null provider
cards.x: It stores input and exposes a triggers_replace argument.

decks.title: Production & Security
decks.summary: Workspaces, import, policy-as-code, scanning and CI/CD.

cards.q: What are Terraform workspaces?
cards.a: Multiple named state instances for one config (e.g. dev, staging)
cards.x: terraform.workspace exposes the current name; they are NOT strong isolation.

cards.q: Are CLI workspaces good isolation for prod vs dev?
cards.a: No — they share backend and config; prefer separate configs/state per environment
cards.x: Workspaces suit lightweight variants, not hard prod boundaries.

cards.q: What does `terraform import` do?
cards.a: Brings an existing, unmanaged resource under Terraform management in state
cards.x: You still write matching config; modern Terraform supports import blocks.

cards.q: What is "policy as code" (Sentinel / OPA)?
cards.a: Automated guardrails that pass/fail plans against rules before apply
cards.x: e.g. "no public S3 buckets", "only approved regions".

cards.q: What do tools like tfsec / Checkov / Trivy do?
cards.a: Statically scan Terraform for insecure configurations
cards.x: e.g. open security groups, unencrypted storage — caught before apply.

cards.q: Where should cloud credentials come from in CI?
cards.a: Short-lived, injected secrets or OIDC federation — never committed to the repo
cards.x: Hard-coding keys in .tf or state is a breach waiting to happen.

cards.q: A safe Terraform CI pipeline runs, in order:
cards.a: fmt/validate → plan (save) → policy/security scan → gated apply of that plan
cards.x: Humans review the plan; apply uses the exact reviewed plan file.
wrong: apply on every push, no review

cards.q: How do you roll back a bad Terraform change?
cards.a: Revert the config in version control and apply the previous state of the code
cards.x: There is no automatic undo; git history is your rollback.
wrong: Restore state from a snapshot only

cards.q: Why run `terraform plan` on every pull request?
cards.a: To review the exact infrastructure impact before it is merged/applied
cards.x: Catches surprises (replacements, deletions) during code review.

cards.q: Biggest risk of an unprotected remote state?
cards.a: It contains secrets and full infra topology — a prime target
cards.x: Encrypt it, lock down access, and enable versioning on the bucket.
wrong: Nothing; state is public by design

puzzles.prompt: Order the stages of a safe Terraform CI pipeline.
puzzles.x: Format and validate, produce a saved plan, scan it, let a human review it, then apply exactly that reviewed plan.

tracks.title: C++
tracks.tagline: Systems programming: performance, memory control and modern C++.

decks.title: Basics & the Compile Model
decks.summary: What C++ is, how a program is built, and hello world.

cards.q: Is C++ compiled or interpreted?
cards.a: Compiled — source is translated to machine code before it runs
cards.x: A compiler (e.g. g++, clang++, MSVC) produces a native executable.
wrong: Run on a virtual machine like Java

cards.q: What are the three build stages for a C++ program?
cards.a: Preprocess → compile → link
cards.x: The preprocessor expands #includes/macros, the compiler makes object files, the linker combines them.

cards.q: What is the entry point of a C++ program?
cards.a: The main() function
cards.x: Execution starts at main; returning 0 means success.

cards.q: What does `#include <iostream>` do?
cards.a: Brings in the standard input/output stream declarations
cards.x: Needed for std::cout and std::cin.

cards.q: How do you print to the console?
cards.a: std::cout << "text"
cards.x: << is the stream insertion operator; std::endl or "\n" ends the line.

cards.q: What is the `std` in `std::cout`?
cards.a: The standard library namespace
