cards.x: std:: qualifies names from the standard library.

cards.q: What does `using namespace std;` do, and why be cautious?
cards.a: Pulls all std names into scope; it can cause name clashes in larger code
cards.x: Prefer std:: qualification in headers and real projects.

cards.q: Does C++ require a semicolon after each statement?
cards.a: Yes — statements end with ;
cards.x: Missing semicolons are a very common compile error.

cards.q: What does `return 0;` from main signal?
cards.a: The program exited successfully
cards.x: A non-zero value signals an error to the OS.

cards.q: Compile a single file with g++ to an executable named app:
cards.a: g++ main.cpp -o app
cards.x: Add -std=c++20 to pick the language standard.

puzzles.prompt: Put the C++ build pipeline in order, from source to running program.
puzzles.x: The preprocessor expands includes and macros, the compiler produces object files, the linker combines them into an executable, then the OS runs it.

puzzles.prompt: What does the expression 7 / 2 evaluate to in C++ when both operands are int?
puzzles.x: Integer division truncates toward zero: 7 / 2 is 3. Use 7.0 / 2 to get 3.5.

decks.title: Types, Variables & Operators
decks.summary: Fundamental types, const, auto and operators.

cards.q: Which type holds a whole number?
cards.a: int
cards.x: double/float hold decimals; char holds a single byte/character.

cards.q: What does `const int x = 5;` mean?
cards.a: x is a read-only integer that cannot be reassigned
cards.x: const catches accidental mutation at compile time.

cards.q: What does `auto` do in `auto x = 3.0;`?
cards.a: Deduces the type from the initialiser (here, double)
cards.x: auto reduces verbosity; the variable is still statically typed.

cards.q: What is the result type of `7 / 2` in C++?
cards.a: int (3) — integer division truncates
cards.x: Use 7.0 / 2 to get a double (3.5).

cards.q: What does `sizeof(int)` return?
cards.a: The number of bytes an int occupies (commonly 4)
cards.x: Sizes are implementation-defined; sizeof gives the actual size.

cards.q: What is the value range risk with signed integer overflow?
cards.a: It is undefined behaviour in C++
cards.x: Unsigned overflow wraps; signed overflow is UB — do not rely on it.
wrong: It always wraps to the minimum

cards.q: What does `bool` store?
cards.a: true or false
cards.x: In C++ true is 1 and false is 0 when converted to int.

cards.q: What is the difference between `=` and `==`?
cards.a: = assigns; == compares for equality
cards.x: Using = inside an if is a classic bug.

cards.q: How do you write a character literal vs a string literal?
cards.a: Single quotes 'a' for char, double quotes "a" for a C-string
cards.x: 'a' is one byte; "a" is a null-terminated array.

cards.q: What does `static_cast<double>(x)` do?
cards.a: Explicitly converts x to a double at compile time
cards.x: Prefer named casts over C-style (double)x casts.

decks.title: Control Flow & Functions
decks.summary: if/switch, loops, and defining functions.

cards.q: Which loop runs its body at least once?
cards.a: do { ... } while (cond);
cards.x: The condition is checked after the body.

cards.q: What does `break;` do in a loop?
cards.a: Exits the innermost loop immediately
cards.x: continue skips to the next iteration instead.

cards.q: What does a function return type of `void` mean?
cards.a: The function returns no value
cards.x: You call it for its side effects.

cards.q: What is pass-by-value?
cards.a: The function gets a copy of the argument; changes do not affect the caller
cards.x: Fine for small types; copies larger objects.

cards.q: How do you let a function modify the caller's variable?
cards.a: Take the parameter by reference: void f(int& x)
cards.x: Or by pointer: void f(int* x).

cards.q: Why pass a large object as `const T&`?
cards.a: To avoid copying it while promising not to modify it
cards.x: Pass-by-const-reference is the default for big read-only params.
wrong: It is required for all params

cards.q: What is function overloading?
cards.a: Multiple functions with the same name but different parameter lists
cards.x: The compiler picks the best match by arguments.

cards.q: What is a default argument?
cards.a: A parameter value used when the caller omits it
cards.x: e.g. int f(int x, int y = 0).

cards.q: Where must a function be declared before you call it?
cards.a: Before its first use — via a definition or a forward declaration (prototype)
cards.x: Headers provide declarations so callers can see them.

cards.q: What does `switch` compare against each `case`?
cards.a: An integral/enumeration value, matched exactly
cards.x: Remember break; or cases fall through.

decks.title: Pointers, References & Memory
decks.summary: Addresses, the stack/heap, and manual allocation.

cards.q: What is a pointer?
cards.a: A variable that stores the memory address of another object
cards.x: Dereference it with * to read/write the pointee.
wrong: A reference that cannot be null

cards.q: What does `&x` give you?
cards.a: The address of x (the 'address-of' operator)
cards.x: Assign it to a pointer: int* p = &x;.

cards.q: What does `*p` do when p is a pointer?
cards.a: Dereferences p: accesses the object it points to
cards.x: *p on the left assigns through the pointer.

cards.q: What should an uninitialised or "points to nothing" pointer be set to?
cards.a: nullptr
cards.x: Dereferencing nullptr (or a wild pointer) is undefined behaviour.

cards.q: How do pointers and references differ?
cards.a: A reference is an alias that must bind on creation and cannot be reseated or null
cards.x: Pointers can be null and re-pointed.

cards.q: Where do local (automatic) variables live?
cards.a: On the stack — freed automatically when the scope ends
cards.x: Heap memory (new) must be freed manually.

cards.q: What does `new` return and who frees it?
cards.a: A pointer to heap memory that YOU must delete
cards.x: Every new needs a matching delete (or use smart pointers).

cards.q: What is a memory leak?
cards.a: Heap memory that is never freed, so it is lost until the program exits
cards.x: Caused by a missing delete or a lost pointer.

cards.q: What is a dangling pointer?
cards.a: A pointer to memory that has already been freed or gone out of scope
cards.x: Using it is undefined behaviour.

cards.q: Match `new[]` with which delete?
cards.a: delete[] (the array form)
cards.x: Mismatching new/delete[] is undefined behaviour.

decks.title: Classes & OOP
decks.summary: Encapsulation, constructors, inheritance and polymorphism.

cards.q: Default member access: class vs struct?
cards.a: class members are private by default; struct members are public
cards.x: Otherwise they are the same in C++.
wrong: class is public, struct is private

cards.q: What is a constructor?
cards.a: A special member function that initialises an object when it is created
cards.x: It has the class name and no return type.

cards.q: What is a destructor for?
cards.a: Cleanup when an object is destroyed (free resources, close handles)
cards.x: Named ~ClassName(); runs automatically at end of lifetime.

cards.q: What does `this` refer to inside a member function?
cards.a: A pointer to the current object
cards.x: Use this->member to disambiguate from parameters.

cards.q: What does `public`/`private`/`protected` control?
cards.a: Access to members: private is class-only, protected adds derived classes, public is open
cards.x: Encapsulation hides internals behind a public interface.

cards.q: What makes a function overridable by a derived class?
cards.a: Declaring it `virtual` in the base class
cards.x: Calls then dispatch to the actual object type at runtime.

cards.q: What is runtime polymorphism in C++?
cards.a: Calling a virtual function through a base pointer/reference dispatches to the derived override
cards.x: Enabled by the virtual table (vtable).

cards.q: Why give a polymorphic base class a virtual destructor?
cards.a: So deleting a derived object via a base pointer runs the derived destructor
cards.x: Without it, that is undefined behaviour / a leak.

cards.q: What is a pure virtual function (`= 0`), and what does it make the class?
cards.a: A function with no base body; it makes the class abstract (not instantiable)
cards.x: Derived classes must override it.

cards.q: What is an initializer list in a constructor?
cards.a: ClassName() : member(value) { } — initialises members before the body runs
cards.x: More efficient than assigning in the body; required for const/reference members.

decks.title: The Standard Library (STL)
decks.summary: Containers, iterators, strings and algorithms.

cards.q: Which container is a dynamic, contiguous array?
cards.a: std::vector
cards.x: It grows as needed and is the default go-to container.

cards.q: How do you add to the end of a vector?
cards.a: v.push_back(x) (or emplace_back)
cards.x: size() reports the count; empty() checks for none.

cards.q: What does `std::map` store, and in what order?
cards.a: Sorted key→value pairs with unique keys
cards.x: std::unordered_map is a hash map (no order, average O(1)).

cards.q: What does `std::string` give you over a C-string?
cards.a: A managed, resizable string that owns its memory
cards.x: No manual null-termination or buffer sizing.
wrong: It is the same as char*

cards.q: What is an iterator?
cards.a: An object that points into a container and can be advanced to traverse it
cards.x: begin()/end() delimit the range.

cards.q: What does `std::sort(v.begin(), v.end())` do?
cards.a: Sorts the range in ascending order (by default <)
cards.x: Pass a comparator for custom order.

cards.q: How do you iterate a container with a range-based for loop?
cards.a: for (const auto& x : container) { ... }
cards.x: Use & to avoid copies; const for read-only.

cards.q: What does `std::find` return when the value is absent?
cards.a: The end() iterator
cards.x: Always compare the result against end() before using it.

cards.q: Which container keeps unique, sorted elements?
cards.a: std::set
cards.x: std::unordered_set is the hash-based, unordered version.

cards.q: What is `std::pair` used for?
cards.a: Holding two values together (e.g. a map entry's .first and .second)
cards.x: std::tuple generalises it to N values.

resources.title: A Tour of C++ / isocpp.org "Get Started"

puzzles.prompt: You push_back three elements onto an empty std::vector. What does v.size() return?
puzzles.x: push_back appends to the end; size() reports the element count — here 3.

decks.title: RAII & Smart Pointers
decks.summary: Deterministic resource management and move semantics.

cards.q: What is RAII?
cards.a: Resource Acquisition Is Initialization: tie a resource's lifetime to an object's scope
cards.x: The destructor releases the resource automatically — C++'s core memory idiom.

cards.q: What does `std::unique_ptr` express?
cards.a: Exclusive ownership of a heap object; it frees it automatically
cards.x: It cannot be copied, only moved.

cards.q: What does `std::shared_ptr` do?
cards.a: Shared ownership via reference counting; frees when the last owner dies
cards.x: Copying increments the count; destruction decrements it.

cards.q: What problem does `std::weak_ptr` solve?
cards.a: It breaks reference cycles by observing a shared_ptr without owning it
cards.x: Two shared_ptrs pointing at each other would never free.

cards.q: Prefer `std::make_unique<T>(...)` over `new` because…
cards.a: It is exception-safe and never leaks if construction throws
cards.x: Also avoids writing the type twice.
wrong: It is faster to type only

cards.q: What are move semantics for?
cards.a: Transferring resources from one object to another without copying
cards.x: std::move casts to an rvalue so the move constructor is chosen.

cards.q: What is the "Rule of Five"?
cards.a: If you define any of destructor, copy/move constructor or copy/move assignment, consider all five
cards.x: Managing a resource usually means defining or deleting them together.

cards.q: What is the "Rule of Zero"?
cards.a: Design classes so you need none of the special members — let members (e.g. smart pointers) manage resources
cards.x: The simplest, safest default in modern C++.

cards.q: How does RAII interact with exceptions?
cards.a: Stack unwinding runs destructors, so resources are released even when an exception propagates
cards.x: This is why RAII beats manual cleanup.

cards.q: After `auto p2 = std::move(p1);` on a unique_ptr, what is p1?
cards.a: Empty (null) — ownership moved to p2
cards.x: The moved-from unique_ptr is left in a valid, null state.

resources.title: A Tour of C++ / isocpp.org "Get Started"

decks.title: Templates & Modern C++
decks.summary: Generics, lambdas, and C++11/17/20 features.

cards.q: What is a template?
cards.a: A blueprint that generates code for many types from one definition
cards.x: e.g. template<typename T> T max(T a, T b).

cards.q: When is a template instantiated?
cards.a: At compile time, once per set of types actually used
cards.x: This is why templates mostly live in headers.

cards.q: What is a lambda?
cards.a: An inline anonymous function object, e.g. [](int x){ return x*2; }
cards.x: The [ ] capture list can grab surrounding variables.
wrong: A pointer to a function only

cards.q: What does the lambda capture `[&]` mean?
cards.a: Capture all used outer variables by reference
cards.x: [=] captures by value; beware dangling references with [&].

cards.q: What does `constexpr` request?
cards.a: That a value/function be evaluated at compile time when possible
cards.x: Enables compile-time constants and computation.

cards.q: What is a namespace for?
cards.a: Grouping related names to avoid collisions
cards.x: Access with ns::name; std is the standard one.

cards.q: Why split a class into a header (.h/.hpp) and a source (.cpp)?
cards.a: The header declares the interface; the .cpp defines it, so callers compile against the declaration
cards.x: Templates are the exception — they usually stay header-only.
wrong: To hide it from the linker

cards.q: What does `nullptr` improve over `NULL`/0?
cards.a: It is a real null-pointer type, so overload resolution is unambiguous
cards.x: NULL is just 0 and can pick the wrong int overload.

cards.q: What does `std::optional<T>` represent?
cards.a: A value that may or may not be present
cards.x: A type-safe alternative to a sentinel or a null pointer.

cards.q: What is `std::vector`'s advantage that makes it the default container?
cards.a: Contiguous storage: cache-friendly, fast index access and iteration
cards.x: Reach for list/map only when you need their specific behaviour.

resources.title: A Tour of C++ / isocpp.org "Get Started"

decks.title: Safety, UB & Performance
decks.summary: Undefined behaviour, memory safety and tooling.

cards.q: What is "undefined behaviour" (UB)?
cards.a: Code the standard gives no meaning to — the compiler may do anything
cards.x: Examples: out-of-bounds access, signed overflow, use-after-free.

cards.q: Why is a buffer overflow dangerous in C++?
cards.a: Writing past an array corrupts memory and is a classic security vulnerability
cards.x: C++ does no bounds checking on raw arrays/[]; the programmer must.

cards.q: How do you avoid most raw-array bounds bugs?
cards.a: Use std::vector/std::array and range-based for or .at()
cards.x: .at() throws std::out_of_range instead of UB.

cards.q: What does `.at(i)` do that `[i]` does not on a vector?
cards.a: Bounds-checks and throws std::out_of_range on a bad index
cards.x: [i] is faster but UB if out of range.

cards.q: Why compile with `-Wall -Wextra`?
cards.a: To enable warnings that catch likely bugs before they ship
cards.x: Treat warnings as errors (-Werror) in CI.

cards.q: What does AddressSanitizer (ASan) detect?
cards.a: Memory errors at runtime: use-after-free, buffer overflows, leaks
cards.x: Build with -fsanitize=address during testing.

cards.q: What does Valgrind help find?
cards.a: Memory leaks and invalid memory use at runtime
cards.x: Complements smart pointers and sanitizers.

cards.q: Best way to prevent leaks in modern C++?
cards.a: Use RAII and smart pointers instead of raw new/delete
cards.x: Let ownership be explicit and automatic.
wrong: Rely on the OS at exit

cards.q: What is a "use-after-free"?
cards.a: Accessing memory through a pointer after it was freed — undefined behaviour and exploitable
cards.x: Null the pointer or use smart pointers to avoid it.

cards.q: Default way to pass a large read-only object to a function?
cards.a: By const reference (const T&) to avoid a copy
cards.x: Pass by value only for small/cheap-to-copy types or when you need a copy.

tracks.title: Go
tracks.tagline: Simple, fast, concurrent: the language of cloud-native tooling.

decks.title: Basics & Tooling
decks.summary: What Go is, modules, and the go command.

cards.q: Is Go compiled or interpreted?
cards.a: Compiled — to a single, statically-linked native binary
cards.x: That self-contained binary is why Go is popular for deployment and containers.
wrong: Compiled to bytecode on a VM

cards.q: What package must an executable program declare?
cards.a: package main
cards.x: It must also contain a func main() entry point.

cards.q: How do you print a line to stdout?
cards.a: fmt.Println("text")
cards.x: Import the "fmt" package first.

cards.q: What does `go run main.go` do?
cards.a: Compiles and runs the program in one step (no binary kept)
cards.x: go build produces a reusable binary instead.

cards.q: How do you start a new module?
cards.a: go mod init <module-path>
cards.x: It creates go.mod, which tracks dependencies and the Go version.

cards.q: What does `gofmt` (go fmt) do?
cards.a: Rewrites code to the single canonical Go formatting
cards.x: Go has one official style; formatting debates do not exist.

cards.q: Does Go allow an unused import or local variable?
cards.a: No — it is a compile error
cards.x: This keeps code clean but surprises newcomers.

cards.q: How are exported (public) names marked in Go?
cards.a: By an uppercase first letter (e.g. Println)
cards.x: lowercase names are package-private.

cards.q: What command downloads and tidies dependencies?
cards.a: go mod tidy
cards.x: It adds missing and removes unused modules in go.mod/go.sum.

cards.q: What is a key part of Go's design philosophy?
cards.a: Simplicity: a small language with one obvious way to do things
cards.x: Few keywords, no inheritance, built-in concurrency and formatting.

puzzles.prompt: Order the steps to create and build a new Go program.
items: write package main and func main
puzzles.x: Initialise the module, write the code, tidy dependencies into go.mod/go.sum, then compile the binary.

puzzles.prompt: How many loop keywords does Go have?
puzzles.x: Just `for` — it covers C-style loops, while-style (for cond {}) and infinite (for {}).

decks.title: Variables, Types & Constants
decks.summary: Declarations, zero values, and constants.

cards.q: What does `x := 5` do?
cards.a: Declares and initialises x, inferring its type (short variable declaration)
cards.x: It works only inside functions; use var at package level.

cards.q: What is the zero value of an int, string, and bool?
cards.a: 0, "" (empty string), and false
cards.x: Every type has a zero value; there is no "undefined".

cards.q: Does Go do implicit numeric conversion, e.g. int to float64?
cards.a: No — conversions must be explicit: float64(i)
cards.x: Mixing types without a conversion is a compile error.

cards.q: What is a `rune` in Go?
cards.a: An alias for int32 representing a Unicode code point
cards.x: Iterating a string with range yields runes.

cards.q: What is a `byte` in Go?
cards.a: An alias for uint8
cards.x: Strings are read-only slices of bytes.

cards.q: How do you declare a constant?
cards.a: const Pi = 3.14159
cards.x: Constants are compile-time; they cannot use := and cannot be addressed.

cards.q: What is `iota` used for?
cards.a: Generating successive untyped integer constants in a const block
cards.x: Common for enums: the first is 0, then 1, 2…

cards.q: Are Go strings mutable?
cards.a: No — strings are immutable
cards.x: Build them with a strings.Builder or convert to []byte.

cards.q: What does `var s string` give s before assignment?
cards.a: The zero value: an empty string ""
cards.x: No nil strings — only the empty string.

cards.q: How do you get the number of bytes in a string s?
cards.a: len(s)
cards.x: Note: len counts bytes, not runes, for multibyte UTF-8.

decks.title: Control Flow & Functions
decks.summary: for, if, switch, multiple returns and defer.

cards.q: How many loop keywords does Go have?
cards.a: One: for (it covers while and infinite loops too)
cards.x: for cond {} is a while; for {} is infinite.

cards.q: How do you write a C-style "while" in Go?
cards.a: for condition { ... }
cards.x: Omit the init and post clauses of the for.

cards.q: What can Go functions return that many languages cannot?
cards.a: Multiple values, e.g. (result, error)
cards.x: This underpins Go's explicit error handling.

cards.q: What does `defer` do?
cards.a: Schedules a call to run when the surrounding function returns
cards.x: Great for cleanup: defer f.Close().

cards.q: If multiple defers run, in what order?
cards.a: Last-in, first-out (LIFO) — reverse of declaration
cards.x: The last defer executes first.

cards.q: Do Go switch cases fall through by default?
cards.a: No — each case breaks automatically
cards.x: Use the fallthrough keyword to continue to the next case.

cards.q: What is a variadic function?
cards.a: One that accepts a variable number of args, e.g. func sum(nums ...int)
cards.x: Inside, nums is a slice.

cards.q: What are "named return values"?
cards.a: Return parameters given names in the signature, pre-initialised to zero values
cards.x: A bare return then returns their current values.

cards.q: Can a Go switch have no condition?
cards.a: Yes — a conditionless switch acts like if/else-if chains
cards.x: Each case holds a boolean expression.

cards.q: How do you ignore a returned value you do not need?
cards.a: Assign it to the blank identifier _
cards.x: e.g. v, _ := f() discards the second return.

decks.title: Slices, Arrays & Maps
decks.summary: Go's core data structures and the range loop.

cards.q: Array vs slice in Go?
cards.a: An array has a fixed length that is part of its type; a slice is a dynamic view into an array
cards.x: Slices are what you use almost everywhere.

cards.q: How do you grow a slice?
cards.a: append(s, value) — and assign the result back: s = append(s, v)
cards.x: append may allocate a new backing array.

cards.q: What do len() and cap() return for a slice?
cards.a: len is the number of elements; cap is the backing array size from the slice start
cards.x: append grows cap when it is exceeded.

cards.q: What does `make([]int, 0, 10)` create?
cards.a: An empty int slice with length 0 and capacity 10
cards.x: Pre-sizing capacity avoids repeated reallocation.

cards.q: How do you create a map?
cards.a: make(map[string]int) or a literal map[string]int{...}
cards.x: Reading a missing key returns the value type's zero value.

cards.q: What is the "comma ok" idiom for maps?
cards.a: v, ok := m[key] — ok is true only if the key exists
cards.x: Distinguishes a missing key from a stored zero value.

cards.q: What does `range` give you over a slice?
cards.a: The index and a copy of the element: for i, v := range s
cards.x: Over a map it gives key, value (unordered).

cards.q: Is map iteration order guaranteed in Go?
cards.a: No — range over a map visits keys in a randomised order
cards.x: Sort the keys if you need determinism.

cards.q: What happens if you modify a slice element inside a range loop variable `v`?
cards.a: Nothing in the slice — v is a copy; index with s[i] to mutate
cards.x: Range copies each element into v.

cards.q: How do you delete a key from a map?
cards.a: delete(m, key)
cards.x: It is a no-op if the key is absent.

decks.title: Structs, Methods & Interfaces
decks.summary: Composition over inheritance; implicit interfaces.

cards.q: What is a struct?
cards.a: A typed collection of named fields
cards.x: Go has no classes; structs plus methods do the job.

cards.q: How do you attach a method to a type?
cards.a: func (r Receiver) Name() { ... } — a receiver before the name
cards.x: The receiver can be a value or a pointer.

cards.q: Value receiver vs pointer receiver?
cards.a: A pointer receiver (*T) can modify the receiver and avoids copying; a value receiver gets a copy
cards.x: Use pointer receivers to mutate or for large structs.

cards.q: How does a type satisfy an interface in Go?
cards.a: Implicitly — by having the required methods; no "implements" keyword
cards.x: Structural typing: if it has the methods, it satisfies the interface.

cards.q: What does Go use instead of class inheritance?
cards.a: Composition via struct embedding
cards.x: An embedded type's fields and methods are promoted.

cards.q: What is the empty interface `interface{}` (or `any`)?
cards.a: A type that any value satisfies
cards.x: Used for heterogeneous values; prefer concrete types or generics when possible.

cards.q: How do you recover the concrete type from an interface value?
cards.a: A type assertion: v, ok := i.(ConcreteType)
cards.x: Or a type switch for many cases.

cards.q: What is idiomatic about small interfaces in Go?
cards.a: Prefer small, focused interfaces (often one method), defined where they are used
cards.x: e.g. io.Reader, io.Writer.

cards.q: What is the zero value of an interface or pointer?
cards.a: nil
cards.x: Calling a method on a nil interface panics.

cards.q: What does embedding `io.Reader` in a struct do?
cards.a: Promotes its Read method, so the struct also satisfies io.Reader
cards.x: Composition builds bigger behaviours from small ones.

decks.title: Errors & Error Handling
decks.summary: Explicit errors, wrapping, and panic/recover.

cards.q: How does Go report most errors?
cards.a: By returning an error value as the last return, which the caller checks
cards.x: if err != nil { ... } is the core pattern.

cards.q: What is the error interface?
cards.a: An interface with a single method: Error() string
cards.x: Any type with that method is an error.

cards.q: How do you create a simple error?
cards.a: errors.New("message") or fmt.Errorf("...: %v", x)
cards.x: fmt.Errorf can format context into the message.

cards.q: What does `%w` in fmt.Errorf do?
cards.a: Wraps an underlying error so it can be unwrapped later
cards.x: e.g. fmt.Errorf("open: %w", err).

cards.q: What does `errors.Is(err, target)` check?
cards.a: Whether err, unwrapped through the chain, matches a specific target error
cards.x: The right way to compare against sentinel errors.

cards.q: What does `errors.As(err, &target)` do?
cards.a: Finds the first error in the chain matching target's type and assigns it
cards.x: Use it to inspect a specific error type.

cards.q: What is `panic` for?
cards.a: Truly exceptional, usually unrecoverable situations — not ordinary errors
cards.x: It unwinds the stack running deferred calls.

cards.q: What does `recover()` do, and where?
cards.a: Stops a panic's unwinding — but only when called inside a deferred function
cards.x: Used to turn a panic into a returned error at a boundary.

cards.q: Should you use panic/recover for ordinary errors?
cards.a: No — return error values; reserve panic for programmer bugs/impossible states
cards.x: Idiomatic Go handles errors explicitly.

cards.q: What does ignoring a returned error cost you?
cards.a: Silent failures — Go makes you handle errors explicitly for a reason
cards.x: At minimum log it; _ = f() is a deliberate (visible) ignore.

decks.title: Goroutines & Channels
decks.summary: Go's concurrency model and synchronisation.

cards.q: What is a goroutine?
cards.a: A lightweight thread managed by the Go runtime, started with the go keyword
cards.x: Thousands can run cheaply; the scheduler multiplexes them onto OS threads.
wrong: A coroutine you must resume manually

cards.q: How do you start a goroutine?
cards.a: go someFunction()
cards.x: It runs concurrently; main does not wait for it by default.

cards.q: What is a channel?
cards.a: A typed conduit to send and receive values between goroutines
cards.x: ch <- v sends; v := <-ch receives.

cards.q: Unbuffered vs buffered channel?
cards.a: An unbuffered channel blocks until sender and receiver meet; a buffered one holds up to N values
cards.x: make(chan int) vs make(chan int, N).

cards.q: What is Go's concurrency motto?
cards.a: "Do not communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating"
cards.x: Prefer channels to coordinate over shared, locked state.

cards.q: What does `select` do?
cards.a: Waits on multiple channel operations, proceeding with whichever is ready
cards.x: A default case makes it non-blocking.

cards.q: What is sync.WaitGroup for?
cards.a: Waiting for a set of goroutines to finish (Add, Done, Wait)
cards.x: Wait blocks until the counter returns to zero.

cards.q: What does sync.Mutex protect?
cards.a: A critical section — Lock/Unlock guard shared data from concurrent access
cards.x: Use defer mu.Unlock() to avoid forgetting.

cards.q: What causes a deadlock like "all goroutines are asleep"?
cards.a: Every goroutine is blocked waiting (e.g. receiving on a channel nobody sends to)
cards.x: The runtime detects and reports it.

cards.q: How do you find data races?
cards.a: Run with the race detector: go test -race / go run -race
cards.x: It flags unsynchronised concurrent access to shared memory.

puzzles.prompt: Order the sync.WaitGroup pattern to wait for N goroutines.
items: launch each goroutine with defer wg.Done()
wg.Wait() blocks until the counter hits zero
puzzles.x: Add the count up front, each goroutine signals Done when it finishes, and Wait blocks until all have.

decks.title: Standard Library & Testing
decks.summary: net/http, json, context, and the testing toolchain.

cards.q: Which package builds HTTP servers and clients?
cards.a: net/http
cards.x: http.HandleFunc + http.ListenAndServe stand up a server in a few lines.

cards.q: How do you encode a struct to JSON?
cards.a: json.Marshal(v) from encoding/json
cards.x: json.Unmarshal goes the other way.

cards.q: What controls which struct fields appear in JSON?
cards.a: Struct tags like `json:"name,omitempty"` and the field being exported
cards.x: Only uppercase (exported) fields are marshalled.

cards.q: What is context.Context for?
cards.a: Carrying deadlines, cancellation and request-scoped values across API boundaries
cards.x: ctx.Done() signals cancellation.

cards.q: Where do Go tests live and how are they named?
cards.a: In *_test.go files, functions func TestXxx(t *testing.T)
cards.x: Run them with go test.

cards.q: What is a table-driven test?
cards.a: A test that loops over a slice of input/expected cases, often with t.Run subtests
cards.x: The idiomatic Go testing style.
wrong: A test using a database table

cards.q: How do you write a benchmark?
cards.a: func BenchmarkXxx(b *testing.B) with a loop to b.N; run go test -bench
cards.x: The framework tunes b.N for a stable measurement.

cards.q: What does `go vet` do?
cards.a: Reports suspicious constructs the compiler allows (e.g. bad Printf verbs)
cards.x: A quick static check beyond compilation.

cards.q: How do you measure test coverage?
cards.a: go test -cover (or -coverprofile for a report)
cards.x: Shows the percentage of statements exercised.

cards.q: What makes Go a strong fit for cloud-native tooling?
cards.a: Static binaries, fast builds, built-in concurrency and a strong stdlib
cards.x: Docker, Kubernetes and Terraform are all written in Go.

tracks.title: Rust
tracks.tagline: Memory-safe systems programming without a garbage collector.

decks.title: Basics & Cargo
decks.summary: What Rust is, the toolchain, and hello world.

cards.q: What is Rust's headline promise?
cards.a: Memory safety without a garbage collector, enforced at compile time
cards.x: The ownership system prevents use-after-free and data races.

cards.q: What is Cargo?
cards.a: Rust's build tool and package manager
cards.x: cargo new / build / run / test drive most workflows.

cards.q: How do you create a new project?
cards.a: cargo new <name>
cards.x: It scaffolds Cargo.toml and src/main.rs.

cards.q: What does `cargo run` do?
cards.a: Compiles the project and runs the resulting binary
cards.x: cargo build just compiles; cargo check type-checks fast without a full build.

cards.q: How do you print a line in Rust?
cards.a: println!("text")
cards.x: println! is a macro — note the exclamation mark.

cards.q: Why is `println!` written with a `!`?
cards.a: It is a macro, not a function
cards.x: Macros expand at compile time and can take variable arguments/format strings.

cards.q: What file lists a project's dependencies?
cards.a: Cargo.toml
cards.x: Cargo.lock pins exact versions for reproducible builds.

cards.q: Where do community crates come from?
cards.a: crates.io, the Rust package registry
cards.x: Add one with cargo add <crate>.

cards.q: What does `cargo check` buy you over `cargo build`?
cards.a: Fast type/borrow checking without producing a binary
cards.x: Great for a tight edit-compile loop.

cards.q: How are statements terminated in Rust?
cards.a: With a semicolon; the last expression without one is the block's value
cards.x: Rust is expression-oriented.

puzzles.prompt: Order the Cargo workflow to run a new Rust program.
puzzles.x: Scaffold the project, write the code, fast-check it compiles/borrows, then build-and-run.

puzzles.prompt: How many values does the range 0..5 produce?
puzzles.x: 0..5 is end-exclusive: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — five values. Use 0..=5 for inclusive.

decks.title: Variables, Types & Mutability
decks.summary: Immutability by default, scalar types and shadowing.

cards.q: Are variables mutable by default in Rust?
cards.a: No — `let x = 5;` is immutable; add `mut` to allow changes
cards.x: Immutability by default prevents a class of bugs.

cards.q: How do you make a variable mutable?
cards.a: let mut x = 5;
cards.x: Then x can be reassigned.

cards.q: What is "shadowing"?
cards.a: Declaring a new variable with the same name using let, replacing the previous binding
cards.x: It can even change the type; different from mutation.

cards.q: What is the difference between a `let` binding and a `const`?
cards.a: const is always immutable, requires a type annotation, and is a compile-time constant
cards.x: let is a normal binding; consts use SCREAMING_CASE.

cards.q: What are Rust's signed/unsigned integer types like?
cards.a: i8..i128 and u8..u128, plus isize/usize
cards.x: The default integer type is i32.

cards.q: What type is a `char` in Rust?
cards.a: A 4-byte Unicode scalar value
cards.x: Not a single byte — that is u8.

cards.q: What is a tuple?
cards.a: A fixed-size, ordered group of values of possibly different types
cards.x: Access by position: t.0, t.1.

cards.q: What does Rust do if integer arithmetic overflows in a debug build?
cards.a: It panics
cards.x: Release builds wrap by default; use checked/wrapping/saturating methods to be explicit.

cards.q: Does Rust do implicit numeric conversions?
cards.a: No — you must convert explicitly, e.g. `x as f64` or .into()
cards.x: Mixing types is a compile error otherwise.

cards.q: What is the type of `let x = 5;`?
cards.a: Inferred as i32 from the literal and usage
cards.x: Rust infers most types but is statically, strongly typed.

decks.title: Control Flow & Functions
decks.summary: if/loop/match as expressions, and functions.

cards.q: Is `if` an expression in Rust?
cards.a: Yes — it returns a value: let n = if cond { 1 } else { 2 };
cards.x: Both branches must have the same type.

cards.q: What are Rust's three loop forms?
cards.a: loop (infinite), while, and for (over an iterator/range)
cards.x: for x in 0..5 iterates a range.

cards.q: How do you return a value from a `loop`?
cards.a: break value; — loop is an expression
cards.x: e.g. let r = loop { break 10; };

cards.q: What does `match` require of its arms?
cards.a: They must be exhaustive — every possible case handled
cards.x: Use _ as a catch-all.

cards.q: How does a function return a value?
cards.a: As the final expression without a semicolon, or with `return`
cards.x: The return type follows -> .

cards.q: What is the difference between an expression and a statement?
cards.a: An expression evaluates to a value; a statement does not. Adding ; turns an expression into a statement
cards.x: This is why the last line of a block has no semicolon.

cards.q: What is `if let` used for?
cards.a: Concise matching of a single pattern, ignoring the rest
cards.x: e.g. if let Some(x) = opt { ... }.

cards.q: What does the range `0..5` include?
cards.a: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 (end-exclusive)
cards.x: Use 0..=5 for an inclusive range.

cards.q: Can `match` bind parts of the matched value?
cards.a: Yes — patterns can destructure and bind, e.g. Some(x) binds x
cards.x: Powerful, exhaustive destructuring.

cards.q: What does a function with no `-> Type` return?
cards.a: The unit type () — effectively nothing
cards.x: Like void elsewhere.

decks.title: Ownership & Borrowing
decks.summary: Rust's central idea: who owns memory, and borrowing rules.

cards.q: What are the three ownership rules?
cards.a: Each value has one owner; there is one owner at a time; when the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped
cards.x: This frees memory deterministically, no GC.

cards.q: What happens on `let b = a;` when a is a String?
cards.a: Ownership MOVES to b; a is no longer usable
cards.x: Using a afterward is a compile error (no shallow copy of the heap data).

cards.q: Why do integers NOT move on assignment?
cards.a: They implement the Copy trait, so they are cheaply copied, not moved
cards.x: Copy types live entirely on the stack.

cards.q: What does borrowing (`&x`) give you?
cards.a: A reference you can use without taking ownership
cards.x: The owner keeps the value; the borrow must not outlive it.

cards.q: What is the borrowing rule about mutability?
cards.a: At any time: either ONE mutable reference OR any number of immutable references — not both
cards.x: This prevents data races at compile time.

cards.q: What is `&mut x`?
cards.a: An exclusive, mutable borrow — only one may exist at a time
cards.x: Lets you modify without owning.

cards.q: What is the borrow checker?
cards.a: The compiler pass that enforces the borrowing/lifetime rules
cards.x: It rejects dangling references and aliasing+mutation at compile time.

cards.q: What is a dangling reference, and does Rust allow one?
cards.a: A reference to freed/out-of-scope memory — Rust rejects it at compile time
cards.x: Lifetimes guarantee a reference never outlives its data.

cards.q: What is a lifetime?
cards.a: A compile-time region for which a reference is valid; sometimes annotated as 'a
cards.x: Most are inferred; annotations relate the lifetimes of inputs/outputs.

cards.q: How do you deep-copy heap data when you really need two owners?
cards.a: Call .clone() explicitly
cards.x: Clone is explicit so copies are never hidden/accidental.

puzzles.prompt: Order the borrowing rules from most to least permissive by count.
items: Never both at the same time
puzzles.x: Share freely OR mutate exclusively — the compiler forbids aliasing and mutation together, which is what prevents data races.

decks.title: Structs, Enums & Matching
decks.summary: Data modelling with structs, enums, Option and Result.

cards.q: How do you add methods to a struct?
cards.a: In an impl block: impl Point { fn dist(&self) -> f64 { ... } }
cards.x: Methods take self, &self, or &mut self.

cards.q: What does an enum model in Rust?
cards.a: A type that is one of several variants, each able to hold data
cards.x: Far richer than C enums.

cards.q: What does `Option<T>` replace?
cards.a: Null — it is Some(T) or None
cards.x: The compiler forces you to handle the None case.

cards.q: What does `Result<T, E>` represent?
cards.a: Success Ok(T) or failure Err(E)
cards.x: Rust's primary error-return type.

cards.q: Why is there no null in Rust?
cards.a: Absence is modelled by Option, so you cannot accidentally use a missing value
cards.x: The "billion-dollar mistake" is designed out.

cards.q: How do you handle every enum variant safely?
cards.a: match — it is exhaustive, so a missed variant is a compile error
cards.x: Add arms or a _ catch-all.

cards.q: What does `if let Some(x) = opt` do?
cards.a: Runs the block with x bound only when opt is Some
cards.x: A concise alternative to a full match.

cards.q: What do you get by deriving `#[derive(Debug)]`?
cards.a: Automatic debug formatting so you can print the struct with {:?}
cards.x: Common derives: Debug, Clone, PartialEq.

cards.q: What is a tuple struct?
cards.a: A struct with unnamed, positional fields, e.g. struct Pair(i32, i32)
cards.x: Access by .0, .1.

cards.q: Does a Rust struct have a null/default state automatically?
cards.a: No — fields must all be initialised (or derive/impl Default)
cards.x: No uninitialised memory.

decks.title: Collections & Error Handling
decks.summary: Vec, String, HashMap, Result and the ? operator.

cards.q: Which type is a growable array?
cards.a: Vec<T>
cards.x: push to add; indexing a bad position panics, .get returns Option.

cards.q: What is the difference between String and &str?
cards.a: String is an owned, growable UTF-8 string; &str is a borrowed string slice
cards.x: Function params usually take &str.

cards.q: Which type is a hash map?
cards.a: HashMap<K, V>
cards.x: Reading a key returns an Option.

cards.q: What does the `?` operator do?
cards.a: Returns early with the Err/None if a Result/Option is not Ok/Some, else unwraps it
cards.x: Clean error propagation without boilerplate.

cards.q: What does `.unwrap()` do on an Err/None?
cards.a: Panics (crashes) — it extracts the value only on Ok/Some
cards.x: Fine for prototypes; prefer ? or match in real code.

cards.q: How is `.expect("msg")` better than `.unwrap()`?
cards.a: It panics with YOUR message, making the failure easier to diagnose
cards.x: Still a panic — use deliberately.

cards.q: When should you call `panic!`?
cards.a: For unrecoverable bugs/invariants, not for expected, handleable errors
cards.x: Expected errors should be Result.

cards.q: How do you safely index a Vec without risking a panic?
cards.a: Use .get(i), which returns Option<&T>
cards.x: v[i] panics on out-of-range.

cards.q: What does iterating with `for x in &v` borrow?
cards.a: Each element by shared reference, leaving v usable afterward
cards.x: Use &mut v to mutate elements.

cards.q: What trait powers `for x in collection`?
cards.a: Iterator (via IntoIterator)
cards.x: Adaptors like map/filter/collect compose lazily.

decks.title: Traits & Generics
decks.summary: Shared behaviour and zero-cost abstraction.

cards.q: What is a trait?
cards.a: A set of method signatures a type can implement — Rust's interface
cards.x: impl Trait for Type provides the behaviour.

cards.q: How do generics plus trait bounds work?
cards.a: fn f<T: Trait>(x: T) accepts any T that implements Trait
cards.x: Monomorphised at compile time — a zero-cost abstraction.

cards.q: What does `#[derive(Clone, Debug)]` do?
cards.a: Auto-implements those traits for your type
cards.x: Saves writing boilerplate impls.

cards.q: Static vs dynamic dispatch in Rust?
cards.a: Generics (impl/<T>) dispatch statically; dyn Trait objects dispatch at runtime via a vtable
cards.x: Static is faster; dyn allows heterogeneous collections.

cards.q: What is `Box<dyn Trait>` for?
cards.a: A heap-allocated trait object for runtime polymorphism
cards.x: Lets a Vec hold different concrete types sharing a trait.
wrong: A smart pointer to a number

cards.q: Can a trait provide default method implementations?
cards.a: Yes — types can use or override them
cards.x: Reduces repetition across implementors.

cards.q: What does the `Default` trait give you?
cards.a: A ::default() that produces a sensible zero/empty value
cards.x: Derive it for simple structs.

cards.q: What do `PartialEq`/`Eq` enable?
cards.a: Comparing values with == and !=
cards.x: Derive them to compare structs field by field.

cards.q: What is "zero-cost abstraction"?
cards.a: High-level constructs (generics, iterators) compile to code as fast as hand-written equivalents
cards.x: You pay nothing at runtime for the abstraction.

cards.q: Where can trait bounds be written for readability?
cards.a: In a where clause: fn f<T>(x: T) where T: Trait + Clone
cards.x: Handy when bounds get long.

decks.title: Fearless Concurrency & Safety
decks.summary: Threads, shared state, and compile-time race freedom.

cards.q: What does "fearless concurrency" mean in Rust?
cards.a: The ownership/borrow rules reject data races at compile time
cards.x: Many concurrency bugs become compile errors.

cards.q: How do you spawn a thread?
cards.a: thread::spawn(|| { ... })
cards.x: Join the handle to wait for it.

cards.q: Why often use `move` with a thread closure?
cards.a: To transfer ownership of captured variables into the thread
cards.x: Ensures the data outlives the borrow across threads.

cards.q: How do you share mutable state across threads safely?
cards.a: Arc<Mutex<T>> — atomic reference counting plus a mutex
cards.x: Arc shares ownership; Mutex guards access.

cards.q: Why Arc instead of Rc across threads?
cards.a: Arc uses atomic reference counting and is thread-safe (Send + Sync); Rc is not
cards.x: Rc is for single-threaded sharing only.

cards.q: What do the Send and Sync marker traits mean?
cards.a: Send: ownership can move to another thread; Sync: a reference can be shared across threads
cards.x: The compiler uses them to enforce thread safety.

cards.q: What is Rust's channel type for message passing?
cards.a: std::sync::mpsc (multi-producer, single-consumer)
cards.x: tx.send(v) and rx.recv() move values between threads.

cards.q: When is the `unsafe` keyword needed?
cards.a: For operations the compiler cannot verify (raw pointers, FFI, some low-level tricks)
cards.x: It narrows, not disables, the checks — keep unsafe blocks small and audited.

cards.q: How does Rust free memory without a GC?
cards.a: Deterministically via ownership: a value is dropped (Drop) when its owner leaves scope
cards.x: Like RAII; predictable, no pauses.

cards.q: Why is Rust attractive for security-sensitive systems code?
cards.a: It eliminates whole bug classes (use-after-free, buffer overflow, data races) at compile time
cards.x: Memory-safety bugs are a huge share of CVEs in C/C++.

tracks.title: SQL
tracks.tagline: Query, shape and protect relational data.

decks.title: Relational Basics
decks.summary: Tables, rows, columns, and what SQL is.

cards.q: What does SQL stand for?
cards.a: Structured Query Language
cards.x: The standard language for relational databases.

cards.q: How is data organised in a relational database?
cards.a: In tables of rows (records) and columns (fields)
cards.x: Each row is one record; each column holds one attribute.

cards.q: Is SQL declarative or imperative?
cards.a: Declarative — you describe WHAT you want, not how to fetch it
cards.x: The query planner decides the execution strategy.

cards.q: Which statement reads data?
cards.a: SELECT
cards.x: INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE change data; SELECT reads it.

cards.q: What does `SELECT * FROM users;` return?
cards.a: Every column of every row in the users table
cards.x: * means "all columns" — avoid it in production queries.

cards.q: What clause names the table to read from?
cards.a: FROM
cards.x: SELECT <cols> FROM <table>.

cards.q: What is a primary key?
cards.a: A column (or set) that uniquely identifies each row
cards.x: It must be unique and not null.

cards.q: What does NULL represent?
cards.a: An unknown or missing value — not zero or empty string
cards.x: NULL is special: NULL = NULL is not true.

cards.q: What is an RDBMS?
cards.a: A Relational Database Management System (e.g. PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server)
cards.x: It stores, enforces and queries relational data.

cards.q: How do you end an SQL statement in most clients?
cards.a: With a semicolon ;
cards.x: It separates statements in a batch.

decks.title: Filtering & Sorting
decks.summary: WHERE, ORDER BY, DISTINCT and operators.

cards.q: Which clause filters rows?
cards.a: WHERE
cards.x: e.g. WHERE age >= 18.

cards.q: How do you sort results descending by a column?
cards.a: ORDER BY column DESC
cards.x: ASC (ascending) is the default.

cards.q: What does DISTINCT do?
cards.a: Removes duplicate rows from the result
cards.x: SELECT DISTINCT country ... lists each once.

cards.q: How do you limit the number of rows returned?
cards.a: LIMIT n (TOP n in SQL Server)
cards.x: Often combined with ORDER BY.

cards.q: Which operator does a pattern match on text?
cards.a: LIKE (with % and _ wildcards)
cards.x: e.g. WHERE name LIKE 'A%' finds names starting with A.

cards.q: What does `WHERE id IN (1, 2, 3)` mean?
cards.a: id equals any value in the list
cards.x: Shorthand for id = 1 OR id = 2 OR id = 3.
wrong: id is one of the columns

cards.q: How do you test for a missing value?
cards.a: WHERE col IS NULL (or IS NOT NULL)
cards.x: col = NULL does NOT work because NULL is unknown.

cards.q: What does `BETWEEN 10 AND 20` include?
cards.a: Values from 10 to 20 inclusive
cards.x: Both endpoints are included.

cards.q: How do you give a column a display name?
cards.a: An alias with AS: SELECT price AS cost
cards.x: Aliases also name computed columns.

cards.q: Which logical operators combine WHERE conditions?
cards.a: AND, OR, NOT
cards.x: Parentheses control precedence.

puzzles.prompt: Put the SQL clauses in the order you write them in a query.
puzzles.x: Written order: choose columns, pick the table, filter rows, group them, filter groups, sort, then limit. (The DB evaluates FROM/WHERE first, but this is how you type it.)

puzzles.prompt: A table has 5 rows; 2 of them have NULL in the "email" column. What does COUNT(email) return?
puzzles.x: COUNT(column) ignores NULLs, so it counts the 3 non-NULL emails. COUNT(*) would return 5.

decks.title: Aggregates & Grouping
decks.summary: COUNT/SUM/AVG, GROUP BY and HAVING.

cards.q: What does COUNT(*) return?
cards.a: The number of rows
cards.x: COUNT(col) ignores NULLs in that column.

cards.q: Which function totals a numeric column?
cards.a: SUM(col)
cards.x: AVG, MIN and MAX are the other common aggregates.

cards.q: What does GROUP BY do?
cards.a: Collapses rows into groups so aggregates are computed per group
cards.x: e.g. total sales per region.

cards.q: WHERE vs HAVING — what is the difference?
cards.a: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation
cards.x: Use HAVING to filter on an aggregate like COUNT(*) > 5.

cards.q: Can you use an aggregate like SUM() in a WHERE clause?
cards.a: No — aggregates belong in HAVING (or a subquery)
cards.x: WHERE is evaluated before groups exist.

cards.q: What does AVG(col) ignore?
cards.a: NULL values in that column
cards.x: Aggregates skip NULLs (except COUNT(*)).

cards.q: In a grouped query, what may the SELECT list contain?
cards.a: The grouping columns and aggregate functions
cards.x: Non-grouped bare columns are an error in strict SQL.

cards.q: How do you count distinct values of a column?
cards.a: COUNT(DISTINCT col)
cards.x: Counts unique non-NULL values.

cards.q: Group sales by region and keep only regions over 1000:
cards.a: GROUP BY region HAVING SUM(sales) > 1000
cards.x: Group first, then filter the groups with HAVING.

cards.q: What does MAX(date) give you?
cards.a: The latest (largest) date in the column
cards.x: MIN gives the earliest.

decks.title: Joins
decks.summary: Combining tables: inner, outer and self joins.

cards.q: What does an INNER JOIN return?
cards.a: Only rows with a match in BOTH tables
cards.x: Unmatched rows are excluded.

cards.q: What does a LEFT (OUTER) JOIN return?
cards.a: All rows from the left table, plus matches from the right (NULLs where none)
cards.x: Great for "find rows with no related record".

cards.q: How do you find customers with NO orders using a LEFT JOIN?
cards.a: LEFT JOIN orders ... WHERE orders.id IS NULL
cards.x: Unmatched right-side columns are NULL.

cards.q: What does a join condition (ON) specify?
cards.a: How rows in the two tables relate, e.g. ON a.id = b.a_id
cards.x: Usually a foreign-key relationship.

cards.q: What is a self join?
cards.a: A table joined to itself (with aliases) to relate rows within it
cards.x: e.g. employees to their managers.

cards.q: What does a CROSS JOIN produce?
cards.a: The Cartesian product — every row of A paired with every row of B
cards.x: Rarely what you want; usually a missing ON.

cards.q: A FULL OUTER JOIN returns…
cards.a: All rows from both tables, matched where possible, NULLs elsewhere
cards.x: Left + right + matches.

cards.q: Why qualify columns like `u.id` in a join?
cards.a: To disambiguate columns that exist in more than one table
cards.x: Table aliases keep queries readable.

cards.q: What enforces the relationship a join relies on?
cards.a: A foreign key referencing another table's primary key
cards.x: It keeps references valid (referential integrity).

cards.q: Can you join more than two tables in one query?
cards.a: Yes — chain multiple JOIN ... ON clauses
cards.x: Each join adds a relationship.

decks.title: Tables & Changing Data
decks.summary: CREATE/ALTER/DROP and INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE.

cards.q: Which statement creates a table?
cards.a: CREATE TABLE name (col type, ...)
cards.x: DDL (Data Definition Language).

cards.q: Which statement adds a new row?
cards.a: INSERT INTO table (cols) VALUES (...)
cards.x: DML (Data Manipulation Language).

cards.q: What does UPDATE ... without a WHERE do?
cards.a: Updates EVERY row — a classic, dangerous mistake
cards.x: Always scope UPDATE/DELETE with WHERE.

cards.q: Which statement removes rows but keeps the table?
cards.a: DELETE FROM table WHERE ...
cards.x: DROP TABLE removes the whole table.

cards.q: What does the NOT NULL constraint enforce?
cards.a: The column must always have a value
cards.x: Inserting NULL into it fails.

cards.q: What does a UNIQUE constraint guarantee?
cards.a: No two rows share the same value in that column
cards.x: Primary keys are unique + not null.

cards.q: What does DEFAULT do on a column?
cards.a: Supplies a value when an INSERT omits that column
cards.x: e.g. created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT now().

cards.q: Which statement changes a table's structure?
cards.a: ALTER TABLE (add/drop/modify columns or constraints)
cards.x: e.g. ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN age INT.

cards.q: Difference between DELETE and TRUNCATE?
cards.a: DELETE removes selected rows and is logged/rollback-able; TRUNCATE quickly empties the whole table
cards.x: TRUNCATE is faster but less granular.

cards.q: What does a CHECK constraint do?
cards.a: Rejects rows that violate a boolean condition
cards.x: e.g. CHECK (price >= 0).

decks.title: Subqueries & CTEs
decks.summary: Nested queries, EXISTS, set operators and WITH.

cards.q: What is a subquery?
cards.a: A query nested inside another query
cards.x: It can feed WHERE, FROM or SELECT.

cards.q: What does `WHERE x IN (SELECT ...)` do?
cards.a: Keeps rows whose x matches any value returned by the inner query
cards.x: A common subquery pattern.

cards.q: What does EXISTS (subquery) test?
cards.a: Whether the subquery returns at least one row
cards.x: Often faster and clearer than IN for correlated checks.

cards.q: What is a correlated subquery?
cards.a: A subquery that references a column from the outer query, re-evaluated per outer row
cards.x: Powerful but can be slow.

cards.q: What does a CTE (`WITH name AS (...)`) give you?
cards.a: A named, readable temporary result you can reference in the main query
cards.x: Great for breaking up complex queries; supports recursion.

cards.q: What does UNION do?
cards.a: Combines the rows of two queries and removes duplicates
cards.x: UNION ALL keeps duplicates and is faster.

cards.q: What does INTERSECT return?
cards.a: Rows present in BOTH query results
cards.x: The common set.

cards.q: What does EXCEPT (MINUS) return?
cards.a: Rows in the first query that are NOT in the second
cards.x: Set difference.

cards.q: Requirement for UNION/INTERSECT/EXCEPT?
cards.a: The queries must have the same number and compatible types of columns
cards.x: Column names come from the first query.

cards.q: A scalar subquery returns…
cards.a: Exactly one row and one column (a single value)
cards.x: Usable anywhere a value is expected.

decks.title: Indexes & Normalization
decks.summary: Performance and well-designed schemas.

cards.q: What is an index, in one line?
cards.a: A data structure (usually a B-tree) that speeds up lookups on indexed columns
cards.x: It is like a book index — find rows without scanning everything.

cards.q: What is the trade-off of adding indexes?
cards.a: Faster reads, but slower writes and more storage
cards.x: Every INSERT/UPDATE must maintain the index.

cards.q: What is a full table scan, and why avoid it?
cards.a: Reading every row to answer a query — slow on big tables
cards.x: A good index lets the DB jump to matching rows.

cards.q: What does First Normal Form (1NF) require?
cards.a: Atomic column values — no repeating groups or arrays in a cell
cards.x: One value per column per row.

cards.q: What does Third Normal Form (3NF) remove?
cards.a: Transitive dependencies — non-key columns depending on other non-key columns
cards.x: Each non-key attribute depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.

cards.q: Why normalize a schema?
cards.a: To reduce redundancy and update anomalies
cards.x: One fact stored in one place.

cards.q: When might you deliberately denormalize?
cards.a: For read performance — trading some redundancy for fewer joins
cards.x: Common in reporting/analytics.

cards.q: What does a composite index on (a, b) help with?
cards.a: Queries filtering on a, or on a AND b (left-most prefix)
cards.x: It does not efficiently serve a query on b alone.

cards.q: What does EXPLAIN (or EXPLAIN ANALYZE) show?
cards.a: The query planner's execution plan — scans, joins, index usage and cost
cards.x: The first tool for diagnosing slow queries.

cards.q: Primary key vs foreign key?
cards.a: A primary key uniquely identifies rows in its table; a foreign key references a primary key in another
cards.x: Foreign keys enforce referential integrity.
wrong: A foreign key is unique in its table

resources.title: Use The Index, Luke! (SQL indexing & performance)

decks.title: Transactions, Views & Security
decks.summary: ACID, views, window functions, and injection defence.

cards.q: What is a transaction?
cards.a: A group of statements that succeed or fail as a single unit
cards.x: BEGIN ... COMMIT; or ROLLBACK to undo.

cards.q: What does ACID stand for?
cards.a: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
cards.x: The guarantees a reliable transaction provides.

cards.q: What does ROLLBACK do?
cards.a: Undoes all changes made in the current (uncommitted) transaction
cards.x: COMMIT makes them permanent.

cards.q: What is a view?
cards.a: A saved SELECT you can query like a table (usually not storing data)
cards.x: Simplifies complex queries and can restrict exposed columns.

cards.q: What do window functions (e.g. ROW_NUMBER() OVER ...) do?
cards.a: Compute values across a set of rows related to the current row, WITHOUT collapsing them
cards.x: Unlike GROUP BY, rows are preserved.

cards.q: What is SQL injection?
cards.a: Injecting malicious SQL through unsanitised input to run unintended queries
cards.x: A top web vulnerability (OWASP).

cards.q: What is the primary defence against SQL injection?
cards.a: Parameterised queries / prepared statements (never string-concatenate input)
cards.x: The driver sends data separately from the SQL.

cards.q: Why grant databases least-privilege accounts?
cards.a: So a compromised app can only do what it needs, limiting blast radius
cards.x: e.g. a read-only reporting user.

cards.q: What does transaction isolation prevent?
cards.a: Concurrent transactions from interfering (dirty/non-repeatable/phantom reads)
cards.x: Higher isolation = fewer anomalies, less concurrency.

cards.q: Why avoid storing passwords in plain text in a table?
cards.a: A breach exposes them directly; store a salted hash instead
cards.x: Use bcrypt/argon2, never reversible encoding.

resources.title: Use The Index, Luke! (SQL indexing & performance)

puzzles.prompt: Order a safe money-transfer transaction.
puzzles.x: Both updates happen atomically between BEGIN and COMMIT; if either fails you ROLLBACK, so money is never lost or created.

tracks.title: Docker
tracks.tagline: Build, ship and run applications in portable containers.

decks.title: Containers & Docker Basics
decks.summary: What containers are and how they differ from VMs.

cards.q: What is a container?
cards.a: A lightweight, isolated process bundling an app with its dependencies, sharing the host kernel
cards.x: Portable and consistent across machines.

cards.q: Container vs virtual machine?
cards.a: Containers share the host OS kernel (lightweight, fast); VMs run a full guest OS (heavier)
cards.x: Containers start in milliseconds and use less memory.

cards.q: What is a Docker image?
cards.a: A read-only template (layers) used to create containers
cards.x: A container is a running instance of an image.

cards.q: What is the relationship between an image and a container?
cards.a: A container is a runnable instance of an image
cards.x: Many containers can run from one image.

cards.q: What does `docker run <image>` do?
cards.a: Creates and starts a container from the image
cards.x: It pulls the image first if it is not present locally.

cards.q: Which command lists running containers?
cards.a: docker ps
cards.x: docker ps -a also shows stopped ones.

cards.q: Which command lists local images?
cards.a: docker images (or docker image ls)
cards.x: Shows repository, tag, id and size.

cards.q: Why are containers valuable?
cards.a: Consistency ("works on my machine" solved), isolation and portability
cards.x: Same artifact runs in dev, CI and prod.
wrong: They remove the need for code

cards.q: Do containers virtualise hardware?
cards.a: No — they virtualise the OS (process/namespace isolation), not hardware
cards.x: That is why they are so lightweight.

cards.q: What is the Docker Engine?
cards.a: The daemon (dockerd) + CLI that builds and runs containers
cards.x: The CLI talks to the daemon over an API.

decks.title: Images & the Dockerfile
decks.summary: Building images with a Dockerfile and layers.

cards.q: What is a Dockerfile?
cards.a: A text recipe of instructions to build an image
cards.x: Each instruction adds a layer.

cards.q: What does the FROM instruction set?
cards.a: The base image to build upon
cards.x: It is (almost always) the first instruction.

cards.q: What does `docker build -t name:tag .` do?
cards.a: Builds an image from the Dockerfile in the current directory and tags it
cards.x: The . is the build context sent to the daemon.

cards.q: COPY vs RUN in a Dockerfile?
cards.a: COPY adds files from the build context into the image; RUN executes a command during build
cards.x: RUN creates a new layer with its result.

cards.q: CMD vs ENTRYPOINT?
cards.a: ENTRYPOINT sets the executable; CMD sets default arguments (or the default command)
cards.x: Together they define what runs when the container starts.

cards.q: What does EXPOSE document?
cards.a: Which port the container listens on (metadata; it does not publish it)
cards.x: You still need -p to publish at run time.

cards.q: Why does Docker cache build layers?
cards.a: To skip rebuilding unchanged steps, speeding up builds
cards.x: Order instructions so frequently-changing ones come last.

cards.q: Why put `COPY package.json` + install BEFORE copying all source?
cards.a: So dependency install is cached and only re-runs when deps change
cards.x: A key layer-caching optimisation.

cards.q: What does a .dockerignore file do?
cards.a: Excludes files from the build context (e.g. .git, node_modules)
cards.x: Smaller context = faster builds and smaller images.

cards.q: What does WORKDIR do?
cards.a: Sets the working directory for subsequent instructions and the container
cards.x: Creates it if needed.

puzzles.prompt: Order a cache-friendly Dockerfile for a Node app.
puzzles.x: Copy and install dependencies BEFORE copying all source, so the install layer is cached and only re-runs when package.json changes.

decks.title: Running Containers
decks.summary: run flags, ports, logs, exec and lifecycle.

cards.q: What does the `-d` flag do on docker run?
cards.a: Runs the container detached (in the background)
cards.x: Without it, the container runs in the foreground.

cards.q: What does `-p 8080:80` do?
cards.a: Publishes host port 8080 to container port 80
cards.x: Format is host:container.

cards.q: What does `--rm` do?
cards.a: Automatically removes the container when it exits
cards.x: Keeps your system tidy for throwaway runs.

cards.q: How do you pass an environment variable?
cards.a: -e KEY=value
cards.x: Or --env-file for many.

cards.q: How do you run a shell inside a RUNNING container?
cards.a: docker exec -it <container> sh (or bash)
cards.x: exec runs a new process in the existing container.

cards.q: How do you view a container's logs?
cards.a: docker logs <container>
cards.x: Add -f to follow them live.

cards.q: How do you stop and remove a container?
cards.a: docker stop <id> then docker rm <id>
cards.x: docker rm -f stops and removes in one step.

cards.q: What does `--name web` give you?
cards.a: A friendly name so you can reference the container without its id
cards.x: Names must be unique.

cards.q: What happens to data written inside a container when it is removed?
cards.a: It is lost — the writable layer is deleted; use a volume to persist
cards.x: Containers are ephemeral by design.
wrong: It goes to the host home dir

cards.q: What does `docker run -it ubuntu bash` give you?
cards.a: An interactive terminal (-i -t) running bash in an Ubuntu container
cards.x: Great for exploring an image.

decks.title: Volumes & Networking
decks.summary: Persisting data and connecting containers.

cards.q: What is a Docker volume?
cards.a: Docker-managed persistent storage that lives beyond a container's lifetime
cards.x: The right way to persist data (databases, uploads).

cards.q: Volume vs bind mount?
cards.a: A volume is managed by Docker; a bind mount maps a specific host path into the container
cards.x: Bind mounts are great for live-editing source in dev.
wrong: Bind mounts are managed by Docker

cards.q: How do you mount a named volume?
cards.a: -v myvol:/data (or --mount)
cards.x: Docker creates myvol if it does not exist.

cards.q: What is the default Docker network type?
cards.a: bridge — containers get a private subnet and can talk by name
cards.x: host shares the host network; none disables networking.

cards.q: On a user-defined bridge network, how do containers reach each other?
cards.a: By container name via built-in DNS
cards.x: e.g. a web container connects to "db".

cards.q: What does `--network host` do?
cards.a: Shares the host's network stack (no port mapping needed)
cards.x: Fast, but less isolation; Linux-only behaviour.

cards.q: Why prefer a volume over writing into the container layer?
cards.a: Data survives container removal and can be shared/backed up
cards.x: The container layer is ephemeral.

cards.q: How do you share one volume between two containers?
cards.a: Mount the same named volume in both with -v
cards.x: They then read/write the same storage.

cards.q: What does `--network none` do?
cards.a: Gives the container no network access (isolation)
cards.x: Useful for untrusted or offline workloads.

cards.q: Where should application config/secrets come from, not the image?
cards.a: Environment variables, mounted files, or a secrets manager at runtime
cards.x: Never bake secrets into image layers.

decks.title: Docker Compose
decks.summary: Defining multi-container apps declaratively.

cards.q: What problem does Docker Compose solve?
cards.a: Defining and running multi-container apps from one YAML file
cards.x: One command brings up the whole stack.

cards.q: What file does Compose use?
cards.a: compose.yaml (or docker-compose.yml)
cards.x: It declares services, networks and volumes.

cards.q: What is a "service" in Compose?
cards.a: A container definition (image/build, ports, env, volumes) that Compose runs
cards.x: Each service can be scaled to multiple containers.

cards.q: What does `docker compose up` do?
cards.a: Creates and starts all services defined in the compose file
cards.x: Add -d to run detached.

cards.q: What does `docker compose down` do?
cards.a: Stops and removes the containers, networks (and optionally volumes)
cards.x: Clean teardown of the stack.

cards.q: How do you express that a web service needs the db first?
cards.a: depends_on: [db]
cards.x: Note: it waits for start, not readiness — add a healthcheck for that.

cards.q: How do Compose services reach each other?
cards.a: By service name over the Compose-created network
cards.x: e.g. the app connects to "db:5432".

cards.q: How do you rebuild images before starting?
cards.a: docker compose up --build
cards.x: Rebuilds services that have a build context.

cards.q: Where do you set per-service environment variables in Compose?
cards.a: The environment: key (or env_file:) under the service
cards.x: Keeps config out of the image.

cards.q: Can Compose scale a service to N containers?
cards.a: Yes — docker compose up --scale web=3
cards.x: A load balancer/ingress then spreads traffic.

decks.title: Registries & Image Lifecycle
decks.summary: Tagging, pushing, pulling and distributing images.

cards.q: What is a container registry?
cards.a: A service that stores and distributes images (e.g. Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR)
cards.x: push to upload, pull to download.

cards.q: What does `docker push repo:tag` do?
cards.a: Uploads the tagged image to its registry
cards.x: You must be logged in (docker login).

cards.q: What does an image tag like `app:1.2.0` identify?
cards.a: A specific named version of a repository
cards.x: latest is just a default tag, not "newest" magically.

cards.q: Is the `latest` tag always the newest image?
cards.a: No — it is only a conventional default tag you must push to keep current
cards.x: Pin explicit versions in production.

cards.q: What is an image digest (sha256:...)?
cards.a: A content-addressed, immutable identifier for an exact image
cards.x: Pin by digest for reproducible, tamper-evident deploys.

cards.q: How do you authenticate to a registry?
cards.a: docker login <registry>
cards.x: Credentials are stored for push/pull.

cards.q: Why run your own/private registry?
cards.a: To keep private images internal and control distribution
cards.x: Common in enterprises and CI.

cards.q: What does `docker pull` do?
cards.a: Downloads an image (and its layers) from a registry to local storage
cards.x: run pulls automatically if the image is missing.

cards.q: How do you re-tag an existing image for a registry?
cards.a: docker tag local:tag registry/repo:tag
cards.x: Then push it.

cards.q: Why scan images from registries before running them?
cards.a: Base images and dependencies can carry known vulnerabilities (CVEs)
cards.x: Scan with Trivy/Docker Scout in CI.

decks.title: Optimization & Security
decks.summary: Small, fast, least-privilege images.

cards.q: What is a multi-stage build?
cards.a: Using multiple FROM stages so build tools stay out of the final image
cards.x: Copy only the built artifact into a slim runtime stage.

cards.q: Why use a small base like alpine or distroless?
cards.a: Smaller attack surface, faster pulls and less to patch
cards.x: Fewer packages = fewer CVEs.

cards.q: Why run the container process as a non-root USER?
cards.a: To limit damage if the app is compromised (least privilege)
cards.x: Add a USER instruction; avoid running as root.

cards.q: Where should secrets NOT go?
cards.a: In image layers or the Dockerfile — they persist and leak via the image
cards.x: Inject them at runtime (env, mounts, secrets manager).

cards.q: Why order Dockerfile layers from least- to most-frequently-changing?
cards.a: To maximise build-cache reuse and minimise rebuild time
cards.x: Deps before source is the classic example.

cards.q: What does a container image vulnerability scanner (Trivy/Scout) do?
cards.a: Reports known CVEs in the base image and dependencies
cards.x: Gate builds on it in CI.

cards.q: Why combine RUN commands with && in one layer?
cards.a: Fewer layers and the ability to clean up caches in the same layer
cards.x: e.g. apt-get update && install && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists.

cards.q: What does running a container read-only (--read-only) help with?
cards.a: Prevents the app from writing to the container filesystem (tamper resistance)
cards.x: Mount a writable volume for the few paths that need it.

cards.q: What is "image signing" (e.g. cosign) for?
cards.a: Proving an image is authentic and untampered (supply-chain security)
cards.x: Verify signatures before deploying.

cards.q: Why avoid baking build-time credentials into layers?
cards.a: They remain recoverable in the image history even if a later layer deletes them
cards.x: Use build secrets / multi-stage instead.
wrong: They are fine if deleted later

puzzles.prompt: Order a multi-stage build that ships only the artifact.
puzzles.x: The heavy build tools stay in the build stage; the final image copies only the compiled output into a slim runtime — smaller and more secure.

decks.title: Operations & Troubleshooting
decks.summary: Health, limits, logs and cleanup.

cards.q: What does a HEALTHCHECK instruction do?
cards.a: Defines a command Docker runs to report whether the container is healthy
cards.x: Orchestrators use it to restart or route around unhealthy containers.

cards.q: How do you limit a container's memory and CPU?
cards.a: --memory and --cpus flags on docker run
cards.x: Prevents one container from starving the host.

cards.q: What does a restart policy like `--restart unless-stopped` do?
cards.a: Restarts the container automatically unless you explicitly stopped it
cards.x: Good default for long-running services.

cards.q: Which command shows live resource usage per container?
cards.a: docker stats
cards.x: CPU, memory, network and I/O in real time.

cards.q: What does `docker inspect <id>` give you?
cards.a: Detailed JSON config/state (mounts, networks, env, etc.)
cards.x: The go-to for "why is this configured like that?".

cards.q: First step to debug a crashing container?
cards.a: Read its logs: docker logs <id>
cards.x: Then exec in or inspect if it stays up.

cards.q: What does `docker system prune` do?
cards.a: Removes stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images (and more with -a)
cards.x: Reclaims disk; be careful with -a --volumes.

cards.q: Why set resource limits in production?
cards.a: To bound the blast radius of a leak or spike and keep the host stable
cards.x: Unbounded containers can OOM the host.

cards.q: What does `docker exec` let you do for debugging?
cards.a: Run commands (e.g. a shell) inside a running container to inspect it
cards.x: Check files, processes and connectivity from inside.

cards.q: Why are small, single-purpose containers preferred?
cards.a: Easier to scale, update, reason about and secure (one process per container)
cards.x: The "one concern per container" principle.
wrong: To run many apps in one

tracks.title: Kubernetes
tracks.tagline: Orchestrate containers at scale: self-healing, declarative infrastructure.

decks.title: Kubernetes Basics
decks.summary: What Kubernetes is and how a cluster is shaped.

cards.q: What is Kubernetes (K8s)?
cards.a: A platform that orchestrates containers across a cluster of machines
cards.x: It schedules, scales, heals and networks containerised workloads.

cards.q: What are the two halves of a cluster?
cards.a: The control plane (brains) and worker nodes (run the workloads)
cards.x: The control plane decides; nodes execute.

cards.q: What runs on the control plane?
cards.a: The API server, scheduler, controller-manager and etcd
cards.x: They make and store cluster decisions.

cards.q: What is etcd?
cards.a: The cluster's key-value store holding all state/configuration
cards.x: The single source of truth; back it up.

cards.q: What is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes?
cards.a: A Pod
cards.x: A pod wraps one (or a few tightly-coupled) containers.

cards.q: What is kubectl?
cards.a: The CLI that talks to the cluster's API server
cards.x: kubectl apply/get/describe/logs drive everything.

cards.q: What is the kubelet?
cards.a: The agent on each node that runs the pods the control plane assigns
cards.x: It talks to the container runtime.

cards.q: Why use Kubernetes over running containers by hand?
cards.a: Self-healing, declarative scaling, rollouts and service discovery across many hosts
cards.x: It keeps the desired state true automatically.

cards.q: Is Kubernetes declarative or imperative by design?
cards.a: Declarative — you describe desired state and controllers reconcile reality to it
cards.x: kubectl apply submits the desired state.

cards.q: What does "desired state reconciliation" mean?
cards.a: Controllers continuously compare actual state to your declared spec and fix drift
cards.x: e.g. a crashed pod is recreated to match the replica count.

decks.title: Pods & Workloads
decks.summary: Pods, ReplicaSets and Deployments.

cards.q: What does a Pod group together?
cards.a: One or more containers that share network and storage, scheduled together
cards.x: They share an IP and can talk over localhost.

cards.q: Should you create bare Pods directly in production?
cards.a: No — use a controller (Deployment) so they are recreated and managed
cards.x: A bare pod is not rescheduled if its node dies.

cards.q: What does a Deployment manage?
cards.a: A desired number of identical Pods, with rolling updates and rollbacks
cards.x: The standard way to run stateless apps.

cards.q: What does a ReplicaSet ensure?
cards.a: That a specified number of pod replicas are running at all times
cards.x: Deployments create and manage ReplicaSets for you.

cards.q: How do you connect a Deployment to its Pods?
cards.a: Labels and a selector that matches them
cards.x: Selectors are how most K8s objects find each other.

cards.q: What does `kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml` do?
cards.a: Creates or updates the resources to match the manifest (declarative)
cards.x: Re-applying converges to the declared state.

cards.q: How do you scale a Deployment to 5 replicas?
cards.a: kubectl scale deploy/name --replicas=5 (or edit the manifest)
cards.x: The ReplicaSet adds/removes pods to match.

cards.q: What does `kubectl get pods` show?
cards.a: The pods in the current namespace with status and restarts
cards.x: Add -o wide for node/IP; -A for all namespaces.

cards.q: What does `kubectl describe pod <name>` help with?
cards.a: Detailed state and recent events — great for debugging why a pod is unhealthy
cards.x: Shows scheduling, image pulls, probe failures.

cards.q: If a pod's node dies, what does a Deployment do?
cards.a: Reschedules replacement pods onto healthy nodes (self-healing)
cards.x: The controller restores the desired replica count.

puzzles.prompt: Order the Kubernetes workload abstractions from smallest to largest.
puzzles.x: A Deployment manages a ReplicaSet, which keeps N Pods running, and each Pod runs one or more Containers.

decks.title: Manifests, Namespaces & Config
decks.summary: YAML objects, namespaces, ConfigMaps and Secrets.

cards.q: What four top-level fields does a K8s manifest have?
cards.a: apiVersion, kind, metadata, spec
cards.x: kind + apiVersion say what it is; spec is the desired state.
