cards.q: What are namespaces for?
cards.a: Logically partitioning a cluster (e.g. dev, staging, team-a)
cards.x: They scope names, quotas and access.

cards.q: What is a ConfigMap?
cards.a: An object holding non-secret configuration as key-value data
cards.x: Inject it as env vars or mounted files.

cards.q: What is a Secret?
cards.a: An object for sensitive data (base64-encoded, access-controlled)
cards.x: Note: base64 is encoding, not encryption — enable encryption at rest + RBAC.

cards.q: Is a K8s Secret encrypted by default?
cards.a: No — it is base64-encoded in etcd; you must enable encryption at rest
cards.x: Protect it with RBAC and etcd encryption.
wrong: It is plaintext in the pod image

cards.q: How do you apply a directory of manifests?
cards.a: kubectl apply -f ./dir/
cards.x: Applies every YAML in the folder.

cards.q: How do you inject a ConfigMap value as an env var?
cards.a: Reference it via valueFrom.configMapKeyRef in the container spec
cards.x: Or mount the whole ConfigMap as files.

cards.q: Why keep config out of the container image?
cards.a: So the same image runs in every environment with env-specific config injected
cards.x: Config changes should not require a rebuild.

cards.q: What does `metadata.labels` enable?
cards.a: Selecting and grouping objects (by Services, Deployments, queries)
cards.x: Labels are the glue of Kubernetes.

cards.q: What does a resource's `spec` describe?
cards.a: The desired state the controllers should make real
cards.x: status (read-only) reports the actual state.

decks.title: Services & Networking
decks.summary: Stable endpoints, DNS and Ingress.

cards.q: Why do Pods need a Service in front of them?
cards.a: Pod IPs are ephemeral; a Service gives a stable virtual IP/name and load-balances to the pods
cards.x: Clients target the Service, not individual pods.

cards.q: What does a ClusterIP Service provide?
cards.a: A stable internal-only virtual IP reachable within the cluster
cards.x: The default Service type.

cards.q: What does a NodePort Service do?
cards.a: Exposes the Service on a static port on every node's IP
cards.x: A simple way to reach a Service from outside.

cards.q: What does a LoadBalancer Service do?
cards.a: Provisions an external load balancer (via the cloud provider) for the Service
cards.x: The common way to expose prod traffic on a managed cluster.

cards.q: How does a Service find its Pods?
cards.a: Via a label selector matching the pods' labels
cards.x: Matching pods become the Service's endpoints.

cards.q: How do pods resolve a Service by name?
cards.a: Cluster DNS: <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local (or just <service> in-namespace)
cards.x: CoreDNS provides service discovery.

cards.q: What is an Ingress for?
cards.a: HTTP(S) routing from outside into Services by host/path, with one entry point
cards.x: An Ingress controller implements the rules.

cards.q: What implements Ingress rules?
cards.a: An Ingress controller (e.g. nginx, Traefik) running in the cluster
cards.x: Without a controller, Ingress objects do nothing.

cards.q: What are a Service's "endpoints"?
cards.a: The actual pod IPs/ports the Service currently routes to
cards.x: They update as pods come and go.

cards.q: Can two namespaces have a Service with the same name?
cards.a: Yes — names are scoped per namespace
cards.x: Fully-qualified DNS disambiguates them.

puzzles.prompt: Order the path external HTTP traffic takes to reach a pod.
puzzles.x: Ingress routes by host/path to a Service, the Service load-balances to a healthy Pod by label selector.

decks.title: Storage & Persistence
decks.summary: Volumes, PersistentVolumes and claims.

cards.q: Why is a pod's container filesystem not enough for data?
cards.a: It is ephemeral — lost when the pod is rescheduled or restarted
cards.x: Persistent data needs a volume.

cards.q: What is a PersistentVolume (PV)?
cards.a: A piece of cluster storage provisioned for use by pods
cards.x: An admin- or dynamically-provisioned resource.

cards.q: What is a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)?
cards.a: A pod's request for storage of a certain size/mode, bound to a PV
cards.x: Pods mount the PVC, not the PV directly.

cards.q: What does a StorageClass enable?
cards.a: Dynamic provisioning of PVs on demand when a PVC is created
cards.x: Defines the type/quality of storage (e.g. SSD).

cards.q: How do you give a pod persistent storage?
cards.a: Create a PVC and mount it as a volume in the pod spec
cards.x: The data survives pod restarts/rescheduling.

cards.q: How do you mount a Secret into a pod?
cards.a: As a volume or env var referencing the Secret
cards.x: Mounted secrets update when the Secret changes.

cards.q: What does ReadWriteOnce (access mode) mean?
cards.a: The volume can be mounted read-write by a single node
cards.x: ReadWriteMany allows many nodes (if the backend supports it).

cards.q: Stateless app vs stateful app on K8s?
cards.a: Stateless pods are interchangeable (Deployment); stateful apps need stable identity/storage (StatefulSet)
cards.x: Databases usually need a StatefulSet + PVCs.

cards.q: Where does data from an emptyDir volume go when the pod is deleted?
cards.a: It is deleted — emptyDir lives only for the pod's lifetime
cards.x: Use a PVC for persistence.

cards.q: Why not store database files in the image?
cards.a: Images are read-only and shared; data must be writable and durable per instance
cards.x: Mount a PVC instead.

decks.title: Rollouts, Scaling & Probes
decks.summary: Rolling updates, autoscaling and health checks.

cards.q: What does a rolling update do?
cards.a: Replaces old pods with new ones gradually, keeping the app available
cards.x: The default Deployment strategy.
wrong: Stops all pods, then starts new

cards.q: How do you undo a bad rollout?
cards.a: kubectl rollout undo deploy/name
cards.x: Deployments keep revision history.

cards.q: What does a liveness probe decide?
cards.a: Whether to RESTART a container that has become unhealthy
cards.x: A failing liveness probe triggers a restart.

cards.q: What does a readiness probe decide?
cards.a: Whether a pod should RECEIVE traffic yet
cards.x: A not-ready pod is removed from Service endpoints.

cards.q: What is a startup probe for?
cards.a: Giving slow-starting containers time before liveness checks begin
cards.x: Prevents premature restarts during boot.

cards.q: What does the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) do?
cards.a: Automatically scales replica count based on metrics (e.g. CPU)
cards.x: It needs metrics (metrics-server) to work.

cards.q: Why set resource requests and limits?
cards.a: Requests guide scheduling; limits cap usage so one pod cannot starve the node
cards.x: Essential for stable, fair clusters.

cards.q: What happens if a container exceeds its memory limit?
cards.a: It is OOM-killed (terminated) and typically restarted
cards.x: CPU over-limit is throttled, not killed.

cards.q: What does `kubectl rollout status deploy/name` show?
cards.a: Whether the rollout has finished and all new pods are ready
cards.x: Use it to gate CD pipelines.

cards.q: Why run multiple replicas of a stateless service?
cards.a: Availability (survive pod/node failure) and horizontal scaling
cards.x: The Service load-balances across them.

decks.title: Workload Types & Operability
decks.summary: StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs and debugging.

cards.q: When do you use a StatefulSet instead of a Deployment?
cards.a: For apps needing stable identity and per-pod storage (databases, queues)
cards.x: Pods get stable names (app-0, app-1) and their own PVCs.

cards.q: What does a DaemonSet do?
cards.a: Runs one copy of a pod on every (or selected) node
cards.x: Used for node agents: log collectors, monitoring, CNI.

cards.q: What is a Job in Kubernetes?
cards.a: A workload that runs pods to completion (batch work), then stops
cards.x: A CronJob runs Jobs on a schedule.

cards.q: First command to debug a failing pod?
cards.a: kubectl logs <pod> (and kubectl describe pod for events)
cards.x: Logs show app errors; describe shows scheduling/probe issues.

cards.q: How do you get a shell in a running pod?
cards.a: kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh
cards.x: Inspect files, env and connectivity from inside.

cards.q: What do `kubectl cordon` and `drain` do?
cards.a: Cordon marks a node unschedulable; drain evicts its pods — for maintenance
cards.x: Pods reschedule elsewhere.

cards.q: What does `kubectl get events` help diagnose?
cards.a: Recent cluster events: failed scheduling, image pull errors, evictions
cards.x: A quick cluster-health signal.

cards.q: What is CrashLoopBackOff?
cards.a: A pod that keeps crashing and restarting, with increasing back-off delay
cards.x: Check logs/describe to find why it exits.

cards.q: Why label and organise resources well?
cards.a: Selection, grouping, policy and cost attribution all key off labels
cards.x: Consistent labels make a cluster operable.

cards.q: What is a controller's core loop?
cards.a: Observe actual state → compare to desired spec → act to reconcile — forever
cards.x: This is how K8s self-heals.

decks.title: Cluster Security
decks.summary: RBAC, network policy, and pod hardening.

cards.q: What does RBAC control in Kubernetes?
cards.a: Who (users/service accounts) can do what to which resources
cards.x: Roles/ClusterRoles grant verbs; bindings assign them.

cards.q: What is a ServiceAccount?
cards.a: An identity that pods use to authenticate to the API server
cards.x: Scope its permissions tightly with RBAC.

cards.q: Why avoid the default ServiceAccount with broad rights?
cards.a: Least privilege — a compromised pod should not be able to control the cluster
cards.x: Give each workload a minimal, dedicated SA.

cards.q: What does a NetworkPolicy do?
cards.a: Restricts which pods/namespaces can talk to each other (and egress)
cards.x: Default is allow-all until a policy selects a pod.

cards.q: Why run containers as non-root in Kubernetes?
cards.a: To limit the impact of a container breakout (least privilege)
cards.x: Set runAsNonRoot and a non-zero runAsUser in securityContext.

cards.q: What does `privileged: true` grant a container?
cards.a: Near-host-level access — a major risk; avoid it
cards.x: Pod Security standards forbid it in restricted profiles.

cards.q: What do Pod Security Standards (restricted) enforce?
cards.a: Hardened defaults: non-root, no privilege escalation, dropped capabilities, etc.
cards.x: Applied via admission control per namespace.

cards.q: Why set ResourceQuotas and LimitRanges per namespace?
cards.a: To cap resource use and prevent a tenant from exhausting the cluster
cards.x: Multi-tenant safety and cost control.

cards.q: How should application secrets reach a pod securely?
cards.a: Via Secrets (with etcd encryption + RBAC) or an external secrets manager
cards.x: Never bake them into images or commit them.

cards.q: Why scan images and pin digests for cluster workloads?
cards.a: To avoid deploying vulnerable or tampered images (supply-chain security)
cards.x: Combine with admission policies that block unsigned/unscanned images.

tracks.title: Git
tracks.tagline: Version control: track, branch, merge and collaborate with confidence.

decks.title: Git Basics
decks.summary: What Git is and the three areas of a repository.

cards.q: What kind of version control system is Git?
cards.a: A distributed VCS — every clone is a full copy with complete history
cards.x: You can commit, branch and view history offline.

cards.q: What does `git init` do?
cards.a: Creates a new, empty Git repository in the current directory
cards.x: It adds a hidden .git folder holding all history.

cards.q: What does `git clone <url>` do?
cards.a: Copies a remote repository, including its full history, to your machine
cards.x: It sets up origin as the remote automatically.

cards.q: What are Git's three main areas?
cards.a: The working directory, the staging area (index), and the repository (.git)
cards.x: You edit in the working dir, stage, then commit.

cards.q: What does `git status` show?
cards.a: Which files are modified, staged, or untracked
cards.x: Your first stop to see the repo's state.

cards.q: What is the staging area (index)?
cards.a: A holding area where you assemble exactly what the next commit will contain
cards.x: It lets you commit part of your changes.

cards.q: What does a commit represent?
cards.a: A snapshot of the staged files at a point in time, with a message and parent
cards.x: Git stores snapshots, not just diffs.

cards.q: What is the .git directory?
cards.a: The hidden folder holding the entire repository: objects, refs and config
cards.x: Delete it and you lose the version history.

cards.q: Why is Git "distributed" an advantage?
cards.a: You work fully offline and every clone is a redundant backup of history
cards.x: No single central point of failure.

cards.q: What does a repository track?
cards.a: The history of changes to a set of files (a project)
cards.x: Commits form a chain back through time.

resources.title: Pro Git (the official Git book, free online)

decks.title: Staging & Committing
decks.summary: add, commit, diff, log and .gitignore.

cards.q: What does `git add <file>` do?
cards.a: Stages the file's current changes for the next commit
cards.x: git add . stages everything in the directory.

cards.q: What does `git commit -m "msg"` do?
cards.a: Records the staged changes as a new commit with that message
cards.x: Only staged changes are committed.

cards.q: What does `git diff` (no args) show?
cards.a: Unstaged changes — working directory vs the staging area
cards.x: git diff --staged shows staged vs the last commit.

cards.q: What does `git log` show?
cards.a: The commit history, newest first
cards.x: --oneline gives a compact view.

cards.q: What does a .gitignore file do?
cards.a: Tells Git which untracked files/patterns to ignore (e.g. node_modules, .env)
cards.x: Keeps build output and secrets out of the repo.

cards.q: What makes a good commit?
cards.a: A small, focused change with a clear message explaining why
cards.x: Atomic commits are easy to review and revert.

cards.q: How do you unstage a file you added by mistake?
cards.a: git restore --staged <file> (older: git reset <file>)
cards.x: It leaves your working changes intact.

cards.q: Does committing send your work to the remote?
cards.a: No — commit is local; you must push to share it
cards.x: Commits accumulate locally until pushed.

cards.q: What does `git show <commit>` display?
cards.a: The details and diff of a specific commit
cards.x: Handy for reviewing exactly what changed.

cards.q: Why should secrets never be committed?
cards.a: Git keeps full history, so a committed secret stays recoverable even after deletion
cards.x: Use .gitignore + a pre-commit scan; rotate anything leaked.

resources.title: Pro Git (the official Git book, free online)

puzzles.prompt: Order the steps to record and share a change in Git.
puzzles.x: Changes flow working directory → staging area → local repo → remote. A commit is local until you push.

decks.title: Remotes & Syncing
decks.summary: push, pull, fetch and tracking branches.

cards.q: What is a "remote" in Git?
cards.a: A named reference to another copy of the repo (e.g. on GitHub)
cards.x: The default remote is called origin.

cards.q: What does `git push` do?
cards.a: Uploads your local commits to the remote branch
cards.x: Set upstream once with -u origin <branch>.

cards.q: What does `git pull` do?
cards.a: Fetches remote changes AND merges them into your current branch
cards.x: It is fetch + merge in one step.

cards.q: What does `git fetch` do that pull does not?
cards.a: Downloads remote changes WITHOUT merging them into your work
cards.x: Lets you review before integrating.

cards.q: What is origin?
cards.a: The conventional default name for the remote you cloned from
cards.x: You can add others (e.g. upstream) with git remote add.

cards.q: What does `git remote -v` show?
cards.a: The configured remotes and their fetch/push URLs
cards.x: Verifies where your code goes.

cards.q: What is a tracking (upstream) branch?
cards.a: A local branch linked to a remote branch, so push/pull know the target
cards.x: git branch --set-upstream-to or push -u sets it.

cards.q: What does `git push -u origin main` do?
cards.a: Pushes main and sets origin/main as its upstream for future push/pull
cards.x: After that, plain git push works.

cards.q: Why run `git pull` before you start work?
cards.a: To integrate others' changes early and reduce conflicts later
cards.x: Working on stale code causes painful merges.

cards.q: What is the risk of `git push --force`?
cards.a: It can overwrite others' commits on a shared branch — data loss
cards.x: Prefer --force-with-lease, and never force-push shared history.

resources.title: Pro Git (the official Git book, free online)

decks.title: Branching & Merging
decks.summary: Lightweight branches, HEAD and merges.

cards.q: What is a Git branch, under the hood?
cards.a: A lightweight, movable pointer to a commit
cards.x: Creating one is nearly free — just a new ref.
wrong: A full copy of the files

cards.q: What is HEAD?
cards.a: A pointer to your current branch (and thus the commit you are on)
cards.x: Checking out moves HEAD.

cards.q: How do you create and switch to a new branch?
cards.a: git switch -c <name> (or git checkout -b <name>)
cards.x: It branches from your current commit.

cards.q: What does `git merge <branch>` do?
cards.a: Integrates another branch's commits into your current branch
cards.x: Creates a merge commit unless it can fast-forward.

cards.q: What is a fast-forward merge?
cards.a: Moving the branch pointer forward when there is no divergent history
cards.x: No merge commit is needed.

cards.q: When is a merge commit created?
cards.a: When both branches have diverging commits (a true 3-way merge)
cards.x: It has two parents, tying the histories together.

cards.q: How do you list branches?
cards.a: git branch (add -a for remotes too)
cards.x: The current branch is marked with *.

cards.q: How do you delete a merged branch?
cards.a: git branch -d <name>
cards.x: -D force-deletes an unmerged branch.

cards.q: Why branch for each feature or fix?
cards.a: To isolate work so main stays stable and changes are reviewable
cards.x: Branches are cheap — use them freely.

cards.q: What does `git switch main` do?
cards.a: Moves HEAD to the main branch, updating your working directory to match
cards.x: Commit or stash first to avoid losing changes.

resources.title: Pro Git (the official Git book, free online)

decks.title: Conflicts, Merge & Rebase
decks.summary: Resolving conflicts and integrating history.

cards.q: What causes a merge conflict?
cards.a: Two branches changed the same lines, so Git cannot auto-merge
cards.x: You must choose the correct result manually.

cards.q: What do the markers <<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>> mean?
cards.a: They delimit the conflicting versions (yours vs theirs) in the file
cards.x: Edit to the right result and DELETE all three markers.

cards.q: After editing a conflicted file, what finishes the merge?
cards.a: git add the file, then git commit (or git merge --continue)
cards.x: Staging marks the conflict resolved.

cards.q: How do you bail out of an in-progress merge?
cards.a: git merge --abort
cards.x: Returns the branch to its pre-merge state.

cards.q: What does `git rebase main` do to your branch?
cards.a: Re-applies your commits on top of the latest main, creating a linear history
cards.x: It rewrites your commits (new hashes).

cards.q: Merge vs rebase — key difference?
cards.a: Merge preserves history with a merge commit; rebase rewrites it into a straight line
cards.x: Rebase gives cleaner history but changes commit hashes.

cards.q: The golden rule of rebasing?
cards.a: Never rebase commits that have been pushed/shared — it rewrites others' history
cards.x: Rebase only local, unpushed work.

cards.q: What makes a 3-way merge?
cards.a: Git uses both branch tips plus their common ancestor to compute the merge
cards.x: The ancestor helps resolve non-conflicting changes automatically.

cards.q: How can you prevent committing conflict markers?
cards.a: A pre-commit hook / git diff --check that blocks <<<<<<< etc.
cards.x: Committed markers break builds (they did here!).

cards.q: What does `git rebase --continue` do?
cards.a: Proceeds after you resolve a conflict mid-rebase (having staged the fix)
cards.x: --abort cancels the whole rebase.

resources.title: Pro Git (the official Git book, free online)
Dangit, Git!? — recovering from common mistakes

puzzles.prompt: Order the steps to resolve a merge conflict.
items: git commit to finish the merge
puzzles.x: You edit to the correct result and delete all three markers, then staging marks it resolved and the commit completes the merge.

decks.title: Undoing Changes
decks.summary: restore, reset, revert, stash and reflog.

cards.q: How do you discard unstaged changes to a file?
cards.a: git restore <file> (older: git checkout -- <file>)
cards.x: This is destructive — the edits are gone.

cards.q: What does `git revert <commit>` do?
cards.a: Creates a NEW commit that undoes the changes of a given commit
cards.x: Safe for shared history — it adds, never rewrites.

cards.q: What does `git reset --soft HEAD~1` do?
cards.a: Undoes the last commit but keeps its changes staged
cards.x: Great for re-committing differently.

cards.q: What does `git reset --hard` do, and the risk?
cards.a: Resets the branch and WIPES working/staged changes — unrecoverable if uncommitted
cards.x: Use with care; prefer stash first.

cards.q: What does `git commit --amend` do?
cards.a: Replaces the last commit (edit its message or add staged changes)
cards.x: Avoid amending commits you have already pushed.

cards.q: What does `git stash` do?
cards.a: Shelves your uncommitted changes and gives you a clean working tree
cards.x: git stash pop reapplies them later.

cards.q: What is the reflog, and why is it a lifesaver?
cards.a: A log of where HEAD has been — it can recover "lost" commits after a bad reset
cards.x: git reflog shows the history of moves.

cards.q: revert vs reset for a commit already pushed?
cards.a: Use revert — it does not rewrite shared history; reset --hard would
cards.x: Rewriting pushed history breaks collaborators.

cards.q: How do you throw away ALL local commits back to origin/main?
cards.a: git reset --hard origin/main (destructive)
cards.x: Make sure nothing valuable is uncommitted.

cards.q: What does `git stash pop` do?
cards.a: Reapplies the most recent stash and removes it from the stash list
cards.x: git stash apply keeps it in the list.

resources.title: Pro Git (the official Git book, free online)
Dangit, Git!? — recovering from common mistakes

decks.title: Workflows & Collaboration
decks.summary: Feature branches, PRs, rebase -i, cherry-pick and tags.

cards.q: What is the feature-branch workflow?
cards.a: Each change is developed on its own branch and merged via review
cards.x: Keeps main releasable and changes isolated.

cards.q: What is a pull request (merge request)?
cards.a: A proposal to merge a branch, with review and discussion before it lands
cards.x: Where code review and CI gates happen.

cards.q: What does `git rebase -i` (interactive) let you do?
cards.a: Reorder, squash, edit or drop commits before sharing them
cards.x: Clean up a messy local history.

cards.q: What does squashing commits do?
cards.a: Combines several commits into one
cards.x: Gives a tidy, single logical change in history.

cards.q: What does `git cherry-pick <commit>` do?
cards.a: Applies a specific commit from one branch onto your current branch
cards.x: Useful for hotfixes across branches.

cards.q: What is a Git tag used for?
cards.a: Marking a specific commit, typically a release (e.g. v1.2.0)
cards.x: Annotated tags store a message and author.

cards.q: What is "forking" on a platform like GitHub?
cards.a: Creating your own server-side copy of a repo to contribute via pull requests
cards.x: Common for open-source contributions.

cards.q: Trunk-based vs GitFlow — one line?
cards.a: Trunk-based: small, frequent merges to main behind flags; GitFlow: long-lived release/develop branches
cards.x: Trunk-based suits continuous delivery.

cards.q: Why keep pull requests small?
cards.a: They are faster to review, lower-risk, and easier to revert
cards.x: Huge PRs hide bugs and stall review.

cards.q: What does a CI check on a PR typically do?

decks.summary: The object model, history integrity and security.

cards.q: What identifies a Git commit?
cards.a: A cryptographic hash (SHA-1, moving to SHA-256) of its content
cards.x: Change anything and the hash changes — tamper-evident.

cards.q: What are Git's core object types?
cards.a: blob (file content), tree (directory), commit, and tag
cards.x: Everything is a hashed object in .git/objects.

cards.q: What data structure is Git history?
cards.a: A directed acyclic graph (DAG) of commits linked to their parents
cards.x: Branches/merges are just nodes and edges.

cards.q: Why does rewriting shared history cause problems?
cards.a: It changes commit hashes, so collaborators' clones diverge and break
cards.x: Only rewrite local, unpushed commits.

cards.q: How do you keep secrets out of a repo?
cards.a: .gitignore + a pre-commit secret scanner (e.g. gitleaks); rotate anything that leaks
cards.x: History makes a committed secret hard to erase.

cards.q: What are signed commits/tags for?
cards.a: Cryptographically proving who authored them (GPG/SSH signatures)
cards.x: Protects against impersonation in the history.

cards.q: What is Git LFS for?
cards.a: Storing large binary files outside normal Git history, via pointers
cards.x: Keeps the repo small and clones fast.

cards.q: Why avoid committing large binaries directly?
cards.a: They bloat every clone's history forever and slow operations
cards.x: Use LFS or keep them out of Git.

cards.q: What does a pre-commit hook enable?
cards.a: Running checks (lint, tests, secret/marker scans) before a commit is recorded
cards.x: Catches problems at the earliest point.

cards.q: Why is a good commit message valuable?
cards.a: It explains WHY a change was made — invaluable when debugging history later
cards.x: Future you (and reviewers) rely on it.

overview: Python is the glue language of IT and security work: short scripts rename a thousand files, parse a firewall log, or call a cloud API. Everything starts with values, the variables that name them, and the operators that combine them.

This lesson covers the core data types (`int`, `float`, `str`, `bool` and `None`), arithmetic including floor division and modulo, converting between types, and working with strings: indexing, immutability and f-strings.

learn.heading: Values, types and variables
body: Every value has a type, and `type(value)` tells you which. `42` is an `int`, `3.0` is a `float` (any literal with a decimal point), `"hi"` is a `str`, `True` and `False` are `bool`, and `None` is the single value that means "nothing here". Functions that do not return anything give back `None`.
A variable is just a name bound to a value: `count = 3`. Python is dynamically typed, so the same name can later refer to a different type, but the value itself always has one definite type.

learn.heading: Operators you will use constantly
body: `+ - * /` work as expected, and `/` always returns a `float` (`7 / 2` is `3.5`). Floor division `//` divides and rounds down (`7 // 2` is `3`), modulo `%` gives the remainder (`7 % 2` is `1`), and `**` raises to a power (`2 ** 3` is `8`).
Modulo is more useful than it looks: `n % 2 == 0` tests for even numbers, and `seconds % 60` turns a duration into the seconds part of minutes:seconds.

learn.heading: Converting types and reading input
body: `input()` always returns a `str`, even if the user types digits. Convert with `int("42")` or `float("3.5")`. If the text is not a valid number, `int()` raises `ValueError`, which you will learn to handle in the Files & Errors lesson.
Going the other way, `str(42)` gives `"42"`. You rarely need that for output, because f-strings convert for you.

learn.heading: Strings: indexing, immutability and f-strings
body: Strings are sequences of characters, indexed from zero: `"abc"[1]` is `"b"`. Negative indices count from the end, so `"hello"[-1]` is `"o"`. `len("hello")` is `5`.
Strings are immutable. Methods such as `.upper()` or `.replace()` return a new string and leave the original unchanged, so you must assign the result: `name = name.strip()`.
To build text from values, use an f-string: `f"Hi {name}, you have {count} alerts"`. Any expression can go inside the braces, including formatting such as `{ratio:.1%}`.

examples.title: Arithmetic and types
examples.code:
print(type(3.0))   # <class 'float'>
print(7 / 2)       # 3.5
print(7 // 2)      # 3  (floor division)
print(7 % 2)       # 1  (remainder)
print(2 ** 3)      # 8
examples.explanation: Run each line in a Python shell (`python` or `python3`) to see the result for yourself.

examples.title: Read a number and report it
examples.code:
raw = input("How many hosts? ")   # always a str
hosts = int(raw)                  # ValueError if not digits
print(f"Scanning {hosts} hosts, about {hosts * 0.5:.0f} seconds")
examples.explanation: Convert input before doing maths with it, then let the f-string format the output.

Parse text to a number (ValueError if invalid)
Methods return a new string; reassign the result

overview: Programs become useful when they make decisions and repeat work. Control flow is how a script decides what to do with each log line, retries a failed request, or stops when it finds what it was looking for.
This lesson covers `if`/`elif`/`else`, truthiness, `for` and `while` loops with `range`, `break`, `continue` and `pass`, and how to package logic into reusable functions.

learn.heading: Decisions: if, elif, else and truthiness
body: Python delimits blocks with indentation, not braces. PEP 8 recommends 4 spaces per level; mixing tabs and spaces causes errors. The "else if" keyword is `elif`.

Conditions do not have to be booleans. The falsy values are `False`, `None`, `0`, `""` and empty collections; everything else is truthy. That is why `if items:` is the idiomatic way to check that a list is not empty.
Use `==` to compare values and `is` to compare identity. In practice `is` is only for singletons: write `if result is None:`.

learn.heading: Loops
body: A `for` loop walks over any iterable: a list, a string, a file, a dictionary. `range(3)` produces `0, 1, 2`: it starts at 0 and stops before the end value. A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition stays true.

`break` leaves the innermost loop immediately, `continue` skips the rest of the current pass and moves to the next one, and `pass` does nothing: it is a placeholder where the syntax needs a statement.

learn.heading: Functions
body: Define a function with `def name(parameters):` and an indented body. `return` sends a value back; a function without a `return` returns `None`.

Parameters can have default values: `def greet(name="world"):`. Never use a mutable default such as `[]` or `{}`: the default is created once, when the function is defined, and shared by every call. Use `None` and create the list inside the function instead.

examples.title: Classify failed logins
examples.explanation: One function holds the rule; the loop applies it to every user.

examples.title: break, continue and the mutable-default trap
examples.code:
with open("auth.log") as f:     # with: see the Files & Errors lesson
    for line in f:
        if not line.strip():
            continue      # skip blank lines
        if "CRITICAL" in line:
            print(line)
            break         # stop at the first critical entry

def add_tag(tag, tags=None):   # not tags=[]
    tags = [] if tags is None else tags
    tags.append(tag)
    return tags
examples.explanation: With `tags=[]`, every call would append to the same shared list.

overview: Real data comes in groups: a list of IP addresses, a mapping of usernames to roles, a set of blocked domains. Choosing the right collection makes code simpler and often dramatically faster.
This lesson compares the four built-in collections (`list`, `tuple`, `set`, `dict`), then covers slicing, comprehensions, and the looping helpers `enumerate` and `.items()`.

learn.heading: Four collections, four jobs
body: A `list` is ordered and mutable: use it for sequences you add to and change. A `tuple` is ordered but immutable: use it for fixed records such as `(host, port)`. Because tuples cannot change, they are hashable and can be dictionary keys.
A `set` holds unique items only; adding a duplicate does nothing, and membership tests (`x in s`) are O(1) on average. A `dict` maps keys to values and has preserved insertion order since Python 3.7.
Dictionary keys must be hashable, which is why a list cannot be a key: it could change after being stored. Convert it to a tuple first.

learn.heading: Working with lists and dicts
body: `my_list.append(x)` adds one item to the end; `extend` adds every item from another iterable. `d["k"]` raises `KeyError` if the key is missing, whereas `d.get("k", 0)` returns the default instead.
Slices take a range: `nums[1:3]` includes index 1 and excludes index 3, so `[10, 20, 30, 40][1:3]` is `[20, 30]`. `nums[::-1]` reverses a list.

learn.heading: Comprehensions and idiomatic loops
body: A list comprehension builds a list from a loop in one expression: `[x * 2 for x in range(3)]` is `[0, 2, 4]`. Add a filter with `if`: `[ip for ip in ips if ip.startswith("10.")]`. Dict and set comprehensions use `{}`.
Loop over a dict's keys and values together with `for k, v in d.items():`. When you need the position as well as the item, use `for i, item in enumerate(items):` instead of `range(len(items))`.

examples.title: Count hits per IP with a dict
examples.explanation: `get` with a default avoids a KeyError the first time each IP appears.

examples.title: Fast membership with a set
examples.code:
blocked = {"evil.example", "phish.example"}   # set literal
requests = ["docs.python.org", "phish.example"]
flagged = [r for r in requests if r in blocked]
print(flagged)   # ['phish.example']
examples.explanation: Checking membership in a set stays fast even with millions of entries.

overview: Automation lives on files: logs to parse, reports to write, configs to read. It also has to survive the real world, where files go missing and input is malformed. A script that crashes halfway through a batch job is worse than no script.
This lesson covers reading and writing files safely, handling and raising exceptions, organising code into modules, isolating dependencies with virtual environments, and choosing a safe data format.

learn.heading: Files and context managers
body: Open files with `with open(path) as f:`. The `with` block uses a context manager that closes the file automatically when the block ends, even if an error occurs inside it.

The `pathlib` module gives object-oriented paths that work on every operating system: `Path("logs") / "app.log"`, `path.exists()`, `path.read_text()`. For structured data, the `json` module converts between JSON text and Python objects with `json.loads` and `json.dumps`.

learn.heading: Exceptions
body: Errors are raised as exceptions. Opening a missing file raises `FileNotFoundError` (a subclass of `OSError`); bad conversions raise `ValueError`. Handle the ones you expect with `try`/`except SpecificError:`.

Avoid a bare `except:`. It swallows every error, including `KeyboardInterrupt` when you press Ctrl+C, and hides bugs. A `finally` block always runs, whether or not an exception happened, which makes it the place for cleanup.
Signal problems in your own code with `raise ValueError("port must be 1-65535")`, choosing the most specific built-in exception or your own subclass.

learn.heading: Modules, __main__ and virtual environments
body: Every `.py` file is a module you can import. Code under `if __name__ == "__main__":` runs only when the file is executed directly, not when it is imported, so a file can be both a reusable library and a script.

A virtual environment isolates a project's dependencies from the system Python: `python -m venv .venv`, activate it, then `pip install`. List dependencies in `requirements.txt` and pin versions so every install is reproducible.

learn.heading: Safe data formats
body: `pickle` can serialise almost any Python object, but `pickle.load` on untrusted data can execute arbitrary code: an insecure deserialization vulnerability. For anything that crosses a trust boundary, use JSON.

examples.title: Read a config file defensively
examples.explanation: Each expected failure is handled specifically; anything unexpected still surfaces as an error.

examples.title: Set up an isolated project
examples.code:
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate        # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install requests
pip freeze > requirements.txt
examples.explanation: Anyone can recreate the environment later with `pip install -r requirements.txt`.

Signal an error from your own code

overview: As scripts grow into tools, you need ways to model things (a host, a finding, a user) and to reuse behaviour without copying code. Object-oriented programming and a few Pythonic features make larger code readable and testable.
This lesson covers classes and `self`, `__init__` and the dunder methods, inheritance, dataclasses, static and class methods, generators, decorators, lambdas, type hints and PEP 8 naming.

learn.heading: Classes, self and dunder methods
body: A class is a blueprint; each object created from it is an instance. `__init__` initialises a new instance's attributes, and every method receives the instance it was called on as its first parameter, named `self` by convention.

Methods with double underscores ("dunder" methods) hook into Python's syntax. `__repr__` controls how an object appears to developers (in the shell and in logs) and should be unambiguous; `__str__` is the friendlier form for end users; `__eq__` defines `==`.
`@dataclass` writes `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` for you from annotated fields, which is ideal for plain data-holding classes.

learn.heading: Inheritance and method types
body: Inheritance lets a class reuse and extend another: `class Admin(User):` gets every `User` method, and `super().__init__(...)` calls the parent's version. Prefer small hierarchies; composition (an object holding another) is often clearer.

`@staticmethod` defines a method that takes neither `self` nor `cls`, a plain function grouped with the class. `@classmethod` receives the class itself as `cls`, which is handy for alternative constructors such as `Host.from_string("10.0.0.1:22")`.

learn.heading: Generators, decorators and lambdas
body: A generator function uses `yield` instead of `return`, producing values lazily, one at a time. It can process a huge file or an endless stream without loading everything into memory.
A decorator is a function that wraps another function to add behaviour: timing, logging, retries, access checks. Writing `@login_required` above a `def` wraps it without editing its body.
`lambda x: x * 2` creates a small anonymous function from one expression, most often as a sort key: `sorted(users, key=lambda u: u.age)`.

learn.heading: Type hints and style
body: Type hints such as `def f(x: int) -> str:` document intent and let tools like mypy and your IDE catch bugs early. They are not enforced at runtime.
PEP 8 naming: `snake_case` for functions and variables, `CapWords` (PascalCase) for classes, `UPPER_CASE` for constants.

examples.title: A dataclass with an alternative constructor
examples.explanation: The dataclass generated `__init__` and `__repr__`; the class method parses a common input format.

examples.title: A generator and a decorator
examples.explanation: The generator streams matching lines; the decorator adds timing without touching `count_errors`.

No self or cls / receives cls
Wraps a function to add behaviour

overview: This is where Python pays for itself: talking to web APIs, running system commands, pulling indicators out of logs, and turning a one-off script into a tool colleagues can use.
This lesson covers HTTP with `requests`, safe use of `subprocess`, regular expressions, CSV parsing, handling secrets, SSH automation, command-line arguments and proper logging.

learn.heading: Calling APIs
body: `requests` is the de facto library for HTTP: `requests.get(url, timeout=5)` then `.json()` for the body. Always set a timeout, or a hung server can hang your script forever.

Check the status code: 2xx means success, 3xx a redirect, 4xx a client error (bad request, not authorised, not found) and 5xx a server error. `response.raise_for_status()` turns 4xx and 5xx into exceptions.
API keys never belong in code. Read them from an environment variable (`os.environ["API_KEY"]`) or a secrets manager. A key committed to git stays in the history and must be rotated.

learn.heading: Running commands safely
body: `subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "1", host], capture_output=True, text=True)` runs a program with its arguments passed as a list. Each item is one argument, so nothing is interpreted by a shell.
Passing a string with `shell=True` and user input enables command injection: a "hostname" of `8.8.8.8; rm -rf /` becomes two commands. Use the list form, and validate input.

learn.heading: Parsing text: regex and CSV
body: The `re` module finds patterns: `re.findall(r"\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+", log)` pulls IPv4-like strings from a log. Write patterns as raw strings (`r"..."`) so Python does not interpret the backslashes before `re` sees them.
The `csv` module handles quoting and commas inside fields correctly. `csv.DictReader` gives each row as a dictionary keyed by the header, which reads far better than numeric column indexes.

learn.heading: From script to tool
body: `argparse` turns hard-coded values into command-line options and generates `--help` automatically. `logging` replaces `print()` for diagnostics, with levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR) you can filter and handlers that write to files.
For servers and network gear, `paramiko` provides SSH, and `netmiko` builds on it with vendor-specific handling for switches and routers.

examples.title: Query an API with a timeout and a secret from the environment
examples.code:
import os, requests

resp = requests.get(
    "https://api.example.com/v1/alerts",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['API_KEY']}"},
    timeout=5,
)
resp.raise_for_status()           # 4xx/5xx -> exception
for alert in resp.json()["alerts"]:
    print(alert["id"], alert["severity"])
examples.explanation: No key in the code, no request without a timeout, no silent failure on an error status.

examples.title: A small log tool with argparse, regex and logging
examples.code:
import argparse, logging, re

IPV4 = re.compile(r"\b(?:\d{1,3}\.){3}\d{1,3}\b")

def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="List unique IPs in a log")
    parser.add_argument("logfile")
    parser.add_argument("-v", "--verbose", action="store_true")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG if args.verbose else logging.INFO)

    with open(args.logfile) as f:
        ips = {ip for line in f for ip in IPV4.findall(line)}
    logging.info("found %d unique IPs", len(ips))
    for ip in sorted(ips):
        print(ip)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
examples.explanation: Run it with `python ips.py auth.log -v`; `python ips.py --help` documents itself.

Run a command; pass arguments as a list
Regular expressions; raw strings keep backslashes

overview: Scanning a /16, pulling data from 500 APIs or hashing a disk image all hit the same wall: doing things one at a time is slow. Concurrency helps, but only if you pick the right tool for the kind of work.

This lesson explains the GIL, when to use threads, processes or asyncio, how race conditions happen, and how to measure and fix performance with profiling, the right data structures, caching and streaming.

learn.heading: The GIL and the two kinds of work
body: CPython has a Global Interpreter Lock (GIL): only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time. CPython 3.13 and later also offer an experimental free-threaded build without it, but the default build still has the GIL.
I/O-bound work (network requests, disk reads, database calls) spends most of its time waiting, and threads release the GIL while waiting. Threads or `asyncio` therefore speed it up well.

CPU-bound work (hashing, compression, number crunching) is limited by the GIL, so use `multiprocessing` or `ProcessPoolExecutor`: separate processes each have their own interpreter and GIL, so they use multiple cores.

learn.heading: Threads, processes and asyncio in practice
body: `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor` gives a pool of worker threads with a simple `submit`/`map` API; `ProcessPoolExecutor` offers the same API with processes. Start with these before reaching for lower-level modules.

`asyncio` runs many tasks on one thread with an event loop. Inside an `async def`, `await` suspends that coroutine until the awaited operation finishes, and the loop runs other tasks meanwhile. It scales to thousands of concurrent connections, but every library in the path must be async-aware.

learn.heading: Race conditions
body: A race condition is when the outcome depends on the unpredictable timing of concurrent access to shared state, for example two threads both reading a counter, adding one, and writing it back. Protect shared state with a `threading.Lock`, or better, avoid sharing: have workers return results and combine them at the end.

learn.heading: Measure, then optimise
body: Profile before changing anything: `python -m cProfile -s cumtime script.py` shows where time actually goes. The fix is often a data structure, not concurrency. `x in my_set` is O(1) on average while `x in my_list` is O(n), so converting a list to a set can turn minutes into milliseconds.

`functools.lru_cache` memoises a pure function's results for repeated arguments. For big inputs, stream with generators: iterating over a file object reads it line by line, so a 10 GB log never has to fit in memory.

examples.title: I/O-bound: check many URLs with a thread pool
examples.explanation: Workers return results instead of writing to shared state, so no lock is needed.

examples.title: CPU-bound: hash files on every core
examples.explanation: The `__main__` guard is required for process pools on Windows and macOS.

Suspend this coroutine; the loop runs others
Result depends on timing; use locks or avoid sharing
Find where the time goes before optimising

overview: A tool other people rely on needs tests that prove it works, a clean way to install it, and dependencies you can trust. Supply-chain attacks against PyPI are real, and untested security tooling fails exactly when it matters.
This lesson covers pytest, fixtures and mocking, coverage, modern packaging with `pyproject.toml` and lock files, and the security checks every Python project should run.

learn.heading: Testing with pytest
body: pytest is the most widely used Python test framework. Tests are plain functions named `test_*` that use ordinary `assert` statements, and pytest explains exactly what differed when one fails. `@pytest.mark.parametrize` runs one test over many inputs.
A fixture is reusable setup code that pytest injects into any test that names it as a parameter. A fixture can `yield` its value and run teardown code after the test finishes.
Mocking replaces a real dependency with a controllable fake. `unittest.mock.patch` stops tests from calling real APIs, databases or clocks, which keeps them fast and repeatable.

learn.heading: Coverage
body: Coverage measures which lines or branches your tests executed. High coverage does not prove the code is correct, since a test can run a line without checking its result, but low coverage clearly shows the blind spots.

learn.heading: Packaging and reproducible installs
body: `pyproject.toml` is the modern standard file for package metadata and build configuration (PEP 517, 518 and 621), replacing most uses of `setup.py`.

A lock file pins the exact version of every dependency, including indirect ones, so installs are reproducible and a compromised new release cannot slip in unnoticed. Tools such as uv, poetry and pip-tools generate them.

learn.heading: Security checks
body: `pip-audit` checks installed packages against the Python Packaging Advisory Database of known vulnerabilities. Typosquatting is a supply-chain attack where malicious packages use names close to popular ones (`reqeusts` instead of `requests`), so check names and publishers.

Bandit is a static security linter (SAST) for Python. It flags insecure patterns such as `eval`, `shell=True` and hard-coded secrets; run it in CI. Never call `eval()` on user input: it executes arbitrary code. Use `ast.literal_eval` to safely parse Python literals.

examples.title: Fixtures, parametrise and mocking
examples.explanation: Assumes `fetch_banner` calls `socket.create_connection(...)` and then `.recv()`. No real network traffic: the fixture patches the socket call, and teardown happens after `yield`.

examples.title: Quality gate for CI
examples.code:
pytest --cov=scanner --cov-report=term-missing
pip-audit
bandit -r scanner/
examples.explanation: Run all three on every pull request: tests with coverage, known-vulnerable dependencies, insecure code patterns.

What ran, not whether it is correct
Exact pinned versions for reproducible installs

overview: Security teams build small tools constantly: a port checker, a hash verifier, a log summariser. Python's standard library covers most of it, and a few well-known libraries fill the gaps, but only if you use the security-sensitive parts correctly.

This lesson covers sockets, hashing and password storage, secure randomness, the cryptography library, constant-time comparison, packet crafting, pandas for log analysis, SQL injection prevention, and the ethics of testing.

learn.heading: Networking and integrity
body: The `socket` module opens raw TCP and UDP connections. `socket.create_connection((host, port), timeout=2)` succeeding means the port is open, which is the basis of a simple port check. Scapy crafts and sniffs arbitrary packets for deeper protocol work.
`hashlib` computes digests: `hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()` produces the fingerprint you compare against a vendor's published hash to verify a download or preserve evidence integrity.

learn.heading: Passwords, tokens and encryption
body: Never store passwords with a fast hash like plain SHA-256: attackers can try billions of guesses per second. Use a slow, salted algorithm designed for passwords: bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2.
Generate tokens, API keys and passwords with the `secrets` module. The `random` module is predictable and must never be used for security values.
For encryption, use the `cryptography` library. Its Fernet recipe gives authenticated symmetric encryption with sensible defaults, so you do not have to assemble primitives yourself.
When comparing secrets such as tokens or HMACs, use `hmac.compare_digest(a, b)`. A normal `==` stops at the first differing character, and that timing difference can leak the secret byte by byte.

learn.heading: Data and databases
body: pandas is the standard library for tabular analysis: `pd.read_csv("auth.csv")` then `groupby` and `value_counts` summarise thousands of log rows in a line or two.

Prevent SQL injection with parameterised queries: `cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?", (name,))`. The driver sends the value separately from the SQL, so input can never change the query. Never build SQL with f-strings or concatenation.

learn.heading: Authorisation first
body: Scanning or probing systems you do not own or have written permission to test can be illegal, and it violates professional codes of ethics such as ISC2's. Get a written scope before running any of these tools against anything but your own lab.

examples.title: A minimal, polite port check
examples.explanation: A timeout keeps it fast, and the `with` block closes each connection immediately.

examples.title: Tokens, constant-time checks and safe SQL
examples.code:
import hmac, secrets, sqlite3

token = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)            # not random.random()

def token_ok(supplied: str) -> bool:
    return hmac.compare_digest(supplied, token)

db = sqlite3.connect("users.db")
name = input("user: ")
rows = db.execute("SELECT id, role FROM users WHERE name = ?", (name,)).fetchall()
examples.explanation: Secure randomness, constant-time comparison, and a parameterised query: three of the most common fixes in real code reviews.

overview: Every network conversation, from loading a web page to a switch forwarding a frame, can be described in layers. Models give you a shared vocabulary ("that is a Layer 2 problem") and a systematic way to troubleshoot from the cable up.
This lesson covers the seven OSI layers and what lives at each, the four-layer TCP/IP model used in practice, the name of the data unit at each layer (the PDU), and encapsulation.

learn.heading: The seven OSI layers
body: Every network conversation — a page loading, a file crossing an ocean — descends through seven layers, each with a single job done well. The upper three serve software directly; the lower four move the data.

items.name: Transport
items.does: End-to-end delivery, steered to the right application by port number.

items.name: Network
items.does: Carries packets between networks, choosing paths through routers.

items.name: Data Link
items.does: Organizes bits into frames addressed by MAC address.

items.name: Physical
items.does: Moves raw bits as electrical pulses, light or radio waves.

mnemonic.lead: Generations of engineers have memorized the order from the wire up with a single sentence:

learn.heading: PDUs and encapsulation
body: Each layer names its unit of data — its protocol data unit — differently: bits at Layer 1, frames at Layer 2, packets at Layer 3, and segments at Layer 4 when TCP delivers them reliably, datagrams when UDP sends them best-effort.

As data descends the stack, every layer wraps what it received in its own header — Layer 2 appends a trailer as well — nesting envelopes within envelopes. This is encapsulation. At the destination the process reverses: each layer strips its own header and passes the payload upward until the original message emerges intact. A router demonstrates it in miniature: it discards the arriving frame, reads the destination IP from the packet within, then builds a fresh frame to carry it across the next link.

learn.heading: The TCP/IP model
body: The internet itself runs on a leaner blueprint: four layers, each absorbing one or more OSI layers. The colours match the OSI layers above.

stack.title: The TCP/IP model and its OSI equivalents

items.name: Application
items.does: Folds OSI’s top three layers into one.

items.name: Transport
items.does: Aligns directly with OSI Layer 4.

items.name: Internet
items.does: Maps to OSI Layer 3: addressing and routing.

items.name: Link
items.does: Sometimes called Network Access; absorbs OSI’s bottom two.

body: Every protocol you will ever configure lives in this model — yet engineers still speak OSI daily, because "that’s a Layer 2 problem" or "it’s failing at Layer 7" tells a colleague exactly where to look.

architecture.caption: Encapsulation as data moves down the stack. Each layer wraps the one above with its own header (Ethernet also adds an FCS trailer); the receiver removes them in reverse.
architecture.diagram:
Layer 7-5  Data                                   [ HTTP request ]
Layer 4    Segment                      [ TCP hdr | HTTP request ]
Layer 3    Packet              [ IP hdr | TCP hdr | HTTP request ]
Layer 2    Frame     [ Eth hdr | IP hdr | TCP hdr | HTTP request ] + FCS
Layer 1    Bits      0101 1001 0111 0100 ... on the wire, fibre or radio

overview: A port number tells the receiving host which service a segment is for. Knowing the common ports lets you read firewall rules, spot suspicious traffic and answer a large share of Network+ and Security+ questions.

This lesson covers TCP versus UDP, the three-way handshake, and the well-known ports grouped by job — each with its full name, so the acronyms stop being alphabet soup — including which cleartext protocols to replace with secure ones.

learn.heading: TCP and UDP
body: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is connection-oriented. It opens a connection with a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), numbers every byte, acknowledges receipt, retransmits losses and delivers data in order. It closes with FIN/ACK exchanges, or abruptly with RST (reset).

UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is connectionless and best-effort: no handshake, no acknowledgements, no ordering. That makes it lighter and faster, which suits DNS queries, VoIP, video, and protocols that handle reliability themselves, such as QUIC (HTTP/3 runs over UDP 443).

learn.heading: Remote access
body: Remote administration is the highest-value target on the network, so its ports deserve the most scrutiny. Encrypted administration is non-negotiable; anything cleartext here is a finding.

items.name: SSH — Secure Shell
items.does: Encrypted remote shell and the secure workhorse of administration. Also carries SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol) and SCP (Secure Copy Protocol), so one port covers shell and file transfer.

items.name: Telnet — Teletype Network
items.does: Unencrypted remote shell from another era. Usernames, passwords and every keystroke cross the wire in cleartext.

items.name: RDP — Remote Desktop Protocol
items.does: Microsoft's graphical remote desktop. Powerful for administration, dangerous when exposed.
items.examples: Never expose to the internet; use a VPN

learn.heading: File transfer
body: Moving files sounds mundane until you realize the oldest protocols do it in cleartext — credentials and data alike. Know which are safe and which are legacy.

items.name: FTP — File Transfer Protocol
items.does: The classic file transfer protocol: port 21 carries the control channel, port 20 carries data in active mode. Everything — including the login — is cleartext.

items.name: SMB — Server Message Block
items.does: Windows file sharing and printer sharing, the protocol behind mapped network drives. A favourite target of ransomware worms.

items.name: TFTP — Trivial File Transfer Protocol
items.does: A stripped-down, unauthenticated cousin of FTP used to push firmware and configs to network devices. Simple, fast, and trusting — by design, not by accident.

learn.heading: Web traffic
body: The web is two ports, and the difference between them is the difference between a private conversation and a postcard.

items.name: HTTP — Hypertext Transfer Protocol
items.does: Unencrypted web traffic. Fine for public, non-sensitive content; unacceptable for logins or anything personal.

items.name: HTTPS — HTTP Secure
items.does: HTTP wrapped in TLS (Transport Layer Security): encrypted, authenticated, and the default for the modern web. HTTP/3 (QUIC) also uses 443, but over UDP.

learn.heading: Email
body: Email is three jobs — sending between servers, submitting from clients, and retrieving to clients — and each job has its own port. Mixing them up is a classic exam trap.

items.name: SMTP — Simple Mail Transfer Protocol
items.does: Server-to-server mail delivery across the internet. Clients submit new mail on 587 instead, and the legacy encrypted variant SMTPS uses 465.

items.name: POP3 — Post Office Protocol v3
items.does: Retrieves mail by downloading it, historically deleting the server copy. Simple, but one device ends up holding the mailbox. Encrypted variant POP3S uses 995.

items.name: IMAP — Internet Message Access Protocol
items.does: Retrieves mail while leaving it on the server, so phone, laptop and webmail stay in sync. The modern default for clients. Encrypted variant IMAPS uses 993.

learn.heading: Name, address and time services
body: These three are the invisible plumbing: without them, nothing resolves, nothing gets an address, and nothing agrees what time it is — and authentication quietly breaks.

items.name: DNS — Domain Name System
items.does: Translates names to IP addresses. Most queries ride UDP; TCP handles zone transfers between servers and responses too large for one datagram.

items.name: DHCP — Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol
items.does: Hands out IP addresses automatically. The server listens on 67, the client on 68 — the conversation is a four-step DORA exchange (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge).

items.name: NTP — Network Time Protocol
items.does: Keeps clocks synchronized across the network. Accurate time is not cosmetic: Kerberos authentication fails when clocks drift, and forensic log correlation depends on it.

learn.heading: Management and directories
body: The protocols that watch the network and the directories that know who everyone is. Both carry sensitive data, so both have encrypted variants you are expected to name.

items.name: SNMP — Simple Network Management Protocol
items.does: Monitors and manages network devices. Managers poll agents on 161; agents send unsolicited alerts (traps) on 162. Versions 1 and 2c use cleartext community strings — use SNMPv3 for encryption and authentication.

items.name: Syslog — System Logging Protocol
items.does: The standard way devices ship log messages to a central collector. Plain syslog is UDP and unencrypted; wrap it in TLS and it commonly moves to 6514/TCP.

items.name: LDAP — Lightweight Directory Access Protocol
items.does: Queries directory services like Active Directory: who is this user, what groups are they in. The encrypted variant LDAPS wraps it in TLS on 636.

examples.title: See what is listening, and test one port
examples.code:
# Windows: listening ports with the owning process ID
netstat -ano | findstr LISTENING

# Linux: listening TCP/UDP sockets and processes
ss -tulpn

# Test whether a remote TCP port answers (PowerShell)
Test-NetConnection 10.0.0.5 -Port 3389
examples.explanation: Compare what is listening with what should be: an unexpected 23 or 3389 is worth investigating.

SMTP — Simple Mail Transfer Protocol / submission / SMTPS
POP3 — Post Office Protocol v3 (995 encrypted)
IMAP — Internet Message Access Protocol (993 encrypted)
DNS — Domain Name System (TCP for zone transfers)

SNMP — Simple Network Management Protocol, polling / traps
