overview: Cryptography is the quiet machinery underneath nearly every security control: the TLS that protects a login, the hash that proves a file is intact, the signature that makes a software update trustworthy. Security+ expects you to know not just the names but when each tool fits.

This lesson covers how strangers agree on secrets (key exchange), how hybrid encryption gets the best of both worlds, what certificates actually prove, and how the pieces — ciphers, hashes, signatures — combine into working systems.

learn.heading: Agreeing on secrets and mixing ciphers
body: Two parties who have never met can still agree on a secret over a public channel using Diffie-Hellman: each combines a private value with the other’s public value, and both arrive at the same secret while eavesdroppers cannot. It solves key distribution without ever transmitting the key itself.

Real systems rarely use one cipher type alone. A digital envelope encrypts the message with a fast symmetric key, then encrypts that key with the recipient’s public key — symmetric speed for the bulk data, asymmetric convenience for the key. TLS handshakes work the same way, and ephemeral keys per session give perfect forward secrecy.

Block ciphers like AES encrypt fixed-size chunks; stream ciphers encrypt bit by bit. Prefer authenticated modes such as AES-GCM, which bundle confidentiality and integrity, over plain CBC, which needs a separate HMAC to detect tampering. And remember the fundamental split: hashing is one-way with no key, encryption is reversible with one.

learn.heading: Certificates and the PKI that backs them
body: A certificate binds a public key to an identity, vouched for by a certificate authority. Domain-validated (DV) certs only prove control of the domain; organization-validated (OV) verify the business; extended-validation (EV) vets rigorously. All three encrypt identically — the difference is how much identity was checked.

Choose wildcards (*.example.com) for many subdomains of one domain, and SAN certificates when one certificate must cover several different names. Self-signed certificates encrypt fine but no trusted third party vouches for them, so browsers warn — acceptable in a lab, not in production.

Trust flows down a chain: the leaf was signed by an intermediate, which was signed by a root your system trusts. Intermediates exist so the root key can stay offline; if an intermediate is compromised it can be revoked without replacing the root. Certificate pinning goes further — an app accepts only one specific key — defeating rogue-CA attacks at the cost of painful rotations.

learn.heading: Keys, signatures, and where they live
body: A digital signature is a hash of the message encrypted with the sender’s private key. Verification decrypts with the public key, re-hashes, and compares. It proves origin and integrity — but not confidentiality, since anyone can read a signed message.

Keys need homes and lifecycles. A hardware security module (HSM) is a network-attached vault serving keys to many systems; a TPM is a chip binding keys to one motherboard. Rotate keys on schedule and immediately on suspected compromise, and never hard-code them into shipped software — anyone who downloads the app owns the key.

Elliptic-curve crypto gives more strength per bit than RSA: a 256-bit curve rivals RSA-3072, which is why ECC dominates on phones and constrained devices. And when secrecy must also hide the message’s very existence, steganography tucks data inside innocent files — but unlike encryption, it provides no mathematical guarantee once discovered.

Third party holds key copies for recovery
Hash, then encrypt hash with private key

overview: Before any tool or protocol, security rests on a handful of ideas that show up on every exam and in every real design review: what you are protecting (the CIA triad), who gets in (AAA), and how you arrange trust (zero trust, defense in depth, least privilege).
This lesson turns those abstractions into working instincts — which goal a ransomware attack hits, why a mantrap beats a polite sign, and how biometric error rates actually trade off.

learn.heading: CIA and AAA in practice
body: Confidentiality keeps secrets secret, integrity keeps data trustworthy, availability keeps systems reachable. Ransomware that encrypts your files attacks availability; when it also steals them for double extortion, confidentiality falls too. A database with wrong balances but no outage is an integrity failure — and only a verified clean copy restores it, not just any backup.

Redundancy — RAID, clustering, generators — buys availability. Hashes, checksums, and version control buy integrity by detecting change. Encryption buys confidentiality. Most real controls serve one goal primarily; knowing which one tells you what a given attack actually breaks.

AAA separates three questions: authentication (prove who you are), authorization (what you may do), and accounting (a record of what you did). A badge that opens the door but logs nothing failed at accounting — and without that record, incident response is blind. Authorization should default to implicit deny: nothing is allowed unless explicitly granted.

learn.heading: Zero trust and layered defense
body: The old castle-and-moat model trusted everything inside the network. Zero trust assumes no implicit trust by location: every request is verified continuously, based on identity, device health, and context. A compromised laptop on the LAN gets no free pass.

Microsegmentation carves the network into tiny isolated zones so breaching one does not open the rest. Continuous validation re-checks throughout the session rather than once at login. The policy engine decides, the administrator configures, and the enforcement point applies — the three logical pieces of a NIST 800-207 architecture.

Defense in depth layers controls so one failure is not a breach: if phishing beats training, MFA and EDR still stand in the way. "Assume breach" designs detection, segmentation, and least privilege as if attackers were already inside — because eventually, they will be.

learn.heading: Physical security and biometrics
body: Physical controls are the outermost layer. Bollards stop vehicle ramming; a mantrap — two interlocked doors where the second opens only after the first closes — defeats tailgating; a Faraday cage blocks all radio signals for rooms where wireless exfiltration is a concern. Cable locks deter opportunistic laptop theft, and visitor logs with escorts keep non-employees accountable.

Biometrics authenticate "something you are": fingerprint, iris, face, voice. Two error rates govern them — the false acceptance rate (wrongly admitting) and false rejection rate (wrongly denying) — and lowering one raises the other. The crossover error rate, where the two are equal, lets you compare systems objectively.
The catch with biometrics is permanence: you cannot revoke a compromised fingerprint. Use them for convenience, and pair them with something revocable — a PIN or token — where the stakes are high.

learn.heading: Design principles that prevent fraud
body: Separation of duties splits critical tasks so no single person can complete fraud alone — the approver of payments cannot also issue them. Dual control goes further, requiring two authorized people for one sensitive action, as in key ceremonies and large transfers.

Job rotation exposes fraud by putting fresh eyes on a role, and mandatory vacations force a break in any scheme that needs constant cover — both are classic anti-fraud controls, especially in finance. "Need to know" limits information access to those whose role requires it.

These principles compose: classification labels data, need-to-know limits who sees it, least privilege limits what they can do with it, and separation of duties ensures no one person controls the whole chain.

overview: Security exists to manage risk, not to eliminate it — and risk is a business language, not a technical one. Leaders decide how much risk to accept; your job is to measure it honestly, price it in dollars or clear ratings, and drive it down to the line they drew.
This lesson covers how risks are assessed and answered, what a business impact analysis produces, and how continuity planning keeps the organisation alive when controls fail.

learn.heading: Measuring and answering risk
body: Qualitative assessments rate risks high, medium, or low — fast and cheap. Quantitative assessments put numbers on them: single loss expectancy times annualized rate of occurrence gives annualized loss expectancy in dollars. Use qualitative for speed, quantitative when you need to justify a budget.

A risk matrix plots likelihood against impact so the red corner — high likelihood times high impact — demands action first. Inherent risk is what you face before controls; residual risk is what remains after. The goal is never zero risk; it is residual risk at or below the appetite leadership set.

Four answers exist for any risk: mitigate it with controls, transfer it with insurance or outsourcing, accept it with formal sign-off, or avoid it by stopping the activity. Acceptance is a documented decision with an expiry date, not neglect — and transfer never removes your residual liability.

learn.heading: Business impact analysis and continuity
body: The business impact analysis identifies critical functions, sets recovery time and recovery point objectives for each, and maps the dependencies they need. Its outputs — not anyone’s gut feeling — drive the continuity budget. Maximum tolerable downtime caps it all: the RTO must fit inside the MTD or recovery is theatre.

The business continuity plan keeps the whole organisation running and belongs to business leadership; the disaster recovery plan restores IT systems and belongs to IT. DRP is a subset of BCP. Succession planning names trained backups for every critical role, because incidents do not wait for the one expert to return.

Match alternate sites to RTO: hot sites run ready for seconds-to-minutes recovery, warm sites need hours, cold sites are empty space for days-long rebuilds. Separate primary and recovery sites geographically — one regional disaster must not take both — and consider power grids and flood plains, not just mileage.

learn.heading: Backups, testing, and communication
body: Full backups copy everything; incremental copies changes since the last backup of any kind (fast daily, slow to restore); differential copies changes since the last full (the middle path). Align backup frequency to the recovery point objective — a weekly tape cannot serve a four-hour RPO.

Test realism in stages: tabletops talk through a scenario, functional exercises actually fail systems over, full-interruption tests run the business from the alternate site. Escalate gradually, because the most realistic tests risk real disruption. Test generators under load monthly — an untested generator is a hope, not a control.

Continuity lives or dies on communication: who contacts whom, over which out-of-band channels, with pre-drafted messages for staff, customers, regulators, and media. Rehearse call trees — people change numbers, and a drill finds the dead branches before 2 a.m. does.

overview: Someone has to decide what "secure enough" means, prove it to outsiders, and keep vendors honest. That is governance: the laws that constrain you, the frameworks that organise you, the audits that verify you, and the contracts that bind your third parties.
This lesson maps the compliance landscape Security+ tests — HIPAA, SOX, PCI DSS, GDPR and friends — plus the frameworks, privacy principles, and vendor-risk practices that turn policy into proof.

learn.heading: The compliance landscape
body: HIPAA protects health information held by covered entities and their business associates, with breach notification within 60 days. Sarbanes-Oxley demands reliable financial reporting, which forces controlled IT systems under Section 404. The GLBA Safeguards Rule requires written security programs at financial institutions — broadly defined enough to include car dealerships offering financing.

California’s CCPA/CPRA grants consumers rights to know, delete, and opt out of sale or sharing of personal data. FERPA guards student education records. FISMA makes federal systems categorise, control, assess, authorise, and continuously monitor via the NIST Risk Management Framework.

PCI DSS is an industry standard, not a law — but its twelve requirement families bind anyone handling card data, and transaction volume decides whether you self-assess or face an on-site Report on Compliance. GDPR adds data-subject rights — access, rectification, erasure, portability, objection — and the ePrivacy Directive layers cookie consent on top.

learn.heading: Frameworks that organise security
body: The NIST Risk Management Framework runs seven steps, authorisation being an explicit risk decision.

items.name: Prepare
items.does: Set context, roles and risk strategy before any system work.

items.name: Categorize
items.does: Rate the system by the impact of losing confidentiality, integrity or availability.

items.name: Select
items.does: Choose a baseline of controls and tailor it.

items.name: Implement
items.does: Put the controls in place and document them.

items.name: Assess
items.does: Test that the controls work as intended.

items.name: Authorize
items.does: A senior official explicitly accepts the residual risk.

items.name: Monitor
items.does: Watch controls and risk continuously, and reassess on change.

body: ISO 27001 states certifiable requirements for an information security management system; ISO 27002 is the companion code of practice, and ISO 27701 extends both into privacy.

The CIS Controls v8 organise eighteen controls into Implementation Groups: IG1 is basic cyber hygiene every organisation should reach, IG2 and IG3 add depth for the mature. SOC 2 reports on five trust services criteria — Security plus Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, and Privacy as needed — under the SSAE 18 auditing standard.
NIST CSF 2.0 added Govern as a sixth top-level function, placing organisational context, risk strategy, and supply-chain oversight above the original five.

items.name: Govern
items.does: Organisational context, risk strategy, policy and supply-chain oversight; sits over the other five.

items.name: Identify
items.does: Understand assets, risks and the business context.

items.name: Protect
items.does: Safeguards that limit or contain an incident.

items.name: Detect
items.does: Find cybersecurity events quickly.

items.name: Respond
items.does: Act on a detected incident.

items.name: Recover
items.does: Restore capabilities and services.

body: For cloud, the CSA Cloud Controls Matrix maps provider controls to ISO, SOC 2, and others, and FedRAMP standardises authorisation for US federal cloud use.

learn.heading: Privacy principles and data rights
body: Collect and keep only what you need — data minimization shrinks both breach blast radius and compliance burden — and use it only for the purpose collected, which is purpose limitation. Know your data regimes: PII identifies a person, PHI is health data, PCI is cardholder data, each triggering different laws and handling.

Data sovereignty means data answers to the laws where it resides, driving residency and cloud-region choices. The right to erasure is easy to promise and hard to deliver: every copy must be found across backups, logs, analytics, and vendor systems. True anonymization escapes GDPR scope; mere de-identification, where re-identification remains possible, does not.

Build privacy in from the start rather than bolting it on. The controller decides purposes and means and carries primary accountability; the processor acts only on instructions. Moving personal data across borders needs an adequacy decision, Standard Contractual Clauses, or Binding Corporate Rules — and high-risk processing triggers a Data Protection Impact Assessment first.

learn.heading: Policies, audits, and third-party risk
body: Policies set intent: acceptable use defines permitted behaviour and consequences; data retention sets how long each type lives and how it dies; BYOD rests on MDM enrolment plus containerisation; and the IR policy authorises, the plan organises, the playbook executes. NIST 800-63B modernised password thinking: long passphrases, no forced rotation without cause, and checks against breached lists.

Internal audits serve management and can run continuously; external audits serve regulators or customers and are point-in-time. A good scope states objectives, systems, period, and criteria before fieldwork. Findings mean a control failed and demand dated responses; continuous auditing replaces annual sampling with automated, always-on testing.

Vet vendors before signing — security posture, financial health, compliance evidence, incident history — because leverage evaporates after the contract is signed. Demand right-to-audit clauses, define SLAs with measurement and remedies (not wishes), and remember fourth-party risk: your vendors’ vendors, whom you never vetted. Offboard completely — orphaned vendor VPN accounts are a classic breach path.

Certifiable ISMS vs code of practice

overview: Security operations is the discipline of turning signals into decisions under pressure. Every scenario in this lesson is a judgement call an analyst actually faces: an alert that could be nothing or everything, a noisy rule everyone has learned to ignore, a user who swears they were “just browsing”. The right move is rarely the technical one first — it is the operational one: contain, verify, escalate, communicate.

This lesson covers SIEM triage and correlation, alert tuning, SOAR playbooks, log pipelines and retention, threat hunting hypotheses, and the handoffs and metrics that keep a SOC honest. If the fundamentals decks taught you the vocabulary, these scenarios teach you the reflexes.

learn.heading: Triage: contain first, investigate second
body: Triage answers one question: is this malicious, and is it still active? Until you know, the defensible posture is containment — disable the account, isolate the host, revoke the sessions. Investigation then proceeds without the attacker watching or spreading. Every minute of authenticated attacker access is potential data loss.

Impossible travel is physics, not policy: an account in two places at once is compromised until proven otherwise, and no manager’s assurance overrides it. Push bombing, lateral movement to a domain controller, and beaconing all share the same tell — machine behaviour that no human explanation justifies. Verify after containment, never before.

Correlation is why SIEMs exist: a failed login from a new country means little alone, but failed login followed by success from that country followed by a large download is a pattern. Train yourself to read combinations, not alerts.

learn.heading: Tuning, pipelines, and honest metrics
body: Alert fatigue is a process failure with a technical fix: noisy rules need precision, not deletion. Narrow the rule’s scope — require an admin logon, exclude known-good sources, add correlation — then measure for two weeks. Bulk-closing is a culture problem that tuning alone will not fix.

The log pipeline is invisible until it breaks: collectors and forwarders, parsing, normalisation, hot/warm/cold retention. A silent EPS drop or an unparsed feed after a firmware upgrade is a detection outage — treat it like one, fix the parser, and backfill from raw logs so the gap stays searchable.
Measure outcomes, not noise: true-positive rate, mean time to detect and respond to full recovery, and repeat causes. Alert volume measures how loud the SOC is; MTTD/MTTR measures how good it is.

learn.heading: Hunting, handoffs, and the human layer
body: Threat hunting starts from a hypothesis and a baseline: enumerate a mechanism across the fleet and investigate the outliers. Stack-counting scheduled tasks or WMI subscriptions works because legitimate activity repeats thousands of times — attackers hide in the rare deviations.

Shift handoffs are where investigations die. A good handoff documents the timeline, the IoCs, what was blocked, and crucially what was not yet checked — persistence, lateral movement — with explicit next steps. Unstated assumptions become missed follow-ups.

SOAR earns its keep on high-volume, low-judgment work: phishing triage, enrichment, ticketing, IoC blocking. New automations graduate from alert-only to human-in-the-loop to autonomous by blast radius — a false positive in an auto-isolation playbook is an outage you caused yourself.

Many prompts then an approval; kill the session
Weak signals compose into strong indicators

overview: Hardening and vulnerability management are where security meets the calendar: every patch competes with uptime, every baseline competes with convenience, and every exception competes with memory. The scenarios in this lesson are the calls a security engineer actually makes — which finding gets the emergency window, what to do about the system that can never be patched, how to answer “are we getting safer?”

This lesson covers patch prioritization by exposure and exploitability, secure baselines and drift, asset discovery, compensating controls for unpatchable systems, exception discipline, and the metrics that prove a vulnerability program works.

learn.heading: Prioritize by exposure, not by severity alone
body: CVSS measures the vulnerability; risk measures the vulnerability in your environment. An internet-facing RCE with a public exploit outranks a critical on an isolated host with no exploit — exposure plus exploitability beats the number. KEV-listed items and crown-jewel adjacency are tiebreakers.

Emergency change exists for exactly this: a publicly exploited edge vulnerability cannot wait for Friday’s change board. But emergencies need discipline too — staged rings, tested rollback, and clear communication, or the patch becomes its own outage.
SLAs must encode risk to be real: internet-facing criticals in days, internal highs in weeks, everything tracked with owners and dates. “Everything is critical” means nothing is.

learn.heading: Baselines, drift, and the unpatchable
body: A secure baseline is an approved, locked-down configuration every system is compared against — CIS benchmarks or STIGs as the template, enforced as code. Drift is the constant enemy: “needed for troubleshooting” changes accumulate until the fleet no longer matches the standard. Alert on drift and require tracked, temporary exceptions.

Some systems can never be patched: the XP box running the press, the bankrupt vendor’s thermostat, the EOL ERP. The playbook is the same every time — isolate on a dedicated segment, allow only the traffic the function needs, monitor the segment, and document the risk exception with a review date.

Golden images, CI guardrails, and default-deny cloud settings make the secure state the default. Repeat misconfigurations — the third public bucket, the same 40 missing patches on every new VM — are guardrail failures, not training failures.

learn.heading: Exceptions, assets, and honest measurement
body: Vulnerability exceptions are time-boxed risk acceptances: written, signed at the right authority level, with compensating controls and an expiry. When the compensating control dies or the review lapses, the exception dies with it. Verbal acceptance evaporates at the first incident.

Unknown assets are unpatched assets. Discovery must be continuous and reconciled against the CMDB, because scans only see what they are pointed at. Decommissioned servers still powered on and domain-joined are attacker infrastructure waiting to happen — isolate, verify dependencies, then wipe and remove properly.

Answer “are we getting safer?” with outcomes: mean time to remediate for exposed criticals, exception aging, repeat findings. Closed-ticket counts reward closing easy findings; the board needs to know how fast the dangerous ones die.

For exploited edge vulns; still needs rings and rollback
Enforce as code; alert; exceptions tracked and temporary
Rebuild monthly in a pipeline, scan before promote
Continuous scans reconciled against the CMDB
Isolate → verify deps → wipe → remove from domain

overview: Tools don’t secure anything — operated tools do. EDR that nobody tunes, NAC that quarantines the wrong laptops, DLP that blocks the legal team into demanding its removal: every control in this lesson is powerful and every one fails when it is misconfigured, unscoped, or trusted blindly. The scenarios are about operating the stack, not buying it.

This lesson covers EDR triage and tamper response, NAC and network access decisions, DLP tuning, identity lifecycle and privileged access operations, and the automation discipline that keeps SOAR from becoming an outage machine.

learn.heading: EDR: trust the telemetry, isolate on tradecraft
body: EDR asks “what did this process just do?” — parent-child relationships, command lines, network egress. Rundll32 sideloading a DLL from Downloads with outbound traffic is living-off-the-land tradecraft no user explanation overrides. When the agent itself is tampered with — service disabled, logs cleared — that is not a glitch; isolate immediately.

EDR is a per-platform configuration, not one control: server workloads need their own memory-scanning and behavioral policies, tested with adversary emulation. And when the attacker owns local admin, local logs are not the system of record — real-time forwarding to the SIEM is what preserves evidence.
Coverage gaps are findings about the control, not the user: a DLP that didn’t fire on a browser upload means the policy scope or agent health failed. Verify scope and health before blaming anyone.

learn.heading: NAC and DLP: enforce, but keep the business working
body: NAC gates on identity plus health: patched, compliant, authenticated. Agentless profiling with fingerprinting gives unmanageable devices — sensors, cameras, BYOD — a segmented home instead of blind trust. Quarantine loops are usually telemetry mismatches: validate what the health check actually measures before bypassing the control.

Guest networks are untrusted by definition: the control that matters is isolation — separate VLAN, client isolation, no corporate routes — not the strength of the captive portal. A pen tester pivoting from guest to corporate LAN means segmentation failed, not onboarding.

DLP dies the day it blocks legitimate work permanently. Tune the patterns, scope exceptions narrowly with approval — legal’s contract workflow, not the whole legal department — because a bypassed control protects nothing.

learn.heading: Identity operations and automation discipline
body: Identity lifecycle runs on the HR system of record: joiner, mover, leaver with role-based templates and same-day revocation. Manual spreadsheets are where orphaned accounts are born — and orphaned privileged accounts are attacker persistence. Ancient service accounts get scoped, replaced with least-privilege managed identities, and retired with a rollback window.

Privileged access is vaulted, just-in-time, session-recorded, and break-glass only under dual control with mandatory rotation after. Session recording is the accountability half of elevation; skipping it “for speed” turns JIT into standing privilege with extra steps.

Automate high-volume, low-judgment work first — phishing triage, enrichment, IoC blocking — and graduate new playbooks from alert-only to human-in-the-loop to autonomous by blast radius. Full auto-remediation on day one turns the first false positive into the outage you caused.

cheatSheet: Judge parent-child + location + egress, not the binary
Isolate completely; onboarding strength is secondary
Narrow exceptions with approval, never blanket disables
HR system of record drives provision/deprovision
Top insider vector; fix the feed, not just the accounts
Dual control, logged, mandatory rotation after
One identity, one MFA policy, one kill switch

overview: Incident response is the exam’s hardest domain because it is the job’s hardest phase: decisions with incomplete information, a clock running, and stakeholders pulling in opposite directions. The scenarios in this lesson run the full NIST lifecycle — preparation through lessons learned — the way it actually unfolds, including the parts nobody puts in the playbook: the CEO who wants to chat with the attackers, the 40-person bridge where nothing gets decided, the scribe who stops taking notes.

This lesson covers scoping before action, evidence handling and chain of custody, containment strategies including cloud, the forensics-vs-business tension, legal and notification duties, command structure, and the post-incident work that decides whether it happens again.

learn.heading: Scope first, preserve as you go
body: The first move in any incident is scoping: how many, how far, patient zero, the vector. Reimaging before scoping destroys evidence without stopping the spread — you will reimage the same machines twice. Declare the incident, assemble the team, establish out-of-band communications, then act.

Evidence handling starts at minute one: capture volatile data in order of volatility — memory and network state before disk — because a rootkit lives in RAM and a powered-off box is a dead end. Hash at acquisition, document every handler, and keep images off shared folders: chain of custody is what makes evidence admissible.

Forensics and the business are not enemies when the plan predates the incident: image the CFO’s laptop, hand over a loaner, and the presentation happens on time. Litigation holds override retention schedules — automated purges during an investigation are spoliation.

learn.heading: Contain by the environment you are in
body: Containment stops the bleeding: isolate affected hosts now, but do not power off yet — memory evidence dies with the power. Short-term containment buys time; long-term containment is hardened fixes while operating. Eradication must be verified before recovery, or you restore into the same vulnerability.

Cloud containment targets identity, not hosts: revoke sessions and keys, attach deny-all policies, snapshot resources for forensics before terminating anything. On-prem instincts applied to the cloud miss the actual control plane.

The ransomware order of operations is fixed: contain, preserve evidence during eradication, then restore from known-good backups in the right sequence — identity and core infrastructure before business apps. Paying the ransom and restoring early are both business-legal decisions, never technical shortcuts.

learn.heading: Command, communicate, and actually learn
body: Incidents are managed, not meeting’d: one incident commander, defined roles — operations, communications, legal liaison, scribe — and observers on a listen-only channel. The scribe’s timeline is the legal record, the notification evidence, and the lessons-learned input; scribing is the actual work.

External communication runs through legal with a holding statement: acknowledge the investigation promptly, never deny what you have not verified. Breach notification clocks start at discovery and do not wait for a complete investigation.

Lessons learned is a phase, not a meeting: blameless by rule, focused on systems not people, and every recommendation gets an owner, a deadline, and a verification check. The same vector succeeding twice means the review failed — track it.

cheatSheet: Declare, scope, out-of-band comms — then act
Suspends purges; spoliation is worse than the breach
One commander, defined roles, scribe, listen-only observers
Holding statement via legal; never deny unverified
Clock starts at discovery; runs parallel to investigation
Tests people and plan: comms, roles, authorities
Blameless, owner + date + verification per item
MTTD/MTTR to full recovery; repeat causes
Centralized tested logging before you need it

overview: Threats don’t arrive labeled. The scenarios in this lesson are the calls a defender actually makes when the evidence is partial: two incidents land the same week — are they one actor or two? Credentials are used from a foreign IP with no malware in sight — what vector do you chase? A trusted vendor’s update turns malicious overnight. The wrong attribution sends the response down the wrong road, and the wrong vector keeps the real door open.

This lesson covers threat-actor profiling (APT vs e-crime vs insider vs hacktivist), initial-access identification (exposed services, trusted relationships, physical media, supply chain), and the structural fixes that remove whole attack classes — network segmentation for vendors, MFA for remote access, and the discipline of never merging incidents by timing alone.

learn.heading: Attribution: dwell, tooling, and objectives
body: Attribution starts from three signals: how long they stayed, how sophisticated their tooling was, and what they wanted. Eleven months of slow IP theft with custom tools and no ransom note is espionage; loud, fast double extortion is e-crime. The two can hit the same week and still be different actors — timing is the weakest attribution signal there is.

Insiders leave access logs instead of malware: authorized credentials at odd hours, data touched that matches no project, no phishing email to find. When the technical trail is empty but the access trail isn’t, test the human vector before chasing the technical one.

Hacktivists want an audience, not assets: defacement is loud by design. Ransomware crews want money fast. Nation-states want persistence and quiet. Match the response to the motive — a graffiti incident doesn’t need a full data-breach response, and a wiper doesn’t negotiate.

learn.heading: Initial access: find the real door
body: Attackers take the easiest path in: exposed RDP with weak credentials needs no phishing, a hijacked vendor mailbox needs no exploit, a labeled USB in the parking lot needs no zero-day. Forensics should identify the actual vector, because the fix for the wrong vector leaves the real door open.

Trusted relationships are attack surface: vendor VPNs, OAuth grants, shared update channels. The structural fix is always the same — replace standing trust with temporary, scoped, expiring access. A vendor that needs support access gets just-in-time access, not a permanent tunnel.

Living-off-the-land techniques (PowerShell, WMI, legitimate cloud services) defeat file-based defenses by having no file to find. When the evidence shows no binary, detection moves to behavior: command-line logging, process trees, and anomaly detection.

learn.heading: Ecosystems, not lone wolves
body: Modern attacks are supply chains: initial-access brokers sell footholds, affiliates deploy ransomware, and the two may never meet. Defending only the ransomware phase misses the business model — killing initial access (phishing, exposed services, valid accounts) starves the whole chain.

Supply-chain compromise inverts trust: the signed update, the vendor’s VPN, the managed service. When multiple customers fall the same day with one common vendor, contain the vendor’s access first and verify out-of-band — the compromised channel can’t be the verification channel.

Mergers, acquisitions, and “temporary” connections are attack vectors with paperwork: acquired networks without your baselines must stay isolated behind strict controls until they meet your standards. “Temporary” flat connections become permanent with none of your controls.

cheatSheet: Slow quiet theft vs loud fast extortion
Defend initial access, not just ransomware

overview: Malware announces itself by behavior, not by name. The scenarios in this lesson are the identifications an analyst actually makes: a worm that needs no user, a RAT with a human behind it, a rootkit that makes every tool lie, ransomware that already stole the data before it encrypted. The right identification drives the right response — and the wrong one wastes the response on the wrong layer.

This lesson covers malware identification from behavior (worms, fileless, RATs, rootkits, keyloggers, trojans, spyware), ransomware variants and the double-extortion reality, persistence below the OS, and the containment choices each type demands — network segmentation for worms, memory forensics for fileless, rebuild-from-gold for rootkits.

learn.heading: Identify from behavior, not signatures
body: Self-propagation without user action is a worm: the response is a network action (segmentation) before a host action, because cleaning hosts on a flat network just re-infects them. Malicious behavior with no file on disk is fileless: signature AV has nothing to find, so the response is memory forensics plus behavioral EDR.

Interactive behavior — windows moving, files browsed in odd order — means a RAT with a live operator, not automated malware. Isolation plus memory capture, and every credential typed on that host is burned. Polymorphic strains that change every infection defeat static signatures by design: judge what code does, not what it looks like.

Persistence below the OS (firmware, bootkits) survives every reinstall: when cleaning fails repeatedly, the fix is reflash from trusted media or hardware replacement. Tools running on a compromised OS can lie — trust must come from outside the compromised environment.

learn.heading: Ransomware: the extortion reality
body: Double extortion defeats the “we have backups” defense: the data was stolen before it was encrypted, and payment doesn’t un-steal it. The response is restore plus legal and notification process — never payment as a plan. A wallet with no identification mechanism and no communication channel is a wiper in costume: there is no recovery path, so don’t pay.

Ransomware hunts backups first: a backup server that’s domain-joined and reachable is just another target. “Offline” must mean truly isolated — air-gapped or immutable, on separate credentials. And check for public decryptors before paying or rebuilding; free, tested decryption beats both.

Paying marks you as willing to pay and funds the next attack. Direct negotiation by executives creates legal exposure (sanctions risk) and worse terms — route all contact through counsel and the IR firm.

learn.heading: Containment by malware type
body: Shared vectors need fleet-wide responses: a keylogger on a shared terminal burns every credential typed there; adware bundled fleet-wide is a data-exfiltration incident, not a nuisance ticket. Scope the response to the blast radius, not the single machine.

Reinfection means the vector is still alive: a shared USB with an autorun payload, a trojanized installer still in use. Clean the vector before the hosts — mopping with the tap running just floods again. And time your defenses to adversary timing: holiday-weekend attacks assume skeleton crews.

Unpatchable and unmanaged devices (IoT cameras, legacy terminals) become attacker infrastructure: when firmware can’t be fixed, segmentation is the compensating control. Isolate them on dedicated VLANs with only required traffic allowed.

cheatSheet: RAM only: memory forensics + behavioral EDR
OS lies: boot from known-good media
Data stolen first: payment buys nothing
Vector still alive: kill it first
Check No More Ransom before paying

overview: The human and the application are the two softest targets, and attackers work both. The scenarios in this lesson are the judgments defenders actually make: a perfectly personalized email to the CFO, a helpdesk call armed with LinkedIn facts, a login form that answers “user not found” a little too helpfully, a coupon that applies twice when double-clicked. Each one pairs the social technique with the technical control that defeats it.

This lesson covers phishing variants (spear, whaling, vishing, smishing, quishing), pretexting and helpdesk verification, credential attacks (spraying, stuffing, enumeration), and the OWASP-class application flaws as incident scenarios — injection, XSS, IDOR, XXE, SSRF, race conditions, and insecure uploads — with the structural fixes for each.

learn.heading: Engineered trust: verify out-of-band
body: Every social attack manufactures trust plus urgency: the accurate board-meeting details in the phish, the employee ID recited to the helpdesk, the “fraud department” demanding an instant wire. The defense is always the same motion — terminate the contact and re-establish it through a channel the attacker doesn’t control.

Public facts are not authentication: names, IDs, and manager names from LinkedIn make pretexting convincing but prove nothing. Helpdesk verification must rely on secrets or callbacks to numbers on file. And some rules must be absolute: MFA codes are never spoken aloud, to anyone, for any reason.

Password managers are phishing detectors: refusal to autofill on a lookalike domain is the signal. Teach staff that the manager’s silence plus a slightly-off URL is the whole verdict — no further investigation needed before closing the tab.

learn.heading: Credential attacks: beyond lockouts
body: Password spraying stays under lockout thresholds by design — a few attempts per user across thousands of users. Account lockouts won’t catch it; MFA plus behavioral throttling will. And any account that authenticated during the spray window gets treated as compromised.

Distinct error messages (“user not found” vs “wrong password”) are account-enumeration oracles that feed targeted phishing. The secure pattern is ambiguous responses (“if an account exists, we’ve emailed it”) plus throttling — helpful to users, useless to attackers.
Credential stuffing uses real passwords from other breaches: the defense is MFA plus breach-corpus monitoring, because the passwords are correct and lockouts won’t save reused credentials.

learn.heading: Application flaws as incidents
body: Injection is a code/data boundary failure: concatenated SQL, reflected input, unescaped ticket content. The structural fixes are parameterized queries and output encoding — blacklists and escaping are bypassable. WAFs are speed bumps, not fixes.

Authorization failures (IDOR, missing function-level checks) are the most common “logged-in but looking at someone else’s data” incidents: every object fetch must verify ownership server-side. Never trust the parameter, the hidden field, or the client.

State-changing actions must be POST with anti-CSRF tokens, uploads must be content-validated and stored outside the web root, and XML parsers must not resolve external entities. Each of these is a secure-defaults failure — the fix is making the safe behavior the default, not a per-case decision.

cheatSheet: Verify via trusted channel, never the message

overview: Vulnerability management is where security meets the calendar: every patch competes with uptime, every scan lies a little, and every “critical” needs context. The scenarios in this lesson are the calls a security engineer actually makes — which of 4,000 findings is real, what to do when there is no patch, how to answer a researcher, and how to tell whether the program is actually working.

This lesson covers scan interpretation (false positives, credentialed vs unauthenticated, scan integrity), risk-based prioritization (CVSS vs exposure vs exploitability, KEV), zero-day and unpatchable-system response with compensating controls, coordinated disclosure and bug bounties, and the metrics that prove a vulnerability program works.

learn.heading: Scans lie: verify before you patch
body: Unauthenticated scans guess from banners; credentialed scans verify from package managers. Treating 4,000 banner matches as findings burns the quarter on ghosts — verify the detection method before reopening the work. And a scan whose credentials expired mid-run is worse than no scan: it reports confidence it doesn’t have.

Stale plugins flag patched systems; version detection misreads backported fixes. The discipline is: reproduce the finding with current, credentialed data before scheduling the work. Re-patching a patched system is pure waste.
Discovery is part of scanning: 60 unknown devices on a scan means shadow IT, and unknown assets are unpatched assets. Quarantine first to a discovery VLAN, identify owners, then onboard or remove.

learn.heading: Risk, not just severity
body: CVSS measures the vulnerability; risk measures the vulnerability in your environment. An internet-facing 7.5 with a public exploit outranks an isolated 9.8 — exposure plus exploitability beats the number. KEV-listed items and crown-jewel adjacency are the tiebreakers.

Zero-days invert the order: when no patch exists, compensating controls become the patch — restrict management interfaces, deploy IPS signatures, increase monitoring — then patch the hour it drops. Waiting unprotected for the vendor is not a strategy.

Unpatchable systems (medical devices, EOL industrial gear) get the standard treatment every time: dedicated segment, allowlisted traffic only, monitoring, and a documented risk exception with a review date. “We’ll replace it someday” is not a control.

learn.heading: Disclosure, bounties, and honest measurement
body: Coordinated disclosure is a contract: acknowledge promptly, validate, fix within the window, credit the researcher. Ghosting a good-faith reporter converts an ally into full disclosure — and a public one. Treat external reports like free pen tests.

Risk acceptance is a decision with paperwork and an expiry: written, signed at the right authority level, with compensating controls and a review date. Silent ignoring is not acceptance — it’s negligence with better branding.

Measure outcomes, not activity: mean time to remediate for exposed criticals, exception aging, repeat findings. When closed-ticket counts look great while MTTR climbs, the program is optimizing easy wins — re-anchor leadership reporting on risk-weighted metrics.

cheatSheet: Compensating controls now, patch at drop

overview: Cloud security is the discipline of controlling what you no longer own: the provider owns the hypervisor and the building, you own everything you configure — and misconfiguration is the number one breach cause. The scenarios in this lesson are the calls cloud engineers actually make — the public bucket with anonymous downloads, the drifted Terraform state, the serverless function with an admin role, the single region that is not a DR plan.

This lesson covers shared responsibility in practice, IaC discipline, container and Kubernetes hardening, identity in the cloud, multi-cloud visibility, and data residency. If the trivia decks taught you the vocabulary, these scenarios teach you the reflexes.

learn.heading: Your half of the shared model
body: Shared responsibility is a boundary, not a blur: the provider secures the hypervisor, the building, and the managed service — you secure your configurations, your identities, your data, and your code. Nearly every headline cloud breach is a customer-side misconfiguration: a public bucket, an open security group, a committed key.

Guardrails beat guidance: SCPs, organization policies, and CI checks make the safe path the default. Relying on every engineer remembering every setting is how 300 open security groups happen. Default-deny and automated remediation turn policy into physics.

Shadow cloud is the enemy of the model: workloads in personal accounts have no logging, no SSO, no offboarding. Bring them under the organization or shut them down — invisible infrastructure is unprotected infrastructure.

learn.heading: IaC, containers, and ephemeral discipline
body: Infrastructure as code only works if the code is the truth: hotfixes that bypass the pipeline become permanent drift, and the next deploy surprises everyone. Reconcile every change into code, scan it before apply, and treat the plan output as a security review.

Containers and serverless trade servers for supply chains: minimal base images, signed artifacts, non-root runtimes, and per-function IAM roles. Ephemeral does not mean invisible — scan functions like any code and scope roles to the exact APIs called.

Kubernetes concentrates privilege: cluster-admin for a CI bot is a standing takeover waiting for a leaked token. Namespace-scoped roles, admission policies, and signed images keep the orchestrator from becoming the attacker’s.

learn.heading: Identity, visibility, and residency
body: Cloud identity is the new perimeter: wildcard trust policies, stale IAM users, and disabled audit logging are the cloud equivalents of open doors. Scope trusts to named principals, deprovision on HR events, and never cut logging to save money.

You cannot protect what you cannot enumerate: multi-cloud without aggregated inventory and consistent tagging is three blind spots. A CSPM or CMDB with enforced tagging turns sprawl into something you can actually defend.

Data residency is decided by contracts and regulators, not latency: when the agreement says EU, the region choice is compliance. Encryption does not override residency — the law cares where the bits sleep.

cheatSheet: Provider: platform; you: config, identity, data
No logging, no SSO = invisible risk
Open door — scope to named principals

overview: Network architecture is the discipline of deciding what can reach what — and proving it. Every scenario in this lesson is a design call with real stakes: the flat /16 that let an attacker cross to the domain controllers in 40 minutes, the vendor who got a full-tunnel VPN for one database, the OT network reachable from the helpdesk for convenience.

This lesson covers segmentation and microsegmentation, zero trust and ZTNA, SD-WAN and SASE choices, wireless hardening, OT boundaries, and the inspection points that make forensics possible. If the trivia decks taught you the components, these scenarios teach you the trade-offs.

learn.heading: Segmentation is the blast-radius control
body: Lateral movement speed is a network-design metric: on a flat network, one phished laptop becomes a domain compromise. Tiered segmentation — user, server, management — with firewall-enforced flows turns a breach into a contained incident instead of a tour.

Microsegmentation takes it to the workload: per-host or per-service policies so a compromised web tier cannot reach the database tier directly. Each layer reaches only the next; skipping tiers is how breaches become disasters.

Special networks get special treatment: OT behind a boundary, IoT on its own VLAN with no LAN path, voice separated from data, guests nowhere near payment systems. Segmentation by function, not by optimism.

learn.heading: Zero trust and the death of the trusted network
body: VPNs trust the network; zero trust verifies every request: identity plus device posture, per application, every time. Migrating remote access from concentrators to ZTNA shrinks the blast radius from the whole network to the one app.
Bastions concentrate privilege and must be hardened like it: MFA, per-admin accounts, session recording, source allow-listing. The jump host is the keys to the kingdom — treat it accordingly.
NAC only works when it can say no: monitor-mode forever is a dashboard, not a control. Pilot on one segment, define the exception policy, then enforce in stages.

learn.heading: Design choices with price tags
body: SD-WAN versus MPLS is threat-model plus cost: encrypted overlay with central policy can replace private circuits, but unencrypted SD-WAN is just the internet. Backhaul versus local breakout is the same math — policy must follow the traffic, not the 2010 diagram.

Wireless is a physical-layer promise: WPA2-PSK shared across 200 people has no attribution and brutal rotation. Enterprise 802.1X with per-user credentials fixes both — and rogue APs get found by WIDS, not by luck.

Inspect where it matters: IDS in detect-first mode before inline blocking, packet capture or flow data at the edge, DNS forced through your resolvers. Firewall logs are the bouncer’s diary; forensics needs the actual traffic.

overview: Data protection is the discipline of treating data according to what it is worth: classification first, then encryption, keys, and DLP that follow the classification instead of fighting the business. The scenarios in this lesson are the calls that decide whether a lost laptop is a hardware expense or a breach notification.

This lesson covers classification-driven handling, encryption choices and key management, TLS and certificate lifecycle, DLP tuning, tokenization versus masking, and the end-of-life of data — retention, sanitization, and the paper nobody thinks about.

learn.heading: Classify first, then protect
body: Controls follow classification: public, internal, confidential, restricted — each with handling rules. Without classes, every file gets the same treatment, which means the crown jewels get the same treatment as the lunch menu.
Logs, backups, and analytics inherit sensitivity: PII in logs shipped to a vendor is PII at the vendor. Scrub, mask, or tokenize at the boundary — the data’s classification travels with it.
Retention is a schedule with a legal-hold process, not a sentiment: keep what law and business require, defensibly delete the rest. Every retained byte is discoverable and breachable.

learn.heading: Encryption is key management
body: Encryption without key protection is decoration: keys belong in a KMS or HSM with access controls and audit, never in config files beside the data. Rotation must be scheduled and automated — five-year-old keys are standing risk.
TLS is negotiated, so the server must remove the weak options: TLS 1.0/1.1 and 3DES go, in stages with compatibility monitoring. Attackers pick the weakest cipher you still offer.

Certificates are a lifecycle, not a purchase: automate issuance and renewal, or they expire at 3 AM on a holiday. Self-signed certs train users to click through warnings — issue from a trusted CA instead.

learn.heading: DLP, tokens, and the human layer
body: DLP that blocks legitimate work teaches circumvention: tune by classification and user context, provide approved paths, and the control gets obeyed instead of bypassed. Blunt DLP is just a suggestion with extra steps.

Tokenization beats encryption for stored card data: no PAN in your systems means no PAN in your scope. Masking keeps format for display; anonymization removes linkability for analytics — choose by whether the value must come back.

Endpoints and paper are data too: full-disk encryption plus MDM remote wipe for the stolen laptop, badge-release printing for the PII on the shared printer, blocked-by-default USB with approved encrypted drives.

overview: Resilience is the discipline of assuming failure and being boring about recovery: backups that survive the compromise, sites that match the RTO, and plans that have been tested instead of admired. Every scenario in this lesson is a recovery call — the night the ransomware found the online backups, the generator that had never been load-tested, the DR plan written for a datacenter that no longer exists.
This lesson covers the 3-2-1 rule and immutable backups, RTO/RPO as architecture requirements, site types, high availability, power, and the testing cadence that turns plans into capability.

learn.heading: Backups must survive the disaster
body: 3-2-1 is the floor: three copies, two media, one offsite. A backup sharing fate with production — same SAN, same account, same building — is a copy, not a recovery plan. Offsite means a different risk zone.
Ransomware hunts backups first: online, writable copies die in the same night as production. Immutability — Object Lock, air gaps, offline tape — puts recovery outside the attacker’s reach.
A backup without a tested restore is a prayer: scheduled restore tests prove the read, not just the write. Corruption, missing keys, and wrong procedures only surface when you actually restore.

learn.heading: RTO and RPO are architecture requirements
body: RTO and RPO are not aspirations — they size the architecture: a one-hour RPO needs sub-hourly backups; a two-hour RTO cannot be met by a cold site. Every resilience design starts from these two numbers.

Site types follow the RTO: hot is running, warm is ready, cold is a building. The cheaper the site, the longer the recovery — match the site to the number the business signed, not the budget you wish you had.
High availability is math, not marketing: single servers, single ISPs, single load balancers, and single masters are all single points of failure. Nines are delivered by redundancy, not optimism.

learn.heading: Test everything, document the order
body: Plans rot: staff leave, systems migrate, vendors change. Tabletop exercises graduate to simulations to full failovers on a cadence — an untested plan describes a world that no longer exists.
Power is a chain: UPS bridges exactly the generator’s start time plus margin, and generators must be load-tested under real load. The chain is only as strong as its untested link.

Changes need backout plans and incidents need owners: every change ships with a tested rollback, every post-mortem action item gets an owner and a deadline. Repeat root causes are a management failure wearing a technical costume.

overview: General security concepts are the vocabulary of every security decision: zero trust, control categories, AAA, defense in depth. The exam tests whether you can apply them to messy real situations, not just recite them.
This lesson covers zero-trust migration decisions, classifying controls by type and function, AAA in real designs, and the human and physical controls that surround the technology.

learn.heading: Zero trust in practice
body: Zero trust assumes breach and verifies explicitly: identity becomes the perimeter. The most defensible migration starts with strong identity (MFA everywhere) before re-architecting networks.
Microsegmentation, continuous validation, and least-privilege access are the implementation levers. Start with the crown jewels — do not try to segment everything on day one.

learn.heading: Control categories and functions
body: Controls are classified by nature — technical, administrative (managerial), physical — and by function: preventive stops, detective finds, corrective fixes, plus deterrent, directive, and compensating. Gap analysis must cover all types.
When the ideal control is impossible (legacy systems, budget), compensating controls reduce risk to an acceptable, documented level: isolate plus monitor.

learn.heading: People and physical controls
body: Separation of duties, mandatory vacations, dual control, and job rotation are detective and preventive controls against fraud and single-person dependency.
Physical controls fail at the weakest door: badge readers mean nothing beside a propped side door. Every entry is the perimeter.

cheatSheet: Preventive, detective, corrective (+ deterrent, directive, compensating)
Authentication, authorization, accounting — all three legs
No single person creates and releases
Honeytokens where no legitimate user goes

overview: Cryptography decisions show up everywhere: how data moves, how passwords are stored, how identities are proven. The exam tests judgment — choosing the right mechanism for the situation — more than math.
This lesson covers protocol and algorithm choices, PKI lifecycle failures, key management and recovery, and the operational side of crypto: rotation, revocation, and agility.

learn.heading: Choosing the right mechanism
body: Match the tool to the job: TLS 1.2+ for data in transit, AES-256 for bulk data at rest, asymmetric crypto for key exchange and signatures. Hybrid encryption — symmetric data key wrapped asymmetrically — is the standard pattern.
Passwords need slow, salted, memory-hard hashing (bcrypt, Argon2, scrypt). Fast hashes like SHA-256 are built for attackers. Tokens need unpredictability from a CSPRNG, not hashing.

learn.heading: PKI that survives reality
body: Certificates expire: automate issuance and renewal (ACME) with alerting. Wildcards trade simplicity for blast radius; SAN certs suit distinct names. Self-signed certs in production train users to click through warnings.
Revocation needs a working story: OCSP stapling gives clients fresh proof without per-user queries. Monitor Certificate Transparency logs for misissued certs on your domains.

learn.heading: Keys, recovery, and agility
body: Key recovery must survive departure and compromise: M-of-N escrow means no single custodian can abuse or lose the keys. Rotate on schedule and on events (departures, suspected compromise).
Crypto agility — knowing where each algorithm is used and being able to swap — is the defensible answer to quantum and to the next broken cipher. Inventory first, panic never.

cheatSheet: One key compromise hits all subdomains
Vault + runtime injection, never in repos

overview: Risk management turns security into business language: dollars, probabilities, and decisions. The exam tests whether you can do the math and then make the call — accept, mitigate, transfer, or avoid.
This lesson covers quantitative analysis (SLE, ALE, ARO), qualitative triage, risk ownership and registers, and the economics of controls.

learn.heading: The math that decides
body: ALE = SLE × ARO. A control is justified when its cost is less than the ALE reduction it delivers. Work the numbers before the sticker price decides for you.

Quantitative analysis speaks to boards in dollars; qualitative (red/yellow/green) is faster for triage. Use each where it fits — and aggregate correlated lows on one asset, because three lows can equal a high.

learn.heading: Owning and treating risk
body: Risk owners are business owners with budget authority — unowned risks are unmanaged risks. The four treatments: mitigate, transfer (insurance, outsourcing), accept (signed, time-bound), avoid (retire the asset).
Acceptance is formal: named owner, compensating controls, expiry date. Transfer moves financial impact, never accountability — the breach is still yours.

learn.heading: Keeping risk alive
body: Risk registers are reviewed quarterly and after major changes, fed by threat intel and control testing — continuous assessment, not an annual ritual.
Track time-to-remediate by severity with escalation. New regulations, vendor breaches, and key-person findings all flow into the same register.

cheatSheet: Correlated lows can equal a high
How much risk vs acceptable variance

overview: Governance is how security gets authority: policies with teeth, audits with scope, and compliance that maps to real obligations. The exam tests whether you can navigate the machinery — and know its limits.
This lesson covers the policy hierarchy, audit types and evidence, regulatory applicability, and privacy roles — plus the honest truth that compliance is a floor, not a ceiling.

learn.heading: Policies, audits, evidence
body: Policy states the requirement (executive-approved), standards name the specific rules, procedures give the steps. Audits need precise scope — systems, period, criteria — and tamper-evident evidence, not screenshots.
External audits serve relying parties (SOC 2 Type II for enterprise deals); internal audit serves management readiness. Respond to findings with owner-dated remediation plans.

learn.heading: Regulations in context
body: Applicability follows the data: EU residents trigger GDPR, patient records trigger HIPAA with BAAs, card data triggers PCI DSS. Reduce scope first — tokenization can make most of PCI fall away.
Breach clocks start at awareness: GDPR gives 72 hours, which is why notification runbooks pre-assign owners and templates.

learn.heading: Privacy and the ceiling
body: Data minimization and purpose limitation are the privacy defaults: collect only what the purpose needs, use it only for that purpose. Controller decides the why, processor handles the how — the DPA must reflect reality.
Passing audits is necessary but not sufficient: keep hardening beyond the checklist, because auditors sample and attackers do not.

cheatSheet: EU data subjects, wherever you sit
PHI + signed BAAs down the chain
Collect only what the purpose needs

overview: Your security now depends on other companies: their breaches become your breach notifications. The exam tests whether you can govern the supply chain — assess, contract, and exit.
This lesson covers vendor assessment, contract instruments, fourth parties, concentration risk, and continuity: the exit strategy you prove before you need it.

learn.heading: Assess before you sign
body: Assess vendors while you have leverage: SOC 2 Type II or equivalent evidence, read the exceptions and scope — not just the opinion letter. Scale the review to data access and criticality.
Fourth parties are your risk too: require disclosure and approval rights over subprocessors. Open source gets the same treatment — SBOM and vulnerability monitoring.

learn.heading: Contract the protections
body: MSA for master terms, SOW for the work, SLA for measurable performance. Demand data ownership with return-and-destroy on exit, breach-notification windows, and right-to-audit for critical vendors.
SLA credits are rebates, not recovery: negotiate termination rights for chronic misses. Use renewals to raise the bar.

learn.heading: Plan the exit
body: A tested exit strategy — proven data export, migration path, contractual cooperation — is proven before it is needed. Tier vendors by BIA impact and reassess on acquisitions.
Shared responsibility: the provider secures the cloud, you secure what you put in it. Misconfigured storage is always your breach.

cheatSheet: Period, exceptions, scope — not just the letter
You own it; return + certified destroy on exit
Rebates, not continuity — get exit rights
Tested export before you need it

overview: Cloud computing changed how organisations buy and run IT: capacity on demand, paid for as it is used, managed through APIs. It also changed who is responsible for what, and misunderstanding that split is behind many cloud breaches.

This lesson covers the NIST definition, the service and deployment models, the shared responsibility model, CapEx versus OpEx, elasticity, regions, availability zones and edge locations, and vendor lock-in.

learn.heading: What makes something "cloud"
body: NIST SP 800-145 defines five essential characteristics: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service. If you cannot provision it yourself in minutes and pay by use, it is hosting, not cloud.

Elasticity means resources scale up and down automatically with demand. Scalability is the ability to grow; elasticity is doing it automatically, in both directions. Financially, cloud shifts spending from CapEx (buying hardware up front) to OpEx (pay as you go).

learn.heading: Service and deployment models
body: The three service models are a sliding scale of who manages what: the further up the stack you rent, the less you operate — and the less you control.

stack.title: Cloud service models: who manages what

items.name: IaaS — Infrastructure as a Service
items.does: The provider runs the hardware, virtualisation and facilities; you manage the operating system, runtime, middleware, data and applications. Most control, most responsibility — including patching the OS yourself.
items.examples: EC2, Azure VMs — exam: you patch the OS

items.name: PaaS — Platform as a Service
items.does: The provider adds the OS, runtime and middleware to its side; you deploy code and data. You stop patching servers but keep owning the application, its configuration and its vulnerabilities.
items.examples: App Service, Elastic Beanstalk — exam: you never touch the OS

items.name: FaaS — Function as a Service
items.does: Serverless: a step past PaaS. You deploy single functions; the provider runs, scales and bills them by the millisecond. No servers to think about — but mind cold starts, execution timeouts and lock-in.
items.examples: Lambda, Azure Functions — exam: billed per invocation

items.name: SaaS — Software as a Service
items.does: The provider runs the whole application; you configure it and own your data, users and access. Least operational burden — but a misconfigured sharing setting is still your breach, not theirs.
items.examples: Microsoft 365, Salesforce — exam: you still own data and access

body: Deployment is a separate question from service model: where the cloud physically lives and who it is shared with.

items.name: Public cloud
items.does: Compute sold to anyone over the internet on shared infrastructure. Cheapest and most elastic; you share the building with strangers, isolated by the provider's controls.

items.name: Private cloud
items.does: Cloud infrastructure operated solely for one organisation, on-premises or hosted. More control and isolation — but you carry the capacity planning that public cloud was meant to remove.

items.name: Community cloud
items.does: Shared by several organisations with common concerns — hospitals, government agencies, research consortia. Splits cost and compliance effort among members with similar needs.

items.name: Hybrid cloud
items.does: On-premises or private cloud working together with public cloud: burst to public for peak demand, keep regulated data at home. The model most real enterprises actually run.
items.examples: Sensitive data local, burst to public

learn.heading: Shared responsibility
body: The provider secures the cloud itself (data centres, hardware, the virtualisation layer); the customer secures what they put in the cloud. The split shifts with the model: in IaaS you patch the OS; in SaaS you do not.
Some responsibilities never move. In every model, the customer owns their data, their users, and access configuration. A misconfigured public storage bucket is always the customer's problem.

learn.heading: Where cloud runs
body: A region is a geographic area; an availability zone (AZ) is one or more isolated data centres within a region, with independent power and networking. Spread workloads across AZs for high availability, and across regions for disaster recovery. Edge locations cache content close to users as part of a CDN, such as CloudFront, Azure Front Door or Cloud CDN.

Vendor lock-in is dependence on one provider's proprietary services. Reduce it with open standards, containers and portable infrastructure as code, and accept it deliberately where a managed service is worth it.

cheatSheet: 5 characteristics: self-service, network access, pooling, elasticity, measured
Customer manages the OS and up
Customer still owns data, users, access
On-prem + public / shared by a sector
Provider: of the cloud; customer: in the cloud

overview: Every cloud offers the same building blocks under different names: virtual machines, storage, databases, networks, identity and logging. Once you know the categories and one provider's names, the others map quickly.
This lesson maps the core services across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, covers storage classes and managed databases, and explains why multi-account organisation is the real isolation boundary.

learn.heading: Compute and storage
body: Virtual machines are EC2 on AWS, Virtual Machines on Azure and Compute Engine on GCP. Managed Kubernetes is EKS, AKS and GKE.

Object storage (S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage) holds files as objects in buckets, accessed over HTTPS: cheap, durable and effectively unlimited. Block storage (EBS on AWS) is a virtual disk attached to one instance; EFS provides shared file storage. For rarely accessed archives, S3 Glacier classes are far cheaper, with Deep Archive the cheapest, but retrieval takes minutes to hours.

learn.heading: Databases and networking
body: Managed relational databases (RDS and Aurora on AWS, Azure SQL Database, Cloud SQL) take over patching, backups and failover. Managed NoSQL key-value stores include DynamoDB, Cosmos DB, and Firestore or Bigtable.
Your isolated virtual network is a VPC on AWS, a VNet on Azure and a VPC on GCP (where VPCs are global rather than regional).

learn.heading: Identity, audit and monitoring
body: Identity is IAM on AWS (with IAM Identity Center for single sign-on), Microsoft Entra ID on Azure and Cloud IAM on GCP. Every API call can be recorded for auditing: CloudTrail on AWS, the Activity Log on Azure and Cloud Audit Logs on GCP. Metrics and logs go to CloudWatch, Azure Monitor, or Cloud Monitoring and Logging.

AWS Organizations centrally manages many accounts with Service Control Policies. Separate accounts for production, development and security are the recommended isolation boundary, because a problem in one account cannot directly touch another.

cheatSheet: CloudTrail · Activity Log · Cloud Audit Logs

overview: Cloud bills surprise people because everything is metered and nothing stops you from spending. Cost control and basic account governance belong on day one, not after the first shocking invoice.
This lesson covers pricing models, tagging, budgets, egress charges, rightsizing, FinOps and TCO, protecting the root account, and landing zones.

learn.heading: Pricing models
body: On-demand pricing is flexible and the most expensive per hour. Reserved Instances and Savings Plans give large discounts for committing to steady usage for one to three years. Spot instances are the cheapest, up to about 90% off, but AWS can reclaim them with two minutes' notice, so they suit interruptible jobs such as batch processing and CI.
Egress, data leaving the cloud to the internet or crossing regions, is charged; ingress is usually free. Architectures that move a lot of data out can cost far more than the compute.

learn.heading: Keeping costs visible
body: Tag every resource (owner, environment, cost-center) for cost allocation, ownership, automation and policy. Set a budget alert on day one of any account, so you are notified when spend crosses a threshold.

Rightsizing, matching instance size to actual usage, is often the quickest cost win. FinOps is collaborative cloud financial management across engineering and finance, in a cycle of inform, optimise and operate. TCO (total cost of ownership) comparisons must include hidden on-premises costs such as power, cooling, staff and hardware refresh.

learn.heading: Account governance
body: The root account has unrestricted power and cannot be limited by IAM policies. Enable MFA on it, lock the credentials away, and do daily work through role-based admin accounts instead.

A landing zone is a pre-configured, secure multi-account baseline (accounts, logging, guardrails, networking) that every new workload starts from. AWS Control Tower and Azure Landing Zones build one for you.

cheatSheet: Data out costs; ingress usually free

overview: Cloud networking looks like on-premises networking with the cables replaced by API calls. The same concepts (subnets, routes, firewalls, DNS) apply, but a single route table entry can make a database internet-facing.

This lesson covers public and private subnets, NAT gateways, security groups versus network ACLs, connecting VPCs and on-premises networks, private endpoints, load balancers, Route 53, IP planning, secure admin access and flow logs.

learn.heading: Subnets and routing
body: In AWS a subnet is "public" only because its route table has a route to an Internet Gateway. Private subnets have no such route; they reach the internet outbound through a NAT gateway, which allows outbound connections (for patches and API calls) but never lets the internet initiate a connection inward.
Plan IP space centrally before you build: VPCs with overlapping CIDR blocks cannot be peered or routed cleanly, and fixing that later means rebuilding.

learn.heading: Filtering traffic
body: Security groups are stateful and attach to instances (network interfaces): return traffic is allowed automatically, and rules can only allow. Network ACLs are stateless and apply to whole subnets: they can allow and deny, are evaluated in rule-number order, and need explicit rules for return traffic.
VPC Flow Logs record IP traffic metadata (source, destination, ports, bytes, accept or reject) for network interfaces. They are essential for investigations, but they do not contain payloads.

learn.heading: Connecting networks and services
body: VPC peering privately connects two VPCs but is not transitive: A to B and B to C does not give A to C. Transit Gateway scales to a hub-and-spoke design. Direct Connect (AWS), ExpressRoute (Azure) and Cloud Interconnect (GCP) are private, dedicated links from on-premises.
VPC endpoints (PrivateLink) reach cloud services privately without the public internet: gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB, interface endpoints for most others.

The Application Load Balancer works at Layer 7 with path- and host-based routing; the Network Load Balancer works at Layer 4 with extreme performance and static IPs. Route 53 provides DNS with health checks and latency-based, weighted, failover and geolocation routing.

learn.heading: Admin access
body: A bastion host is a hardened jump box that admins SSH through. The modern alternative, AWS Systems Manager Session Manager, needs no open inbound ports at all and logs every session.

architecture.caption: A classic two-tier VPC across two availability zones. Only the load balancer is reachable from the internet.
architecture.diagram:
Internet
