overview: Resilient architectures assume failure. An Availability Zone will eventually have a bad day, and the exam expects your designs to survive it without a human being paged: traffic reroutes, unhealthy instances are replaced, and the database fails over on its own. Roughly a quarter of the exam tests this domain, and nearly every question is a variation on one theme — no single point of failure.

This lesson covers the three pillars of highly available compute: spreading work across zones, balancing and scaling it automatically, and routing around failure with DNS. The details matter — ALB versus NLB, Multi-AZ versus read replica, target tracking versus step scaling — because the exam distinguishes designs by exactly these choices.

learn.heading: Designing for the zone that fails
body: The minimum viable resilient network spans two Availability Zones; production VPCs routinely span three. Every tier that can be multi-AZ should be: compute in an Auto Scaling group across zones, data in a replicated store, and nothing stateful trapped on a single instance. The exam's bluntest resilience question — survive an AZ failure with no manual intervention — is answered by this shape every time.

State is the enemy of horizontal scaling. A web application that stores sessions on local disk breaks the moment the load balancer sends a returning user to a different instance, so sessions move to ElastiCache or DynamoDB and instances become interchangeable. Where affinity is genuinely required, it is configured at the load balancer as stickiness — a deliberate choice, not an accident of local disks.

For the database tier, RDS Multi-AZ provides automatic failover to a synchronous standby in another zone; the standby takes no reads and exists solely to be promoted. Read replicas are a different tool: asynchronous copies that absorb read traffic and can be promoted manually, including across regions. The exam tests the distinction relentlessly — automatic failover means Multi-AZ, read scaling means replicas — and for Aurora, a reader endpoint load-balances reads across replicas while the cluster handles failover itself.

learn.heading: Balancing and scaling the fleet
body: Load balancers come in three flavors, chosen by layer. The Application Load Balancer works at Layer 7: path- and host-based routing for HTTP and HTTPS, the default for web tiers. The Network Load Balancer works at Layer 4: static IP addresses, ultra-low latency, preservation of the client source IP, and millions of requests per second — the choice for TCP workloads and for anything that must present a fixed IP. The Gateway Load Balancer exists for one job: chaining third-party virtual appliances like firewalls and intrusion detection into the traffic path.

Auto Scaling groups keep the fleet at the right size and the right health. A target-tracking policy holds a metric at a set value — request count per target is the canonical example — scaling out under load and in on calm. Health checks do the janitorial work: when an instance fails its checks, the group terminates it and launches a replacement without being asked. Lifecycle hooks pause those transitions for custom actions — warming a cache on launch, draining connections on termination.

Scale-in deserves the same care as scale-out. Terminating an instance mid-request drops work, so the load balancer's deregistration delay gives in-flight requests time to finish before the target is removed. And for the legacy application that cannot scale at all, the exam still has an answer: an Auto Scaling group with minimum, maximum, and desired all set to one, spread across zones — it cannot grow, but it auto-recovers.

learn.heading: DNS as a control plane
body: Route 53 is more than a phone book; its routing policies are failover machinery. Failover routing pairs a primary record with a secondary, flipping traffic when health checks declare the primary unhealthy — the standard shape for active/passive multi-region designs. Weighted routing splits traffic by proportion, which makes it the tool for blue/green deployments and canary releases. Latency-based routing sends each user to the region that answers fastest.

Health checks are the senses of this system, and they must monitor what users actually experience: a check against the application endpoint, not just a ping of the host. Target-group health checks and Route 53 health checks serve different masters — the former decides whether a load balancer sends traffic to an instance, the latter decides whether DNS sends traffic to a region — and a resilient design uses both.

For disciplined failover at organizational scale, Route 53 Application Recovery Controller adds readiness checks — continuous verification that the recovery environment can actually take over — and routing controls, the authoritative switches operators flip during an event. Geolocation routing answers by the user's location for compliance and localization; geoproximity adds a bias knob so traffic can be steered toward or away from a region by distance.

cheatSheet: Production spans 2+ AZs; single-AZ designs fail the resilience bar.
Layer-7 balancer: path/host routing for HTTP(S) web tiers.
Layer-4 balancer: static IPs, ultra-low latency, preserves source IP.
Chains third-party virtual appliances (firewalls, IDS) into traffic.
ASG policy holding a metric — e.g. requests per target — at a set value.
Pauses scale-out/in for custom warm-up or drain actions.
Lets in-flight requests finish before a target is removed.
Synchronous standby with automatic failover; takes no reads.
Asynchronous readable copy for read scaling; promotable, not automatic.
Readiness checks plus routing controls for disciplined failover.

overview: Tightly coupled architectures fail together: one slow component backs up into the next until the whole system stalls. Decoupled architectures fail separately — a queue absorbs the surge, a failed message is isolated and retried, and each tier scales on its own schedule. This is the heart of the resilience domain, and the exam returns to it constantly.

This lesson covers the decoupling toolkit: SQS queues that buffer, SNS topics that fan out, EventBridge for event-driven routing, and Step Functions for orchestrated workflows. The skill being tested is selection — knowing which service fits which shape of problem — and the failure modes each one exists to contain.

learn.heading: Queues absorb, topics broadcast
body: SQS is a pull-based buffer between producers and consumers. When a web tier spikes and the backend cannot keep up, messages wait in the queue instead of overwhelming workers; when a downstream API rate-limits you, the queue meters the work to a pace it can accept. Consumers poll, process, and delete — and if processing fails, the message simply becomes visible again for another attempt.

Two queue types serve two contracts. Standard queues offer at-least-once delivery, best-effort ordering, and near-unlimited throughput — the default for decoupled work. FIFO queues offer exactly-once processing and strict ordering within a message group, at lower throughput: the choice when messages must be processed in exact order per customer, with the customer ID as the message group. Retention stretches to 14 days, and long polling — waiting for messages rather than returning empty — cuts both cost and latency versus short polling.

SNS is the complementary shape: push-based publish/subscribe. One message published to a topic fans out to every subscriber — SQS queues, Lambda functions, email endpoints — simultaneously. The canonical fan-out pattern is an SNS topic feeding one SQS queue per consumer, so inventory, billing, and shipping each process the same order event at their own pace, in their own queue, with their own retries.

learn.heading: Poison pills and idempotency
body: Every queue eventually receives a message no consumer can process — malformed data, a poison pill that crashes each worker that touches it. Without protection, that message cycles forever, consuming capacity. The dead-letter queue is the isolation ward: after a configured number of failed receives, the message is moved aside for inspection, and once the bug is fixed it can be redriven back into the main queue.

Because standard queues deliver at-least-once, duplicates are a fact of life: a consumer can crash after processing but before deleting, and the message returns. Consumers must therefore be idempotent — processing the same message twice produces the same result as once. Deduplication keys, conditional writes, and transactional outboxes are the implementation; the exam tests the principle, which is that retries are safe only when repetition is harmless.

The visibility timeout is the mechanism that makes all of this work. When a consumer receives a message, it becomes invisible to other consumers for the timeout period — long enough to finish processing. Set it too short and a slow consumer's message reappears mid-processing, creating duplicates; set it generously relative to actual processing time and the system stays calm.

learn.heading: Orchestration and events
body: Some workflows are not a queue but a sequence: step one, then step two, with retries, branching, and occasionally a human approval in the middle. Step Functions orchestrates these — state machines that coordinate Lambda functions and services, retry failed steps with backoff, and pause for human input via callbacks. A saga across microservices, where each step needs a compensating action on failure, is the textbook case.

EventBridge is the event bus for loosely coupled systems: producers emit events, rules route them to targets based on content, and a schema registry keeps everyone honest about the shape. Choose it over SNS when routing logic matters — events filtered by type, transformed en route, or sourced from SaaS applications — and keep SNS for simple fan-out. EventBridge Scheduler, the successor to scheduled CloudWatch rules, fires one-time or recurring schedules without running any infrastructure.

Two integration patterns tie the toolkit together. When Lambda throttles on a burst of S3 uploads, inserting an SQS queue between the S3 event notification and the function absorbs the spike — data waits instead of being lost. And when the workload is a true stream — ordered, replayable, consumed by many analytics applications at scale — Kinesis Data Streams replaces the queue with a sharded, replayable log. Queues carry discrete messages; streams carry ordered history.

cheatSheet: Exactly-once, ordered per message group; lower throughput.
How long a received message hides; must exceed processing time.
Isolates repeatedly failing messages; redrive after fixing.
Pub/sub fan-out: one message pushed to many subscribers.
SNS topic feeding one SQS queue per consumer team.
Orchestrates sequential workflows with retries and human approval.
Event bus with content-based rules, schema registry, SaaS sources.
Safe to process twice; required because queues deliver at-least-once.
Ordered, replayable streams; choose over SQS at streaming scale.

overview: Every disaster-recovery decision is a negotiation between two numbers: how long you can be down, and how much data you can afford to lose. The exam frames the entire backup and DR landscape through RTO and RPO, and the winning design is the cheapest one that still meets both — not the most elaborate one you can draw.

This lesson covers the four DR strategies in cost order, the backup machinery that makes them real, and the operational discipline — testing, runbooks, rehearsal — that separates a plan from a hope. Recovery is a system you operate, not a document you file.

learn.heading: RTO, RPO, and the strategy spectrum
body: RTO — recovery time objective — is how long the business can wait for the system to return. RPO — recovery point objective — is how much data loss is tolerable, measured as the age of the newest restorable backup. A seconds-level RPO demands continuous replication; a 24-hour RPO is satisfied by nightly backups. Every DR question on the exam is answered by matching the strategy's cost and recovery profile to these two numbers.

The four strategies form a ladder. Backup and restore is the cheapest and slowest: data is backed up, infrastructure is rebuilt from scratch on failure — fine for dev environments and tolerant workloads. Pilot light keeps a minimal core running in the recovery region — the database replicating, the essential services idling — and scales to full capacity on failover. Warm standby runs a scaled-down but fully functional copy, cutting over faster. Multi-site active/active serves traffic from two or more regions continuously: the fastest recovery and the highest bill.

The exam's classic trap is recommending active/active for a workload whose RTO tolerates hours. Cost-optimization applies to resilience too: buy the recovery speed the business case requires, and not a minute faster.

learn.heading: Backups that survive the worst day
body: AWS Backup is the centralized control plane: one place to define backup policies, schedules, and retention across EC2, RDS, EFS, and DynamoDB, instead of per-service scripts that drift. For ransomware resistance, Vault Lock puts backups in WORM compliance mode — immutable for the retention period, undeletable even by a compromised admin account. The 3-2-1 rule translates cleanly: versioned S3 as the second copy, cross-region replication as the offsite third, vault-locked backups as the immutable last resort.

RDS offers two backup shapes with different jobs. Automated backups give point-in-time recovery within the retention window — up to 35 days — and vanish with the instance. Manual snapshots persist until deleted, are the unit of cross-region copy, and are how you seed new environments. EBS snapshots work the same way: incremental, stored in S3, copied across regions for DR.

Know the difference between a snapshot and an AMI, because the exam asks. A snapshot is a point-in-time copy of a disk. An AMI is a launchable image — snapshots plus the metadata describing how to boot them. For fast instance recovery, keep AMIs current with EC2 Image Builder pipelines that rebuild golden images on a schedule, so failover launches today's software, not last quarter's.

learn.heading: Failover mechanics and rehearsal
body: Data replication sets the RPO floor. S3 Cross-Region Replication copies objects — including, with the right configuration, existing objects and delete markers — to a second region, underpinning static-website and data-lake DR. For relational data with seconds-level RPO, Aurora Global Database maintains cross-region clusters with typically sub-second replication lag and managed failover measured in seconds, not hours.

Traffic failover is Route 53's job: health checks against real application endpoints drive failover routing to the recovery region, or Application Recovery Controller's routing controls flip traffic under operator command. The runbook is the human half of the system — it names who decides, the exact sequence of steps, how to verify each one, and the rollback criteria — and it is tested, not shelved.

Testing without impacting production is a design requirement, not a luxury. Fail over to isolated environments, run game days against the recovery region, and use ARC readiness checks to verify continuously that the recovery environment could take over today. An untested DR plan is a hypothesis; the exam treats rehearsal as part of the architecture.

cheatSheet: How long recovery may take / how much data loss is tolerable.
Cheapest DR; slowest — rebuild from backups on failure.
Minimal core idles in the recovery region; scale up on failover.
Scaled-down live copy; faster cutover than pilot light.
Full capacity in 2+ regions; fastest recovery, highest cost.
Centralized backup policies across EC2, RDS, EFS, DynamoDB.
WORM compliance lock; backups survive even compromised admins.
Cross-region clusters, typically sub-second replication lag.
Point-in-time recovery; retained up to 35 days.
Snapshot = disk copy. AMI = launchable image (snapshots + boot metadata).

overview: Storage questions reward a simple mental model: block, file, and object storage solve different problems, and the exam tests whether you can match the workload to the shape. A database wants block. A hundred web servers sharing uploads want file. A data lake queried by Athena wants object. Get the shape right and the service choice usually follows.

This lesson maps the storage portfolio — EBS and instance store, EFS and FSx, S3 — and the data-movement tools that get bytes in and out at speed. The through-line is fitness for purpose: each service has a workload it was built for and several it merely tolerates.

learn.heading: Three shapes of storage
body: EBS is network-attached block storage for a single instance in a single Availability Zone: the virtual hard drive behind EC2. Volumes persist independently of the instance, which is why databases and stateful applications live on them. Within EBS, gp3 is the general-purpose default — baseline 3,000 IOPS with throughput and IOPS tunable independently of size — while io2 serves latency-sensitive databases needing up to 64,000 provisioned IOPS. Instance store is the opposite shape: physically attached, ephemeral disks that are fast and free but lose everything on stop or termination — scratch space, caches, nothing you cannot rebuild.

EFS is the shared file option: a POSIX file system that hundreds of instances mount simultaneously across Availability Zones, with file locking intact — the answer for the CMS cluster or the hundred web servers sharing uploads. Infrequent Access lifecycle management moves cold files to a cheaper tier automatically. When the workload needs Windows SMB shares, it is FSx for Windows File Server; when it needs raw throughput for a render farm or HPC scratch, FSx for Lustre; ONTAP and OpenZFS cover the remaining enterprise file shapes.

S3 is object storage: flat, effectively unlimited, with strong read-after-write consistency for all operations. It is the data lake's home — Athena, EMR, and Redshift Spectrum query it in place — and the durable tier everything else archives to. The exam's storage-selection questions are usually decided here: shared POSIX means EFS, SMB means FSx Windows, analytics over a lake means S3, a single instance's disk means EBS.

learn.heading: Sharing disks and copying them
body: EBS volumes attach to one instance — with one exception. Multi-Attach lets io1 and io2 volumes attach to multiple instances in the same AZ, which is how clustered file systems and tightly coupled database clusters share block storage. It is a specialist feature for specialist software; reaching for it for ordinary sharing is a design smell, and the exam will offer EFS as the correct alternative.

EBS snapshots are the copy mechanism: incremental point-in-time copies stored in S3, so only changed blocks are billed after the first. They are the unit of backup, of cross-region DR for stateful instances, and of volume migration. An AMI builds on them — snapshots plus the launch metadata that turns a disk copy into a bootable image — which is why golden-image pipelines snapshot, register, and test on a schedule.

S3 has its own selection tools for getting data out selectively. S3 Select filters and retrieves a subset of an object's data without downloading the whole thing — ideal for pulling a few columns from a large CSV. Athena is the heavier instrument: SQL across many objects and prefixes. The rule of thumb is scope: one object, S3 Select; a dataset, Athena.

learn.heading: Moving data at speed and at scale
body: Large uploads from a single host go through multipart upload: the object is split, parts upload in parallel, and the transfer is resumable — interrupted uploads pick up where they stopped rather than starting over. For clients far from the bucket's region, Transfer Acceleration routes uploads through the nearest CloudFront edge location onto the AWS backbone, which beats the public internet across oceans.

Hybrid architectures bridge on-premises storage with Storage Gateway: file, volume, and tape gateway modes that present familiar interfaces locally while tiering to S3 behind the scenes. It is the answer for the workload that cannot move yet but must stop growing on-premises. And for the 50 TB migration over a constrained link, the exam's answer is offline: a Snowball appliance ships the data physically, because no clever protocol beats a truck full of disks when bandwidth is the constraint.

S3 Object Lambda adds a final twist: transform data on retrieval. Instead of storing a redacted copy, a thumbnail copy, and a full copy, store one object and let Object Lambda derive the variants as they are requested — less duplication, one source of truth, transformations applied at read time.

cheatSheet: Persistent block storage for one instance in one AZ.
Ephemeral attached disks; fastest, but data dies with the host.
General-purpose SSD; IOPS and throughput tuned independently of size.
Provisioned-IOPS SSD for latency-sensitive databases (to 64,000 IOPS).
Shared POSIX file system across AZs; IA tier for cold files.
Managed file systems: Windows (SMB), Lustre (HPC), ONTAP, OpenZFS.
Object storage with strong consistency; the data-lake default.
Share io1/io2 volumes across instances; for clustered file systems only.
Parallel, resumable uploads for large objects.
Offline bulk-transfer appliance for tens of terabytes.

overview: Database selection is the exam's purest test of architectural judgment: a dozen managed engines, each with a workload it dominates and several it merely survives. The questions describe access patterns — millisecond key lookups at planetary scale, petabyte joins, graph traversals — and the correct answer is the engine built for that pattern.

This lesson covers the relational core (RDS and Aurora), the purpose-built engines (DynamoDB, ElastiCache, Neptune, Redshift, and the rest), and migration with minimal downtime. The decision framework is consistent throughout: match the data model and the access pattern first, and let cost and operations follow.

learn.heading: Relational: RDS and Aurora
body: RDS is managed relational database service in the straightforward sense: you keep your engine — PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server — and AWS handles patching, backups, and failover mechanics. Choose it when the workload is relational but ordinary: moderate throughput, standard availability needs, and a budget that appreciates RDS's lower price. Aurora is the cloud-native sibling: same wire compatibility with PostgreSQL and MySQL, but a distributed storage layer that delivers higher throughput, faster failover, and storage that grows automatically.

Scaling reads and surviving failure are separate mechanisms. Read replicas are asynchronous copies that absorb read traffic — including across regions — and can be promoted to standalone primaries; they do not provide automatic failover. Multi-AZ standby is the failover mechanism: a synchronous copy in another zone that takes over automatically but serves no reads. Aurora unifies more of this: an Aurora reader endpoint load-balances reads across replicas while the cluster manages failover internally.

Two features solve specific pain the exam likes to probe. Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity in fine-grained units for workloads with variable or unpredictable load — pay for the ACUs you use, not the instance you sized. RDS Proxy sits between application fleets and the database as a connection pooler: thousands of Lambda invocations share a small pool of database connections instead of overwhelming the engine with a connection storm, which is exactly the failure mode serverless applications hit at scale.

learn.heading: Purpose-built engines
body: DynamoDB is the serverless NoSQL answer for key-value access at any scale: single-digit-millisecond reads and writes, flexible schema, throughput that scales without servers. The design discipline is the partition key — high-cardinality keys spread load evenly, while a low-cardinality key funnels traffic into a hot partition that throttles. Billing follows the access pattern: provisioned capacity with auto scaling for predictable workloads, on-demand for spiky or unknown traffic; Global Tables replicate across regions for active-active applications.

Caching layers sit in front of the database, not beside it. DAX is DynamoDB's dedicated in-memory cache, dropping reads to microseconds for the hottest keys. ElastiCache is the general cache: choose Redis for rich data structures — sorted sets powering leaderboards, pub/sub channels, persistence options — and Memcached for simple, multithreaded key-value caching with no need for replication or persistence.

The remaining engines each own a pattern. Neptune traverses relationships in milliseconds for fraud detection and recommendation graphs. DocumentDB serves MongoDB-compatible document workloads. Timestream is built for time-series telemetry. Redshift is the petabyte OLAP warehouse for complex analytic joins. The exam's phrasing is the giveaway: millisecond graph traversals mean Neptune, petabyte joins mean Redshift, flexible-schema millisecond reads mean DynamoDB.

learn.heading: Migration with minimal downtime
body: Moving a production database is a migration, not a copy, and the exam cares about the downtime. AWS Database Migration Service performs the full load of existing data and then continuously replicates changes — change data capture — so the cutover window shrinks to minutes: the classic answer for migrating Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL without extended outage. The Schema Conversion Tool handles the heterogeneous half, translating schemas and flagging the constructs that need human attention.

The RDS-versus-DynamoDB decision deserves its own framing because it recurs across the exam. Choose RDS when the workload needs the relational model: complex joins, ad-hoc SQL, transactions across entities, and a schema the business already understands. Choose DynamoDB when the access pattern is key-based at scale: known query shapes, single-digit-millisecond latency, flexible schema, and traffic that would require constant re-sharding on a relational engine.

A final operational note: encrypt the database, and plan for it early. An existing unencrypted RDS instance cannot be flipped in place — the path is snapshot, copy the snapshot with encryption enabled, restore — which is one more reason new databases launch encrypted by default and stay that way.

cheatSheet: Managed relational engines; AWS handles patching, backups, failover mechanics.
Cloud-native relational: faster failover, auto-growing storage, global clusters.
Async readable copy for read scaling; promotable, not automatic failover.
Serverless NoSQL; single-digit-ms at any scale; partition-key design is the discipline.
Low-cardinality key funneling traffic; fix with higher-cardinality keys.
In-memory microsecond cache dedicated to DynamoDB.
Rich structures (sorted sets, pub/sub) with persistence options.
Simple multithreaded cache; no replication, no persistence.
Connection pooling that shields RDS from Lambda connection storms.
Minimal-downtime migration via full load plus continuous change capture.

overview: Performance on AWS is rarely about bigger instances; it is about putting data closer to the request. Edge caches absorb global traffic, in-memory caches absorb database load, and each layer you add multiplies the capacity of the layers beneath it. The exam tests caching as architecture: where the cache sits, what it holds, and what happens when it misses.

This lesson covers CloudFront and Global Accelerator at the edge, the caching strategies inside the architecture, and the cost and consistency trade-offs every cache introduces. A cache is a performance decision with a correctness bill attached — the lesson is in reading both sides.

learn.heading: CloudFront as the front door
body: CloudFront is the content delivery network: a global mesh of edge locations that cache responses close to viewers, so a user in Sydney does not wait on an origin in Virginia. It serves static assets by default and accelerates dynamic content too, and private S3 origins stay private through Origin Access Control — the bucket policy grants access to the CloudFront distribution, never to the public.

Restricted content uses signed URLs or signed cookies: time-limited, optionally IP-bound tokens that grant access without exposing the origin. When deployments change content, invalidation purges the edge cache — effective but metered, which is why versioned filenames (app-v2.js rather than app.js) are the cleaner pattern: new names bypass the cache naturally, no purge required. Origin failover adds resilience: a primary origin group with a secondary that takes over when health checks fail.

Edge compute splits by weight. CloudFront Functions run lightweight JavaScript at viewer request and response — header rewrites, simple redirects, token checks. Lambda@Edge runs full Lambda functions at more trigger points, including origin request and response, for heavier work like authentication flows and content transformation. The exam's distinction is scope: simple and viewer-facing means CloudFront Functions; complex or origin-touching means Lambda@Edge.

learn.heading: When the CDN is not enough
body: CloudFront speaks HTTP and HTTPS. For everything else — gaming protocols, VoIP, custom TCP and UDP — Global Accelerator provides two static anycast IP addresses that route each user to the optimal AWS endpoint. The static IPs solve real operational problems: client firewalls can allowlist them, DNS propagation delay disappears from failover, and users get the AWS backbone instead of the public internet from the nearest edge.

Route 53's latency-based routing is the DNS-layer complement: each user resolves to the region with the lowest measured latency. API Gateway caching plays the same role one layer up, caching API responses at the gateway so repeated identical calls never reach the backend. The pattern is consistent: identify the repeated work, intercept it as close to the requester as possible.

Price classes are CloudFront's cost lever: restrict the distribution to fewer edge locations — North America and Europe only, say — when the audience is regional and the global footprint is wasted spend. Performance design and cost design are the same exercise here, which is why the exam places caching questions in both the performance and cost domains.

learn.heading: Caching inside the architecture
body: Behind the edge, application caches protect the database. Cache-aside is the default strategy for read-heavy workloads: the application checks the cache, falls back to the database on a miss, and populates the cache with the result — the catalog page that is read a thousand times for every write. Write-through suits write-heavy consistency needs but is rarer in exam scenarios. ElastiCache implements both: Redis for data structures and persistence, Memcached for simple multithreaded speed.

Every cache introduces two failure modes the exam probes. Stale data: TTLs must reflect how fresh the answer needs to be, and invalidation must be a designed path, not an afterthought. Thundering herd: when a popular key expires, a thousand simultaneous misses slam the database — mitigated with jittered TTLs, staggered expirations, request coalescing, or serving slightly stale data while refreshing in the background.

Two cost details hide in caching designs. Cross-AZ data transfer is billed, so chatty services — application tiers hammering a cache cluster — should sit in the same AZ as their cache, or use zonal endpoints to keep traffic local. And DAX versus ElastiCache is a scoping question: DAX is DynamoDB's dedicated microsecond cache, while ElastiCache serves any workload — choose the specialist when the database is DynamoDB and the generalist otherwise.

cheatSheet: Global CDN caching at edge locations for low-latency delivery.
Lets CloudFront serve private S3 content securely.
Time-limited access tokens for private CloudFront content.
Lightweight edge code at viewer request/response.
Full Lambda at more edge triggers; heavier than CF Functions.
Static anycast IPs for TCP/UDP; optimal-endpoint routing off the internet.
App checks cache, falls back to DB, populates on miss; best read-heavy.
Rich structures (sorted sets, pub/sub) with persistence options.
Simple multithreaded cache; no replication, no persistence.
Restrict CloudFront edge locations to cut cost for regional audiences.

overview: Compute is usually the largest line on an AWS bill, and the exam treats cost optimization as a design discipline, not an accounting afterthought. The same workload can cost triple or a third depending on three decisions: which pricing model matches its shape, whether it is sized correctly, and whether it runs only when needed.

This lesson covers the EC2 pricing ladder, commitment instruments, rightsizing and scheduling, and the serverless trade-offs. The mental model is simple: pay for flexibility where you need it, commit where you are certain, and never pay for idle.

learn.heading: The pricing ladder
body: On-Demand is the top of the ladder: no commitment, highest price, the right choice for unpredictable, spiky, or short-lived workloads — the startup whose traffic cannot be forecast buys flexibility here. Spot instances are the bottom: spare EC2 capacity at discounts up to around 90%, reclaimable with two minutes' notice, perfect for fault-tolerant batch jobs that run nightly and tolerate interruption. Spot Fleets improve on single requests by diversifying across instance pools and maintaining target capacity as prices shift.

Steady-state workloads commit. Reserved Instances lock a configuration for one or three years at a deep discount; Savings Plans commit to a dollar-per-hour spend instead, which is why the exam prefers them — a Compute Savings Plan applies across instance families, regions, operating systems, Fargate, and even Lambda, trading a slightly smaller discount for far more flexibility. An EC2 Instance Savings Plan goes deeper but stays narrow: one family, one region.

The web tier running 24/7 for two years is the textbook commitment case: a Compute Savings Plan for flexibility, or an EC2 Instance Savings Plan if the family is certain. Unpredictable traffic stays On-Demand. Nightly interruptible batch goes Spot. The exam's cost questions are almost always this matching exercise in disguise.

learn.heading: Rightsizing and scheduling
body: The most expensive instance is the one doing nothing. Compute Optimizer applies machine learning to CloudWatch history and recommends smaller instance types, and the exam expects you to reach for it whenever a question mentions over-provisioned or underutilized fleets. The quieter version of the same waste is the over-provisioned Auto Scaling minimum: capacity that never scales in still bills around the clock.

Scheduling attacks the time dimension. A development environment used eight hours a day on weekdays has no business running the other 128 hours — Instance Scheduler stops and starts resources on a timetable, and scheduled scaling adjusts ASG minimums for known patterns. Idle resources that nobody remembers are found through Cost Explorer and Trusted Advisor, which flag the unattached volumes and forgotten instances every account accumulates.

Graviton changes the price-performance math itself: ARM-based instances delivering materially better price-performance — AWS cites up to 40% — for compatible workloads, which increasingly means most of them. And Lambda inverts the comparison for spiky APIs: when traffic is intermittent, paying per request beats paying per hour for an instance waiting between requests. Fargate sits between: pay-per-use containers without server management, cheaper than idle EC2 at low utilization, more expensive than well-packed EC2 at sustained high utilization.

learn.heading: Structure and visibility
body: Multiple AWS accounts are a cost-management tool, not just a security one. Separate accounts isolate each team's spend for chargeback, let service control policies guard the expensive actions, and still aggregate under consolidated billing so volume discounts apply across the organization. The Cost and Usage Report provides the line-item detail — every hour of every resource — that feeds serious analysis and anomaly detection.

Dedicated tenancy has its own pricing shape worth knowing. Dedicated Instances run on isolated hardware billed per instance — the compliance answer for noisy-neighbor concerns. Dedicated Hosts allocate whole physical servers, billed per host, and exist for socket-based licensing: bring your own Oracle or Windows Server licenses and the host-level visibility satisfies the auditors.

The Free Tier deserves a cautionary paragraph because the exam sets traps there. The tier covers specific usage amounts of specific services — and nothing else. Forgotten resources keep billing after the trial project ends, and services the tier does not cover, like NAT gateway hours and data transfer, bill from the first byte. The trap is assuming 'free tier' means 'free account'.

cheatSheet: No commitment; for unpredictable, spiky, or short-lived workloads.
Spare capacity up to ~90% off; for interruption-tolerant batch.
Commit $/hour for 1–3 years; flexible across family, region, Fargate, Lambda.
Deeper discount locked to one instance family and region.
ML-driven rightsizing recommendations from CloudWatch history.
ARM instances with materially better price-performance for compatible workloads.
Stops dev/test resources on a timetable instead of 24/7.
Cost and Usage Report: line-item detail for deep cost analysis.
One payer account aggregates volume discounts across accounts.
Whole physical servers for socket-based BYOL licensing.

overview: Storage bills hide in the details: the tier an object sits in, the requests made against it, the transfers that move it, and the queries that scan it. S3 is cheap per gigabyte and expensive per mistake — the exam's cost questions probe exactly the mistakes: objects in the wrong tier, chatty request patterns, forgotten multipart uploads, and Athena queries scanning terabytes of CSV.

This lesson covers lifecycle-driven tiering, the hidden meters of requests and transfer, and data-format economics. The discipline is lifecycle thinking: data has a temperature, and every temperature has a price.

learn.heading: Tiering as a strategy
body: S3 lifecycle policies automate the temperature curve: recent logs sit in Standard, age into Infrequent Access after 30 days, then into Glacier Flexible and finally Deep Archive for the seven-year compliance tail. Each tier trades retrieval speed for price, and each carries a minimum storage duration — 30 days for IA, 90 for Glacier Flexible, 180 for Deep Archive — billed pro-rata if you delete early. Tiering data you will retrieve next week into Deep Archive is not savings; it is a penalty with extra steps.

Choose the tier by access pattern, not by price tag alone. S3 Intelligent-Tiering monitors access and moves objects between frequent and infrequent tiers automatically — the answer when patterns are unknown or shifting, for a small monitoring fee. Standard-IA versus One Zone-IA is a durability question: One Zone-IA is cheaper because it stores in a single AZ, suitable only for reproducible data like transcoded media. Glacier Deep Archive, at roughly a dollar per terabyte-month, is the cheapest retention for the annual-audit backup set — with 12-to-48-hour retrieval that annual audits easily tolerate.

Two subtleties catch people. Small objects in Glacier tiers incur minimum billable sizes, so archiving millions of tiny files costs more than the bytes suggest — aggregate first. And Object Lock in Compliance mode makes retention a cost commitment: objects cannot be deleted early by anyone, so an over-long retention period bills in full with no escape hatch.

learn.heading: The hidden meters: requests and transfer
body: S3 charges per request as well as per byte, and high-request workloads can spend more on GETs and LISTs than on storage. The fixes are architectural: fewer, larger objects instead of millions of tiny ones; lifecycle rules instead of application-driven transitions; CloudFront in front of hot objects so the edge absorbs repeat requests. A workload doing ten million small reads a day is a request-cost problem wearing a storage costume.

Incomplete multipart uploads are pure waste: every part uploaded so far is billed until the upload completes or is aborted. The exam's answer is a lifecycle rule that aborts incomplete uploads after N days — set it on every bucket that takes large uploads. Replication doubles the storage bill plus cross-region transfer fees, so replicate selectively with prefix or tag filters rather than whole buckets.

Data transfer has its own geography. Transfer into AWS is free; transfer out to the internet is billed; transfer between AZs is billed; same-region transfers between AWS services — EC2 to S3 in the same region, for example — are generally free. CloudFront reduces the egress bill two ways: cached content serves from the edge, and price classes trim the edge footprint for regional audiences. EBS snapshots bill incrementally per gigabyte-month of changed blocks, which is why snapshot retention policies matter as much as snapshot schedules.

learn.heading: Data-format and query economics
body: Athena bills per terabyte scanned, which makes data format a cost decision. Partitioning by date lets queries skip entire prefixes; columnar formats like Parquet let queries read only the columns they need; compression shrinks everything. The same query over CSV can cost orders of magnitude more than over partitioned Parquet — the exam's data-lake cost question is always answered with format and partitioning, never with a bigger budget.

EBS rightsizing follows the same 'measure, then tune' loop as compute: CloudWatch reveals the actual IOPS and throughput, gp3 lets you dial provisioned IOPS and throughput independently of volume size, and unused provisioned IOPS on io volumes are money for nothing. Downsizing is safe when the metrics support it; the waste is in the volumes nobody measured.

Visibility closes the loop. S3 Storage Lens gives organization-wide insight into usage, access patterns, and cost drivers across every bucket — the tool for finding the anomalies. Cost-allocation tags, activated in the Billing console, let Cost Explorer break spend down by team or project for chargeback. And before any of it is built, the AWS Pricing Calculator models the architecture's cost so the estimate exists before the bill does.

overview: Threat detection in AWS is not one service but a layered system: something that finds the threats, something that collects the findings, something that protects the data those threats target, and something that reconstructs the story after the fact. On SCS-C02, those roles are played by GuardDuty, Security Hub, Macie, and Detective, and the exam expects you to know exactly which one answers which question.

This lesson covers the detection layer end to end: how GuardDuty finds compromise without agents, how Security Hub normalises and prioritises everything into one console, how Macie classifies the sensitive data worth stealing, and how Detective turns scattered findings into an investigation timeline. (SCS-C02 Domain 1.0: Threat Detection and Incident Response.)

learn.heading: GuardDuty: detection without agents
body: Amazon GuardDuty is a threat detection service that never installs anything on your workloads. It analyses log sources AWS already collects — CloudTrail management events, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS query logs — with machine learning and threat intelligence, looking for signs of compromise: an EC2 instance talking to a known command-and-control domain, API calls from an unusual geography, a user exfiltrating data to an unfamiliar S3 bucket.

GuardDuty is regional. Enabling it in us-east-1 protects nothing in eu-west-1. The exam will test this relentlessly: the correct multi-account, multi-region answer is always to enable GuardDuty in every region through AWS Organizations with a delegated administrator account, which gives one pane of glass without anyone logging into fifty consoles.

Beyond the foundational sources, GuardDuty offers separately enabled protection plans that cost extra because of their data volume: S3 protection for object-level data events, EBS malware protection, RDS protection, Lambda protection, and EKS protection covering audit logs and runtime monitoring. Findings carry a severity — high means act now, and a high-severity IAM finding (anomalous API calls, unusual credential use) should be treated as compromised credentials until proven otherwise.

The recommended containment for a compromised EC2 instance is instructive about AWS-native IR: isolate the instance by swapping its security group for one that denies all traffic, then take snapshots for forensics. Do not delete it first — deletion destroys the evidence you need to answer what the attacker touched.

learn.heading: Security Hub: one console, one format
body: If GuardDuty is the sensor, AWS Security Hub is the dashboard. It aggregates findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, IAM Access Analyzer, and partner products into the AWS Security Finding Format — ASFF — a normalised schema with standard severity, resource, and remediation fields. Normalisation is the point: automation and SIEMs can parse any finding uniformly instead of learning each product's dialect.

Security Hub also runs automated security checks against standards like the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark, so it doubles as a posture tool: not just "what happened" but "what is misconfigured." Its insights group related findings into patterns — every finding tied to one instance, say — which is how you prioritise during an incident instead of drowning in fifty tabs.

Know the vocabulary distinction cold: a finding is a single detection event; an insight is a grouped collection of findings matching a pattern. Security Hub detects nothing itself — it aggregates, normalises, and prioritises.

learn.heading: Macie and Detective: data and investigation
body: Amazon Macie answers a different question: what sensitive data do we actually have? It uses machine learning to discover and classify PII, PHI, and other sensitive data types in S3 buckets — national ID numbers sitting unencrypted in a log bucket, for instance. The remediation pattern is always the same two moves: fix the exposure (enable default encryption, restrict access with bucket policies and Block Public Access), then protect the data class going forward. Macie also feeds findings into Security Hub for continuous monitoring as new objects land.

Amazon Detective is the investigation tool. Where GuardDuty says "this instance talked to a malicious domain," Detective builds a visual entity graph — the IP addresses, users, and roles that interacted over time — so an analyst can answer "what else did this actor touch" without manually correlating logs. It shortens investigations from hours of Athena queries to clicks.

Together the four form the detection story the exam expects you to tell: GuardDuty finds, Security Hub consolidates, Macie watches the data, Detective reconstructs the attack. Any question about centralising threat detection across many accounts resolves to Organizations plus delegated administration — the management pattern, not a bigger console.

cheatSheet: Agentless ML threat detection over CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs; regional, enable everywhere via delegated admin.
S3, EBS malware, RDS, Lambda, EKS — enabled and billed separately from foundational detection.

overview: You cannot secure what you cannot see, and in AWS, visibility is a design decision. CloudTrail, CloudWatch Logs, and VPC Flow Logs each record a different slice of reality — API activity, application and system logs, network metadata — and the security architect's job is to make sure every slice is collected, tamper-evident, centralised, and queryable when an incident demands it.

This lesson covers the logging foundations the exam builds everything on: management versus data events, organization trails, log file validation, CloudTrail Lake and Athena for analysis, CloudWatch metric filters and alarms, and the immutable log archive that makes the whole edifice trustworthy. (SCS-C02 Domain 2.0: Logging and Monitoring.)

learn.heading: CloudTrail: the control plane on record
body: CloudTrail records API activity in your account — who called what, from where, and when. Management events cover control-plane calls (launching instances, changing policies) and are logged by default at no extra charge. Data events cover data-plane calls — S3 object-level access, Lambda invocations — and are billed per event, which is why the exam expects you to enable them selectively on sensitive resources rather than everywhere.

A trail that covers one region is a trail with blind spots. The correct architecture is an organization trail, created in the management account, logging all regions for every member account and delivering to one central S3 bucket. Future regions are included automatically, which closes the gap an attacker would otherwise exploit by operating somewhere logging was never enabled.

Logs must be tamper-evident. Store them in a dedicated log-archive account — not the workload accounts — with restricted write access and MFA Delete, so a compromised admin cannot erase their own trail. Enable log file validation, which writes digest files with hashes proving the delivered logs were not modified after the fact. And for analysis across months of history, CloudTrail Lake provides managed, immutable, SQL-queryable storage with up to seven years of retention; Athena against the raw S3 bucket is the flexible, do-it-yourself alternative.

learn.heading: CloudWatch: from log text to alarms
body: CloudWatch Logs collects the logs; the security value comes from what you extract from them. A metric filter watches a log group for a pattern — say, the string "AccessDenied" or console sign-in failures — and publishes a numeric metric every time it matches. A CloudWatch alarm then evaluates that metric: more than five failed console logins in ten minutes, page the security team. The exam's canonical root-usage alarm is exactly this pattern: organization trail, metric filter for root API calls, alarm to SNS.

Two defaults deserve attention. CloudWatch log groups retain logs indefinitely ("Never Expire") unless you set a retention period — free only in the sense that nobody configured it, and expensive in storage and incident-scoping terms. Set retention deliberately. And alarms are not just notifications: they can invoke EC2 actions (reboot, stop, terminate, recover an impaired instance), Auto Scaling policies, or EventBridge rules, which makes them the bridge from monitoring to automated response.

For event-driven automation, EventBridge is the evolved successor to CloudWatch Events — the same event-bus concept with SaaS integrations, a schema registry, and archives. GuardDuty findings, Config compliance changes, and alarm state changes all flow through EventBridge to Lambda or Systems Manager Automation runbooks, which is how detection becomes response in seconds.

learn.heading: Network visibility and the immutable archive
body: VPC Flow Logs record network metadata — source and destination IPs, ports, protocol, bytes, and whether traffic was accepted or rejected. They do not contain packet payloads; they show who talked to whom, never what was said. For long-term analysis, send them to S3 rather than CloudWatch Logs: S3 is far cheaper for high-volume, long-retention storage and queries directly with Athena.

The archive design ties it together. Seven years of CloudTrail for audit is cheapest as an organization trail to S3 with lifecycle policies transitioning older logs to Glacier and Deep Archive — compliance retention does not need hot, queryable storage. For tamper-proofing beyond digest validation, S3 Object Lock in compliance mode makes the log bucket WORM: not even the root user can delete objects until retention expires.

One more exam favourite: CloudTrail Insights detects unusual API activity — spikes in call volume, anomalous patterns — statistically rather than by signature. It will not find malware or open buckets; it finds behaviour that deviates, which is often the first signal that credentials are being misused.

cheatSheet: Control-plane API calls (free, default) vs data-plane calls like S3 object access (billed per event, enable selectively).
Logs all regions and member accounts to one central bucket; covers future regions automatically.
Dedicated, locked-down account for logs with MFA Delete — separation of duties against tampering.

overview: Identity is the primary security boundary in AWS. There is no corporate firewall that matters more than the question of who — or what — is allowed to call which API on which resource. Every breach story in the cloud eventually resolves to an identity question: a key that should not have existed, a policy broader than the job required, a role assumed from somewhere it should never have been.

This lesson builds the IAM mental model the specialty exam assumes you already own: policy evaluation order, roles versus long-lived keys, identity versus resource policies, MFA, and the hygiene practices — credential reports, policy simulation, least privilege — that keep the identity plane clean. (SCS-C02 Domain 4.0: Identity and Access Management.)

learn.heading: How authorization is decided
body: Every API call passes through IAM policy evaluation, and the order is fixed: start with an implicit deny, then look for an explicit allow, then let any explicit deny override everything. The sentence to memorise is that an explicit deny always wins. It wins over allows in identity policies, resource policies, SCPs, and permission boundaries alike, which is why deny-based guardrails are the reliable way to draw lines nobody can cross.

Two kinds of policy attach to two kinds of thing. Identity-based policies attach to users, groups, and roles and describe what that identity may do. Resource-based policies attach to resources — S3 buckets, KMS keys, Lambda functions — and describe who may act on that resource. Cross-account access typically needs both sides to agree: the identity policy allows the action, and the resource policy trusts the external principal.

Within a policy, the elements have distinct jobs. Action names the API calls, Resource scopes where they apply, Condition constrains when, and Effect allows or denies. A policy that allows s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::data/* permits reading objects inside the bucket but not listing the bucket itself — S3 ARNs distinguish bucket-level from object-level permissions, and the exam will catch you if you blur them.

learn.heading: Roles, not keys; MFA, not hope
body: Applications running on EC2 — or Lambda, ECS, or anywhere else — should use IAM roles, never embedded access keys. A role delivers temporary credentials through the instance metadata service that rotate automatically; there is no secret to leak, commit to a repository, or forget to rotate. An instance profile is simply the container that passes a role to an EC2 instance. When a human needs elevated access for two hours, the same principle applies: assume a role and let the credentials expire, rather than widening a permanent permission.

MFA protects against credential theft: a stolen password alone no longer suffices. Enforce it for console access and especially for privileged role assumption — a trust policy condition on aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent makes MFA a gate before any session begins. And the root user deserves special handling: no IAM policy or SCP can limit it, so lock it with MFA, never use it for daily work, and alarm on any root API activity at all. Root usage should be rare enough that every occurrence is worth a page.

Hygiene is a practice, not a project. The IAM credential report shows password and key age, MFA status, and last-used timestamps for every user — the fastest way to find stale keys and MFA-less accounts. IAM Access Analyzer goes further, identifying unused permissions and generating policies from actual CloudTrail activity so you can rightsize toward least privilege based on observed behaviour instead of guesses. And before deploying any policy change, run it through the IAM Policy Simulator: it answers "would this allow or deny that action" without touching production.

overview: Incident response in AWS rewards preparation and punishes improvisation. The platform gives you extraordinary leverage — snapshots in seconds, automation that isolates hosts faster than any human, logs centralised by architecture — but only if the runbooks, roles, and forensic accounts exist before the alert fires. The exam tests whether you would reach for the right building blocks in the right order.

This lesson covers the AWS IR playbook: the correct order of operations, forensic preservation with EBS snapshots, session revocation that actually works, EventBridge-driven automated containment, and the rehearsal discipline that makes it all real. (SCS-C02 Domain 1.0: Threat Detection and Incident Response.)

learn.heading: The order of operations
body: For a compromised EC2 instance, the sequence is: detect and scope, contain, collect forensic evidence, eradicate, recover, then lessons learned. The ordering is load-bearing. Containment — isolating the instance by replacing its security group with a deny-all — stops lateral movement and exfiltration. Forensic collection — EBS snapshots taken before any remediation — preserves the evidence that tells you what the attacker did. Eradication first destroys both.

Forensic images belong in a dedicated forensic account, not the compromised one. Create EBS snapshots, share or copy them to the isolated account, and restrict access — snapshots are point-in-time and immutable, and the separation maintains chain of custody. Watch for attacker tradecraft in the process: ransomware playbooks specifically include checking for encrypted volumes and unfamiliar snapshots or AMIs shared from other accounts, because attackers plant their own images.

Compromised credentials need more than a password change. Deleting an IAM user's access keys does not invalidate already-issued temporary session tokens — the attacker's existing session keeps working. The reliable kill is an inline policy with an explicit deny keyed on aws:TokenIssueTime, which invalidates every session issued before a chosen moment, or deleting and deactivating the user and keys together. Treat high-severity GuardDuty IAM findings as credential compromise until proven otherwise, and rotate everything the compromised identity could reach: for a Lambda function, that means its execution role's reachable secrets, environment variables, and the code itself if tampered with.

learn.heading: Automate the response, rehearse the team
body: Detection-to-containment should be measured in seconds, which means automation. EventBridge rules matching GuardDuty findings can trigger Lambda functions or Systems Manager Automation runbooks — isolate the instance, snapshot the volumes, revoke the sessions — without waiting for a human to finish reading the alert. During a multi-account incident, Security Hub insights group related findings so responders work one prioritised queue instead of dozens of consoles.

Amazon Detective compresses the investigation itself: it pre-correlates GuardDuty findings into timelines of IP, user, and role activity across accounts, so analysts pivot from one finding to the full blast radius in clicks rather than hours of manual log correlation.

None of this matters if the team has never run it. A game day — a simulated incident exercising detection, runbooks, and coordination — is how you discover that the automation role lacks a permission or that nobody knows the forensic account's break-glass procedure at 2 AM. The exam expects preparation over improvisation, and it expects the automation itself to follow least privilege: an over-permissive remediation role is both an attack path and an outage waiting to happen. Scope Lambda and SSM response roles to exactly the actions the playbook needs.

After the dust settles, AWS Artifact provides the compliance reports — SOC 2, ISO 27001 — that regulators and customers will demand as breach-notification evidence. Have access to them before you need them; "we are still gathering our audit reports" is not a sentence you want to say during an incident.

overview: Logging collects the evidence; monitoring turns it into judgement. This is the detective-control layer of the security program: continuously evaluating whether resources are configured the way policy demands, analysing network and API data at a scale no human can read raw, and surfacing the drift between "approved" and "actual" before an attacker exploits it.

This lesson covers the monitoring toolkit: AWS Config and its rules, conformance packs, and aggregators; large-scale log analysis with Athena and CloudTrail Lake; and the EventBridge wiring that turns a compliance change into a notification or an automatic fix. (SCS-C02 Domain 2.0: Logging and Monitoring.)

learn.heading: Config: the compliance sensor
body: CloudTrail tells you who did what; AWS Config tells you what the resource became. It records configuration history and evaluates compliance state continuously: this S3 bucket was compliant yesterday, a policy change at 14:32 made it non-compliant, and here is the API call responsible. The timeline view gives you attribution plus state history in one place, which is exactly what auditors and incident responders need.

Config rules are the evaluations — managed rules for common checks, custom Lambda-backed rules for your own. A conformance pack bundles rules and remediation actions into one deployable package, such as the CIS benchmark, so baseline compliance lands across accounts quickly. And a Config aggregator collects configuration and compliance data from multiple accounts and regions into one central view, which is the only sane way to govern a hundred-account organization.

Know how Config relates to its neighbours. Config rules evaluate resource compliance continuously; Security Hub aggregates those evaluations among its findings. Config is the sensor; Security Hub is one of the dashboards that consumes it. They are complementary, not competing.

learn.heading: Analysis at scale, and closing the loop
body: Thirty days of VPC Flow Logs across a fleet is not a dataset you open in a console. The pattern is S3 plus Athena: flow logs delivered to a bucket partitioned by date, queried with SQL for the compromised IP's conversations. Partitioning matters — a full scan of unpartitioned data is slow and billed by the byte scanned. CloudTrail Lake is the managed alternative when you want immutable, queryable event storage with up to seven years of retention without managing the S3 lifecycle yourself.

For interactive investigation of centralised logs, CloudWatch Logs Insights runs ad-hoc queries over log groups — all 403s from one IP in the last hour — faster than exporting when the logs are already in place. Sharing KMS-encrypted log groups with a central security account requires both halves of the permission: a resource-based log destination policy and KMS key policies granting the central account decrypt rights.

Monitoring closes the loop when a detection triggers action. A Config rule flags the bucket policy that just went non-compliant; EventBridge catches the compliance-change event and routes it to SNS or a Lambda that remediates. That detect-notify-remediate chain — Config rule plus EventBridge plus response — is the exam's standard answer for near-real-time drift detection, whether the drift is an S3 policy, an unencrypted volume, or a security group someone opened to the world.

Cost discipline belongs in the design. Data events are high-volume and billed per event, so enable them on sensitive resources rather than everywhere. Management events already cover the control plane for free. And when retention is about audit rather than investigation, Glacier-class storage behind lifecycle policies beats any queryable store on price.

overview: Network security in AWS is a stack of overlapping controls, and the exam tests whether you know which layer answers which threat. Security groups guard instances, NACLs guard subnets, WAF guards web applications, Shield guards against DDoS, and account boundaries guard everything. Misplace a control — expecting WAF to stop a volumetric flood, or a NACL to behave like a security group — and the architecture fails where it matters.

This lesson maps the network security stack: stateful versus stateless filtering, three-tier VPC design, private connectivity through endpoints, Layer 7 protection with WAF, DDoS with Shield, and why multi-account structure is itself a network security decision. (SCS-C02 Domain 3.0: Infrastructure Security.)

learn.heading: Filtering: security groups and NACLs
body: Security groups and network ACLs both filter traffic, and they behave differently in the ways that matter. Security groups are stateful: return traffic for an allowed connection is automatically permitted, so you never think about ephemeral ports. They are also allow-only — there is no deny rule in a security group. NACLs are stateless: each direction is evaluated independently, so a NACL that allows inbound web traffic must also allow the outbound ephemeral-port range for the response. And NACLs support explicit deny rules, evaluated in ascending rule-number order with first match winning.

The canonical three-tier layout puts load balancers in public subnets and application and data tiers in private subnets across at least two Availability Zones, with NAT gateways providing outbound-only internet access. A web security group allows 443 from the internet; the application security group allows traffic only from the web security group — referenced by security group ID, not by IP, so the rules stay correct as instances scale. No instance that users reach directly should hold data.

For AWS service access without internet exposure, VPC endpoints keep traffic on the private AWS network. Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are route-table targets and free; interface endpoints for most other services are elastic network interfaces with hourly and data charges. Endpoint policies add a further control: even with broad IAM permissions, an endpoint policy can deny access to sensitive buckets, containing exfiltration paths. And an instance with no internet route can still be managed — private subnets with interface endpoints for SSM, EC2 Messages, and SSM Messages give you Session Manager with no internet path at all.

learn.heading: WAF, Shield, and the account boundary
body: AWS WAF filters Layer 7 web traffic — SQL injection, cross-site scripting, bot control — in front of CloudFront, Application Load Balancers, and API Gateway. It is not a network firewall; it never sees Layers 3 and 4 the way security groups do. Start with AWS managed rule groups for common threats like the OWASP Top 10, then add custom rules for business logic — blocking specific paths, headers, or geographies. If a managed rule update starts blocking legitimate traffic, switch it to Count mode: matches are logged but not blocked, giving you visibility to tune exclusions without an outage.

DDoS protection comes in two tiers. Shield Standard is automatic and free for CloudFront, Route 53, ALBs, and Elastic IPs. Shield Advanced adds cost but brings 24/7 access to the DDoS Response Team, deeper Layer 7 mitigations, and cost protection against scaling charges during an attack. The exam's pairing is deliberate: WAF rate-based rules handle application-layer request floods per IP, while Shield Advanced handles volumetric Layers 3, 4, and 7 attacks. Use both; neither replaces the other.

For centralised, stateful inspection across VPCs — Suricata-compatible rules at Layers 3 through 7 — AWS Network Firewall sits as a transit inspection point, typically in a dedicated security VPC in a hub-and-spoke Transit Gateway design. AWS Firewall Manager then deploys WAF rules, Shield Advanced protections, and security group policies centrally across the organization.

Finally, the strongest network boundary in AWS is not a firewall rule but an account. Separate accounts per environment, governed by SCPs with separate CloudTrail and Config, eliminate entire classes of accidental cross-environment privilege paths. Combined with account-level S3 Block Public Access — which guarantees no bucket can become public via ACLs or policies regardless of individual settings — the multi-account structure is the foundation every other network control rests on.
