acn-3.example: A NACL denies inbound traffic from an attacker's IP range to every subnet, while security groups continue to control which services talk to which.
acn-3.tip: A stateless NACL that allows inbound 443 but forgets outbound ephemeral ports silently breaks connections. A classic troubleshooting trap.

acn-4.body:
Choosing a load-balancing strategy depends on the protocol and the features needed. Layer 4 network load balancers suit TCP/UDP, extreme throughput, static IPs, source IP preservation, and non-HTTP protocols. Layer 7 application load balancers suit HTTP/HTTPS with host and path routing, redirects, header-based rules, authentication integration, TLS termination with managed certificates, and WAF attachment.

Within a pool, algorithms such as round robin or least outstanding requests spread load, while sticky sessions keep a user on one target (useful for legacy stateful apps, but it hinders even scaling). Global load balancing across regions uses DNS policies or anycast front ends. Balance latency, cost, observability, and security requirements when choosing.
acn-4.example: A company uses an ALB with path-based routing for its microservices and a separate NLB for an MQTT IoT broker that needs static IPs for device firewall rules.
acn-4.tip: Prefer stateless applications over sticky sessions. Stickiness makes scaling uneven and failover disruptive.

acn-5.body:
Private connectivity keeps traffic off the public internet or protects it across it. Site-to-site VPNs encrypt traffic over the internet: quick to set up and cheap, but performance varies with internet conditions and each tunnel has limited bandwidth. Dedicated connections (AWS Direct Connect, Azure ExpressRoute, Google Cloud Interconnect) provide private circuits with consistent latency and high bandwidth, but take weeks to provision and are not encrypted by default.

Private Link and private endpoints expose individual services privately inside your VPC. Production designs typically combine a dedicated connection for primary traffic, a VPN for backup or encryption overlay, and private endpoints for cloud services, all with BGP for dynamic failover.
acn-5.example: A hospital uses ExpressRoute for its EHR integration with Azure, with a site-to-site VPN as backup, and private endpoints for Azure SQL and Storage.
acn-5.tip: Match the option to the need: fast setup = VPN; consistent high bandwidth = dedicated link; single-service exposure = PrivateLink.

acn-6.body:
Cloud DNS is a traffic-management layer. Public hosted zones publish internet-facing names; private hosted zones resolve names only inside associated VPCs, enabling internal names such as db.internal.example.com without exposing them. Hybrid resolvers (such as Route 53 Resolver endpoints) forward queries between on-premises DNS and cloud private zones.

Routing policies (weighted, latency-based, geolocation, and failover with health checks) steer users to the right endpoints, enabling active-active multi-region deployments and disaster-recovery cutovers. Combine low TTLs during changes with higher TTLs for stability, enable DNSSEC for public zones, and log queries for security monitoring.
acn-6.example: A two-region application uses latency routing with health checks so users go to the nearest healthy region, while private zones handle internal service names.
acn-6.tip: DNS query logs are a strong security signal. Malware often reveals itself through unusual domain lookups.

acn-7.body:
Service endpoints and private endpoints let workloads reach cloud provider services (object storage, databases, secrets managers, queues) and SaaS offerings over private IP addresses rather than public endpoints. AWS offers gateway endpoints (S3 and DynamoDB, routed through route tables at no extra charge) and interface endpoints powered by PrivateLink; Azure offers Private Endpoints; Google offers Private Service Connect.

Benefits include removing the need for NAT or internet access for these services, reducing data-transfer costs, and a better security posture. Resource policies can require that data is only accessed through your private endpoint (for example an S3 bucket policy with aws:SourceVpce), which blocks access from anywhere else even with valid credentials.
acn-7.example: An S3 bucket policy allows access only via the company's VPC endpoint, so stolen access keys used from the internet are denied.
acn-7.tip: Endpoint policies plus resource policies are a strong defence against data exfiltration with stolen credentials.

acn-8.body:
Packet or traffic mirroring copies network traffic from chosen interfaces (entire packets, not just metadata) and sends it to a collector or appliance for analysis. In the cloud, AWS VPC Traffic Mirroring, Azure virtual network TAP, and Google Packet Mirroring provide this without physical taps.

Mirrored traffic feeds intrusion detection and prevention systems (Suricata, Snort), network security monitoring tools (Zeek), forensic capture during incidents, and performance troubleshooting. Because full packets can include sensitive data, restrict and secure the collectors. Mirroring every interface all the time is expensive, so mirror critical segments or enable it on demand, and use flow logs for broad coverage.
acn-8.example: During an incident, the SOC mirrors a suspected compromised instance's traffic to a Zeek sensor and discovers DNS tunnelling to an attacker's domain.
acn-8.tip: Flow logs tell you who talked to whom; mirroring tells you what was said. Use each where it fits.

o1-1.body:
Active Directory Domain Services is Microsoft's directory service. It stores objects (users, computers, groups, service accounts, printers) in a hierarchical database organised into domains, trees, and forests, and provides authentication (mainly Kerberos, with NTLM as a legacy fallback) and authorisation information across the network.

Users sign in once with domain credentials and are granted access to resources based on group membership, instead of having separate accounts on every machine. AD also underpins Group Policy, certificate services, and single sign-on to many applications, and it can be synchronised to Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) for cloud services. Because it controls access to nearly everything, AD is a prime attack target: attackers who reach Domain Admin effectively own the organisation.
o1-1.example: A new employee's account is created once in AD, added to 'Finance' and 'VPN Users' groups, and immediately works on any company PC, file share, and VPN.
o1-1.tip: Protect AD with tiered admin accounts, few Domain Admins, LAPS for local admin passwords, and monitoring for attacks such as Kerberoasting and DCSync.

o1-2.body:
A domain controller is a Windows Server that runs AD DS and holds a writable copy of the directory database (NTDS.dit). DCs authenticate users and computers (acting as the Kerberos Key Distribution Center), apply security policy, and serve LDAP queries. Most organisations run at least two DCs per domain, and several per site in larger networks, for redundancy and fast local logons.

DCs replicate changes to each other automatically (multi-master replication). A few special roles, the FSMO roles such as the PDC Emulator and RID Master, live on specific DCs. Read-only domain controllers (RODCs) suit branch offices with weak physical security. Because a DC holds every password hash in the domain, DCs must be tightly secured, patched, backed up, and accessed only from privileged admin workstations.
o1-2.example: When the only DC at a branch fails, users there still log in because their computers find another DC through DNS SRV records and site links.
o1-2.tip: Never browse the web or read email on a domain controller. Treat DCs as Tier 0: only Tier 0 admins log on to them.

o1-3.body:
Group Policy lets administrators define configuration and security settings once and apply them to many users and computers. Group Policy Objects (GPOs) contain computer settings (applied at startup) and user settings (applied at logon), covering password and lockout policies, security baselines, firewall rules, software installation, drive mappings, scripts, desktop restrictions, and more.

GPOs are linked to sites, domains, or OUs and processed in the order LSDOU: Local, Site, Domain, OU (closest OU last), so later GPOs override earlier ones unless 'Enforced' or blocked. Security filtering and WMI filters target specific groups or machines. Tools include gpupdate /force to apply changes immediately, and gpresult /r or the Resultant Set of Policy report to see what actually applied.
o1-3.example: A security baseline GPO linked to the Workstations OU disables SMBv1, enables BitLocker, and restricts local admin rights across 5,000 PCs in one change.
o1-3.tip: Troubleshoot GPOs with `gpresult /h report.html` to see which policies applied, which were filtered, and why.

o1-4.body:
NTFS permissions control access to files and folders on NTFS volumes through access control lists (ACLs). Each entry (ACE) grants or denies permissions such as Read, Read & Execute, List Folder Contents, Write, Modify, and Full Control to a user or group. Permissions inherit from parent folders by default, and explicit deny entries override allows.

When files are accessed over the network, share permissions apply as well, and the most restrictive combination of share and NTFS permissions wins. Best practice is to set share permissions broadly (for example Authenticated Users: Change) and control access precisely with NTFS permissions assigned to groups, never to individual users, following least privilege. Moving files within the same volume keeps their permissions; copying them inherits the destination's.
o1-4.example: HR staff get Modify on \\files\HR through the 'HR-Staff' group, while everyone else has no access; a departing employee loses access the moment they leave the group.
o1-4.tip: Effective permission = most restrictive of share and NTFS permissions over the network. Deny beats allow.

o1-5.body:
Windows Server is Microsoft's server operating system. It is role-based: you install only the roles and features a server needs, such as AD DS (domain controller), DNS, DHCP, File and Storage Services, Print Services, Hyper-V (virtualisation), IIS (web server), Remote Desktop Services, AD Certificate Services, and Windows Server Update Services (WSUS).

Editions and installation options affect its footprint: Server Core has no desktop GUI, which means a smaller attack surface and fewer patches, and is managed remotely with PowerShell, Windows Admin Center, or RSAT tools. Key administration practices include regular patching, security baselines (CIS or Microsoft), minimal installed roles, remote management over secure channels, and monitoring event logs.
o1-5.example: A company runs its domain controllers and DNS on Server Core to reduce patching and attack surface, managing them remotely with PowerShell.
o1-5.tip: Install only needed roles and prefer Server Core where possible. Every extra role is extra attack surface.

o1-6.body:
Organizational Units are containers inside an AD domain that hold users, computers, groups, and other OUs, forming a hierarchy that usually mirrors how you manage things: by location, department, or device type. OUs serve two main purposes: linking Group Policy (a GPO linked to an OU applies to the objects inside it) and delegating administration (for example letting the helpdesk reset passwords only in the 'Branch-London' OU).

An OU is not a security boundary: you cannot grant access to a file share 'to an OU'. Security groups are what you use to grant access to resources. Design OUs around administration and policy needs, keep the structure reasonably flat, and avoid leaving objects in the default Users and Computers containers, which cannot have GPOs linked to them.
o1-6.example: Laptops live in the 'Workstations/Laptops' OU with a GPO enforcing BitLocker, and helpdesk staff are delegated rights to that OU only.
o1-6.tip: OUs = policy and delegation. Security groups = permissions. A common exam distinction.

o1-7.body:
Active Directory depends completely on DNS. Clients find domain controllers by querying SRV records (such as _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.example.local), which DCs register automatically. If clients point to the wrong DNS server (for example a public resolver), they cannot find a DC, and domain logons, Group Policy, and Kerberos fail.

AD-integrated DNS zones are stored inside the AD database instead of text files, so they replicate automatically to other DCs with AD replication, support multi-master updates, and allow secure dynamic updates, where only authenticated domain members can register or change their records. Domain members should use internal DNS servers only; those servers forward external queries to the internet.
o1-7.example: Logons start failing after someone sets office PCs to use 8.8.8.8 for DNS; the PCs can no longer locate a domain controller through SRV records.
o1-7.tip: In AD troubleshooting, check DNS first: `nslookup -type=SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.yourdomain` and `dcdiag /test:dns`.

o1-8.body:
Windows records events in logs viewable with Event Viewer or PowerShell (Get-WinEvent). The main logs are System (drivers, services, OS events), Application (software events), and Security (audited logons, privilege use, policy and account changes), plus many specialised logs such as PowerShell, Sysmon, and Windows Defender.

Key security event IDs include 4624 (successful logon), 4625 (failed logon), 4672 (special privileges assigned), 4720 (user created), 4728/4732 (user added to a group), 4740 (account locked out), 4688 (process created), and 1102 (audit log cleared). Enable advanced audit policies through GPO and forward events to a SIEM with Windows Event Forwarding or an agent, because attackers clear local logs.
o1-8.example: A SIEM alert fires on many 4625 failures followed by a 4624 success from the same IP, a sign of a successful password-guessing attack.
o1-8.tip: Event ID 1102 (security log cleared) on a server is a strong indicator of attacker anti-forensics.

o2-1.body:
Every Linux file and directory has an owner, a group, and three permission sets: owner (u), group (g), and others (o). Each set has read (r), write (w), and execute (x) bits. For files, x means the file can be run; for directories, r lists contents, w creates or deletes entries, and x allows entering (traversing) the directory.

ls -l shows permissions as a 10-character string such as -rwxr-xr--: the first character is the type (- file, d directory, l symlink), followed by the owner, group, and others triplets. Special bits add behaviour: setuid (s on the owner) runs a program with its owner's privileges, setgid (s on the group) inherits group ownership in directories, and the sticky bit (t, as on /tmp) lets only the owner delete their files.
o2-1.example: `-rw-r-----  root  shadow  /etc/shadow` means root can read and write, the shadow group can read, and everyone else has no access to password hashes.
o2-1.tip: Unexpected setuid-root binaries are a classic privilege escalation path. Audit them with `find / -perm -4000 -type f`.

o2-2.body:
chmod changes permissions, using either octal numbers or symbolic notation. In octal, r=4, w=2, x=1 are summed for each of owner, group, and others: chmod 755 script.sh gives rwxr-xr-x, and chmod 600 id_rsa gives rw------- (owner only). Symbolically: chmod u+x script.sh adds execute for the owner, and chmod g-w,o-r file removes group write and others' read.

chown changes ownership: chown alice file, chown alice:developers file, or recursively chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www. chgrp changes only the group. The umask sets default permissions for new files. Least privilege applies: config files with secrets should be 600 or 640, never world-readable, and avoid chmod 777, which lets anyone modify the file.
o2-2.example: SSH refuses a private key with 'permissions are too open' until `chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519` restricts it to the owner.
o2-2.tip: `chmod 777` is almost always wrong. It lets any user modify or replace the file, including scripts run by root.

term:systemd & Services.body:
systemd is the init system and service manager on most modern Linux distributions. It starts as process ID 1 at boot, brings up the system in parallel according to unit dependencies, and supervises services (daemons), restarting them if configured to do so. Units describe what systemd manages: .service (daemons), .timer (scheduled jobs, a cron alternative), .socket, .mount, and .target (groups of units, such as multi-user.target).

systemctl controls it: systemctl status nginx, start, stop, restart, reload (re-read the configuration), enable and disable (start at boot or not), and systemctl list-units --failed. Logs go to the journal, read with journalctl -u nginx -f (follow one service) or journalctl -b (the current boot). Custom services are defined in unit files under /etc/systemd/system.
term:systemd & Services.example: After a reboot a web app is down; `systemctl status myapp` shows it was never enabled, so `systemctl enable --now myapp` starts it now and at every boot.
term:systemd & Services.tip: `start` runs a service now; `enable` makes it start at boot. You usually want both (`enable --now`).

o2-4.body:
Package managers install, update, and remove software from trusted repositories, handling dependencies automatically and verifying package signatures. Debian and Ubuntu use apt (apt update refreshes indexes, apt install nginx, apt upgrade) on top of dpkg. RHEL, Fedora, Rocky, and Alma use dnf (formerly yum) on top of rpm. Others include zypper (SUSE), pacman (Arch), and apk (Alpine).

Using packages keeps software patched through normal update processes and makes installations auditable (dpkg -l, rpm -qa list what is installed). Downloading random binaries or piping curl output into bash bypasses signature checks and update management. Enterprises often mirror repositories internally and automate patching with unattended-upgrades, dnf-automatic, or configuration management tools.
o2-4.example: `sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade` patches OpenSSL along with everything else on an Ubuntu server within minutes of a security advisory.
o2-4.tip: Patch regularly and verify repositories are signed. A compromised or untrusted repository is a supply-chain attack path.

o2-5.body:
A Bash script is a text file of shell commands that runs in sequence, starting with a shebang line (#!/usr/bin/env bash) and made executable with chmod +x. Scripts use variables (NAME=value, used as "$NAME"), command substitution ($(date +%F)), conditionals (if [[ -f file ]]; then ... fi), loops (for f in *.log; do ... done), functions, and exit codes (0 means success).

Scripts automate backups, log rotation, user provisioning, deployments, and health checks. Robust scripts start with set -euo pipefail (stop on errors, undefined variables, and pipeline failures), quote every variable, validate input, log what they do, and are tested with shellcheck. For complex logic, move to Python or configuration management.
o2-5.example: A nightly script dumps the database with a dated file name, compresses it, uploads it to object storage, and deletes local copies older than seven days.
o2-5.tip: Always quote variables ("$file"). Unquoted variables break on spaces and enable injection bugs; run `shellcheck` on every script.

o2-6.body:
Linux accounts are defined in /etc/passwd (username, UID, GID, home directory, shell), password hashes live in /etc/shadow (readable only by root), and groups in /etc/group. useradd or adduser creates users, usermod modifies them (usermod -aG docker alice adds a supplementary group), passwd sets passwords, and userdel removes accounts. System accounts for services typically have no login shell (/usr/sbin/nologin).

sudo lets authorised users run specific commands as root or another user, logging every use, without sharing the root password. Rules live in /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d/ (always edit with visudo). Grant the narrowest rules possible, disable direct root login, remove or lock accounts of leavers promptly, and review group memberships regularly.
o2-6.example: A deploy user is allowed only `sudo systemctl restart myapp` via a sudoers rule, rather than full root access.
o2-6.tip: Broad sudo rules (such as `ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL`) or sudo access to editors and interpreters are easy privilege escalation paths.

o2-7.body:
Processes can be inspected with ps aux (a snapshot of all processes with user, CPU, memory, and command), top or htop (live views sorted by resource use), pgrep and pidof (find process IDs), and lsof or ss -p (open files and sockets per process). kill PID sends SIGTERM (a polite stop); kill -9 PID sends SIGKILL (immediate, no cleanup) and should be a last resort.

Logs are the first stop when something misbehaves. Traditional text logs live in /var/log: syslog or messages (general), auth.log or secure (logins and sudo), kern.log, and application directories such as /var/log/nginx. On systemd systems, journalctl queries the journal, and dmesg shows kernel messages such as hardware errors and out-of-memory kills.
o2-7.example: A server is slow; `top` shows a runaway process at 100% CPU, and `journalctl -u app --since '10 min ago'` reveals it is stuck retrying a failed database connection.
o2-7.tip: Check `dmesg` for 'Out of memory: Killed process'. The OOM killer silently terminating services explains many mystery crashes.

o2-8.body:
SSH provides encrypted remote shell access (ssh user@host), secure file transfer (scp, sftp, rsync over SSH), and tunnelling or port forwarding. The server daemon sshd is configured in /etc/ssh/sshd_config. Key-based authentication uses a key pair: the private key stays on your machine (protected by a passphrase), and the public key goes into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server.

Hardening steps: disable password authentication (PasswordAuthentication no), disable direct root login (PermitRootLogin no), allow only specific users or groups (AllowGroups), use modern key types such as Ed25519, keep OpenSSH patched, and rate-limit or block brute force with fail2ban. For fleets, use a bastion or an SSH certificate authority, or cloud session managers that avoid exposing port 22.
o2-8.example: Internet-facing servers see thousands of SSH password-guessing attempts a day; disabling password authentication makes them all irrelevant.
o2-8.tip: Always verify host key fingerprints on first connection. A changed host key warning can indicate a man-in-the-middle.

l1-1.body:
The shell is the command interpreter that sits between the user and the operating system. It reads commands, expands variables and wildcards (globbing), handles pipes and redirection, and asks the kernel to run programs. Common shells are Bash (the default on most Linux systems), Zsh (the macOS default), Fish, and the minimal POSIX sh or dash used for system scripts.

The shell is also a programming environment, with variables, conditionals, loops, functions, and job control (running tasks in the background with &, and managing them with jobs, fg, and bg). Configuration files such as ~/.bashrc and ~/.zshrc set aliases, PATH, and the prompt. Scripting the shell is the foundation of Linux automation.
l1-1.example: `for host in web01 web02 web03; do ssh "$host" uptime; done` checks load on three servers in one line.
l1-1.tip: Know your PATH. A writable directory early in root's PATH lets attackers hijack commands.

l1-2.body:
Linux follows the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard: one tree rooted at /, where extra disks are mounted as directories. /etc holds system configuration, /home holds user directories (/root for the root user), /var holds variable data such as logs (/var/log), spools, caches, and databases, and /tmp holds temporary files (often cleared on reboot).

/bin, /sbin, /usr/bin, and /usr/sbin hold programs (often merged into /usr on modern distributions), and /lib holds shared libraries. /opt holds add-on software and /srv service data. /boot holds the kernel and bootloader files. /proc and /sys are virtual file systems exposing process and kernel information, and /dev contains device files. /mnt and /media are mount points.
l1-2.example: Web server configuration is in /etc/nginx, its logs in /var/log/nginx, and its site files in /var/www or /srv; knowing this, you find anything in seconds.
l1-2.tip: Watch /var and /tmp disk usage. A full /var/log can stop services and logging entirely.

l1-3.body:
Each Linux file has an owner, a group, and permissions for owner, group, and others, with read, write, and execute bits (rwx). The octal shorthand adds r=4, w=2, x=1 per class. 755 (rwxr-xr-x) suits executables and directories anyone may enter, 644 (rw-r--r--) suits ordinary readable files, 600 (rw-------) suits private files such as SSH keys and secrets, and 700 (rwx------) suits private directories.

chmod changes permissions, chown changes owner and group, and umask sets the default permissions for new files (a common umask of 022 yields 644 files and 755 directories). Access Control Lists (setfacl, getfacl) provide finer-grained permissions when the owner/group/other model is not enough.
l1-3.example: A web app's config file containing database passwords is set to 640, owned by root with group www-data, so the app can read it but other users cannot.
l1-3.tip: Read the octal digits as owner-group-others. 640 = owner rw, group r, others nothing.

l1-4.body:
Linux is multi-user by design. Each account has a numeric UID (root is 0) and a primary group, and it can belong to supplementary groups that grant shared access (for example docker, sudo or wheel, www-data). Account data lives in /etc/passwd, hashed passwords in /etc/shadow, and groups in /etc/group; the id command shows a user's UID, GID, and groups.

sudo delegates privilege precisely: users run specific commands as root (or another user), with each use logged, and no one needs to know the root password. Policies live in /etc/sudoers and drop-in files under /etc/sudoers.d/, edited safely with visudo. Membership in the sudo or wheel group typically grants full admin rights, so keep it small.
l1-4.example: Adding a developer to the docker group effectively gives them root on that host, because Docker can mount the host file system.
l1-4.tip: Some group memberships (docker, lxd, disk) are equivalent to root. Treat them as privileged.

l1-5.body:
Every running program is a process with a PID, a parent (PPID), an owner, and a state (running, sleeping, stopped, zombie). Inspect processes with ps aux, ps -ef --forest (showing parent and child trees), top or htop, and pgrep name.

Signals let you communicate with processes: SIGTERM (15, the default for kill) asks a program to shut down cleanly; SIGKILL (9) forces immediate termination with no cleanup; SIGHUP (1) traditionally makes daemons reload their configuration; SIGINT (2) is what Ctrl+C sends; SIGSTOP and SIGCONT pause and resume. killall and pkill signal processes by name. Use SIGTERM first and SIGKILL only if the process does not respond.
l1-5.example: `kill -HUP $(pidof nginx)` or `systemctl reload nginx` applies a configuration change without dropping active connections.
l1-5.tip: An unusual parent-child relationship (such as a web server spawning a shell) is a classic sign of compromise. Use `ps -ef --forest`.

l1-6.body:
Every process has three standard streams: stdin (0, input), stdout (1, normal output), and stderr (2, error output). Redirection changes where they go: > writes stdout to a file (overwriting), >> appends, < reads input from a file, 2> redirects errors, and 2>&1 sends errors wherever stdout goes. /dev/null discards output.

Pipes (|) connect one command's stdout to the next command's stdin, so small tools combine into powerful pipelines. tee writes output to a file and the screen at the same time. Here-documents (<<EOF) feed multi-line input to commands. This composability, many small tools each doing one thing well, is the core of the Unix philosophy.
l1-6.example: `grep 'Failed password' /var/log/auth.log | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head` lists the IPs with the most failed SSH logins.
l1-6.tip: `cmd > out.txt 2>&1` captures both output and errors. The order matters: `2>&1 > file` does not do the same thing.

l1-7.body:
Linux text tools turn logs and command output into answers. grep searches for patterns (-i ignore case, -r recursive, -v invert, -E extended regex, -c count). sed edits streams, for example sed 's/old/new/g' to substitute. awk processes columns and fields ('{print $1, $9}' prints fields 1 and 9 of access logs) and can sum and filter. cut extracts fields by delimiter, and tr translates characters.

sort orders lines (-n numeric, -r reverse), and uniq collapses duplicates (-c counts them, but it needs sorted input). wc counts lines and words, head and tail show the start or end (tail -f follows a growing log), and xargs turns input lines into arguments for another command. Together they replace spreadsheets for quick analysis.
l1-7.example: `awk '{print $9}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr` counts HTTP status codes in a web log in one second.
l1-7.tip: `uniq` only removes adjacent duplicates. Always `sort` first.

l1-8.body:
Package management differs by distribution family. Debian and Ubuntu use .deb packages via apt and dpkg; RHEL, Fedora, Rocky, and Alma use .rpm packages via dnf (formerly yum) and rpm; Arch uses pacman; Alpine, popular in containers, uses apk; SUSE uses zypper. Universal formats such as Snap, Flatpak, and AppImage bundle dependencies for desktop apps.

Package managers resolve dependencies, verify signatures with repository GPG keys, track installed files for clean removal, and make patching a single command. Pinning or holding versions (apt-mark hold, dnf versionlock) prevents unwanted upgrades of critical packages. Prefer official and vendor repositories, verify third-party repository keys, and avoid building software from source on servers unless necessary.
l1-8.example: An Alpine-based container image installs tools with `apk add --no-cache curl`, keeping the image small and the package list auditable.
l1-8.tip: Know your distribution family. Exam and interview scenarios often hinge on `apt` versus `dnf`.

l1-10.body:
SSH is the standard for secure remote administration. Generate a key pair with ssh-keygen -t ed25519, protect the private key with a passphrase, copy the public key to servers with ssh-copy-id user@host, and let ssh-agent cache the unlocked key for the session. The ~/.ssh/config file defines host aliases, users, keys, and jump hosts (ProxyJump) to simplify connections.

SSH also tunnels traffic: local forwarding (-L) reaches a remote service through the SSH connection, remote forwarding (-R) exposes a local service, and dynamic forwarding (-D) creates a SOCKS proxy. Harden servers by disabling password and root logins, restricting users, keeping OpenSSH patched, and monitoring authentication logs.
l1-10.example: `ssh -J bastion.example.com admin@10.0.2.15` connects to a private server through a bastion host in one command using ProxyJump.
l1-10.tip: Protect private keys like passwords. A stolen unencrypted key gives immediate access to every server that trusts it.

v-1.body:
A hypervisor, or virtual machine monitor (VMM), creates and runs virtual machines by abstracting the physical hardware. It divides CPU time, memory, storage, and network access among VMs, presents each with virtual hardware, and keeps them isolated so that a crash or compromise in one VM does not affect the others or the host.

Modern CPUs include hardware virtualisation extensions (Intel VT-x, AMD-V) that let hypervisors run guests efficiently. Hypervisors also enable snapshots, live migration of running VMs between hosts, resource over-commitment, and high-availability restarts. They are the foundation of data-centre consolidation and of public cloud infrastructure.
v-1.example: One physical server with 64 cores and 512 GB of RAM runs 40 VMs for different teams, each believing it has its own dedicated computer.
v-1.tip: VM escape vulnerabilities, where code breaks out of a guest into the hypervisor, are critical. Patch hypervisors promptly.

v-2.body:
A Type 1, or bare-metal, hypervisor installs directly on the physical hardware with no general-purpose host operating system underneath. Because it controls the hardware directly, it offers the best performance, efficiency, and security isolation, and it is what data centres and cloud providers run.

Examples include VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V (a thin hypervisor layer beneath Windows), Xen, KVM (built into the Linux kernel, so Linux effectively becomes the hypervisor), Proxmox VE (KVM-based), and AWS Nitro. Type 1 hypervisors are managed remotely through management consoles such as vCenter or System Center, and support clustering, live migration, and high availability.
v-2.example: An enterprise runs VMware ESXi clusters; when a host fails, its VMs restart automatically on other hosts in the cluster.
v-2.tip: Type 1 = bare metal = production data centres and clouds. Type 2 = hosted on an OS = desktops and labs.

v-3.body:
A Type 2, or hosted, hypervisor runs as an application on top of an existing operating system such as Windows, macOS, or Linux. The host OS manages the hardware, and the hypervisor requests resources through it, which adds overhead and makes the VMs depend on the host OS's stability and security.

Examples include Oracle VirtualBox, VMware Workstation and Fusion, and Parallels Desktop. Type 2 hypervisors are easy to install and ideal for developers, students, testers, and security labs, for example running Kali Linux and a vulnerable Windows VM on a laptop to practise safely. Snapshots let you revert a lab VM to a clean state in seconds.
v-3.example: A student builds a home lab in VirtualBox with a Windows Server domain controller and a Windows 10 client on an isolated internal network.
v-3.tip: Keep malware-analysis and attack lab VMs on host-only or isolated networks so nothing escapes to your real LAN.

v-4.body:
A virtual machine is a complete software-defined computer: virtual CPUs, memory, disks (image files such as VMDK, VHDX, or qcow2), and network adapters, running its own full guest operating system and kernel. To the guest, it looks like real hardware. VMs are strongly isolated from each other by the hypervisor.

Because each VM carries a whole OS, VMs are relatively heavy: gigabytes of disk and RAM, and boot times of tens of seconds or more. In return, they can run any OS (Windows next to Linux on the same host), provide strong security isolation, and can be snapshotted, cloned, templated, backed up, and live-migrated. Cloud instances such as EC2 and Azure VMs are VMs.
v-4.example: A company keeps a legacy Windows Server 2012 application running inside an isolated VM while modernising the rest of its infrastructure.
v-4.tip: Snapshots are not backups. They live on the same storage and degrade performance if kept for long.

term:Container.body:
A container packages an application together with its libraries, dependencies, and configuration, and runs it as an isolated process on a host that shares its operating system kernel with other containers. Isolation comes from Linux kernel features: namespaces give each container its own view of processes, network, file system mounts, and users, while cgroups limit its CPU and memory.

Because there is no guest OS, containers start in milliseconds to seconds, use megabytes rather than gigabytes, and pack densely onto hosts. The same image runs identically on a laptop, a test server, and production. The trade-off is weaker isolation than VMs: a kernel vulnerability or a misconfigured container (privileged mode, a mounted Docker socket, running as root) can let an attacker reach the host.
term:Container.example: A microservice runs as 30 identical containers across 5 hosts, and new replicas start in under two seconds during a traffic spike.
term:Container.tip: Harden containers: run as non-root, drop capabilities, use read-only file systems, never run privileged containers in production, and scan images for vulnerabilities.

v-6.body:
Docker popularised containers by making them easy to build, share, and run. A Dockerfile describes how to build an image: a base image (FROM), commands to install software (RUN), files to copy (COPY), environment settings, and the startup command (CMD or ENTRYPOINT). docker build produces an image made of cached layers, docker push stores it in a registry, and docker run starts containers from it.

Docker Compose defines multi-container applications (such as an app, a database, and a cache) in one YAML file for local development. Best practices include small base images (distroless, Alpine, or slim variants), multi-stage builds so compilers stay out of the final image, pinned versions, a non-root USER, no secrets baked into images, and regular vulnerability scanning.
v-6.example: A developer runs `docker compose up` and gets the same app, Postgres, and Redis versions as production, which ends 'works on my machine' problems.
v-6.tip: Anyone with access to the Docker socket (/var/run/docker.sock) effectively has root on the host.

v-7.body:
Kubernetes is an open-source platform that orchestrates containers across a cluster of machines. You declare the desired state (for example 'run five replicas of this image, exposed on port 443') in YAML manifests, and Kubernetes continuously works to make reality match: scheduling Pods onto nodes, restarting failed containers, replacing Pods on failed nodes, and rolling out new versions gradually.

Key objects include Pods, Deployments (manage replicas and rolling updates), Services (stable networking and load balancing), Ingress (HTTP routing), ConfigMaps and Secrets (configuration), and Namespaces (logical separation). The control plane (API server, scheduler, controller manager, etcd) manages the worker nodes, where the kubelet runs containers. Managed services include EKS, AKS, and GKE.
v-7.example: A node crashes at 3 a.m.; Kubernetes automatically reschedules its Pods onto healthy nodes and the service stays up without anyone being paged.
v-7.tip: Kubernetes security basics: RBAC least privilege, network policies, Pod Security Standards, secrets encryption, and restricted API server access.

term:Pod.body:
A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes: a wrapper around one or more containers that are scheduled together on the same node, share a network namespace (one IP address, so they talk over localhost), and can share storage volumes. Most Pods run a single main container; multi-container Pods add helpers such as sidecars (log shippers, service-mesh proxies) or init containers that run setup steps first.

Pods are ephemeral and disposable: they are not repaired or patched in place, but replaced. When a Pod dies, a controller such as a Deployment or StatefulSet creates a new one, usually with a new IP address, which is why applications reach Pods through Services rather than Pod IPs. Resource requests and limits tell the scheduler how much CPU and memory each Pod needs.
term:Pod.example: An app Pod runs the application container plus an Envoy sidecar that handles mTLS for all its network traffic.
term:Pod.tip: Set resource requests and limits on every Pod. Without them, one noisy Pod can starve its neighbours on the node.

v-9.body:
Virtual machines and containers solve different problems. A VM virtualises hardware and runs a full guest OS with its own kernel, giving strong isolation, the ability to run any OS, and compatibility with legacy software, at the cost of gigabytes of overhead and slower startup. A container virtualises the operating system: it shares the host kernel and isolates processes, giving tiny footprints, near-instant startup, high density, and consistent packaging, but weaker isolation.

In practice they are complementary: containers usually run inside VMs (cloud Kubernetes nodes are VMs), combining VM-level isolation between tenants with container efficiency within them. Sandboxed runtimes such as gVisor and Kata Containers, and micro-VMs such as Firecracker (used by AWS Lambda), blur the line by giving containers VM-like isolation.
v-9.example: A SaaS provider isolates each customer on separate VMs (strong boundary) while running each customer's microservices as containers inside those VMs.
v-9.tip: Need to run Windows and Linux side by side, or require strong isolation between untrusted tenants? Use VMs. Need density and fast deploys? Use containers.

v-10.body:
A container image is a read-only, versioned template for creating containers. It consists of stacked file-system layers (a base OS layer, then dependencies, then application code) plus metadata such as the default command and environment variables. Layers are cached and shared between images, so builds and downloads are fast.

Images are stored in registries (Docker Hub, Amazon ECR, Azure ACR, GitHub Container Registry, Harbor) and identified by a tag (app:1.4.2) or, immutably, by a content digest (app@sha256:…). Because images are immutable, the same artifact moves from test to production unchanged. Security practices include trusted base images, vulnerability scanning in CI, signing images (Sigstore/cosign), deploying by digest, and generating SBOMs.
v-10.example: Production deploys pin `myapp@sha256:9f86d0…` so the exact tested image runs, even if someone pushes a new image with the same tag.
v-10.tip: Tags such as `latest` are mutable. Pin versions or digests to avoid surprise changes and supply-chain attacks.

tr-1.body:
Effective troubleshooting is a disciplined, evidence-driven process. Start by clarifying the problem: what exactly is failing, for whom, since when, and what changed recently (a deploy, a config change, a patch, a certificate expiry, or traffic growth)? Reproduce it if you can, and gather facts from logs, metrics, and error messages before forming theories.

Then form a hypothesis, test it, change only one thing at a time, and observe the result. Resist random fixes and 'restart and hope', which can destroy evidence and hide the real cause. Build a mental model of how the system should work, and compare it with what you observe. Write down what you check as you go, which helps teammates and the eventual postmortem.
tr-1.example: Before rebooting a failing server, the engineer captures memory usage, the process list, and recent logs, and finds a memory leak that a reboot would have hidden until the next outage.
tr-1.tip: Ask 'what changed?' first. Most incidents follow a change.

tr-2.body:
Layered diagnostics use the OSI or TCP/IP model to narrow down where a fault lives. Bottom-up starts at Layer 1 (cables, link lights, interface errors), then Layer 2 (VLAN, MAC learning), Layer 3 (IP configuration, routing, ping), Layer 4 (is the port reachable? use nc, telnet, or Test-NetConnection), and finally the application (HTTP status codes, logs, certificates). Top-down starts with the application error and works downward. Divide-and-conquer starts in the middle, for example with a ping, and moves up or down depending on the result.

Each layer has typical tools: interface counters, arp and ip neigh, ping, traceroute, ss or netstat, tcpdump or Wireshark, curl -v, and application logs and metrics. Localise the fault to one layer and component before trying to fix it.
tr-2.example: Ping to the server works (L3 fine), but `curl -v https://app` fails the TLS handshake, so the problem is an expired certificate at the application layer, not the network.
tr-2.tip: When unsure, start in the middle with ping. It instantly tells you whether to look up or down the stack.

tr-3.body:
The 5 Whys is a simple root cause analysis technique from Toyota: state the problem, ask why it happened, then ask why again about that answer, repeating (often about five times) until you reach a cause that, if fixed, prevents recurrence. The goal is to move past symptoms and proximate triggers to process or design causes.

For example: the site went down (why?) because the database ran out of disk (why?) because logs filled the volume (why?) because log rotation was not configured on the new server (why?) because the build template lacked it (why?) because there is no standard server baseline. The fix is the baseline, not just deleting logs. For complex incidents there are often several contributing causes, so pair 5 Whys with fishbone (Ishikawa) diagrams or timelines.
tr-3.example: A failed deploy's 5 Whys ends at 'integration tests do not run on the release branch', which produces a pipeline fix rather than blaming the engineer.
tr-3.tip: If a 'why' ends with a person's name, keep asking. Look for the system or process that allowed the mistake.

tr-4.body:
An error budget turns reliability targets into a shared decision tool. If a service's SLO is 99.9% availability per month, the error budget is the remaining 0.1%, about 43 minutes of downtime or the equivalent fraction of failed requests. While budget remains, teams can ship features and take risks; if it is burned quickly, the agreed policy slows or freezes risky changes and shifts effort to reliability work.

Blameless culture is the human side: postmortems focus on how the system, tools, and processes allowed a failure, not on punishing individuals. When people feel safe, they report problems and near misses honestly, which surfaces the real causes. Punishing mistakes drives them underground and makes systems less reliable.
tr-4.example: After a bad release burns 80% of the monthly error budget, the team pauses feature launches for two weeks to add canary deployments and automated rollback.
tr-4.tip: Blameless does not mean no accountability. People own the follow-up actions, but the analysis targets systems.

tr-5.body:
Logs, metrics, and traces are the three core observability signals. Metrics are numeric time series (request rate, error rate, latency percentiles, CPU, queue depth). They are cheap to store and ideal for dashboards and alerts, showing that something is wrong and when it started. Logs are timestamped records of discrete events with rich context, such as error messages, request details, and stack traces. They explain what happened.

Traces follow a single request across services, showing each step (span) and its duration, which pinpoints where time is spent or where errors originate in distributed systems. Used together, they form a workflow: an alert on a metric, a trace that finds the slow or failing service, and logs from that service that explain the cause. Correlate them with shared request or trace IDs.
tr-5.example: A latency alert fires; traces show 90% of the time is spent in the payment service; its logs reveal connection-pool timeouts to the database.
tr-5.tip: Structured logs (JSON with consistent fields such as trace_id) make correlation across signals fast.

tr-6.body:
Many incidents fall into recurring failure modes. Resource exhaustion covers CPU saturation, memory leaks and OOM kills, full disks (often logs), exhausted file descriptors, connection pools, NAT ports, or API rate limits. Configuration errors include wrong environment variables, typos, expired certificates or secrets, stale DNS, and mismatched versions between environments.

Dependency failures include slow or failing downstream services, timeouts, and retry storms, where many clients retry simultaneously and overload a recovering service, triggering cascading failures across the system. Knowing these patterns speeds up diagnosis, and each has standard defences: capacity alerts, config validation, certificate expiry monitoring, timeouts, exponential backoff with jitter, circuit breakers, and bulkheads.
tr-6.example: A brief database blip causes every app server to retry immediately and repeatedly; the retry storm keeps the database overloaded long after the blip ended.
tr-6.tip: Always set timeouts on network calls, and retry with exponential backoff and jitter. Never retry in tight loops.

tr-7.body:
During an incident, restoring service comes before finding the root cause. The fastest safe path is often rolling back to the last known good version or configuration, which is why every deployment should have a tested, quick rollback. Mitigations buy time when rollback is not possible: disabling a feature with a feature flag, shedding load or rate limiting, failing over to another region, scaling out, opening circuit breakers to failing dependencies, or serving degraded but functional responses.

Once users are protected, investigate the root cause calmly, with the evidence preserved. Communicate status regularly to stakeholders throughout. Afterwards, fix the underlying issue properly and hold a postmortem.
tr-7.example: A new release causes checkout errors; the on-call engineer rolls back within five minutes, then the team debugs the release in staging the next morning.
tr-7.tip: Mitigate first, then investigate. Make rollback a one-click, routinely exercised operation.

tr-8.body:
A runbook documents how to handle a specific known situation: what the alert means, the dashboards and logs to check, diagnostic commands, remediation steps, escalation contacts, and how to verify recovery. A playbook covers a broader scenario, such as a ransomware response or a major outage, coordinating multiple people and decisions.

Runbooks reduce cognitive load under pressure, speed up response, and let less experienced on-call engineers act safely. Link each alert directly to its runbook, keep runbooks in version control, test them in game days, and update them after every incident. Frequently used manual runbooks are prime candidates for automation.
tr-8.example: A 'disk 90% full' alert links to a runbook listing which directories to check, safe clean-up commands, and when to expand the volume instead.
tr-8.tip: If an alert has no runbook, either write one or ask whether the alert is actionable at all.

tr-9.body:
Reproducing a problem reliably is often the turning point in solving it. Try to recreate the failure in a controlled environment such as staging, a local container, or a test account, using the same inputs, data, configuration, and versions. Then shrink it: remove components, inputs, and steps until you have the minimal case that still fails.

Binary search helps. Revert half the recent changes (git bisect automates this for code), disable half the features, or test with half the data, and see which half contains the trigger. A minimal reproduction clearly separates data problems from configuration, code, and dependency problems, makes the fix testable, and can become a regression test so the bug never returns silently.
tr-9.example: `git bisect` pinpoints the one commit, out of 200, that introduced a memory leak by testing a handful of builds.
tr-9.tip: Turn every reproduced bug into an automated test before fixing it, so the fix is proven.

tr-10.body:
Organisations get more reliable only if they learn from each incident. Capture knowledge in blameless postmortems (timeline, impact, root and contributing causes, what went well, and action items with owners and deadlines), commit messages and pull requests that explain why a fix works, updated runbooks and diagrams, and searchable knowledge-base articles.

Share lessons broadly through incident reviews, internal talks, and training, so other teams avoid the same failure. Track postmortem action items to completion; unfinished action items are how the same incident happens twice. Good documentation also shortens onboarding and reduces dependence on a few key people.
tr-10.example: A monthly incident review walks through the top three postmortems, and another team discovers it has the same certificate-expiry risk and fixes it proactively.
tr-10.tip: An incident is not closed until its action items are done and the runbooks are updated.

term:Data Lake.body:
A data lake is a central repository that stores large volumes of raw data in its native format (structured tables, semi-structured JSON and logs, and unstructured files such as images) at low cost, usually on object storage such as Amazon S3, Azure Data Lake Storage, or Google Cloud Storage. Unlike a warehouse, it applies schema on read: structure is imposed when the data is queried, not when it is loaded.

That flexibility suits machine learning, log analytics, IoT data, and questions you have not thought of yet. Query engines such as Athena, Spark, Presto/Trino, and BigQuery external tables read directly from the lake, especially efficiently when data is stored in columnar formats (Parquet, ORC) and partitioned. Without governance (a data catalogue, ownership, quality checks, access control, and lifecycle policies), a lake degrades into a 'data swamp' that nobody trusts.
term:Data Lake.example: A retailer lands clickstream JSON, point-of-sale CSVs, and product images in S3, then uses Spark for recommendation models and Athena for ad-hoc analysis.
term:Data Lake.tip: Classify and control access to sensitive data in the lake from day one. Lakes often become the largest store of PII in the company.

term:Distributed Tracing.body:
Distributed tracing follows a single request as it travels through many services. The first service creates a trace ID, and each unit of work (an HTTP call, database query, or queue message) records a span with its start time, duration, attributes, and parent span. Context propagation passes the trace ID between services in headers (the W3C traceparent standard), so the backend can reassemble the complete request tree.

Traces show exactly where latency accumulates and where errors originate, which is nearly impossible to reconstruct from logs alone in microservice architectures. Tools include OpenTelemetry for instrumentation plus backends such as Jaeger, Zipkin, Tempo, AWS X-Ray, and commercial APM products. Because tracing every request is expensive, systems use sampling: head-based (decide at the start) or tail-based (keep traces that were slow or failed).
term:Distributed Tracing.example: A checkout request takes 4 seconds; its trace shows 3.5 seconds spent in one call from the pricing service to a third-party tax API.
term:Distributed Tracing.tip: Add trace IDs to your logs so you can jump from a slow trace straight to the relevant log lines.

cf-1.body:
Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of computing resources (servers, storage, databases, networking, software, analytics, and AI) over the internet, with pay-as-you-go pricing. Instead of buying and running hardware in your own data centre, you rent capacity from a provider such as AWS, Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud, and can provision it in minutes through a console or API.

NIST defines five essential characteristics: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling (multi-tenancy), rapid elasticity, and measured service (pay for what you use). Benefits include speed, global reach, elasticity, and trading capital expense for operating expense. The trade-offs are ongoing costs that must be managed, dependence on the provider, and new security responsibilities for configuration and identity.
cf-1.example: A startup launches its app worldwide without buying a single server, scaling from 10 to 10,000 users in a month by adding cloud resources as needed.
cf-1.tip: Remember NIST's five characteristics; they are a common exam definition question.

cf-2.body:
Infrastructure as a Service provides virtualised computing building blocks: virtual machines, block and object storage, virtual networks, load balancers, and IP addresses, which you configure much like physical hardware. Examples include Amazon EC2, Azure Virtual Machines, and Google Compute Engine.

IaaS gives the most flexibility and control among the service models: you choose the operating system, install any software, and configure networking and security in detail. It also brings the most responsibility. You must patch and harden the OS, manage middleware and applications, configure firewalls, back up data, and control access. The provider manages the physical data centre, hardware, and virtualisation layer. IaaS suits lift-and-shift migrations, custom software stacks, and workloads needing specific OS control.
cf-2.example: A company migrates its legacy ERP servers to EC2 instances unchanged, keeping full control of the Windows Server OS and the application.
cf-2.tip: In IaaS, OS patching is your job. Unpatched cloud VMs are breached just like on-premises servers.

cf-3.body:
Platform as a Service provides a managed environment for building, deploying, and running applications without managing the underlying servers or operating systems. You supply the code (and configuration); the provider handles the OS, runtime, middleware, patching, scaling, and often load balancing and monitoring. Examples include Heroku, AWS Elastic Beanstalk, Azure App Service, Google App Engine, and managed databases (RDS, Cloud SQL), which are often counted as PaaS.

PaaS speeds development and reduces operational toil, but it offers less control over the environment, may constrain supported languages and versions, and can create lock-in to provider-specific features. Customers remain responsible for application code security, configuration, identity and access, and data.
cf-3.example: A development team deploys a Python web app to Azure App Service with `git push`, while Microsoft patches the OS and scales instances automatically.
cf-3.tip: PaaS moves OS responsibility to the provider, but your code, configuration, secrets, and access control are still yours.

cf-4.body:
Software as a Service delivers complete applications over the internet, usually through a browser or mobile app, on a subscription basis. The provider runs everything: infrastructure, operating system, application, updates, and availability. Examples include Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Salesforce, Slack, Zoom, and Dropbox.

For users, SaaS means no installation or maintenance and access from anywhere. The customer still owns critical security responsibilities: configuring the service securely, managing who has access (ideally through SSO with MFA), protecting and classifying data, controlling sharing settings, and monitoring activity. SaaS sprawl and shadow IT (employees signing up for unapproved apps) are common governance challenges.
cf-4.example: A company uses Microsoft 365 for email and documents; Microsoft runs the servers, but the company must configure MFA, sharing policies, and data retention itself.
cf-4.tip: Most SaaS data breaches are customer-side misconfigurations, such as publicly shared links or no MFA, not provider hacks.

cf-5.body:
Public cloud infrastructure is owned and operated by a third-party provider and shared by many customers (tenants) over the internet. Each customer's resources are logically isolated through virtualisation, networking, and identity controls, while the physical hardware is pooled.

Advantages include no upfront hardware cost, massive scale, global regions, rapid innovation, and pay-per-use pricing. Considerations include ongoing spend management, data residency, dependence on the provider's availability, and correctly configuring your own security. The major providers are AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud, followed by Oracle, IBM, and Alibaba Cloud. Dedicated options such as dedicated hosts give single-tenant hardware inside the public cloud when licensing or compliance requires it.
cf-5.example: An e-commerce company runs entirely on AWS, scaling up for holiday traffic and paying only for the extra capacity during those weeks.
cf-5.tip: Multi-tenancy is safe when isolation holds. Provider isolation is strong, but your configuration determines your exposure.

cf-6.body:
A private cloud provides cloud capabilities (self-service, automation, and elastic pooled resources) to a single organisation. It can run on-premises in the organisation's own data centre (for example with VMware Cloud Foundation, OpenStack, or Nutanix) or be hosted by a provider on dedicated hardware.

Private clouds offer greater control over hardware, data location, security configuration, and customisation, which appeals to regulated industries, organisations with strict data sovereignty needs, and steady, predictable workloads. The trade-offs are higher capital costs, the organisation's own responsibility for capacity, maintenance, and staffing, and less elasticity: you can only scale to the hardware you own.
cf-6.example: A bank runs its core transaction systems on an on-premises private cloud for regulatory control, while its marketing site runs in the public cloud.
cf-6.tip: A virtualised data centre is not automatically a private cloud; it needs self-service and automation too.

cf-7.body:
Hybrid cloud combines public cloud with private cloud or on-premises infrastructure, connected so workloads and data can move between them or work together. Connectivity typically uses VPNs or dedicated links (Direct Connect, ExpressRoute), with consistent identity, networking, security policy, and management across environments.

Organisations choose hybrid to keep sensitive or latency-critical systems on-premises while using the public cloud for elasticity (cloud bursting), new applications, analytics, or disaster recovery; to migrate gradually; or to meet data residency rules. Tools such as Azure Arc, AWS Outposts, Google Anthos, and Kubernetes help manage hybrid estates. Multi-cloud, using several public clouds, is related but different.
cf-7.example: A hospital keeps patient records on-premises for compliance, but runs its analytics and patient-portal website in Azure, linked by ExpressRoute.
cf-7.tip: Hybrid multiplies the attack surface. Apply consistent identity, logging, and security policies across every environment.

cf-8.body:
Capital expenditure (CapEx) is spending on long-lived assets, such as servers, storage arrays, and data-centre build-outs, paid up front and depreciated over several years. It requires forecasting capacity years ahead, often leading to over-provisioning (idle waste) or under-provisioning (outages and slowdowns).

Operational expenditure (OpEx) is ongoing spending on services consumed, such as cloud usage billed monthly. Cloud shifts IT spending from CapEx to OpEx: no large upfront purchases, costs that track actual usage, and faster experimentation. But OpEx can grow unexpectedly without cost management, and steady long-term workloads can sometimes be cheaper on owned hardware or with committed-use discounts (Reserved Instances, Savings Plans).
cf-8.example: Instead of spending $500,000 up front on servers for a new product, a company runs it in the cloud for $8,000 a month and scales spending as revenue grows.
cf-8.tip: Cloud is not automatically cheaper. It is more flexible. Cost optimisation is a continuous discipline.

cf-9.body:
Elasticity is the ability to automatically add resources when demand rises and remove them when it falls, closely matching capacity to load in near real time. Scalability is the broader ability of a system to handle growth, either vertically (a bigger instance) or horizontally (more instances). Elasticity is scalability that happens automatically and in both directions.

Cloud services achieve elasticity through auto-scaling groups, serverless functions that scale per request (including down to zero), managed databases with automatic capacity, and container orchestration. The benefit is paying only for what is used while handling spikes gracefully. Applications must be designed for it: stateless servers, externalised session state, and fast startup times.
cf-9.example: A ticketing site scales from 4 to 200 instances in minutes when concert tickets go on sale, then back down to 4 an hour later.
cf-9.tip: Scale out (more instances) is usually preferred to scale up (bigger instances) for elasticity and resilience.

cf-10.body:
A Region is a separate geographic area (for example AWS us-east-1 in Northern Virginia, or Azure West Europe) containing multiple Availability Zones. Each AZ is one or more discrete data centres with independent power, cooling, and networking, located far enough apart to avoid shared disasters but connected by low-latency private links.

Deploying across multiple AZs protects against the failure of a single data centre, which is the standard for high availability. Deploying across multiple Regions protects against a whole-region outage and serves users with lower latency worldwide, but adds cost and data-replication complexity. Region choice also affects data residency and compliance, service availability, and price. Edge locations, local zones, and wavelength zones push some services even closer to users.
cf-10.example: A web app runs in three AZs within eu-west-1, so an entire data centre can fail with no customer impact, and data stays in the EU for GDPR.
cf-10.tip: Multi-AZ = high availability; multi-region = disaster recovery and global latency. Know the difference.

cs-1.body:
Object storage stores data as objects, each consisting of the data itself, metadata, and a unique key, inside flat containers called buckets. It is accessed over HTTP(S) APIs (PUT, GET, DELETE) rather than mounted as a file system. Services include Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, and Google Cloud Storage, with S3-compatible options such as MinIO and Wasabi.

Object storage scales virtually without limit, is extremely durable (S3 is designed for 99.999999999%, 'eleven nines', of durability by replicating across multiple facilities), and is cheap per gigabyte, with storage classes for different access patterns. It is ideal for backups, logs, media, data lakes, and static website hosting. It is not suited to databases or anything needing frequent small in-place updates. Security relies on bucket policies, IAM, blocking public access, encryption, and versioning or object lock.
cs-1.example: A photo-sharing app stores billions of user images in S3 and serves them through a CDN, while metadata lives in a database.
cs-1.tip: Misconfigured public buckets are a top cause of cloud data leaks. Enable 'Block Public Access' at the account level.

cs-2.body:
Block storage provides raw storage volumes that attach to a virtual machine and appear to its operating system as a local disk, which it formats with a file system. Examples include Amazon EBS, Azure Managed Disks, and Google Persistent Disk. Data is stored in fixed-size blocks, giving low latency and high IOPS, ideal for boot volumes, databases, and transactional applications.

Volumes persist independently of the instance: they can be detached and reattached, resized, snapshotted, and encrypted. They live in a single Availability Zone and generally attach to one instance at a time (some multi-attach options exist for clustered applications). Performance tiers range from cost-effective general-purpose SSDs to provisioned-IOPS SSDs for demanding databases and throughput-optimised HDDs for large sequential workloads.
cs-2.example: A PostgreSQL server on EC2 stores its data on a provisioned-IOPS EBS volume, with nightly snapshots copied to another region for disaster recovery.
cs-2.tip: Block volumes are zonal. To survive an AZ failure, replicate the data or restore from snapshots in another AZ.

cs-3.body:
Cloud file storage provides a fully managed shared file system that many servers can mount at the same time using standard protocols: NFS (Linux) or SMB (Windows). Examples include Amazon EFS and FSx, Azure Files, and Google Filestore. It offers a familiar hierarchical directory structure with file locking and permissions.

It suits workloads that need shared access to the same files: content management systems, shared home directories, media processing, legacy lift-and-shift applications expecting a network share, and container volumes shared across pods. Managed file services scale capacity automatically and can span AZs. They cost more per gigabyte than object storage and may have higher latency than local block storage, so choose based on access pattern.
cs-3.example: Ten web servers behind a load balancer all mount the same EFS file system, so uploaded images are instantly visible to every server.
cs-3.tip: Shared storage for many servers = file storage. One server with high IOPS = block storage. Massive cheap unstructured data = object storage.

cs-3b.body:
Network Attached Storage (NAS) is a dedicated file server or appliance that shares files over a standard network using file-level protocols (SMB/CIFS for Windows, NFS for Linux and Unix). Clients see folders and files; the NAS manages the file system. NAS is simple to deploy, relatively inexpensive, works with virtually any OS, and is ideal for shared documents, home directories, and backups, but the file-protocol layer and network add overhead.

A Storage Area Network (SAN) is a dedicated high-speed network that presents raw block storage (LUNs) to servers, which format and manage the file systems themselves, as if the storage were a local disk. SANs use Fibre Channel (with HBAs and FC switches) or iSCSI over Ethernet, and deliver very high performance, low latency, and features such as snapshots and replication. They are more complex and expensive, and suit databases, virtualisation clusters, and high-performance applications.
cs-3b.example: An office uses a Synology NAS for shared department folders, while its VMware cluster runs on a Fibre Channel SAN for performance and live migration.
cs-3b.tip: NAS = file-level access over the network (SMB/NFS). SAN = block-level access (Fibre Channel/iSCSI). A classic exam pairing.

cs-3c.body:
RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) combines multiple drives into one logical volume for performance, redundancy, or both. RAID 0 (striping) splits data across disks for speed and full capacity but has no redundancy: one failed disk loses everything. RAID 1 (mirroring) writes identical copies to two disks and survives one failure, at half the capacity. RAID 5 stripes data with distributed parity across three or more disks and survives one disk failure. RAID 6 uses double parity with four or more disks and survives two failures.

RAID 10 (1+0) stripes across mirrored pairs, giving high performance and redundancy, and is favoured for databases, at 50% capacity. Hardware RAID uses a dedicated controller, often with battery-backed cache; software RAID (mdadm, Storage Spaces, ZFS) uses the host CPU and is more flexible. Rebuilding large arrays takes a long time, and a second failure during a rebuild is a real risk, so RAID 6 or 10 is preferred for big disks.
cs-3c.example: A file server with six 8 TB disks in RAID 6 loses one disk, keeps running, and rebuilds onto a hot spare while staying protected against another failure.
cs-3c.tip: RAID is not a backup. It does not protect against deletion, ransomware, corruption, or site loss. Keep separate backups.

cs-4.body:
A managed database service runs a database engine for you: provisioning, OS and engine patching, automated backups with point-in-time restore, monitoring, replication, and automatic failover. Examples include Amazon RDS and Aurora, Azure SQL Database, Google Cloud SQL and AlloyDB, and managed NoSQL such as DynamoDB, Cosmos DB, and MongoDB Atlas.

You keep responsibility for schema design, query performance, access control, network exposure, encryption settings, and choosing the right size and tier. In return you avoid most DBA operational toil and get high availability (for example Multi-AZ deployments with synchronous standby replicas) with a few settings. The trade-offs are less control over the engine (limited superuser access and extensions) and higher cost than self-managed databases on VMs.
cs-4.example: A team moves from a self-managed MySQL VM to RDS Multi-AZ; when the primary's AZ has an outage, RDS fails over to the standby in about a minute.
cs-4.tip: Keep managed databases in private subnets, require TLS, and use IAM or secret rotation instead of shared static passwords.

cs-5.body:
Cloud NoSQL databases (Amazon DynamoDB, Azure Cosmos DB, Google Firestore and Bigtable, MongoDB Atlas) store data in non-relational models: key-value, document, wide-column, or graph. They typically have flexible schemas and scale horizontally across many nodes, delivering consistent single-digit-millisecond latency at very high throughput.

They excel at predictable access patterns at scale: user profiles and sessions, shopping carts, product catalogues, IoT telemetry, gaming leaderboards, and event data. Design starts from the queries (access patterns) rather than normalised tables, and partition keys must spread load evenly to avoid hot partitions. Many offer tunable consistency, global multi-region replication, serverless on-demand capacity, time-to-live expiry, and change streams.
cs-5.example: A mobile game stores player profiles and leaderboards in DynamoDB global tables, serving players on three continents with low latency.
cs-5.tip: Choose a high-cardinality partition key (such as userId). A low-cardinality key (such as country) creates hot partitions and throttling.

cs-7.body:
A snapshot is a point-in-time copy of a storage volume, file system, or database. In the cloud, the first snapshot copies all data, and later snapshots are incremental, storing only blocks changed since the previous one, which makes frequent snapshots efficient. Snapshots are stored durably (for example in S3 behind the scenes for EBS).

They are used for backups, restoring after mistakes, creating new volumes and cloning environments, and migrating data across AZs or regions (by copying snapshots). For consistency, databases should be quiesced or use application-consistent snapshot tools. Automate snapshot schedules and retention (AWS Data Lifecycle Manager, AWS Backup), copy critical snapshots to another region or account, and protect them from deletion, because ransomware operators target backups.
cs-7.example: Before a risky upgrade, an admin snapshots the server's volumes; when the upgrade fails, a new volume from the snapshot restores service in minutes.
cs-7.tip: Copy backups to a separate account with restricted access (or vault lock) so a compromised production account cannot delete them.

cs-8.body:
Storage tiers price storage according to how often data is accessed. Hot tiers (such as S3 Standard) offer instant, frequent access at the highest storage price. Cool or infrequent-access tiers (S3 Standard-IA, Azure Cool) cost less to store but charge per retrieval and may have minimum storage durations. Archive tiers (S3 Glacier and Glacier Deep Archive, Azure Archive) are the cheapest to store, but retrieval takes minutes to hours and costs more.

Lifecycle policies automate transitions, for example moving logs to infrequent access after 30 days, to archive after 90, and deleting after 7 years, which dramatically cuts costs for aging data. Intelligent tiering services move objects automatically based on observed access. Consider retrieval time requirements, retrieval fees, and minimum durations when choosing a tier.
cs-8.example: A company keeps 30 days of logs in hot storage for troubleshooting, then archives them to Glacier Deep Archive for compliance, cutting storage costs by over 90%.
cs-8.tip: Archive tiers are cheap to store but slow and costly to restore. Make sure restore times meet your RTO.

cs-9.body:
Data replication maintains copies of data in multiple locations so it survives failures and can be served closer to users. Within a region, managed services replicate across Availability Zones (for example Multi-AZ databases and S3's multi-facility storage), protecting against a data-centre outage. Cross-region replication (S3 CRR, database read replicas and global tables, geo-redundant storage) protects against a regional disaster and supports global low-latency reads.

Synchronous replication confirms writes on replicas before acknowledging them: no data loss on failover, but higher write latency. Asynchronous replication acknowledges immediately and replicates afterwards: faster, but recent writes can be lost on failover (non-zero RPO). Replication multiplies storage and transfer costs, and it faithfully replicates mistakes and ransomware encryption too, so it complements rather than replaces backups.
cs-9.example: An S3 bucket in us-east-1 replicates to eu-west-1, so the data survives even if an entire region becomes unavailable.
cs-9.tip: Replication protects availability, not against deletion or corruption. You still need versioned, point-in-time backups.

cs-10.body:
Ephemeral (instance store) storage consists of disks physically attached to the host machine that runs a VM. It is often very fast NVMe SSD with high IOPS and no network latency, and it is usually included in the instance price. But data on it exists only as long as the instance runs on that host: stopping, terminating, or hibernating the instance, or a host failure, erases it.

Use ephemeral storage only for temporary data that can be recreated: caches, buffers, scratch space for processing, swap, or replicated data in distributed systems that keep copies on other nodes (such as some Cassandra or Kafka deployments). Container file systems and many serverless /tmp directories are ephemeral too. Never keep the only copy of important data there.
cs-10.example: A video transcoding job writes intermediate files to fast instance-store NVMe, then uploads the finished video to S3 before the instance is terminated.
cs-10.tip: Stopping an instance with instance-store volumes wipes them. Persistent data belongs on block, file, or object storage.

ca-1.body:
Microservices architecture splits an application into small, independently deployable services, each owning one business capability (such as orders, payments, or inventory) and its own data store, and communicating over APIs or events. Teams can develop, deploy, and scale their services independently, choose appropriate technologies, and limit the blast radius of failures.

The costs are real: distributed-systems complexity (network latency and failures, retries, timeouts), data consistency across services (sagas instead of single transactions), harder testing and debugging (requiring distributed tracing and centralised logging), service discovery, versioned APIs, and heavier operational overhead. Many organisations do well starting with a well-structured modular monolith and splitting out services only when team size or scaling needs justify it.
ca-1.example: An e-commerce company splits checkout into its own service so it can scale independently during sales and deploy fixes without redeploying the product catalogue.
ca-1.tip: Microservices trade code complexity for operational complexity. Invest in observability, CI/CD, and automation first.

ca-2.body:
Serverless computing lets you run code without provisioning or managing servers. With Functions as a Service (AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, Google Cloud Functions), you upload a function and the provider runs it in response to events such as HTTP requests, file uploads, queue messages, and schedules, scaling automatically from zero to thousands of concurrent executions. You pay per invocation and per millisecond of execution, and nothing when idle.

Serverless also includes managed services such as API gateways, queues, and serverless databases. It suits event-driven, bursty, and glue workloads. Limitations include cold-start latency, maximum execution times (for example 15 minutes for Lambda), statelessness, per-request costs that can exceed containers at sustained high volume, and provider lock-in. Security focuses on least-privilege function roles, input validation, and dependency scanning.
