ca-2.example: When a user uploads a photo to S3, a Lambda function automatically creates thumbnails. The company pays only for the milliseconds each resize takes.
ca-2.tip: Give each function its own minimal IAM role. One over-privileged function can expose the whole account.

ca-3.body:
Auto scaling automatically adjusts the number of compute resources (VM instances, containers, and in some services database capacity) to match demand. Policies define minimum, maximum, and desired capacity. Target-tracking policies keep a metric near a target (for example average CPU at 60% or requests per target at 1,000); step policies react to alarm thresholds; scheduled scaling handles predictable patterns; and predictive scaling uses historical trends.

Scaling out adds capacity during spikes; scaling in removes it to save money when load falls. Auto scaling works with load balancers (new instances register automatically after passing health checks) and replaces unhealthy instances, which provides self-healing. Applications must be stateless and start quickly, and scale-in should drain connections gracefully. Cooldown periods prevent flapping.
ca-3.example: An auto-scaling group keeps CPU near 50%, running 3 instances overnight and 30 at lunchtime peak, and it automatically replaces an instance whose health check fails.
ca-3.tip: Set a sensible maximum and a budget alert. A bug or attack can otherwise scale your bill without limit.

ca-4.body:
High availability means designing a system to keep operating through component failures with minimal downtime. The core principle is eliminating single points of failure through redundancy: multiple instances behind load balancers, spread across Availability Zones, replicated databases with automatic failover, redundant network paths, and health checks that detect failures and shift traffic automatically.

Availability is expressed in 'nines': 99.9% allows about 8.8 hours of downtime a year (about 43 minutes a month); 99.99% about 52.6 minutes a year; 99.999% about 5.3 minutes a year. Each extra nine costs significantly more. A system's overall availability is limited by its dependencies: chaining components multiplies their availabilities, so redundancy is needed at every critical layer.
ca-4.example: A web tier runs in three AZs; when one AZ fails, the load balancer routes all traffic to the remaining two, and customers notice nothing.
ca-4.tip: Compound availability: two 99.9% dependencies in series give only about 99.8%. Remove single points of failure everywhere.

ca-5.body:
The Recovery Time Objective (RTO) is the maximum acceptable time to restore a service after a disruption: how quickly you must be back up. The Recovery Point Objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time: how far back your last good copy can be. They are business decisions, set through a business impact analysis, and they drive technical design and cost.

An RTO of 4 hours and an RPO of 24 hours might be met with nightly backups and a documented restore. An RTO of minutes and an RPO near zero needs synchronous replication and a hot standby or active-active multi-region design. Disaster-recovery strategies range from backup and restore, through pilot light and warm standby, to multi-site active-active, from cheapest and slowest to most expensive and fastest. Test restores regularly to prove the objectives can actually be met.
ca-5.example: An online store sets RTO 1 hour and RPO 5 minutes for checkout, so it runs a warm standby in a second region with continuous database replication.
ca-5.tip: RTO = time to recover (downtime); RPO = data loss window. Also know MTD (maximum tolerable downtime); RTO must be shorter than MTD.

ca-6.body:
A multi-region architecture deploys an application across two or more geographically separate cloud regions. Active-passive designs keep a standby region ready (warm or pilot light) to take over if the primary fails. Active-active designs serve traffic from all regions at once, routing users to the nearest healthy region for low latency.

Multi-region provides the highest resilience, surviving the loss of an entire region, and improves global performance, but it is the most complex and expensive option. Challenges include cross-region data replication and consistency (conflict resolution for multi-writer databases), global traffic routing (DNS latency or failover routing, global load balancers, anycast), duplicated infrastructure costs, and keeping configurations identical, which is best done with infrastructure as code and automated failover testing.
ca-6.example: A payments company runs active-active in us-east-1 and us-west-2 with DynamoDB global tables; a regional outage shifts traffic to the other region automatically.
ca-6.tip: Most applications meet their goals with multi-AZ. Go multi-region only when the business impact of a region outage justifies the cost.

ca-8.body:
CI/CD automates the path from code change to production. Continuous Integration means developers merge small changes frequently into a shared branch, and every change triggers an automated build plus unit, integration, and security tests, so integration problems are caught within minutes. Continuous Delivery keeps the code always in a releasable state, with automated deployment through environments and a manual approval for production. Continuous Deployment removes the manual gate, so every change that passes the pipeline goes to production automatically.

Pipelines (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, Azure DevOps, AWS CodePipeline) typically run: build, test, scan (SAST, dependency, container image, and IaC scans), package an immutable artifact, deploy to staging, run smoke tests, deploy to production using a safe strategy (rolling, blue/green, or canary), and monitor with automated rollback. Small, frequent releases lower risk.
ca-8.example: A developer merges a fix at 10:00; tests, security scans, and a canary deployment run automatically, and it reaches all users by 10:25 with no manual steps.
ca-8.tip: Secure the pipeline itself. It holds production credentials, so a compromised CI system is a supply-chain attack path.

ca-9.body:
In an event-driven architecture, services communicate by producing and consuming events (records that something happened, such as 'OrderPlaced') through a message broker or event bus instead of calling each other directly. Examples include Amazon EventBridge, SNS and SQS, Apache Kafka, Azure Event Grid and Service Bus, and Google Pub/Sub.

Producers do not need to know who consumes their events, so services are loosely coupled and can be added, scaled, or fail independently, and queues absorb traffic spikes and buffer during outages. The trade-offs include eventual consistency, harder end-to-end tracing and debugging, the need for idempotent consumers (events may be delivered more than once), ordering challenges, dead-letter queues for poison messages, and careful schema versioning.
ca-9.example: When an order is placed, one event triggers the inventory, email, analytics, and fraud services independently. Adding a loyalty-points service needs no change to the order service.
ca-9.tip: Make consumers idempotent. At-least-once delivery means the same event can arrive twice.

ca-10.body:
FinOps is the practice of bringing financial accountability to variable cloud spending through collaboration between engineering, finance, and business teams. The FinOps Foundation describes a cycle of Inform (visibility and allocation: tagging, showback and chargeback, dashboards), Optimize (right-sizing, removing idle resources, choosing pricing models such as Savings Plans, Reserved Instances, and Spot, and storage lifecycle policies), and Operate (budgets, policies, forecasting, and continuous improvement).

The goal is not simply spending less but maximising business value per dollar: understanding unit economics such as cost per customer or per transaction. Common quick wins include shutting down non-production resources out of hours, deleting unattached volumes and old snapshots, right-sizing over-provisioned instances, and using committed-use discounts for steady workloads.
ca-10.example: Tagging reveals that 30% of spend comes from forgotten test environments; scheduling them to shut down nights and weekends saves $40,000 a month.
ca-10.tip: You cannot optimise what you cannot attribute. Enforce cost-allocation tags from day one.

cda-1.body:
A data warehouse is a central store of structured, cleaned, and integrated data optimised for analytics and business intelligence. Data from operational systems is loaded through ETL or ELT pipelines and modelled, commonly as star schemas with fact tables (measurements such as sales) and dimension tables (context such as customer, product, and date), so analysts can run fast SQL queries across large histories.

Cloud warehouses such as Snowflake, Amazon Redshift, Google BigQuery, and Azure Synapse separate storage from compute, use columnar storage and massively parallel processing, and scale on demand. They apply schema on write: data must fit the model before loading, which ensures consistency and trusted reporting. Warehouses are best when the questions are known and the data is structured.
cda-1.example: A retailer's warehouse combines sales, inventory, and marketing data so the finance team can report daily revenue by store, product, and campaign in seconds.
cda-1.tip: Warehouses concentrate sensitive business data. Apply role-based access, column masking, and audit logging.

cda-3.body:
A lakehouse combines the low-cost, flexible storage of a data lake with the reliability and performance features of a warehouse. Open table formats such as Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, and Apache Hudi sit on top of files in object storage and add ACID transactions, schema enforcement and evolution, time travel (querying older versions), efficient updates and deletes, and metadata for fast queries.

This lets one copy of data serve both BI and SQL analytics and data science and ML, avoiding duplicate pipelines between separate lakes and warehouses. Platforms include Databricks, Snowflake with Iceberg tables, AWS (Athena, EMR, and Glue with Iceberg), and Microsoft Fabric. Governance catalogues such as Unity Catalog and AWS Lake Formation provide central access control and lineage.
cda-3.example: A bank stores transaction data once in Iceberg tables on S3; analysts query it with SQL for reports while data scientists train fraud models on the same tables.
cda-3.tip: Time travel and ACID deletes make lakehouses practical for GDPR 'right to erasure' requests on large datasets.

cda-4.body:
ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) extracts data from sources, transforms it (cleaning, joining, aggregating, and conforming to the target schema) on a separate processing engine, and then loads the finished result into the warehouse. It suited older warehouses with expensive, limited compute, and it is still useful when sensitive data must be masked or filtered before it lands.

ELT (Extract, Load, Transform) loads raw data into the cloud warehouse or lakehouse first, then transforms it there using the platform's scalable compute, typically with SQL-based tools such as dbt. It is the modern cloud default: ingestion is faster and simpler, raw data is preserved for reprocessing when requirements change, and transformations are version-controlled and tested like code. Tools such as Fivetran and Airbyte handle extract and load.
cda-4.example: A company loads raw Salesforce and Stripe data into Snowflake nightly with Fivetran, then dbt models transform it into tested revenue and churn tables.
cda-4.tip: With ELT, raw sensitive data lands first. Apply access controls and masking to the raw layer too.

cda-5.body:
Batch processing collects data over a period and processes it all at once on a schedule, such as hourly, nightly, or monthly. It is simpler, cheaper, easier to reprocess, and well suited to historical reporting, billing, payroll, and ML training. Its drawback is latency: results are only as fresh as the last run.

Stream processing handles events continuously as they arrive, with latency in milliseconds to seconds, using platforms such as Apache Kafka, Amazon Kinesis, Google Pub/Sub, and processors such as Apache Flink or Spark Structured Streaming. It enables real-time fraud detection, monitoring, alerting, live dashboards, and personalisation, but is more complex to build and operate (ordering, late data, exactly-once semantics, state management). Many architectures combine both.
cda-5.example: A card issuer scores each transaction in real time with a streaming pipeline to block fraud, while producing monthly statements with nightly batch jobs.
cda-5.tip: Choose streaming only when the business truly needs low latency. Batch is simpler and cheaper for everything else.

cda-6.body:
Streaming analytics computes results continuously over data in motion. Because streams never end, calculations use windows: tumbling windows (fixed, non-overlapping periods, such as each minute), sliding or hopping windows (overlapping periods), and session windows (activity separated by gaps). Engines also perform stream enrichment (joining events with reference data), pattern detection (complex event processing), and stateful aggregations.

Challenges include late or out-of-order events (handled with event-time processing and watermarks), exactly-once processing guarantees, state checkpointing for recovery, and back-pressure. Tools include Apache Flink, Spark Structured Streaming, Kafka Streams, Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, Google Dataflow, and Azure Stream Analytics.
cda-6.example: A security platform counts failed logins per user in 5-minute sliding windows and triggers an alert when any user exceeds 20.
cda-6.tip: Use event time (when it happened), not processing time (when it arrived), for accurate results with delayed data.

cda-7.body:
Business intelligence tools, such as Microsoft Power BI, Tableau, Looker, Amazon QuickSight, and Apache Superset, connect to warehouses, lakehouses, and databases and let people explore data through interactive dashboards, reports, and visual analysis without writing code. Semantic layers define shared business metrics (such as 'active customer' and 'net revenue') once so everyone gets consistent numbers.

Real value comes from trusted, governed data and well-designed dashboards aimed at decisions, not from more charts. Good practice includes certified datasets, row-level security so users see only their data, clear metric definitions, performance optimisation through extracts, caching, and aggregates, scheduled report delivery, and self-service within guardrails.
cda-7.example: Regional managers open a Power BI dashboard filtered by row-level security to their own stores, showing sales against target and inventory alerts.
cda-7.tip: Row-level security in BI tools prevents one department or customer from seeing another's data.

cda-8.body:
Data mesh is an organisational and architectural approach for large companies where a central data team has become a bottleneck. It rests on four principles: domain ownership (the teams closest to the data, such as orders or marketing, own their analytical data), data as a product (datasets are published with owners, documentation, SLAs, schemas, and quality guarantees), a self-serve data platform (shared infrastructure and tooling so domains can build products easily), and federated computational governance (global standards for security, interoperability, and privacy, enforced automatically).

Consumers discover data products through a catalogue. Data mesh can improve scalability and data quality at large organisations but requires mature teams, platform investment, and cultural change, so it is usually overkill for small teams.
cda-8.example: The payments domain team publishes a 'settled_transactions' data product with a documented schema, freshness SLA, and quality tests that finance and risk teams consume.
cda-8.tip: Federated governance is essential. Without shared standards, a mesh becomes many incompatible data silos.

cda-9.body:
Partitioning organises a large dataset into separate folders or segments based on column values, most commonly date (year/month/day), region, or tenant. When a query filters on the partition column, the engine skips all irrelevant partitions (partition pruning) and reads far less data. In pay-per-scan systems such as Athena and BigQuery, that directly cuts cost as well as time.

Partitioning works best combined with columnar file formats (Parquet, ORC), which let engines read only the needed columns, with compression, and with appropriately sized files (avoiding millions of tiny files). Clustering or sorting within partitions and file statistics (min/max per column) enable further skipping. Choose partition keys that match common filters and avoid over-partitioning into too many small partitions.
cda-9.example: Partitioning three years of web logs by date means a query for yesterday scans 1 GB instead of 1 TB, and costs about a thousandth as much.
cda-9.tip: Filter on the partition column in your WHERE clause. Otherwise the engine scans everything anyway.

cda-10.body:
Data observability monitors the health of data pipelines and datasets the way application observability monitors services. Key signals are freshness (is the data up to date, and did the pipeline run?), volume (did row counts suddenly drop or spike?), schema (did columns change unexpectedly?), quality or distribution (null rates, duplicates, out-of-range values, referential integrity), and lineage (which sources and transformations produced each table, and what depends on it downstream).

Tools include dbt tests, Great Expectations and Soda for assertions, and data observability platforms such as Monte Carlo that detect anomalies automatically. Lineage speeds root cause analysis and impact assessment. Catching bad data before it reaches dashboards and ML models protects decisions and trust.
cda-10.example: A volume check alerts that yesterday's orders table has 40% fewer rows than normal; lineage traces it to a failed API extraction before executives see a false sales drop.
cda-10.tip: Treat data tests like unit tests. Run them in the pipeline and block bad data from being published.

cmo-1.body:
Monitoring collects predefined metrics and checks them against known thresholds to answer questions you already know to ask: is CPU above 90%? Is the error rate above 1%? Is the site up? It is essential for detecting known failure modes and triggering alerts.

Observability is the ability to understand a system's internal state from its external outputs well enough to answer new questions you did not anticipate, without deploying new code. It relies on rich, high-cardinality telemetry, meaning metrics, logs, and traces with detailed attributes (customer ID, version, region), so engineers can slice and correlate data to explain novel failures in complex distributed systems. In short, monitoring tells you that something is wrong, and observability helps you discover why.
cmo-1.example: Monitoring alerts that p99 latency jumped; observability lets the engineer find that only users of app version 4.2 in one region, calling one endpoint, are affected.
cmo-1.tip: You need both: monitoring for known problems and fast alerting, observability for investigating the unknown.

cmo-2.body:
Metrics are numeric measurements recorded over time as time series: request rate, error count, latency percentiles, CPU and memory utilisation, queue depth, disk I/O. They are compact and cheap to store and query, which makes them ideal for dashboards, trend analysis, capacity planning, and alerting.

Two frameworks guide what to measure. The RED method for request-driven services tracks Rate (requests per second), Errors (failed requests), and Duration (latency distribution). The USE method for resources tracks Utilisation, Saturation (queued work), and Errors. Use percentiles (p50, p95, p99) rather than averages for latency, because averages hide slow outliers. Watch cardinality: labels with unbounded values, such as user IDs, create huge numbers of time series and costs.
cmo-2.example: A dashboard shows request rate, 5xx error percentage, and p95 latency for each API; p95 rising from 200 ms to 2 s triggers investigation before users complain.
cmo-2.tip: Averages lie. Alert on percentiles and error rates tied to user experience.

cmo-3.body:
Logs are timestamped records of discrete events: HTTP requests, authentication attempts, errors with stack traces, configuration changes, and deployments. They provide the detailed context needed to explain what happened. Structured logging writes each entry as machine-parseable data (typically JSON) with consistent fields such as timestamp, level, service, environment, trace_id, and user_id, making logs searchable and aggregatable.

Centralise logs from all hosts, containers, and services into one platform (CloudWatch Logs, Elasticsearch or OpenSearch, Splunk, Loki, Datadog) using agents or collectors; otherwise debugging means SSHing into dozens of machines, and logs vanish when containers die. Manage volume with log levels, sampling, and retention tiers; never log secrets, passwords, or unnecessary personal data; and protect security logs from tampering.
cmo-3.example: Searching all services for trace_id=abc123 instantly shows the full sequence of log lines for one failed customer checkout across five microservices.
cmo-3.tip: Redact secrets and PII before logs leave the application. Leaked tokens in logs are a common breach source.

cmo-5.body:
Alerting notifies people when a system needs attention. Good alerts are actionable (someone must do something now), urgent, tied to user impact rather than internal symptoms, few in number, and linked to a runbook. Critical alerts page the on-call engineer through tools such as PagerDuty or Opsgenie; lower-severity issues create tickets or chat messages to handle during working hours.

Too many noisy, non-actionable alerts cause alert fatigue, and real incidents get ignored. Improve signal by alerting on SLO burn rate and error rates rather than raw CPU, using durations and multiple windows to avoid flapping, grouping related alerts, suppressing alerts during maintenance, and reviewing every page afterwards: was it useful, and should it be tuned, automated, or deleted?
cmo-5.example: Instead of paging on 'CPU > 80%', the team pages on 'checkout error budget burning 10x faster than sustainable', which cuts pages by 70% while catching real outages sooner.
cmo-5.tip: Every page should answer: what is broken, how badly are users affected, and where is the runbook?

cmo-6.body:
A Service Level Indicator is a quantitative measure of service behaviour from the user's point of view, such as the proportion of successful requests or the proportion of requests served faster than 300 ms. A Service Level Objective is an internal target for an SLI over a time window, such as 99.9% of requests succeeding over 30 days. A Service Level Agreement is an external contract with customers that specifies consequences, typically service credits, if targets are missed; SLAs are usually looser than internal SLOs.

The error budget is the allowed unreliability implied by the SLO: 100% − 99.9% = 0.1%, about 43 minutes of downtime or 1 in 1,000 failed requests per month. Teams spend it on releases and experiments; when it runs low, they slow changes and prioritise reliability. This makes reliability versus velocity a data-driven decision.
cmo-6.example: An API with a 99.95% monthly SLO has an error budget of about 21.6 minutes; after an incident uses 18 minutes, risky launches are postponed to next month.
cmo-6.tip: Set SLOs from user expectations. 100% is the wrong target for almost everything.

cmo-7.body:
Synthetic monitoring runs scripted, artificial transactions against your service on a schedule from multiple locations, whether or not real users are active. Checks range from simple HTTP and TCP pings, DNS resolution, and TLS certificate validity and expiry, to multi-step browser scripts that log in, search, and complete a checkout. Tools include CloudWatch Synthetics, Datadog Synthetics, Checkly, and Pingdom.

Synthetics catch outages, broken user journeys, regional problems, and expiring certificates before users report them, and they give consistent baselines. Canary releases are a different but related idea: deploying a new version to a small slice of real traffic first, and comparing its error and latency metrics with the stable version before rolling out further, with automatic rollback if it degrades.
cmo-7.example: A synthetic browser test detects at 3 a.m. that the login page fails in Europe after a CDN change, and the on-call engineer fixes it before business hours.
cmo-7.tip: Monitor certificate expiry with synthetics. Expired certificates cause surprisingly many major outages.

cmo-8.body:
A runbook documents the response to a specific alert or known issue: what it means, how to assess impact, which dashboards, logs, and queries to check, common causes, step-by-step mitigation (including exact commands and rollback procedures), escalation contacts, and how to verify recovery. It lets any on-call engineer respond quickly and consistently, even at 3 a.m. or on an unfamiliar service.

Incident response organises the human side: detect (an alert or report), triage (severity and impact), mobilise (an incident commander, communications lead, and subject-matter experts), mitigate (restore service first, often by rollback or failover), resolve, and learn through a blameless postmortem with tracked action items. Status pages and regular stakeholder updates keep everyone informed.
cmo-8.example: A database-replication-lag alert links to a runbook that checks the replica's metrics, identifies a long-running query, and shows the safe command to terminate it.
cmo-8.tip: Update the runbook after every incident, while the details are fresh.

cmo-9.body:
Each major cloud has a native observability stack. AWS CloudWatch provides metrics, logs (Logs Insights queries), alarms, dashboards, synthetics (canaries), and application signals, with X-Ray for tracing and CloudTrail for API audit. Azure Monitor includes metrics, Log Analytics (KQL queries), Application Insights for APM, alerts, and workbooks. Google Cloud Observability (formerly Stackdriver) provides Cloud Monitoring, Logging, Trace, and Profiler.

Native tools integrate automatically with provider services and IAM, need little setup, and are often enough for cloud-native workloads. Limitations include cross-cloud and hybrid visibility, query and visualisation depth compared with specialist tools, and costs at high log volumes. Many organisations combine native services with OpenTelemetry-based instrumentation and third-party platforms (Datadog, Grafana, New Relic, Splunk) for a unified multi-cloud view.
cmo-9.example: A team sets CloudWatch alarms on ALB 5xx rates and Lambda errors, and uses Logs Insights to query error patterns across all functions in seconds.
cmo-9.tip: Control log ingestion and retention settings. Default 'never expire' log retention quietly grows costs.

cmo-10.body:
OpenTelemetry (OTel) is a vendor-neutral, open-source standard (a CNCF project) for generating and collecting telemetry: traces, metrics, and logs. It provides language SDKs and APIs, automatic instrumentation for popular frameworks and libraries (HTTP servers, database clients, messaging), semantic conventions for consistent attribute names, and the OTLP protocol for sending data.

The OpenTelemetry Collector receives, processes (batching, filtering, sampling, redacting sensitive data), and exports telemetry to any compatible backend: Prometheus, Jaeger, Tempo, Elasticsearch, Datadog, Honeycomb, New Relic, or cloud-native services. Instrument once and switch or combine backends without re-instrumenting code, which avoids vendor lock-in. It has become the industry standard supported by virtually all observability vendors.
cmo-10.example: A company instruments all services with OpenTelemetry and later moves from one APM vendor to another by changing the Collector's exporter configuration, not application code.
cmo-10.tip: Use the Collector to scrub sensitive attributes and sample centrally, rather than configuring every service individually.

cgc-1.body:
Cloud governance is the framework of policies, processes, roles, and automated controls that keeps cloud usage secure, compliant, cost-effective, and aligned with business goals as it scales across many accounts, regions, and teams. It covers identity and access, security baselines, network architecture, data protection and residency, cost management, resource tagging, and approved services.

Modern governance is automated rather than based on manual approvals: landing zones (AWS Control Tower, Azure Landing Zones) create standardised, pre-secured accounts; organisation-level guardrails (service control policies, Azure Policy) prevent forbidden actions; detective controls (AWS Config, CSPM) flag drift; and dashboards give visibility. Good governance enables teams to move fast safely instead of blocking them. Without it, cloud sprawl produces uncontrolled costs, security gaps, and compliance failures.
cgc-1.example: A new team requests an AWS account and receives one in minutes through Control Tower, already configured with logging, guardrails blocking public S3, and budget alerts.
cgc-1.tip: Prefer preventive guardrails (block the action) over detective ones (alert afterwards) for high-risk misconfigurations.

cgc-2.body:
Policy as code expresses governance and security rules in machine-readable files that are version-controlled, peer-reviewed, tested, and evaluated automatically, instead of written checklists and manual reviews. Policies can run at several points: in CI/CD against infrastructure-as-code plans before deployment (Checkov, tfsec, OPA/Conftest, Terraform Sentinel), at admission time in Kubernetes (OPA Gatekeeper, Kyverno), and continuously at runtime against deployed resources (AWS Config rules, Azure Policy, GCP Organization Policy).

Examples include requiring encryption on all storage, blocking public buckets, enforcing mandatory tags, restricting regions, and forbidding privileged containers. Benefits are consistency, fast feedback to developers, an audit trail of policy changes, and scalability across thousands of resources. Exceptions should be explicit, documented, and time-limited.
cgc-2.example: A pull request adding an unencrypted RDS database fails the pipeline because a Checkov policy requires storage encryption; the developer fixes it before merging.
cgc-2.tip: Shift left: catching violations in CI is far cheaper than finding them in production.

cgc-3.body:
Cloud Security Posture Management tools continuously scan cloud accounts and services for misconfigurations and compliance violations, such as publicly accessible storage, unencrypted volumes and databases, overly permissive IAM policies, security groups open to the internet, disabled logging, and missing MFA on privileged accounts. They compare configurations with benchmarks such as the CIS Benchmarks, NIST, PCI DSS, and ISO 27001, and prioritise findings by risk.

Examples include AWS Security Hub, Microsoft Defender for Cloud, Google Security Command Center, and third-party platforms (Wiz, Prisma Cloud, Orca), which often combine CSPM with workload protection and identity analysis as part of a CNAPP. Value comes from acting on findings: assigning owners, automating remediation for common issues, and tracking the posture score over time.
cgc-3.example: CSPM flags a newly created S3 bucket that allows public read and an IAM user with no MFA; automated remediation blocks public access within minutes.
cgc-3.tip: Misconfiguration, not zero-day exploits, causes most cloud breaches. CSPM targets exactly that risk.

cgc-4.body:
SOC 2 is an attestation framework from the AICPA in which an independent auditor reports on a service organisation's controls against the Trust Services Criteria: security (required), availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy. A Type I report assesses control design at a point in time; a Type II report tests operating effectiveness over a period, usually 6–12 months, which is what customers typically ask SaaS vendors for.

ISO/IEC 27001 is an international, certifiable standard for an information security management system (ISMS): a risk-based management process with policies, a risk assessment, a Statement of Applicability selecting controls from Annex A, internal audits, and continual improvement, verified by accredited certification bodies. Both require evidence and continuous operation, not one-time documents. Cloud providers publish their reports, and customers inherit infrastructure controls but must implement their own.
cgc-4.example: An enterprise customer requires a SaaS vendor's SOC 2 Type II report and ISO 27001 certificate before signing, and reviews the vendor's control exceptions.
cgc-4.tip: SOC 2 = an auditor's attestation report (Type I or II). ISO 27001 = certification of a management system.

cgc-5.body:
PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard, currently version 4.0) applies to any organisation that stores, processes, or transmits cardholder data. Its twelve requirements cover network security controls, secure configurations, protecting stored account data (encryption, masking, and minimal retention), encrypting transmission, anti-malware, secure development, restricting access by need to know, strong authentication with MFA, physical security, logging and monitoring, regular testing (scans and penetration tests), and security policies.

HIPAA protects US protected health information (PHI) through the Privacy Rule, Security Rule (administrative, physical, and technical safeguards), and Breach Notification Rule; cloud providers handling PHI must sign a Business Associate Agreement (BAA). Reducing scope (for example tokenising card data or using a payment provider's hosted checkout) is often the most effective compliance strategy.
cgc-5.example: An online shop uses a payment provider's hosted checkout page, so card numbers never touch its servers, dramatically shrinking its PCI DSS scope.
cgc-5.tip: Scope reduction beats scope compliance. Keep regulated data out of systems that do not need it.

cgc-6.body:
Cost governance applies policies and automation so cloud spending stays visible, attributable, and controlled. Foundations include mandatory tagging (owner, cost centre, environment, application) enforced by policy, account structure aligned to teams or products, and cost allocation reports and dashboards. Budgets with alerts at thresholds (for example 50%, 80%, and 100% of forecast) warn owners before overruns, and cost anomaly detection flags unexpected spikes, often caused by misconfigurations, runaway autoscaling, forgotten resources, or compromised accounts used for crypto-mining.

Preventive guardrails can restrict expensive instance types or regions, require approval for large purchases, and automatically shut down idle non-production resources. FinOps provides the culture and collaboration; governance provides the automated enforcement.
cgc-6.example: An anomaly alert shows GPU spend jumping from $50 to $4,000 a day; investigation finds leaked credentials being used for crypto-mining, and the keys are revoked.
cgc-6.tip: Cost anomalies can be security incidents. Route anomaly alerts to security as well as finance.

cgc-7.body:
Audit logs record who did what, when, from where, and with what result across cloud control planes and data access: AWS CloudTrail (API calls), Azure Activity Log and resource logs, Google Cloud Audit Logs, plus service-specific data-access logs, VPC flow logs, and identity provider sign-in logs. They are essential for compliance evidence, security monitoring, and incident investigation.

Protect their integrity and availability: enable logging organisation-wide in every region, deliver logs to a separate, locked-down logging or security account with write-once (object lock or immutable) storage and log-file integrity validation, restrict access tightly, set retention to meet regulatory and investigative needs (often a year or more), and stream them to a SIEM for real-time detection. Attackers routinely try to disable or delete logs to cover their tracks.
cgc-7.example: During an investigation, CloudTrail logs in the isolated security account show exactly which access key created new IAM users at 02:14 and from which IP.
cgc-7.tip: Alert immediately on attempts to stop or delete audit logging (for example CloudTrail StopLogging).

cgc-8.body:
Data residency is the requirement that data be stored, and sometimes processed, in a particular geographic location. Data sovereignty goes further: data is subject to the laws and jurisdiction of the country where it resides, which can include government access rights. Regulations and contracts (GDPR transfer rules, national data localisation laws, public-sector requirements) often dictate where personal, financial, or government data may live.

Cloud controls include choosing specific regions, restricting allowed regions with organisation policies, disabling cross-region replication and global services for regulated data, customer-managed keys (optionally held outside the provider), and sovereign or dedicated cloud offerings. Compliance requires knowing your data flows, including backups, logs, analytics copies, support access, and third-party SaaS processors, and documenting them.
cgc-8.example: A German public-sector client requires all data in Germany; the architecture uses the Frankfurt region only, with a policy blocking resource creation elsewhere.
cgc-8.tip: Backups, logs, and disaster-recovery copies count too. They often silently replicate data outside the required region.

cgc-9.body:
An IAM permission boundary is an advanced AWS feature that sets the maximum permissions an IAM user or role can ever have. Effective permissions are the intersection of the identity's policies and its boundary, so even if someone attaches AdministratorAccess, the identity can do only what the boundary also allows. (Service control policies provide a similar cap at the account or organisation level, and Azure uses scoped roles and management groups for comparable control.)

Boundaries enable safe delegation: a platform team can let application teams create their own IAM roles for their services, but require that every role they create carries a boundary, so teams cannot create roles more powerful than themselves or escalate privileges. This combines developer autonomy with centrally controlled limits.
cgc-9.example: Developers may create Lambda execution roles, but only with the 'app-boundary' policy attached, which forbids IAM changes and access outside their project's resources.
cgc-9.tip: Effective permissions = identity policy ∩ permission boundary ∩ SCPs, with any explicit Deny winning.

cgc-10.body:
Joiner-Mover-Leaver (JML) processes manage access across an identity's lifecycle. Joiners receive baseline access for their role automatically on day one. Movers who change roles gain the new role's access and, critically, lose the old role's; missing this step causes privilege creep. Leavers have all access revoked promptly (ideally automatically, triggered by HR systems), including accounts, tokens, keys, and shared credentials.

Periodic access reviews (user access recertification) have managers or resource owners confirm that each person still needs each entitlement, removing what is unnecessary; privileged and sensitive access is reviewed more often. Identity governance tools (such as SailPoint, Entra ID Governance, and Okta Identity Governance) automate provisioning through SCIM, reviews, and reporting. Stale and orphaned accounts are a frequent breach cause and a common audit finding.
cgc-10.example: When an employee transfers from finance to marketing, automation removes their access to the accounting system the same day, before their new marketing access is granted.
cgc-10.tip: Revoke leavers' access on or before their last day, including API keys and personal access tokens, not just their main login.

moa-1.body:
OpenTelemetry's architecture has three parts. First, instrumentation in each application, either automatic (agents and libraries that instrument frameworks without code changes) or manual (the API used to add custom spans, metrics, and business attributes). Second, the OpenTelemetry Collector, deployed as an agent on each host or node and/or as a central gateway, which receives telemetry over OTLP and other protocols, processes it (batching, memory limiting, attribute enrichment such as Kubernetes metadata, redaction, and tail-based sampling), and exports it. Third, one or more backends that store and analyse the data.

This decoupling means you can change or combine backends by reconfiguring exporters, add enrichment centrally, and control costs through sampling in one place. Semantic conventions keep attribute names consistent across languages and teams.
moa-1.example: A Collector gateway enriches all spans with Kubernetes pod and namespace labels, drops health-check traces, keeps 100% of error traces, and sends the data to two backends during a vendor migration.
moa-1.tip: Deploy Collectors close to workloads (agent mode) plus a gateway tier, so application SDKs stay simple and configuration lives centrally.

moa-2.body:
Service maps (dependency or topology maps) are generated automatically from tracing data: every span that calls another service defines an edge, building a live graph of which services call which, with request rates, error rates, and latency on each connection. Because they are derived from real traffic, they reveal dependencies nobody documented, unexpected callers, circular dependencies, and changes after deployments.

During incidents, service maps show blast radius at a glance: which upstream services are affected by a failing dependency, and where errors originate versus where they surface. They also support architecture reviews, capacity planning, and security reviews by showing actual data flows.
moa-2.example: During an outage, the service map shows the failing recommendation service is called synchronously by checkout, explaining why a 'non-critical' service broke purchases.
moa-2.tip: Critical user paths should not depend synchronously on non-critical services. Service maps expose those hidden couplings.

moa-3.body:
Google's SRE book defines four golden signals for monitoring user-facing systems. Latency is the time taken to serve requests, measured as a distribution (p50, p95, p99), with successful and failed requests tracked separately, because fast errors can make averages look good. Traffic is the demand on the system, such as requests per second, transactions, or concurrent sessions.

Errors are the rate of failing requests, whether explicit (HTTP 5xx), implicit (wrong content returned with a 200), or policy-based (responses slower than the SLO). Saturation is how 'full' the service is: utilisation of its most constrained resource (CPU, memory, disk I/O, connection or thread pools, queue depth), which often predicts problems before errors appear. Dashboards and alerts built around these four cover most user-impacting failures.
moa-3.example: Queue depth (saturation) climbs for 20 minutes before latency and errors spike, so alerting on saturation gives the team time to scale out first.
moa-3.tip: Track latency of successful and failed requests separately. Quick failures can mask a real outage in averages.

moa-4.body:
Application Performance Monitoring (APM) instruments application code to measure transactions end to end: response times per endpoint, slow database queries, external API calls, errors with stack traces, and throughput, often linking directly to distributed traces. It answers 'which part of this request is slow?' at the code level.

Continuous profiling samples CPU usage, memory allocations, locks, and I/O across production processes at low overhead, aggregating them into flame graphs that show which functions consume resources over time. It catches issues APM can miss: memory leaks, inefficient serialisation, regex backtracking, excessive garbage collection, and gradual performance regressions between releases. Tools include Pyroscope and Grafana, Datadog, Parca, and cloud profilers. Use APM for latency paths and profiling for resource hotspots.
moa-4.example: Continuous profiling reveals that JSON serialisation of a large response object uses 40% of CPU after a release; switching the serialiser halves the server count needed.
moa-4.tip: Compare profiles before and after each release to catch performance regressions early.

moa-5.body:
Log aggregation collects logs from every host, container, function, and service into a central platform where they can be searched, correlated, visualised, and alerted on. Collectors and shippers (Fluent Bit, Fluentd, Vector, the OpenTelemetry Collector, and cloud agents) read logs, parse and enrich them (adding host, pod, and environment metadata), filter and redact sensitive fields, and send them to backends such as Elasticsearch or OpenSearch, Loki, Splunk, or cloud log services.

For useful analysis, use consistent structured fields (timestamp, service, severity, trace_id, user or tenant ID), index what you search frequently, build saved queries and dashboards, and feed security detections and anomaly alerts. Plan retention by value: short hot retention for debugging, longer cold or archive retention for compliance and forensics, and tight access controls.
moa-5.example: A security analyst searches a year of centralised authentication logs to find every login by a compromised account across all systems in under a minute.
moa-5.tip: Centralise logs off the host quickly. Attackers delete local logs, and containers take theirs with them when they die.

moa-6.body:
Burn rate measures how fast an SLO's error budget is being consumed relative to the rate that would use it up exactly at the end of the SLO window. A burn rate of 1 means you will use the whole budget in 30 days; a burn rate of 14.4 sustained for an hour consumes about 2% of a 30-day budget, a typical threshold for paging.

Multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerting (from the Google SRE Workbook) pairs a long window with a short one, for example page if the 1-hour and 5-minute burn rates both exceed 14.4, and open a ticket if the 3-day and 6-hour rates both exceed 1. The long window proves the problem is significant; the short window confirms it is still happening, so alerts reset quickly after recovery. This yields fewer false pages, fast detection of severe outages, and alerts aligned with business tolerance.
moa-6.example: A brief 2-minute error spike no longer pages anyone, but a sustained 5% error rate pages within minutes because it would exhaust the monthly budget in hours.
moa-6.tip: Page on fast burn, ticket on slow burn. Both are tied to the SLO, not to arbitrary thresholds.

moa-7.body:
Runbook automation turns repetitive, well-understood response steps into code triggered by alerts or run with one click: gathering diagnostics (logs, thread dumps, recent deploys, and metrics snapshots attached to the incident), restarting a known-safe stuck process, clearing a cache, scaling out, failing over, rotating a leaked credential, or rolling back the last deployment. Tools include AWS Systems Manager Automation, Rundeck, StackStorm, PagerDuty Runbook Automation, and SOAR platforms for security.

Automation reduces mean time to recovery and removes error-prone manual steps under pressure. Keep humans in the loop for novel or high-risk situations: automate what is safe, idempotent, and well tested, add guardrails and rate limits, log every automated action, and review automations after incidents.
moa-7.example: A disk-full alert automatically runs a job that compresses old logs and, if space is still low, expands the volume, notifying the on-call engineer only if both steps fail.
moa-7.tip: Only automate actions that are safe to run repeatedly (idempotent), with clear limits on how often they fire.

moa-8.body:
Chaos engineering deliberately injects failures, such as terminating instances or pods, adding network latency or packet loss, exhausting CPU or memory, failing a dependency, or blocking a zone, to test whether systems and teams handle them as expected. It is run as controlled experiments: define the steady state, hypothesise what will happen, limit the blast radius, run the experiment, and observe. Tools include AWS Fault Injection Service, Gremlin, Chaos Mesh, and LitmusChaos; Netflix's Chaos Monkey pioneered the approach.

Fault injection also validates observability: if the dashboards, alerts, and runbooks do not detect an injected failure, they will not detect a real one. Game days bring teams together to practise realistic scenarios, test on-call readiness, and find gaps safely.
moa-8.example: A game day that blocks one AZ reveals that a critical cache runs in a single AZ; the team fixes it before a real outage exposes the weakness.
moa-8.tip: Start small in non-production, with an abort button, then graduate to carefully scoped production experiments.

moa-9.body:
Telemetry costs grow with volume (log bytes ingested, spans stored), metric cardinality (unique label combinations), and retention. Unmanaged, observability can become one of the largest items on the infrastructure bill. Cost-aware observability keeps the diagnostic value while controlling spend.

Techniques include: sampling traces (head-based sampling for routine traffic, and tail-based sampling that keeps all errors and slow requests); dropping or aggregating noisy, low-value logs (debug logs, health checks) at the collector; converting high-volume logs into metrics; limiting high-cardinality labels to those with clear diagnostic value; tiered retention (hot for recent debugging, cheaper warm storage for weeks, archive for compliance); and attributing telemetry costs to the teams that generate them.
moa-9.example: Tail-based sampling keeps 100% of error traces but only 5% of successful ones, cutting tracing costs by 80% while preserving everything needed to debug failures.
moa-9.tip: Never put unbounded values such as user IDs or request IDs in metric labels. Put them in logs or traces instead.

moa-10.body:
Effective incident diagnosis correlates signals across telemetry types and change events. Start from the symptom (an SLO or golden-signal alert), narrow the scope with metrics (which service, region, version, or customer segment?), use traces to find the failing or slow component, read that component's logs for the specific error, and check change events: deployments, feature flag flips, configuration changes, infrastructure events, and dependency incidents.

Shared identifiers make this fast: trace IDs in logs, request IDs, deployment version labels on metrics, and deployment markers on dashboards. Afterwards, document the causal chain in the postmortem with concrete evidence (graphs, log lines, and trace links) rather than guesses, and distinguish the root cause from contributing factors and triggers.
moa-10.example: A latency spike lines up exactly with a deployment marker; traces point to a new database query, and logs show it running without an index.
moa-10.tip: Always overlay deployment and config-change markers on dashboards. Changes are the most common incident trigger.

mo-1.body:
Prometheus is the leading open-source metrics system for cloud-native environments (a CNCF graduated project). It uses a pull model: the Prometheus server scrapes HTTP /metrics endpoints on targets at regular intervals, discovering targets dynamically (for example via Kubernetes service discovery), and stores the samples in a time-series database. Exporters expose metrics for systems that do not do so natively (node_exporter for hosts, database exporters, and so on).

Metric types are counters (only increase, such as total requests), gauges (go up and down, such as memory in use), histograms (bucketed observations such as request duration, enabling percentiles), and summaries. PromQL queries them: rate() computes per-second rates from counters, increase() gives totals over a window, and histogram_quantile() computes percentiles. Recording rules precompute expensive queries; alerting rules feed Alertmanager for routing, grouping, and silencing.
mo-1.example: `histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, service))` shows p95 latency per service.
mo-1.tip: Always apply rate() to counters. Raw counter values only ever grow and are meaningless on their own.

mo-2.body:
Structured logging emits each log event as machine-parseable data, usually a JSON object, instead of free-form text. Consistent fields such as timestamp (ISO 8601 in UTC), level, service, environment, version, message, trace_id and span_id, request_id, and relevant business keys (order_id, tenant_id) make logs easy to filter, aggregate, and correlate across services.

Most languages have structured logging libraries (for example Python's structlog, Java's Logback with a JSON encoder, Go's slog, and Node's pino). Ship logs to a centralised store (Loki, Elasticsearch or OpenSearch, Splunk, or cloud log services) with consistent parsing. Redact secrets, tokens, passwords, and unnecessary personal data before shipping, and use log levels thoughtfully so production is not flooded with debug output.
mo-2.example: `{"ts":"2026-09-27T10:15:02Z","level":"error","service":"payments","trace_id":"7f3a…","order_id":"A1021","msg":"card declined by issuer"}` can be searched by any field.
mo-2.tip: Agree on field names across teams (or use OpenTelemetry semantic conventions) so cross-service searches just work.

mo-3.body:
In microservices, one user request may touch a dozen services, queues, and databases. Distributed tracing reconstructs that journey: the entry point (often the API gateway) starts a trace, and each service records spans for its work, with timing, status, and attributes, passing the trace context to the next service through headers or message metadata (W3C Trace Context).

The resulting trace, displayed as a timeline (waterfall), shows the critical path, parallel versus sequential calls, retries, and where errors originate. OpenTelemetry provides the instrumentation; Jaeger, Zipkin, Grafana Tempo, AWS X-Ray, and commercial APM tools provide storage and visualisation. Span metrics derived from traces feed service maps and RED dashboards.
mo-3.example: A trace shows an order request calling inventory, pricing, and shipping sequentially; making the three calls in parallel cuts latency from 900 ms to 350 ms.
mo-3.tip: Propagate trace context through message queues and async jobs too, or traces break at every asynchronous hop.

mo-5.body:
SLO-based alerting ties alerts to user-visible reliability rather than to internal resource thresholds. Define SLIs that reflect the user experience (availability as successful requests over total, latency as the proportion of requests under a threshold), set SLOs (for example 99.9% over 28 days), and derive the error budget.

Alert on how fast the error budget is burning, not on each individual missed request or CPU spike: multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts page for fast, significant burns and create tickets for slow burns. This catches real outages quickly, ignores brief blips, and reduces pager noise. Revisit SLOs periodically as user expectations and system capabilities change, and use remaining error budget to guide release decisions.
mo-5.example: A team replaces 40 threshold alerts with 6 burn-rate alerts on 3 SLOs; pages drop by 80% while every real customer-impacting incident is still caught.
mo-5.tip: If an alert does not correspond to user pain or imminent risk, it should not page a human.

mo-6.body:
Dashboards turn telemetry into understanding, but only if they are designed for a purpose and an audience. Service dashboards typically follow the RED method (Rate, Errors, Duration) and the golden signals, plus SLO status and error budget remaining, saturation of key resources, dependency health, and deployment markers. Executive and business dashboards show SLO compliance, availability trends, and key business metrics.

Good practice: a clear hierarchy (overview first, with drill-down links), consistent time ranges and units, percentiles rather than averages, annotations for deployments and incidents, and dashboards defined as code (for example Grafana JSON or Terraform) so they are versioned and reviewed. Avoid dashboard sprawl, meaning hundreds of unmaintained dashboards nobody trusts.
mo-6.example: The on-call overview dashboard shows every service's SLO status in green, amber, or red; clicking a red one opens that service's RED dashboard with recent deploys marked.
mo-6.tip: If nobody has opened a dashboard in 90 days, archive it. Curated beats comprehensive.

mo-8.body:
Synthetic monitoring actively probes services from the outside on a schedule, simulating users: uptime checks for HTTP, TCP, ICMP, and DNS; API checks that validate response content and latency; SSL certificate checks; and scripted browser journeys (using tools such as Playwright) that log in, search, add to cart, and check out. Probes run from multiple geographic locations and private locations inside your network.

Because synthetics run even when there is no real traffic, such as at night or for new features, they detect outages and regressions before users report them and give a consistent performance baseline. Combine them with passive, real-user telemetry (RUM, server metrics, and traces) for full coverage from outside and inside. Alert on consecutive failures from multiple locations to avoid false alarms from a single flaky probe.
mo-8.example: A scripted checkout journey runs every 5 minutes from four continents; after a payment-provider change, it fails in Asia only, pinpointing a regional routing problem.
mo-8.tip: Use dedicated test accounts and data for synthetic transactions, and exclude them from business analytics.

mo-9.body:
Reliable incident response depends on well-designed on-call practices. Rotations should be sustainable (reasonable frequency, follow-the-sun where possible, and compensation or time off), with clear escalation policies and handoff notes between shifts. Alerts route by severity: pages for urgent, user-impacting issues, and tickets for everything else. Each page links to a runbook.

During significant incidents, defined roles keep response organised: an incident commander coordinating, a communications lead updating stakeholders and status pages, and responders investigating and mitigating. Track metrics such as MTTA (mean time to acknowledge), MTTR (mean time to recover), and pages per shift. After each incident, run a blameless review and tune or remove alerts that were noisy or unhelpful.
mo-9.example: A team measures that half its night pages were self-resolving blips; tuning those alerts lets on-call engineers sleep, and response times to real incidents improve.
mo-9.tip: Pager fatigue is a reliability risk. Burnt-out responders make slower, worse decisions.

monitoring-observability-advanced-c22.body:
Alert quality determines whether on-call engineers trust and act on alerts. A high-quality alert requires human action now, reflects real or imminent user impact, is specific about what is wrong, and links to a runbook and relevant dashboards. Low-quality alerts, such as flapping thresholds, duplicate notifications, informational messages, or problems that fix themselves, create noise that trains people to ignore pages.

Improve quality by alerting on symptoms (SLO burn, error rate) rather than every possible cause, requiring conditions to persist before firing, using multi-window checks, grouping related alerts, routing by severity, suppressing during planned maintenance and temporarily after deployments, and reviewing alert statistics regularly. Delete or downgrade any alert that has not led to meaningful action.
monitoring-observability-advanced-c22.example: An alert review finds a disk alert that fired 200 times last month with no action taken; it is changed to a ticket at a higher threshold, freeing on-call attention.
monitoring-observability-advanced-c22.tip: Measure alert precision: of the pages sent, how many required action? Aim for nearly all of them.

term:CIA Triad.body:
The CIA triad is the core model of information security. Confidentiality means only authorised people and systems can read information. It is protected by encryption, access controls, classification, and MFA. Integrity means information is accurate and has not been altered without authorisation or detection, protected by hashing, digital signatures, checksums, version control, and change management.

Availability means systems and data are accessible when needed, protected by redundancy, backups, patching, capacity planning, DDoS protection, and disaster recovery. Every security control supports at least one of the three, and every breach is a failure of at least one. The goals can conflict: stronger confidentiality controls can reduce availability, so balance them against business needs. Related concepts often added are authenticity, non-repudiation, and privacy.
term:CIA Triad.example: Ransomware attacks all three at once: it encrypts files (availability), often steals them first (confidentiality), and can tamper with backups (integrity).
term:CIA Triad.tip: When an exam asks which principle a control supports: encryption = confidentiality, hashing = integrity, redundancy and backups = availability.

term:Zero Trust.body:
Zero trust is a security model built on 'never trust, always verify'. It rejects the old castle-and-moat assumption that anything inside the corporate network is trustworthy. Every access request, from any user, device, or workload, and from any location, is explicitly authenticated and authorised based on identity, device health, and context, and is encrypted.

Core principles, as in NIST SP 800-207, include verifying explicitly, using least-privilege access (just-in-time and just-enough), and assuming breach, which means minimising blast radius with micro-segmentation and continuously monitoring. Enablers include strong identity with MFA and SSO, device posture checks, micro-segmentation, ZTNA instead of broad VPN access, and comprehensive logging. Zero trust is a strategy adopted incrementally, not a single product.
term:Zero Trust.example: An employee on the office network still needs MFA and a compliant, managed laptop to open the finance app, and gets access to that app only, not the whole network.
term:Zero Trust.tip: The key components are the policy decision point and the policy enforcement point, which evaluate each request continuously rather than once at login.

term:Incident Response.body:
Incident response is the structured process for handling security incidents to limit damage, recover quickly, and learn. NIST SP 800-61 defines the lifecycle: Preparation (plans, playbooks, tools, contacts, training), Detection and Analysis (spotting, validating, scoping, and prioritising incidents), Containment, Eradication and Recovery, and Post-Incident Activity (lessons learned). SANS describes six steps: prepare, identify, contain, eradicate, recover, and lessons learned.

Containment stops the spread, for example by isolating hosts, disabling compromised accounts, or blocking C2 domains. Eradication removes the attacker's tools and persistence and closes the entry point. Recovery restores systems from clean sources and monitors for reinfection. Throughout, preserve evidence (volatile data first, chain of custody), communicate through defined channels, and involve legal and PR for notification duties. Practise with tabletop exercises.
term:Incident Response.example: A ransomware playbook says: isolate affected hosts from the network (but do not power them off), disable the compromised admin account, notify the IR lead and legal, and identify the initial access vector.
term:Incident Response.tip: Do not rush to wipe a compromised machine. You lose the evidence needed to find how the attacker got in.

s1-2.body:
Malware is any software designed to harm, exploit, or gain unauthorised access to systems. A virus attaches itself to legitimate files or programs and spreads when they are run. A worm self-replicates across networks without user action by exploiting vulnerabilities (as WannaCry did via SMB). A Trojan pretends to be legitimate software while carrying a malicious payload, often a remote access Trojan (RAT) giving attackers control.

Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment, often after stealing data for double extortion. Other types include spyware and keyloggers (stealing information), rootkits (hiding deep in the OS), botnets (networks of infected machines controlled remotely), fileless malware (living in memory and abusing tools such as PowerShell), and logic bombs. Defences include EDR, patching, least privilege, application allow-listing, email filtering, user awareness, and offline immutable backups.
s1-2.example: A user downloads a 'free PDF converter' that is really a Trojan; it installs a RAT, and attackers use it to deploy ransomware across the network a week later.
s1-2.tip: Worms spread without user action; viruses need a host file and user execution. A frequent exam distinction.

s1-3.body:
Phishing uses fraudulent emails, texts (smishing), calls (vishing), or websites to trick people into revealing credentials, approving payments, or running malware. Messages impersonate trusted brands, colleagues, or suppliers and create urgency ('your account will be locked', 'invoice overdue'). Spear phishing targets specific individuals with researched details; whaling targets executives; business email compromise (BEC) uses hijacked or look-alike accounts to redirect payments.

Phishing is the most common initial attack vector. Defences are layered: email authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC), secure email gateways and link sandboxing, phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2 passkeys), user training with simulations, an easy 'report phish' button, and payment-verification procedures that confirm requests through a separate channel.
s1-3.example: A finance clerk receives an email that appears to come from the CEO asking for an urgent wire transfer; a call-back verification policy stops a $250,000 loss.
s1-3.tip: MFA stops most credential phishing, but adversary-in-the-middle kits can steal session cookies. FIDO2/passkeys resist even those.

s1-4.body:
A Distributed Denial-of-Service attack overwhelms a target with traffic or requests from many sources, usually a botnet of compromised devices (IoT cameras and routers are common recruits), so legitimate users cannot be served. It attacks availability.

Types include volumetric attacks (floods of UDP or amplified traffic, measured in Gbps or Tbps, often using reflection and amplification through DNS, NTP, or memcached), protocol attacks (SYN floods exhausting connection tables), and application-layer (Layer 7) attacks (HTTP request floods that are hard to tell apart from real users). Defences include upstream scrubbing services, CDNs and anycast networks, cloud DDoS protection (AWS Shield, Cloudflare), rate limiting, WAF rules, auto scaling, and a pre-arranged DDoS response plan with your ISP.
s1-4.example: The 2016 Mirai botnet used hundreds of thousands of hijacked IoT devices to knock DNS provider Dyn offline, taking down major sites such as Twitter and Netflix.
s1-4.tip: You cannot out-provision a large DDoS attack yourself. Absorb it upstream with a CDN or scrubbing service.

s1-5.body:
In a man-in-the-middle (MITM) or on-path attack, the attacker secretly positions themselves between two communicating parties, so they can eavesdrop on, relay, or alter traffic while both sides believe they are talking directly. Techniques include ARP spoofing on LANs, rogue or 'evil twin' Wi-Fi access points, DNS spoofing, BGP hijacking, malicious proxies, and SSL stripping (downgrading HTTPS to HTTP).

The main defence is strong encryption with authentication: TLS with proper certificate validation (so attackers cannot impersonate the server), HSTS to force HTTPS, SSH host key verification, and mutual TLS between services. Network controls such as Dynamic ARP Inspection, DHCP snooping, WPA3, and 802.1X reduce opportunities, and VPNs protect users on untrusted networks such as public Wi-Fi.
s1-5.example: An attacker in a café sets up a Wi-Fi network named 'CoffeeShop_Free'. Users who connect have their unencrypted traffic captured and are shown fake login pages.
s1-5.tip: Never click through certificate warnings. They are exactly what a MITM attack looks like to a user.

s1-6.body:
Network defences work in layers. Firewalls enforce which traffic is allowed, by IP, port, and protocol (stateful firewalls) or by application and user (next-generation firewalls). An intrusion detection system (IDS) monitors traffic or hosts for malicious patterns (signatures) or anomalies and raises alerts. An intrusion prevention system (IPS) sits inline and blocks malicious traffic automatically.

Network-based IDS/IPS (such as Suricata or Snort) watch traffic; host-based versions (HIDS/HIPS, often part of EDR) watch the system itself. VPNs create encrypted tunnels for remote users and between sites across untrusted networks. None is sufficient alone: defence in depth combines them with segmentation, strong identity, endpoint protection, and monitoring.
s1-6.example: An IPS inline at the internet edge blocks an exploit attempt against an unpatched web server while the IDS inside the network alerts on the internal scanning that follows a phishing compromise.
s1-6.tip: IDS = detect and alert (passive); IPS = detect and block (inline). An IPS false positive can block legitimate traffic, so tune it.

s1-7.body:
The OWASP Top 10 is a widely used awareness list of the most critical web application security risks, updated every few years from real-world data. The 2021 edition includes Broken Access Control (users acting outside their permissions, the number one risk), Cryptographic Failures, Injection (SQL injection and XSS, among others), Insecure Design, Security Misconfiguration, Vulnerable and Outdated Components, Identification and Authentication Failures, Software and Data Integrity Failures, Security Logging and Monitoring Failures, and Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF).

It serves as a baseline for secure development training, code review, and testing. Most entries are addressed by server-side authorisation checks, input validation and output encoding, parameterised queries, secure defaults, patched dependencies, strong authentication, and good logging. OWASP also publishes the ASVS, cheat sheets, and Top 10 lists for APIs and LLM applications.
s1-7.example: An API returns other customers' invoices when the invoice ID in the URL is changed, a classic Broken Access Control (IDOR) flaw.
s1-7.tip: Broken Access Control is number one: always enforce authorisation on the server for every request, never just by hiding buttons.

s1-8.body:
Multi-factor authentication requires two or more different types of factor: something you know (password or PIN), something you have (authenticator app, hardware key, smart card), and something you are (fingerprint, face). A stolen or guessed password alone is no longer enough, which stops the vast majority of account-takeover attacks. Phishing-resistant options such as FIDO2 security keys and passkeys are strongest; SMS codes are the weakest because of SIM swapping and interception.

Least privilege means every user, service account, and application gets only the permissions needed for its task, and only for as long as needed. It limits the damage a compromised account or insider can do. It is implemented with role-based access, separate admin accounts, just-in-time elevation, removal of standing admin rights, and regular access reviews.
s1-8.example: An attacker phishes an employee's password but cannot sign in without the hardware key; even if they could, the account has no admin rights to abuse.
s1-8.tip: Prioritise MFA for admins, remote access, email, and cloud consoles first. These accounts give attackers the most leverage.

cybersecurity-basics-c2.body:
A threat is anything that could cause harm, such as a criminal gang, a malicious insider, or a flood. A vulnerability is a weakness it could exploit, such as unpatched software, a weak password, or an untrained employee. A risk is the likelihood and impact of a threat exploiting a vulnerability. Understanding common attack patterns helps you recognise them early.

Malware infects systems to steal, spy, or destroy. Phishing tricks people into giving up credentials or running malware. Ransomware encrypts, and often steals, data to extort payment. Social engineering exploits human trust through pretexting, impersonation, tailgating into buildings, and baiting with infected USB drives. Other common attacks include password spraying and credential stuffing, exploitation of public-facing applications, and supply-chain compromises of trusted vendors.
cybersecurity-basics-c2.example: An attacker phones the helpdesk pretending to be a stressed executive locked out before a board meeting and convinces the agent to reset the password, pure social engineering.
cybersecurity-basics-c2.tip: Attackers usually go for the easiest path: people and unpatched internet-facing systems. Train staff and patch exposed services first.

cybersecurity-basics-c3.body:
Authentication (AuthN) proves identity: who are you? Methods include passwords, one-time codes, certificates, hardware security keys, passkeys, and biometrics, ideally combined as MFA. Authorisation (AuthZ) happens after authentication and decides what an authenticated identity may do: which data it can read, which actions it can perform, which resources it can reach.

Authorisation models include role-based access control (RBAC, permissions assigned to roles such as 'HR Manager'), attribute-based access control (ABAC, decisions based on attributes such as department, location, and data classification), and discretionary and mandatory models. OAuth 2.0 scopes limit what applications may do on a user's behalf. Accounting or auditing, the third 'A' in AAA, logs what identities actually did.
cybersecurity-basics-c3.example: Logging into the HR portal with a password and a passkey is authentication; being allowed to view only your own team's salaries is authorisation.
cybersecurity-basics-c3.tip: AuthN ≠ AuthZ. Many breaches come from apps that authenticate users correctly but never check authorisation per request.

cybersecurity-basics-c4.body:
Encryption transforms readable plaintext into unreadable ciphertext using an algorithm and a key; only holders of the right key can decrypt it. Symmetric encryption, such as AES, uses one shared secret key for both encryption and decryption. It is fast and used for bulk data. Asymmetric encryption, such as RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography, uses a public and private key pair. It solves key distribution and enables digital signatures but is slower.

Encryption in transit (TLS, VPNs, SSH) protects data moving across networks; encryption at rest (full-disk encryption, database and storage encryption) protects stored data and backups if media are stolen. Key management is the hard part: generating, storing, rotating, and controlling access to keys, often with a KMS or HSM. Lose the key and the data is gone; leak the key and the encryption is worthless.
cybersecurity-basics-c4.example: A stolen laptop with BitLocker full-disk encryption exposes nothing, because the data is unreadable without the TPM-protected key and the user's PIN.
cybersecurity-basics-c4.tip: Encryption protects confidentiality only if the keys are protected. Never store keys next to the data they protect.

cybersecurity-basics-c6.body:
Vulnerability management is the continuous cycle of discovering, prioritising, remediating, and verifying weaknesses in systems and software. Discovery uses authenticated vulnerability scanners (such as Nessus, Qualys, or OpenVAS), software composition analysis for application dependencies, cloud posture tools, and asset inventories, because you cannot patch what you do not know you have.

Prioritisation goes beyond the CVSS severity score: consider whether the vulnerability is actively exploited (the CISA KEV catalogue, EPSS scores), whether the asset is exposed to the internet, the asset's criticality and data sensitivity, and compensating controls. Remediate by patching (tested, then deployed within agreed SLAs, for example critical internet-facing flaws within days), configuration changes, or mitigations. When fixing is not feasible, document a formal risk acceptance with an owner and an expiry date.
cybersecurity-basics-c6.example: A scanner finds 4,000 issues; the team fixes the 12 actively exploited vulnerabilities on internet-facing systems first, which removes most of the real risk.
cybersecurity-basics-c6.tip: Asset inventory is step zero. Unknown, unmanaged assets are where attackers get in.

cybersecurity-basics-c7.body:
Network defences apply defence in depth so that no single failure gives an attacker full access. Firewalls enforce which traffic may pass at the perimeter and between internal zones. Segmentation, through VLANs, subnets, ACLs, and micro-segmentation, splits the network so that a compromise in one zone cannot spread freely, and it keeps sensitive systems such as payment or medical devices apart.

IDS monitors traffic for malicious activity and alerts, while IPS blocks it inline. Proxies (forward proxies and secure web gateways) inspect and filter users' web traffic, blocking malicious sites and data exfiltration; reverse proxies protect servers. DNS filtering blocks known-bad domains. Network access control (802.1X) keeps unknown devices off the network, and centralised logging of all these controls feeds detection.
cybersecurity-basics-c7.example: Because the guest Wi-Fi, office, and server networks are segmented, a malware-infected guest laptop can reach the internet but nothing inside the company.
cybersecurity-basics-c7.tip: Flat networks are an attacker's dream. Segmentation is one of the highest-value controls against ransomware spreading.

cybersecurity-basics-c8.body:
Secure coding means writing software that resists attack by design. Validate all input on the server (type, length, format, range) using allow-lists, and encode output for its context (HTML, JavaScript, SQL, shell) to stop injection attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting. Use parameterised queries or safe ORM features instead of building SQL strings. Avoid dangerous functions and insecure deserialisation of untrusted data, and in memory-unsafe languages prevent buffer overflows.

Rely on well-reviewed libraries for authentication, session management, and cryptography rather than writing your own. Enforce authorisation on every request, handle errors without leaking details, keep secrets out of code, and keep dependencies patched. Build security into the development lifecycle with threat modelling, code review, SAST, DAST, and dependency scanning in CI.
cybersecurity-basics-c8.example: Replacing `"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='" + name + "'"` with a parameterised query closes a SQL injection hole that allowed dumping the whole user table.
