cybersecurity-basics-c8.tip: Never trust client-side validation alone. Attackers bypass the browser and call your API directly.

cybersecurity-basics-c10.body:
Security governance is written down in documents with different levels of authority. Policies are high-level management statements of intent and requirements ('all remote access requires MFA'). Standards specify mandatory technical requirements ('use FIDO2 or authenticator-app MFA; SMS is not permitted'). Procedures are step-by-step instructions, and guidelines are recommended but optional practices.

Frameworks provide tested baselines: the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover), the CIS Critical Security Controls (prioritised technical safeguards), ISO/IEC 27001 (a certifiable information security management system), and MITRE ATT&CK (a knowledge base of adversary techniques for building detections). Regulations such as GDPR, HIPAA, and PCI DSS impose legal or contractual obligations. Compliance shows controls exist at audit time; security maturity shows they work every day.
cybersecurity-basics-c10.example: A company maps its controls to CIS Controls v8 to prioritise improvements, pursues ISO 27001 certification for customers, and uses ATT&CK to test detection coverage.
cybersecurity-basics-c10.tip: Compliant does not mean secure. Many breached organisations passed their last audit.

s2-1.body:
Symmetric encryption uses the same secret key to encrypt and decrypt. It is very fast, even in hardware (CPUs include AES instructions), so it is used for bulk data: full-disk encryption, database and file encryption, VPN tunnels, and the data phase of every TLS connection. AES (with 128- or 256-bit keys) is the standard; ChaCha20 is a fast alternative on devices without AES hardware.

Modes of operation matter. Authenticated encryption modes such as AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 provide confidentiality and integrity together, while ECB mode leaks patterns and must never be used. The central challenge is key distribution: both parties need the same secret without exposing it, which is why asymmetric cryptography or key exchange is used to agree on symmetric keys.
s2-1.example: BitLocker and FileVault encrypt entire drives with AES; the AES key is itself protected by the TPM or the user's password.
s2-1.tip: Symmetric = one shared key, fast, bulk data. Weakness: securely sharing the key. Legacy algorithms such as DES, 3DES, and RC4 are broken or deprecated.

s2-2.body:
Asymmetric (public-key) cryptography uses a mathematically linked key pair. The public key can be shared with anyone; the private key must stay secret. Data encrypted with the public key can be decrypted only with the private key, which gives confidentiality to the key owner. A signature made with the private key can be verified by anyone with the public key, which gives authentication, integrity, and non-repudiation.

Common algorithms are RSA (2048-bit or larger) and elliptic-curve cryptography (ECDSA, Ed25519, ECDH), which offers equivalent security with much smaller keys. Asymmetric operations are far slower than symmetric ones, so in practice they are used to exchange or protect symmetric keys and to sign data, not to encrypt bulk data. This hybrid approach is exactly how TLS, PGP, and S/MIME work. Post-quantum algorithms such as ML-KEM and ML-DSA are being adopted to resist future quantum attacks.
s2-2.example: To send Bob a secret, Alice encrypts it with Bob's public key; only Bob's private key can decrypt it. To prove she sent it, Alice signs it with her own private key.
s2-2.tip: Encrypt with the recipient's public key; sign with your own private key. Mixing these up is the classic exam trap.

s2-3.body:
A cryptographic hash function turns input of any size into a fixed-size digest (SHA-256 produces 256 bits) with three key properties: it is one-way (you cannot recover the input from the hash), deterministic (the same input always gives the same hash), and collision-resistant (it is infeasible to find two inputs with the same hash). A tiny change to the input produces a completely different hash, the avalanche effect.

Hashes verify integrity (download checksums, file integrity monitoring, blockchain), underpin digital signatures and HMACs (hash plus secret key, for message authentication), and are used for password storage. For passwords, use deliberately slow, salted algorithms such as Argon2id, bcrypt, scrypt, or PBKDF2, because fast hashes such as SHA-256 can be brute-forced at billions of guesses per second on GPUs. MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for security use.
s2-3.example: A software vendor publishes the SHA-256 hash of its installer; if your download's hash matches, the file was not corrupted or tampered with in transit.
s2-3.tip: Hashing is not encryption. It cannot be reversed with a key. Hashing supports integrity, not confidentiality.

s2-4.body:
Transport Layer Security (the successor to the deprecated SSL) protects data in transit between a client and a server, providing confidentiality (encryption), integrity (tamper detection), and server authentication (certificates). HTTPS is HTTP over TLS, and TLS also secures email transport, VPNs, APIs, and database connections.

In the handshake, the client and server agree on a protocol version and cipher suite, the server presents its certificate for the client to validate (chain of trust, host name, and expiry), and both sides perform an ephemeral key exchange (ECDHE) to derive shared session keys, which provides forward secrecy. TLS 1.3 simplified this to one round trip and removed weak algorithms. Use TLS 1.2 or 1.3 only; SSL 2.0/3.0 and TLS 1.0/1.1 are deprecated.
s2-4.example: A browser connecting to your bank validates the bank's certificate, negotiates TLS 1.3 with an AES-GCM cipher, and shows the padlock. An expired certificate would trigger a warning.
s2-4.tip: Forward secrecy (ephemeral Diffie-Hellman) means stealing the server's private key later cannot decrypt previously recorded sessions.

s2-5.body:
Public Key Infrastructure is the system of roles, policies, and technology that binds public keys to identities. A Certificate Authority (CA) verifies an identity and issues an X.509 certificate containing the subject's name (and Subject Alternative Names), public key, validity period, and issuer, signed with the CA's private key. Trust flows through a chain: a trusted root CA (preinstalled in operating systems and browsers) signs intermediate CAs, which sign end-entity certificates.

Certificates expire and can be revoked before expiry if a key is compromised, with revocation checked through CRLs or OCSP (often with OCSP stapling). Registration Authorities handle identity verification. Organisations also run private internal CAs, for example AD Certificate Services, for internal services and devices. Let's Encrypt issues free, automated 90-day certificates via the ACME protocol, making automated renewal the norm.
s2-5.example: A website's certificate chain: example.com, signed by an intermediate CA, signed by a root CA that the browser already trusts.
s2-5.tip: Certificate expiry is a leading cause of outages. Automate renewal (ACME) and monitor expiry dates.

s2-6.body:
A digital signature proves who created data and that it has not changed since. The signer hashes the data and signs that hash with their private key. A verifier hashes the data themselves and uses the signer's public key to check the signature; if the check passes, the data came from the private-key holder (authentication), was not altered (integrity), and the signer cannot credibly deny signing it (non-repudiation).

Signatures secure software updates and code signing, operating-system drivers and bootloaders (Secure Boot), TLS certificates, documents and contracts, emails (S/MIME, DKIM), container images (Sigstore/cosign), and blockchain transactions. Algorithms include RSA-PSS, ECDSA, and Ed25519. A signature is only as trustworthy as the protection of the private key and the certificate binding the public key to an identity.
s2-6.example: An operating system installs a driver update only if it carries a valid signature from the vendor, blocking tampered or fake drivers.
s2-6.tip: Signing provides integrity, authentication, and non-repudiation, but not confidentiality. Signed data can still be read by anyone.

s2-7.body:
Diffie-Hellman key exchange lets two parties who have never met agree on a shared secret over a public, monitored channel. Each side generates a private value and sends a public value derived from it; combining their own private value with the other's public value gives both the same secret, while an eavesdropper seeing only the public values cannot feasibly compute it. The shared secret then becomes the key for fast symmetric encryption.

Modern systems use ephemeral elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE), generating fresh values for every session. This provides perfect forward secrecy: compromising a server's long-term private key later does not expose past sessions. Plain Diffie-Hellman does not authenticate the parties, so it is combined with certificates and signatures to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks, as in TLS and SSH.
s2-7.example: Every TLS 1.3 connection performs an ECDHE exchange, so even an attacker who records traffic and later steals the server key cannot decrypt it.
s2-7.tip: Diffie-Hellman provides key agreement, not authentication. Without signatures or certificates it is vulnerable to MITM.

s2-8.body:
Passwords must never be stored in plaintext or with reversible encryption. Instead, store a salted, slow hash. A salt is a unique random value generated per password and stored alongside the hash. It ensures identical passwords produce different hashes and makes precomputed rainbow tables useless.

The hash function must be deliberately slow and ideally memory-hard, so each guess is expensive: Argon2id (the current recommendation), bcrypt, scrypt, or PBKDF2 with a high iteration count, tuned so one check takes tens to hundreds of milliseconds. A pepper, a secret key stored separately from the database, adds protection if only the database leaks. Combine this with breached-password checks, rate limiting, and MFA. When a breach happens, attackers get hashes that are expensive to crack rather than usable passwords.
s2-8.example: Two users both choose 'Summer2026!'; with unique salts their stored bcrypt hashes look completely different, so cracking one does not reveal the other.
s2-8.tip: Fast hashes (MD5, SHA-1, even plain SHA-256) are wrong for passwords. Use Argon2id or bcrypt.

s3-1.body:
A penetration test is an authorised, simulated attack against defined systems to find and demonstrate exploitable weaknesses before real attackers do. It begins with scoping and rules of engagement: written permission, targets in and out of scope, testing windows, allowed techniques, and emergency contacts. Testing without authorisation is illegal.

Typical phases are reconnaissance, scanning and enumeration, exploitation, post-exploitation (privilege escalation, lateral movement, and showing business impact), and reporting. Knowledge levels vary: black box (no inside information, simulating an outsider), white box (full access to documentation and code), and grey box (partial knowledge, such as a user account). The deliverable is a report with an executive summary, findings rated by risk, evidence, and clear remediation guidance, followed by a retest to confirm fixes.
s3-1.example: A grey-box test starting with a standard employee account reaches Domain Admin in two days through a misconfigured service account, a finding that drives a tiering project.
s3-1.tip: No written authorisation = no test. Get sign-off from someone with the authority to approve it.

s3-2.body:
Ethical hacking uses the same knowledge, tools, and techniques as malicious attackers, but with permission and to improve security. Ethical hackers work within a defined scope and rules of engagement, avoid causing damage, protect any data they encounter, and report findings responsibly to the organisation. Roles include penetration testers, red teamers, bug bounty hunters, and security researchers.

The discipline requires broad skills (networking, operating systems, web applications, cloud, Active Directory, scripting) and constant learning as new vulnerabilities and techniques appear. Certifications include CEH, OSCP, and PNPT, and legal practice environments include TryHackMe, Hack The Box, and PortSwigger's Web Security Academy. Responsible disclosure and coordinated vulnerability disclosure programmes govern how researchers report flaws they find.
s3-2.example: A bug bounty researcher finds an access-control flaw in an airline's booking API, reports it through the official programme, and is paid a reward once it is fixed.
s3-2.tip: Stay inside scope. Testing a system you were not authorised to test is illegal even with good intentions.

s3-3.body:
Nmap is the standard network scanner for discovering hosts, open ports, running services and versions (-sV), and operating systems (-O), with the Nmap Scripting Engine adding vulnerability checks. Metasploit Framework is a modular exploitation platform: pick an exploit for a known vulnerability, pair it with a payload (such as Meterpreter), set options, and run it, plus post-exploitation modules for privilege escalation and pivoting.

Burp Suite is the leading web application testing proxy. It intercepts and modifies HTTP traffic between the browser and the application, and provides a scanner, Repeater (manually resend and tweak requests), Intruder (automated fuzzing), and many extensions for finding injection, authentication, access-control, and business-logic flaws. OWASP ZAP is a free alternative. Other essentials include Wireshark, Hashcat and John the Ripper, BloodHound, and Impacket.
s3-3.example: A tester uses Nmap to find an outdated web server, Burp Suite to discover an IDOR flaw in its API, and Metasploit to demonstrate remote code execution on an unpatched service.
s3-3.tip: Defenders should know these tools too. Their traffic patterns and artifacts are what your detections must catch.

s3-4.body:
A Security Operations Center is the team, processes, and technology that monitor an organisation's environment around the clock and respond to threats. Analysts work from a SIEM (centralised log correlation and alerting), EDR and XDR (endpoint and extended detection and response), network detection, email security, and threat intelligence, and often use SOAR (security orchestration, automation and response) to automate repetitive enrichment and containment steps.

Work is often tiered: Tier 1 triages alerts, dismissing false positives and escalating real ones; Tier 2 investigates incidents in depth and contains them; Tier 3 handles complex incidents, threat hunting, malware analysis, and detection engineering. Key metrics include mean time to detect (MTTD) and mean time to respond (MTTR). Alert fatigue is a major challenge, addressed by tuning detections and automation. Some organisations outsource this to managed detection and response (MDR) providers.
s3-4.example: At 2 a.m. the SIEM correlates an impossible-travel sign-in with a new mailbox forwarding rule; a Tier 1 analyst escalates, and Tier 2 disables the account and revokes its sessions within 15 minutes.
s3-4.tip: Detections are only valuable if someone acts on them. Tune noisy rules, because alert fatigue hides real attacks.

s3-5.body:
Threat hunting is the proactive search for attackers who have evaded automated detection. Instead of waiting for alerts, hunters assume compromise and form hypotheses based on threat intelligence, MITRE ATT&CK techniques, or anomalies, then query telemetry (EDR data, logs, network flows, DNS) to confirm or refute them.

Examples of hypotheses: 'An attacker is using scheduled tasks for persistence', 'Service accounts are logging in interactively', or 'A host is beaconing to a newly registered domain at regular intervals'. Techniques include stacking (finding rare values across the fleet), baselining normal behaviour, and pivoting on indicators. Successful hunts either find intrusions or become new automated detections, so every hunt improves future coverage.
s3-5.example: A hunt for rare parent-child process pairs finds Excel spawning PowerShell on three machines, revealing a malicious macro campaign that no alert had caught.
s3-5.tip: Hunting needs good telemetry. You cannot hunt in data you are not collecting.

s3-6.body:
Incident response is how an organisation handles a confirmed or suspected security breach. The lifecycle runs from preparation (IR plan, playbooks, roles, contact lists, tools, retainers) through detection and analysis (confirming, scoping, and prioritising the incident), containment (stopping the spread by isolating hosts, disabling accounts, and blocking indicators), eradication (removing malware, persistence, and the root-cause vulnerability), and recovery (restoring from clean backups and monitoring closely), to lessons learned.

Speed limits damage, but evidence matters too: collect volatile data first (memory, network connections), maintain chain of custody, and keep a detailed timeline. Communication runs through defined channels, out of band if email may be compromised, with legal counsel involved early because of breach-notification laws (such as GDPR's 72-hour rule) and regulators. Rehearse with tabletop exercises and technical drills.
s3-6.example: During a ransomware incident, the team isolates infected segments, preserves memory images of patient-zero machines, restores from immutable backups, and notifies regulators within the legal deadline.
s3-6.tip: Prepare before you need it: decide in advance who can authorise shutting down systems, and keep offline copies of the IR plan.

s3-7.body:
A red team emulates a real adversary. It is often objective-based ('access the payment database without being detected') and uses stealth, social engineering, physical intrusion, and custom tooling over weeks, testing the organisation's ability to detect and respond rather than just finding vulnerabilities. A blue team is the defence: SOC analysts, incident responders, and engineers who monitor, detect, and respond.

Purple teaming brings them together: red executes specific techniques (often mapped to MITRE ATT&CK), while blue watches detections in real time; gaps are fixed immediately and retested. This collaborative loop improves detection coverage much faster than adversarial exercises alone. Tools such as Atomic Red Team, CALDERA, and breach-and-attack simulation platforms help automate technique testing.
s3-7.example: A red team phishes its way in and moves laterally for a week unnoticed; the follow-up purple-team sessions build detections for each technique it used.
s3-7.tip: Pentest = find as many vulnerabilities as possible in scope. Red team = test detection and response against a realistic adversary.

s3-8.body:
Zero trust architecture, formalised in NIST SP 800-207, removes implicit trust based on network location. Every access request is evaluated by a policy engine using identity (strong authentication), device posture (managed, patched, EDR healthy), resource sensitivity, and context (location, time, behaviour), and enforced by policy enforcement points in front of resources. Access is least privilege and time-limited, sessions are continuously re-evaluated, and all traffic is encrypted and logged.

Practical building blocks include an identity provider with MFA and conditional access, device management, ZTNA replacing broad VPN access, micro-segmentation for workloads, and strong monitoring with analytics. Zero trust is especially suited to cloud, SaaS, and remote work, where the traditional network perimeter no longer exists. It is adopted as a journey, starting with identity and the most critical assets.
s3-8.example: A developer on home Wi-Fi reaches the production console only through a ZTNA gateway after passkey MFA, from a compliant company laptop, with a session that expires after one hour.
s3-8.tip: Zero trust assumes breach. Design so that one compromised device or account gives access to as little as possible.

sec-1.body:
Cloud Identity and Access Management controls who (a principal: user, group, role, or service identity) can perform which actions on which resources, under which conditions. In AWS, JSON policies allow or deny actions (s3:GetObject) on resources (specific ARNs). Every API call, from the console, CLI, or SDK, is authenticated and then evaluated against the applicable identity policies, resource policies, permission boundaries, session policies, and organisation-level controls (service control policies).

Evaluation logic in AWS starts from an implicit deny; an explicit allow is required, and any explicit deny overrides all allows. Best practices include using roles with temporary credentials instead of long-lived access keys, federating human access through SSO, requiring MFA, granting least privilege, using conditions (such as source IP, MFA present, or tags), and continuously reviewing permissions. Misconfigured IAM, meaning over-broad permissions and leaked keys, is a leading cause of cloud breaches.
sec-1.example: An EC2 instance uses an IAM role granting read access to only one S3 bucket, so there are no stored access keys to leak and no access to any other data.
sec-1.tip: An explicit Deny always wins in AWS policy evaluation. Use SCP guardrails to deny dangerous actions organisation-wide.

sec-2.body:
Least privilege means each identity, whether human, service account, application, or pipeline, receives only the permissions required to do its job, scoped to specific resources and, ideally, only for the time needed. It shrinks the blast radius when credentials are stolen or misused and limits insider risk.

In practice: start from no access and add specific permissions; avoid wildcards such as "Action": "*" and "Resource": "*"; separate duties (the person who writes code is not the one approving production access); use just-in-time elevation for admin tasks instead of standing admin rights; and continuously right-size using access analysis tools (such as AWS IAM Access Analyzer, last-accessed data, and CIEM products) that show which permissions are actually used. Review access regularly, especially when people change roles or leave.
sec-2.example: Access analysis shows a CI pipeline role with AdministratorAccess only ever uses 11 actions; restricting it to those removes a huge risk if the pipeline is compromised.
sec-2.tip: Permissions tend to grow over time (privilege creep). Schedule periodic access reviews and remove unused rights.

sec-4.body:
Encryption at rest protects data stored in databases, block volumes, object storage, file systems, snapshots, and backups, so that stolen, leaked, or improperly disposed storage media are unreadable without the keys. Cloud services typically use AES-256 with envelope encryption: data is encrypted with a data key, and that data key is itself encrypted by a master key held in a key management service.

Most cloud services now enable encryption at rest by default. The meaningful decision is who controls the keys: provider-managed keys (simplest), customer-managed keys in KMS (you control the key policy, rotation, and auditing, and can disable the key to cut off access), or customer-supplied or external keys held in your own HSM for the strictest requirements. Encryption at rest does not protect against an attacker who gains authorised access through the application, since the service decrypts data for authorised callers.
sec-4.example: An S3 bucket encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key denies reads to anyone whose role lacks kms:Decrypt on that key, even if the bucket policy were misconfigured.
sec-4.tip: Encryption at rest protects against media theft and some misconfigurations, but not against compromised valid credentials.

sec-5.body:
Encryption in transit protects data moving over networks, between users and services, between services, and to databases and APIs, from eavesdropping and tampering. The main tool is TLS (1.2 or 1.3), used for HTTPS, database connections, message queues, and internal service calls. Mutual TLS (mTLS), where both client and server present certificates, adds strong service-to-service authentication, often provided automatically by a service mesh.

Encrypt in transit everywhere, including inside VPCs and private networks, because zero trust assumes internal networks can be compromised. Enforce HTTPS with HSTS and redirects, require TLS on database and cache connections, disable old protocols and weak ciphers, manage certificates automatically (for example with AWS Certificate Manager or cert-manager), and use IPsec or MACsec for network-level encryption where needed.
sec-5.example: A bank enables TLS between its application pods and the database cluster, so an attacker who compromises one host on the subnet cannot sniff customer data.
sec-5.tip: 'It's inside our VPC' is not a reason to skip TLS. Internal traffic is a common target for lateral-movement sniffing.

sec-6.body:
A Key Management Service (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, Google Cloud KMS) creates, stores, and controls cryptographic keys inside hardware security modules that never expose raw key material. Services and applications call the KMS to encrypt, decrypt, or generate data keys (envelope encryption), and every use is authorised by key policies and IAM and logged, for example to CloudTrail, which gives a full audit trail of who used which key.

Key features include automatic rotation of key material, separation between key administrators and key users, grants for temporary delegated use, multi-region keys, disabling or scheduling deletion of keys (which effectively crypto-shreds all data encrypted with them), and import of your own key material. Protect key administration tightly, because whoever controls the keys controls the data.
sec-6.example: An application encrypts customer documents with data keys from KMS; auditors review CloudTrail logs showing exactly which service role decrypted which documents and when.
sec-6.tip: Separate duties: people who manage keys should not automatically be able to use them to decrypt data, and vice versa.

sec-7.body:
The shared responsibility model divides security duties between the cloud provider and the customer. The provider is responsible for security of the cloud: physical data centres, hardware, the hypervisor and host infrastructure, and the global network. The customer is responsible for security in the cloud: their data, identities and access, configurations, and whatever software they manage.

The split depends on the service model. With IaaS (VMs), the customer manages the guest OS, patching, applications, firewall rules, and data. With PaaS (managed databases, serverless), the provider also handles the OS and runtime, while the customer manages configuration, access, and data. With SaaS, the provider runs almost everything, but the customer still owns user access, data, and settings. Most cloud breaches, such as public storage buckets, leaked keys, and over-permissive IAM, fall on the customer's side.
sec-7.example: AWS patches the hypervisor under your EC2 instance, but if you never patch the instance's Linux OS and it gets exploited, that is your responsibility.
sec-7.tip: In every model, data classification, identity and access management, and configuration remain the customer's responsibility.

sec-8.body:
Multi-factor authentication requires a user to present two or more independent factors (knowledge, possession, inherence) before access is granted. In the cloud it is essential because consoles and APIs are reachable from anywhere on the internet. MFA should be mandatory for the root or global administrator account, all privileged roles, and increasingly for every user, typically enforced centrally at the identity provider with conditional access policies.

Strength varies. FIDO2 security keys and passkeys are phishing-resistant, because they are cryptographically bound to the real site. Authenticator app codes and push notifications are good but can be phished or abused through 'MFA fatigue' prompt bombing, which number matching mitigates. SMS and voice codes are the weakest, vulnerable to SIM swapping. Protect the account recovery process too, since it can bypass MFA entirely.
sec-8.example: Attackers with a leaked root-account password are stopped by the hardware security key required for every root sign-in.
sec-8.tip: Lock the root account away: strong MFA, no access keys, and use it only for the few tasks that truly require it.

sec-9.body:
Single sign-on lets users authenticate once with a central identity provider (IdP), such as Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, or Google Workspace, and then access many applications without signing in again. Applications (service providers) trust the IdP through federation standards: SAML 2.0 (XML assertions, common for enterprise SaaS) and OpenID Connect (built on OAuth 2.0 with JSON Web Tokens, common for modern and mobile apps).

SSO improves usability (one strong credential instead of dozens of reused passwords) and security: MFA and conditional access are enforced in one place, access is logged centrally, and disabling one account cuts off every connected app at once, which is crucial when people leave. The trade-off is that the IdP becomes a high-value target, so protect it with strong MFA, admin separation, and monitoring. SCIM automates provisioning and deprovisioning of accounts into apps.
sec-9.example: When an employee leaves, disabling their single Entra ID account instantly revokes access to Salesforce, Slack, AWS, and 40 other SSO-connected apps.
sec-9.tip: SAML = XML assertions for enterprise SSO; OIDC = identity layer on OAuth 2.0; OAuth 2.0 itself is for authorisation (delegated access), not authentication.

sec-10.body:
Compliance means demonstrating that security and privacy controls meet an external standard, regulation, or contract. Common frameworks include SOC 2 (independent attestation of controls for security, availability, confidentiality, processing integrity, and privacy; Type II covers a period of operation), ISO/IEC 27001 (a certifiable information security management system), PCI DSS (payment card data), HIPAA (US healthcare information), GDPR (EU personal data), and FedRAMP (US government cloud).

Cloud providers hold many certifications, and customers can inherit controls for the provider's side (physical security, infrastructure) through provider reports such as AWS Artifact. The customer must still configure and evidence their own side: access control, encryption, logging, data residency, and incident response. Continuous compliance tooling (such as AWS Config, Azure Policy, and CSPM products) monitors configurations against these frameworks between audits.
sec-10.example: A SaaS startup uses its cloud provider's SOC 2 report for infrastructure controls, and implements and evidences its own access reviews, encryption, and logging to pass its own SOC 2 Type II audit.
sec-10.tip: Using a compliant cloud provider does not make your application compliant. Your configuration is still in scope.

term:Infrastructure as Code.body:
Infrastructure as Code (IaC) defines servers, networks, databases, load balancers, IAM policies, and other resources in machine-readable files rather than creating them by hand in a console. Declarative tools such as Terraform and OpenTofu, AWS CloudFormation and CDK, Azure Bicep, and Pulumi describe the desired end state and work out the changes needed; configuration management tools such as Ansible, Chef, and Puppet configure what runs on the servers.

Because infrastructure lives in version control, every change is reviewed in a pull request, tested, and applied through the same CI/CD pipelines as application code. Environments can be recreated identically (dev matching production), drift from the defined state can be detected, and disasters can be recovered by re-applying code. Security and compliance checks (policy as code, IaC scanners) run before anything is deployed.
term:Infrastructure as Code.example: A team rebuilds its entire staging environment (VPC, subnets, EKS cluster, and databases) from Terraform in 20 minutes after it is accidentally deleted.
term:Infrastructure as Code.tip: Treat IaC like application code: code review, automated tests and scans, and no manual console changes in production.

term:GitOps.body:
GitOps is an operating model in which Git holds the declarative desired state of applications and infrastructure, and an automated agent continuously reconciles the live environment to match it. Changes happen only through commits and pull requests, which are reviewed, tested, and auditable. The agent, such as Argo CD or Flux for Kubernetes, pulls changes from Git rather than having CI push credentials into production.

Key benefits include a complete audit trail of who changed what and when, easy rollback with git revert, automatic correction of manual drift (someone's kubectl edit is reverted), consistent multi-cluster deployment, and a smaller attack surface because CI pipelines do not need direct production credentials. The four OpenGitOps principles are: declarative, versioned and immutable, pulled automatically, and continuously reconciled.
term:GitOps.example: A developer merges a pull request that bumps an image tag; Argo CD notices within a minute and rolls the new version out to three clusters, with no one running kubectl.
term:GitOps.tip: In GitOps, protect the Git repository like production: branch protection, required reviews, and signed commits.

d1-1.body:
Git is a distributed version control system that records the complete history of a codebase as a series of commits, each a snapshot with an author, timestamp, and message. Every developer has a full copy of the repository, so work continues offline and history is never held in one place.

Branches let people work on features and fixes in isolation, then merge them back, usually through pull (merge) requests on platforms such as GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket, where teammates review the code and CI runs automated checks. Common workflows include trunk-based development (short-lived branches merged into main frequently) and GitFlow (long-lived develop and release branches). Git makes it possible to find when a bug was introduced (git bisect), roll back safely, and collaborate at scale. Protecting the main branch and scanning for committed secrets are essential security practices.
d1-1.example: A bug appears in production; `git log` and `git blame` show which commit changed the code, and `git revert` safely undoes it within minutes.
d1-1.tip: Anything committed stays in history. Rotate secrets that were ever committed, even if later deleted.

d1-2.body:
Continuous Integration is the practice of merging developers' changes into a shared main branch frequently, at least daily, with every push automatically triggering a build and a test suite. Problems surface within minutes of being introduced, while the change is small and the context fresh, instead of weeks later during a painful 'integration phase'.

A healthy CI setup has fast, reliable tests (unit tests first, then integration), static analysis and linting, security scans (SAST, dependency, and secret scanning), and a rule that a failing build blocks merging and gets fixed immediately. Short-lived branches or trunk-based development plus feature flags keep changes small. The result is a main branch that is always in a working, releasable state.
d1-2.example: A pull request fails CI because a unit test catches an off-by-one error in pricing logic; it is fixed before merge, so no customer ever sees the bug.
d1-2.tip: Keep the CI pipeline fast (ideally under 10 minutes). Slow pipelines encourage big batches and skipped tests.

d1-3.body:
Continuous Delivery extends CI so that every change that passes the pipeline is automatically built into a deployable artifact, tested in production-like environments, and ready to release to production at any time, usually with a one-click, human-approved deployment. Continuous Deployment goes one step further: every change that passes all automated checks is released to production automatically, with no manual gate.

Both depend on thorough automated testing, repeatable deployments, infrastructure as code, and good monitoring. They make releases small, frequent, and boring, which reduces risk because each change is easy to understand and roll back. Safe release strategies (canary, blue/green, feature flags) and automated rollback on bad metrics make high deployment frequency practical.
d1-3.example: An online retailer deploys to production 50 times a day with continuous deployment; each change is small, and a canary automatically rolls back any release that raises errors.
d1-3.tip: Delivery = always releasable, manual trigger. Deployment = automatic release to production.

d1-4.body:
A CI/CD pipeline is the automated sequence of stages that takes code from commit to production: checkout, build, unit tests, static analysis and security scans, packaging an immutable artifact (a container image or package), deploying to test or staging environments, integration and end-to-end tests, approval (if required), production deployment, and post-deployment verification.

Each stage acts as a quality gate: a failure stops the change from progressing. Pipelines are defined as code (YAML in GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Azure Pipelines, or Jenkinsfiles), stored in the repository, reviewed, and versioned like application code. Build once and promote the same artifact through environments, so what was tested is exactly what ships. Pipelines hold powerful credentials, so they must be secured.
d1-4.example: A GitHub Actions workflow runs tests, builds a Docker image, scans it with Trivy, pushes it to ECR, and deploys it to staging; a manual approval promotes the same image digest to production.
d1-4.tip: Build the artifact once and promote it. Rebuilding for each environment means production runs something you never tested.

d1-6.body:
Automated tests give confidence to change code quickly. The test pyramid guides the mix: many fast unit tests at the base (individual functions and classes in isolation, running in milliseconds), fewer integration tests in the middle (components working together with real databases, queues, or APIs), and a small number of slow end-to-end tests at the top (full user journeys through the UI or API).

Other useful types include contract tests (verifying API agreements between services), smoke tests (quick checks after deployment), performance and load tests, and security tests (SAST, DAST, and dependency scanning). All run automatically in the pipeline and block releases on failure. Tests must be reliable, because flaky tests erode trust and get ignored. Coverage is a guide, not a goal: test the behaviour and risks that matter.
d1-6.example: A payment service has 800 unit tests (2 seconds), 60 integration tests against a test database (1 minute), and 5 end-to-end checkout tests (3 minutes), all run on every merge.
d1-6.tip: Fix or quarantine flaky tests immediately. A test suite nobody trusts is worse than no tests.

d1-7.body:
Monitoring and observability give teams visibility into how systems behave in production. Monitoring collects metrics (CPU, memory, request rate, error rate, latency), logs, and health checks, and alerts when something crosses a threshold or an SLO starts burning. Tools include AWS CloudWatch, Azure Monitor, Google Cloud Monitoring, Prometheus with Grafana, Datadog, and New Relic.

Observability goes further, adding distributed traces and rich, high-cardinality telemetry so engineers can ask new questions about unexpected failures without shipping new code. In DevOps, observability closes the feedback loop: every deployment is watched for regressions, automated rollback reacts to bad metrics, and production data informs development priorities. Good alerts are actionable and tied to runbooks.
d1-7.example: After a deployment, dashboards show error rates rising for one endpoint; traces identify the new code path, and the team rolls back within minutes.
d1-7.tip: You cannot safely deploy often without good observability. Invest in it before increasing deployment frequency.

a1-1.body:
A distributed system is a collection of independent computers that communicate over a network and coordinate to appear as a single system to users. Distribution delivers horizontal scalability, fault tolerance through redundancy, and low latency by placing nodes near users.

It also introduces fundamental difficulties: partial failures (some nodes or links fail while others keep working), unreliable networks with variable latency and dropped or duplicated messages, the lack of a global clock (making ordering hard), consistency trade-offs (the CAP theorem), and concurrency issues. The 'fallacies of distributed computing', such as 'the network is reliable' and 'latency is zero', describe assumptions that break real systems. Designing for failure (timeouts, retries with backoff, idempotency, replication, consensus algorithms such as Raft, and graceful degradation) is the core skill.
a1-1.example: An online store's order service times out calling payments; without idempotency keys, a retry could charge the customer twice.
a1-1.tip: Assume every network call can fail, be slow, or happen twice, and design for each case.

a1-2.body:
Microservices architecture structures an application as a set of small services, each aligned to a business capability (bounded context), independently deployable, owning its own data, and communicating through well-defined APIs or events. Teams can own services end to end, deploy them independently, choose suitable technologies, and scale hot services without scaling everything.

The trade-offs are significant: network calls replace in-process calls (latency and failures), data consistency spans services (sagas and eventual consistency instead of ACID transactions), and operations require service discovery, API gateways, centralised logging, distributed tracing, and mature CI/CD. Organisational fit matters (Conway's law: systems mirror team communication structures). Many teams do better with a modular monolith until scale or team size clearly justifies splitting.
a1-2.example: A streaming company runs hundreds of microservices so the recommendations team can deploy several times a day without coordinating with the billing team.
a1-2.tip: Do not split into microservices to fix messy code. A distributed mess is harder to fix than a monolithic one.

a1-3.body:
Event-driven systems communicate by publishing events (facts about something that happened, such as 'PaymentReceived') to a broker or event bus, and letting any interested services consume them asynchronously. Common infrastructure includes Apache Kafka, RabbitMQ, Amazon EventBridge, SNS and SQS, Azure Service Bus, and Google Pub/Sub.

Benefits include loose coupling (producers do not know or wait for consumers), independent scaling, buffering of traffic spikes, easy addition of new consumers, and resilience when downstream services are temporarily unavailable. Patterns include publish/subscribe, event sourcing (storing state as a sequence of events), and CQRS. Challenges include eventual consistency, debugging flows across services, message ordering, duplicate delivery (consumers must be idempotent), schema evolution, and handling failed messages with dead-letter queues.
a1-3.example: When a user signs up, one 'UserRegistered' event triggers the welcome email, CRM sync, analytics, and fraud-screening services independently.
a1-3.tip: Design consumers to be idempotent and monitor dead-letter queues. Unprocessed events are silent data loss.

a1-4.body:
An API is a contract between systems, and good design keeps it clear, consistent, and stable. REST APIs model resources with nouns and HTTP methods (GET /orders/123, POST /orders), use proper status codes, support pagination, filtering, and sorting, return consistent error formats, and are documented with OpenAPI. gRPC uses Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2 for efficient, strongly typed, streaming-capable communication, which suits internal service-to-service calls. GraphQL lets clients request exactly the data they need.

Version APIs (for example /v2/ or header-based versioning) and evolve them backward-compatibly, adding fields rather than removing or renaming them, so existing clients do not break. Make operations idempotent where retries are likely (idempotency keys for POSTs). Secure APIs with authentication (OAuth 2.0 and OIDC), per-request authorisation, rate limiting, and input validation, following the OWASP API Security Top 10.
a1-4.example: A payments API accepts an Idempotency-Key header, so a mobile app retrying a timed-out 'charge' request never creates a duplicate payment.
a1-4.tip: Broken object-level authorisation (users accessing others' objects by ID) is the top API risk. Check authorisation for every object.

term:Observability.body:
Observability is the ability to understand what is happening inside a system by examining its outputs, well enough to explain behaviour you did not predict. It rests on three main signal types. Logs are timestamped records of discrete events with rich context. Metrics are numeric time series (latency, error rate, throughput, saturation) that are cheap to store and ideal for dashboards and alerts. Traces follow individual requests across services, revealing where time is spent and where failures originate.

In distributed systems, observability is essential because failures emerge from interactions between many components. Correlating the signals (trace IDs in logs, deployment markers on metrics), instrumenting with OpenTelemetry, and emitting high-cardinality context (version, region, customer tier) enable fast diagnosis. Some add profiles and events as further signals.
term:Observability.example: An alert on rising error rates leads to a trace showing failures in the inventory service, whose logs reveal a new database migration locking a table.
term:Observability.tip: Instrument before you need it. You cannot debug last night's outage with telemetry you were not collecting.

a1-6.body:
Service Level Indicators (SLIs) are carefully chosen measurements of service behaviour that users care about: availability (the ratio of successful requests), latency (the proportion of requests faster than a threshold), throughput, durability, or freshness. Service Level Objectives (SLOs) are internal targets for SLIs over a window, for example 99.9% of requests succeed and 95% complete within 300 ms over 30 days. Service Level Agreements (SLAs) are contractual commitments to customers, with penalties such as service credits, and are normally set looser than the SLOs.

The error budget (100% minus the SLO) quantifies acceptable unreliability. Teams spend it on releases and experiments; when it is exhausted, they prioritise reliability work over features. This aligns product and engineering on a shared, measurable definition of 'reliable enough', because 100% is neither achievable nor worth the cost.
a1-6.example: A 99.9% availability SLO over 30 days allows about 43 minutes of errors; an SLA promising 99.5% gives the provider margin before credits are owed.
a1-6.tip: Define SLIs from the user's perspective, measured as close to the user as possible, not just server CPU.

a1-7.body:
Chaos engineering is the discipline of experimenting on a system to build confidence that it can withstand turbulent real-world conditions. Teams deliberately inject failures, such as terminating instances or containers, adding network latency or packet loss, exhausting CPU, memory, or disk, failing dependencies, or simulating an Availability Zone outage, and verify that the system keeps meeting its steady-state behaviour (for example SLOs).

Experiments follow the scientific method: define the steady state, form a hypothesis, limit the blast radius, run the experiment with an abort mechanism, and learn from the results. Netflix pioneered the practice with Chaos Monkey and the Simian Army; modern tools include AWS Fault Injection Service, Gremlin, Chaos Mesh, and LitmusChaos. Findings, such as missing timeouts, single points of failure, and untested failover, are fixed before a real outage exposes them.
a1-7.example: An experiment adding 500 ms of latency to the payment dependency shows checkout threads piling up; adding a timeout and a circuit breaker fixes a hidden cascading-failure risk.
a1-7.tip: Start in staging with small blast radii and clear abort criteria before running chaos experiments in production.

a1-8.body:
Scalability patterns target specific bottlenecks. Caching (in-memory stores such as Redis or Memcached, CDNs, HTTP caching) serves repeated reads without hitting the database or origin. Horizontal scaling adds stateless instances behind load balancers. Read replicas offload read traffic from a primary database. Sharding partitions data across multiple databases by a key to scale writes and storage.

Asynchronous processing with queues (SQS, Kafka, RabbitMQ) decouples producers from consumers, absorbs spikes, and lets work proceed at a sustainable rate. Other tools include connection pooling, rate limiting and back-pressure, denormalisation and precomputation, and CQRS. The key is to measure first, find the real constraint (CPU, database connections, I/O, or a hot key), and apply the pattern that addresses it, since each adds complexity.
a1-8.example: A news site survives a viral story by serving pages from a CDN cache and moving comment processing onto a queue, instead of adding database servers.
a1-8.tip: Measure before optimising. Scaling the wrong tier wastes money and leaves the real bottleneck in place.

k8-3.body:
A Deployment is a Kubernetes object that declares the desired state for a stateless application: which container image to run, how many replicas, resource requests and limits, environment configuration, and the update strategy. The Deployment controller manages ReplicaSets, which in turn keep the requested number of identical Pods running, recreating Pods that crash or are evicted.

When you change the image or configuration, the Deployment performs a rolling update by default: it gradually creates new Pods and removes old ones, respecting maxSurge and maxUnavailable settings and waiting for readiness probes, so the service stays available. kubectl rollout status shows progress, kubectl rollout history lists revisions, and kubectl rollout undo returns to the previous version. Stateful workloads use StatefulSets instead.
k8-3.example: Updating a Deployment's image from v1.4 to v1.5 replaces Pods two at a time; when v1.5 fails its readiness checks, the rollout halts and `kubectl rollout undo` restores v1.4.
k8-3.tip: Always set readiness probes. Without them, rolling updates send traffic to Pods that are not ready yet.

k8-4.body:
Pods are ephemeral and get new IP addresses when they are recreated, so Kubernetes Services provide a stable virtual IP and DNS name that load-balances across the healthy Pods matching a label selector. Cluster DNS (CoreDNS) resolves names such as orders.shop.svc.cluster.local, so applications call each other by name.

Service types: ClusterIP (the default; reachable only inside the cluster), NodePort (opens the same port on every node for external access), LoadBalancer (asks the cloud provider to create an external load balancer), and ExternalName (a DNS alias to an outside name). Headless Services (clusterIP: None) skip the virtual IP and return individual Pod IPs, which StatefulSets use for stable per-Pod identities. EndpointSlices track which Pod IPs currently back each Service.
k8-4.example: The frontend calls http://cart:8080; as cart Pods scale from 3 to 12 and restart, the Service keeps routing to whichever Pods are ready.
k8-4.tip: Only expose Services externally when needed. Prefer ClusterIP plus an Ingress or Gateway with TLS and authentication.

k8-5.body:
An Ingress defines HTTP and HTTPS routing rules from outside the cluster to internal Services, based on host names and URL paths, for example api.example.com/orders to the orders Service and www.example.com to the web Service. It typically terminates TLS using certificates stored as Secrets, often issued automatically by cert-manager with Let's Encrypt.

An Ingress resource does nothing by itself: an Ingress controller must be installed to implement it, such as NGINX Ingress, Traefik, HAProxy, or cloud controllers like the AWS Load Balancer Controller and GKE Ingress. Controllers add features such as rate limiting, authentication, redirects, and WAF integration through annotations. The newer Gateway API is the more expressive, role-oriented successor to Ingress, supporting traffic splitting and more protocols.
k8-5.example: One Ingress with a single cloud load balancer routes traffic for 15 microservices by host and path, each with an automatically renewed TLS certificate.
k8-5.tip: Ingress is Layer 7 HTTP routing and needs a controller; a Service of type LoadBalancer is simpler Layer 4 exposure.

k8-6.body:
ConfigMaps store non-sensitive configuration (feature settings, URLs, configuration files) separately from container images, so the same image can run in dev, staging, and production with different settings. Secrets store sensitive values such as passwords, API tokens, and TLS keys. Both can be injected into Pods as environment variables or mounted as files; mounted files can update without restarting the Pod.

Kubernetes Secrets are only base64-encoded by default, not encrypted. Anyone who can read them through the API, or read etcd, can decode them. Secure them by enabling encryption at rest for etcd (ideally with a KMS provider), restricting access with RBAC, avoiding environment variables for highly sensitive data where practical, and preferably using external secret managers (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault, Azure Key Vault) via the External Secrets Operator or the CSI Secrets Store driver, with rotation and auditing.
k8-6.example: A database password lives in AWS Secrets Manager; the External Secrets Operator syncs it into a Kubernetes Secret, and rotation updates it automatically.
k8-6.tip: Base64 is encoding, not encryption. Never commit Secret manifests with real values to Git unless they are encrypted (for example with SOPS or Sealed Secrets).

k8-7.body:
Kubernetes health probes tell the kubelet about a container's state. A liveness probe checks whether the container is still healthy; if it fails repeatedly, Kubernetes restarts the container (useful for deadlocks and hung processes). A readiness probe checks whether the container can serve traffic now; while it fails, the Pod is removed from Service endpoints but not restarted (useful during warm-up, dependency outages, or overload).

A startup probe gives slow-starting applications time to boot: liveness and readiness checks begin only after it succeeds, preventing premature restarts. Probes can be HTTP GET requests, TCP socket checks, gRPC checks, or commands (exec). Tune initialDelaySeconds, periodSeconds, timeoutSeconds, and failureThreshold carefully: an aggressive liveness probe that fails under load can cause restart loops that worsen outages.
k8-7.example: A Java service needs 60 seconds to start; a startup probe prevents the liveness probe from killing it during boot, while readiness keeps traffic away until it is warm.
k8-7.tip: Liveness probes should not check external dependencies, or one database blip restarts every Pod at once.

k8-8.body:
Containers' file systems are ephemeral, so Kubernetes provides volumes for data that must be shared or must outlive a container. emptyDir is scratch space that lasts as long as the Pod, shared between its containers. For durable data, a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) requests storage of a given size and access mode (ReadWriteOnce, ReadOnlyMany, ReadWriteMany), and Kubernetes binds it to a PersistentVolume (PV).

StorageClasses enable dynamic provisioning: a PVC referencing a StorageClass automatically creates the underlying disk through a CSI driver, such as AWS EBS, Azure Disk, or Google Persistent Disk for block storage, or EFS, Azure Files, and NFS for shared file storage. StorageClasses define disk type, performance, reclaim policy (Delete or Retain), and volume expansion. StatefulSets use volumeClaimTemplates to give each replica its own persistent volume.
k8-8.example: A PostgreSQL StatefulSet gets a 100 GB gp3 EBS volume per replica through a StorageClass; when a Pod moves nodes, its volume reattaches and the data persists.
k8-8.tip: Set the reclaim policy to Retain for important data. The Delete default removes the disk when the PVC is deleted.

k8-9.body:
Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes. A chart bundles templated Kubernetes manifests with a values.yaml file of defaults; installing a chart renders the templates with your values and creates a release that Helm tracks, so you can upgrade, roll back (helm rollback), or uninstall it as a unit. Public charts package common software (ingress controllers, Prometheus, databases), and teams write internal charts for their own services.

Use per-environment values files (values-dev.yaml, values-prod.yaml) instead of copying manifests, pin chart and image versions in version control, review rendered output (helm template or helm diff) before applying, and scan charts for insecure defaults. Alternatives and complements include Kustomize (overlays without templating) and GitOps tools such as Argo CD and Flux, which can deploy Helm charts declaratively.
k8-9.example: The platform team installs ingress-nginx, cert-manager, and kube-prometheus-stack from pinned Helm chart versions defined in a GitOps repository.
k8-9.tip: Review third-party chart defaults. Many enable features, privileges, or exposure you do not want in production.

k8-10.body:
Kubernetes observability covers the cluster itself and the workloads on it. Metrics come from node_exporter (host resources), cAdvisor via the kubelet (per-container CPU, memory, and network), kube-state-metrics (the state of Kubernetes objects, such as desired versus available replicas, Pod restarts, and pending Pods), the control-plane components, and application metrics, typically scraped by Prometheus (often through the kube-prometheus-stack) and visualised in Grafana.

Logs are written by containers to stdout and stderr and collected from nodes by agents such as Fluent Bit, Vector, or the OpenTelemetry Collector, enriched with Pod and namespace metadata and shipped to a central store. Kubernetes Events record scheduler and controller decisions (failed scheduling, image pull errors, OOMKilled), which are invaluable for troubleshooting. OpenTelemetry provides tracing inside clusters, and audit logs record who did what through the API.
k8-10.example: An alert on high Pod restarts plus a Kubernetes Event showing 'OOMKilled' tells the team the new release needs a higher memory limit, or has a leak.
k8-10.tip: Collect Kubernetes Events and API audit logs centrally. They disappear from the cluster quickly and are key forensic evidence.

cicd-1.body:
Continuous Integration means every developer integrates small changes into the main branch frequently, with each commit or pull request automatically built and tested. The goal is to keep main always releasable and to catch integration problems within minutes.

Practices that make CI work: trunk-based development or short-lived branches (hours to a couple of days), feature flags to merge incomplete features safely, a fast pipeline (lint, unit tests, static and security analysis, then build), a rule that the build is never left broken, and required status checks before merging. Pre-commit hooks catch simple issues even earlier. Measuring build duration and flakiness keeps the pipeline healthy as the codebase grows.
cicd-1.example: Twenty engineers merge into main dozens of times a day; each merge runs a 7-minute pipeline, and a failure notifies the author immediately so it is fixed before others are blocked.
cicd-1.tip: Long-lived branches are the enemy of CI. The longer a branch lives, the more painful and risky the merge.

cicd-2.body:
After CI proves a change works, Continuous Delivery automates the rest of the release process: building a versioned artifact, running security scans, deploying to staging, running smoke, integration, and acceptance tests, and making the change deployable to production at the push of a button (often with a required approval). Continuous Deployment removes the final manual step, so every change that passes all automated checks goes to production automatically.

Both require high confidence in automated testing, repeatable infrastructure, safe release strategies, and strong observability with automated rollback. Which to choose depends on risk tolerance, regulatory requirements, and test maturity; many teams continuously deploy to lower environments and use a manual gate for production.
cicd-2.example: A SaaS team continuously deploys to staging on every merge; production releases happen via one-click approval several times a day after automated tests pass.
cicd-2.tip: Regulated environments can still do continuous delivery. The approval step can be automated evidence plus a recorded sign-off.

cicd-3.body:
A pipeline codifies every step from commit to production. Typical stages include source checkout and dependency restore; linting and formatting; unit tests; static application security testing (SAST) and secret scanning; build; integration tests; packaging into an immutable artifact such as a container image; software composition analysis and image vulnerability scanning; SBOM generation and artifact signing; deployment to staging; smoke and end-to-end tests; approval if required; production deployment with a progressive strategy; and post-deploy verification.

Each stage is a gate: a failure stops promotion and notifies the team. Run fast checks first for quick feedback, parallelise independent jobs, cache dependencies, and keep pipeline definitions in version control. Protect the pipeline itself: least-privilege credentials, pinned third-party actions, and isolated runners.
cicd-3.example: A pipeline fails at the image-scan stage because a base image contains a critical OpenSSL CVE; updating the base image fixes it before staging deployment.
cicd-3.tip: Pin third-party CI actions and plugins to specific versions or commit SHAs. Compromised actions are a real supply-chain attack vector.

cicd-6.body:
Release strategies reduce the risk of shipping changes. Rolling updates replace instances gradually (the Kubernetes default): simple and with no extra capacity needed, but old and new versions run side by side during the rollout. Blue/green deployment runs two full environments: the new version (green) is deployed and tested alongside the current one (blue), then traffic switches over at once, and switching back is instant.

Canary releases send a small percentage of real traffic (for example 1%, then 10%, then 50%) to the new version while comparing its error rates and latency with the stable version, promoting or rolling back automatically. Feature flags separate deploying code from releasing features: code ships dark and is turned on for specific users, percentages, or regions, and can be switched off instantly without a redeploy. Choose based on risk, cost, and observability maturity.
cicd-6.example: A new recommendation algorithm ships behind a feature flag, is enabled for 5% of users, shows a conversion drop, and is switched off in seconds without any deployment.
cicd-6.tip: Database schema changes need backward-compatible migrations (expand, then contract) so old and new versions can run at the same time.

cicd-7.body:
CI/CD pipelines need credentials to push images, deploy to cloud accounts, and access registries, which makes them high-value targets. Never hard-code secrets in pipeline files or repositories, and never print them in logs. Prefer short-lived credentials: OIDC federation lets GitHub Actions, GitLab, and other CI systems exchange a signed identity token for temporary cloud credentials (for example an AWS IAM role) scoped to a specific repository and branch, so there are no long-lived keys to leak.

Where static secrets are unavoidable, store them in the CI platform's encrypted secret store or a vault (HashiCorp Vault, cloud secret managers), scope them to specific environments with protected branches and required approvals, rotate them regularly, and audit access. Grant the pipeline least privilege, separate deployment identities per environment, and run secret scanning to catch accidental commits.
cicd-7.example: A GitHub Actions workflow assumes an AWS role through OIDC that only works from the main branch of one repository; no AWS access keys exist anywhere in CI.
cicd-7.tip: Pull requests from forks must not have access to deployment secrets. Configure CI so untrusted code cannot read them.

cicd-8.body:
Artifact management stores the outputs of builds, such as container images, language packages (npm, PyPI, Maven), Helm charts, and binaries, in registries and repositories such as Amazon ECR, Azure Container Registry, Google Artifact Registry, GitHub Packages, JFrog Artifactory, Sonatype Nexus, or Harbor.

Good practice: tag artifacts with immutable, meaningful versions (semantic versions plus the Git commit SHA), enable tag immutability, deploy by content digest in production, and never rely on the floating latest tag. Scan artifacts for vulnerabilities when built and continuously afterwards, generate SBOMs, sign artifacts (Sigstore/cosign) and verify signatures at deployment, apply retention policies to control storage, and proxy public registries through a controlled internal cache to reduce supply-chain risk.
cicd-8.example: An admission policy in production only allows images from the company registry that are signed by the CI system and have no critical vulnerabilities.
cicd-8.tip: Promote the exact same signed artifact through every environment. Never rebuild for production.

cicd-9.body:
An effective testing strategy balances confidence, speed, and cost. Unit tests validate small pieces of logic in isolation, and they are fast and numerous. Integration tests validate how components work together with real dependencies (databases, message queues), often using containers (Testcontainers). Contract tests (for example Pact) verify that a service provider still meets the expectations of its consumers, catching breaking API changes without full end-to-end environments.

End-to-end tests validate critical user journeys through the whole system, but they are slow and brittle, so keep them few. Performance and load tests (k6, JMeter, Locust) catch regressions under realistic load. Security tests include SAST, DAST, dependency scanning, and IaC scanning. Not every test type needs to cover everything: concentrate effort on business-critical and high-risk paths, and track flakiness.
cicd-9.example: Contract tests catch that the orders service renamed a field the billing service depends on, before either is deployed.
cicd-9.tip: Test in proportion to risk. Checkout and authentication deserve far more coverage than an admin report page.

cicd-10.body:
Release observability measures both delivery performance and the health of each change. The four DORA metrics are deployment frequency, lead time for changes (commit to production), change failure rate (the percentage of deployments causing a failure in production), and time to restore service (MTTR). Research shows elite teams deploy frequently and have low failure rates at the same time; speed and stability reinforce each other.

For each release, monitor error rates, latency percentiles, saturation, and key business metrics, compared with the previous version and with deployment markers on dashboards. Automated analysis (for example Argo Rollouts or Flagger checking Prometheus metrics during a canary) can promote a release when metrics stay healthy and roll back automatically when they degrade, which dramatically reduces MTTR for bad deployments.
cicd-10.example: A canary's error rate rises to 2% against 0.1% for the stable version; automated analysis aborts the rollout and routes all traffic back within 3 minutes.
cicd-10.tip: Track the DORA metrics over time. They show whether process changes actually improve delivery.

k2-1.body:
The Kubernetes control plane manages the cluster's desired and actual state. The kube-apiserver is the front door: every request from kubectl, controllers, kubelets, and operators goes through it, where it is authenticated, authorised with RBAC, validated, passed through admission controllers, and persisted. The scheduler assigns new Pods to nodes based on resource requests, affinity and anti-affinity rules, taints and tolerations, and topology constraints.

The controller manager runs reconciliation loops (Deployment, ReplicaSet, Node, Job, and other controllers) that continually drive actual state towards desired state. The cloud controller manager integrates cloud resources such as load balancers and routes. etcd stores all cluster data. Managed services (EKS, AKS, GKE) run the control plane for you, but you still control access to it. Whoever controls the API server controls the cluster, so restrict network access, use strong authentication, and minimise cluster-admin rights.
k2-1.example: A misconfigured RBAC binding gives a CI service account cluster-admin; an attacker who compromises the pipeline can create privileged Pods and take over every node.
k2-1.tip: Keep the API server endpoint private or IP-restricted, and audit every cluster-admin binding.

k2-2.body:
Custom Resource Definitions extend the Kubernetes API with new object types, such as PostgresCluster, Certificate, KafkaTopic, or Rollout, that behave like built-in resources: you create them with YAML, and kubectl, RBAC, admission control, and GitOps tools all work with them. On their own, CRDs only store data; a controller (often part of an operator) watches the custom resources and acts on them.

CRDs let platform teams offer higher-level, domain-specific abstractions: developers declare 'a Postgres database with 3 replicas and daily backups' instead of wiring together StatefulSets, Services, and CronJobs. Treat CRDs as APIs: define schemas with validation (OpenAPI v3), version them (v1alpha1, v1beta1, v1) with conversion webhooks when they change, document them, and govern who can create or modify both the definitions and the instances.
k2-2.example: cert-manager's Certificate CRD lets a team request a TLS certificate declaratively; its controller obtains and renews it automatically from Let's Encrypt.
k2-2.tip: Installing a CRD and its controller extends your cluster's attack surface. Review what permissions the controller needs.

k2-3.body:
The operator pattern packages human operational knowledge into software. An operator is a controller that watches custom resources and automates the full lifecycle of a complex, often stateful application: provisioning, configuration, scaling, backups and restores, upgrades, failover, and self-healing, continuously reconciling the application to the declared desired state.

Examples include the Prometheus Operator, database operators (CloudNativePG, Zalando Postgres, Percona), Strimzi for Kafka, Elastic Cloud on Kubernetes, and cert-manager. Frameworks such as Kubebuilder, the Operator SDK, and kopf (Python) help build them. Operators replace runbooks for routine operations, but they need careful RBAC (they often hold broad permissions), testing of upgrade paths, and monitoring of the operator itself.
k2-3.example: A CloudNativePG operator detects that the primary database Pod failed, promotes a replica, and repoints the service in seconds, without a DBA being paged.
k2-3.tip: Evaluate an operator's maturity (the capability levels, from basic install to autopilot) before trusting it with production data.

k2-4.body:
Progressive delivery reduces release risk by exposing new versions to gradually increasing traffic or users, while automatically evaluating their health. Techniques include canary releases (shifting traffic in steps such as 5%, 25%, 50%, and 100%), blue/green with automated verification, A/B testing, and feature flags for user-level control.

In Kubernetes, Argo Rollouts and Flagger implement this, using service meshes, ingress controllers, or the Gateway API to split traffic and querying metrics providers (Prometheus, Datadog, CloudWatch) against success criteria based on SLOs, such as error rate below 1% and p99 latency below 500 ms. Releases are promoted automatically when healthy and rolled back automatically when not, turning deployment from a risky event into a routine, low-stress operation.
k2-4.example: Argo Rollouts shifts 10% of traffic to v2, runs a 10-minute analysis against Prometheus error-rate queries, then continues to 50% and 100% only if the thresholds hold.
k2-4.tip: Automated analysis is only as good as its metrics. Include business signals (such as orders per minute), not just HTTP status codes.

k2-5.body:
A GitOps architecture typically separates application source repositories from environment configuration repositories, which hold the Kubernetes manifests, Helm values, or Kustomize overlays for each cluster and environment. CI builds and tests code, publishes a signed image, and then updates the image reference in the config repository through a pull request, or automatically via image automation.

A GitOps controller running inside each cluster (Argo CD or Flux) pulls the config repository, compares it with the live cluster state, and reconciles differences, reporting sync and health status. Patterns include app-of-apps or ApplicationSets for managing many applications and clusters, sync waves for ordering, and automated drift correction. Because the controller pulls changes, CI never needs cluster credentials, and git revert provides instant, audited rollback.
k2-5.example: An ApplicationSet deploys the same service to 40 regional clusters from one Git repository; promoting to production is a reviewed pull request that changes one values file.
k2-5.tip: Keep secrets out of plain Git. Use SOPS, Sealed Secrets, or an external secrets operator with GitOps.

k2-6.body:
Admission control is the Kubernetes API server's final checkpoint before an object is stored. Validating admission webhooks can reject non-compliant requests, and mutating webhooks can modify them (for example injecting sidecars or default labels). Policy engines, namely OPA Gatekeeper (with Rego policies), Kyverno (policies written in YAML), and built-in ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (using CEL expressions), use this mechanism to enforce guardrails.

Typical policies include requiring resource requests and limits, mandatory labels, allowing images only from approved registries (with signature verification), blocking privileged containers, host networking, and hostPath mounts, enforcing runAsNonRoot and read-only root file systems, and restricting Ingress host names. Pod Security Admission provides built-in baseline and restricted profiles. Enforcing at deploy time shifts governance left from after-the-fact audits, and running policies in audit mode first avoids breaking teams.
k2-6.example: Kyverno rejects a Deployment that runs a privileged container from Docker Hub, returning a clear message explaining which policy failed and how to fix it.
k2-6.tip: Roll out new policies in audit or warn mode first, fix violations, then switch to enforce.

k2-7.body:
Multi-tenancy runs workloads for many teams, applications, or customers on shared clusters while keeping them isolated. Soft multi-tenancy, for trusted internal teams, typically uses a namespace per tenant with RBAC limiting each team to its namespaces, ResourceQuotas and LimitRanges to cap and default CPU, memory, and object counts, NetworkPolicies to block cross-namespace traffic by default, and Pod Security standards.

Hard multi-tenancy, for untrusted tenants such as different customers, needs stronger boundaries: dedicated node pools with taints and tolerations, sandboxed runtimes (gVisor, Kata Containers), virtual clusters (vCluster), or separate clusters per tenant. The three pillars are identity and access isolation, resource isolation (quotas and fair scheduling), and network isolation. Cost, operational overhead, and the level of trust between tenants determine the right model.
k2-7.example: Each product team gets its own namespace with a quota of 20 CPUs, default-deny network policies, and RBAC to manage only its own resources.
k2-7.tip: Namespaces are not a hard security boundary. Untrusted tenants need node, runtime, or cluster-level isolation.

k2-8.body:
etcd is the distributed, strongly consistent key-value store that holds all Kubernetes cluster data: every object, secret, and status. It uses the Raft consensus algorithm, so a cluster of 3 or 5 members stays available as long as a majority (quorum) survives; losing quorum makes the cluster read-only and unmanageable, although existing workloads keep running.

etcd performance directly affects the whole control plane: slow disks (high fsync latency) or network latency between members slow down every API request and can cause leader elections. Operate it with fast SSDs, low-latency networking, regular compaction and defragmentation, and monitoring of leader changes, database size, and request latency. Take frequent snapshots (etcdctl snapshot save) and practise restores, because an unrecoverable etcd means rebuilding the cluster. Encrypt it at rest, and restrict access to its endpoints and client certificates, since it contains every Secret.
k2-8.example: A self-managed cluster's etcd disk fills up; API writes fail until the team compacts and defragments it. Monitoring on database size would have warned them days earlier.
k2-8.tip: Test etcd restores regularly. A backup you have never restored is only a hope.

k2-9.body:
A service mesh adds a dedicated infrastructure layer for service-to-service communication. A data plane of proxies, either Envoy sidecars injected into each Pod or node-level and eBPF-based proxies in 'ambient' or sidecarless modes, intercepts traffic and applies policy set by a control plane. It provides, without application code changes, automatic mutual TLS (encryption plus workload identity), fine-grained authorisation between services, retries, timeouts and circuit breaking, traffic splitting for canaries, and consistent metrics and traces for every call.

Popular meshes include Istio, Linkerd, Consul, and Cilium's service mesh. The costs are operational complexity, added latency and resource use from proxies, and a steeper learning curve. Adopt a mesh when cross-cutting needs such as zero-trust mTLS, traffic management, and uniform observability across many services outgrow what libraries and ingress can handle cleanly.
k2-9.example: Enabling Istio strict mTLS encrypts all traffic between 200 microservices and allows the payments service to accept calls only from the checkout service's identity.
k2-9.tip: Start with the features you need, typically mTLS and observability, and add advanced traffic management later.

k2-10.body:
Cluster API (CAPI) is a Kubernetes sub-project that manages Kubernetes clusters declaratively using Kubernetes itself. A management cluster runs CAPI controllers, and the workload clusters you want are described as custom resources (Cluster, MachineDeployment, and control-plane objects).
