Infrastructure providers implement those resources on AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, vSphere, bare metal, and others, creating the machines, networking, and control planes.

This brings the Deployment model to whole clusters: create them from templates, scale node groups, perform rolling Kubernetes version upgrades by changing a field, and replace unhealthy machines automatically with MachineHealthChecks. Combined with GitOps, cluster definitions live in Git, so entire fleets of clusters are version-controlled, reviewable, and reproducible, which is ideal for platform teams managing many clusters across environments and regions.
k2-10.example: A platform team upgrades 25 clusters from Kubernetes 1.30 to 1.31 by changing the version in Git; Cluster API rolls new control-plane and worker machines cluster by cluster.
k2-10.tip: Protect the management cluster carefully. It holds credentials to create and destroy every workload cluster.

kg-8.body:
StatefulSets manage stateful applications that need stable identities and persistent storage, such as databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB), message brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ), and coordination services (ZooKeeper, etcd). Unlike Deployments, each Pod gets a stable, ordinal name (kafka-0, kafka-1, kafka-2) and a stable DNS name through a headless Service, which it keeps across rescheduling.

volumeClaimTemplates give each replica its own PersistentVolumeClaim, which stays bound to that ordinal even if the Pod moves to another node. Pods are created, scaled, and updated in order (by default one at a time, from lowest to highest ordinal on creation and highest to lowest on termination), which respects clustering requirements. Running stateful services on Kubernetes still requires careful backup, restore, and upgrade procedures, which is why operators are often used on top of StatefulSets.
kg-8.example: A 3-node Kafka cluster runs as a StatefulSet; kafka-1 is rescheduled after a node failure, keeps its name and its disk, and rejoins the cluster with its data intact.
kg-8.tip: Deleting a StatefulSet does not delete its PVCs by default, which protects data but can leave orphaned volumes and costs.

kg-9.body:
Organisations often run many Kubernetes clusters: per environment, per region for latency and resilience, per compliance boundary, per cloud, or at the edge. Multi-cluster management coordinates workloads, configuration, identity, and policy across them. Approaches include GitOps fleet tools (Argo CD ApplicationSets, Flux, Rancher Fleet), control-plane federation projects (such as Karmada and the older KubeFed), Crossplane for managing cloud infrastructure and clusters declaratively, and multi-cluster service meshes and networking (Istio multi-cluster, Cilium Cluster Mesh) for cross-cluster service discovery and failover.

Challenges include keeping configuration and policies consistent, cross-cluster networking and latency, data locality and replication, split-brain risks during partitions, unified observability, and consistent identity and access control across clusters.
kg-9.example: An online game runs clusters in five regions; GitOps deploys identical services to all of them, and global DNS routes players to the nearest healthy region.
kg-9.tip: Prefer independent clusters with shared GitOps and policy over tightly coupled federation. Simpler failure domains are easier to reason about.

sre-1.body:
Site Reliability Engineering, created at Google, treats operations as a software engineering problem. SRE teams apply engineering to reliability: defining SLOs from the user's perspective, using error budgets to balance feature velocity against stability, automating away repetitive operational work (toil), building monitoring and alerting around user-visible symptoms, managing incidents methodically, and running blameless postmortems.

A common guideline caps toil at about 50% of an SRE's time, with the rest spent on engineering projects that improve reliability and scalability, so systems can grow without operations headcount growing linearly. SRE also emphasises capacity planning, change management (most outages follow changes), simplicity, and shared ownership of production between developers and SREs. The Google SRE books, including the free Site Reliability Engineering and The Site Reliability Workbook, are the classic references.
sre-1.example: An SRE team spends a quarter automating certificate renewal and database failover, eliminating two of the most common causes of pages.
sre-1.tip: SRE is not 'ops with a new name'. Its hallmark is engineering work that removes operational burden and manages reliability with data.

sre-2.body:
An error budget is the amount of unreliability a service is allowed within its SLO window: error budget = 100% − SLO. With a 99.9% monthly availability SLO, the budget is 0.1%, about 43 minutes of full downtime or the equivalent share of failed requests. Budgets turn reliability into a measurable resource that product and engineering share.

While budget remains, teams can release freely and take calculated risks. An agreed error budget policy defines what happens when it is exhausted or burning too fast: for example freezing risky feature releases, requiring extra review, and redirecting engineering effort to reliability work until the service recovers. This replaces subjective arguments ('we need more stability' versus 'we need to ship') with data, and it discourages over-investing in reliability users do not need.
sre-2.example: After two incidents consume the quarter's error budget, the product team agrees to pause launches for two weeks while engineers fix the underlying database failover issue.
sre-2.tip: Get product leadership to sign the error budget policy in advance; enforcing it during an incident without agreement rarely works.

sre-3.body:
Toil is operational work that is manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical (reactive rather than strategic), without lasting value, and that grows linearly with service size: manually restarting services, running the same fix for recurring alerts, provisioning accounts by hand, copying data, rotating certificates manually, or processing routine tickets.

SRE measures toil (through surveys, ticket analysis, and time tracking) and deliberately reduces it through automation, self-service tools, better system design, and eliminating the root causes of recurring issues. A common target keeps toil below 50% of the team's time. Some toil is unavoidable, but unchecked toil crowds out improvement work, burns people out, and does not scale. A useful heuristic: if you have done a task manually three times, consider automating it.
sre-3.example: An SRE team replaces manual weekly database user provisioning (about 6 hours a week) with a self-service workflow and approval, freeing time for reliability projects.
sre-3.tip: Measure toil before and after automation to prove value and prioritise the next target.

sre-4.body:
Incident management provides a structured, calm way to restore service during significant outages. Incidents are detected through SLO-based alerts, monitoring, or customer reports, then declared and assigned a severity. Clear roles prevent chaos: the incident commander coordinates and makes decisions but does not debug hands-on; the communications lead updates stakeholders and status pages; the operations or technical lead directs the investigation; and subject-matter experts investigate and act. Many organisations use frameworks based on the Incident Command System.

The priority is mitigation, restoring service quickly by rollback, failover, feature flag, or scaling, before root cause analysis. Maintain a timeline in a dedicated channel, communicate at regular intervals, and hand over explicitly between shifts. Every significant incident ends with a blameless postmortem that produces tracked action items.
sre-4.example: During a regional outage, the incident commander assigns one engineer to failover, one to investigate, and the communications lead posts status updates every 20 minutes.
sre-4.tip: The incident commander should not also be the person debugging. Coordination is a full-time job during major incidents.

sre-5.body:
A blameless postmortem is a written review after an incident that focuses on how the system, processes, and tools allowed the failure, not on who made a mistake. It assumes everyone acted reasonably with the information they had. That psychological safety encourages honest, detailed accounts, which surface the real contributing factors.

A good postmortem includes a summary, impact (users affected, duration, SLO and error budget consumed), a detailed timeline, root cause and contributing factors, what went well, what went poorly, where the team got lucky, and specific action items with owners, priorities, and due dates. Postmortems are shared widely so other teams learn, and action items are tracked to completion. Organisations that blame individuals learn less and see incidents repeat.
sre-5.example: A postmortem for a bad config push identifies missing validation in the deploy tool and no canary stage; both are fixed, and the same failure cannot recur.
sre-5.tip: Replace 'human error' as a root cause with the question: why did the system make that error easy and its impact large?

sre-6.body:
Capacity planning ensures a service has enough resources to meet demand and its SLOs, including peak periods and failure scenarios, without wasteful over-provisioning. Inputs include organic growth trends, seasonality (holidays, month-end, sporting events), planned launches and marketing campaigns, and constraints in dependencies (database connections, third-party API quotas, cloud service limits).

Plan for peak load plus headroom, and for N+1 or N+2 redundancy: the system must still handle peak load after losing a node or an entire Availability Zone. Validate assumptions with load testing and track utilisation against thresholds. In the cloud, auto scaling covers much short-term variation, but you still need to plan quotas, reserved capacity, database scaling, and cost. Poor capacity planning leads to throttling, saturation, and outages at the worst moments.
sre-6.example: Before Black Friday, load tests reveal the database connection pool saturates at 3x normal traffic; the team adds read replicas and connection pooling weeks in advance.
sre-6.tip: Check cloud service quotas (instance limits, IP addresses, API rate limits) before peak events. Hitting a quota blocks auto scaling.

sre-7.body:
Changes, meaning code deployments, configuration pushes, infrastructure updates, and feature flag flips, are the single largest cause of production incidents. SRE-style change management reduces this risk without slowing delivery to a crawl: make changes small and frequent, automate them through pipelines, roll them out progressively (canaries and staged rollouts across zones and regions), gate them on automated health checks, and ensure fast, tested rollback.

Other practices include change freezes or extra scrutiny during high-risk periods, preventing simultaneous risky changes, peer review for configuration changes as well as code, and correlating changes with anomalies by overlaying deployment and config-change markers on dashboards, so responders can immediately ask 'what changed?'
sre-7.example: A global configuration change rolls out to one region first, and automated checks detect elevated errors and halt it before the other nine regions are affected.
sre-7.tip: Treat configuration changes like code: reviewed, tested, and rolled out progressively. Many major outages were 'just a config change'.

sre-8.body:
Alerting hygiene keeps paging trustworthy and on-call sustainable. Page only when a human must act now to prevent or reduce user impact; route everything else to tickets or chat. Base alerts on symptoms that users feel (SLO burn rate, error rates, latency) rather than every internal cause. Every alert needs a clear severity, an owner, and a runbook link.

Reduce noise by requiring conditions to persist, deduplicating and grouping related alerts, suppressing alerts during maintenance, and deleting alerts that never lead to action. Track pages per on-call shift, off-hours pages, mean time to acknowledge (MTTA), mean time to resolve (MTTR), and alert precision. Review alerts regularly as a team. Protect on-call engineers from alert storms with routing, escalation policies, and sustainable rotation sizes.
sre-8.example: A quarterly alert review deletes 30 alerts that never required action and converts 12 into tickets, halving night pages without missing any real incidents.
sre-8.tip: If a page can safely wait until morning, it should not be a page.

sre-9.body:
Reliability is ultimately about whether users can accomplish what they came to do: log in, search, pay, stream. Backend health checks can show all green while users suffer from broken JavaScript, CDN misconfiguration, DNS problems, mobile app crashes, third-party script failures, or regional network issues.

Measure user-facing reliability as close to the user as possible: SLIs defined on critical user journeys, real user monitoring (RUM) and client-side error and performance metrics (such as Core Web Vitals), synthetic probes that exercise key flows from real user locations, and edge or load-balancer logs instead of only application server logs. Include dependencies users rely on, such as payment providers and authentication, in the picture. Prioritise reliability work by user impact.
sre-9.example: Server dashboards are green, but RUM shows checkout failing for Safari users after a front-end release; a synthetic browser test is added to catch this in future.
sre-9.tip: Define SLOs per critical user journey (such as 'checkout completes') rather than per server.

sre-10.body:
SRE culture aligns development and operations around shared ownership of production and shared incentives for reliability. Developers participate in on-call for the services they build ('you build it, you run it'), often with SRE support; production readiness reviews happen before launch; and reliability work (automation, capacity, resilience) is planned and valued alongside features.

Healthy culture is blameless, treating incidents as learning opportunities; data-driven, using SLOs and error budgets; and sustainable, with reasonable on-call load, compensation, and no reliance on individual heroics. Career paths should reward engineering that prevents outages (automation, design reviews, tooling) as much as dramatic firefighting. Knowledge sharing through postmortem reviews, runbooks, and training spreads reliability expertise across the organisation.
sre-10.example: A company adds reliability objectives to every product team's quarterly goals and recognises engineers who eliminate recurring incidents, not just those who fix outages at 3 a.m.
sre-10.tip: Rewarding heroics encourages fragile systems. Reward the work that makes heroics unnecessary.

site-reliability-engineering-c11.body:
SLIs, SLOs, and SLAs form the measurement backbone of SRE. An SLI (Service Level Indicator) is a metric of good behaviour, usually a ratio of good events to valid events: successful requests over total requests, requests faster than 300 ms over total, or fresh records over total. An SLO (Service Level Objective) is the target for that SLI over a rolling window, such as 99.9% over 28 days. An SLA (Service Level Agreement) is an external, contractual promise with consequences (service credits or penalties), deliberately set looser than the internal SLO so there is room to react.

Choose a few SLIs per service tied to critical user journeys, set SLOs based on what users actually need and what the system can realistically achieve rather than maximum possible reliability, publish them, review them regularly, and use missed or burning SLOs to trigger error budget decisions.
site-reliability-engineering-c11.example: A search API defines two SLIs, availability (non-5xx responses) and latency (p95 under 400 ms), each with a 99.5% SLO, and an SLA of 99% in customer contracts.
site-reliability-engineering-c11.tip: If every metric is an SLO, nothing is. Keep a small number of SLOs that genuinely reflect user happiness.

site-reliability-engineering-c14.body:
Reliability testing proactively exercises the failure modes and load conditions a system will eventually face in production. Load and stress testing (k6, Locust, Gatling, JMeter) validates capacity and finds breaking points and bottlenecks. Soak tests run sustained load for hours to reveal memory leaks and resource exhaustion. Chaos experiments inject failures such as instance termination, zone outages, dependency latency and errors, network partitions, and resource saturation to confirm that redundancy, timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, and failover actually work.

Disaster recovery tests restore backups and fail over whole regions to prove that RTO and RPO targets can be met. Game days rehearse realistic incidents end to end, testing people, runbooks, alerts, and communication as well as technology. Regular testing uncovers hidden dependencies and technical debt before real outages do.
site-reliability-engineering-c14.example: A game day simulating the loss of the primary region reveals that the DR runbook references a decommissioned server; it is fixed months before a real regional outage.
site-reliability-engineering-c14.tip: An untested failover or backup should be treated as not working until proven otherwise.

iac-1.body:
Declarative IaC describes the desired end state (for example 'three subnets, a load balancer, and an encrypted database of this size') and lets the tool work out how to get there: which resources to create, update in place, replace, or delete. Terraform and OpenTofu, CloudFormation, Bicep and ARM, Pulumi (declarative state described with general-purpose languages), and Kubernetes manifests all work this way.

The engine compares the desired configuration with the current real state and computes a plan, making changes idempotent (applying the same code twice changes nothing the second time) and predictable. By contrast, imperative scripts (a series of CLI commands) describe steps, break when the starting state differs, are hard to review, and cannot easily detect drift, so they are not true IaC even if stored in Git. Declarative definitions become the single source of truth, reviewed as diffs in pull requests.
iac-1.example: Changing `instance_count = 3` to `5` in Terraform makes the plan add exactly two instances; applying the same code again reports 'no changes'.
iac-1.tip: Idempotency is the key property: re-running declarative IaC should be safe and converge on the same result.

iac-2.body:
Terraform's core workflow is init, plan, and apply. terraform init downloads providers and modules and configures the state backend. terraform plan refreshes knowledge of the real infrastructure, compares it with the configuration and state, and produces an execution plan showing each resource to be created (+), updated in place (~), replaced (-/+, destroy and recreate), or destroyed (-), including which attribute changes force replacement.

Humans, or automated policy checks, review the plan before terraform apply executes it. In CI/CD, the plan is saved as an artifact (terraform plan -out=tfplan), posted to the pull request for review, and exactly that saved plan is applied after approval, so what was reviewed is what runs. Watch for unexpected replacements or destroys of stateful resources, protect critical resources with lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }, and never run apply blindly against production.
iac-2.example: A plan unexpectedly shows `-/+` for the production database because a renamed parameter forces replacement; the reviewer catches it and the change is reworked to avoid data loss.
iac-2.tip: Read every 'must be replaced' and 'destroy' line in a plan. Those are where data loss happens.

iac-3.body:
Terraform state is a file that maps every resource in your configuration to the real object it manages (IDs, attributes, and dependencies), so Terraform knows what exists and what to change. For teams, state must be stored in a remote backend, such as S3 (with DynamoDB, or native S3 locking in newer versions), Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, or Terraform Cloud and HCP, with locking to prevent two people from applying at once and corrupting it, versioning to recover from mistakes, and encryption at rest.

State often contains sensitive values in plain text, including generated passwords, private keys, and connection strings, so restrict access tightly and treat any state leak like a credential leak. Split state by environment and component to limit the blast radius. Never hand-edit state files; use terraform state mv, rm, and import (or moved and import blocks) for deliberate changes.
iac-3.example: Two engineers run apply simultaneously without locking, corrupting state; after moving to an S3 backend with locking and versioning, the team restores the previous state version in minutes.
iac-3.tip: Never commit terraform.tfstate to Git. It frequently contains secrets.

iac-4.body:
Drift is any difference between the infrastructure your code describes and what actually exists. It is caused by manual console changes ('quick fixes' during incidents), other automation or scripts, provider-side defaults changing, or resources modified by other tools. Drift makes environments inconsistent, breaks the assumption that code is the source of truth, and can hide security problems such as a security group opened by hand.

Detect it by running scheduled terraform plan (or plan -refresh-only) jobs and alerting when changes appear, or with CloudFormation drift detection, Terraform Cloud drift detection, or CSPM tools. Resolve each case deliberately: either revert the manual change by re-applying the code, or, if the change was intended, update the code to match and import resources where needed. Reduce drift by limiting console write access in production and routing changes through pipelines.
iac-4.example: A nightly drift check flags that someone opened port 22 to 0.0.0.0/0 on a production security group; re-applying Terraform closes it and the incident is investigated.
iac-4.tip: Restrict production write access in the console to break-glass roles, so IaC stays the only normal way to change infrastructure.

iac-5.body:
Modules package reusable infrastructure patterns, such as a standard VPC with subnets and flow logs, an encrypted S3 bucket with logging, or a database cluster with backups and monitoring, behind a small interface of input variables and outputs. Teams compose modules to build environments rather than copying hundreds of lines of resources.

Modules encode organisational standards (encryption on, public access off, mandatory tags) so every team gets secure defaults automatically. Distribute approved modules through a private registry (Terraform Cloud, Artifactory, a Git repository with tags), version them with semantic versioning, document their inputs and outputs, test them, and pin versions in consuming code (version = "~> 3.2") so upstream changes are adopted deliberately. Avoid over-abstraction: modules with dozens of options become as complex as the resources they wrap.
iac-5.example: A platform team's 'secure-bucket' module enforces encryption, versioning, and blocked public access; 60 application teams use it, so no bucket is ever created insecurely.
iac-5.tip: Pin module versions in production. Referencing a moving branch means someone else's change can alter your infrastructure unexpectedly.

iac-6.body:
Environment strategy keeps development, staging, and production isolated yet consistent. Each environment should have its own state (and usually its own cloud account or subscription), so an experiment in dev can never modify production. The same modules are reused across environments with different variable values (instance sizes, replica counts, domain names), typically through per-environment directories or configuration files, Terragrunt, or workspaces (used carefully).

Promote code, not state: a change is merged, applied to dev, validated, then applied to staging and production through the pipeline, with reviews and approvals at each gate. Layer variables as global defaults, then environment overrides, then secrets injected at runtime. Ephemeral environments created per pull request give realistic testing and are destroyed automatically afterwards to control cost.
iac-6.example: The same Terraform root module deploys dev with 1 small instance and prod with 6 large instances across 3 AZs, driven by separate tfvars files and separate state in separate accounts.
iac-6.tip: Separate accounts or subscriptions per environment are the strongest isolation. Workspaces alone share credentials and backends.

iac-7.body:
Infrastructure code deserves tests, just like application code. Static checks run in seconds: terraform fmt and validate, linters (TFLint), and security and compliance scanners (Checkov, tfsec and Trivy, KICS) that flag issues such as unencrypted storage, public exposure, or missing logging. Plan-level tests assert on the terraform plan output, for example that no resources are destroyed or that tags are present, often with policy as code (OPA/Conftest, Sentinel).

Unit-style tests (Terraform's native terraform test framework) validate module logic with mocked or real providers. Integration tests (such as Terratest in Go) deploy real infrastructure into an isolated test account, verify behaviour (the website responds, the database accepts connections, the security group blocks other ports), then destroy everything. Run these in CI on every change so infrastructure defects are caught before they reach production.
iac-7.example: A Checkov scan in CI blocks a pull request that creates an RDS instance without encryption and with public accessibility enabled.
iac-7.tip: Run integration tests in a dedicated sandbox account with budgets and automatic clean-up to avoid orphaned, costly resources.

iac-8.body:
Secrets such as database passwords, API keys, and TLS private keys must never be hard-coded in IaC templates, variable files committed to Git, or pipeline logs. Instead, reference secrets stored in managed secret stores (AWS Secrets Manager and SSM Parameter Store, Azure Key Vault, Google Secret Manager, HashiCorp Vault), generate them at deploy time (for example a random password stored directly into Secrets Manager), or use dynamic, short-lived credentials from Vault.

Be aware that Terraform state can still record secret values in plain text even when variables are marked sensitive, so encrypt and restrict state, and prefer designs where the secret never passes through Terraform, such as managed master passwords handled by the database service or ephemeral resources in newer Terraform versions. Mark sensitive variables and outputs, scan repositories for committed secrets, and immediately rotate any secret that ever appeared in code, state, logs, or chat.
iac-8.example: An RDS instance uses the provider-managed master password feature, so the password lives only in Secrets Manager and never appears in Terraform code or state.
iac-8.tip: `sensitive = true` hides values from CLI output. It does not remove them from state.

iac-9.body:
AWS CloudFormation is AWS's native IaC service: templates in YAML or JSON (or generated by AWS CDK in TypeScript, Python, and other languages) are deployed as stacks, with state managed by AWS, automatic rollback on failure, change sets for previewing changes, drift detection, StackSets for multi-account deployment, and day-one support for many new AWS features. It only manages AWS (plus registry extensions).

Terraform (and its open-source fork OpenTofu) is multi-cloud and multi-service. Thousands of providers manage AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, GitHub, Datadog, Cloudflare, and more with one language (HCL) and workflow. You manage state yourself (or via Terraform Cloud and HCP) and review plans before apply. Both are declarative. Choose CloudFormation or CDK for AWS-only organisations wanting deep native integration and managed state; choose Terraform for multi-cloud, hybrid, or SaaS-heavy estates and a large module ecosystem.
iac-9.example: An AWS-only startup uses CDK for its app stacks, while a multinational manages AWS, Azure, Cloudflare DNS, and GitHub repositories from one Terraform codebase.
iac-9.tip: Consistency matters more than the tool. Standardise on one primary IaC tool per organisation where possible.

iac-10.body:
Policy and governance for IaC enforce organisational standards automatically before infrastructure is created. Policy as code tools evaluate plans or templates in CI/CD: HashiCorp Sentinel in Terraform Cloud and Enterprise, Open Policy Agent (OPA) with Conftest, Checkov custom policies, AWS CloudFormation Guard and Hooks, and Azure Policy for Bicep and ARM deployments. Typical rules include mandatory tags, approved regions and instance types, encryption required, no public storage or databases, cost limits, and prohibited services.

The pipeline blocks non-compliant changes regardless of who wrote them, with clear messages explaining how to fix them. Exceptions go through a documented, time-limited approval process. Policies are versioned and tested like code, and evaluation results provide audit evidence for compliance frameworks. Complement pre-deployment checks with runtime guardrails (SCPs, Azure Policy, AWS Config) to catch anything created outside IaC.
iac-10.example: An OPA policy in the pipeline blocks a Terraform plan that would create resources outside the approved EU regions, keeping the company within its data residency rules.
iac-10.tip: Combine preventive checks in CI with runtime guardrails. Not every change goes through your pipeline.

infrastructure-as-code-deep-dive-c15.body:
Immutable infrastructure means servers, containers, and other components are never modified after deployment. To change anything (patch the OS, update the application, change configuration), you build a new, versioned image and replace the old instances with new ones. Images are built by pipelines using tools such as HashiCorp Packer (VM images such as AMIs), EC2 Image Builder, or Dockerfiles (container images), tested, and then rolled out.

Because every instance comes from the same tested image, environments stay consistent, configuration drift and 'snowflake servers' disappear, rollbacks are simple (redeploy the previous image), and scaling out is fast and predictable. Immutable infrastructure pairs naturally with auto-scaling groups, blue/green and canary deployments, and containers. It also improves security: SSH access and in-place changes can be disabled entirely, and compromised instances are simply replaced.
infrastructure-as-code-deep-dive-c15.example: Monthly OS patching becomes 'build a new AMI with Packer, test it, and roll the auto-scaling group'; no one logs into production servers to run updates.
infrastructure-as-code-deep-dive-c15.tip: If you must SSH in to change production servers, you are not immutable. Rebuild the image instead.

cipherNotes.sec-concepts: Exam trap: a security camera is detective, not preventive — it identifies what happened; deterrence is just a side effect.
cipherNotes.net-switch-route: Longest prefix match is decided before administrative distance — a /24 beats a /16 even from a more trusted source.
cipherNotes.net-osi: Don't call a packet a frame: segments live at Layer 4, packets at Layer 3, frames at Layer 2, bits at Layer 1.
